title: One Wrong Shadow Database URL Wiped 22 Tables. 4 Guards for Agent-Run Migrations
description:
• Book: Database Playbook
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The command didn't contain the word DROP. It was prisma migrate diff, a command whose job is to describe the difference between two schemas. One argument, --shadow-database-url, got the production connection string. According to the AI Incident Database, incident 1676, all 22 tables in a live Supabase database were dropped.

Per the incident record and a postmortem by Tokenstead, a developer had given a Claude Opus 5 coding agent production access to a personal project and asked it to fix schema problems. The agent passed $DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED, the direct production connection string, as the shadow database, then reported the damage itself. AIID notes that most content was later recovered or rebuilt. The postmortem adds that two tables, BlogPost and ApiKey, had no migration files, so rebuilding from prisma/migrations could not bring them back.

The same mistake doesn't need an agent. On July 14, 2026, a developer posted on Railway's forum that they had run prisma migrate diff with their production URL as --shadow-database-url, lost every table behind 66 applied migrations, and had no backup to restore from. Their post doesn't mention an agent.

Exemplar's writeup put the problem in one line: "The risk is entirely a function of where it points, not what it says." Where a URL points is something a script can check before the command runs, and each guard below does it in a few lines of SQL or bash.

What Prisma does to a shadow database

Prisma Migrate uses a second, throwaway database to work out what your migration history produces. prisma migrate dev replays your existing migrations into it to detect drift, then generates a new migration from your schema changes. When you configure that database yourself with shadowDatabaseUrl, the Prisma docs say such databases "are not dropped, but are reset at the start of the migrate dev command." migrate diff needs one too whenever one side of the diff is a local migrations directory, which is the command in the Railway post.

Reset is the whole contract. Whatever URL you hand Prisma as the shadow gets emptied. The same docs warn against giving url and shadowDatabaseUrl the same value for exactly that reason, and state that the shadow database "is not required in production." prisma migrate deploy "does not rely on a shadow database" and "does not reset the database."

Prisma 7 removed --shadow-database-url from migrate diff. The shadow URL now comes from datasource.shadowDatabaseUrl in prisma.config.ts:

import "dotenv/config";
import { defineConfig, env } from "prisma/config";

export default defineConfig({
  schema: "prisma/schema.prisma",
  migrations: { path: "prisma/migrations" },
  datasource: {
    url: env("DATABASE_URL"),
    shadowDatabaseUrl: env("SHADOW_DATABASE_URL"),
  },
});

That moves the failure from a flag to an environment variable. An agent that exports the wrong value into SHADOW_DATABASE_URL gets the same result, so the guards below read those two variables.


The shadow database exists to be emptied and refilled. Production must never be the one in that slot.

Guard 1: a sentinel table that says "production"

Give production a marker a script can read. Put it in its own schema so Prisma never sees it: a table in public that isn't in your Prisma schema would show up in a diff as something to drop.

-- run once, on production only
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS ops;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ops.prod_sentinel (
  env text PRIMARY KEY CHECK (env = 'production')
);
INSERT INTO ops.prod_sentinel VALUES ('production')
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

The check is one query. to_regclass returns NULL instead of raising an error when the table doesn't exist, so it is safe to run against any database:

SELECT to_regclass('ops.prod_sentinel') IS NOT NULL;

If that returns t on the database you are about to use as a shadow, stop. A staging database restored from a production dump inherits the sentinel too, and that is what you want: it holds real data.

Guard 2: refuse when both URLs reach the same database

The obvious check compares the two URL strings. It misses the likely shape of incident 1676. The shadow got $DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED, the direct string, while an app's main URL on Supabase usually goes through the pooler on a different host or port. Two different strings can reach one database. Ask the server instead. current_database() and pg_postmaster_start_time() return the same pair for every connection to one database, whichever pooler or hostname it came through, and that pair practically never repeats across two different servers.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/db-guard.sh: refuse when the shadow database
# is production, or is the main database.
set -euo pipefail

: "${DATABASE_URL:?DATABASE_URL is not set}"
: "${SHADOW_DATABASE_URL:?SHADOW_DATABASE_URL is not set}"

# psql rejects Prisma-only params like ?pgbouncer=true
q() {
  psql "${1%%\?*}" -X -tAq -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c "$2"
}

SENT="SELECT to_regclass('ops.prod_sentinel') IS NOT NULL"
FP="SELECT current_database()::text || '@'
    || pg_postmaster_start_time()::text"

is_prod="$(q "$SHADOW_DATABASE_URL" "$SENT")"
if [[ "$is_prod" == "t" ]]; then
  echo "db-guard: shadow URL is production" >&2
  exit 1
fi

main_fp="$(q "$DATABASE_URL" "$FP")"
shadow_fp="$(q "$SHADOW_DATABASE_URL" "$FP")"
if [[ "$main_fp" == "$shadow_fp" ]]; then
  echo "db-guard: shadow and main are one database" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "db-guard: ok"

Each query result is assigned to a variable before it is compared, so if either database is unreachable, psql exits non-zero and set -e stops the script: the guard fails closed. Stripping the query string also drops sslmode, so set PGSSLMODE=require (or stricter) in the environment if your provider needs it. And -X skips any local .psqlrc that could change the output format.

Guard 3: a role that can't drop, and a tripwire for the one that can

Postgres has no DROP privilege to revoke. The docs on privileges say: "The right to modify or destroy an object is inherent in being the object's owner, and cannot be granted or revoked in itself." So the guard is ownership. The credentials an agent holds for looking at production should not belong to the role that owns the tables.

-- what the agent connects as: reads, never DDL
CREATE ROLE agent_ro LOGIN;
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE app TO agent_ro;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO agent_ro;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO agent_ro;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO agent_ro;

Replace app with your database name, run it as the role that owns the tables (on Supabase, postgres; default privileges apply to tables that role creates later), and set the password with psql's \password agent_ro so it never lands in a file. Anything that tries to drop a table through agent_ro gets a permission error from Postgres. Never grant agent_ro membership in the owner role, because the same Postgres page says members of the owning role inherit the right to drop. The Tokenstead postmortem makes the same recommendation: a read-only role for exploration, production credentials out of the agent's environment.


Ownership decides who can drop a table. The tripwire catches the owner's own tools.

Migrations still run as the owner. For that role, add an event trigger on sql_drop that refuses to drop a table unless the session opted in. It catches cascaded drops too, because pg_event_trigger_dropped_objects() lists every object the command removed, not only the one it named. This follows the drop-protection example in Supabase's docs:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ops.block_table_drops()
RETURNS event_trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  obj record;
BEGIN
  IF current_setting('ops.allow_drop', true) = 'on' THEN
    RETURN;
  END IF;
  FOR obj IN SELECT * FROM pg_event_trigger_dropped_objects()
  LOOP
    IF obj.object_type = 'table' THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'drop of % blocked, set ops.allow_drop',
        obj.object_identity;
    END IF;
  END LOOP;
END;
$$;

CREATE EVENT TRIGGER block_table_drops
  ON sql_drop
  EXECUTE FUNCTION ops.block_table_drops();

In plain Postgres, creating an event trigger requires a superuser. On Supabase, the postgres role can do it through the supautils extension, per the same Supabase page. A migration that drops a table on purpose opts in on its first line and turns it off on its last:

SET ops.allow_drop = 'on';
DROP TABLE "LegacyAudit";
RESET ops.allow_drop;

Know the limits. Any session can set ops.allow_drop, so this catches a tool doing its normal job, and anyone who knows the setting can turn it off. TRUNCATE and DELETE don't drop anything, so the trigger never sees them. The read-only role is what covers those.

Guard 4: only migrate deploy touches a database that isn't local

migrate dev is documented as "for use in development environments only," and migrate diff against a migrations folder needs a shadow too. Make the rule mechanical. Anything that resets a shadow runs only when both URLs point at localhost and Guard 2 passes. Everything else goes through migrate deploy.

Both incidents above passed --shadow-database-url, so they ran a pre-7 CLI. If you are still on Prisma 6, the shadow database page notes that shadowDatabaseUrl belongs in the datasource block of schema.prisma there. Set it to env("SHADOW_DATABASE_URL") so the guards read the URL Prisma uses, and let the wrapper refuse the old flag so nobody hands Prisma a different one.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/migrate.sh: the one door to Prisma Migrate.
set -euo pipefail
cmd="${1:?usage: migrate.sh dev|diff|deploy [args]}"
shift

# Prisma 6 still accepts the flag; the guards can't see it
for a in "$@"; do
  case "$a" in
    --shadow-database-url*)
      echo "migrate.sh: set SHADOW_DATABASE_URL" >&2
      exit 1 ;;
  esac
done

host_of() {
  local rest="${1#*://}"
  rest="${rest#*@}"
  printf '%s' "${rest%%[:/?]*}"
}

local_only() {
  local url
  for url in "$DATABASE_URL" "$SHADOW_DATABASE_URL"; do
    case "$(host_of "$url")" in
      localhost|127.0.0.1) ;;
      *) echo "migrate.sh: $cmd is local-only" >&2
         exit 1 ;;
    esac
  done
  ./scripts/db-guard.sh
}

case "$cmd" in
  dev)    local_only; npx prisma migrate dev "$@" ;;
  diff)   local_only; npx prisma migrate diff "$@" ;;
  deploy) npx prisma migrate deploy "$@" ;;
  *) echo "migrate.sh: unknown command $cmd" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

Then send the agent through that door. In Claude Code, deny rules in .claude/settings.json block direct Prisma calls, so the agent gets refused and reaches for ./scripts/migrate.sh instead:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Bash(prisma migrate *)",
      "Bash(* prisma migrate *)"
    ]
  }
}

The * in a rule matches any sequence of characters, so the second rule covers npx, pnpm exec and bunx. The wrapper's own command text is ./scripts/migrate.sh dev, which neither rule matches. The same Claude Code docs warn that Bash patterns which constrain arguments are fragile: a script that calls Prisma on the agent's behalf walks straight past them. Treat the deny rules as a signpost and the read-only role from Guard 3 as the barrier.

The order to add them in

Start by removing production credentials from the agent's environment. In incident 1676 the agent reached production because the URL was sitting in its environment, and none of the four guards matter as much as that. Next comes Guard 2, which catches the pooled-versus-direct case string comparison misses, with the Guard 1 sentinel behind it. The read-only role from Guard 3 still holds after every script is bypassed, and the wrapper keeps the destructive commands on your laptop.

Then check your backups. Railway's reply to the July post was that it is "not able to restore data lost to user-initiated actions." Whatever your provider says in that situation, find out before you need it.

If this was useful

The shadow-database trap is a migration-workflow problem more than a Prisma problem: a tool that resets a scratch database will empty whatever you point it at. The guards above are the operational side of a bigger question: what your data store is, who owns it, and how it changes over time. The Database Playbook is my guide to choosing the right store for each system you build, Postgres included. If agents are about to start touching your schema, it is a good moment to be sure that choice was deliberate.

title: XSS: When Your Own Site Runs the Attacker's Code
description:
Cross-site scripting is a strange kind of betrayal. Your site, the one your users trust, turns around and runs the attacker's code inside their browser. Not your server. Their browser. Their session. Their logged-in tab.

And the browser has no reason to be suspicious. The script arrived from your domain, wrapped in your padlock, under your name. So it runs with all the trust your users handed you.

That is XSS in one breath. Let me slow it down.

The concept: output you forgot to escape becomes code

A browser reads HTML and runs any script it finds inside it. That is its entire job.

XSS happens when attacker-controlled text lands in your page without being treated as plain text. You meant to display a comment, a username, a search term. But you dropped it straight into the HTML, so the browser cannot tell the difference between the words you wanted to show and a script someone slipped in. If the input contains markup, the browser runs it.

Input becomes output becomes code. Same shape as SQL injection, different stage. There the database gets tricked. Here it is the browser.

Stored versus reflected, quickly

Two flavors you should know.

Reflected XSS bounces off a single request. The malicious input rides in on a crafted link or form, the server echoes it straight back into the response, and it fires for whoever clicked. It is a trap you have to lure someone into.

Stored XSS is worse. The payload gets saved. A comment, a profile bio, a support ticket. It sits in your database and fires for every single person who loads that page. One poisoned comment, thousands of victims. No link required.

There is a third kind, DOM-based, where the whole thing plays out in client-side JavaScript that writes untrusted data into the page. Same root cause. Untrusted data, trusted context.

What an attacker actually does with it

This is where people stop taking it seriously, so let me be blunt.

Once attacker script runs in your user's browser, it can read whatever that browser can. It can lift session tokens and ride in as that user. It can quietly rewrite the page, drop a fake login form over the real one, and harvest whatever gets typed. It can deface the site. It can act on the user's behalf, click their buttons, change their email, all while looking exactly like them.

Session theft is the big one. If a script can read the session, it can become the user. Game over, no password required.

The fix: escape, frameworks, CSP

Good news. We know how to stop this.

  • Escape output based on context. Text going into HTML gets HTML-encoded, so markup renders as harmless characters instead of running. This is the core defense.
  • Lean on your framework. React, Vue, and Angular auto-escape by default. Render user text the normal way and they turn it into text, not code. Use that behavior on purpose.
  • Set a Content Security Policy. CSP is your safety net, a header that tells the browser which scripts are allowed to run. Even if something slips through, a tight policy can stop it from executing.
  • Set HttpOnly on session cookies so client-side script cannot read them. That alone takes the most common session-theft path off the table.

The footguns

Here is where teams quietly reintroduce it. Every framework has an "I know what I am doing" door. In React it is dangerouslySetInnerHTML. In plain JavaScript it is innerHTML. The name is a warning, not a suggestion.

The moment you push raw, unescaped user content through one of those, every auto-escape protection you had is gone. If you genuinely must render user-supplied HTML, sanitize it first with a trusted, maintained library. Never trust it raw.

Your framework escapes by default for a reason. The day you switch that off, you had better be certain the input is clean. Because the browser will run whatever you give it, and it will never ask whose side it is on.

I am Ksatria Bintang Samudra, an AI-native full-stack engineer with a penetration-testing background and a deep interest in digital forensics, open to remote work worldwide. More of what I build at ksatriabintangsamudra.com.

title: What We Learned Benchmarking AI App Builders on 103 Real Creative Tasks
description:
Most AI coding benchmarks ask whether a model can solve a bounded programming problem. That is useful, but it misses much of what happens when a real person asks an agent to create an app.

A real request may arrive with screenshots, videos, PDFs, a half-working repository, conflicting follow-ups, or a design the user already approved. The agent has to decide whether to discuss, plan, prototype, or build. It then has to preserve earlier decisions, produce a runnable result, test it, and recover when the user changes direction.

Eazo recently published a benchmark built around that full creative chain rather than a collection of isolated code-generation prompts.

The benchmark shape

The benchmark contains 103 real-user creative tasks across seven capability sections:

  1. Inputs and references
  2. Intent routing and design depth
  3. Asset sourcing, presentation, and integration
  4. Development and runtime
  5. Disruption and recovery
  6. Delivery and publishing
  7. Cross-cutting capabilities

The tasks include multi-turn work involving images, video, CAD/STEP files, documents, existing projects, design feedback, rollback requests, browser QA, exports, and publishing.

The user's words are sent verbatim. When the agent asks a question, the simulated user answers only with facts available in the task; it does not reveal the scoring criteria.

That detail matters. A benchmark becomes much easier if the evaluator quietly helps the agent toward the expected answer.

Separate quality from completion

Every task is judged in two ways.

First, a weighted quality score across eight dimensions:

  • Correct stage routing
  • Clear deliverable per step
  • Continuity of prior state
  • Asset, design, and code reuse
  • Core feature completeness
  • Interaction and failure states
  • Responsiveness, performance, and accessibility
  • Self-testing and delivery quality

Second, item-by-item acceptance. Each task has explicit deliverable and process requirements. An item only passes when the frozen evidence supports it.

This distinction prevents a common failure mode: a polished final message claiming success when the app, files, or runtime do not actually support the claim.

The browser—not the agent's narration—is the evidence

At the end of a run, the conversation, files, screenshots, and runtime state are frozen. Reviewers judge that evidence without asking the agent follow-up questions or modifying the result.

For runnable apps, a separate tester opens the product in a real browser, exercises the interactions, and captures desktop and mobile evidence. Reviewers then decide whether each requirement passed.

A useful rule emerges:

“The agent said it works” is not evidence that it works.

This sounds obvious, but it changes benchmark design. A build command exiting successfully does not prove that the main interaction works. A screenshot does not prove that state changes correctly. A deployed URL does not prove that the requested version was deployed.

Five lessons from the 103 tasks

1. Routing errors happen before coding errors

An agent can write competent code and still fail the user's request by going too far.

If the user asked to compare options, building an app is not a bonus. If they said “read the existing project and wait,” editing files is a failure. If they asked for one lightweight prototype, producing a full product can make iteration harder.

The benchmark treats the correct stage—discussion, plan, artifact, prototype, or runnable app—as a dedicated quality dimension.

2. Continuity is a first-class capability

Many real failures are not syntax errors. They are quiet reversals of earlier decisions:

  • A selected design disappears during implementation.
  • A supplied asset is replaced with a generic substitute.
  • A local-only requirement turns into a public deployment.
  • A rollback restores the UI but not the underlying behavior.

Single-turn benchmarks rarely expose this. Multi-turn tasks do.

3. Multimodal input is only valuable when it changes the result

“Supports images” can mean anything from accepting an upload to actually using local details from the image in the product.

The same applies to PDFs, CAD assemblies, videos, and existing repositories. A meaningful evaluation checks whether the agent parsed the material, understood the relevant parts, and carried those facts into the deliverable—not whether it merely acknowledged the attachment.

4. Recovery deserves dedicated tests

Users change their minds. Tools fail. A generated asset may be unusable. A design direction may be rejected after implementation begins.

Rollback, mid-task pivots, asset locking, and failure recovery need explicit tasks. Otherwise a benchmark over-rewards agents that work only when every earlier step goes perfectly.

5. Aggregate scores hide important failures

Across the benchmark, Eazo's average composite quality score was 88.5, compared with 84.2 for Codex. Average task time was 11.1 minutes versus 11.7 minutes, and total token usage was 158M versus 179M.

But the deliverable pass rate was 60% for both systems. The process pass rate was 52% for Eazo and 47% for Codex.

Those numbers are a useful reminder: a higher average quality score does not mean every required item passed. The detailed task evidence is more informative than a single leaderboard number.

The methodology, task-level cases, scoring dimensions, and current aggregate results are available on the full Eazo benchmark.

A reusable checklist for agent benchmarks

When evaluating an app-building agent, check whether the benchmark includes:

  • Raw user language rather than evaluator-cleaned prompts
  • Multi-turn changes and corrections
  • Existing files and projects
  • Images, documents, video, or structured data
  • A distinction between discussion, planning, prototyping, and building
  • Frozen evidence after execution
  • Independent browser testing
  • Mobile and desktop checks
  • Loading, empty, and error states
  • Rollback and recovery tasks
  • Item-level evidence citations
  • Separate deliverable and process requirements
  • A way to record review corrections rather than overwrite them

The goal is not to make the benchmark complicated for its own sake. It is to make it difficult for a system to receive credit for work a user could not actually use.

Keep the limitations visible

Any benchmark reflects its task selection, scoring weights, product versions, and review process. A comparison between two systems is not a universal ranking of every coding agent, and aggregate scores can obscure individual failures.

The most useful benchmark is therefore not just a leaderboard. It is an inspectable collection of tasks, artifacts, runtime evidence, and review decisions that other people can question.

title: React: un inbox de prueba con layout estable
description:
Una bandeja de correo de prueba puede parecer un componente sencillo: un botón para iniciar la consulta, una lista de mensajes y un estado vacío. En la practica, los estados intermedios suelen causar más problemas que la lista final. Un spinner aparece, desaparece, mueve el botón y deja al equipo de QA buscando el mensaje en otra posición.

Este artículo propone un enfoque pequeño para React: reservar desde el principio el espacio de la bandeja, comunicar cada estado y mantener el foco donde el usuario espera. La idea sirve para flujos que revisan una dirección de correo desechable, un buzón de staging o cualquier integración de verificación por email.

El problema no es la bandeja: es el movimiento

Cuando una consulta tarda 300 ms, el cambio de layout casi no se nota. Si tarda dos segundos, el usuario ya ha empezado a leer otra cosa. Si falla y vuelve a intentarse, la interfaz puede cambiar tres veces: carga, vacío, error y finalmente mensajes.

Ese movimiento tiene un coste práctico. El clic siguiente ocurre sobre otro elemento, el lector de pantalla recibe anuncios poco claros y una captura de evidencia queda desactualizada. Además, cada prueba necesitan una forma visible de saber si el sistema sigue esperando o si ya terminó.

Por eso conviene modelar el inbox como una máquina de estados simple:

type InboxState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "loading" }
  | { kind: "ready"; messages: Message[] }
  | { kind: "empty" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

No hace falta enseñar todos los detalles internos. Basta con que la UI pueda distinguir una consulta que todavía no termina de una consulta que terminó sin mensajes.

Diseñar un estado estable antes de traer mensajes

El componente debe tener una estructura que no cambie entre estados. Un encabezado, una región de estado y una lista ocupan siempre el mismo lugar. El contenido de la lista sí puede variar, pero el botón de actualizar no debería saltar hacia arriba o abajo.

También es útil mostrar una explicación breve: “Buscando mensajes”, “No hay mensajes todavía” o “No pudimos consultar el buzón”. “Cargando” a secas informa poco, especialmente cuando la respuesta tarda mas de lo esperado.

Un ejemplo de renderizado legible podría ser:

function TestInbox({ state }: { state: InboxState }) {
  return (
    <section className="test-inbox" aria-labelledby="inbox-title">
      <div className="test-inbox__header">
        <h2 id="inbox-title">Correo de prueba</h2>
        <button type="button">Actualizar</button>
      </div>

      <p className="test-inbox__status" role="status" aria-live="polite">
        {statusText(state)}
      </p>

      <div className="test-inbox__viewport">
        {state.kind === "ready" && <MessageList messages={state.messages} />}
        {state.kind === "empty" && <EmptyState />}
        {state.kind === "error" && <ErrorState message={state.message} />}
      </div>
    </section>
  );
}

La región aria-live comunica el cambio sin robar el foco. El botón conserva su posición y puede seguir usándose con teclado. Si la consulta es larga, es mejor indicar progreso en ese texto que hacer que el lector de pantalla anuncian cada modificación de la lista.

CSS para reservar espacio sin ocultar información

La reserva de espacio no significa fingir que ya hay mensajes. Significa dar una altura mínima razonable al viewport y usar un estado vacío que explica qué está pasando. Así el layout permanece reconocible cuando llega la respuesta.

.test-inbox__viewport {
  min-height: 16rem;
  display: grid;
  align-content: start;
  gap: 0.75rem;
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #d8dee9;
  border-radius: 0.75rem;
  background: #fff;
}

.test-inbox__status {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
  margin: 0.5rem 0;
  color: #52606d;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    scroll-behavior: auto;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms;
  }
}

El min-height evita el salto principal y align-content: start mantiene el mensaje cerca del encabezado. En pantallas pequeñas, una altura mínima demasiado grande tambien puede ser incómoda; conviene probarla con zoom y con contenido largo, no solo en el viewport del portátil.

Este patrón combina bien con pruebas que necesitan esperar un mensaje concreto. Para separar la experiencia del frontend de la lógica del servicio, puedes probar correos de renovación en un SaaS y revisar el contrato de entrega en otra capa. Si el backend usa una espera asíncrona, también ayuda entender una espera útil para correos asíncronos antes de poner otro spinner en React.

Accesibilidad y rendimiento en la misma revisión

Una interfaz accesible no tiene que ser pesada. El componente puede mostrar una sola región viva, evitar animaciones permanentes y renderizar únicamente los mensajes visibles. Para una bandeja pequeña, eso es suficiente y mantiene el código mas claro.

Hay cuatro comprobaciones rápidas:

  1. El foco queda en el botón después de actualizar, salvo que el usuario haya abierto un mensaje.
  2. Un teclado puede iniciar una consulta, leer el estado y llegar a cada mensaje.
  3. El texto de estado diferencia loading, empty y error; no todo es “sin resultados”.
  4. El contraste sigue siendo legible en el estado deshabilitado y en el mensaje de error.

Si el equipo busca términos como dummy e mail o tem email durante una prueba de búsqueda, pueden aparecer como datos de fixture, pero no deberían colarse en etiquetas visibles de producción. Es mejor conservar esos valores en un escenario controlado y documentado.

Para flujos de QA que usan un correo temporal, el componente debería tratar el buzón como una fuente de evidencia de corta duración, no como un historial permanente. Guarda el identificador de la ejecución, el asunto esperado y la hora de consulta. No hace falta copiar todo el contenido del mensaje si solo se valida que llegó el enlace correcto.

Checklist para una sesión de QA

  • [ ] El título y el botón no cambian de posición entre estados.
  • [ ] La región de estado anuncia cambios útiles, no cada detalle técnico.
  • [ ] El área de mensajes tiene una altura mínima y un estado vacío explicativo.
  • [ ] La interfaz funciona con teclado, zoom y reducción de movimiento.
  • [ ] La prueba identifica el mensaje por un dato estable, como un asunto o un token de ejecución.
  • [ ] Los fallos dejan una evidencia que se puede leer sin repetir la consulta a ciegas.

Una bandeja de prueba bien diseñada no intenta ocultar la latencia. La hace comprensible. Con estados explícitos, CSS predecible y una revisión de accesibilidad desde el inicio, el equipo puede validar correo sin perseguir elementos que se mueven. Es una mejora sencilla y bastante util para cualquier frontend que dependa de mensajes asíncronos.

title: Python Retrieval Design with 3 Cache Boundaries for a Travel Planner
description:
Short answer: Use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context, then cache three different artifacts instead of treating every travel-planning result as interchangeable. The deciding constraint is retrieval quality versus latency: a fast cache hit is wrong when it hides a newly changed listing or loses the evidence an itinerary needs to cite.

For a travel media product aggregating hotel, activity, and event listings, I would try Infrai for the web-to-vector boundary when a small team wants plain HTTP instead of another SDK. Its primary fit here is practical: one REST API can cover web search, scraping, and vector operations, so Python can call the service without installing or tracking a vendor client library. One key across those stages also narrows credential plumbing and invoice reconciliation. It isn't the automatic answer for every retrieval stack.

What retrieval architecture should a travel itinerary planner use for caching?

Start with the answer contract, not the cache. A useful itinerary result needs the listing identity, source context, collection, freshness requirement, and enough trace data to explain why the item appeared. Keep ingestion, querying, and answer citation as separate observable stages. That split makes a stale source document distinguishable from a poor nearest-neighbor match or a citation assembly mistake.

The three cache boundaries have different invalidation rules:

  1. Cache normalized source documents by source identity and freshness policy. A changed opening time should invalidate the derived document before it reaches retrieval.
  2. Cache bounded retrieval results by collection, normalized query, metadata filters, and retrieval configuration. A query cache key that omits filters can quietly mix cities or dates.
  3. Cache the final itinerary only when its source references and freshness window remain valid. This is the most tempting layer to over-cache because it produces the largest visible latency win, but it also freezes the most assumptions.

Keep those keys boring.

A media listing can be duplicated across a publisher feed and a venue page, while two listings with similar prose can refer to different dates. The retrieval unit therefore cannot be chosen by text length alone. Define whether one vector represents a venue, a dated event, a room offer, or a paragraph before selecting an endpoint. Then make collection and metadata boundaries explicit. This is the same kind of edge case that makes OTP delivery work deceptively hard: the happy path is short, but identity, expiry, and replay semantics determine whether the system is trustworthy.

Before production rollout, measure retrieval quality on a small labeled evaluation set. I'm not sure any cache is helping until cached and uncached runs are judged against the same labels; lower latency by itself can't show that the right listing survived.

Decision invariants and failure boundaries

The first invariant is isolation: a result for one collection or metadata scope must never satisfy another. The second is traceability: every itinerary claim must retain source context through cache reads. The third is bounded work: query limits and cache admission rules should prevent a broad request from turning into an unreviewable candidate pool. The fourth is freshness: each source class gets an explicit expiry or invalidation rule rather than one global TTL.

A cache miss is routine. A cache hit with the wrong scope is a correctness failure.

Treat invalidation as part of ingestion. When a source is refreshed, update the retrieval unit and invalidate result keys that depend on its prior version; don't ask the answer layer to infer staleness after retrieval. Log the collection, normalized filter set, source identifiers, cache outcome, and request trace at their respective stage boundaries. That gives an operator a path from a questionable itinerary sentence back to the retrieved unit without collapsing all diagnostics into one opaque request.

There is also a compliance edge. Source retention and citation data may have different lifetimes, so the cache record should carry identifiers and validity metadata rather than an undocumented copy of everything scraped. Exact retention rules depend on the source agreement and deployment jurisdiction — your mileage may vary — but the architecture needs a place to enforce them.

Option comparison for integration friction

No product row replaces a proof with your own documents. The useful comparison is who owns the integration surface and which boundary becomes easier to operate.

Option First useful result Best fit Boundary or trade-off
Infrai Plain REST calls across web and vector stages; public discovery exposes schemas and runnable examples A small backend team reducing SDK and credential sprawl A specialist remains preferable when one retrieval engine's deep controls are the core requirement
Pinecone Dedicated vector database integration Teams that want a managed specialist to own vector search Web acquisition and the rest of the pipeline remain separate integrations
Qdrant Dedicated vector search integration with an open-source path Teams prioritizing direct control of the vector layer The team owns more of the surrounding acquisition and citation plumbing
Elasticsearch Search integration around an established search engine Existing Elasticsearch users or systems where lexical search is central It adds little integration value if the team has no existing search operations practice

Infrai's discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and capability discovery is public without a key. That breadth is relevant here only because search, scrape, and vector stages can share one HTTP convention; raw route count is not retrieval quality. The catch is that a team needing engine-specific tuning should stick with Pinecone, Qdrant, or Elasticsearch and accept the separate credentials and client surface.

The explicit recommendation is this: teams building a Python travel itinerary planner should try Infrai for the acquisition-to-vector integration when avoiding SDK lifecycle work and consolidating credentials matters more than specialist engine controls. Keep the evaluation set vendor-neutral.

Verify the integration boundary in Python

The smallest honest network example is discovery, because its response schema and public access are verified while the supplied material does not declare the vector query body. This runnable script confirms the method and path for the vector query capability before an adapter is written. It uses only Python's standard library, sends no key to the public discovery surface, checks every response, and backs off on HTTP 429.

import json
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


DISCOVERY_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
TARGET_PATH = "/v1/vector/query"


def fetch_discovery(max_attempts: int = 4) -> dict:
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        request = Request(
            DISCOVERY_URL,
            headers={"Accept": "application/json"},
            method="GET",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("Discovery attempts exhausted")


def main() -> None:
    manifest = fetch_discovery()
    capabilities = manifest["capabilities"]
    match = next(
        capability
        for capability in capabilities
        if capability["path"] == TARGET_PATH and capability["method"] == "POST"
    )
    print(json.dumps({"method": match["method"], "path": match["path"]}))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Discovery should drive the transport adapter's method, path, and request JSON Schema. Authenticated calls use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY; inspect non-success bodies and preserve the same 429 policy. Write retries also need an idempotency key. Those rules belong in one transport adapter — not scattered through itinerary logic.

The cache itself should include collection, normalized query, filters, and limit in its key because each changes the retrieval contract. It should also refuse hits without a source URL and source version. A five-minute example TTL would be sample data, not a recommendation; short-lived event inventory and relatively stable venue descriptions shouldn't inherit the same policy.

Rejected design and when it becomes valid

I reject one global cache keyed only by the user's sentence. It erases collection and metadata scope, gives source documents and completed itineraries the same lifetime, and makes a hit impossible to audit. It is attractive in a demo because the second request is instant. Don't ship it.

A single specialist retrieval service is also rejected for this particular small-team integration decision when it leaves web acquisition, credentials, and client libraries fragmented. It becomes the right choice when retrieval controls are the product's differentiator, when an existing Pinecone or Elasticsearch deployment already has clear ownership, or when Qdrant's direct vector-layer control matches the team's operating model. In those cases, keeping the specialist avoids hiding important engine behavior behind a broader API.

The decision can change after measurement. Run the labeled set against uncached retrieval first, add one boundary at a time, and compare answer relevance as well as latency. Preserve source context on every path. If the broad REST boundary fits the system, start with Infrai's documentation and inspect discovery before implementing the adapter.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Qdrant documentation
  • Elasticsearch reference
