title: PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE: What I Actually Look At in Query Plans
description:
PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE: What I Actually Look At in Query Plans

Every slow query I have ever chased started the same way: someone guessing. "Probably needs an index." "The join is too big." "Postgres is slow today." Guessing is how you add three indexes, change nothing, and learn nothing.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE ends the guessing. It runs the query and tells you exactly where the time went. Here is how I read one, in the order I actually read it, and what each part is telling me.

One warning first, because it bites people: ANALYZE executes the statement. On a SELECT that is fine. On an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, wrap it in a transaction and roll back:

BEGIN;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) UPDATE orders SET status = 'x' WHERE id = 1;
ROLLBACK;

Forget the rollback once and you will remember it forever.

1. Always add BUFFERS

Plain EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you time. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) tells you time plus where the data came from:

Buffers: shared hit=42 read=8190

hit means the page was already in Postgres's cache. read means it went to disk. A query with 8000 reads and 42 hits is not slow because the plan is bad. It is slow because nothing it needs is cached. That is a completely different problem from a bad join, and it changes everything you do next. Without BUFFERS you cannot tell them apart, so I never run a plan without it.

If you want the disk time broken out too, track_io_timing needs to be on, but the hit/read split alone answers most questions.

2. Read bottom-up, and multiply by loops

A plan is a tree. Postgres executes the leaves first and the results flow upward, so the most expensive thing is usually near the bottom, not the top. Start at the bottom.

Two mechanics people get wrong:

Time is cumulative. The actual time on a node includes all its children. To get what a node itself cost, subtract the children. The node with the biggest exclusive time is where your query is actually dying.

Loops multiply. This line is the classic killer:

->  Index Scan using orders_user_id_idx on orders  (actual time=0.012..0.031 rows=3 loops=184200)

That index scan looks cheap: 0.03 milliseconds. But it ran 184,200 times, once per outer row. That is 184,200 tiny index probes, which is 184,200 rounds of random I/O. The per-loop number lies to you. The total is what you pay.

Whenever I see a high loop count on an inner node, I already know the shape of the fix before reading further: the outer side is too big for a nested loop, or the inner side needs to be cheaper.

3. Estimated rows vs actual rows: the gap is the signal

Every node shows two row counts: what the planner guessed (rows=) and what actually came back (actual rows=). The single most informative number in the whole plan is the ratio between them.

Seq Scan on events  (actual rows=4 loops=1)
   Filter: (created_at > '2026-10-01')
   Rows Removed by Filter: 987331

The planner thought this filter would match a lot of rows. It matched 4. When the estimate is off by orders of magnitude, the planner picks the wrong strategy for the wrong data shape, and everything downstream is built on that lie.

Do not tune the query first. Fix the estimate. Nine times out of ten it is stale statistics: run ANALYZE on the table and look again. If the stats are fresh and the gap persists, the query is shaped in a way statistics cannot model: a function applied to the column (WHERE lower(email) = ...), a LIKE '%...%' with a leading wildcard, or a predicate the planner has no stats for. Then you change the query shape or add an expression index, not another prayer.

4. Seq Scan is not automatically the villain

A sequential scan on a 200-row lookup table is the correct plan. Postgres knows it, and you should let it. The seq scan becomes the villain in exactly one situation: it is scanning a large table and throwing almost all of it away.

Rows Removed by Filter is the field that tells you. If a seq scan reads a million rows and the filter removes 999,996 of them, that is either a missing index or an index the query cannot use. Check whether the filtered column has an index. If it does and Postgres still chose the seq scan, the estimate was probably wrong (see section 3) or the filter is not sargable, like a function call wrapping the column.

Small table, full scan: fine. Big table, filter discards everything: that is your problem.

5. Nested loops: the silent killer

Nested loop joins are perfect when the outer side is small. Ten outer rows, index probe each, done. They become catastrophic when the outer side grows and nobody notices, because the plan shape does not change, only the loop count does. A query that ran fine for a year starts timing out, and the plan looks "the same" except loops= went from 50 to 500,000.

My rule: if the outer side returns more than a few thousand rows, I want a hash join or a merge join, not a nested loop doing random I/O per row. The fix is usually upstream, make the outer side smaller (a better filter, a better estimate), rather than forcing the join type.

6. Hash joins, sorts, and work_mem

When a hash join or a sort does not fit in work_mem, Postgres spills to disk. The plan tells you plainly:

Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 18432kB

or for a hash join, multiple batches instead of one. Disk is orders of magnitude slower than memory, and this is the easiest big win in query tuning: SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB' for that session or transaction and re-run. If the plan flips to an in-memory quicksort and the time collapses, you found it.

I do not raise work_mem globally for this. It is per-operation memory, and a global bump gets multiplied by every concurrent sort and hash in the system. Session-local, for the query that needs it, is the disciplined move.

7. Index-only scans and heap fetches

An index-only scan is Postgres's cheapest access path, but it has a catch: it still visits the table (the heap) for any row whose visibility is not confirmed in the visibility map. The plan shows this as Heap Fetches. A high number means the table is not vacuumed often enough and the "index-only" scan is quietly doing heap I/O anyway.

If you see an index-only scan with thousands of heap fetches on a table that updates a lot, the fix is not a better index. It is autovacuum tuning, or a manual VACUUM, so the visibility map actually reflects reality.

8. CTEs can be an optimization fence

On Postgres 12 and later, a CTE that is referenced once gets inlined into the main query like a subquery, and the planner can optimize across it. Before 12, every CTE was materialized: fully computed, stored in a temp table, then read. That fence still exists on demand with the MATERIALIZED keyword.

When I see a plan where a CTE materializes millions of rows and the outer query filters down to a hundred, I check whether inlining would let the planner push the filter inside. On modern Postgres this usually happens automatically, but a MATERIALIZED left over from an older version, or a CTE referenced twice, will still fence it. Small thing, big difference on large CTEs.

9. My 60-second routine for any slow query

This is the actual order I go in, every time:

  1. Find the node with the largest exclusive time (subtract children, multiply loops). That is the bottleneck. Everything else is context.
  2. On that node and its parents, compare estimated rows to actual rows. A big gap means fix statistics or query shape before touching anything else.
  3. Check BUFFERS on the expensive nodes. Mostly reads means a caching problem, not a plan problem.
  4. Look for disk: external merge, hash batches, temp files. That is work_mem, session-local.
  5. Check the join strategy against the outer row count. Nested loop with a huge outer side is the usual suspect for queries that "used to be fast."

Most slow queries I have chased were not exotic. A wrong estimate, a missing index, or a nested loop that outgrew its welcome. The plan tells you which one in about a minute, if you read it bottom-up and trust the numbers over your first guess.

title: CSS Concepts Beginners Should Learn First: A Practical Learning Roadmap
description:
Learning CSS can feel confusing at first.

You start with something simple like changing the color of a heading. Then suddenly you're introduced to:

  • Selectors
  • Properties
  • Values
  • The Box Model
  • Flexbox
  • Grid
  • Positioning
  • Media queries
  • Responsive design
  • Animations
  • Transitions
  • CSS variables
  • And dozens of other concepts

Before long, you may find yourself asking:

“What am I actually supposed to learn first?”

The good news is that you don't need to learn everything at once.

CSS becomes much easier when you learn its concepts in a logical order.

Instead of trying to memorize hundreds of properties, focus on understanding the fundamentals, practising them, and gradually building more advanced skills.

In this guide, we'll create a practical CSS learning roadmap for beginners.

What Is CSS?

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.

It is the language used to control the presentation and layout of HTML content.

HTML provides the structure of a webpage.

CSS controls how that structure is presented.

For example, HTML can create a heading:

Welcome to My Website

CSS can control its appearance:

h1 {
color: darkblue;
font-size: 36px;
}

HTML essentially tells the browser:

“This is a heading.”

CSS tells the browser:

“Make this heading dark blue and 36 pixels.”

Once you understand this relationship, you can begin learning CSS systematically.

  1. Start With CSS Selectors

Selectors are one of the first concepts you should understand.

A selector tells CSS which HTML element or elements you want to style.

For example:

p {
color: gray;
}

The p is the selector.

It targets paragraph elements.

You should become comfortable with common selectors such as:

h1
p
button

You should also learn class and ID selectors.

For example:

Learning CSS is fun.

You can target the class with:

.description {
color: blue;
}

Understanding selectors gives you control over what gets styled.

Before worrying about advanced CSS, make sure you understand how CSS identifies elements.

  1. Learn Properties and Values

After selectors, understand the basic structure of a CSS rule.

For example:

h1 {
color: blue;
}

Here:

  • h1 = selector
  • color = property
  • blue = value

The property tells CSS what you want to change.

The value tells CSS how you want to change it.

You will see this pattern repeatedly throughout your CSS journey.

For example:

p {
font-size: 18px;
}

Here, font-size is the property and 18px is the value.

Understanding this structure is more important than memorizing every available property.

  1. Learn Colors

Colors are usually one of the most enjoyable things for beginners to experiment with.

You can change text color:

h1 {
color: blue;
}

You can also change the background:

body {
background-color: lightgray;
}

As you progress, learn different ways of representing colors, including:

  • Color names
  • HEX values
  • RGB
  • RGBA
  • HSL

For example:

h1 {
color: #800020;
}

You don't need to memorize color codes.

The important thing is understanding how CSS applies color to different elements.

  1. Learn Fonts and Text Styling

Typography is another important part of CSS.

Start with properties such as:

font-family
font-size
font-weight
font-style

For example:

h1 {
font-size: 36px;
font-weight: bold;
}

You should also learn text-related properties such as:

text-align
text-decoration
line-height
letter-spacing

These properties help control how readable and visually organized your text appears.

At this stage, you're still learning the fundamentals.

Don't worry about creating elaborate designs.

Focus on understanding what each property does and when you might use it.

  1. Understand the CSS Box Model

This is where CSS starts becoming much more interesting.

Every element on a webpage can be understood through the CSS Box Model.

The box model consists of:

Content → Padding → Border → Margin

Imagine a paragraph inside a box.

The content is the actual text.

Padding creates space between the content and the border.

The border surrounds the element.

Margin creates space outside the element.

A simplified structure looks like this:

Margin
┌─────────────────────┐
│ Border │
│ ┌───────────────┐ │
│ │ Padding │ │
│ │ ┌─────────┐ │ │
│ │ │ Content │ │ │
│ │ └─────────┘ │ │
│ └───────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────┘

If you don't understand the Box Model, you may eventually find yourself asking:

“Why is there so much space around this element?”

Learning the Box Model helps answer that question.

  1. Learn Width and Height

Once you understand the Box Model, learn how to control an element's dimensions.

For example:

.card {
width: 300px;
height: 200px;
}

But don't stop at fixed pixel values.

As you progress, you'll encounter units such as:

  • %
  • em
  • rem
  • vw
  • vh

You don't need to master every CSS unit immediately.

Start by understanding what width and height do, then gradually learn when different units are useful.

  1. Learn Margin and Padding

Margin and padding are frequently confused by beginners.

A simple way to remember the difference is:

Padding = space inside the element

Margin = space outside the element

For example:

.card {
padding: 20px;
margin: 30px;
}

Padding creates space between the content and the edge of the card.

Margin creates space between the card and other elements.

Understanding this difference will save you from many frustrating CSS problems.

  1. Learn Borders

Borders are another basic but useful CSS concept.

For example:

.card {
border: 1px solid black;
}

You can control:

  • Border width
  • Border style
  • Border color
  • Individual sides

Later, you can explore things like:

border-radius

which allows you to create rounded corners.

Borders may seem simple, but they help you understand how the visual boundaries of elements work.

  1. Learn Display

Now we start moving toward layout.

The display property affects how an element participates in the layout of a webpage.

You'll encounter values such as:

display: block;
display: inline;
display: inline-block;
display: flex;
display: grid;

Understanding display creates a foundation for learning modern CSS layouts.

This is an important transition:

You're moving from:

“How do I style this element?”

to:

“How do I arrange these elements?”

  1. Learn Flexbox

Flexbox is one of the most useful CSS layout systems for beginners.

It makes it easier to arrange elements along a row or column.

For example:

.container {
display: flex;
gap: 20px;
}

You can then learn properties such as:

flex-direction
justify-content
align-items
flex-wrap
gap

Flexbox is particularly useful for:

  • Navigation bars
  • Buttons
  • Cards
  • Rows of content
  • Simple page layouts
  • Aligning elements

Once Flexbox starts making sense, many layouts that previously seemed difficult become much easier.

  1. Learn CSS Grid

After gaining some confidence with Flexbox, move on to CSS Grid.

Grid is particularly useful for creating two-dimensional layouts involving rows and columns.

For example:

.container {
display: grid;
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
gap: 20px;
}

Grid is useful for layouts such as:

  • Product displays
  • Image galleries
  • Dashboard interfaces
  • Card grids
  • Larger page structures

You don't need to choose between Flexbox and Grid.

They solve different layout problems and can be used together.

A good beginner goal is to understand when each one is useful.

  1. Learn Positioning

CSS positioning allows you to control how elements are positioned within a page.

Start with the concepts:

  • static
  • relative
  • absolute
  • fixed
  • sticky

For example:

.card {
position: relative;
}

And:

.badge {
position: absolute;
top: 10px;
right: 10px;
}

Positioning can be extremely useful, but it can also become confusing if you don't understand the underlying concepts.

That's why it makes sense to learn it after you understand basic layout.

  1. Learn Responsive Design

Now it's time to think beyond one screen size.

A website might be viewed on:

📱 A smartphone

💻 A laptop

🖥️ A desktop monitor

📱 A tablet

The layout shouldn't fall apart simply because the screen becomes smaller.

That's where responsive design comes in.

Responsive design is the approach of creating interfaces that adapt to different screen sizes and devices.

Instead of designing only for one screen, you learn to think:

“How will this layout behave when the available space changes?”

This is an important mindset for modern web development.

  1. Learn Media Queries

Media queries allow you to apply CSS based on conditions such as the viewport size.

For example:

@media (max-width: 768px) {
.container {
flex-direction: column;
}
}

This tells the browser to apply the rule when the viewport is at or below the specified width.

Media queries are an important part of responsive design.

However, don't think of responsive design as simply adding a few media queries at the end.

Good responsive thinking should begin while you're designing your layout.

What Should You Learn Later?

Once you are comfortable with the fundamentals above, you can gradually explore more advanced CSS concepts.

These may include:

Advanced Selectors

Learn more complex ways of targeting elements.

Pseudo-classes and Pseudo-elements

For example:

button:hover

and:

p::before

Transitions

Create smoother changes between CSS states.

Animations

Create more complex movement and visual effects.

CSS Variables

Create reusable values in your stylesheet.

For example:

:root {
--primary-color: #800020;
}

Advanced Responsive Techniques

Explore more sophisticated approaches to building adaptable layouts.

CSS Architecture

As projects become larger, you'll need better ways to organize and maintain your styles.

CSS Frameworks and Utility Systems

Tools such as frameworks and utility-based approaches can become useful once you understand the underlying CSS concepts.

The important thing is not to rush into them before understanding CSS itself.

A Simple CSS Learning Roadmap

If you want a straightforward path, think about your learning journey like this:

Stage 1 — Fundamentals

Selectors
Properties & values
Colors
Fonts
Text styling

↓

Stage 2 — Box Model

Width & height
Margin
Padding
Borders

↓

Stage 3 — Layout

Display
Flexbox
Grid
Positioning

↓

Stage 4 — Responsive Design

Responsive layouts
Media queries
Different screen sizes

↓

Stage 5 — Advanced CSS

Pseudo-classes
Pseudo-elements
Transitions
Animations
CSS variables
Advanced selectors
CSS architecture

This gives you a progression instead of a pile of unrelated topics.

Don't Try to Memorize CSS

One common mistake beginners make is believing they need to memorize every CSS property.

You don't.

Even experienced developers look things up.

The important skills are:

Understanding → Applying → Debugging → Practising

For example, you might forget the exact syntax for a particular CSS property.

That's okay.

You can look it up.

What matters is knowing what you're trying to accomplish and understanding the concept well enough to implement it.

Build Small Projects While Learning

Don't spend months only watching tutorials.

Build.

After learning basic CSS, create a simple profile card.

After learning Flexbox, create a navigation bar.

After learning Grid, create a product-card layout.

After learning responsive design, make your page adapt to mobile screens.

Small projects help turn theoretical knowledge into practical understanding.

You will also encounter real problems.

And those problems are valuable.

You might discover that:

  • Your element isn't where you expected.
  • Your margin isn't behaving as expected.
  • Your Flexbox alignment is wrong.
  • Your Grid columns don't fit.
  • Your mobile layout breaks.

That's when CSS starts becoming more than something you're reading about.

You're actually learning how to solve layout problems.

The Goal Isn't to Know Everything

CSS is a large subject.

There will always be another property, technique, layout challenge, or browser behavior to learn.

That's normal.

Your goal as a beginner isn't:

“I must know all of CSS.”

Instead, aim for:

“I understand the fundamentals and can use them to build and troubleshoot a webpage.”

That's a much more realistic goal.

Start small.

Learn the basics.

Understand the Box Model.

Learn how layouts work.

Practise Flexbox and Grid.

Understand positioning.

Learn responsive design.

Then gradually move into advanced CSS.

You don't need to master everything before you start building.

Build while you learn.

Because the more you practise turning ideas into actual webpages, the more naturally CSS concepts begin to connect.

And eventually, instead of looking at a CSS problem and thinking:

“I have no idea what to do.”

You'll start thinking:

“Okay. I know what concept I need to check.”

That's real progress.

Final Thoughts

Learning CSS doesn't have to feel like memorizing a giant dictionary of properties.

It becomes much easier when you approach it as a progression.

Start with:

Selectors → Properties → Box Model → Layout → Responsive Design → Advanced Concepts

Give yourself time to understand each stage.

Experiment.

Break things.

Fix them.

Build small projects.

And don't be afraid to look things up.

The goal isn't to know every CSS property from memory.

The goal is to become comfortable enough with CSS to turn structured HTML into responsive, organized and visually effective webpages.

Learn the foundation first. Then build on it.

title: When Your AI Assistant Gets Frontier Brains: The Work You Can Newly Hand Over (and What to Verify)
description:
Every few months, the model inside a consumer AI assistant gets quietly replaced with a smarter one. Most coverage treats this as a leaderboard event — who's on top, who got embarrassed. For a small business owner, it's something more practical: a moving line. Capability jumps move the line between work you have to do yourself and work you can hand over.

Meta just moved the line. The Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models are the company's first genuine frontier models, and they were built specifically for agentic tasks — the release examples are navigating an insurance claim, making sense of a lease, and working through someone's finances. Two details matter beyond the benchmarks: Active Memory, which carries what matters to you across conversations, and Active Focus, which keeps a task moving when it gets hard — trying other approaches, recovering from errors, and checking in before following through on anything important.

One honesty note before the hype: Wonder is rolling out to subscribers first, not the entire free tier today. So the shift is arriving in tiers, not all at once. But the direction is set — the assistant you already use is getting a brain that doesn't just summarize work, it does work. Here's how to think about what newly crosses the line, and where you still have to be the checkpoint.

What a capability jump actually changes

The question is never "which model is smartest." It's "which of my tasks just crossed from assistant-shaped to doer-shaped." Assistant-shaped work produces a summary of a job. Doer-shaped work produces the job. Every tier jump converts a category you used to babysit into a category you can delegate, and the conversion is worth real money — but only if you notice it.

The Wonder-class jump is specifically about long, multi-step work over messy real documents. That's the category that used to bounce. Three task families just crossed the line:

  1. Document wrangling. Hand over a lease, a supplier contract, an insurance policy, or a franchise agreement and ask for the obligations extracted: what you owe, when, what triggers penalties, what's unusual compared to a standard agreement. A weaker model gives you a generic summary. A frontier-class one reads the actual text in front of it and works the problem — and with memory, it remembers what it found when you ask a follow-up next week.

  2. Disputes and claims. Assembling the timeline from a messy email thread, drafting the escalation chain for an unpaid invoice or a rejected insurance claim, and keeping it moving across multiple touchpoints over days. This is exactly the multi-step, follow-through-shaped work agentic models are now built for — the claim-navigation example in Meta's release is not a hypothetical use case; it's the design target.

  3. Financial sense-making. "Here's my last three months of statements — what changed, what should I worry about?" Not bookkeeping; a first-pass read that tells you where to look. You verify before acting, but the hours of gathering and initial pattern-spotting move off your desk.

Notice what's not on the list: anything where the output goes straight to a customer without review, anything requiring knowledge of facts you can't verify, and anything that's your actual judgment. Capability jumps convert tasks, not responsibility.

The boundary that didn't move

Here's the part the benchmark charts won't tell you: Wonder Full scores 30 on AA-Omniscience — a factual-recall test — versus 46 for Claude Opus 5.5. Knowledge is the model's thin side. Its relatively low hallucination rate means it's less likely to invent missing facts, which is a real mitigation. It is not a license to skip verification.

So draw the verify line explicitly. Before anything derived from Wonder-class work touches reality, check:

  • Dates and deadlines. Renewal windows, notice periods, claim filing limits. A missed deadline is where a summarized document becomes a lawsuit.
  • Dollar amounts. Every figure extracted from a contract, policy, or statement gets checked against the source. Transposition errors are cheap to catch and expensive to miss.
  • Legal and policy references. If the output cites a statute, a clause, or a coverage term — open the source and confirm it says what the assistant says it says.
  • Anything with regulatory or financial force. The pattern is simple: the stronger the consequence of being wrong, the less delegable the verification.

The useful feature here is Active Focus's check-in behavior — the model is built to pause and confirm before following through on anything important. That's a natural checkpoint, if you use it. Set the expectation up front: "Show me the draft and the extracted facts before anything gets sent or filed." A frontier brain with a checkpoint habit is an employee. Without one, it's a liability with good prose.

Run the conversion test this month

Don't take a benchmark's word for it — run your own. Pick two real tasks from the doer-shaped categories above, one document wrangle and one dispute or claim that's actually rotting on your list. Give the full messy inputs, not a cleaned-up version. Then score it the only way that matters: did the job get done — obligations extracted, timeline assembled, escalation drafted — or did you get a nice summary of a job that still needs doing? Verify the facts on the short list above, and time-box the whole thing to a week.

If it finishes, you've just converted hours of skilled reading and drafting into review work. If it doesn't, you've learned the line hasn't moved for your use case yet — and it will, probably within a quarter, because the direction of frontier capability arriving inside consumer assistants is now the least uncertain thing in technology.

The models will keep improving. The owner's job doesn't change: decide what crosses the line, keep the verify list short and non-negotiable, and let the checkpoint — not the benchmark — be the thing you trust.

If you want the full delegation framework — the permission ladder that matches tasks to trust levels, the first-month inspection habit, and the escalation contract format that tells an agent exactly when to come back to you — it's written down in The AI Agent Owner's Playbook. $49 CAD, instant download.

title: The Field Type You Pick in Ten Minutes Is a Ten-Year Decision
description:
Mei runs procurement at an equipment manufacturer with about 700 people. Their platform went live three years ago. Last month she asked me a question that sounded like a two-minute request.

"Sales wants to sort the contract amount from high to low. Right now it sorts like text. Can we just change the field type?"

The field is amount. It was created in the second week of the project, in a workshop room, by an analyst who had a dropdown and a deadline. She picked single-line text, because the number came from a PDF and she was not sure yet whether it needed decimals.

Three years and roughly nine thousand contracts later, that ten-second choice has become a six-week project.

The dropdown is not a label

Renaming a field takes a minute. Moving it on a form takes a minute. Changing its type is a different category of work entirely, and almost nobody knows that at the moment they choose.

In a platform like ours, the type is not metadata that sits above the table. It is the table. Every data table compiles down to a real physical table in PostgreSQL, one column per field, and the field type decides what that column is. Single-line text is a bounded string. Multi-selects and attachments are stored as JSON. There is no neutral layer underneath where a type can be reconsidered later.

So the analyst was not picking a display format. She was writing DDL.

Type decides what the database is allowed to do

The second-order effects show up slowly, in reporting.

Indexes are the clearest case. Ours can be created on ordinary columns, but the documentation is honest about the exceptions: function fields, related-record fields, lookup fields, static text and custom components cannot be indexed. Which means the moment you model something as a lookup instead of a stored value, you have also decided that this column will never be a fast filter.

Nobody thinks about that in a workshop. They think about not typing the same supplier name forty times, and they are right to — denormalization for convenience is usually correct. The convenience is just paid for by whoever, two years later, builds a dashboard filtered on that column and watches it time out.

The type also decides what sorting means. Text sorts lexicographically, so "9" comes after "10", and the amount column becomes useless for the one question finance asks every Monday. A float sorts correctly and rounds incorrectly. A precise decimal sorts and rounds correctly and is the only one of the three that survives a reconciliation.

These are ordinary database distinctions. What is unusual is that in a low-code platform, the person making the decision was never taught them, and the interface does not teach them either.

Type decides how many states the world has

My favourite example is the checkbox.

A boolean has two states. A procurement approval has three: approved, rejected, and nobody has looked at it yet. Model it as a checkbox and the third state does not disappear — it becomes null, which is indistinguishable from "the field was added after this record was created" and from "the form did not require it".

The platform will not save you here either. Generated tables ship with exactly one not-null column, the system id; every business column is nullable by default, because nullability is a form setting rather than a storage decision. So the third state exists physically and is unnameable semantically. Reporting on it becomes a negotiation: does blank mean no, or does blank mean unknown? Two analysts will answer differently, and both will be able to point at real rows.

A single-select with three options costs the same ten seconds and keeps the third state.

The type is a statement about the business. We treat it as a statement about the widget.

Type is a promise to every consumer downstream

The database is only the first reader. By year two, a field has many more.

The WebAPI returns what is stored, so a JSON-encoded multi-select becomes a parsing problem for every integration that touches it. The Excel export renders it one way, the dashboard another, the mobile app a third. The importer expects a template that matches the current type, and every historical spreadsheet your team has been emailing around matches the old one.

Expressions are the quietest and most expensive reader. Formulas reference fields and coerce values, and when the type changes, the coercion changes underneath the formula without the formula changing at all. A comparison that meant one thing when both sides were strings means something else when one side becomes a number. Nothing errors. The report just starts disagreeing with last quarter.

And when the type finally changes, it is not an alter table. It is a data rewrite, plus every expression that touched the field, plus every view and dashboard and export template, plus every integration contract, plus the import templates stored in someone's shared drive. The rewrite cannot even be proven lossless, because the old column had no constraints: it contains values that were never valid for the type you are moving to, and somebody has to decide, row by row, what "N/A", "TBD", "1.2M" and "-" were supposed to mean.

The economics are backwards

Here is what bothers me most.

Adding a field is cheap and removing one is politically expensive. So platforms are optimized, culturally and technically, for addition. Every project accumulates fields. Each one is a type decision made by whoever was closest to the requirement that day, usually under time pressure, usually without knowing what the reports would need.

The decisions that take the least time have the longest half-life. A workflow can be redesigned in a week. A permission model can be tightened in an afternoon. A field type, once nine thousand records depend on it, is a migration project with a steering committee.

We have built an interface where the cheapest action is the most permanent one, and we have not labelled it.

What the platform owes the person at the dropdown

Some of this is unavoidable. Types must be types, and a platform that pretends otherwise is lying.

But there is a difference between a hard decision and an invisible one.

A field type should show what it forecloses at the moment of choosing: whether it can be indexed, how it sorts, how it will appear in exports and in the API, and what changing it later will cost. Not a warning dialog on every field — that becomes noise. A single line, in the same place where you pick the type, saying what you are giving up.

A type change should be an operation with a plan rather than a quiet edit: show every expression, view, export and integration that reads the column; run the conversion in dry mode against real values; tell me how many rows will fail to parse before I click. We do the opposite. We let the change succeed and let the failures surface later, as a report that no longer adds up.

And a platform should treat a small number of fields as architecture rather than content. Amount, date, status, owner, and the identifier that everything joins on. Those five deserve a review before go-live, in the same way a schema review happens in a codebase. Not because they are hard to name, but because they are expensive to be wrong about.

The uncomfortable conclusion

The tempting fix is to make types flexible: store everything as text, parse at the edges, let each application decide what the value means.

That does not remove the decision. It moves it to every consumer, and it removes the one thing a type was giving you — a single, enforced, queryable definition of what the column contains. You get a platform that never blocks a migration because it never knew what the data was.

The real failure is not that the analyst chose text for an amount. Given what she knew in week two, text was defensible.

The failure is that the platform let a ten-second decision stay invisible for three years, and then presented the bill as a six-week project nobody had budgeted for.

We are very good at making the first ten minutes feel effortless.

We have never once shown the customer what the next ten years cost.

title: Intersection Observer API
description:
Watching the Web: How the Intersection Observer API Lets Your JavaScript See What's Happening

Ever felt like your web page is a bit… oblivious? It loads content, scrolls, and just keeps going, even if half of its elements are off-screen, taking up valuable resources for no good reason. Well, say hello to the Intersection Observer API, your JavaScript's new superpower for understanding what's visible and what's not. Think of it as giving your code eyes that can see exactly when things pop into view, or more importantly, when they leave view.

This isn't just about fancy animations. The Intersection Observer API is a game-changer for performance, user experience, and building more dynamic, engaging web applications. Let's dive deep into this awesome API, breaking down what it is, why you should care, and how to wield its power.

🤯 What's All the Fuss About? A Gentle Introduction

Imagine you're browsing an online store. Products are listed, and as you scroll down, more products magically appear. Or maybe a "Back to Top" button only shows up when you've scrolled a bit. These aren't just clever tricks; they're often powered by the Intersection Observer API.

Traditionally, detecting when an element enters or leaves the viewport (that visible area of your browser window) was a bit of a hassle. You'd have to attach scroll event listeners, calculate element positions, and constantly re-evaluate. This could lead to janky scrolling, high CPU usage, and a generally sluggish experience, especially on less powerful devices.

The Intersection Observer API elegantly solves this. Instead of you actively asking "Is this element visible?", you tell the browser, "Hey, let me know when this element intersects with this other element (or the viewport)." The browser then handles all the heavy lifting, notifying you only when an intersection change occurs. It's a more efficient, declarative approach that feels like a breath of fresh air for web developers.

🧠 What You Need to Know Before We Begin (Prerequisites)

While the Intersection Observer API is quite accessible, having a basic understanding of a few web development concepts will make this journey smoother:

  • JavaScript Fundamentals: You should be comfortable with basic JavaScript syntax, variables, functions, and DOM manipulation.
  • DOM Basics: Knowing how to select elements from the Document Object Model (DOM) is crucial. Think document.getElementById(), document.querySelector(), etc.
  • Viewport: Understanding what the viewport is – the visible part of the web page in the browser window – is key.
  • Browser Compatibility: While the Intersection Observer API has excellent browser support now, it's always good practice to check Can I Use (caniuse.com) for the latest information.

That's it! No complex algorithms or arcane knowledge required. We're going to build on these fundamentals.

✨ The Superpowers: Why You'll Love the Intersection Observer API

This API isn't just a minor improvement; it brings some serious advantages to the table:

  • Performance Boost: This is the big one. By offloading intersection detection to the browser, you dramatically reduce the need for frequent JavaScript calculations on scroll. This means smoother scrolling, less CPU strain, and a more responsive website, especially on mobile devices.
  • Simplified Code: Gone are the days of complex scroll event handlers and manual position calculations. The API provides a clean, declarative way to manage intersections, making your code more readable and maintainable.
  • Lazy Loading Excellence: Image lazy loading, infinite scrolling, and loading ad banners only when they're about to be seen? These are prime use cases for Intersection Observer, significantly improving initial page load times.
  • Animations on Scroll: Want elements to fade in, slide up, or animate when they enter the viewport? Intersection Observer makes this incredibly easy and performant.
  • Analytics and Tracking: Trigger specific JavaScript actions or send analytics events when certain elements become visible to the user.
  • Resource Management: Only load and render resources (like images, videos, or even entire components) when they are actually needed, saving bandwidth and improving user experience.

🚧 The Not-So-Sunny Side: Potential Downsides

Every superhero has a weakness, and the Intersection Observer API is no different. While its advantages far outweigh its disadvantages, it's good to be aware of them:

  • Browser Support (Historically): While now widely supported, in its early days, polyfills were necessary for older browsers. Always check compatibility if you need to support very old browsers.
  • Complexity for Edge Cases: For extremely intricate intersection scenarios or custom intersection logic that goes beyond simple visibility checks, you might still need to supplement it with other techniques. However, for the vast majority of use cases, it's sufficient.
  • Understanding the Concepts: While the API itself is simple, grasping the nuances of thresholds, root margins, and how they interact can take a little getting used to.

🛠️ Let's Get Practical: Features and How to Use Them

The core of the Intersection Observer API revolves around a IntersectionObserver object. You create one, configure it, and then tell it which elements to observe.

1. Creating an IntersectionObserver

The constructor takes two main arguments:

  • callback: A function that gets executed every time the observed element's intersection status changes.
  • options (optional): An object to configure the observer's behavior. 
const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries, observer) => {
  // This callback function will be executed when an observed element's
  // intersection status changes.
  // 'entries' is an array of IntersectionObserverEntry objects.
  // 'observer' is the IntersectionObserver instance itself.

  entries.forEach(entry => {
    // We'll explore what 'entry' contains in a moment.
    console.log('Intersection changed for:', entry.target);
  });
}, {
  // Options object goes here
});

2. The Callback Function: What Happens When Things Change

The callback function receives two arguments:

  • entries: An array of IntersectionObserverEntry objects. Each entry represents a specific observed element and its intersection status.
  • observer: A reference to the IntersectionObserver instance that triggered the callback.

Let's break down the IntersectionObserverEntry object. This is where the magic lies:

  • target: The DOM element that triggered the intersection change.
  • isIntersecting: A boolean value. true if the element is currently at least partially visible within the root (usually the viewport), false otherwise. This is your primary tool!
  • intersectionRatio: A number between 0.0 and 1.0, indicating how much of the target element is currently visible within the root. 0.0 means none is visible, 1.0 means the entire element is visible.
  • boundingClientRect: The DOMRect object for the target element. Similar to element.getBoundingClientRect().
  • intersectionRect: The DOMRect object representing the intersection of the target element and the root.
  • rootBounds: The DOMRect object for the root element. If the root is the viewport, this will be the viewport's dimensions.

3. Observing Elements: Telling the Observer What to Watch

Once you have your IntersectionObserver instance, you use its observe() method to tell it which elements to watch.

const myElement = document.getElementById('my-awesome-element');
if (myElement) {
  observer.observe(myElement);
}

4. Stopping Observation: Cleaning Up

When you're done observing an element or want to unregister the observer entirely, you use unobserve() and disconnect() respectively.

// To stop observing a specific element:
observer.unobserve(myElement);

// To stop observing all elements and clean up the observer:
observer.disconnect();

5. The options Object: Fine-Tuning the Magic

The options object allows you to customize how and when the callback is triggered.

  • root: The element that is used as the "viewport" for checking visibility of the target. If not specified or null, the browser's viewport is used.

    // Observe intersections relative to a specific container
const container = document.getElementById('scrollable-container');
const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
  root: container
});

  • rootMargin: This is like adding a margin around the root. You can use it to expand or shrink the area around the root that counts as "intersecting." Values are similar to CSS margin properties (e.g., '10px 20px', '5% 10px 0 0'). This is incredibly useful for triggering content before it's fully visible.

    // Trigger the callback when an element is 100px *away* from entering the viewport
const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
  rootMargin: '100px'
});

    Imagine you want an image to load just before it's visible. You can use rootMargin to achieve this.

  • threshold: This is where you define how much of the target element needs to be visible for the callback to fire. It can be a single number between 0.0 and 1.0, or an array of numbers.

    // Callback fires when at least 50% of the element is visible
const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
  threshold: 0.5
});

// Callback fires when 25%, 50%, and 75% of the element is visible
const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
  threshold: [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
});

    This is powerful for triggering animations at different stages of visibility.

🚀 Practical Examples: Bringing the API to Life

Let's see some real-world scenarios in action.

Example 1: Simple Lazy Loading for Images

This is the most common use case. We'll replace the src attribute of an image with its data-src attribute when it becomes visible.

HTML:

<img data-src="path/to/your/image.jpg" alt="A descriptive alt text" class="lazy-load">

JavaScript:

const lazyImages = document.querySelectorAll('.lazy-load');

const imageObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries, observer) => {
  entries.forEach(entry => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      const img = entry.target;
      img.src = img.dataset.src; // Load the actual image
      img.removeAttribute('data-src'); // Clean up
      observer.unobserve(img); // Stop observing this image once loaded
    }
  });
}, {
  threshold: 0.1 // Trigger when 10% of the image is visible
});

lazyImages.forEach(img => {
  imageObserver.observe(img);
});

In this example, the threshold: 0.1 ensures that we start loading the image slightly before it's fully in view, providing a smoother experience. We also unobserve once loaded, so the observer doesn't keep checking an already loaded image.

Example 2: Fade-in Animation on Scroll

Let's make elements gracefully fade in as they enter the viewport.

HTML:

<div class="fade-in-element">This will fade in!</div>
<div class="fade-in-element">Another one!</div>

CSS:

.fade-in-element {
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 0.5s ease-in-out;
}

.fade-in-element.is-visible {
  opacity: 1;
}

JavaScript:

const fadeInElements = document.querySelectorAll('.fade-in-element');

const fadeInObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries, observer) => {
  entries.forEach(entry => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      entry.target.classList.add('is-visible');
      observer.unobserve(entry.target); // Stop observing once it's visible
    }
  });
}, {
  threshold: 0.2 // Trigger when 20% of the element is visible
});

fadeInElements.forEach(el => {
  fadeInObserver.observe(el);
});

Here, we add a CSS class is-visible when the element intersects. The CSS transition handles the actual fading.

Example 3: Infinite Scrolling

This is a bit more involved but demonstrates the power of triggering actions based on visibility.

HTML:

<div id="content-container">
  <!-- Initial content will be loaded here -->
</div>
<div id="loading-indicator" style="display: none;">Loading more...</div>

JavaScript (Conceptual - you'd fetch data in a real app):

const contentContainer = document.getElementById('content-container');
const loadingIndicator = document.getElementById('loading-indicator');
let currentPage = 1;
const itemsPerPage = 10;

// Function to simulate fetching more content
function loadMoreContent() {
  loadingIndicator.style.display = 'block';
  setTimeout(() => { // Simulate network delay
    for (let i = 0; i < itemsPerPage; i++) {
      const newItem = document.createElement('div');
      newItem.textContent = `Item ${currentPage * itemsPerPage + i + 1}`;
      newItem.style.padding = '10px';
      newItem.style.borderBottom = '1px solid #eee';
      contentContainer.appendChild(newItem);
    }
    currentPage++;
    loadingIndicator.style.display = 'none';
    // Re-observe the loading indicator after adding new content
    observer.observe(loadingIndicator);
  }, 1000);
}

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries, observer) => {
  entries.forEach(entry => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      observer.unobserve(entry.target); // Unobserve immediately to prevent multiple fetches
      loadMoreContent();
    }
  });
}, {
  // No root or rootMargin needed if observing against viewport
});

// Initial load of some content
loadMoreContent(); // Load the first batch

// We need to observe the loading indicator *after* it's visible and has content
// The first loadMoreContent() will add content and we'll then observe the indicator.
// For subsequent loads, the loadMoreContent() function itself re-observes the indicator.

// To make sure the indicator is observed initially if it's the last thing on screen:
observer.observe(loadingIndicator);

In this infinite scroll example, the loadingIndicator is observed. When it becomes visible, we trigger loadMoreContent(). Crucially, loadMoreContent() then re-observes the loadingIndicator itself, ensuring that the next batch of content can be loaded when that indicator becomes visible.

🌐 Browser Compatibility and Polyfills

As of late 2023 and early 2024, the Intersection Observer API is very well supported across modern browsers. You can generally use it without worrying about polyfills for Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, and most mobile browsers.

However, if you have a strict requirement to support very old browsers (like Internet Explorer 11 without Edge's compatibility modes), you might need a polyfill. You can find reliable polyfills on resources like GitHub.

🚀 Conclusion: Your New Favorite Tool for Dynamic Web Experiences

The Intersection Observer API is a powerful, elegant, and performant way to make your web pages more dynamic and responsive. It simplifies common tasks like lazy loading and scroll-based animations, leading to better user experiences and improved performance.

By understanding how to create observers, interpret the IntersectionObserverEntry objects, and configure options like rootMargin and threshold, you unlock a whole new level of control over your web application's behavior.

So, next time you're thinking about adding a touch of interactivity or optimizing your page's loading speed, remember the Intersection Observer API. It's your JavaScript's eye on the web, helping it see what truly matters – what's in view! Happy observing!

title: Pause workflows for approval with Chat SDK
description:
You can build human-in-the-loop approvals with Chat SDK through the new chat/workflow subpath. One requestApproval call posts a card with Approve and Deny buttons and suspends a Workflow SDK workflow until someone decides.

The wait can last seconds or days and survives deploys and restarts. You don't need an approvals table, an onAction handler, or a polling loop:

Start the workflow from any handler, and Thread instances serialize across the workflow boundary automatically. The card handles the rest:

  • Scoped approvers: Pass approvers to restrict who can decide. Clicks from anyone else post a notice, and the workflow keeps waiting.

  • Verified decisions: Chat SDK checks the platform's signature on every click, so the user.id on the result is the person who decided.

  • Audit trail: Once a decision lands or the timeout elapses, the card is edited in place with an outcome line, preventing stale clicks.

Get started by reading the approvals documentation.

The Bun runtime for Vercel Functions now supports Bun.serve() as a function entrypoint, including WebSocket handlers. The server you run locally with Bun deploys as-is, without being wrapped in a framework.

Enable the runtime by setting "bunVersion": "1.x" in vercel.json.

Deploy a routes-based server

Create a server with a routes map in server.ts at the project root.

Accept WebSocket connections

Add a websocket handler and call server.upgrade(request) in fetch to upgrade matching requests. The rest of the server stays the same.

WebSocket connections run on Fluid compute with Active CPU pricing, so you pay only for time spent processing messages, not idle connection time. A connection is pinned to one function instance for its lifetime, and a single instance can handle multiple concurrent connections. Use an external data store to coordinate messages across instances.

title: The 1M-Token Training Run: How Alibaba Trains Coding Agents on 8-Hour Bug Hunts
description:
Your coding agent doesn't train on code snippets anymore. The frontier trains on full workdays: one execution can run for hours, hit hundreds of tool calls, and burn through nearly a million tokens. Alibaba's Qwen team just published the machinery that makes that training tractable — QwenGyre, an elastic reinforcement-learning framework for what they call "xLong-horizon" agents (arXiv 2609.33848).

The headline numbers: on their flagship Qwen 3.8 2.4T with ~700K tokens per rollout, NL2RepoBench went from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps, and the full run took 75.42 hours instead of 134.55 (Async baseline) or 91.47 (Colocate) — up to 1.85× faster at matched scores.

The ELI5 version

Training an agent with RL is like coaching a junior engineer: they try a task, you score the result, they adjust. But when one "try" takes 3 hours and another takes 20 minutes, two things break:

  1. The straggler tax. GPUs sit idle waiting for the slowest execution to finish — like a classroom where everyone stares at the ceiling until the last kid hands in the exam.
  2. The redundancy tax. One execution branches into many possible paths that mostly share the same beginning. Training on all of them naively means recomputing the same prefix over and over.

QwenGyre attacks both. It's not a model — it's the training system around the model.

How it works, part 1: the elastic scheduler

Normal RL setups pick one of two bad options. Colocate: all GPUs do rollouts, then all GPUs train — the whole pool waits for the slowest agent execution. Async: split the pool statically, half rollouts, half training — but neither side can borrow the other's spare GPUs, so capacity sits stranded while stragglers dribble in.

QwenGyre organizes hardware into independently switchable cells. As rollout executions finish, cells flip from inference to training on the fly. Live harness runs are never interrupted: model requests get rerouted to the remaining rollout engines mid-flight, KV caches migrate over RDMA (no recomputation), and the freed cells join the ongoing training step as extra data-parallel replicas.

The switching is fast: 8.52 seconds rollout→training, 3.46 seconds back. Against executions that last hours, that's rounding error.

How it works, part 2: the trajectory processor

The second innovation is how training samples are built from branching agent histories. The framework:

  • Reconstructs branching histories as prefix-shared trajectory trees — the shared beginning of an execution is stored and trained on once, not once per branch.
  • Scores partial progress — timed-out executions aren't thrown away; the preserved workspace is scored as-is, so an 80%-done 3-hour run still teaches.
  • Deduplicates redundant paths — at most 5 trajectories per execution. Evaluator failures are excluded rather than scored zero (a broken grader shouldn't poison the signal).

The 5-trajectory cap matched uncapped scores while cutting forward-backward time 25.2%. At 8 branches per execution, prefix sharing alone gives 2.1×, and the cap pushes it to 3.1×.

The state of the art

The scale test is serious: Qwen 3.6 122B on 24–32 nodes, and Qwen 3.8 2.4T on 192 nodes (4 cells of 48), with rollouts served by SGLang and training in Megatron, running inside an unmodified black-box harness (Claude Code 2.1.220 — the framework doesn't get to cheat by changing the agent's tools).

What the numbers say:

  • +6.06pp on NL2RepoBench (52.48% → 58.54%) in 48 steps — repository-level coding, not quiz questions.
  • 1.78× faster than Async, 1.85× faster than Colocate end-to-end. The gap shrinks when many queries hit the timeout (worst case 1.21× on the 2.4T) — stragglers still bite, just less.
  • 8.5s / 3.5s cell switches — the migration machinery costs nothing measurable.

The honest caveat: QwenGyre's numbers are vendor-reported, and the paper links no public code release. Treat the framework as an existence proof of a technique, not a download.

Takeaways

  • The agent frontier moved to the training loop. When single executions run hours and cost ~1M tokens, the bottleneck isn't the model — it's GPU scheduling and trajectory hygiene. The harness and the RL system around the model now decide who wins, exactly the way agent harnesses decided capability earlier this year.
  • Elasticity beats partitioning. Any time you have highly variable work, fixed splits strand capacity. Let the hardware follow the work.
  • Don't discard partial work. Scoring timed-out executions on their preserved state recovers a learning signal that naive "reward = 0" throws away — in my toy simulation above, the naive rule kills the signal entirely while partial scoring stays correlated 0.91 with true capability.
  • If you build agents: long-horizon evaluation is now the benchmark that matters (NL2RepoBench, TerminalBench). If your agent can't hold a task together for an hour, no amount of prompt engineering closes the gap — it has to be trained there.

Companion notebook: the runnable tutorial for this post — download it here (open in Colab/Jupyter).

title: A flex child that is allowed to shrink overflows from its centre, so the title left the top of the screen and the button left the bottom
description:
Every practice game on CogniPrep renders inside one component. It is a header with a back button, a question counter and a clock, and below it the game. No page scroll, no site chrome, because a timed assessment that moves under you while you are answering it is a different test from the one the candidate is sitting.

The whole shell is about fifteen lines of JSX, and four class names in it were each paid for by a bug.

h-dvh, not h-screen 

<div className="bg-background flex h-dvh w-full flex-col overflow-hidden">

h-screen is 100vh. On mobile browsers 100vh is the viewport with the browser chrome hidden, which is taller than what is actually on screen while the URL bar is showing. A 100vh shell with overflow-hidden on it therefore puts its own bottom strip underneath the URL bar, and because the shell does not scroll, there is no way to reach it.

The bottom strip is where the Start and Next buttons live. So the first version of this was a game you could not start on a phone until you scrolled the page, and the page did not scroll.

h-dvh is 100dvh, which tracks the visible area as the chrome comes and goes. It is the entire fix, and it is worth knowing that the failure it prevents is not "the layout looks slightly off", it is "the primary action is unreachable".

min-h-0, so overflow-auto can do its job 

<main className="flex min-h-0 flex-1 flex-col overflow-auto">

flex-1 says take the space left over after the header. That is not enough on its own, because a flex item's default min-height is auto, meaning it refuses to be smaller than its content. A box that will not shrink below its content cannot have a scrollbar, since there is nothing to scroll: the content simply makes the box taller and the box pushes past the bottom of the shell, which is clipped by overflow-hidden.

min-h-0 lets it shrink to the space that is actually left. Then overflow-auto has something to work with.

This is the Tailwind spelling of the oldest flexbox gotcha there is, and I will keep paying for it in some new codebase about once a year.

The one that is not obvious: shrink-0 on the children 

<main className="flex min-h-0 flex-1 flex-col overflow-auto [&>*]:shrink-0">

Having just told the main box it may shrink, we tell everything inside it that it may not. That looks like undoing the previous fix. It is not, and the reason is the most interesting thing in this component.

Every game screen inside the shell is a centred box, roughly:

<div className="flex min-h-full flex-col items-center justify-center">

That is what puts a short screen, an instruction panel or a result, in the middle of the available space instead of pinned to the top. Now let that box shrink. justify-center is still in force, so when the content is taller than the box, the overflow is distributed to both ends. The content overflows centred.

Centred overflow is the worst kind, because scrolling cannot recover it. The top of the content is above the box's top edge, which is not a position overflow-auto will scroll to, so the heading is simply gone. At the same time the primary button is below the bottom edge. One screen, two pieces of content amputated, and a scrollbar that behaves as if everything is fine.

[&>*]:shrink-0 stops the screen from being squashed below its content at all. The box grows to its content, the main element becomes genuinely scrollable, and scrollTop 0 shows the heading.

The 320px rules in the header

The header has three things that only exist from sm up, and all three are the same decision.

The back button's text label:

{/* Label drops below sm so the arrow alone remains. At 320px the
    full label plus the question counter did not fit and the two
    overlapped; aria-label carries the meaning either way. */}
<span className="hidden sm:inline">Back to Games</span>

The arrow stays, the words go, and the button keeps its aria-label, so what a screen reader announces does not change with the viewport. A hidden label and an unlabelled icon button look identical in a screenshot and are not the same component.

The width reservation on the counter and clock:

<div className="text-muted-foreground text-right text-xs tabular-nums sm:min-w-[120px] sm:text-sm">

Reserved width is there so the header does not twitch as the counter and the clock change, which is worth having and is also 120 pixels you do not own on a 320 pixel screen. tabular-nums does most of the same work for free, so the reservation starts at sm and the small screen keeps its space for the label beside it.

And the divider between the button and the game name is hidden sm:block, because a separator between two things when one of them is not rendered is a line in the middle of nothing.

The general shape of it

A full screen app layout is four claims, and every one of them is a bug if you leave it out:

  1. The shell is exactly as tall as the visible viewport. h-dvh.
  2. The shell does not scroll. overflow-hidden.
  3. The scrolling region may be shorter than its content. min-h-0 plus overflow-auto.
  4. The content inside that region may not be shorter than itself. shrink-0.

Three and four sound contradictory, and that is exactly why the combination takes an afternoon to find.

The shell wraps every game in the library, so the quickest way to see it is to start one: the Arctic Shores games include free games you can try with a free account, and the provider list covers the other 55. The same layout problem in a three pane form, which is a longer story, is behind the assessment centre exercises.
