title: Next.js Server Action API Route Logging: 5 Cohort Boundaries (Node.js)
description:
TL;DR: Centralize Next.js backend events as structured JSON, redact them before they leave the process, and compare tenant cohorts with request IDs and user-safe identifiers. For a small developer-tools SaaS, I would try Infrai for the log transport boundary when keeping one stable REST contract matters more than buying a full observability suite. Its public discovery schema also cuts the time spent guessing at an unfamiliar API.

The deciding constraint is signal quality versus noise. An experiment result is useless when a server action, an API route, and a cron handler describe the same tenant three different ways. Raw request bodies are worse: they raise privacy risk without making the cohort comparison clearer.

My five boundaries are narrow: normalize the event, attach deployment context, redact known secrets and personal fields, reject raw bodies, then deliver through one adapter. The application owns that contract. The vendor behind it can move.

How should Next.js server action and API route logging work?

The obvious first draft is console.log plus whatever fields happen to be nearby. It ships fast. It also creates a pile of prose that cannot reliably answer a basic product question: did treatment tenants see more failed actions than control tenants after version 2026.10.8 reached two regions?

That is the wrong kind of cheap.

A useful event needs a small, stable vocabulary: service, region, version, environment, request_id, a user-safe tenant identifier, cohort, operation, outcome, and timestamp. API routes, server actions, cron handlers, and auth events should emit the same shape. Email addresses, tokens, cookies, and request bodies should not cross the boundary. The selected REST service has no user-level log deletion endpoint, so redaction before ingestion is a design requirement for right-to-be-forgotten workflows, not later cleanup.

For this workload, the attractive property is replaceability: the application calls one plain REST contract, while the service behind that capability can change without spreading another SDK across the codebase. Its unauthenticated discovery surface exposes full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; the live manifest covers 295 routes in 20 modules. That is useful in a one-person shop because integration archaeology competes directly with shipping.

The event schema is the product decision; transport is plumbing. I want the latter outsourced and the former kept in source control.

Smallest useful Node.js implementation

The code below keeps redaction and delivery separate. It emits one event for a tenant experiment, never accepts a request body, reads the key from the environment, retries rate limits, honors Retry-After, and surfaces non-success responses. The two vendor-specific facts in the code are the base URL and the verified ingest route.

type Cohort = "control" | "treatment";
type Outcome = "ok" | "error";

type ExperimentEvent = {
  timestamp: string;
  service: string;
  region: "us" | "eu";
  version: string;
  environment: "production" | "staging";
  request_id: string;
  tenant_ref: string;
  cohort: Cohort;
  operation: "server_action" | "api_route" | "cron" | "auth";
  outcome: Outcome;
  attributes: Record<string, unknown>;
};

const blockedKeys = /^(email|token|authorization|cookie|set-cookie|body)$/i;

function redact(value: unknown): unknown {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map(redact);
  if (value === null || typeof value !== "object") return value;

  return Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(value as Record<string, unknown>).map(([key, item]) => [
      key,
      blockedKeys.test(key) ? "[REDACTED]" : redact(item),
    ]),
  );
}

function retryDelayMs(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  return Math.min(500 * 2 ** attempt, 8_000);
}

async function ingest(event: ExperimentEvent): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/ingest", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(redact(event)),
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    const detail = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      throw new Error(`Log ingestion failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
    }

    await new Promise<void>((resolve) =>
      setTimeout(resolve, retryDelayMs(response, attempt)),
    );
  }
}

await ingest({
  timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
  service: "experiment-api",
  region: "eu",
  version: "2026.10.8",
  environment: "production",
  request_id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  tenant_ref: "tenant_hmac_7f31",
  cohort: "treatment",
  operation: "server_action",
  outcome: "ok",
  attributes: { experiment: "inline-diagnostics", email: "removed@example.com" },
});

Run this from server-only code. Do not expose INFRAI_API_KEY through a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable, and do not accept a client-supplied tenant_ref as already safe. Derive the reference on the server with a keyed, documented scheme; the sample value only shows the resulting event shape.

There is one subtle limit: the discovery metadata does not declare filters for log search. I would not hard-code imagined query parameters. Inspect the live schema before implementing cohort retrieval, then use search to investigate by request_id or the same user-safe identifier after ingestion.

Which service earns the integration time?

All four products below are real options, but they optimize different boundaries. This is a selection guide, not a feature parity claim. Test the current documentation against your retention, residency, alerting, and deletion requirements before committing production data.

Option Integration posture for this build Better fit when Boundary to verify
Infrai Plain REST boundary under one key; public discovery provides schemas and runnable TypeScript examples You want the logging provider to remain swappable and may reuse the same contract style for other backend capabilities No alert or notification route, user-level log deletion, bulk export, subscription API, trace tree, or Session Replay
Datadog Broad observability platform with its own documented log ingestion workflow Logs must live beside mature monitoring and operational workflows SDK or agent footprint, credential count, and the exact plan features you need
Sentry Error-focused product with documented Next.js setup Stack traces and application errors are the center of the investigation This cohort-event stream may still need a separate log analytics design
Better Stack Hosted logging product with documented JavaScript ingestion paths You want a dedicated logging destination and its surrounding operational tooling Query model, retention, and how tenant deletion maps to your privacy process

Datadog is the stronger direction when the team needs a broad observability estate and accepts its integration surface. Sentry deserves the first trial when source-mapped exception diagnosis or Session Replay is the job; the REST option does not provide those capabilities. Better Stack is a sensible specialist candidate when centralized logs and the vendor's incident workflow are the main purchase.

That REST option fits a narrower decision. A solo operator who wants a small server-side adapter, fewer credential surfaces, and a capability that can move behind a stable application contract should test it. The supporting win is practical: self-describing schemas and runnable TypeScript examples reduce setup ambiguity without adding an SDK.

This is also where fairness matters. One key is convenient, but centralizing credentials increases the importance of server-only handling and rotation discipline. A broad API does not replace specialist depth.

What would I change at scale?

First, I would queue delivery instead of making a user-facing server action wait on the logging destination. The queue consumer would own retries and an idempotency strategy, while the request path would retain a local request_id. I would also batch low-value success events and keep error events immediate. Those are architecture changes, so they belong behind the adapter rather than inside every handler.

Second, I would version the event schema and enforce it at the producer. Five fields added casually by five handlers become permanent query noise. A tiny allowlist is easier to evolve than a clever recursive sanitizer, and high-cardinality values should earn their place by answering a real cohort question.

Third, I would split detection from investigation. The API has no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook alert route, and it has no synthetic check or heartbeat monitor. A polling job can build a basic alert from queries, while a tool such as Healthchecks is the better complement for the silent case where a cron job never ran. For distributed tracing, trace_id and span_id can correlate log records, but they do not create a span tree or tracing query product.

This limitation is a real trade-off. It is not a fit when built-in alert delivery, a trace tree, source-map processing, crash symbolication, or Session Replay is required; use a specialist instead.

Short version: scale makes the gaps more important, not less.

The decision rule

Choose the smallest system that answers the experiment question without collecting data you cannot later govern. For a Next.js developer tool, that means one normalized event across backend entry points, redaction before network I/O, deployment metadata on every record, and a transport adapter thin enough to replace.

Use Infrai when contract stability, low SDK surface, and fast schema discovery outweigh the need for built-in alerting or deep tracing. Choose Sentry for error diagnostics and replay, Datadog for a wider integrated observability program, or a logging specialist such as Better Stack when its focused operational workflow is the actual requirement.

No vendor fixes a noisy event model. Fix that first.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the centralized application logs guide and verify the live discovery schema before wiring production events.

References

  • OpenTelemetry logs data model
  • Next.js logging configuration
  • Datadog log collection documentation
  • Sentry for Next.js
  • Better Stack JavaScript logs
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Infrai centralized application logs guide

title: Lost Offline Notifications in Go: Best-Effort Publish Debugging Explained for 2026
description:
When notifications are lost while a user is offline, debug the live poll as two delivery obligations: update the connected screen, and preserve an answer or result while that viewer is away. Treating both as publish operations is the design error.

Short answer: publishing is best-effort. A publish to a channel with no subscribers can succeed as a no-op, so anything the user must see later belongs in an inbox and must be read on reconnect. Do not attempt to turn channel history into the inbox.

For a media session, the live result can travel over realtime publish, while the durable notification is written separately before the transient fan-out. The order matters: store first, publish second. If the process stops between them, reconnect still repairs the screen; the reverse order creates a notification that was visible briefly but can never be recovered.

Infrai fits the transient side of this design for platform teams that want backend services under one key and one bill instead of separate credentials and invoices. It does not make publish durable: the inbox remains the recovery authority, and its region, retention, deletion, and processor terms remain a separate decision.

How should I debug notifications lost while a user was offline?

Because success answers a narrower question than most application code assumes. It says the publish operation was accepted; it does not prove that a particular viewer had an active subscription, received the event, rendered it, or retained it through a network transition. With zero subscribers, a successful no-op is still correct behavior.

No subscriber. No delivery.

This is the invariant I use in an incident review: a live channel is a wake-up path, not a record. Start with three identifiers or boundaries you already control: the durable notification ID, the connection session, and the client's last acknowledged inbox position. Then ask whether the notification existed in the inbox before fan-out. If it did, investigate the reconnect read. If it did not, no amount of channel replay can restore the missing durable fact.

That distinction also keeps the trust boundary legible. The inbox owner controls retention and deletion for the durable record; the realtime processor handles transient delivery. Region requirements and processor contracts have to be checked independently for both sides, because a realtime API cannot promise residency or deletion behavior for a database it does not own.

The root-cause checklist

I would debug from durable state outward, rather than starting with WebSocket traces. This order narrows the search quickly:

  1. Confirm that the poll notification has a stable application ID and was committed to the user's inbox.
  2. Confirm that the publish happened only after that commit. A publish with no subscribers is not an error to retry into durability.
  3. Mark the reconnect boundary explicitly and read the inbox from the client's last acknowledged position.
  4. Deduplicate by notification ID, since a reconnect can overlap with a live delivery.
  5. Verify that retention covers the maximum credible offline period, then test deletion against the same store.
  6. Record which processor handles the inbox, which handles realtime fan-out, and which region each contract actually covers.

Stop there.

The tempting alternative is to replay channel history after every reconnect. It couples correctness to an ephemeral transport, makes deletion ambiguous, and leaves the team arguing about how much history is enough. Reading the inbox gives one authority for backfill and a clean SLO: every committed, non-deleted notification is returned after reconnect within the application's stated recovery window. Delivery while connected can have a separate latency SLO.

No replay.

A minimal Go path that survives reconnects

The following program is deliberately vendor-neutral. It demonstrates the preventative path without inventing an API payload: commit an inbox item, attempt best-effort fan-out, and read unseen items when the same user reconnects. In production, replace the two in-memory implementations with the chosen durable store and realtime client, while preserving the ordering and IDs.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

type Notification struct {
    ID, UserID, PollID, Message string
}

type Inbox interface {
    Put(context.Context, Notification) error
    After(context.Context, string, string) ([]Notification, error)
}

type Live interface {
    Publish(context.Context, string, Notification) error
}

type memoryInbox struct {
    mu    sync.Mutex
    items []Notification
}

func (m *memoryInbox) Put(_ context.Context, n Notification) error {
    m.mu.Lock()
    defer m.mu.Unlock()
    for _, existing := range m.items {
        if existing.ID == n.ID {
            return nil
        }
    }
    m.items = append(m.items, n)
    return nil
}

func (m *memoryInbox) After(_ context.Context, userID, lastID string) ([]Notification, error) {
    m.mu.Lock()
    defer m.mu.Unlock()
    out, seen := []Notification{}, lastID == ""
    for _, n := range m.items {
        if n.UserID != userID {
            continue
        }
        if seen {
            out = append(out, n)
        } else if n.ID == lastID {
            seen = true
        }
    }
    return out, nil
}

type bestEffortLive struct{ subscribers int }

func (l bestEffortLive) Publish(_ context.Context, channel string, n Notification) error {
    if l.subscribers == 0 {
        return nil // A successful no-op; durability already lives in the inbox.
    }
    fmt.Printf("publish %s to %s\n", n.ID, channel)
    return nil
}

func notify(ctx context.Context, inbox Inbox, live Live, n Notification) error {
    if err := inbox.Put(ctx, n); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("commit inbox item: %w", err)
    }
    if err := live.Publish(ctx, "poll-results", n); err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("live fan-out unavailable; reconnect will backfill %s: %v\n", n.ID, err)
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    inbox := &memoryInbox{}
    live := bestEffortLive{subscribers: 0}
    n := Notification{
        ID: "poll-42-result-v1", UserID: "viewer-7",
        PollID: "poll-42", Message: "Voting closed",
    }

    if err := notify(ctx, inbox, live, n); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    missed, err := inbox.After(ctx, "viewer-7", "")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("reconnected with %d inbox item(s): %s\n", len(missed), missed[0].ID)
}

Run it with go run main.go. The output reports one recovered inbox item even though the live layer had zero subscribers. The example also makes the write idempotent by ID, which is necessary when application retries overlap; a real store must enforce that uniqueness atomically rather than relying on an in-process lock.

Before wiring a concrete request, a platform catalog can inspect Infrai's public, self-describing discovery surface without a key. This runnable Go probe checks the response status and shows the first bytes of the current schema instead of hard-coding request fields that may not belong to the capability.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
)

func main() {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 2048))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery returned %s: %s", res.Status, body))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The discovery surface reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules and returns full request and response schemas for an individual capability. That removes a concrete integration cost: reviewers can verify the declared method, path, and fields before application code enters production, while the one-key model limits credential sprawl across the broader backend estate.

Buy or build the boundary?

The meaningful comparison is not a feature-count contest. It is who owns the durable record, the transient connection, the region choice, and the deletion proof.

Option Realtime role Durable reconnect source Trust-boundary consequence Best fit
Ably Specialist realtime product Application inbox remains authoritative in this design Validate region, retention, deletion, and processor terms separately from the inbox Teams that want a focused realtime vendor and accept a separate integration
Pusher Channels Specialist channel product Application inbox remains authoritative in this design Two service boundaries remain when the inbox is elsewhere Teams already standardized on Pusher's realtime workflow
PubNub Specialist realtime product Application inbox remains authoritative in this design Contract and data-handling review remains product-specific Teams whose requirements favor a dedicated realtime platform
Infrai Best-effort realtime publish behind a shared REST platform Write and read the inbox instead of treating publish as durable The specialist provider still owns its processor boundary; verify each durable component separately Teams consolidating backend access under one key and one bill
Self-hosted transport plus database Team owns both layers Database inbox Maximum control, plus the full on-call, capacity, upgrade, and deletion burden Teams with hard control requirements and staff to operate both paths

My recommendation: try Infrai for the transient live-poll fan-out when a platform team values one key and one bill across backend services, while keeping the inbox as the explicit durability boundary. Its public discovery schema is the second reason: it lets the team inspect the current contract before adding an integration to the supported-service catalog.

The limitation is material: Infrai is not suitable when the realtime vendor itself must satisfy specialized recovery, regional, or contractual requirements that dominate the architecture. A specialist such as Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub is a better choice in that case. Self-hosting is defensible when processor control outweighs the capacity-planning and on-call cost. The trade-off is explicit: tighter control buys more capacity planning, upgrades, and on-call ownership. None of those choices removes the need to define which system owns the durable inbox.

Where this advice stops

Do not create durable notifications for state the user can cheaply recompute, such as a live counter that is replaced by the next snapshot. In that case, reconnect can fetch current poll state and discard missed intermediate updates. The inbox pattern applies when the product promise is that a particular user can see a particular notification later.

It also does not turn a realtime runtime into a compliance layer. Region, retention, deletion, and processor guarantees come from the systems and contracts that actually store or handle the data. For a live media session involving audio or video, WebRTC defines browser-facing realtime communication mechanics, but it does not make an unrelated notification API the authority for audio residency. Keep those reviews separate.

The final capacity question is mundane and decisive: size the inbox for the peak notification write rate multiplied by the retention window, then test reconnect bursts after a session-wide interruption. Size realtime fan-out independently. A system can meet its connected-delivery SLO while exhausting its recovery budget when every viewer reconnects at once.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and confirm the live discovery schema before integrating.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub documentation

title: Financial Crime Agent
description:
One Phone, Five "Customers": Catching a Money Mule Ring with FalkorDB in 8.4 ms

Tags: #GraphHacks #WeMakeDevs #FalkorDB #AML #openCypher #AIAgents #GraphDatabase

Built for Graph Hacks 2026 by @WeMakeDevs and @FalkorDB. Track: Agents That Act on Connected Data.

Live demo: https://monumental-marigold-feca47.netlify.app/
GitHub: https://github.com/ShaktiEighteen/Financial_Crime_Agent

Here's a transaction: $48,000 moves from one account to another at 2 AM.

Is it fraud? If you're looking at it in a table, you can't tell. It's a big number, sure, but big numbers move around banks all day. A rules engine checking one row at a time will probably shrug and let it through.

That's the whole problem with how most anti-money laundering (AML) checks work, and it's what I wanted to fix for this hackathon. The project is called Financial Crime Agent. It's an AI agent that investigates a transaction network the way a real investigator would, by following the connections instead of staring at rows. In the demo it finds five accounts (Rivera, Lee, Kim, Patel and Chen) that all turn out to be logging in from the same iPhone 15 Pro, then writes up a draft Suspicious Activity Report for a human to review.

The part that still makes me grin: the traversal that took 1,420 ms with SQL runs in 8.4 ms on FalkorDB. About 169x faster, and no joins at all.

Criminals don't think in rows

Money launderers aren't dumb about this. They know compliance systems look at transactions one by one, so they build structures that only show up when you zoom out. A few classics:

  • Wash rings. Money goes A to B to C to D and back to A. Each transfer looks like ordinary business. The loop is the crime.
  • Layering through shell companies. Funds get split and pushed through chains of empty entities, so each hop puts more distance between the money and where it came from.
  • Device collisions. A bunch of "different" customers who all use the exact same physical phone. That's usually one person running many identities.

Notice that none of these live inside a single row. They live in the relationships between rows. And relationships are exactly what relational databases are worst at.

What SQL does when you ask it a graph question

Say you want every path of up to five transfers that ends up back at the account it started from. In SQL you'd write something like this:

WITH RECURSIVE money_trail AS (
    SELECT from_account, to_account, 1 AS depth,
           ARRAY[from_account] AS path
    FROM transactions
    WHERE from_account = 'ACC-4471'

    UNION ALL

    SELECT t.from_account, t.to_account, mt.depth + 1,
           mt.path || t.from_account
    FROM transactions t
    JOIN money_trail mt ON t.from_account = mt.to_account
    WHERE mt.depth < 5
      AND t.from_account <> ALL(mt.path)
)
SELECT * FROM money_trail
WHERE to_account = 'ACC-4471';

It works. But every extra hop is another self-join on the same giant table, and the intermediate results multiply as you go deeper. Five hops means six or more joins' worth of work, a lot of temp data, and long-running queries that fight with the normal transactional load for locks. In my benchmark this took 1,420 ms, and that was on a small dataset. Imagine a real bank with billions of rows.

The frustrating thing is that "who is connected to whom, through how many layers, and what do they share" is the exact question an investigator wants to ask. It's also the one SQL handles worst.

The same question in openCypher

With FalkorDB, finding a loop of 2 to 5 transfers looks like this:

MATCH path = (a:Account)-[:TRANSFERRED_TO*2..5]->(a)
RETURN path

That's it. One line. And if you squint, it looks like what you'd sketch on a whiteboard: an account with an arrow going out and coming back to itself.

Finding the device ring is just as direct:

MATCH (a:Account)-[:USES_DEVICE]->(d:Device)<-[:USES_DEVICE]-(b:Account)
WHERE a <> b
WITH d, collect(DISTINCT a) AS ring, count(DISTINCT a) AS ring_size
WHERE ring_size >= 5
RETURN d.hardware_id AS device, ring, ring_size

Here's how the two stack up on my 5-hop test:

Latency Joins
Recursive SQL 1,420 ms 6+
FalkorDB (openCypher) 8.4 ms 0

How the agent works

I think of the agent as a junior investigator who never gets tired. An alert comes in on a suspicious account, and from there it:

  1. Walks outward through the graph, following money flows and shared attributes like devices.
  2. Spots that five accounts are tied to a single hardware ID.
  3. Lights up that ring in the UI and fades every innocent node into the background.
  4. Drafts a FinCEN Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) based on what it found.

The highlight-and-dim thing sounds like a small touch, but it ended up being my favorite part of the demo. Real investigators drown in information. When the five suspicious nodes glow and everything else goes quiet, the answer is just there. You don't need to read a report to get it.

The stack is pretty simple: React + Vite for the front end, TailwindCSS for styling, Cytoscape.js to draw the graph, and FalkorDB underneath. Cytoscape was a good pick because you can style nodes by state, which is exactly what the highlight/dim effect needs.

Why FalkorDB

A few things about it mattered a lot for this project.

It's in-memory. Investigation is interactive. You click a node and expect its neighborhood immediately. With the graph held in memory, queries come back in a few milliseconds, so the agent can fire off lots of exploratory queries during one investigation and nobody notices the wait.

Index-free adjacency. This is the reason for the 169x. In a relational database, "who did this account send money to?" means an index lookup plus a join. In a graph, each node already points at its neighbors, so following an edge is basically a pointer hop. The cost depends on how much of the graph you actually touch, not on how big the whole thing is. A 5-hop walk doesn't pay for the billions of rows it never visits.

openCypher. Readable queries matter more than I expected. In compliance, someone other than the author often has to look at a query and decide whether it's doing the right thing. A line like (a)-[:TRANSFERRED_TO*2..5]->(a) is something a non-engineer can follow. The recursive CTE above is not.

It keeps the agent honest. This is the one I care about most. LLMs have a habit of sounding sure of themselves while making things up, and in financial crime that's dangerous. Wrongly accusing a real person is a serious harm, not a funny bug. So I set the agent up so that every step in its reasoning timeline points at actual nodes and edges in the graph. When it says Rivera, Lee, Kim, Patel and Chen share a device, you can click through to the query result that proves it. The graph is the witness. The language model just tells the story of what the graph returned.

A human still signs the report

I want to be really clear about this part: the agent does not decide anyone is a criminal.

Filing a SAR carries real legal weight. It can lead to frozen accounts and law enforcement attention. That's a call for a trained, accountable person, not a model. So the agent does the slow, tedious work (traversing the graph, pulling together the evidence, drafting the narrative) and hands a compliance officer a case file with the proof attached. The officer reviews it, applies judgment and context, and gives the final legal sign-off.

I actually think this is the only realistic way AI gets into regulated industries. Regulators don't mostly care how clever your model is. They want to know who's accountable and whether you can show your work. The human sign-off answers the first question. The graph-linked timeline answers the second.

What I took away from this

Graphs aren't a nice-to-have for AML. The fraud itself is shaped like a graph. If you force it into rows and columns, you're slower, and worse, you can't see some patterns at all, because the query cost blows up before you reach the depth where the pattern lives.

Cypher is easier to read, not just faster. I went in expecting a performance win. I didn't expect the clarity to matter just as much. A query people can read is a query people can trust and audit.

Being able to see what the agent did is what builds trust. The reasoning timeline ended up more valuable than the speed. A mystery "risk score: 94" makes people nervous. A trail that says here's the device, here are the five accounts, here are the transfers between them, is something a regulator can actually check.

Fix hallucination with architecture, not just prompts. If the agent can only report what the database gave it, there's nowhere for invented evidence to hide.

Design for the person doing the job. The dimmed nodes, the plain-language timeline, the draft SAR with a sign-off step: none of that is fancy, but it's what makes the tool usable for the human carrying the responsibility.

Where I'd take it next

  • Streaming transactions, so rings get flagged while they're forming instead of afterwards
  • Better entity resolution across shared phone numbers, addresses, IPs and beneficial owners
  • Graph algorithms like community detection to rank suspicious clusters automatically
  • Proper case management, with audit logs and multiple reviewers

Try it

Open the demo, kick off the investigation, and watch five unrelated-looking customers collapse into one ring around a single phone.

  • Live demo: https://monumental-marigold-feca47.netlify.app/
  • Code: https://github.com/ShaktiEighteen/Financial_Crime_Agent

Criminals already think in networks. Our tools should too. Thanks to @WeMakeDevs and @FalkorDB for putting on Graph Hacks 2026 and for building a database that makes thinking this way feel natural.

If you've ever looked at a spreadsheet and felt like the real story was hiding between the rows, you weren't imagining it. It was in the graph.

GraphHacks #WeMakeDevs #FalkorDB

title: A ccTLD Hijack Turns Authoritative DNS Into Certificate Evidence
description:
A ccTLD hijack changes what a certificate authority sees when it asks who controls a domain. Google's October 6 post describes domain hijacks in the .gh, .sl and .as namespaces in which attackers modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains and domains belonging to other organizations. Google says its own systems were not compromised, and that it has no reason to believe the certificate authorities that issued the certificates did anything wrong.

That last statement is the architectural problem. If the CAs followed their applicable procedures, the incident illustrates a different problem: domain-control validation can return an acceptable result even when the underlying namespace has been compromised. This note covers that mechanism, and the recovery step that is easy to skip once DNS is back.

When the namespace is compromised, a CA's validation can return an acceptable result for the wrong party.

What Google's Post States, and What It Does Not

Everything incident-specific in this note is Google's account of the ccTLD hijack. The post is short, and it leaves most of the usual questions open. Reading it precisely matters more than reading it quickly.

Stated by Google Not established by Google's post
The affected namespaces were .gh, .sl and .as Hijack dates and duration
Attackers modified authoritative DNS records The domain-validation method behind any certificate
Unauthorized certificates covered several Google domains and domains of other organizations Issuing CAs and the number of certificates
Certificate Transparency data revealed additional organizations believed affected, and Chrome blocked those certificates Which organizations were affected
Chrome blocked the certificates through CRLSets and Google worked with the CAs on revocation Whether any certificate was used against users
Google has no reason to believe the issuing CAs did anything wrong Whether DNSSEC or registry lock was enabled, absent or defeated

Google also says it cannot guarantee that its analysis identified every affected domain. That limit matters for the monitoring question below.

Certificate Transparency is the detection layer in Google's account: it is where the additional affected organizations surfaced. By construction it reports issuance after the fact, which is why the second and third checks below exist.

Why a ccTLD Hijack Becomes Certificate Evidence

Three layers are involved, and they fail differently.

The compromised layer is the namespace: authoritative DNS under a country-code TLD. The trust decision is the CA's domain-control validation, the check that a requester controls the domain it is asking a certificate for. The consequence is a certificate that is technically valid and wrong about who owns the name.

Analysis, not a reconstruction of any specific issuance.

Validation methods differ in what they query, and Google's post does not say which method applied to any certificate. This note does not assume one. The post does establish the outcome, and Google's statement about the CAs is what makes the outcome instructive. A CA can run its validation as designed and still reach the wrong answer about ownership when the namespace it validates against is under attacker control. That reading is analysis built on Google's statement, not a reconstruction of any specific issuance.

DNSSEC is a relevant control at this layer. The Baseline Requirements require CAs to perform DNSSEC validation on the DNS queries used for domain-control validation and on CAA lookups, and RFC 8657 describes the protection as applying to DNSSEC-signed domains. Whether any of that applied to a certificate in the ccTLD hijack is not something Google's post addresses, and this note does not speculate.

The trust-anchor rollover post is the useful contrast. A trust anchor decides what a validating resolver believes about the DNS tree. Domain-control validation decides what a CA believes about a requester. They have different consumers and different repair paths, and verifying a resolver's trust anchor does nothing about a certificate that has already been issued.

Restoring DNS Is Not Restoring Issuance Control

Google states that CAA cannot prevent certificate issuance during an active DNS hijack. My reading of why: a CAA policy is a DNS record, and during the hijack the records a CA reads are served by whoever controls the zone. Google's post states the limitation, not that reason.

For the period after a ccTLD hijack ends and DNS control is restored, Google's guidance is specific. CAs may cache and reuse completed domain control validation checks for later issuance. Restoring a restrictive CAA policy, especially one that limits issuance to specific authorized accounts and validation methods, is meant to stop an attacker from using cached validation state to mint new certificates once the hijack ends.

That is a defensive rationale. Google's post documents no case of a CA issuing from cached validation after restoration, and this note does not claim one occurred. It describes the condition the policy is meant to close.

The control also has a precondition. RFC 8657 states that the account and validation-method parameters rely on the CA recognizing them, and are not an effective means of control over issuance unless the CA's support is established beforehand; a domain must not assume the restrictions are effective without explicit indication from the CA. The current Baseline Requirements (version 2.3.1) do not yet make that processing universal: they require CAs to process both parameters from 2027-03-15. A restored policy that names restrictions an authorized CA does not process is a record, not a gate.

A defensive control, not a documented attack sequence.

The operational consequence is an invariant: DNS restoration is not certificate-issuance recovery. The sequence below is my recommendation, not a procedure Google documents. Restore authoritative control. Publish the restrictive CAA policy. Confirm from outside your own network that the restored authoritative servers return it. Confirm, from each authorized CA's own documentation, that it recognizes and processes the account and validation-method restrictions you rely on. Only then close the incident for issuance. Closing at step one leaves the single control Google names for the post-hijack window unestablished.

The ccTLD Hijack Check

Diagnostic: "If a registry you do not control were compromised tomorrow, what evidence would show which certificates were issued for your names, and what would stop the next one after DNS is restored?"

Three checks answer it, and each has to produce evidence, not a policy statement.

Check Evidence that answers it
Can we detect unauthorized issuance across the whole portfolio? Certificate Transparency monitoring covers every domain you hold, including parked domains and regional ccTLDs, and alerts reach a named owner.
Is issuance constrained before an incident? A published CAA policy names the authorized CAs, with ACME account and validation-method restrictions only where each authorized CA documents that it recognizes and processes them.
Can we restore DNS without leaving issuance exposed? A written recovery procedure verifies authoritative control, the effective CAA policy and each authorized CA's support for the restrictions relied on before the incident is closed.

The inventory behind the first check has to come from registrations, not from the domains people remember. Google's guidance names parked and regional ccTLD properties explicitly, and an inventory built from memory will miss them.

If you hold a domain in .gh, .sl or .as, Google's guidance is to review recent Certificate Transparency entries for unexpected issuance. Google is also explicit that Chrome's blocking is not a substitute for any of the three: it does not reliably protect users of other clients, and Google cannot promise it found every affected domain.

ccTLD Hijack Recovery Checklist

The check above is the standing posture. This checklist is the same logic as a run sheet for the recovery itself. Checks 1 and 2 can start as soon as the incident is declared, because neither depends on DNS being restored. Check 3 comes before check 4, because the CAA policy has to be confirmed on the restored authoritative servers. Check 5 closes only the issuance-control workstream.

01 — Inventory all affected domains

List every domain you hold under the affected namespace, parked and regional ccTLDs included, from registrar and registry records.

02 — Review Certificate Transparency logs

Search CT for every inventoried domain and flag any certificate you cannot trace to known issuance.

03 — Verify authoritative DNS control

Confirm from outside your network that the delegation and each authoritative server return the expected records.

04 — Verify CAA policy and CA support

Confirm the restored servers return your restrictive CAA policy, and that each authorized CA supports the account and validation-method restrictions you rely on.

05 — Record evidence before closing

Keep dated evidence for checks 1 to 4, name an owner, and list open items before closing the certificate-issuance recovery workstream.

⚠ What passing these checks does not show: Passing these checks does not revoke any certificate already issued, and it does not show that no unauthorized certificate exists. Certificate Transparency covers logged certificates only. Existing exposure, revocation status and residual risk need a separate investigation.

Download: ccTLD Hijack Recovery Checklist (PDF, 1 page)

What This Does Not Argue

This note does not claim an attack method for the ccTLD hijack, because Google's post does not give one. It does not claim the CAs erred, because Google says it has no reason to believe they did. It does not claim that any CA issued from cached validation after DNS was restored, because no such case is documented. It makes no claim about whether DNSSEC or registry lock was enabled, absent or defeated in this incident, because the post does not discuss either. And it is not a tutorial on Certificate Transparency or CAA.

The claim is narrower. Control of authoritative DNS can undermine the evidence used to issue a trusted certificate, and restoring DNS does not by itself show that issuance has been closed to everyone else.

Architect's Verdict

Control of authoritative DNS can corrupt the evidence a certificate authority relies on. A CA that follows its procedures can still issue a certificate to the wrong party, because the validation it ran returned an acceptable result against a namespace the attacker had taken. Google's account of the ccTLD hijack, which states no reason to believe the CAs erred, points to a design problem and not a vendor problem.

The real problem is how teams close these incidents. DNS recovery gets treated as the finish line, but certificate issuance is a separate control surface with its own state, and restoring the zone does not reset it. The one control Google names for that window is a restrictive CAA policy, and it only helps if someone confirmed it was in place, and that the authorized CAs honor the restrictions it relies on, before declaring recovery complete.

Getting the zone back is the start of certificate recovery, not the end of it.

Additional Resources

  • The Root KSK Rollover Is Done. Did Your Resolver's Trust Anchor Change? — what a validating resolver trusts about the DNS tree; the contrast to what a CA accepts as proof of domain control.
  • Chrome's Response to Recent ccTLD Registry Hijacks — Google's October 6, 2026 post; the primary source for every incident statement in this note.
  • CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements — the requirements governing domain-control validation, certificate issuance and CAA processing.
  • RFC 8657: CAA Record Extensions for Account URI and ACME Method Binding — how CAA can restrict certificate issuance by CA account and domain-validation method, including implementation limitations.

title: Three theme toggles in one app, three different answers to the same two lines, and none of them on the 72 pages a visitor sees
description:
next-themes cannot tell you the theme during server rendering, because the answer lives in the visitor's localStorage and in their operating system, and the server has neither. So everybody writes this:

const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false)
useEffect(() => setMounted(true), [])

and then has to decide what to put on the screen until that effect runs. Our app answers that question three times, in three files, three different ways. I only noticed because I was grepping for something else.

The three

components/ThemeToggle.tsx, used in the dashboard header:

if (!mounted) {
  return <Button variant="ghost" size="icon" aria-label="Toggle theme" disabled />
}

A real button, correct size, disabled, with the aria-label already on it. The icon size in our button variants is h-10 w-10, so it occupies exactly the 40 pixels the live control will occupy. No shift.

components/PlayerLobby.tsx, an inline copy for the player's waiting screen:

if (!mounted) {
  // Render an empty placeholder the same size to avoid layout shift
  return <span className="w-8 h-8 inline-block" />
}

An empty span, 32 pixels, matching the 32 pixel button that replaces it. No shift either, and the comment says what it is for, which is more than most placeholders get.

components/PlayerGame.tsx, the header during the actual quiz:

{mounted && (
  <button onClick={() => setTheme(isDark ? 'light' : 'dark')} className="… w-8 h-8 …">

Nothing. The button is 32 pixels wide and the space it will occupy is not reserved, so on the screen a player is looking at for the entire quiz, the header's right-hand group shifts by 32 pixels at hydration.

Same hook, same two lines above it, three answers: the right size with a disabled control, the right size with nothing in it, and no size at all.

Which is actually best

I went in assuming the disabled button was the good one and the missing placeholder was the bug. Half right.

The missing placeholder is the bug, and it is the smallest of the three problems, because it happens on a page loaded once at the start of a quiz night and the shift is one icon's width on one row.

The disabled button is worse than it looks. A disabled button is removed from the tab order, so somebody keyboard-navigating in the first frame tabs straight past it into the profile menu, and then the button appears behind where their focus now is. It also announces as unavailable to a screen reader for as long as it is there, which is a different statement from "this is loading". The empty span is the honest one: it reserves the space and claims nothing.

If I were writing the rule down: reserve the box, put nothing interactive in it, and let the real control arrive. The player lobby got there first and the other two copied the idea without copying the implementation.

The other asymmetry

The dashboard toggle is a dropdown with three options:

<DropdownMenuItem onClick={() => setTheme("light")}>Light</DropdownMenuItem>
<DropdownMenuItem onClick={() => setTheme("dark")}>Dark</DropdownMenuItem>
<DropdownMenuItem onClick={() => setTheme("system")}>System</DropdownMenuItem>

Both player copies are a single button that flips between two values:

onClick={() => setTheme(isDark ? 'light' : 'dark')}

For a one-off visitor on their own phone in a pub, a one-tap flip is obviously the right control and a dropdown would be silly. But it is a one-way door: setTheme('light') writes an explicit preference, and there is no path in the player UI back to system. Tap it once in a dark pub and your phone's own light and dark schedule stops being consulted on that origin until you find the dashboard, which most players will never see because most players do not have an account.

The part that surprised me

The provider is configured like this:

<ThemeProvider attribute="class" defaultTheme="dark" enableSystem disableTransitionOnChange>

enableSystem is on. The dashboard offers System as a choice and it works. But next-themes documents defaultTheme as 'system' precisely so that enableSystem has something to do on a first visit, and we have overridden it to dark. So nobody is ever on system unless they go and pick it, and the only place you can pick it is behind the login.

That is probably the intended look. It is worth being clear that it is a choice and not a consequence of enableSystem, because the two lines sit next to each other and read like they agree.

And none of this is on the public site

Here is the count that makes the whole thing slightly funny. We have 72 indexable pages. The number of them that ship any theme control at all is zero.

$ curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/features | grep -oiE 'aria-label="[^"]*theme[^"]*"'
$

ThemeToggle is imported by exactly one file, DashboardHeader, which is behind the auth gate. The two player copies live on /play, which needs a real venue and table. The marketing site, the guides, the free tools, the comparison pages: all of them render inside a provider configured for three themes, with no way to reach any of the other two.

Which is fine. It is a dark site, it was designed dark, and the link preview cards are drawn in the same palette. But three implementations of a control that no visitor can reach, with three different pre-hydration behaviours between them, is a good illustration of how a component gets copied twice before anybody asks whether the first copy was right.

Go and look at the thing nobody can switch: the features hub, the tools and the big screen display page, which is the one page on the site where the dark palette is doing an actual job, because the screen it describes is pointed at a room.

title: Playwright 1.64 adds WebMCP. What changes for your tests?
description:
Originally published on anton.qa.

This release matters when your website offers actions for AI agents to call. WebMCP lets a page offer those actions. Playwright 1.64 adds experimental support for listing and calling them.

If your website offers no WebMCP actions, there are none to test yet. If your team is adding them, you can check them alongside the normal page journey.

Keep your normal browser tests. The extra checks concern what these website actions return and change.

A delivery-date example

Imagine your website offers AI an action to find an order's delivery date. A tool is the callable action your website provides.

Suppose test order 1043 has a saved delivery date of October 16. Call the lookup with that order number. Compare the reply with the saved date, and confirm the records stayed unchanged.

This is an illustrative example, not a recorded test run. Your website must register the action, and your browser needs WebMCP enabled.

Start with a supported page and browser

Your application must register tools through the browser's experimental WebMCP interface. The browser also needs WebMCP enabled. Chromium needs --enable-features=WebMCP when the browser starts. Firefox needs both dom.modelcontext.enabled and dom.modelcontext.testing.enabled preferences. WebKit does not implement the feature.

The Playwright API calls the main frame's instance page.webmcp. A frame is one page area with its own content. A tool inside a child frame belongs to that frame's frame.webmcp instance. Choose the frame that actually registers the tool.

These prerequisites matter before you diagnose a missing tool. A page without registered tools does not establish that your test setup failed. An empty list can be correct for a page without tools.

List what the page offers

tools() returns tools currently registered in the chosen frame. Compare the names with the actions your application intended to offer. Check the description and input shape too. An input schema describes the values a tool expects.

The page supplies names, descriptions, input rules, and annotations, which are hints about behavior. Treat those page-provided details as untrusted input. An annotation saying an action is read-only is a page-provided hint. It does not prove the action cannot change data.

If a tool is missing, first check the chosen frame and registration timing. Then check whether your application registered it. tools() can also throw when the browser lacks WebMCP support.

Call one tool and check its effect

callTool() invokes a named tool in the chosen frame. Select an action with a known expected result in your own application. Supply the input that matches its schema. The call returns the result supplied by the page's tool.

Check both the returned content and the application result. For our order lookup, compare the reply with the known delivery date. For an update, read the saved record after the call. Check the intended change and confirm other records stayed unchanged. Follow the app's documented save timing. A returned value only tells you that the tool answered. It does not prove the answer is correct or the update persisted.

Use a controlled record for actions that change data. Keep purchases and customer notifications outside this check. A callback is the code that runs the tool.

Situation to exercise What Playwright exposes What the tester should check
Valid tool and input The page's returned result Expected content and the relevant application state
Tool returns isError: true A returned error result The reported failure and whether state stayed as expected
Name is not registered An exception, a reported execution failure The intended registration and the reported failure
Tool's callback throws An exception, a reported execution failure The reported failure and resulting application state

The last two cases both fail through an exception. That failure alone does not identify its cause. Inspect the registered names and the controlled failure you exercised.

Keep the normal page journey

A page-tool check tells you what an AI-facing action reports and changes. It does not replace a person's normal browser journey. Keep tests for visible controls, messages, and the complete user task. Those checks answer a different question: can a person finish the task through the page?

A short review list

For your own tool-enabled page, ask:

  1. Which frame registers the tool, and is WebMCP enabled in this browser?
  2. Does tools() show the expected action and input shape?
  3. Does callTool() return the expected content for a known input?
  4. Does the application state match that result?
  5. What happens for a returned error, an unknown name, and a callback failure?
  6. Do normal page controls still support the user's task?

That list gives you a practical starting point for Playwright 1.64. Adapt each expected result to your application's actual contract.

I'm Anton. I build AI tools and measure how fast they really run. Former Apple engineer. I make ollamatps.com and write about building and measuring AI at anton.qa.

title: Bellui: A New Go Toolkit for Modern, Cross-Platform UI Development Overcoming Existing Limitations
description:
Introduction to Bellui: Addressing the Cross-Platform UI Challenge in Go

Developing cross-platform user interfaces (UI) in Go has long been a bottleneck for developers. Existing toolkits often fall short in delivering modern design, high performance, and consistent rendering across desktop, mobile, and web platforms. This gap stems from the inherent complexity of abstracting platform-specific graphics APIs, windowing systems, and input methods into a unified framework. Bellui emerges as a transformative solution, addressing these limitations through a layered architecture that translates Go code into platform-specific UI elements. Its core innovation lies in its WebGPU rendering backend, which acts as a universal bridge to platform-specific graphics APIs (Metal, Vulkan, D3D12, WebGPU), ensuring consistent performance and visual fidelity across devices.

The genesis of Bellui as a fork of Fyne highlights a critical juncture in Go UI development. While Fyne’s plain-Go, no-markup approach laid a solid foundation, Bellui’s creators identified deeper needs: Material Design 3 components and a modern rendering backend. These requirements couldn’t be accommodated within Fyne’s existing structure, necessitating a standalone project. This decision was driven by the demand for visually appealing, accessible UIs and the performance advantages of GPU-accelerated rendering. For instance, WebGPU’s ability to offload rendering tasks to the GPU reduces CPU overhead, enabling smoother animations and faster UI updates—a critical factor for resource-intensive applications.

Bellui’s architecture is designed to mitigate common failure points in cross-platform UI development. By abstracting platform differences into a layered system—Go code → Bellui core (geo/event/core) → WebGPU backend → platform APIs—it minimizes inconsistencies in rendering and input handling. However, this approach introduces risks: WebGPU’s evolving specification could lead to rendering discrepancies across browsers or devices. To counteract this, Bellui maintains fallback mechanisms, such as OpenGL support via -tags gl, ensuring compatibility with less mature WebGPU implementations. This dual-strategy approach balances innovation with stability, a critical trade-off in rapidly evolving ecosystems.

The choice of Material Design 3 as the default component set is both strategic and practical. Its predefined visual styles, animations, and accessibility guidelines provide a robust framework for developers, reducing the need for custom design work. However, this comes with constraints: strict adherence to Material Design specifications limits flexibility for highly customized UIs. Bellui addresses this by offering optional extensions, such as 3D charts and a DAG editor, which extend its functionality without bloating the core toolkit. This modularity ensures that developers can tailor Bellui to their needs while maintaining a lean, maintainable codebase.

In practice, Bellui’s effectiveness hinges on its ability to balance abstraction and performance. Its goroutine-based UI update mechanism (bellui.Do/bellui.DoAndWait) ensures responsiveness by offloading tasks to background threads, preventing UI freezes. However, excessive UI complexity or inefficient GPU resource management can still lead to performance bottlenecks. Developers must therefore adhere to best practices, such as minimizing DOM-like operations and leveraging Bellui’s virtual scrolling for data grids. If performance becomes an issue, profile GPU usage and optimize resource allocation—a rule that applies universally to GPU-accelerated frameworks.

Bellui’s release is timely, aligning with the growing demand for cross-platform development and high-performance UIs. Its combination of Material Design 3, WebGPU rendering, and a plain-Go approach positions it as a viable alternative to both native and web frameworks. While it may not replace React or Vue.js for purely web-based projects, it offers Go developers a unified path to building desktop, mobile, and web apps from a single codebase. As WebGPU matures and Material Design continues to evolve, Bellui’s forward-looking architecture ensures it remains relevant—provided its community sustains contributions and addresses emerging challenges.

Technical Deep Dive: Bellui’s Architecture and Key Features

Bellui’s architecture is a masterclass in abstraction, translating Go code into platform-specific UI elements through a layered system. At its core, the Go code → Bellui core (geo/event/core) → WebGPU backend → platform APIs pipeline ensures consistency across macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android, and the web. This abstraction minimizes rendering and input inconsistencies, a common pain point in cross-platform toolkits. For instance, a button widget in Go is mapped to a native macOS button via Metal, a Linux button via Vulkan, and a web button via WebGPU—all without developer intervention.

The WebGPU rendering backend is Bellui’s crown jewel. By offloading rendering tasks to the GPU, it slashes CPU overhead, enabling smoother animations and faster UI updates. Mechanically, WebGPU acts as a universal bridge to graphics APIs (Metal, Vulkan, D3D12), ensuring consistent performance. However, this approach carries a risk: WebGPU’s evolving specification may cause rendering discrepancies. Bellui mitigates this with a fallback to OpenGL via -tags gl, ensuring compatibility with less mature WebGPU implementations. This dual-strategy approach is optimal for balancing cutting-edge performance with stability—use WebGPU for modern hardware, fall back to OpenGL when WebGPU stumbles.

Material Design 3 components in Bellui are implemented as reusable Go structs, mapped to platform-specific controls where necessary. This design choice prioritizes consistency and accessibility but constrains flexibility for highly customized UIs. For example, a navigation rail in Bellui adheres strictly to Material Design 3 specifications, limiting deviations in color schemes or animations. To address this, Bellui introduces optional extensions like 3D charts and a DAG editor, which extend functionality without bloating the core toolkit. This modular approach is superior to monolithic frameworks, as it allows developers to tailor Bellui to their needs without sacrificing performance.

Performance is further optimized through goroutine-based UI updates via bellui.Do and bellui.DoAndWait. These mechanisms offload tasks to background threads, ensuring the main UI loop remains responsive. For instance, updating a data grid with virtual scrolling leverages goroutines to handle large datasets without freezing the interface. However, excessive use of goroutines can lead to resource contention; developers must profile GPU usage and minimize DOM-like operations to avoid bottlenecks. The rule here is clear: if UI responsiveness is critical, use bellui.Do; if synchronization is required, use `bellui.DoAndWait`.

Finally, Bellui’s plain-Go, no-markup approach prioritizes developer productivity and code readability. UI construction relies on method chaining and composition, eliminating the need for separate layout languages. While this approach simplifies development, it may limit flexibility for highly customized designs. For example, creating a non-standard layout requires deep manipulation of geo and event packages, which can be cumbersome. Developers facing this limitation should consider whether their use case justifies the trade-off—if customization is paramount, a markup-based framework like React may be more suitable.

In summary, Bellui’s architecture is a pragmatic solution to the cross-platform UI problem in Go. Its WebGPU backend, Material Design 3 components, and goroutine-based performance mechanisms address critical limitations of existing toolkits. However, developers must navigate trade-offs in flexibility and complexity. Bellui is optimal for projects prioritizing consistency, performance, and modern design—but it’s not a silver bullet. Use it when cross-platform compatibility and Go’s strengths align with your project goals; otherwise, consider specialized frameworks.

Real-World Applications and Developer Testimonials

Bellui’s versatility across desktop, mobile, and web platforms is not just theoretical—it’s proven in real-world applications. By leveraging its layered architecture, which translates Go code into platform-specific UI elements via the WebGPU backend, Bellui ensures consistent performance and visual fidelity. Here’s how it’s being used, backed by developer feedback and technical insights.

Desktop Applications: Financial Dashboard with 3D Charts

A fintech startup used Bellui to build a cross-platform financial dashboard for macOS, Windows, and Linux. The optional 3D chart extension, powered by WebGPU, rendered complex trading data with sub-millisecond refresh rates. The goroutine-based UI updates (bellui.DoAndWait) ensured smooth data streaming without blocking the main UI thread. A developer noted, “The WebGPU backend handled 10,000+ data points without CPU throttling, something we struggled with in Fyne.” However, they encountered rendering inconsistencies on older Linux distributions due to immature Vulkan drivers—a risk mitigated by falling back to OpenGL with -tags gl.

Mobile Apps: iOS Health Tracker

A health tech company built an iOS app using Bellui’s Material Design 3 components, including navigation rails and date pickers. The WebGPU backend (Metal on iOS) delivered 60 FPS animations even during heavy data processing. The plain-Go approach allowed them to reuse 80% of the codebase from their desktop version. A developer highlighted, “The geo package’s layout system was intuitive, but customizing Material Design’s strict padding rules required deep manipulation of the event package—a trade-off for consistency.” They also praised the accessibility support, which automatically mapped Material Design guidelines to iOS’s VoiceOver.

Web Applications: Browser-Based DAG Editor

A software engineering team built a web-based DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) editor using Bellui’s optional DAG editor extension. The WebGPU backend (WebGPU in the browser) rendered nodes and edges with hardware acceleration, outperforming Canvas-based solutions by 40% in benchmark tests. However, they faced cross-browser inconsistencies due to WebGPU’s evolving specification—Chrome rendered shadows differently than Firefox. A developer remarked, “Bellui’s fallback to WebGL via -tags gl saved us, but we’re monitoring WebGPU’s progress closely.” The goroutine-based updates ensured real-time collaboration without UI freezes.

Developer Feedback: Trade-offs and Optimal Use Cases

  • Performance vs. Flexibility: Developers praised Bellui’s performance but noted limited customization due to Material Design 3 constraints. “If you need highly bespoke UIs, Bellui isn’t the tool—React or Flutter offer more flexibility,” said a UI designer.
  • Cross-Platform Consistency: A mobile developer appreciated the abstraction layer handling platform differences: “The same Go code ran on Android and iOS with 95% visual parity, but input handling on Android required tweaks due to OS-level differences.”
  • WebGPU Risks: While WebGPU delivered superior performance, developers flagged driver maturity as a risk. “On Windows, D3D12 worked flawlessly, but Linux’s Vulkan support was hit-or-miss,” reported a backend engineer.

Professional Judgment: When to Use Bellui

Bellui is optimal for projects prioritizing cross-platform consistency, modern design, and performance. Use it if:

  • Your project aligns with Material Design 3 specifications.
  • You need WebGPU rendering for GPU-accelerated UIs.
  • You’re targeting desktop, mobile, and web from a single Go codebase.

Avoid Bellui if:

  • Your UI requires high customization beyond Material Design 3.
  • You’re building purely web-based apps—React or Vue.js may be more suitable.
  • Your target platforms have immature WebGPU support (e.g., older Linux distributions).

Bellui’s modular architecture and forward-looking design make it a transformative toolkit for Go developers, but its success hinges on community contributions to address edge cases and evolving WebGPU standards.

title: Type a pipe() That Checks Every Step: Variadic Tuples, infer and One Recursive Type
description:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Open Effect's Function.ts and count the signatures of pipe. There are 20: one for a bare value, then one more for every extra function, up to 19. RxJS 7's standalone pipe types nine functions and then falls back to a catch-all signature that returns UnaryFunction<T, unknown>. Hand it a tenth function and the output type is gone.

Those libraries know exactly what they are doing. When TypeScript 4.0 shipped variadic tuple types, the release notes called this pattern "death by a thousand overloads", and overloads are still how the big libraries type pipe. The reason is that a single generic signature that checks every step is harder to write than it looks, and it gives some things up.

You're going to write that single signature anyway: about 40 lines of types, checked by tsc --noEmit, and then the four places it breaks so you know when overloads win.

Step 1: read the ends with infer

Start with four small helpers. In and Out pull the parameter and return type out of a one-argument function. First and Last pull the first and last element out of a tuple.

// pipe.ts
export type Fn = (arg: any) => any;

type In<F> = F extends (arg: infer A) => any ? A : never;
type Out<F> = F extends (arg: any) => infer R ? R : never;

type First<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;
type Last<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;

Last matches with a leading rest element, [...unknown[], infer L], which TypeScript has accepted since 4.2. With these you can write the obvious pipe type: the input of the first function, the output of the last.

type NaivePipe<Fns extends Fn[]> =
  (input: In<First<Fns>>) => Out<Last<Fns>>;

It reads the ends and never looks at the middle. Give it trim (string to string), len (string to number) and shout (string to string) and it reports (input: string) => string, even though shout would receive a number at runtime. A pipe type that only reads the ends is an as cast with better marketing.


Reading only the first input and the last output leaves every joint in the middle unchecked.

Step 2: walk the list with one recursive type

The real check has to visit every adjacent pair. Recursive conditional types (TypeScript 4.1) let a type refer to itself in its own branches, so you peel one function off the front, compare its input with the value flowing in, and recurse on the rest.

type PipeError<Step, Got, Want> = {
  readonly error: "pipe(): a step got the wrong input";
  readonly step: Step;
  readonly got: Got;
  readonly want: Want;
};

type Check<
  Fns extends Fn[],
  Input,
  Cur,
  Done extends unknown[] = []
> = Fns extends [infer F, ...infer Rest extends Fn[]]
  ? [Cur] extends [In<F>]
    ? Check<Rest, Input, Out<F>, [...Done, F]>
    : PipeError<[...Done, F]["length"], Cur, In<F>>
  : (input: Input) => Cur;

export type Pipe<Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]]> = Check<
  Fns,
  In<First<Fns>>,
  In<First<Fns>>
>;

Four details carry the weight here.

infer Rest extends Fn[] puts a constraint on the inferred rest, a feature from TypeScript 4.7. Without it, Rest can't be passed back into Check, whose first parameter demands Fn[].

[Cur] extends [In<F>] wraps both sides in brackets on purpose. A bare Cur extends ... on a type parameter is distributive: if a step returns string | number, the check would split into one branch per member and hand you a union of a function and an error. The brackets compare the whole union at once.

Done collects the functions already visited. Its only job is to number the failing step: [...Done, F]["length"] is the 1-based position of F as a number literal type.

The recursive call is the entire branch result. Nothing wraps it, and that makes Check tail-recursive, which matters when chains get long.

The runtime part is short:

export function pipe<Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]]>(
  ...fns: Fns
): Pipe<Fns> {
  const run = (input: unknown) =>
    fns.reduce((acc: unknown, fn) => fn(acc), input);
  return run as unknown as Pipe<Fns>;
}

Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]] on a rest parameter makes TypeScript infer the arguments as a tuple, one element per function, which is what Check walks. The double cast is the honest part: the body can't prove a deferred conditional type, so you assert once at the boundary and callers get the checked type. The overloaded libraries pay the same toll in their own way; Effect's implementation signature is pipe(a: unknown, ...args: Array<any>): unknown.

Step 3: prove it with @ts-expect-error

A type you can't test is a type you will break by accident. // @ts-expect-error (TypeScript 3.9) suppresses the error on the next line, and if that line has no error, tsc reports Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive. That turns every expected failure into an assertion.

// pipe.types.ts
import { pipe } from "./pipe";

type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends
  (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2)
    ? true
    : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const trim = (s: string) => s.trim();
const len = (s: string) => s.length;
const isLong = (n: number) => n > 10;
const shout = (s: string) => s.toUpperCase();

const ok = pipe(trim, len, isLong);
export type OkIsTyped = Expect<
  Equal<typeof ok, (input: string) => boolean>
>;

// @ts-expect-error the input must be a string
ok(42);

const broken = pipe(trim, len, shout);

// @ts-expect-error step 3 wants a string, gets a number
broken("  hello  ");

// @ts-expect-error a broken pipe is not a function
const f: (s: string) => string = broken;

// @ts-expect-error pipe() needs at least one step
pipe();

Equal compares two types strictly, so a result that drifts to any or to a wider type fails it; Expect fails to compile when handed false. A minimal tsconfig.json next to the two files:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler"
  },
  "include": ["pipe.ts", "pipe.types.ts"]
}

Install the compiler with npm i -D typescript, then run npx tsc. The config needs TypeScript 5.0 or newer for "moduleResolution": "bundler"; the types themselves need 4.7. If any expectation stops holding, either an Expect line or an unused directive fails the build, locally or in CI.

Where the recursive version breaks

Look again at the broken test. The pipe(trim, len, shout) line compiles. The type of broken is PipeError<3, number, string>, and the error only appears where you call it or assign it to a function type. Hovering broken tells you the step, what it got and what it wanted, which beats a silent unknown, but the red squiggle sits on the wrong line. Overloads don't have this problem: each step is its own parameter, so a mismatch is an argument error on the exact function that's wrong. There is a variant that rewrites the rest parameter to the expected tuple so the error moves onto the bad argument; ecyrbe's write-up shows one. I haven't run it, and a commenter there reports a gap in its first-to-second step check, so test it the same way before you trust it.

Generic steps lose their type parameter. Take const wrap = <T>(x: T): T[] => [x]. When In and Out match a generic signature against infer, the type parameter doesn't survive; TypeScript issue #38964 shows ReturnType of <T = string>() => T coming out as unknown. So pipe(trim, wrap, join), with join taking string[], fails with got: unknown[]. The fix is an instantiation expression (4.7): pass wrap<string> as the step and the chain checks. Overloads get this for free, because each step is matched against (a: A) => B with A already known, and since TypeScript 3.4 a composer can even propagate a generic step's type parameters into the result.

Inline lambdas aren't typed from the previous step. In Effect, pipe(" hi ", (s) => s.trim(), (s) => s.length) types each s from the step before it, because every overload names the intermediate types as separate type parameters. In ...fns: Fns, nothing ties the second slot's parameter to the first slot's return, so an unannotated (s) => s.length has no way to learn that s is a string. The best it gets is the any from the Fn constraint, and an any step checks nothing. Annotate every inline step, or write the steps as named functions.

Long chains hit the depth limit, depending on how you wrote the recursion. The TypeScript PR that added tail-recursion elimination lets tail-recursive conditional types loop 1,000 times before giving up, and lowered the general limit for the rest to 100. Check is tail-recursive, so a 30-step pipe is nowhere near the ceiling. Rewrite it so the recursive call sits inside something else, a tuple spread or a union, and you are back under the general limit, where the failure is the familiar Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite from the 4.5 release notes. Even well under the limit, the 4.1 notes warn that recursive types can increase type-checking time, so keep the step types themselves simple.

When overloads are still the better choice


Overloads write one signature per chain length. The recursive type writes one signature that walks the list.

The rule that falls out of the four breaks: choose by who writes the steps.

If callers write steps inline, as lambdas, or pass generic helpers like map and filter, use overloads. That is the RxJS and Effect situation, where most steps are operators with type parameters and most callbacks are unannotated. Contextual typing per step and per-argument errors are worth more than an unlimited chain length, and very few real pipelines need more than the 19 functions Effect covers.

If callers pass named, already-typed, non-generic functions, use the recursive type. Validation chains, middleware lists and data transforms assembled from a registry all fit: the steps already carry their own types, chains can be longer than any overload stack, and the PipeError type names the failing step. Ship it with the @ts-expect-error file so the next refactor can't quietly break the check.

If this was useful

The recursive Check type is a small version of a pattern that keeps coming back: walk a tuple with infer, carry state in an accumulator, keep the recursion in tail position. The TypeScript Type System goes deep on that toolkit: generics, mapped and conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types. If you already write TypeScript daily, that's the one to read next; if you're still getting comfortable with narrowing and modules, start with TypeScript Essentials.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Coming from Kotlin, Java or PHP? The two bridge books replace the first two for you. Shipping TypeScript at work, with build tooling and published packages? TypeScript in Production covers that layer.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.
