title: [Agent Platform in Action (1)] Building a LINE AI Business Card Master with Go and Google ADK 2.0: From Fan-Out Parallel Retrieval to HITL Pause
description:
Recap

During the AI Agent development craze over the past year, the first Agent many developers wrote often looked like this: writing an incredibly long System Instruction, then stuffing five or six Tools into the same LLMAgent, and praying the model would obediently follow steps A → B → C → D.

It looks impressive as a Demo initially, but as soon as it hits a production environment, problems immediately surface:

  • The more steps, the higher the rate of losing control: When a Prompt is stuffed with "First do OCR, then check the database for duplicates, simultaneously search online for what this company does, then assemble a preview card to ask the user, if the user wants to change the job title then regenerate the preview, and only write to the DB and write an icebreaker email after confirmation," the model occasionally skips the duplicate check or writes directly to the database before waiting for user confirmation.
  • Burning money and waiting in places where Tokens shouldn't be spent: Logic that is 100% deterministic, such as "shunting based on LINE event type" or "normalizing phone number formats," is not only slow when handed to an LLM but also prone to errors.
  • Independent tasks are forced to execute in a queue: Checking the database, Google searching company backgrounds, and comparing recent conversation records are clearly independent of each other, yet they become sequential waits due to the linear conversation loop of a single Agent.

To solve this pain point, Google officially introduced a heavyweight feature in Agent Development Kit (ADK) 2.0 —— Graph Workflows, with simultaneous support for Python and Go (google.golang.org/adk/v2/workflow)!

After seeing this update, I immediately decided to use my most familiar Golang + LINE Messaging API SDK v8 to build a complete open-source project line-card-assistant (LINE AI Business Card Master). I put all the core weapons of ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow (AddRoute conditional routing, AddFanOut / AddFanIn parallel processing and aggregation, NewRequestInputEvent Human-in-the-Loop pause/wait and loop correction) through a real-world battle test and deployed it on Google Cloud Run.

This article will first guide you through two core technical documents that are must-reads for Google's official ADK Graph Workflows, and then break down step-by-step how we used Go code to implement these graph workflow patterns in a LINE Bot!

I. How Google Officially Defines Graph Workflow? Analysis of Two Must-Read Guides

Before looking at the code, it is strongly recommended to understand the core philosophy of the ADK team's design for Graph Workflows. Google recently released two very critical developer guides:

  1. Google Cloud Official Blog: Graph Workflows in ADK: Everything You Need to Know (Written by Annie Wang and Shangjie Chen of the ADK team)
  2. ADK Official Technical Documentation: Graph-based agent workflows (adk.dev/graphs)

We have condensed and organized the essence of these two official articles as follows:

1. What is "Graph Engineering"?

In the article "Graph Workflows in ADK: Everything You Need to Know", the authors use a "Customer Refund Workflow" as an example to point out a core concept:

As workflows become more complex, reliability comes from separating "Workflow Control" from "Model Reasoning." The essence of Graph Engineering is to decompose tasks into independent nodes, connect them with edges, and explicitly decide at each step whether "Code," "Models," or "People" should determine the next step.

The article summarizes five of the most commonly used Graph Workflow design patterns in the real world:

Core Pattern What pain point does it solve? ADK 2.0 Corresponding Mechanism
1. Fan-out and Fan-in Parallel Aggregation Multiple independent data collection steps (e.g., checking orders, payments, customer records) slow down overall latency if executed sequentially. Use AddFanOut to trigger multiple nodes to execute in parallel, then use a JoinNode (AddFanIn) to wait for all branches to complete before aggregating, consuming zero extra LLM calls in between.
2. Deterministic Routing vs. Agent Routing Some shunting rules are black and white (e.g., amount > $100 goes to manual review) and shouldn't be guessed by an LLM; others require understanding natural language intent. Deterministic Router: Pure code logic sets ev.Routes, 0 Token consumption, 100% testable.
Agent Router: Intent is judged by the LLM, but graph edges strictly limit valid jump targets.
3. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Pause and Resume High-risk actions (e.g., large refunds, writing to production databases) must be confirmed by a human, but traditional Webhooks are stateless short connections. A node issues a RequestInput event to freeze the execution state (Checkpoint) and pause the Graph; after receiving an external human response, RerunOnResume wakes up the same node to continue.
4. Parallel Workers vs. Fan-out Distinguishes between "performing three different checks on the same data" and "performing the same processing on N items." Fan-out: Different nodes perform different responsibilities.
Parallel Workers: The same node expands in parallel for array elements.
5. Static Graph vs. Dynamic Orchestration How to balance "architectural visualization/maintainability" with "dynamic loop correction"? Use static Edges to define clear routing and Conditional Cycles (e.g., generate draft → check/modify → regenerate), making the entire system's state machine clear at a glance.

2. The Four Core Building Blocks of ADK Go v2.0 (adk.dev/graphs)

In the official document "Graph-based agent workflows", the API design for ADK 2.0 in the Go language (google.golang.org/adk/v2/workflow) is shown in detail. To assemble a Graph in Go, you mainly need to master the following four components:

  1. Nodes:
    • workflow.NewFunctionNode / workflow.NewEmittingFunctionNode: Wraps any standard Go function into a graph node, suitable for DB queries, data cleaning, API calls, or assembling LINE Flex Messages.
    • llmagent.RunLLMAgentAsNode: Encapsulates an llmagent with a specific Prompt and tools (e.g., geminitool.GoogleSearch{}) into a single node, allowing the LLM to focus on doing "one thing" well.
  2. State & Data Flow:
    • In addition to passing strongly-typed Output between nodes, structured data can be written to the Session State (ctx.Session().State()) via ev.Actions.StateDelta for downstream or aggregation nodes to read.
  3. Edges & EdgeBuilder:
    • eb.Add(from, to): Unidirectional straight connection.
    • eb.AddRoute(from, workflow.StringRoute("route_name", targetNode), ...): Conditional branch routing (can also be used to create Cycles!).
    • eb.AddFanOut(from, branch1, branch2, ...) and eb.AddFanIn(joinNode, branch1, branch2, ...): Parallel branching and synchronous aggregation.
  4. WorkflowAgent:
    • Finally, call workflowagent.New(workflowagent.Config{Edges: edges}), and the entire Graph becomes a standard ADK agent.Agent, which is then handed over to the runner.Runner for execution and Session management!

II. Practical Project Architecture: LINE AI Business Card Master (line-card-assistant)

Having understood the official theory, let's see how to apply these concepts to a real-world LINE Bot scenario.

Business professionals receive a large number of paper business cards at exhibitions or meetings every day. Traditional business card apps only offer simple OCR recognition but lack features like "What has this company been doing lately?", "At which event did I meet this person?", and "How can I correct recognition errors directly by speaking in the chat room?".

Therefore, we designed line-card-assistant, with an overall architecture that fully corresponds to ADK 2.0's Graph Workflow:

[LINE Webhook] 
      │
      ▼
[Router Node (AddRoutes)]
  ├── (Received business card photo) ──► [Vision OCR Node] 
  │ │
  │ (AddFanOut Parallel Processing)
  │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
  │ ▼ ▼ ▼
  │ [DB Dup Check & Validation] [Company Background Search] [Past Interaction Retrieval]
  │ └──────────────┼──────────────┘
  │ (AddFanIn Aggregation)
  │ ▼
  │ [Generate Flex Message Preview Card]
  │ │
  │ ⏸️ NewRequestInputEvent (HITL Pause & Wait)
  │ │
  │ ┌────────────────────┴────────────────────┐
  │ ▼ (Click: Confirm Save) ▼ (Click: Modify Field / Add Note)
  │ [Write to DB + Generate Icebreaker Draft] [Re-entry Loop Correction Node]
  │
  └── (Received query text) ──► [Query Rewrite] ──► [SQL + Vector Hybrid Retrieval] ──► [Flex Carousel Card Rotation]

This architecture diagram covers three core paths:

  1. Business Card Recognition and Enrichment Pipeline (Ingest Pipeline): Receive photo → Vision OCR → Execute three tasks in parallel (DB duplicate check + Google Search company background + Conversation context inference for meeting occasion) → Aggregate to generate LINE Flex preview card → HITL pause to wait for user confirmation or modification.
  2. HITL Loop Correction (Re-entry Loop): When the graph is paused at HITLConfirmNode, if the user enters text directly in LINE (e.g., "Change job title to Director, met at Cloud Summit"), the workflow wakes up and takes the RouteEdit branch into ApplyEditNode, updates the fields, and loops back to BuildPreviewNode to regenerate the preview card and pause again, until the user clicks "✅ Confirm Save" to actually write to the database and generate the icebreaker email!
  3. Natural Language Hybrid Retrieval Pipeline (Search Pipeline): Receive query text (e.g., "Help me find people doing AI I met at Cloud Summit last week") → Query Rewrite structural decomposition → SQL + Keyword/Tag hybrid retrieval → Return LINE Flex Carousel business card rotation.

III. Go Code Deep Dive: Writing Graph Workflow into a LINE Bot

Next, let's look directly at the Go implementation of internal/workflow/graph.go and various nodes to see how clean the ADK 2.0 API looks in Go.

1. A Global View: Assembling the Graph with EdgeBuilder

In internal/workflow/graph.go, we declare and connect all nodes via the BuildEdges function. You can clearly see the topological structure of the entire graph:

func BuildEdges(deps *Dependencies) ([]workflow.Edge, error) {
    // 1. Entry Router Node
    routerNode, _ := NewRouterNode()

    // 2. Business Card Recognition and Fan-Out Three Parallel Nodes
    visionOCRNode, _ := NewVisionOCRNode(deps)
    cleanAndDedupNode, _ := NewCleanAndDedupNode(deps)
    companyEnrichNode, _ := NewCompanyEnrichNode(deps)
    contextMatchNode, _ := NewContextMatchNode(deps)
    joinPreviewNode := workflow.NewJoinNode("JoinPreviewNode")

    // 3. Preview Card Generation, HITL Pause, and Confirm/Modify Branch Nodes
    buildPreviewNode, _ := NewBuildPreviewNode(deps)
    hitlConfirmNode, _ := NewHITLConfirmNode(deps)
    saveCardNode, _ := NewSaveCardNode(deps)
    applyEditNode, _ := NewApplyEditNode(deps)

    // 4. Natural Language Search and Icebreaker Email Nodes
    queryIntentNode, _ := NewQueryIntentNode(deps)
    hybridSearchNode, _ := NewHybridSearchNode(deps)
    broadSearchNode, _ := NewBroadSearchNode(deps)
    formatCarouselNode, _ := NewFormatCarouselNode(deps)
    emailDraftNode, _ := NewEmailDraftNode(deps)

    eb := workflow.NewEdgeBuilder()

    // Entry -> Deterministic Router
    eb.Add(workflow.Start, routerNode)
    eb.AddRoute(routerNode,
        workflow.StringRoute(RouteImage, visionOCRNode),
        workflow.StringRoute(RouteText, queryIntentNode),
        workflow.StringRoute(RoutePostbackDraft, emailDraftNode),
    )

    // Ingest Pipeline: Vision OCR -> Parallel Fan-Out -> JoinNode Fan-In -> Preview
    eb.AddFanOut(visionOCRNode, cleanAndDedupNode, companyEnrichNode, contextMatchNode)
    eb.AddFanIn(joinPreviewNode, cleanAndDedupNode, companyEnrichNode, contextMatchNode)
    eb.Add(joinPreviewNode, buildPreviewNode)
    eb.Add(buildPreviewNode, hitlConfirmNode)

    // Conditional branches after HITL pause: Confirm Save vs. Modify Field Loop
    eb.AddRoute(hitlConfirmNode,
        workflow.StringRoute(RouteConfirm, saveCardNode),
        workflow.StringRoute(RouteEdit, applyEditNode),
    )
    // ★ Key Cycle: After modifying fields, route back to buildPreviewNode to regenerate Flex preview card and enter HITL again!
    eb.AddRoute(applyEditNode,
        workflow.StringRoute(RoutePreview, buildPreviewNode),
    )

    // Search Pipeline: Query Rewrite -> Hybrid Search -> (Found / Empty Fallback) -> Carousel
    eb.Add(queryIntentNode, hybridSearchNode)
    eb.AddRoute(hybridSearchNode,
        workflow.StringRoute(RouteFound, formatCarouselNode),
        workflow.StringRoute(RouteEmpty, broadSearchNode),
    )
    eb.Add(broadSearchNode, formatCarouselNode)

    return eb.Build()
}

This code perfectly embodies the Static Graph advantage mentioned in the Google Cloud Blog: you don't need to flip through thousands of lines of Prompts or track down Tool Calls scattered everywhere. Just by looking at the 30 lines of code in BuildEdges, you can 100% grasp all possible paths and loop boundaries of the entire Agent system.

2. Deterministic Router: Precise Shunting with 0 Token Consumption

When the LINE Webhook receives an event, we don't need to waste a Gemini API call to ask the model "Is the user sending a picture or text?". We use workflow.NewEmittingFunctionNode to create a pure code deterministic routing node RouterNode:

const (
    RouteImage = "route_image"
    RouteText = "route_text"
    RoutePostbackDraft = "route_postback_draft"
)

func NewRouterNode() (workflow.Node, error) {
    return workflow.NewEmittingFunctionNode("RouterNode", func(ctx workflow.Context, _ struct{}) (string, error) {
        inputType, err := getStateString(ctx, StateKeyInputType)
        if err != nil || inputType == "" {
            inputType = "text"
        }

        var route string
        switch inputType {
        case "image":
            route = RouteImage
        case "postback_draft":
            route = RoutePostbackDraft
        default:
            route = RouteText
        }

        // Emit an event with Routes tags to let EdgeBuilder's AddRoute decide the next node
        ev := workflow.NewEvent(ctx, "route_selected")
        ev.Routes = []string{route}
        if err := ctx.Emit(ev); err != nil {
            return "", err
        }
        return route, nil
    }, workflow.WithDeclaredRoutes(RouteImage, RouteText, RoutePostbackDraft))
}

As long as you set ev.Routes = []string{route} when emitting a workflow.Event, and use workflow.WithDeclaredRoutes(...) to validate route legitimacy during construction, ADK will automatically check for misspelled Route names during the startup phase!

3. Fan-Out / Fan-In Parallel Processing: Running DB Dup Check, Google Search, and Context Inference Simultaneously

Once VisionOCRNode extracts a structured models.BusinessCard from the business card photo via gemini-2.5-flash's multimodal capabilities, we have three completely independent tasks to perform:

  1. CleanAndDedupNode (Pure Code + DB Query): Normalizes Taiwan mobile and landline numbers to +886-... format and queries the SQLite database to see if a business card for the same person already exists (if the job title is different, it can even mark a "Promotion/Transfer Reminder"!).
  2. CompanyEnrichNode (Embedded llmagent with Google Search tool): Automatically searches the web for the latest background of the company based on the company name on the business card, condensing it into a 2-sentence summary and 3~5 industry tags.
  3. ContextMatchNode (LLM Context Inference): Reads the user's most recent LINE conversation records before and after sending the photo (e.g., the user just sent "I'm attending Cloud Summit today") to automatically infer the meeting occasion for this business card (MetContext).

In internal/workflow/nodes_ingest.go, we can even use llmagent.RunLLMAgentAsNode inside CompanyEnrichNode to call a sub-agent with geminitool.GoogleSearch{}:

// Combine LLMAgent with Google Search Grounding capability within a Graph node
searchAgent, err := llmagent.New(llmagent.Config{
    Name: "CompanySearchSubAgent",
    Description: "Searches the web for company background and industry tags.",
    Model: deps.SearchModel,
    Instruction: "Given a company name, search Google and return JSON with summary (2 sentences in Traditional Chinese) and tags (3 to 5 industry tags).",
    Tools: []tool.Tool{geminitool.GoogleSearch{}},
})
if err == nil {
    _ = llmagent.RunLLMAgentAsNode(searchAgent, llmagent.NodeConfig{Name: "CompanySearchSubAgentNode"})
}

💡 Practical Details of Go Parallel Nodes: How to Avoid Race Conditions?

When running eb.AddFanOut in Go, the three branch nodes execute in parallel in different Goroutines. If three nodes simultaneously read and write to the same BusinessCard JSON object and write back to the same State Key, a Lost Update (last write wins) race condition will occur!

To solve this problem, we adopted a very clean technique in the implementation:

  • Write to independent StateDelta Keys:
    • CleanAndDedupNode only writes to StateKeyDedupCard, StateKeyIsDuplicate, StateKeyOldTitle.
    • CompanyEnrichNode only writes to StateKeyCompanySummary and StateKeyCompanyTags.
    • ContextMatchNode only writes to StateKeyMetContext.
  • ADK 2.0's Runner will sequentially Commit the ev.Actions.StateDelta emitted by each node in the main Goroutine.
  • Once JoinPreviewNode (eb.AddFanIn) confirms that the three parallel branches are complete, the single-threaded BuildPreviewNode uses loadMergedCardFromState(ctx) to safely merge the results of the three branches into a complete BusinessCard and renders a beautiful LINE Flex Message preview card!

4. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL): NewRequestInputEvent Pause and Re-entry Loop Correction

The most exciting part of this entire system is the Human-in-the-Loop pause and resume mechanism.

In traditional LINE Bot development, if you want to achieve "send preview card → wait for user to click confirm or type modification → send new preview card after modification → save after confirmation," you usually have to maintain a complex user_state_machine table in the database yourself.

But in ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow, this is built directly into HITLConfirmNode! Let's see how NewHITLConfirmNode in internal/workflow/nodes_ingest.go is written:

func NewHITLConfirmNode(_ *Dependencies) (workflow.Node, error) {
    rerun := true
    return workflow.NewEmittingFunctionNode("HITLConfirmNode", func(ctx workflow.Context, _ struct{}) (string, error) {
        activeID, _ := getStateString(ctx, StateKeyActiveInterruptID)

        // [Phase 1: First entry to node] Not yet paused, emit NewRequestInputEvent to pause Graph!
        if activeID == "" {
            interruptID := fmt.Sprintf("hitl-card-%d", time.Now().UnixNano())
            if err := emitStateDelta(ctx, map[string]any{
                StateKeyActiveInterruptID: interruptID,
            }); err != nil {
                return "", err
            }

            reqEv := workflow.NewRequestInputEvent(ctx, session.RequestInput{
                InterruptID: interruptID,
                Payload: map[string]any{
                    "prompt": "Please confirm if the business card info is correct. Click 'Confirm Save' or enter modifications directly (e.g., change title to Director).",
                },
            })
            if err := ctx.Emit(reqEv); err != nil {
                return "", err
            }
            return "waiting_for_user", nil
        }

        // [Phase 2: Wake up and rerun after receiving user response (RerunOnResume: true)]
        resumedVal, err := ctx.ResumedInput(activeID)
        var decision HITLResumePayload
        if err == nil && resumedVal != nil {
            _ = decodeViaJSON(resumedVal, &decision)
        }

        // Clear the consumed InterruptID so that if the Edit loop comes back later, it can trigger a pause again!
        _ = emitStateDelta(ctx, map[string]any{
            StateKeyActiveInterruptID: "",
            StateKeyHITLAction: decision.Action,
            StateKeyHITLEditText: decision.EditText,
        })

        route := RouteConfirm
        if strings.EqualFold(decision.Action, "edit") || (decision.Action != "confirm" && strings.TrimSpace(decision.EditText) != "") {
            route = RouteEdit
        }

        ev := workflow.NewEvent(ctx, "hitl_decision")
        ev.Routes = []string{route}
        if err := ctx.Emit(ev); err != nil {
            return "", err
        }
        return route, nil
    }, workflow.WithNodeConfig(workflow.NodeConfig{
        RerunOnResume: &rerun, // ★ Key setting: Rerun this node function when external input resumes
    }), workflow.WithDeclaredRoutes(RouteConfirm, RouteEdit))
}

How does the LINE Webhook feed user button clicks or text back to the paused Graph?

When HITLConfirmNode emits a NewRequestInputEvent, our Engine (located in internal/workflow/engine.go) captures this InterruptID and pushes the LINE Flex Message preview card generated by BuildPreviewNode to the user.

Then:

  • If the user clicks the "✅ Confirm Save" button (Postback Event) on the Flex Message, the LINE Webhook calls Engine.ResumeHITL(ctx, userID, HITLResumePayload{Action: "confirm"}).
  • If the user types directly in the chat room "Change title to Technical Director, met at AI conference" (Text Event), the LINE Webhook detects that the user has a PendingHITL waiting, automatically intercepts this text, and calls Engine.ResumeHITL(ctx, userID, HITLResumePayload{Action: "edit", EditText: text})!

Inside Engine.ResumeHITL, you only need to send a FunctionResponse with workflow.WorkflowInputFunctionCallName to the ADK Runner, and the frozen Graph will seamlessly continue execution:

msg := &genai.Content{
    Role: string(genai.RoleUser),
    Parts: []*genai.Part{
        {
            FunctionResponse: &genai.FunctionResponse{
                ID: pending.InterruptID,
                Name: workflow.WorkflowInputFunctionCallName,
                Response: map[string]any{
                    "action": payload.Action,
                    "edit_text": payload.EditText,
                },
            },
        },
    },
}

Once it enters RouteEdit, ApplyEditNode corrects the business card data, then loops back to BuildPreviewNode via eb.AddRoute(applyEditNode, workflow.StringRoute(RoutePreview, buildPreviewNode)), generating an updated Flex preview card and stopping again at HITLConfirmNode to wait for user confirmation. This is where Graph Workflow is most powerful for handling multi-turn interactive corrections!

5. Natural Language Hybrid Retrieval Pipeline (Query Rewrite + Hybrid Search + Flex Carousel)

When the user is not waiting for business card confirmation but directly enters query text (e.g., "Help me find people doing AI I met at Cloud Summit last week"), the RouterNode directs the request to the RouteText branch (defined in internal/workflow/nodes_search.go):

  1. QueryIntentNode: Uses Gemini to decompose natural language into a structured SearchFilter (including Keywords, Tags, Company, Title, MetContext).
  2. HybridSearchNode: Combines SQL condition filtering with tag/keyword matching and simultaneously acts as a Deterministic Router:
    • If business cards are found → Emit RouteFound to go directly to FormatCarouselNode.
    • If precise conditions yield no results → Emit RouteEmpty to automatically enter BroadSearchNode for fuzzy/relaxed retrieval (Fallback), and finally FormatCarouselNode renders up to 10 LINE Flex Carousel business cards, each with a one-click "✉️ Generate Icebreaker" Postback button!

IV. Deployment: Cloud Run + Self-Identity Security Authentication

After completing development and passing all unit tests (go test ./...), we deployed the service to Google Cloud Run (asia-east1).

In the cloud deployment architecture, we can use Cloud Run's Service Account Self-Identity (Application Default Credentials, ADC) mechanism:

  • By binding a Service Account with roles/aiplatform.user permissions to Cloud Run and setting environment variables GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=true and GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT, the application can directly call Vertex AI / Gemini models using the Identity provided by the Cloud Run execution environment, eliminating the risk of managing static API Key leaks.
  • If developing locally or using the Gemini Developer API, you can easily switch via environment variables: 
gcloud run deploy line-card-assistant \
  --source . \
  --region asia-east1 \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --set-env-vars="LINE_CHANNEL_SECRET=your_secret,LINE_CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN=your_token,GEMINI_MODEL=gemini-2.5-flash"

V. Summary of Pitfalls and Practical Experience

After deeply integrating Google ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow (google.golang.org/adk/v2/workflow) with LINE Bot, there are several practical insights worth sharing with Go developers:

  1. Keep Prompts Small, Leave the Flow to the Graph: Previously, a single super Agent required hundreds of lines of Prompts and often missed steps; now, the Prompt for each node (such as VisionOCRNode, CompanyEnrichNode, ContextMatchNode) is only a few lines long, with a single responsibility and fixed output format, resulting in a quantum leap in stability.
  2. AddFanOut Significantly Reduces Perceived Latency: In a LINE chat room, users hate waiting after sending a business card photo. By using AddFanOut to simultaneously perform DB duplicate checks, Google Search company background investigations, and context inference, the total time taken depends only on the slowest branch, rather than the sum of all three steps.
  3. Use StateDelta to Isolate Parallel Writes: When using AddFanOut in Go, remember to have each parallel branch write to its own dedicated Session State Key, and then merge them uniformly after passing through the JoinNode (AddFanIn) to elegantly avoid concurrent overwrite issues.
  4. NewRequestInputEvent + RerunOnResume is a Secret Weapon for Chatbots: Whether it's a LINE Postback button or free text input, they can all be uniformly encapsulated into a FunctionResponse for WorkflowInputFunctionCallName to wake up the same Graph Session, completely bidding farewell to hand-coded spaghetti-style state machines!

The complete project source code, architecture diagrams, and deployment scripts are all open-sourced on GitHub. You are welcome to clone it and play around, or directly transform it into your own enterprise-grade LINE Agent workflow!

References and Further Reading

  • Open Source Code for this Project: kkdai/line-card-assistant (GitHub)
  • Google Cloud Official Blog: Graph Workflows in ADK: Everything You Need to Know
  • ADK Official Documentation: Graph-based agent workflows - Agent Development Kit (ADK)

title: I built a tray app to see where my Claude Code tokens actually go
description:
You're deep in a refactor with Claude Code, everything is flowing, and then:

You've hit your limit. Resets at 3:10 PM.

Two hours of nothing. And the worst part isn't the wait — it's that I had no idea what burned the quota. Was it that one giant conversation? The 20 skills I installed "just in case"? A turn that re-read half the repo?

So I built Bumeter: a small desktop app that reads the logs Claude Code and Kiro already write on your machine and answers two questions:

  1. Where did my tokens go? Per conversation, per turn, per skill.
  2. How close am I to being blocked? Your 5-hour and 7-day quota (and Kiro's monthly credits), always visible in the system tray.

It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), and nothing is uploaded — it only reads files that are already on your disk.

What it shows

A quota bar in your tray

The tray menu shows one bar per tool. The mascot, Bum 🔥, changes face with your usage — calm, happy, worried, on fire, or asleep — and the highest percentage sits next to it in the top bar.

Claude Code
▰▰▰▰▰▱▱▱▱▱ 🟢  5 hours · 49% · reset 13:10
▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▱ 🔴  7 days · 90% · reset Oct 16
Kiro
▰▰▰▱▱▱▱▱▱▱ 🟢  Month · 27% · 271/1000 credits · reset Nov 1

You also get a notification when a quota passes your thresholds (70% / 90% by default) or when a single turn costs far more than usual.

Conversations and turns

Every conversation, grouped by day, with a fuel bar showing how much it cost. Filter by project, model, "costly", "large context", "interrupted" or starred, then open a conversation to see every turn: what you asked, which tools ran, and why it was expensive.

Context analysis

For any session: what is filling the context window (your messages, tool output, re-reads…), when it was compacted, and which tool calls were huge.

The hidden cost of skills

This one surprised me. A skill's description sits in the system prompt of every request in every session, whether you use the skill or not. Bumeter shows each skill's always-on cost next to how often you actually used it — and you can disable, resize or remove skills with undo.

How it works

Claude Code writes a JSONL log for every session under ~/.claude/projects/. Each API call records its token usage: input, cache writes, cache reads, output. Bumeter tails those files, de-duplicates the streamed entries, attributes each call to the turn and skill that caused it, and stores the result in a local SQLite database.

The 5-hour / 7-day percentages are trickier: they aren't in the logs. But Claude Code passes them to your status line command as JSON. So Bumeter puts a tiny bum statusline --tee in front of your existing status line command: it saves the numbers and passes the input through untouched, so your status line keeps working. The change to ~/.claude/settings.json is backed up and has an undo button.

Kiro doesn't log tokens at all, so context size is estimated from the per-turn context percentage, and cost is shown in credits. The monthly limit comes from kiro-cli /usage (only when it's installed and you're logged in), or you can type it in.

Each tool is an adapter behind one interface, so adding Codex, Cursor or Gemini CLI is a new adapter plus one line in a registry — the UI already has per-tool tabs.

The stack

  • Rust workspace: ingestion engine, SQLite (rusqlite), file watching (notify), a background host with JSON-RPC over a local socket
  • Tauri 2 for the window, tray and notifications
  • TypeScript with no framework for the UI (a tiny h() helper, Vite, Vitest)
  • A bum CLI: bum status, bum scan, bum session, bum skills, and bum audit

Numbers I care about

I checked it against my own data (38 MB of logs, ~16,500 lines):

  • Token totals match an independent count 100% (bum audit recounts the raw logs separately), with 0 parse errors.
  • First full scan: ~220 ms. A new log line reaches the app in ~31 ms.
  • Analysing my largest session — 224 prompts, 726 API calls — takes 48 ms.
  • Idle CPU: ~0%.

What I learned from my own data

97% of my tokens were cache reads. Of ~757M tokens, ~735M were cache reads. A "2 million token conversation" sounds scary, but most of it is the same context being re-read on every request — which is much cheaper than fresh input. Raw token counts can make you panic about the wrong thing.

Long sessions get expensive by themselves. Every request re-reads the whole context, so the same short question costs more at turn 200 than at turn 2. Watching context size per turn makes it obvious when /compact or a fresh session is worth it.

Skills you never use still cost something. Small per request, but paid on every request. Worth pruning.

Website: https://bumeter.cc/
Github: https://github.com/chieund/bumeter

Try it

  • Linux: .deb and AppImage
  • Windows: installer (.exe / .msi)
  • macOS: builds are set up in CI but untested — testers very welcome!

👉 github.com/chieund/bumeter

The UI is in English and Vietnamese, with light and dark themes.

What's next

  • Limit forecast: "at your current pace you'll hit the 5-hour limit at ~14:20, 50 minutes before it resets" — in the tray, with one notification.
  • More tools: Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode.
  • Context coaching: suggest /compact or a new session when the context is large and being re-read heavily.

If you use Claude Code or Kiro every day, I'd love to hear what you'd want from a tool like this — and which assistant I should support next. Issues and PRs are welcome. ⭐

title: IPTV and Streaming: How to Choose the Right Setup for Your Devices
description:
Internet streaming has changed how people watch digital content. Instead of relying only on traditional television services, viewers can use internet-connected devices to access video content at home or while travelling. However, choosing a suitable streaming setup requires more than looking at picture quality or subscription prices.

In this article, we will explore device compatibility, internet speed, streaming quality, security, and a few practical considerations that can help users make informed decisions.

  1. Understand How IPTV Works

IPTV stands for Internet Protocol Television. It refers to delivering television content through internet protocol networks rather than exclusively through traditional broadcast or cable systems.

The viewing experience depends on several factors, including the service provider, atlas pro abonnement, the user's internet connection, the device being used, and the format in which the content is delivered.

Before choosing a service, check that it provides access to content you are legally entitled to watch.

  1. Check Device Compatibility

Not every streaming service works equally well on every device. Some solutions support Android TV, smartphones, tablets, computers, or compatible smart televisions, while others may require specific applications or hardware.

Before subscribing, consider the following questions:

Does the service support your operating system?

Is the application compatible with your television or streaming device?

Can you use it comfortably with a remote control?

Are setup instructions and customer support available?

Checking these details in advance can help prevent compatibility problems later.

  1. Choose an Appropriate Internet Connection

A stable connection is often more important than simply having the highest advertised internet speed. Network congestion, Wi-Fi interference, and router placement can all affect playback.

For a better experience, try connecting your device through Ethernet when possible. atlas pro ontv, If you use Wi-Fi, position the router in an open area and avoid placing it too far from your streaming device.

You can also test your connection at different times of day to identify whether slowdowns occur during busy periods.

  1. Understand HD, Full HD, and 4K

Streaming services may advertise different video resolutions, but the actual picture quality depends on more than the resolution label.

HD: Suitable for many everyday viewing situations.

Full HD: Offers greater detail than standard HD.

4K: Provides a higher resolution and can look sharper on compatible screens.

To benefit from 4K, you generally need a compatible display, a device that supports the format, sufficient bandwidth, and content actually provided in 4K. A service advertising 4K does not automatically mean every video is available at that resolution.

  1. Review Security and Subscription Terms

Before signing up for a streaming service, read its terms and privacy policy. Check the subscription price, renewal conditions, cancellation process, supported devices, and any trial-period restrictions.

Use trusted payment methods, avoid sharing account credentials, and be cautious of websites that promise unrealistic features or request unnecessary personal information.

It is also important to confirm that a provider has the appropriate rights to distribute the content it offers in your country. https://atlasprontv4k.fr/

  1. Troubleshoot Common Streaming Problems

If a video repeatedly buffers or the application freezes, try these basic steps:

Restart the streaming application.

Restart your router and streaming device.

Check whether other devices are using substantial bandwidth.

Update the application and device software.

Test a wired connection if one is available.

Contact the provider if the problem continues.

Changing several settings at once can make it difficult to identify the cause, so test one adjustment at a time.

title: A date is not a version: strict parsing under OSV ranges
description:
A vulnerability range is a claim about ordering, and it is worth no more than the version parser sitting underneath it. Walk an OSV range's events in whatever order they happen to sit in the file, compare them against leniently parsed versions, and you get two silent failures: verdicts that flip when the advisory is re-serialised, and a component calling itself 2023-08-01 that lands outside every affected range forever.

Neither failure announces itself, and both land on the one verdict nobody rechecks. An affected finding gets read, argued about, and then either fixed or justified in writing. not_affected gets counted. So a comparator that quietly produces not_affected out of an ordering it invented is worse than one that refuses to answer. A good part of the design work in the internal/match package of vexdesk (the tool I wrote to turn an SBOM and a pile of OSV advisories into an OpenVEX document) goes into making the refusal the cheap path rather than the embarrassing one.

not_affected is version arithmetic and nothing else

Worth pinning down what the verdict means before I defend it. When the matcher says not_affected, it says this version sits outside every range the advisory gives. It is not saying the vulnerable code is unreachable in the product. That is an engineering judgement, it belongs to a person, and it arrives later as a decision file: anything still undecided leaves the document as under_investigation, not as not_affected.

The narrowness is deliberate. A claim about arithmetic over an ordering is the kind of claim you can get exactly right, and the kind that is indefensible to get wrong, because there is nothing subjective left to hide behind. So the ordering has to be real, and where you cannot establish it, the honest output is unknown with the reason attached.

A lenient parser invents an ordering

vexdesk's parseSemver demands exactly major.minor.patch and refuses leading zeros. 1.2 is an error. 2023-08-01 is an error. Both come out as unknown with the parse error as the reason, and the first reaction you hear is that this is pedantry inflating the unknown count. It runs the other way: this is the one place where pedantry carries load.

Think about what a tolerant parser does with a date. Split on non-digit separators, coerce the parts, and 2023-08-01 turns into something that orders as 2023.8.1, a version above every real version anyone will ever publish. Now measure it against a perfectly ordinary range, introduced: 0, fixed: 2.1.4. The date sits above the fix, so it falls outside the interval, so the component is not_affected. Permanently, for every advisory, for a version string that carries no ordering information at all. The tolerant parser did not fail to compare: it succeeded at comparing a number it made up.

The leading-zero refusal is the same argument at smaller scale. Accept 1.08.0 and read it numerically, and now two spellings of one version exist, equality and ordering stop agreeing with each other, and whether a component sits inside a range starts depending on which spelling reached you. Cheaper to have no answer than an answer that depends on that.

Everything the comparison cannot establish ends up in one list, and the list is kept whole:

    var unknown []string
    for _, r := range aff.Ranges {
        switch r.Type {
        case osv.RangeSemver:
            // fall through to comparison
        case osv.RangeEcosystem:
            if !eco.semverOrdered {
                unknown = append(unknown, fmt.Sprintf(
                    "ECOSYSTEM range for %s needs that ecosystem's own version ordering, which is not implemented",
                    eco.name))
                continue
            }
        case osv.RangeGit:
            unknown = append(unknown, "GIT range: commit ranges cannot be compared against a version string")
            continue
        default:
            unknown = append(unknown, fmt.Sprintf("range type %q is not recognised", r.Type))
            continue
        }

        hit, err := inSemverRange(version, r)
        if err != nil {
            unknown = append(unknown, err.Error())
            continue
        }
        if hit {
            return Affected, "version falls inside the advisory's affected range"
        }
    }

    if len(unknown) > 0 {
        // Every reason survives: the person clearing this finding needs the
        // whole list, not the first item of it.
        return Unknown, strings.Join(unknown, "; ")
    }

The ECOSYSTEM branch is the same discipline applied to a whole ecosystem instead of one string. An ECOSYSTEM range means "use this ecosystem's own version ordering", and only a few ecosystems in the tool are marked semverOrdered: golang, npm, cargo. Anything else leaves the range unknown, carrying the reason, rather than quietly compared with semver rules that do not apply to it. Here is what a PyPI component looks like on the way out:

$ vexdesk match -sbom sbom.cyclonedx.json -advisories ./advisories
4 component(s) compared against the advisory set

STATUS    ADVISORY      COMPONENT        VERSION  REASON
affected  FIXTURE-0001  widget           1.2.3    version falls inside the advisory's affected range
affected  FIXTURE-0004  cogwheel         4.0.0    version is in the advisory's affected version list
unknown   FIXTURE-0003  Example_Fixture  3.1.2    ECOSYSTEM range for PyPI needs that ecosystem's own version ordering, which is not implemented

File order is not a sort order

The second failure is subtler, because nothing about it looks like a parsing problem.

An OSV range is a JSON array of events: introduced opens an interval, fixed and last_affected close it. JSON preserves array order, so walking the array and flipping a boolean as you go feels natural. The trouble: the schema's meaning does not live in the array order. A well-formed range can list its events in an order that has nothing to do with their version order, and any tool that reads, filters, merges or re-emits an advisory feed is free to hand you the same claim with the array arranged differently.

This range is the same claim whichever way round you print it:

{
  "affected": [
    {
      "package": { "ecosystem": "Go", "name": "github.com/example/widget" },
      "ranges": [
        {
          "type": "SEMVER",
          "events": [
            { "introduced": "1.5.0" },
            { "fixed": "2.0.0" },
            { "introduced": "0" },
            { "fixed": "1.2.0" }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Walked in array order, 1.1.0 opens at 1.5.0, closes at 2.0.0, opens again at 0, closes at 1.2.0, and whether it comes out inside depends entirely on how you carried that state. Shuffle the four lines and the same advisory gives you a different answer. Not a wrong answer: an unstable one, which is harder to notice and much harder to explain to someone who has already shipped a document built on it.

So inSemverRange sorts the events before walking them. Two rules do the work. First, "introduced": "0" sorts ahead of everything: it is the schema's sentinel for "from the beginning", it is not a parseable major.minor.patch triple, and it needs its own case rather than a parser loose enough to swallow it. Second, at equal versions the closing event sorts before the introduced event that reopens. That pair is a real shape and not a hypothetical: a branch gets closed at a version and a new line of releases opens at the same version. Sorted that way the walk closes and then reopens, so the interval is open at that version, and the verdict holds regardless of the order the file used. internal/match/range_order_test.go exists to hold that property down: the same range, shuffled, one verdict.

The strongest verdict wins across entries

One more place where order would otherwise leak in. Advisories routinely split a single claim across several affected entries: one per branch, one per range type, one per distribution. Stating each separately would put several statements in the document for one claim, and a claim-by-claim reader keeps only the last one it sees, which puts the output back at the mercy of entry order. So the entries fold into one verdict, and the verdict that asks most of a person wins:

    for _, aff := range a.Affected {
        if !samePackage(aff.Package.Ecosystem, aff.Package.Name, eco, name) {
            continue
        }
        s, reason := evaluate(version, aff, eco)
        switch {
        case !stated || rank(s) > rank(status):
            stated, status, reasons = true, s, []string{reason}
        case rank(s) == rank(status) && !slices.Contains(reasons, reason):
            reasons = append(reasons, reason)
        }
    }

// rank orders verdicts by how much they ask of a person.
func rank(s Status) int {
    switch s {
    case Affected:
        return 2
    case Unknown:
        return 1
    default:
        return 0
    }
}

unknown outranking not_affected is the thesis of this whole post compressed into one integer. An entry that could not be compared does not get cleared by a sibling entry that could. And because match exits 1 when anything needs attention, an unknown stops a pipeline instead of sitting as a line in a report nobody opens.

Where leniency does belong

Strictness is not a general virtue here, and it is worth being precise about where it stops.

An explicit affected version list is exact set membership, not ordering, and there I do apply one normalisation: the leading v gets trimmed on both sides, because Go components carry it and OSV lists mostly do not, and a string mismatch there would clear a version that is plainly on the list. Safe, because nothing is being ordered, and deliberately nowhere near the comparator.

The same split runs through the document side of the tool. openvex.New validates what it builds, and Statement.Validate is severe about it: a not_affected with an impact_statement and no justification code gets refused, because prose cannot be compared against every other not_affected the way a code can. But openvex.Parse never calls Validate, so documents already issued are read leniently, including ones that break the rules the tool enforces on write. Refusing them would hide statements someone needs to read.

The rule is not "be strict everywhere". It is: never let leniency manufacture a fact. A tolerant read of a document's shape loses nothing. A tolerant read of a version string produces an ordering that was not in the input, and then a verdict that was not in the input either.

What I would do differently

I would stop treating the unknown count as a defect to engineer down. My first instinct here was the wrong one: a long unknown list reads like the tool failing, and the obvious fix looks like a cleverer parser that gets an answer out of 2023-08-01 somehow. That instinct comes from the wrong domain. In payment systems I have spent years on the opposite reflex: an unsettled transfer is not a successful one, and the unknown state is the expensive one precisely because you cannot collapse it into either neighbour without lying. Vulnerability matching has the same shape. unknown with a reason attached is a work item for a named person; not_affected derived from a guess is a liability with a signature under it.

And I would write the order-independence test before the comparator, not after it. The property (same range, any permutation, one verdict) runs about ten lines, it fails immediately against a naive in-order walk, and it is probably the cheapest way to find out that your evaluator's answer depends on something as fragile as how a feed happened to serialise an array.

The parser is not a detail underneath the range. It is the range.

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: PaperPilot: Turning Messy GST Invoices into Clean Records with Gemma
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

PaperPilot is an invoice and expense assistant for freelancers, consultants, and small agencies.

Anyone who works for themselves ends up with a folder of PDF invoices and a dreaded tax season. Someone has to type every vendor, date, and total into a spreadsheet, spot the invoice that was uploaded twice, and remember who hasn't paid. In India there's an extra layer: GSTIN numbers and CGST, SGST, and IGST splits that generic tools handle poorly.

With PaperPilot you upload a digital PDF invoice and the app:

  • Extracts the vendor, invoice number, dates, subtotal, GST amounts, and total
  • Checks the numbers instead of trusting the AI blindly
  • Lets you review and fix anything before saving
  • Catches duplicate invoices before they are saved
  • Flags overdue invoices from their due dates
  • Matches a bank statement CSV to mark invoices as paid
  • Exports everything to CSV, with search and filters

Demo

paper-pilot-zq9h.onrender.com

Code

SahilNagpure07 / paper-pilot

🧾 PaperPilot: Invoice & Expense Assistant

PaperPilot reads PDF invoices with Gemma, an open-weight AI model, checks the results and organises everything into searchable records and CSV exports Built for freelancers, consultants, and small agencies.

Features

  • Upload digital PDF invoices (scanned or image files are not supported)
  • Gemma extracts vendor, dates, subtotal, tax and total
  • India GST support: GSTIN, CGST / SGST / IGST, HSN / SAC codes
  • Duplicate invoice detection
  • Overdue payment flags based on due date
  • Bank statement matching: upload a CSV and mark paid invoices automatically
  • Safety checks: totals that do not add up, bad GSTINs, or amounts missing from the document are flagged for review
  • Search, filter, and CSV export

Why an open model?

  • Open weights: Gemma's weights are public, so the same model can later be self-hosted by anyone who needs full control.
  • Low cost: hosted Gemma is inexpensive to call, which suits a…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The open model is Gemma. I use Gemma, Google's open-weight model, called through the Gemini API with a standard API key.

Pipeline:

  1. Read: PyMuPDF pulls the text out of a digital PDF.
  2. Redact: a small module blanks out emails, phone numbers, PAN, Aadhaar, and bank account numbers before anything is sent to the model. The GSTIN is kept, since it's a business number the app needs.
  3. Extract: Gemma returns the invoice fields as JSON. I prompt for a strict set of keys and parse the reply defensively (stripping code fences, converting numbers) because models don't always follow instructions perfectly.
  4. Validate: this is the part I care about most. Small models can misread numbers, so the app flags a subtotal plus tax that doesn't equal the total, a total that doesn't appear anywhere in the document, an invalid GSTIN, and unequal CGST and SGST. The AI suggests, the code checks, and the human confirms.
  5. Store and use: records go in SQLite. Duplicate detection, overdue flags, and bank matching are plain Python, not AI. I deliberately kept AI to the one task it's good at, which is reading messy layouts.

Stack: Python, Streamlit, PyMuPDF, SQLite, pandas, and Gemma via the Gemini API.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • No lock-in. The model is a single setting. Swapping to another Gemma model is one line, and the rest of the app doesn't change.
  • A path to full control. Because Gemma's weights are public, a business that doesn't want any data leaving its network can self-host the same model later. A closed model offers no such option, since you can only rent it.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Render
  • Best Use of Gemma

title: How I finally undestood what loosely coupled modules are
description:
Photo by Glen Carrie on Unsplash

The Intro

Here goes another one of those "it finally clicked" posts. This time it's about something you've probably heard a hundred times in code reviews, job interviews and conference talks: loosely coupled modules.

Everyone says it's good. Almost nobody shows you a case where you actually feel the difference.

So today we are going to build a tiny app that sends an email, break it, and then fix it in a way that will make you say "oh... that's why".

The What

First things first. If we ask Wikipedia, this is what we get:

In computing and systems design, a loosely coupled system is one in which components are weakly associated (have breakable relationships) with each other, and thus changes in one component least affect existence or performance of another component.

Crystal clear, right? Great, post over, go enjoy your day...

Nah, I'm messing with you. Definitions never clicked for me either.

Let's make it real instead. Picture this: we are building a web app with a "Sign up" form. When someone signs up, we want to send them a welcome email.

Simple, right?

To send real emails we are going to use Resend, which has a free tier and a very small API. And since we are using TypeScript and Node, the code is going to be as short as it gets.

The How

Here's the first (and most honest) version of our code:

// src/welcome.ts
import { Resend } from 'resend'

const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY)

export async function sendWelcomeEmail(to: string) {
  await resend.emails.send({
    from: 'onboarding@resend.dev',
    to,
    subject: 'Welcome!',
    text: 'Thanks for signing up 🤝',
  })
}

And our main:

// src/main.ts
import { sendWelcomeEmail } from './welcome.js'

await sendWelcomeEmail('chris@example.com')
console.log('Sent!')

Run it with a valid RESEND_API_KEY and the email shows up in our inbox a second later.

Ship it! 🚀

Now, let's say you keep working on the app. You run main.ts 20 more times while testing the sign up flow.

What happens?

  • Every run sends a real email.
  • Your coworkers get spammed when they test with their own address.
  • Resend's free tier starts counting those emails.
  • And if someone forgets to set RESEND_API_KEY... boom, the app crashes.

Not great, huh? 😅

What we really want is: send real emails only in production. Everywhere else, just let me see the email without it going anywhere.

Turns out there's a tool made exactly for that: Mailpit. It's a fake SMTP server with a little web UI where you can read every email your app "sent". We can run it with Docker in one line:

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit
    ports:
      - '1025:1025' # SMTP (your app talks to this one)
      - '8025:8025' # Web UI (you look at this one)

Run docker compose up -d and open http://localhost:8025. Empty inbox, for now.

Since Mailpit speaks SMTP, we can talk to it with Nodemailer. Let's add that to our function:

// src/welcome.ts
import { Resend } from 'resend'
import nodemailer from 'nodemailer'

const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY)
const smtp = nodemailer.createTransport({ host: 'localhost', port: 1025 })

export async function sendWelcomeEmail(to: string) {
  const message = {
    from: 'onboarding@resend.dev',
    to,
    subject: 'Welcome!',
    text: 'Thanks for signing up 🤝',
  }

  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') {
    await resend.emails.send(message)
  } else {
    await smtp.sendMail(message)
  }
}

Run main.ts again (without NODE_ENV), refresh Mailpit and... there it is!

Problem solved! 🎉

Now, be honest with me. Did something feel a little bit off while reading that code?

Let me help you out:

  • sendWelcomeEmail() is supposed to be about welcoming people. But now it also knows about Resend, Nodemailer, SMTP ports and NODE_ENV.
  • The next function (sendPasswordResetEmail()) will need the exact same if/else. And the next one. And the next one.
  • Want to try a third provider some day? Have fun finding every if in the project.
  • And the Resend client gets created at import time even when we will never use it. That's where the "forgot the API key" crash comes from.

This, right here, is what tightly coupled code looks like. Our welcome email is glued to two vendors and one environment variable. You cannot touch one without touching the others.

Let's fix it.

Step 1: describe what we need, not who does it

What does our app actually need? To send an email. That's it. It doesn't care who delivers it.

So let's write that down as an interface:

// src/mail/mailer.ts
export interface Email {
  to: string
  subject: string
  text: string
}

export interface Mailer {
  send(email: Email): Promise<void>
}

Notice there's no from here. The provider knows what address it is allowed to send from, our app doesn't need to.

Step 2: one class per provider

Now we give each vendor its own little box. Each class is the only file in the whole project that knows that vendor exists:

// src/mail/resend-mailer.ts
import { Resend } from 'resend'
import type { Email, Mailer } from './mailer.js'

export class ResendMailer implements Mailer {
  private readonly client: Resend

  constructor(apiKey: string) {
    this.client = new Resend(apiKey)
  }

  async send(email: Email) {
    const { error } = await this.client.emails.send({
      from: 'onboarding@resend.dev',
      ...email,
    })
    if (error) throw new Error(error.message)
  }
}

// src/mail/mailpit-mailer.ts
import nodemailer, { type Transporter } from 'nodemailer'
import type { Email, Mailer } from './mailer.js'

export class MailpitMailer implements Mailer {
  private readonly transport: Transporter

  constructor(host = 'localhost', port = 1025) {
    this.transport = nodemailer.createTransport({ host, port })
  }

  async send(email: Email) {
    await this.transport.sendMail({ from: 'dev@localhost', ...email })
  }
}

(Yes, this is TypeScript. If your thing is Kotlin, C#, Go or whatever else, the same idea maps over almost one to one. Pinky promise.)

Step 3: the welcome email goes back to being boring 

// src/welcome.ts
import type { Mailer } from './mail/mailer.js'

export async function sendWelcomeEmail(mailer: Mailer, to: string) {
  await mailer.send({
    to,
    subject: 'Welcome!',
    text: 'Thanks for signing up 🤝',
  })
}

Look at the imports. No Resend. No Nodemailer. No process.env. Just the shape of a thing that can send emails.

Step 4: decide once, at the front door

There's exactly one place in the app that knows which environment we are in, and that's where the app starts:

// src/main.ts
import { ResendMailer } from './mail/resend-mailer.js'
import { MailpitMailer } from './mail/mailpit-mailer.js'
import { sendWelcomeEmail } from './welcome.js'

const isProduction = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'

const mailer = isProduction
  ? new ResendMailer(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY!)
  : new MailpitMailer()

await sendWelcomeEmail(mailer, 'chris@example.com')
console.log('Sent!')

Now let's try it both ways.

Locally:

npx tsx src/main.ts

Refresh http://localhost:8025 and the email is right there. No API key, no internet, no spam.

And "in production":

NODE_ENV=production RESEND_API_KEY=re_123... npx tsx src/main.ts

Check your real inbox. Same code, same sendWelcomeEmail(), different delivery guy.

Quick note on the test account: Resend's free tier lets you send from onboarding@resend.dev only to the email you signed up with. So use that one as your to while testing and you will get the email without having to verify a domain.

The Why

So, what did we actually win here? Let's count:

  • sendWelcomeEmail() has one reason to change: the content of the welcome email. Not the vendor, not the environment.
  • The NODE_ENV check exists in exactly one line of the whole project. Add 10 more kinds of emails and that line doesn't move.
  • Want to try a third provider (SES, Postmark, you name it)? Write one new class, change one line in main.ts. Nothing else even knows it happened.
  • The Resend SDK is only imported by ResendMailer. If you never create one, you never touch it. The "forgot the API key" crash is gone for free.
  • And testing becomes stupidly easy: pass a Mailer that just pushes emails into an array and assert on it. No mocking libraries, no network.

That's what people mean when they say loosely coupled. Our welcome email and Resend used to be glued together. Now they are just two things that happen to agree on a tiny contract called Mailer.

The welcome email doesn't know Resend exists. Resend doesn't know the welcome email exists. And main.ts is the only one who introduces them to each other.

I know it looks like extra ceremony for a two-line email. The day you have to swap a vendor on a Friday afternoon and only one file changes, you will remember this post.

The Goodbye

And that's a wrap. If you've read How I finally understood what Encapsulation is, you might notice this is the same trick at a bigger scale: push the messy details behind a small, dull contract and let everything else lean on the dull thing. Dull is good. Dull doesn't wake you up at 3 AM.

Go send some fake emails. Happy coding 🤝

title: Build a Grok Voice 3.0 Voice Agent in Node.js: Mic In, Speaker Out, Live Transcripts
description:
You open a WebSocket to a speech-to-speech model, start streaming your microphone, and three things go wrong at once: the model answers itself because it hears its own voice through your speakers, your transcript prints the same sentence a dozen times, and when you ask "who are you?" it describes its origin wrong. All three have small, specific fixes, and this tutorial builds them in from the start.

Grok Voice 3.0 is xAI's speech-to-speech model for realtime voice agents, released on 14 October 2026: you stream 16-bit PCM audio over one WebSocket and the same model answers with audio, using events that xAI describes as compatible with the OpenAI Realtime API. By the end you will have a terminal voice agent in Node.js that listens to your mic, plays replies, prints live transcripts and calls a function, plus the browser variant that never exposes your API key.

Disclosure: I work on apimodels.app, the API gateway the examples connect to, and the relay behaviour described below comes from its source code.

What you need

  • Node.js 18 or newer and the ws package 8.x (pnpm add ws or npm install ws)
  • SoX on your PATH for microphone and speaker I/O: brew install sox on macOS, sudo apt install sox on Debian or Ubuntu. The script uses its rec and play commands.
  • An apimodels.app API key in the APIMODELS_API_KEY environment variable, with at least one minute of balance ($0.104), which the server checks before it accepts the connection
  • Headphones. With open speakers the model hears its own voice and keeps answering itself.

How a Grok Voice session flows

A Grok Voice 3.0 session is a single WebSocket that carries JSON events in both directions, with audio inside the events as base64. You connect, send one session.update to set the voice, instructions and turn detection, then keep appending microphone audio with input_audio_buffer.append. With turn_detection: {"type": "server_vad"} the server decides when you stopped talking and starts answering on its own; you never send a "done" signal.

The answer arrives as a stream: response.output_audio.delta events carry base64 PCM chunks to play in order, response.output_audio_transcript.delta events carry the text of what the model is saying, and response.done closes the turn. Your own speech comes back as conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.updated.

That last event is where the "same sentence a dozen times" bug comes from. xAI's input transcription is cumulative: each updated event carries the whole transcript so far, which may correct earlier words, not a delta to append. Code written for OpenAI-style incremental deltas prints every partial version.

The default audio format is 16-bit PCM, 24 kHz, mono, little-endian, in both directions, so 100 ms of audio is 2,400 samples or 4,800 bytes.

Step 1: Connect and surface handshake errors

Save the four blocks in Steps 1 to 4 into one file, voice-agent.mjs, in order. This first block opens the socket with your key in the Authorization header and prints the server's reason if the handshake is rejected.

// voice-agent.mjs (example). Node 18+, ws 8.x, SoX on PATH. Use headphones.
import { spawn } from "node:child_process";
import WebSocket from "ws";

const URL = "wss://api.apimodels.app/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-3.0";
const SOX = ["-q", "-t", "raw", "-r", "24000", "-e", "signed-integer", "-b", "16", "-c", "1", "-"];

const ws = new WebSocket(URL, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.APIMODELS_API_KEY}` },
});
const send = (event) => ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN && ws.send(JSON.stringify(event));

// A rejected handshake is a plain HTTP response with a JSON body:
// 401 bad key, 400 wrong model, 402 less than one minute of balance, 429 more than 5 sessions.
ws.on("unexpected-response", (_req, res) => {
  let body = "";
  res.on("data", (c) => (body += c));
  res.on("end", () => {
    console.error(`handshake rejected: ${res.statusCode} ${body}`);
    process.exit(1);
  });
});

With a wrong or missing key you see handshake rejected: 401 {"error":{"type":"invalid_api_key","code":"invalid_api_key","message":"Invalid or missing API key / client secret."}} and nothing is charged.

Step 2: Configure the session, identity included

As soon as the socket opens, send session.update. The voice, instructions and turn_detection fields sit directly under session.

ws.on("open", () => {
  send({
    type: "session.update",
    session: {
      voice: "eve", // one of 28 built-in voices; each one speaks every supported language
      instructions:
        "You are Grok Voice 3.0, a realtime voice assistant built by xAI, " +
        "answering for the Acme help desk. Keep answers under three sentences.",
      turn_detection: { type: "server_vad" },
      audio: {
        input: { format: { type: "audio/pcm", rate: 24000 } },
        output: { format: { type: "audio/pcm", rate: 24000 } },
      },
      tools: [
        {
          type: "function",
          name: "get_order_status",
          description: "Look up an order by its id",
          parameters: {
            type: "object",
            properties: { order_id: { type: "string" } },
            required: ["order_id"],
          },
        },
      ],
    },
  });
});

The first sentence of instructions is the fix for the third bug. Setting custom instructions replaces the model's default persona, and without an identity in your prompt the model may describe its origin incorrectly when a caller asks who it is. If your product has its own persona ("Mia from Acme"), write that instead; just write something.

Step 3: Stream the microphone in 100 ms frames

Start the mic only after the server confirms the session with session.updated, so your first words are not processed with default settings. SoX's rec writes raw PCM to stdout; the code cuts it into 4,800-byte frames so no 16-bit sample is ever split across two events.

let mic = null;
function startMic() {
  mic = spawn("rec", SOX, { stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"] }); // raw 16-bit PCM, 24 kHz, mono
  let pending = Buffer.alloc(0);
  mic.stdout.on("data", (chunk) => {
    pending = Buffer.concat([pending, chunk]);
    while (pending.length >= 4800) { // 100 ms = 2,400 samples x 2 bytes
      send({ type: "input_audio_buffer.append", audio: pending.subarray(0, 4800).toString("base64") });
      pending = pending.subarray(4800);
    }
  });
}

function newSpeaker() {
  const p = spawn("play", SOX, { stdio: ["pipe", "ignore", "ignore"] }); // reads raw PCM on stdin
  p.stdin.on("error", () => {}); // ignore EPIPE after we kill it for a barge-in
  return p;
}
let speaker = newSpeaker();

Step 4: Play replies, print transcripts, answer function calls

One message handler does the rest. Note the transcription case: it overwrites the current line instead of appending, because each event already holds the full sentence.

ws.on("message", (raw) => {
  const ev = JSON.parse(raw.toString());
  switch (ev.type) {
    case "session.updated":
      if (!mic) { startMic(); console.log("listening... (Ctrl+C to hang up)"); }
      break;

    case "input_audio_buffer.speech_started":
      // Caller started talking over the model: drop queued audio.
      // (Our browser playground handles this event the same way.)
      speaker.kill();
      speaker = newSpeaker();
      break;

    case "conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.updated":
    case "conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed":
      // Cumulative: overwrite the line, never append.
      process.stdout.write(`\r\x1b[2Kyou:  ${ev.transcript ?? ""}`);
      break;

    case "response.created":
      process.stdout.write("\ngrok: ");
      break;
    case "response.output_audio_transcript.delta":
      process.stdout.write(ev.delta);
      break;
    case "response.output_audio.delta":
      speaker.stdin.write(Buffer.from(ev.delta, "base64"));
      break;
    case "response.done":
      process.stdout.write("\n");
      break;

    case "response.function_call_arguments.done": {
      const args = JSON.parse(ev.arguments || "{}");
      const result = { order_id: args.order_id, status: "shipped" }; // replace with your lookup
      send({
        type: "conversation.item.create",
        item: { type: "function_call_output", call_id: ev.call_id, output: JSON.stringify(result) },
      });
      send({ type: "response.create" }); // ask the model to speak the result
      break;
    }

    case "error":
      console.error(`\n[error] ${ev.error?.code}: ${ev.error?.message}`);
      break;
  }
});

function hangUp() { mic?.kill(); speaker.kill(); ws.close(); }
process.on("SIGINT", hangUp);
ws.on("close", (code, reason) => {
  console.log(`\nsession closed (${code} ${reason})`);
  mic?.kill(); speaker.kill();
});

Closing the socket is not cleanup trivia: it is what stops the billing clock. Sessions are billed by connected time, and the relay only treats a session as idle after 10 minutes with no client events at all. A process that keeps streaming microphone audio, even silence, is never idle and runs until the 60-minute cap.

Verify it works

Run it with headphones on:

APIMODELS_API_KEY=your_key_here node voice-agent.mjs

You should see listening..., then your own words appear on a you: line that updates in place while you speak. Ask "Who are you, and where is order A-1001?" The reply should introduce itself as Grok Voice 3.0 built by xAI (from your instructions), and the function call should come back as a spoken "shipped". Press Ctrl+C; the session appears as one record in your console call history with its duration and cost.

Do the same from a browser

Browsers cannot set headers on a WebSocket, so never put the API key in front-end code. Your server mints a short-lived token and the page passes it as a subprotocol.

// On your server (example): exchange the key for a token valid 10 to 600 seconds (default 60)
export async function mintRealtimeToken() {
  const res = await fetch("https://api.apimodels.app/v1/realtime/client_secrets", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.APIMODELS_API_KEY}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ expires_after: { seconds: 60 } }),
  });
  return res.json(); // { value, expires_at }
}

// In the browser (example), from a click handler so audio is allowed to start
const { value } = await (await fetch("/api/realtime-token", { method: "POST" })).json();
const ws = new WebSocket(
  "wss://api.apimodels.app/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-3.0",
  ["xai-client-secret." + value],
);

The token only governs when a connection can be opened; an open session keeps running after it expires. The rest of the event handling is the same as in Node. For microphone capture, use an AudioWorklet and resample to 24 kHz yourself: Firefox refuses to connect a microphone to an AudioContext created at a non-default sample rate, which is why our own browser playground captures at the device rate and resamples in JavaScript. The Grok Voice 3.0 API docs on apimodels.app have a complete browser example.

Where apimodels.app fits

apimodels.app is a multi-model API gateway: one API key and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for 140+ image, video, audio and language models. Most mainstream models there have multiple upstream channels with automatic failover, failed requests are not charged, long jobs run asynchronously with webhooks, and any request's charge can be looked up with GET /v1/records/{id}. Grok Voice 3.0 itself has a single upstream route, so there is no failover for it; a session that cannot reach the model is not charged.

For this tutorial it supplied the endpoint, the key and the billing: $0.104 per minute of connected session, billed per second (a 90-second call costs $0.156), $0.0052 per typed text message, and no extra fee for function calls. You can also talk to the model with your microphone on the Grok Voice 3.0 model page before writing any code.

Do not route through it if you only use xAI, already have direct xAI access and want the lowest per-minute price: connect to xAI directly, where the same events work. The same goes if you need sessions longer than 60 minutes, more than 5 concurrent sessions per account, or xAI's server-side tools (web_search, x_search, file_search, mcp) inside the voice session, which the relay rejects.

Common errors

  • handshake rejected: 401 ... invalid_api_key: missing or wrong key, or a browser trying to send the key as a header. Use the Authorization header from Node, or a client secret from a browser.
  • handshake rejected: 400 ... "Model gpt-realtime is not available for realtime. Use grok-voice-3.0.": the model query parameter is wrong. Use grok-voice-3.0 (or grok-voice-latest).
  • handshake rejected: 404 ... Unknown API endpoint: GET /api/v1/realtime: you connected to apimodels.app/api/v1/realtime. The endpoint only exists on api.apimodels.app, because the main site's hosting layer cannot proxy WebSockets.
  • 402 insufficient_balance at connect, or an error event with that code mid-call: balance below one minute. Each minute is charged when it starts, so the session closes when the next minute cannot be covered.
  • 429 too_many_sessions: more than 5 open sessions on one account. Close sockets you no longer use.
  • [error] unsupported_tool: your session.update included web_search, x_search, file_search or mcp. Only function tools are accepted.
  • The model keeps answering itself: speaker echo. Use headphones, or echo cancellation in the browser.
  • The same sentence printed many times: you appended cumulative transcription events. Overwrite instead.

Limits

  • This script is an example built from the documented event protocol; run it once with headphones before you build on it. SoX device handling differs by OS, and the SoX arguments above are the only platform-specific part.
  • Barge-in via input_audio_buffer.speech_started is what our browser playground uses; xAI's documentation page does not list that event, so treat it as best-effort.
  • Sessions end at 60 minutes with a session_limit error; reconnect to continue.

What did you use for audio I/O in Node: SoX, a native addon, or a browser-only setup? I'd like to know what held up in production.

This post was written with AI assistance from the apimodels.app source code and public docs, and reviewed before publishing.
