title: Joins in SQL; A Deep Dive
description:
In SQL, joins are operations used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them. Joins are essential in relational databases because they allow you to retrieve data that is spread across multiple tables and present it in a unified way. This is particularly useful in normalized databases where related data is stored in separate tables to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity.

Why do we use Joins?
1.Data Normalization: In relational databases, data is often divided into multiple tables to eliminate redundancy. Joins allow you to reassemble this data as needed.
2.Complex Queries: Joins enable complex queries that can extract meaningful insights from multiple related tables.
3.Data Integrity: By linking tables through joins, you maintain data integrity and consistency, ensuring that related data is accurate and synchronized.

Types of SQL Joins
There are various types of SQL joins. Let’s explore some of the most widely used ones:

1.INNER JOIN
An INNER JOIN is one of the most used joins in SQL. It returns only the rows that have matching values in both tables. If there is no match, the row is not included in the result set.
The INNER JOIN essentially combines the data from two or more tables based on a related column, and it filters out rows that do not satisfy the join condition.

Query

SELECT columns
FROM table1
INNER JOIN table2
ON table1.common_column = table2.common_column;

•table1 and table2 are the names of the tables you want to join.
•common_column is the column that exists in both tables and is used as the join condition.
•columns are the columns you want to select in the result set.

2.LEFT JOIN
A LEFT JOIN, also referred to as a LEFT OUTER JOIN, is a type of SQL join where all rows from the left table (table1) are returned regardless of whether there is a match in the right table (table2). It includes the matching rows from the right table based on a related column specified in the ON clause of the LEFT JOIN statement.

This join condition ensures that for each row from the left table, the LEFT JOIN includes the corresponding matching rows from the right table in the result set. If there is no match found in the right table, NULL values are returned for the columns from the right table.

Query

SELECT columns
FROM table1
LEFT JOIN table2
ON table1.common_column = table2.common_column;

•SELECT columns specifies the columns you want to select from the combined result set.
•table1 and table2 are the names of the tables you want to join.
•LEFT JOIN indicates that you're performing a left join.
•ON table1.common_column = table2.common_column specifies the join condition, where common_column is the column that exists in both tables and is used to match rows between them.

3.RIGHT JOIN
A RIGHT JOIN, also known as RIGHT OUTER JOIN, is a type of SQL join that returns all rows from the right table (table2) and includes matching rows from the left table (table1). The join condition is based on a related column between the two tables, specified in the ON clause of the RIGHT JOIN statement.

The RIGHT JOIN ensures that all rows from the right table are retained in the result set, and for each row from the right table, it includes the corresponding matching rows from the left table based on the join condition. If there is no match found in the left table, NULL values are returned for the columns from the left table.

Query

SELECT columns
FROM table1
RIGHT JOIN table2
ON table1.common_column = table2.common_column;

•SELECT columns specifies the columns you want to select from the combined result set.
•table1 and table2 are the names of the tables you want to join.
•RIGHT JOIN indicates that you're performing a right join.
•ON table1.common_column = table2.common_column specifies the join condition, where common_column is the column that exists in both tables and is used to match rows between them.

Conclusion
SQL joins are integral for combining data from multiple related tables to generate meaningful relationships, that facilitate better insights. Understanding INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and RIGHT JOIN helps us retrieve the exact data needed for the analysis.

title: Idempotency Keys - The Double-Charge Trap
description:
The Problem

You click Pay. The server charges your card, but the response is lost on the way back (network drop, timeout, tab freeze). The UI thinks it failed, so you click Pay again and get charged twice.

A timeout means "I don't know what happened", not "payment failed".

The Idea

Idempotent = doing the same thing twice has the same effect as doing it once.

Action Repeat it twice Idempotent?
Set notifications to OFF Still OFF Yes
Add USD 50 to the balance USD 100 added No
Create a payment Two charges No, unless we add a key

An idempotency key is a unique ID for one payment attempt. The UI sends it with the request. If the same key arrives again, the backend says "I've already handled this one" and returns the saved result instead of charging again.

  • UI's job: create the key once, keep it, and resend the same key on every retry.
  • Backend's job: remember each key and its result, so repeats are not executed again.

Full Flow Diagram

Example: user pays USD 50 for order O100.

sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant UI as Browser UI
    participant SS as sessionStorage
    participant API as Backend
    participant DB as Database
    participant PSP as Payment Provider

    User->>UI: Click "Pay"
    UI->>SS: Key for O100?
    SS-->>UI: None
    UI->>UI: key = crypto.randomUUID() → K1
    UI->>SS: Save payment-key:O100 = K1
    UI->>UI: Disable Pay button, show "Processing..."

    UI->>API: POST /orders/O100/pay<br/>Idempotency-Key: K1
    API->>DB: Insert (user, K1, O100, processing)
    DB-->>API: Inserted (K1 is new)
    API->>PSP: Charge USD 50 (provider key derived from K1)
    PSP-->>API: Success, payment P900
    API->>DB: Update K1 → succeeded, result P900
    API--xUI: 200 OK (response LOST)

    UI->>UI: Timeout → show "Checking payment status..."
    UI->>SS: Read key for O100
    SS-->>UI: K1 (same key)
    UI->>API: POST /orders/O100/pay<br/>Idempotency-Key: K1 (retry)
    API->>DB: Find K1
    DB-->>API: K1 = succeeded, P900
    Note over API,PSP: Provider NOT called again
    API-->>UI: 200 OK, payment P900 (saved result)
    UI->>SS: Remove payment-key:O100
    UI-->>User: Show receipt ✅ (charged once)

Step-by-Step

Step 1: User clicks "Pay" — UI gets a key

The UI first checks whether this order already has a key (from an earlier attempt or before a refresh).

  • Key found → reuse it. This is a retry of the same payment.
  • No key → generate a new one with crypto.randomUUID(). 
payment-key:O100  →  K1   (e.g. "6f13d95a-e6c1-4bf2-9459-99b502098dc1")

Use crypto.randomUUID() — it is random and practically never collides. Do not use Date.now(), Math.random(), or the amount; two different payments could produce the same value.

Step 2: Save the key BEFORE sending the request 

sessionStorage.setItem("payment-key:O100", key);

Save first, then send. If the page crashes or reloads mid-request, the key is still there and the next attempt reuses it.

Where to store on the UI:

Place Survives refresh? Use it?
Variable / React state No Only for the current screen
sessionStorage Yes (same tab) Recommended — cleared when the tab closes
localStorage Yes (even after browser restart) Avoid — leftover keys on shared devices, shared across tabs
Cookie Yes Avoid — sent with every request for no reason

Also disable the Pay button while the request is in flight. This stops accidental double clicks, but it is only a UX helper; the key is the real protection.

Step 3: Send the payment request with the key 

POST /orders/O100/pay
Idempotency-Key: K1
Cookie: session=...   (user is logged in)

The UI sends only the order ID and key. The backend loads the amount from the order itself; never trust a price sent by the browser.

Step 4: Backend checks the key

Why does the backend store the key? Because the UI can't know whether the first request was charged — only the backend can remember.

The backend saves one row per key:

User Key Order Status Result
U1 K1 O100 processing → succeeded P900

When a request arrives:

Backend finds... Backend does
K1 not found New payment: save processing, charge, save result, respond
K1 = processing Another request is already charging → reply "in progress, check again" (e.g. 409)
K1 = succeeded / declined Return the saved result. Do not charge again
K1 exists but for a different order Reject (e.g. 422) — key misuse

The insert must be atomic (a unique constraint on user + key). If two identical requests arrive at the same moment, only one insert succeeds, so only one charge happens.

Step 5: Backend charges and saves the result

The backend calls the payment provider and passes its own provider idempotency key derived from K1, saved before the call. If the backend crashes after the provider charged but before saving the result, a retry reuses that provider key, so the provider returns the original charge instead of creating a new one.

Then it updates the row to succeeded with result P900 and responds.

Step 6: UI handles the response

What the UI gets What it means UI action Key?
200 success Paid Show receipt Remove key
Card declined (clear failure) Not charged Show error, let user try again Remove key; next try gets a new one
409 in progress Still charging Show "Processing...", check again shortly Keep
Timeout / network error / 5xx Unknown! Show "Checking payment status...", retry Keep

The key rule: only remove the key when you know the final outcome.

Step 7: Retry after timeout

The UI retries with the same K1 (a few times, with increasing delays like 1s, 2s, 4s).

Two possible cases, both safe:

  • First request never reached the backend → K1 is new → backend charges once now.
  • First request was already charged → K1 = succeeded → backend returns P900, no second charge.

That's the whole point: the UI doesn't need to know which case happened.

Step 8: User refreshes the page 

flowchart TD
    A[Page loads / user clicks Pay] --> B{Key for O100 in sessionStorage?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Reuse the same key]
    B -- No --> D[Generate new key with crypto.randomUUID]
    D --> E[Save key in sessionStorage]
    C --> F[POST /orders/O100/pay with key]
    E --> F
    F --> G{Response}
    G -- Success --> H[Show receipt, remove key]
    G -- Declined --> I[Show error, remove key]
    G -- In progress / timeout / 5xx --> J[Show 'Checking...', keep key, retry later]
    J --> F

After refresh, the UI finds K1 in sessionStorage and sends the request with K1 again. The backend returns the saved result or "in progress" — never a second charge.

UI Code Example

Illustrative only; status codes depend on your API.

function getOrCreateKey(orderId) {
  const name = `payment-key:${orderId}`;
  let key = sessionStorage.getItem(name);
  if (!key) {
    key = crypto.randomUUID();
    sessionStorage.setItem(name, key); // save BEFORE sending
  }
  return key;
}

async function pay(orderId) {
  const key = getOrCreateKey(orderId);

  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/orders/${orderId}/pay`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Idempotency-Key": key },
      credentials: "include",
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000),
    });

    if (res.ok) {
      sessionStorage.removeItem(`payment-key:${orderId}`);
      return { status: "paid", payment: await res.json() };
    }
    if (res.status === 402) {
      // Clear decline: not charged, a new attempt may use a new key
      sessionStorage.removeItem(`payment-key:${orderId}`);
      return { status: "declined" };
    }
    // 409 in progress, 5xx, etc.: outcome unknown, keep the key
    return { status: "unknown" };
  } catch {
    // Timeout or network error: outcome unknown, keep the key
    return { status: "unknown" };
  }
}

On "unknown", show "Checking payment status..." and call pay(orderId) again after a delay — it automatically reuses the same key.

sessionStorage can throw (e.g. storage full or blocked). In that case, keep the key in memory for this page and avoid letting the user start a fresh payment while one is unresolved.

When Is a New Key Needed?

Situation Same key or new?
Timeout, network error, server error Same
Page refresh during payment Same (read from sessionStorage)
User double-clicks Pay Same
Payment succeeded No more payment needed
Card clearly declined, user tries again New
User changes amount / card / order New (old attempt must be finished first)
A different order New

Simple rule: same intention → same key. New intention → new key.

Security Checklist

  • Store only the key in sessionStorage. Never store card number, CVV, or tokens.
  • The key is not a password. The backend must still check that the logged-in user owns order O100.
  • The backend scopes keys per user, so one user's key can't read another user's payment.
  • Never trust amount or status from the browser; the backend decides both.
  • Clear payment keys on logout.

What If sessionStorage Is Lost?

New tab, cleared storage, or another device → the UI generates a new key for the same order. The idempotency key can't catch this, so the backend needs one more rule:

An order that is already paid, or has a payment in progress, cannot start another charge.

Keys stop duplicate requests. Order rules stop duplicate payments for the same order. You need both.

System Design: Key Creation, Change Detection, and Cancellation

So far, one key = one payment. Real checkouts are messier: the user changes the cart, applies a coupon, or switches cards while a payment is unclear. This section designs a setup that answers three questions:

  1. When should the UI create a key?
  2. How do UI and backend detect that the payment details changed?
  3. How is an old attempt safely cancelled so a new key can be used?

Core idea: a key belongs to a checkout snapshot

A key represents "pay for exactly this checkout". The checkout is identified by a small snapshot:

Snapshot field Changes when...
orderId A different order
orderVersion Backend bumps it on any change to items, quantity, coupon, address, or total
paymentMethodId User picks another saved card or method (an ID like pm_123, never the card number) 
Same snapshot      → same intention → reuse the key
Different snapshot → new intention  → old attempt must be finished/cancelled, then a new key

orderVersion is the important part: the UI doesn't have to compare cart items itself. The backend increases the version whenever anything affecting the price changes.

Architecture 

flowchart LR
    subgraph Browser
        UI[Checkout UI]
        KM[Key Manager]
        SS[(sessionStorage)]
        UI --> KM
        KM <--> SS
    end

    KM -->|Pay / Cancel + Idempotency-Key| GW[API Gateway<br/>auth, rate limit]
    GW --> PS[Payment Service<br/>idempotency check]
    GW --> OS[Order Service<br/>cart, orderVersion, lock]
    PS <--> IDB[(Idempotency Store<br/>key, fingerprint, status, result)]
    PS <--> OS
    PS -->|charge with provider key| PSP[Payment Provider]
    PSP -->|webhook: final result| WH[Webhook Handler]
    WH --> PS
    RJ[Reconciliation Job] -->|resolve stuck attempts| PS
    CJ[Cleanup Job] -->|expire old finished keys| IDB
Component Responsibility
Key Manager (UI) Creates, reuses, stores, and clears keys based on the snapshot
API Gateway Authenticates the user, rate-limits Pay clicks
Order Service Owns the cart and orderVersion; blocks cart edits while a payment is active
Payment Service Checks the key, compares fingerprints, charges, saves results, handles cancel
Idempotency Store Database table with a unique constraint; the source of truth. A cache like Redis can speed up lookups but must not be the only store
Webhook Handler Receives the provider's final result if the original response was lost
Reconciliation Job Periodically asks the provider about attempts stuck in processing
Cleanup Job Deletes finished keys after the retry window (e.g. 24h). Never deletes processing ones

Data model

Idempotency store (one row per key):

Column Example Purpose
user_id + key U1 + K1 Unique together, so duplicates can't both insert
order_id O100 Which order this attempt pays
fingerprint hash of O100, v3, 5000, USD, pm_123 Detects the same key reused with different details
status processing, succeeded, declined, failed, cancelled Current state
response { paymentId: "P900" } Saved result to replay
provider_key derived from K1, saved before charging Prevents duplicate charges at the provider
expires_at now + 24h Cleanup time (only once finished)

Order (relevant columns):

Column Example Purpose
version 3 Increases on every cart/price change
status unpaid / paid Paid orders can't be charged again
active_attempt K1 or empty Only one payment may be in progress per order

The backend calculates the fingerprint from its own data (loaded order + amount), not from values the browser claims.

Attempt lifecycle 

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> processing: Pay request accepted (new key)
    [*] --> cancelled: Cancel arrives before Pay
    processing --> succeeded: Provider approved
    processing --> declined: Provider declined
    processing --> processing: Provider timeout, waiting for webhook / reconciliation
    processing --> failed: Reconciliation found no charge
    succeeded --> [*]
    declined --> [*]
    failed --> [*]
    cancelled --> [*]
  • Cancel is only possible before charging starts. Once processing, the UI must wait for the final result.
  • A succeeded payment cannot be "cancelled". Undoing it is a refund, a separate operation with its own key.

When should the UI create a key?

Moment Create a key? Why
Checkout page loads No User hasn't decided to pay; details may still change
User edits cart / coupon / address No Nothing to pay yet
User clicks Pay, no saved attempt Yes Intention is now fixed. Bind the key to the current snapshot
User clicks Pay again, same snapshot No, reuse Same intention (retry, double click, refresh)
Snapshot changed while an attempt is unresolved Not yet Cancel/resolve the old attempt first
Old attempt declined, failed, or cancelled Yes, on next Pay Previous intention is finished, nothing was charged
Old attempt succeeded No Order is paid. Show the receipt

Rule: create the key at the moment of commitment (the Pay click), never earlier.

Backend rules on POST /orders/O100/pay

The request now carries the snapshot:

POST /orders/O100/pay
Idempotency-Key: K1
Content-Type: application/json

{ "orderVersion": 3, "paymentMethodId": "pm_123" }

The backend checks in this order:

  1. Authenticate and confirm the user owns O100.
  2. Look up the key. If it already exists:
    • Fingerprint differs → 422 KEY_REUSED_WITH_DIFFERENT_DETAILS. Nothing is charged.
    • succeeded / declined / failed → replay the saved result.
    • processing → 409 IN_PROGRESS.
    • cancelled → 409 ATTEMPT_CANCELLED. This blocks a late, delayed request from charging after the user cancelled.
  3. New key. In one database transaction:
    • Request orderVersion ≠ current version → 409 ORDER_CHANGED (UI must refresh the checkout).
    • Order is paid or already has an active_attempt → 409 PAYMENT_ALREADY_ACTIVE.
    • Otherwise insert the key as processing and set order.active_attempt = K1.
  4. Charge using the saved provider key, then save the result:
    • Success → key succeeded, order paid.
    • Decline → key declined, clear active_attempt.
    • Timeout → stays processing; webhook or reconciliation finishes it later.

Key lookup comes before the version check, so a retry of an already-paid attempt still gets its saved receipt.

Cart edits while a payment is active

The Order Service rejects cart changes while active_attempt is set:

PATCH /orders/O100/cart  →  409 PAYMENT_IN_PROGRESS

The UI also disables editing during payment. The backend check is what actually guarantees it (another tab or device could try to edit).

Cancel endpoint 

POST /orders/O100/payment-attempts/cancel
Content-Type: application/json

{ "key": "K1" }

The key goes in the body, not the URL, so it doesn't end up in access logs or browser history.

Backend finds K1... Backend does Response
Not found (Pay never arrived) Inserts K1 as cancelled (a "tombstone") cancelled
processing Cannot cancel, a charge may be happening processing — wait
declined / failed / cancelled Nothing to do Same status
succeeded Cannot cancel succeeded — show receipt or offer refund

Why insert a tombstone for an unknown key? Because the original Pay request might be stuck in the network and arrive later. The tombstone uses the same unique (user_id, key) slot, so whichever arrives first wins, and the late Pay is rejected instead of charging.

Scenario: user changes the cart after a timeout 

sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant UI as Checkout UI
    participant SS as sessionStorage
    participant API as Backend

    User->>UI: Click Pay (cart v3, card pm_123)
    UI->>SS: Save {key: K1, snapshot: "v3:pm_123"}
    UI->>API: POST /pay, key K1, v3
    API--xUI: Timeout (outcome unknown)
    UI-->>User: "Checking payment status..."

    User->>UI: "I want to change my cart"
    UI->>API: Cancel K1
    alt K1 never reached backend
        API->>API: Insert K1 as cancelled (tombstone)
        API-->>UI: cancelled
        UI->>SS: Remove K1
        UI-->>User: Cart unlocked
        User->>UI: Edit cart → backend bumps to v4
        User->>UI: Click Pay
        UI->>SS: Save {key: K2, snapshot: "v4:pm_123"}
        UI->>API: POST /pay, key K2, v4
        API-->>UI: Success ✅
        Note over API: If delayed K1 arrives now → cancelled, no charge
    else K1 is processing
        API-->>UI: processing
        UI-->>User: "Payment in progress, please wait"
    else K1 already succeeded
        API-->>UI: succeeded, P900
        UI->>SS: Remove K1
        UI-->>User: Show receipt (refund if they still want changes)
    end

Scenario: backend crashes mid-payment (K1 stuck in processing)

The key reached the backend and was saved as processing, but the status was never updated. Now the user retries with K1. What happens?

Why K1 gets stuck:

1. UI sends Pay with K1
2. Backend saves K1 = processing (+ provider key PK1)   ✅ saved
3. Backend calls the provider
4. One of these happens:
   a) Backend crashes before or during the provider call  → maybe NOT charged
   b) Provider charged, backend crashed before saving      → charged
   c) Provider is slow or timed out                       → unknown
5. K1 is still "processing" in the DB

The backend itself doesn't know whether money moved.

What the retry does:

UI      -> Backend: Pay O100 with K1 (retry)
Backend -> DB:      Find K1
DB      -> Backend: K1 = processing
Backend -> UI:      409 "Payment in progress"   (provider NOT called)
UI:     shows "Checking payment status...", asks again in a few seconds

Rule: a retry request never starts a charge for a key that is already processing. It could be case (b) or (c), where money already moved or is moving.

Who fixes the stuck status?

  1. Provider webhook (usually first). When the provider finishes the charge, it notifies the backend's webhook handler, which updates K1 to succeeded or declined.
  2. Reconciliation job (safety net). Every minute or so, it finds attempts stuck in processing for longer than a threshold (e.g. 2 minutes) and asks the provider about them using PK1, which was saved with K1 before calling the provider.
Provider says (for PK1) Reconciliation job does
Charge succeeded K1 → succeeded, save P900, order → paid
Charge declined K1 → declined, unlock the order
No charge found (crashed before calling) Retry the charge with the same PK1, or mark K1 failed (not charged) and unlock the order

Retrying with the same PK1 is safe: if the charge already exists, the provider returns it instead of creating a second one.

If the provider can't be reached, or offers no idempotency or status lookup, K1 stays processing and the order stays locked. It is flagged for manual review, never charged blindly.

sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as Checkout UI
    participant API as Backend
    participant DB as Database
    participant PSP as Payment Provider
    participant RJ as Webhook / Reconciliation

    UI->>API: Pay with K1
    API->>DB: K1 = processing, save PK1
    API->>PSP: Charge with PK1
    PSP->>PSP: Charge succeeds
    Note over API: 💥 Backend crashes. K1 still processing
    API--xUI: No response

    UI->>API: Retry with K1
    API->>DB: Find K1 → processing
    API-->>UI: 409 In progress (no charge)
    UI->>UI: "Checking payment status..."

    RJ->>PSP: Status of PK1?
    PSP-->>RJ: Succeeded, P900
    RJ->>DB: K1 = succeeded, P900, order paid

    UI->>API: Retry with K1
    API->>DB: Find K1 → succeeded
    API-->>UI: 200 Paid, P900 (saved result)
    UI->>UI: Show receipt, remove K1

Timeline:

12:00:00  UI: Pay with K1
12:00:00  Backend: K1 = processing, PK1 saved
12:00:01  Backend calls provider with PK1 → provider charges
12:00:01  Backend CRASHES (K1 still processing)
12:00:15  UI timeout → "Checking payment status..."
12:00:20  UI retries K1 → 409 in progress (no charge)
12:00:30  UI retries K1 → 409 in progress (no charge)
12:00:40  Webhook arrives: PK1 succeeded → K1 = succeeded, P900
12:00:45  UI retries K1 → 200 "Paid, P900" (saved result)
          UI shows receipt, removes K1 from sessionStorage
          Customer charged ONCE ✅

If the webhook never arrives, the reconciliation job performs the same update around 12:02.

What the user sees:

  • While processing: "Payment in progress, please don't close this page." Pay button and cart stay locked.
  • After a long wait (e.g. 1-2 minutes): "We're confirming your payment. We'll email you when it's done." The UI can stop polling; the backend still finishes the work.
  • On refresh: the UI reads K1 from sessionStorage and asks again, getting the latest status.
  • If the attempt ends as failed (not charged), the backend replays it like a decline (e.g. 402 in the UI example), so the UI removes K1 and the next Pay creates a new key.

Why it's safe:

Protection Prevents
K1 saved as processing before charging A retry starting a second charge
PK1 saved before calling the provider The provider creating two charges
Webhook + reconciliation job K1 staying stuck forever
Order lock (active_attempt) A new key starting another payment for the same order

Key Manager code (UI)

Illustrative; extends the earlier example with a snapshot and cancel.

const nameFor = (orderId) => `payment-attempt:${orderId}`;
const snapshotOf = (c) => `${c.orderVersion}:${c.paymentMethodId}`;

// Called only when the user clicks Pay
function getOrCreateAttempt(checkout) {
  const name = nameFor(checkout.orderId);
  const saved = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(name) ?? "null");
  const snapshot = snapshotOf(checkout);

  if (saved && saved.snapshot === snapshot) {
    return saved; // same intention: reuse key
  }
  if (saved) {
    // Details changed but the old attempt is unresolved
    throw new Error("Resolve the previous payment attempt first");
  }

  const attempt = { key: crypto.randomUUID(), snapshot };
  sessionStorage.setItem(name, JSON.stringify(attempt)); // save BEFORE sending
  return attempt;
}

// Called when the user wants to change details during an unclear payment
async function cancelAttempt(orderId) {
  const saved = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(nameFor(orderId)) ?? "null");
  if (!saved) return { status: "none" };

  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/orders/${orderId}/payment-attempts/cancel`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      credentials: "include",
      body: JSON.stringify({ key: saved.key }),
    });
    if (!res.ok) return { status: "unknown" }; // keep key, try later

    const { status } = await res.json();
    if (["cancelled", "declined", "failed", "succeeded"].includes(status)) {
      sessionStorage.removeItem(nameFor(orderId)); // final: key no longer needed
    }
    return { status }; // "processing" → keep key and wait
  } catch {
    return { status: "unknown" }; // network error: keep key
  }
}

UI reactions:

  • cancelled / declined → unlock the cart; the next Pay creates a new key.
  • processing / unknown → keep the cart locked, show "Payment in progress".
  • succeeded → show the receipt; offer a refund if the user still wants changes.
  • Pay returns 409 ORDER_CHANGED → the order changed elsewhere (another tab). Reload the checkout, show the new total, and let the user confirm. The old key was never accepted, so remove it; the confirmation Pay creates a new key.

Design summary

Concern Handled by
Create key at the right time UI Key Manager, on Pay click only
Reuse on retry / refresh UI snapshot match + sessionStorage
Detect changed details with the same key Backend fingerprint check (422)
Detect stale checkout orderVersion check (409 ORDER_CHANGED)
Prevent edits during payment Order lock (active_attempt)
Cancel before charging Cancel endpoint + tombstone
Late request after cancel Tombstone blocks it
Lost response / crash Saved result, provider key, webhook, reconciliation
Key stuck in processing Retries get 409, reconciliation resolves via provider key
Storage growth Cleanup job removes finished keys after the retry window

Summary 

Click Pay
  → UI: reuse key, or create one with crypto.randomUUID()
  → UI: save key in sessionStorage
  → UI: POST with Idempotency-Key
  → Backend: new key? charge and save result. Known key? return saved result
  → UI: success/decline → remove key | unknown → keep key and retry

title: TrafficMirror: The Definitive Guide to Zero-Risk Production Traffic Shadowing and Automated Regression Testing
description:
In modern distributed systems, testing in staging environments is fundamentally broken. Synthetic load generators, mock services, and sanitized database dumps fail to replicate the sheer entropy, concurrency spikes, edge-case payloads, and network anomalies inherent to live production environments. As systems grow in complexity, the phrase "it worked in staging" has transitioned from an industry joke to a multi-million-dollar operational liability.

Deploying untested regressions, unoptimized database queries, or breaking schema updates directly to production endangers revenue and brand equity. While blue-green and canary deployments mitigate some blast radiuses, they still expose a percentage of live users to potential failures.

Enter TrafficMirror: the next-generation, high-throughput, cloud-native traffic replication, shadowing, and real-time diffing engine.

Designed for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), Platform Architects, and Enterprise Engineering teams, TrafficMirror transparently duplicates real-world HTTP, gRPC, and raw TCP traffic at the network layer and replays it asynchronously against candidate clusters—delivering zero-latency-impact validation before a single user ever touches new code.

1. The Architectural Impasse of Modern QA

Traditional verification pipelines rely on three outdated assumptions:

  1. Mocks represent reality: Handcrafted mocks drift from production API contracts within days of deployment.
  2. Synthetic tests catch edge cases: Synthetic testing tools simulate expected behaviors, whereas production traffic is defined by unexpected behaviors.
  3. Canaries isolate risk entirely: A canary deployment routing 1% of live traffic to a faulty microservice still subjects hundreds or thousands of paying users to 500-series errors or corrupted state transitions. 
[ Traditional Canary Deployments ]
User Request ---> [ Ingress Router ] 
                        │
                        ├── (99%) ──> [ Production Service v1.0 ] (Safe)
                        └── (1%)  ──> [ Canary Service v1.1 ]    (Real Users Impacted on Failure)

[ TrafficMirror Architecture ]
User Request ---> [ Ingress / eBPF Tap ]
                        │
                        ├── (Primary Sync) ────> [ Production Service v1.0 ] ---> Response to User
                        │
                        └── (Async Shadow) ───> [ TrafficMirror Engine ]
                                                        │
                                                        ├── (Sanitization / PII Scrub)
                                                        └── (Zero-Impact Replay) ──> [ Candidate Service v1.1 ]
                                                                                              │
                                                                [ Diff Engine & Analytics ] <─┘

TrafficMirror inverts this paradigm. By tapping directly into the network data plane (via eBPF hooks or high-performance sidecars), TrafficMirror duplicates inbound requests, scrubs sensitive data at the wire level, and asynchronously streams the payload to non-production clusters. Responses from the target services are intercepted, compared, and discarded—guaranteeing that zero live users are affected by regressions, memory leaks, or unhandled exceptions.

2. Core Technical Architecture of TrafficMirror

TrafficMirror is engineered in Rust to achieve single-digit microsecond overhead, leveraging memory safety, lock-free concurrency, and asynchronous I/O primitives.

A. The Capture Plane: Kernel-Level Packet Interception

Instead of routing production traffic through heavy, unoptimized application-level proxies, TrafficMirror utilizes eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) at the Linux socket layer (sockops / tc egress/ingress hooks).

When a TCP handshake completes on a designated port, TrafficMirror clones the sk_buff buffer at the kernel level. This ensures:

  • Zero context-switching penalties: The kernel duplicates the data stream without traversing user-space boundaries twice.
  • No latency impact on the primary path: The downstream client receives the response directly from the stable upstream service, completely decoupled from shadow stream execution.

B. Payload Sanitization & Dynamic PII Redaction

Replaying production payloads into staging environments presents immediate compliance hurdles (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS). TrafficMirror features a zero-allocation streaming parser that identifies and transforms sensitive fields on the fly:

// Original Inbound Payload (Production)
{
  "user_id": "usr_998124",
  "credit_card": "4532-7598-1234-5678",
  "cvv": "882",
  "auth_token": "bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
}

// Replayed Payload to Candidate Cluster
{
  "user_id": "usr_998124",
  "credit_card": "4532-XXXX-XXXX-5678",
  "cvv": "000",
  "auth_token": "test-mock-token-session-valid"
}

Dynamic mutation rules allow teams to inject deterministic synthetic test credentials, swap out production API tokens, and rewrite host headers without incurring serialization bottlenecks.

C. The Diffing & Drift Engine

Replaying traffic is useless without granular validation. TrafficMirror collects the responses from both the primary (v1.0) and shadow (v1.1) environments, piping them into a distributed diffing pipeline.

The engine accounts for:

  • Timestamp Drift: Dynamic fields like generated_at, nonce, or trace_id are automatically ignored using structural AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) matching.
  • JSON Structure vs. Whitespace: Semantic comparisons instead of raw string checks.
  • Latency & Resource Profiling: Measuring p95, p99, and p99.9 latency variance between builds under identical concurrency.

3. Production Deployment: Kubernetes & Cloud-Native Integration

title: Sign the Sentences, Not the PR: An Approval Ledger for Model-Drafted Doc Blocks
description:
Most documentation reviews approve a pull request, not a sentence. That is the failure mode worth fixing first, because a single approval granted in October can silently keep covering paragraphs a model rewrote in December. The workflow below binds every human signature to a hash of the exact text it approved, so re-approval becomes a mechanical consequence of editing rather than a matter of reviewer vigilance.

The artifact is a ~90-line Python checker that runs in pre-commit and CI. It does not gate generation and it does not judge prose quality; it answers one narrow question per block: has a named human signed this exact text?

The failure mode: approvals outlive their text

A PR approval is scoped to a diff, and a diff is scoped to a moment. Once merged, the approval record lives in review history while the file keeps moving under other PRs, refreshes, and routine edits. When a model later rewrites a command block inside an already-approved page, nothing in the toolchain notices that the signature no longer describes the content.

If you already pin blocks to a source hash to decide what may be refreshed, this is the complementary half. A source hash says "the input changed, so re-draft." An approval hash says "a human still vouches for this sentence." You want both, because either one alone produces a page where the provenance of the prose is unverifiable.

Who may draft what

Before any tooling, write down the boundary. The table below is a defensible starting contract; adapt the rows to your own risk surface rather than copying them wholesale.

Block type Model may draft Human must own
Install and upgrade commands Yes, with a pinned tool version That the command was executed on a clean machine
API signatures and parameter names Yes, from a pinned release artifact Reconciliation against the release being documented
Limits, quotas, prices, deprecation dates No Any figure, date, or contractual statement
Security warnings and data-handling notes Draft as a prompt only The final wording and its applicability
Migration and rollback steps Draft per step Ordering, reversibility, and blast radius
Troubleshooting symptoms Yes, from issue text That the symptom was reproduced

The rows marked "No" are not a comment on model quality; they are a statement about who is accountable when a number is wrong. Ownership is a liability question before it is a writing question.

Step 1: Mark ownership boundaries in the source

Wrap each unit you want to attribute in an HTML comment pair, and keep the body plain Markdown so the page still renders anywhere.

<!-- doc:block id="install-linux" owner="model" -->
Run `make install` from the repository root. The command writes binaries to `./bin`.
<!-- /doc:block -->

<!-- doc:block id="limits-note" owner="human" -->
Rate limits are documented in the pricing page and change without notice.
<!-- /doc:block -->

Blocks marked owner="human" are exempt from checking, which keeps the ledger small and the escape hatch explicit. Blocks marked owner="model" need a signature, and the signature is invalid the moment the body changes.

Step 2: Draft under a restricted instruction

Give the model the marked file and the draft-rights table together, and require it to leave owner="human" blocks byte-identical. A workable instruction is: rewrite only blocks with owner="model", never introduce a number, date, or version not present in the supplied release artifact, and return the full file so the markers survive.

This is where free model access from MonkeyCode is genuinely useful in my setup, because the drafting pass is cheap, repetitive, and worth running several times while you tune the contract. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The drafting pass and the checker job are both small enough to run on the free server option, which keeps the whole workflow inside a single environment while you decide whether it earns a place in your pipeline. Availability is operator-supplied and can change, so keep the checker provider-agnostic and never let it depend on a specific model being reachable.

Step 3: Hash the block and record the signature

The checker below normalizes trailing whitespace, hashes each model-drafted body, and compares it against a JSON ledger stored beside the docs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""doc_provenance.py — fail when a model-drafted block changed without a fresh approval."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import pathlib
import re
import sys

BLOCK_RE = re.compile(
    r'<!--\s*doc:block\s+id="(?P<id>[a-z0-9][a-z0-9\-]*)"\s+owner="(?P<owner>model|human)"\s*-->'
    r'\n(?P<body>.*?)\n'
    r'<!--\s*/doc:block\s*-->',
    re.DOTALL,
)
LEDGER = pathlib.Path(".docprovenance")


def digest(body: str) -> str:
    normalized = "\n".join(line.rstrip() for line in body.strip().splitlines())
    return hashlib.sha256(normalized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def ledger_path(doc: pathlib.Path) -> pathlib.Path:
    return LEDGER / (doc.as_posix().replace("/", "__") + ".json")


def read_ledger(doc: pathlib.Path) -> dict:
    path = ledger_path(doc)
    return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else {"blocks": {}}


def check(doc: pathlib.Path) -> list[str]:
    text, seen, problems = doc.read_text(), set(), []
    records = read_ledger(doc)["blocks"]
    for match in BLOCK_RE.finditer(text):
        block_id, owner, body = match.group("id"), match.group("owner"), match.group("body")
        seen.add(block_id)
        if owner != "model":
            continue
        record = records.get(block_id)
        if record is None:
            problems.append(f"{doc}:{block_id}: model-drafted block has no approval")
        elif record["sha256"] != digest(body):
            problems.append(f"{doc}:{block_id}: text changed since approval by {record['reviewer']}")
    for block_id in records:
        if block_id not in seen:
            problems.append(f"{doc}:{block_id}: approval record for a deleted block")
    return problems


def approve(doc: pathlib.Path, block_id: str, reviewer: str) -> None:
    text = doc.read_text()
    for match in BLOCK_RE.finditer(text):
        if match.group("id") == block_id:
            data = read_ledger(doc)
            data["blocks"][block_id] = {"sha256": digest(match.group("body")), "reviewer": reviewer}
            ledger_path(doc).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            ledger_path(doc).write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n")
            return
    raise SystemExit(f"no block named {block_id} in {doc}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("command", choices=["check", "approve"])
    parser.add_argument("paths", nargs="+")
    parser.add_argument("--block")
    parser.add_argument("--reviewer", default="")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    docs = [pathlib.Path(p) for p in args.paths]
    if args.command == "approve":
        approve(docs[0], args.block, args.reviewer)
        sys.exit(0)
    failures = [problem for doc in docs for problem in check(doc)]
    print("\n".join(failures) or "doc provenance: ok")
    sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)

The approval command writes a record you can review as a diff, which is the point: the signature becomes an artifact in the repository rather than a fact buried in a review thread.

python3 tools/doc_provenance.py approve docs/install.md --block install-linux --reviewer alin
python3 tools/doc_provenance.py check docs/

Illustrative output when a model refreshes a command block without a re-sign:

docs/install.md:install-linux: text changed since approval by alin
doc provenance: exit 1

Step 4: Enforce it in pre-commit and CI

Run the check locally so authors see the failure before pushing, and run the same command in CI so the hook can never be the only gate. A local hook costs about a second on a docs tree of a few hundred files.

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: doc-provenance
        name: doc provenance
        entry: python3 tools/doc_provenance.py check
        language: system
        files: ^docs/.*\.md$
        pass_filenames: true

# CI step, provider-neutral
- run: python3 tools/doc_provenance.py check docs/

Step 5: Review the ledger diff, not the prose diff

In review, the interesting question is which blocks changed and who signed them, so put .docprovenance/ in the same PR as the doc edit and read that diff first. Each added record names a person and a hash; each removed record marks a block that no longer exists.

Limitations and who should not use this

The checker verifies integrity of the binding, not the correctness of the text; a careless reviewer can approve a wrong command in one keystroke. It also adds friction proportional to block count, so start with the ten blocks that carry commands, numbers, or security claims rather than the whole tree.

Skip this approach if your docs are auto-generated from source, if you have no named human who can credibly sign, or if your team cannot enforce a hook in CI. In those cases the ledger becomes ceremony that duplicates whatever your generator already guarantees.

Measure two things before scaling: time from block change to re-approval, and the share of CI runs that fail on staleness. If the second number stays high, your blocks are too granular or your contract is assigned to the wrong owner.

title: Strengthening App Review Guidelines against nonconsensual intimate imagery and bait-and-switch apps
description:
The App Review Guidelines are a core part of the safe and trusted experience that the App Store strives to offer users around the world — and the foundation of that trust is clear standards that are consistently enforced.

As outlined in our App Review Guidelines, pornographic material has long been prohibited on the App Store — this includes apps that generate nudity or sexually explicit imagery, such as “nudification” apps that create sexually explicit images of real individuals without their consent. Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch.

We want great apps and the innovative developers behind them to succeed on the App Store, and as new risks and novel user experiences emerge, we evolve our App Review Guidelines to maintain the trust of users and developers alike. Today we’re publishing updates that strengthen and extend the existing App Store protections, continuing to build on our long-held standards for privacy, quality, and safety.

For complete details, see the App Review Guidelines.

Changes

1.2: Content moderation requirements now explicitly cover nonconsensual intimate imagery — including imagery generated using AI tools — as content that apps must proactively prevent and remove from their platforms. Developers who fail to implement adequate safeguards — or don’t remedy violations after notice — risk violating the Developer Code of Conduct and being removed from the App Store.

2.5.19: This rule clarifies our longstanding prohibition on apps misrepresenting what they do during the App Review process and then changing after approval — for example, adding features or functionality that weren’t included in the version of the app that was submitted to App Review. Apps found engaging in this conduct are subject to removal from the App Store and removal from the Apple Developer Program.

Section 5: The App Store has always prohibited apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children (including child sexual abuse material). When we find instances of apps containing such content, we remove them from the App Store. We’ve updated Section 5 of the App Review guidelines to make clear that apps with such content will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.

We’re committed to keeping bad actors off the App Store, with established processes in place to review and act on apps that violate our guidelines. Last year, we prevented over 150K apps with safety issues from reaching customers and terminated over 193K developer accounts for engaging in fraud and abuse. These violations trace back to malicious actors — in some cases coordinated fraud operations — working to conceal harmful content that only becomes active once an app is approved, and as their tactics evolve, we continue to evolve our own tools and resources to prevent and catch this kind of behavior even faster. We do not hesitate to remove apps, and terminate the developers behind them, when they violate these guidelines.
