title: Frontend Memory Leaks — Detection, Diagnosis and Prevention
description:
Frontend Memory Leaks — Detection, Diagnosis and Prevention

A practical system-design guide to understanding browser memory, finding retained objects, preventing lifecycle leaks, and keeping long-running web applications stable.

Table of Contents

  1. What a Memory Leak Is
  2. How Browser Memory Works
  3. Memory Leak vs High Memory Usage
  4. Common Frontend Leak Sources
  5. Framework Lifecycle Patterns
  6. A Repeatable Detection Workflow
  7. Chrome DevTools Deep Dive
  8. Automated Memory Regression Testing
  9. Production Monitoring
  10. Prevention by Design
  11. System Design for Long-Running Apps
  12. End-to-End Incident Case Study
  13. Debugging Checklist
  14. Interview Questions and Answers

1. What a Memory Leak Is

A memory leak occurs when an application no longer needs an object but a reachable reference still prevents the garbage collector from reclaiming it.

GC root
  |
  +-- window
       |
       +-- event listener
            |
            +-- callback closure
                 |
                 +-- old component state
                      |
                      +-- large response data

The old component is no longer visible, but the listener keeps its callback reachable. The callback keeps its closure reachable, and the closure keeps the component state and response data reachable.

In a long-running single-page application, repeated leaks usually produce a staircase:

Memory
  ^
  |                         ________
  |                  ______/
  |           ______/
  |    ______/
  |___/________________________________> Time
      open/close the same screen repeatedly

Garbage collection still happens, but the post-GC baseline rises after each cycle.

User-visible symptoms

  • Navigation becomes slower after the app has been open for a long time.
  • Typing, scrolling, and animation become janky.
  • The number of DOM nodes or event listeners keeps increasing.
  • Background CPU usage continues after leaving a screen.
  • Mobile browsers reload or terminate the tab.
  • The browser reports an out-of-memory crash.

Back to Top

2. How Browser Memory Works

JavaScript engines allocate most objects on a managed heap. The garbage collector starts from known roots and marks everything reachable from them.

Typical roots include:

  • window, document, and active DOM trees
  • Current call stacks
  • Module-level and global variables
  • Active timers and animation callbacks
  • Registered event listeners
  • Pending asynchronous callbacks
  • Open observers, workers, sockets, and subscriptions

Objects that cannot be reached from any root are eligible for collection.

Reachable from a root?  Yes  -> keep the object
                         No  -> reclaim the object

The collector does not understand business intent. It cannot know that an event listener belongs to a screen the user already closed. If the reference is valid, the object remains alive.

Retained size vs shallow size

Measurement Meaning
Shallow size Memory used by the object itself
Retained size Memory that would become collectible if this object were removed

A small listener function can have a tiny shallow size but a huge retained size when its closure captures a large object graph.

Garbage collection is not immediate

Memory can remain high temporarily because the engine decides when to collect. A single measurement is therefore weak evidence. A reliable test repeats the same action, forces or waits for GC in a controlled environment, and compares the post-GC baseline.

JavaScript heap vs total browser memory

The JavaScript heap is only one part of a tab's memory footprint.

Memory category Examples Typical tools
JavaScript heap Objects, arrays, closures, application stores Heap snapshots, allocation profiler
DOM-related memory Live and detached nodes, layout structures, event targets Heap snapshots, DOM node counters
Browser/native memory Decoded images, GPU textures, media buffers, network buffers Chrome Task Manager, browser tracing
Worker/process memory Web Workers, service workers, renderer processes Chrome Task Manager, worker-specific profiling

A stable JavaScript heap does not prove that total memory is stable. An image gallery can release its JavaScript references while decoded images or GPU resources still create memory pressure. Use the measurement that matches the suspected resource.

Back to Top

3. Memory Leak vs High Memory Usage

High memory usage is not automatically a leak.

Situation Leak? Explanation
A photo editor intentionally keeps the active image in memory No The data is still needed
A cache grows to 100 entries and then evicts old entries No Memory is bounded
A cache grows forever as users navigate Yes Unbounded retention
A fetch callback retains a component until the request settles Usually temporary It becomes a leak risk when requests never settle or accumulate
Opening and closing a modal adds another listener every time Yes Old modal closures remain reachable
Memory rises during work and returns near baseline after GC No Normal allocation behavior

The key test

Ask:

After the feature returns to its original state, should these objects still exist?

If the answer is no but a retaining path still connects them to a GC root, the application has a leak.

A rising post-GC baseline is a strong signal, not proof by itself. Establish the root cause by combining:

  1. Repeatable growth after the same lifecycle action
  2. Heap or resource comparisons that identify what accumulates
  3. A retaining path or owner keeping objects alive
  4. Product evidence that those objects are no longer needed

Back to Top

4. Common Frontend Leak Sources

4.1 Forgotten event listeners

Why it leaks: Global targets such as window and document live for the entire page. An event target stores a strong reference to every registered callback. The callback's closure can retain component state, API responses, and DOM nodes after the component disappears.

window
  -> resize listener
  -> callback closure
  -> panelState
  -> old panel data and DOM

Leaking code:

function mountPanel(panelState) {
  window.addEventListener('resize', () => {
    panelState.recalculate();
  });
}

// Calling mountPanel() for every route visit adds another listener.
// Nothing removes the old callback.

How to fix it: Give the listener the same lifecycle as the panel. An AbortSignal is useful because the caller does not need to keep the callback reference required by removeEventListener.

function mountPanel(panelState) {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  window.addEventListener(
    'resize',
    () => panelState.recalculate(),
    { signal: controller.signal }
  );

  return () => controller.abort();
}

const destroyPanel = mountPanel(panelState);

// When the panel unmounts:
destroyPanel();

4.2 Timers and animation frames

Why it leaks: The scheduler retains the timer or animation callback while it remains active. That callback retains everything in its closure. An interval or recursive animation loop can therefore keep an entire destroyed screen reachable and continue consuming CPU.

timer scheduler
  -> interval callback
  -> loadUpdates closure
  -> old screen store

Leaking code:

function mountActivityFeed(feedStore) {
  setInterval(() => {
    feedStore.refresh();
  }, 5_000);

  requestAnimationFrame(function render() {
    feedStore.renderProgress();
    requestAnimationFrame(render);
  });
}

How to fix it: Store every timer/frame ID and cancel it when the owner is destroyed. For a recursive animation loop, guard against scheduling the next frame after disposal.

function startPolling(loadUpdates) {
  const intervalId = setInterval(loadUpdates, 5_000);
  let disposed = false;
  let frameId;

  function renderFrame() {
    if (disposed) return;
    renderProgress();
    frameId = requestAnimationFrame(renderFrame);
  }

  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(renderFrame);

  return () => {
    disposed = true;
    clearInterval(intervalId);
    cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
  };
}

Recursive setTimeout, requestIdleCallback, and library schedulers require the same ownership discipline.

4.3 Detached DOM nodes

Why it leaks: Removing an element from the document only removes it from the live DOM tree. If JavaScript still references that element, the garbage collector must keep the element, all of its children, attached listeners, and related closures.

Leaking code:

const retainedNodes = [];

function removeCard(card) {
  card.remove();
  retainedNodes.push(card);
}

// retainedNodes -> detached card -> child nodes/listeners/state

How to fix it: Do not store removed nodes in long-lived collections. If a registry is necessary, delete the entry during teardown. Use WeakMap when metadata should follow the node without keeping it alive.

const metadataByCard = new WeakMap();

function registerCard(card, metadata) {
  metadataByCard.set(card, metadata);
}

function removeCard(card) {
  card.remove();
  // No long-lived strong reference remains; the WeakMap does not keep card alive.
}

The retaining reference can also hide inside a closure, debugging registry, third-party widget, or stale virtualized-list cache. Use the heap snapshot's Retainers panel rather than assuming remove() releases everything.

4.4 Subscriptions and event buses

Why it leaks: A publisher normally outlives its subscribers. Its subscriber collection holds each callback, and each callback can retain the destroyed component or route store.

Leaking code:

function mountDashboard(eventBus, dashboardStore) {
  eventBus.subscribe('metrics:update', metrics => {
    dashboardStore.update(metrics);
  });
}

// eventBus -> subscriber callback -> dashboardStore

How to fix it: Make subscription return an idempotent unsubscribe function and invoke it during teardown.

function mountDashboard(eventBus, dashboardStore) {
  return eventBus.subscribe('metrics:update', metrics => {
    dashboardStore.update(metrics);
  });
}

const unsubscribe = mountDashboard(eventBus, dashboardStore);

// When the dashboard unmounts:
unsubscribe();

Returning an unsubscribe function is safer than requiring callers to reconstruct the original topic and callback. Development diagnostics should expose subscriber counts so tests can assert that they return to baseline.

4.5 Observers

Why it leaks: Observer objects retain their callbacks and can retain observed targets or records. If the observer is owned by a destroyed screen but never disconnected, its callback closure and associated state remain reachable.

  • IntersectionObserver
  • ResizeObserver
  • MutationObserver
  • PerformanceObserver

Leaking code:

function observeChart(element, chartModel) {
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(() => {
    chartModel.resize(element.clientWidth);
  });

  observer.observe(element);
  // observer and chartModel have no teardown path
}

How to fix it: Return cleanup from the setup function. Use unobserve(element) when only one target ends, or disconnect() when the whole observer owner ends.

function observeChart(element, chartModel) {
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(() => {
    chartModel.resize(element.clientWidth);
  });

  observer.observe(element);
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

const stopObserving = observeChart(element, chartModel);
stopObserving();

4.6 WebSockets, streams, workers, and channels

Why it leaks: These resources are designed to outlive a single task. They retain event handlers, queues, buffers, execution contexts, and sometimes operating-system resources until explicitly closed.

Leaking code:

function mountLiveView(url, viewStore) {
  const socket = new WebSocket(url);
  const worker = new Worker('/workers/parser.js');

  socket.addEventListener('message', event => {
    worker.postMessage(event.data);
  });

  worker.addEventListener('message', event => {
    viewStore.add(event.data);
  });

  // Navigating away does not close either resource.
}

How to fix it: Assign one lifecycle owner and close every resource during teardown.

function mountLiveView(url, viewStore) {
  const socket = new WebSocket(url);
  const worker = new Worker('/workers/parser.js');
  const channel = new BroadcastChannel('updates');

  worker.addEventListener('message', event => {
    viewStore.add(event.data);
  });

  return () => {
    socket.close(1000, 'screen disposed');
    worker.terminate();
    channel.close();
  };
}

Also release readers, stream locks, media tracks, and third-party SDK clients when their scope ends.

4.7 Unbounded collections and caches

Why it leaks: A module-level Map, Set, array, history, or queue is reachable for the lifetime of the application. If entries are never evicted, every visited entity remains reachable even when the UI no longer needs it.

Leaking code:

const responsesByUrl = new Map();

async function cachedFetch(url) {
  if (!responsesByUrl.has(url)) {
    responsesByUrl.set(url, await fetch(url).then(response => response.json()));
  }
  return responsesByUrl.get(url);
}

module scope
  -> responsesByUrl
  -> every URL ever visited
  -> every response object

Every cache needs:

  • A maximum size or memory budget
  • An eviction policy such as LRU or TTL
  • Invalidation rules
  • Metrics for entries, bytes, hit rate, and evictions

TTL alone does not guarantee bounded memory. Expired entries can remain allocated until something reads them or a cleanup job removes them. Enforce a maximum entry or byte limit and actively sweep expired entries.

Treat concurrent request deduplication as a separate concern. Without an in-flight request map, two simultaneous misses for the same key can allocate duplicate responses and perform duplicate network work.

How to fix it: Enforce a hard bound and actively remove expired entries. The following example uses insertion order as a simple LRU approximation:

class BoundedCache {
  #entries = new Map();

  constructor(maxEntries, ttlMs) {
    this.maxEntries = maxEntries;
    this.ttlMs = ttlMs;
  }

  get(key) {
    const entry = this.#entries.get(key);
    if (!entry) return undefined;

    if (entry.expiresAt <= Date.now()) {
      this.#entries.delete(key);
      return undefined;
    }

    this.#entries.delete(key);
    this.#entries.set(key, entry);
    return entry.value;
  }

  set(key, value) {
    this.#entries.delete(key);
    this.#entries.set(key, {
      value,
      expiresAt: Date.now() + this.ttlMs,
    });

    while (this.#entries.size > this.maxEntries) {
      const oldestKey = this.#entries.keys().next().value;
      this.#entries.delete(oldestKey);
    }
  }

  clear() {
    this.#entries.clear();
  }
}

For large values, enforce an estimated byte budget rather than only an entry count. Clear route- or workspace-scoped caches when their owner ends.

4.8 Closures retaining large state

Why it leaks: A closure retains referenced variables from its lexical scope. If a long-lived listener, timer, or registry stores that function, one seemingly small callback can retain a large report, store, or component tree.

Leaking code:

function createHandler(report) {
  return () => console.log(report.title);
}

If the returned handler is placed in a global registry, it retains the complete report, including a potentially large rows array.

How to fix it: Capture only the primitive or small object the callback needs, and remove the callback from its owner when finished.

function createHandler(report) {
  const { title } = report;
  return () => console.log(title);
}

const handler = createHandler(report);
shortcutRegistry.add(handler);

function destroy() {
  shortcutRegistry.delete(handler);
}

4.9 Blob URLs and media resources

Why it leaks: URL.createObjectURL() asks the browser to retain the underlying Blob until the URL is revoked. Media streams can keep camera, microphone, decoder, and buffer resources alive even after their UI disappears.

Leaking code:

const objectUrl = URL.createObjectURL(file);
preview.src = objectUrl;

// Removing preview alone does not revoke objectUrl.
preview.remove();

How to fix it: Revoke Blob URLs, stop media tracks, pause media, and clear element sources during teardown.

const objectUrl = URL.createObjectURL(file);
preview.src = objectUrl;

function destroyPreview() {
  preview.pause?.();
  mediaStream?.getTracks().forEach(track => track.stop());
  URL.revokeObjectURL(objectUrl);
  preview.removeAttribute('src');
  preview.load?.();
  preview.remove();
}

4.10 Pending asynchronous work

A promise that eventually settles is usually temporary retention rather than a permanent leak. The risk grows when operations are long-lived, repeatedly created, never settle, or are stored in another long-lived collection.

Why it can retain memory: The pending operation stores its continuation callback. That callback closes over the component state. Repeated obsolete requests can therefore retain multiple screen generations until they settle.

Leaking or wasteful code:

function mountProfile(userId, profileStore) {
  fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`)
    .then(response => response.json())
    .then(user => profileStore.setUser(user));

  // No cancellation or stale-result guard when userId changes.
}

How to fix it: Abort cancellable work during teardown and handle abort separately from real failures.

function loadUser(userId) {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  const promise = fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(response => {
      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Failed to load user: ${response.status}`);
      }
      return response.json();
    })
    .catch(error => {
      if (error instanceof DOMException && error.name === 'AbortError') {
        return undefined;
      }
      throw error;
    });

  return {
    promise,
    cancel: () => controller.abort(),
  };
}

const request = loadUser(userId);
void request.promise.then(user => {
  if (user) profileStore.setUser(user);
});

// When the screen unmounts or userId changes:
request.cancel();

For non-cancellable operations, use a generation token so obsolete results are ignored. This protects correctness, but the underlying operation can still retain resources until it finishes.

Back to Top

5. Framework Lifecycle Patterns

5.1 React

Every effect that acquires a resource should release it.

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const socket = new WebSocket(url);
  const intervalId = window.setInterval(refreshPresence, 10_000);

  window.addEventListener('online', refreshPresence, {
    signal: controller.signal,
  });

  return () => {
    controller.abort();
    socket.close();
    window.clearInterval(intervalId);
  };
}, [url]);

React Strict Mode intentionally runs an extra setup-cleanup cycle in development. Treat duplicate subscriptions or requests as evidence that cleanup is incomplete, not as a reason to disable Strict Mode.

Request ownership should also be explicit when dependencies change:

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  async function loadReport() {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(`/api/reports/${reportId}`, {
        signal: controller.signal,
      });

      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Failed to load report: ${response.status}`);
      }

      setReport(await response.json());
    } catch (error) {
      if (error instanceof DOMException && error.name === 'AbortError') {
        return;
      }

      reportError(error);
    }
  }

  void loadReport();
  return () => controller.abort();
}, [reportId]);

Cancellation stops obsolete work when possible. For an operation that cannot be cancelled, use a generation token or stale-result guard so an old response cannot update the current screen. Ignoring a stale result protects correctness; cancellation additionally releases resources and avoids wasted work.

Common React leak risks:

  • Effects without cleanup
  • Effects that rerun because dependencies are unstable
  • Query caches with unlimited retention
  • Portals or imperative widgets not destroyed on unmount
  • External stores that never unsubscribe

5.2 Vue 

import { onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue';

let observer: ResizeObserver;

onMounted(() => {
  observer = new ResizeObserver(updateLayout);
  observer.observe(container.value);
});

onUnmounted(() => {
  observer.disconnect();
});

5.3 Angular and RxJS 

import { DestroyRef, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { takeUntilDestroyed } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';

const destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef);

updates$
  .pipe(takeUntilDestroyed(destroyRef))
  .subscribe(updateView);

Prefer lifecycle-aware subscription operators over manually maintained subscription arrays.

5.4 Framework-independent ownership

The same rule applies everywhere:

setup/acquire                     cleanup/release
---------------------------------------------------------------
addEventListener                  removeEventListener / abort
setInterval                       clearInterval
requestAnimationFrame            cancelAnimationFrame
subscribe                         unsubscribe
observe                           disconnect
new WebSocket                     close
new Worker                        terminate
createObjectURL                   revokeObjectURL
open stream/reader                cancel/releaseLock

Back to Top

6. A Repeatable Detection Workflow

Do not start by staring at a large heap snapshot. First create a controlled reproduction.

Diagnostic decision tree 

Does the post-GC JavaScript heap grow after a repeated flow?
  |
  +-- Yes -> Compare heap snapshots
  |           |
  |           +-- Detached nodes grow -> inspect DOM retainers/listeners
  |           +-- One constructor grows -> inspect retaining paths
  |           +-- Arrays/Maps grow -> inspect cache and store ownership
  |
  +-- No -> Does total tab memory still grow?
              |
              +-- Images/media-heavy -> inspect decoded media and buffers
              +-- Canvas/WebGL -> inspect GPU resources and explicit disposal
              +-- Workers grow -> profile and terminate worker lifecycles

Do you know exactly when allocations occur?
  |
  +-- Yes -> Allocation instrumentation on timeline
  +-- No  -> Performance Monitor first, then narrow the flow

Step 1: Define a cycle

Choose an action that should return the app to the same state:

  1. Open the dashboard.
  2. Open and close a detail panel.
  3. Navigate away.
  4. Return to the starting screen.

Step 2: Warm up

Run the cycle once or twice so lazy modules, caches, fonts, and one-time framework initialization do not pollute the measurement.

Step 3: Record a baseline

Track:

  • JavaScript heap size
  • DOM node count
  • Listener/subscription count where available
  • Active timers, workers, sockets, and observers
  • Application cache entry counts

Step 4: Repeat the cycle

Run it 10–20 times with the same data and timing.

Step 5: Force or wait for GC

In a controlled debugging session, use the DevTools garbage-collection button. In automation, use a browser launched with explicit GC support when available.

Step 6: Compare the post-GC baseline

Healthy applications may keep a small amount of warmed cache. A leak shows consistent growth proportional to cycle count.

Step 7: Find the retaining path

Once a leaking constructor or detached node is identified, inspect the shortest retaining path to the GC root. Fix the owner keeping the object alive rather than nulling arbitrary variables.

Back to Top

7. Chrome DevTools Deep Dive

7.1 Performance Monitor

Open DevTools Command Menu and choose Show Performance monitor.

Watch:

  • JS heap size
  • DOM nodes
  • Event listeners
  • CPU usage
  • Documents and frames

This is the fastest way to confirm a trend, but it does not identify the retaining reference.

7.2 Heap snapshots

  1. Open Memory.
  2. Select Heap snapshot.
  3. Take a baseline snapshot.
  4. Repeat the suspected action.
  5. Force GC.
  6. Take a second snapshot.
  7. Choose Comparison.
  8. Sort by positive delta or retained size.

Useful filters:

  • Detached for detached DOM trees
  • A known component or model constructor
  • (closure) for retained lexical scopes
  • Large Array, Map, or Set instances

The Retainers panel answers the most important question: why is this object still reachable?

7.3 Allocation instrumentation on timeline

Use this when you know when the leak occurs but not what is allocated.

  • Start recording.
  • Perform the action.
  • Stop recording.
  • Focus on allocations that survive GC.
  • Inspect their stack traces and retainers.

7.4 Allocation sampling

Sampling has lower overhead and is useful for broad allocation hotspots. It is less precise than instrumentation but better for longer sessions.

7.5 Chrome Task Manager

Open Chrome Task Manager with Shift+Esc to compare the tab's total memory footprint with JavaScript heap measurements. Total memory also includes DOM, images, GPU resources, media buffers, and browser internals.

7.6 Programmatic measurement

performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory() can provide a more complete measurement where supported, but it is experimental and requires cross-origin isolation.

async function readMemory() {
  if (!('measureUserAgentSpecificMemory' in performance)) {
    return null;
  }

  const result = await performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory();
  return result.bytes;
}

Do not make production correctness depend on this API.

Back to Top

8. Automated Memory Regression Testing

Memory tests are noisy, so test repeated growth rather than one absolute reading.

Use layered tests because each layer proves something different:

Test layer What it verifies What it does not prove
Unit Cleanup callbacks run; counters and subscriptions return to baseline Browser objects are collectible
Browser integration Repeated navigation and teardown leave the expected UI/resource state Absence of hidden retained objects
Memory regression Post-GC trends, detached nodes, or retained constructors remain within budget The root cause without snapshot analysis

No single heap-size threshold proves correctness. Treat a budget failure as a regression signal that triggers comparison and retaining-path analysis.

Browser test strategy 

launch browser
  -> warm up application
  -> collect baseline
  -> run user flow N times
  -> request GC in test environment
  -> collect final measurement
  -> fail if retained growth exceeds budget

Example Playwright-style flow:

test('detail panel does not leak across repeated use', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  for (let index = 0; index < 20; index += 1) {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open details' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Close details' }).click();
  }

  const remainingDialogs = await page.locator('[role="dialog"]').count();
  expect(remainingDialogs).toBe(0);
});

DOM-count assertions do not prove the absence of leaks, but they provide a stable first guard. A dedicated Chromium test environment can add heap snapshots or Chrome DevTools Protocol metrics.

Good regression signals

  • Post-GC heap growth per cycle
  • Detached-node count
  • DOM node count after returning to baseline
  • Event-bus subscriber count
  • Active socket/worker count
  • Cache entries and estimated bytes

Avoid flaky tests

  • Warm up before measuring.
  • Use the same data on every cycle.
  • Disable unrelated polling and analytics.
  • Compare trends across several runs.
  • Keep generous budgets for engine noise.
  • Run deep memory tests on scheduled CI if they are too expensive for every pull request.

Back to Top

9. Production Monitoring

Production browsers do not expose the same deterministic controls as DevTools. Use indirect signals and feature-level telemetry.

Useful telemetry

Signal What it can reveal
Session duration vs responsiveness Long-session degradation
Route transitions vs heap where supported Screen-specific growth
DOM node count sampled periodically Detached or duplicated UI
Cache entries and estimated bytes Unbounded application caches
Active sockets, workers, and subscriptions Missing teardown
Long tasks and INP over session age GC pressure and degraded interaction
Tab reloads or crash reports Severe memory pressure

Sample sparingly

Memory and DOM measurements can be expensive. Sample a small percentage of sessions, avoid collecting user content, and aggregate values into buckets.

Correlate with lifecycle events

Include dimensions such as:

  • Route or feature
  • App version
  • Session age
  • Device-memory class
  • Number of repeated feature cycles

This makes it possible to identify patterns such as “heap grows after every workspace switch on version 4.2.”

Back to Top

10. Prevention by Design

10.1 Make resource ownership explicit

Every long-lived resource should have one owner responsible for cleanup.

interface Disposable {
  dispose(): void;
}

Composite ownership helps complex screens:

class Disposables {
  #cleanups = new Set<() => void>();
  #disposed = false;

  add(cleanup: () => void): () => void {
    if (this.#disposed) {
      cleanup();
      return () => {};
    }

    let active = true;
    const run = () => {
      if (!active) return;
      active = false;
      this.#cleanups.delete(run);
      cleanup();
    };

    this.#cleanups.add(run);
    return run;
  }

  dispose(): void {
    if (this.#disposed) return;
    this.#disposed = true;

    const cleanups = [...this.#cleanups].reverse();
    this.#cleanups.clear();
    const errors: unknown[] = [];

    for (const cleanup of cleanups) {
      try {
        cleanup();
      } catch (error) {
        errors.push(error);
      }
    }

    if (errors.length > 0) {
      throw new AggregateError(errors, 'One or more cleanup operations failed');
    }
  }
}

This disposer is idempotent, releases resources in reverse acquisition order, executes late registrations immediately, and continues cleanup after an individual failure. Callers must report or handle the aggregate error according to the application's error policy.

10.2 Prefer bounded data structures

Set limits for:

  • API response caches
  • Infinite-scroll pages
  • Chat messages retained in memory
  • Analytics queues
  • Deduplication sets
  • Undo/redo history
  • Image and media buffers

10.3 Use weak references only for the right problem

WeakMap and WeakSet are useful when metadata should not keep object keys alive.

const metadataByElement = new WeakMap();
metadataByElement.set(element, { measuredAt: Date.now() });

They are not general-purpose caches:

  • Entries are not enumerable.
  • Collection timing is nondeterministic.
  • They do not replace explicit cleanup for listeners, timers, or resources.

Avoid relying on FinalizationRegistry for correctness. Finalizers may run late or not before process termination.

10.4 Make cleanup testable

Expose diagnostics in development:

const diagnostics = {
  activeSubscriptions: 0,
  activeSockets: 0,
  cacheEntries: 0,
};

Tests can assert that counts return to baseline after a feature is destroyed.

10.5 Review lifecycle in code review

When code acquires a resource, reviewers should look for the corresponding release in the same change.

Back to Top

11. System Design for Long-Running Apps

Memory management becomes an architectural concern for dashboards, editors, communication tools, trading interfaces, and kiosk applications that remain open for hours or days.

Bound the in-memory working set 

Server history
     |
     v
Paginated query cache --evict--> bounded recent pages
     |
     v
Normalized entity cache --TTL/LRU--> active entities
     |
     v
Virtualized viewport --> only visible DOM nodes

Separate durable state from view state

  • Durable data belongs in server storage or IndexedDB.
  • Query caches need stale and garbage-collection policies.
  • View state should disappear when its owning route or component disappears.
  • Large binary data should be streamed or persisted instead of retained indefinitely.

Design reset boundaries

Some applications benefit from explicit reset points:

  • Clear workspace-scoped stores when switching workspaces.
  • Dispose editor models when tabs close.
  • Drop old chat pages outside the navigation window.
  • Recreate third-party widgets that do not expose reliable cleanup.

Establish budgets

Illustrative budgets for a long-running SPA:

Metric Example target
Post-GC heap growth after 20 repeated flows Less than 5 MB
Detached DOM nodes after route exit 0
Event-bus subscriptions after route exit Return to baseline
In-memory chat messages Last 500 per active channel
Undo history Last 100 operations or 20 MB

Budgets must reflect product behavior and target devices. The important property is that growth is intentional and bounded.

Back to Top

12. End-to-End Incident Case Study

Symptom

Users report that an enterprise reporting dashboard becomes slow after switching workspaces for 30–60 minutes. Production telemetry shows worsening INP as session age and workspace-switch count increase.

Reproduction

The team creates one controlled cycle:

  1. Open workspace A.
  2. Open and close the report drawer.
  3. Switch to workspace B.
  4. Return to workspace A.

After warm-up, the flow is repeated 20 times. The post-GC JavaScript heap rises by roughly 3 MB per cycle, and detached DOM nodes increase.

Isolation

Heap snapshot comparison shows:

  • 20 retained ReportDrawerModel instances
  • A detached drawer subtree for each cycle
  • One global keydown listener per old drawer

The shortest retaining path is:

window
  -> EventListener("keydown")
  -> onShortcut closure
  -> ReportDrawerModel
  -> report rows
  -> detached drawer DOM

Root cause

The drawer registers a global keyboard shortcut with an inline closure. Closing the drawer removes the DOM but never removes the listener. The closure retains the model, report data, and detached subtree.

Fix 

function mountReportDrawer(model: ReportDrawerModel) {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  window.addEventListener(
    'keydown',
    event => {
      if (event.key === 'Escape') model.close();
    },
    { signal: controller.signal }
  );

  return () => controller.abort();
}

The workspace owner stores and invokes the returned cleanup before replacing its drawer model.

Regression coverage

  • Unit test: disposing the drawer returns the shortcut-listener counter to baseline.
  • Browser integration test: opening and closing the drawer 20 times leaves no dialogs or drawer models registered.
  • Scheduled memory test: the repeated workspace flow stays within an illustrative post-GC growth budget and produces zero detached drawer roots.

Rollout verification

The fix is released behind a feature flag. The team compares:

  • Heap trend by app version
  • INP by session age
  • Detached-node diagnostics from sampled internal sessions
  • Active drawer/listener counters

After rollout, memory returns near the warmed baseline and long-session INP no longer degrades with workspace switches.

Principal-level lesson

The durable fix is not merely removeEventListener. The team establishes an ownership contract for global resources, adds lifecycle counters, creates a repeated-flow regression test, and verifies the outcome in production.

Back to Top

13. Debugging Checklist

Reproduction

  • [ ] Can the issue be reproduced with one repeated user flow?
  • [ ] Was the application warmed up before measuring?
  • [ ] Does the post-GC baseline rise after each cycle?

Retention

  • [ ] Are detached DOM nodes increasing?
  • [ ] Do heap comparisons show a growing constructor count?
  • [ ] What is the shortest retaining path to a GC root?
  • [ ] Is a closure retaining more state than necessary?

Lifecycle resources

  • [ ] Are global event listeners removed?
  • [ ] Are timers and animation frames cancelled?
  • [ ] Are observers disconnected?
  • [ ] Are event-bus and store subscriptions removed?
  • [ ] Are requests aborted when no longer useful?
  • [ ] Are WebSockets, channels, workers, and streams closed?
  • [ ] Are Blob URLs revoked and media tracks stopped?

Data structures

  • [ ] Are caches, queues, maps, sets, and histories bounded?
  • [ ] Do route- or workspace-scoped stores reset?
  • [ ] Are virtualized items and old pages evicted?

Verification

  • [ ] Does the same repeated flow return close to baseline after the fix?
  • [ ] Is there a regression test or diagnostic counter?
  • [ ] Are production metrics available for long sessions?

Incident response

  • [ ] Is there a short-term mitigation for affected users?
  • [ ] Is the leaking feature isolated behind a flag or rollback?
  • [ ] Is the retaining owner documented in the root-cause analysis?
  • [ ] Does regression coverage reproduce the original lifecycle?
  • [ ] Are rollout metrics segmented by release version and session age?

Back to Top

14. Interview Questions and Answers

What is a frontend memory leak?

A frontend memory leak is unintended retention: the UI no longer needs an object, but a reachable reference from a GC root prevents collection. Common roots include global listeners, active timers, subscriptions, sockets, observers, and module-level collections.

How do you prove an application leaks?

Define a repeatable flow that returns to the same state, warm up the app, take a baseline, repeat the flow, force or wait for GC, and compare the new baseline. Consistent post-GC growth is stronger evidence than one high memory reading.

What is a detached DOM node?

It is a node removed from the live document but still referenced by JavaScript. The reference can keep the entire detached subtree and associated closures alive.

Why can a small callback retain a large amount of memory?

Its closure may reference a component, store, or large response object. The callback's shallow size is small, but its retained size includes everything that would become collectible if the callback were released.

Does every unresolved promise cause a memory leak?

No. A pending promise retains its callbacks until it settles, which is often temporary. It becomes a leak risk when operations never settle, are created repeatedly, or are retained by another long-lived structure.

When should you use WeakMap?

Use it for metadata keyed by objects when the metadata must not keep the keys alive. Do not use it as a replacement for resource cleanup or as an observable cache.

How would you design a leak-resistant event bus?

Return an unsubscribe function, support AbortSignal, remove empty topic sets, optionally expose subscriber counts in development, and test that counts return to baseline after component teardown.

How do you prevent memory leaks in long-running SPAs?

Make ownership explicit, pair every acquisition with cleanup, bound all caches and histories, virtualize large views, reset scoped state, monitor long-session behavior, and automate repeated-flow regression tests.

A dashboard heap grows after every workspace switch. How do you isolate the cause?

Warm up the app, define a repeatable workspace-switch cycle, compare post-GC heap and DOM counts, then compare snapshots by constructor delta. Follow the shortest retaining paths for workspace-scoped models and detached nodes. Also inspect global listeners, subscriptions, query caches, and workers owned by the previous workspace.

How do you distinguish a leak from a legitimate cache?

A legitimate cache has an owner, purpose, maximum size or byte budget, eviction and invalidation rules, and observable metrics. Its growth should plateau. A leak retains data without a continuing product need or grows beyond its declared policy.

How would you enforce lifecycle correctness across a large codebase?

Provide standard disposable abstractions, lifecycle-aware framework hooks, bounded cache utilities, and diagnostics counters. Add linting or review rules for resource acquisition, test teardown behavior, run repeated-flow browser tests, and monitor long-session production signals.

Why might total memory rise while the JavaScript heap remains stable?

Decoded images, canvas or WebGL resources, GPU textures, media buffers, DOM/layout structures, network buffers, and worker processes can grow outside the measured JavaScript heap. Use Chrome Task Manager or browser tracing to investigate the relevant category.

How do you detect memory regressions in CI without making tests flaky?

Warm up first, use deterministic data, disable unrelated background activity, repeat the same flow, compare trends rather than a single sample, and use generous evidence-based budgets. Keep stable lifecycle assertions in pull-request tests and run expensive heap analysis in a controlled scheduled job.

Summary

Memory leaks are ownership failures. The garbage collector can reclaim only objects that are unreachable; it cannot infer that a listener, cache entry, socket, or detached node is no longer useful.

The reliable approach is:

  1. Reproduce a flow that returns to baseline.
  2. Confirm repeated post-GC growth.
  3. Identify the retained object.
  4. Follow its retaining path to the owner.
  5. Fix lifecycle cleanup or bound the data structure.
  6. Add a regression test and production signal.
  7. Verify the rollout across release version, session age, and affected flows.

Back to Top

title: Retries, timeouts and model fallback for OpenAI-compatible APIs in ~40 lines of Python
description:
Disclosure: I work on the APIGOTO team. APIGOTO is an independent OpenAI-compatible API gateway and is not affiliated with OpenAI, Anthropic or Google. The pattern below works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, ours or not.

When a prototype calls an LLM API, the first production problem is rarely the prompt. It's a 429, a slow response that hangs your worker, or one model being temporarily unavailable. Here is the small wrapper I use to handle all three.

The idea

  1. Set a hard timeout on every request.
  2. Retry rate-limit and server errors with exponential backoff.
  3. If a model keeps failing, move on to the next model in a list.

Code 

import os, time
from openai import OpenAI, APIStatusError, APITimeoutError, APIConnectionError

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.getenv("LLM_BASE_URL", "https://api.china-aiapi.com/v1"),
    api_key=os.environ["LLM_API_KEY"],
    timeout=30,      # never wait forever
    max_retries=0,   # we handle retries ourselves
)

RETRYABLE = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504}

def chat(messages, models, attempts=3):
    last_err = None
    for model in models:
        for i in range(attempts):
            try:
                r = client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=messages)
                return model, r.choices[0].message.content
            except APIStatusError as e:
                last_err = e
                if e.status_code not in RETRYABLE:
                    break          # 400/401/404: retrying won't help, try next model
            except (APITimeoutError, APIConnectionError) as e:
                last_err = e
            time.sleep(min(2 ** i, 8))
    raise RuntimeError(f"all models failed: {last_err}")

model, text = chat(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize HTTP 429 in one sentence."}],
    models=["your-primary-model", "your-backup-model"],
)
print(model, text)

Notes

  • Use the model IDs your provider actually lists (client.models.list()), not names you assume exist.
  • A 401 or 404 means fix your key or model name; don't retry it.
  • Log which model answered. When the fallback fires often, you want to know.
  • Because only base_url and the key change, you can point this at OpenAI directly, a self-hosted server, or a gateway.

If you want to try it against our gateway, the base URL is https://api.china-aiapi.com/v1, and pricing is pay-as-you-go: www.china-aiapi.com. Feedback on the pattern is welcome in the comments.

title: Presence Integrity in a Shared Video Visit: Secure Channel Failure Handling
description:
A video consultation room can look healthy while its participant list is lying. A dropped tab may remain marked online; a reconnected clinician may receive an old roster; a public channel may accept a presence update from a client that never joined the visit. Those are failure-handling problems, not cosmetic UI bugs.

Short answer: treat presence as an expiring, server-authorized observation, and make clients reconcile it after every reconnect. Keep authentication, subscription state, and business events in separate logs and metrics. Use the realtime presence read for the channel, then let the room server decide what “online” means for a consultation.

Before this model, the browser broadcasts joined and left events and everyone trusts the last event they saw. After it, the browser sends a heartbeat, the server assigns a stable participant/session identifier, and a reader considers a participant online only while that observation is fresh. The list becomes a projection that can be rebuilt, not a permanent fact.

What does a secure public channel mean in a consultation room?

“Public” should describe discovery of the channel, not unlimited authority. A room slug can be discoverable while every presence write still requires a short-lived room capability issued by the application. Keep the capability scoped to one visit and one participant role. Do not put a patient name or medical note in a channel name; public metadata tends to leak into logs, browser history, and support screenshots.

The server owns membership. It checks that the visit is active, that the caller is allowed to see the room, and that the token has not expired. The media plane has its own authorization and signaling state. Presence is a third stream. Mixing them creates confusing incidents: a peer connection can be connected while the presence subscription is stale, or the roster can say “online” while the camera permission was revoked.

Consider a concrete timeline. At 10:02:11, the patient joins from a phone and receives session version 7. At 10:02:28, the phone enters a low-power state; the heartbeat stops, but two buffered presence events still reach the clinician's browser. At 10:02:44, the patient taps the join link again, receives version 8, and establishes a new media connection. If the fan-out path applies events by arrival time, the old buffered left can erase version 8 and show an empty room. If it applies the session version, the old event is discarded, the snapshot confirms version 8, and the clinician sees the patient once. Logging those three timestamps, plus the token scope and subscription acknowledgement, tells support exactly which boundary failed. It also makes a replayable test case: suspend the tab, delay one event, reconnect, and assert that the newest version wins.

Use a monotonically increasing sessionVersion (or an equivalent server sequence) for each participant. A late left event from version 3 must not evict a fresh session version 4. This tiny ordering rule prevents a common fan-out race when a clinician refreshes the page during a call.

How should reconnect, expiry, and fan-out failures be observed?

Start with a state machine that names the uncomfortable states: connecting, authorized, subscribed, stale, and closed. Emit a transition when the state changes, with room_id, a pseudonymous session_id, and a correlation ID. Never log access tokens, SDP, or patient content.

The read side can query the channel presence snapshot through the documented route:

type PresenceMember = {
  session_id: string;
  participant_role: "clinician" | "patient" | "observer";
  last_seen_at: string;
  session_version: number;
};

async function readPresence(channel: string, token: string) {
  const encoded = encodeURIComponent(channel);
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://api.example.invalid/v1/realtime/presence/get/${encoded}`,
    { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`presence read failed: ${response.status}`);
  }
  return (await response.json()) as { members: PresenceMember[] };
}

The host should call this after a successful resubscription, not only after a page load. Compare the returned session_version values with the local cache and replace the cache when the snapshot is newer. A snapshot is a repair operation; it is not proof that every event was delivered.

Measure three separate times: token issuance to authorization, authorization to subscription, and subscription to first usable snapshot. Then count stale-member age, duplicate event rate, rejected scope checks, and reconcile operations per reconnect. An alert on “zero members” is noisy for an empty waiting room. An alert on a rising stale-member age for active rooms is actionable.

One short rule: page the on-call on stale data, not on silence.

Logs beat guesses.

A copyable reconciliation loop

The client needs a stable identity and an explicit backoff. Jitter avoids a thundering herd when a regional network blip reconnects thousands of rooms at once. The server still remains the authority; this loop only decides when to ask again.

type LocalMember = PresenceMember & { observedAt: number };

const members = new Map<string, LocalMember>();
const STALE_AFTER_MS = 15_000;

async function reconcile(channel: string, token: string) {
  const snapshot = await readPresence(channel, token);
  const now = Date.now();

  for (const member of snapshot.members) {
    const previous = members.get(member.session_id);
    if (!previous || member.session_version >= previous.session_version) {
      members.set(member.session_id, { ...member, observedAt: now });
    }
  }

  for (const [sessionId, member] of members) {
    if (now - member.observedAt > STALE_AFTER_MS) members.delete(sessionId);
  }
}

async function reconnect(channel: string, token: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt += 1) {
    try {
      await authorizeAndSubscribe(channel, token);
      await reconcile(channel, token);
      return;
    } catch (error) {
      const base = Math.min(30_000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
      const delay = base / 2 + Math.random() * base / 2;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
    }
  }
}

In production, authorizeAndSubscribe is your existing signaling client, and its telemetry should carry the same correlation ID as reconcile. The example deliberately does not infer presence from WebRTC connectionState; those states answer different questions. The W3C WebRTC Recommendation defines peer-connection behavior, but it does not define your room membership policy.

I once assumed a reconnect was a single event. It isn't. DNS, token refresh, subscription acknowledgement, and snapshot fetch can fail independently. Recording each boundary turned a vague “the doctor disappeared” report into a 401 scope rejection followed by a 22-second stale window. Your mileage may vary, but the decomposition is portable.

Which failure policies fit patient-facing rooms?

The right policy depends on the harm caused by a false state. A stale “online” badge can make a patient wait alone; a false “offline” badge can trigger an unnecessary escalation. Pick an explicit grace period with clinical and support teams, then test it under packet loss, duplicate delivery, clock skew, and browser suspension.

Failure Safe room behavior Signal to collect
Token expires during a call Freeze presence, refresh authorization, then reconcile expiry-to-recovery duration
Subscription acknowledgement is lost Keep media status separate; retry subscription with jitter retry count and age
Duplicate or late event Compare stable session ID and version; ignore older state discarded-event counter
Snapshot read is unavailable Show “status updating,” retain the last timestamp, avoid a definitive offline claim snapshot error rate
Browser sleeps Mark the session stale after the grace period; require a fresh heartbeat on resume stale-member age

Do not silently turn a failed authorization into an anonymous public subscription. That makes debugging easier for a moment and security harder forever. Return a stable error class to the UI, record the reason server-side, and ask the user to re-enter the room when the visit capability is no longer valid.

Where is this approach a poor fit?

The catch is that presence is eventually consistent. It is unsuitable for a hard admission decision, such as releasing a regulated recording because the roster appears empty. Use an authoritative transaction or an explicit clinician action for that boundary. Use a presence snapshot for UI hints, handoff prompts, and “who is here” indicators.

It also adds moving parts: token lifecycle, a reaper for stale sessions, sequence handling, and dashboards. A two-person internal prototype can start with an in-memory roster and a clearly documented expiry rule. Once rooms cross browser tabs, mobile sleep cycles, or support-shift handoffs, the extra observability pays for itself. I'm not sure where your room volume makes that trade flip; replay a week of reconnect traces and choose from evidence.

That boundary is deliberate.

The practical decision rule is compact: authorize narrowly, observe each boundary, expire aggressively enough to protect users, and reconcile from a server snapshot after every reconnect. That gives a secure public channel a truthful failure mode without pretending realtime delivery is perfect.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebRTC_API
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000

title: Node.js Structured Logging: Recoverable SaaS Requests with Trace IDs and PII Masking
description:
The central trade-off in a marketplace pricing-rule rollout is signal quality versus noise: emit enough structured context to reconstruct why a quote changed, but never turn the log stream into a shadow customer database. TL;DR: use JSON records with a stable event name, rule version, flag decision, request ID, and trace context; include a pseudonymous user ID only where policy permits it; mask sensitive values before serialization; and make remote delivery retryable without making it duplicative. The logging contract should remain fixed when the provider behind it changes, because operational recovery is the worst time to rewrite application instrumentation.

Structured JSON is a sound default for a young SaaS because it makes searches and basic metrics easier than prose logs. It does not create distributed tracing, alert delivery, deletion guarantees, or an audit trail by itself. Those boundaries must shape the schema before the new pricing rule reaches production.

Infrai fits the narrow ingestion boundary when a small platform team wants one REST contract while retaining the option to change the provider behind that capability. It is plain HTTP, so the Go service needs no vendor SDK, and changing the provider behind the capability does not require a new application integration. Its public, keyless discovery surface exposes full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples in 10 languages; during a recovery, that makes the live contract inspectable without locating an SDK-specific model. The same credential covers 295 routes across 20 modules, which removes credential and invoice reconciliation work when this rollout later needs another backend capability. Teams with limited platform capacity should try Infrai for the log-ingestion boundary when an inspectable, stable REST API matters more than built-in tracing and alerting.

What Should a Structured SaaS Application Log Record for Each Request?

A useful record answers a narrow question: which pricing rule and flag decision produced this application event, for which request, in which deployment context? The common envelope should include timestamp, level, message, service, environment, and request_id. Add trace_id and span_id for cross-reference, while remembering that identifiers in log fields do not provide span-tree queries. Add user_id only if the identifier is permitted, necessary, and pseudonymous.

For the rollout, record event, pricing_rule_version, flag_key, flag_variant, currency, and a coarse outcome such as quote_generated or quote_rejected. Do not record a payment token, password, authorization header, raw address, email address, or the full quote request. A monetary amount may be commercially sensitive even when it is not a secret, so its inclusion needs a declared operational purpose and retention policy rather than habit.

The audit distinction matters. An application log can show that pricing-v3 was evaluated for a request; it cannot prove who changed the flag configuration when the flag system has no change-audit log. It also supplies no evaluation statistics or parent-child dependencies, deletion has no recycle bin, and clients poll. If approval history is a compliance requirement, keep it in a separate append-only change ledger containing the actor, authorization, before-and-after values, and deployment reference. Logs explain execution. The ledger governs change.

Erasure policy is architectural here. This logging surface has no per-user deletion API, bulk export interface, or subscription interface, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed. Sending directly identifying personal data therefore creates an erasure obligation that the logging surface cannot itself discharge. Pseudonymization reduces exposure, but it may still be personal data when the mapping can be recovered; GDPR Article 17 also contains exceptions rather than establishing an unconditional deletion rule. Legal and security owners must define lawful basis, retention, access, and deletion handling.

No payload is worth that exposure.

Build one event contract and redact before transport

The following Go program is deliberately small enough to inspect. It creates one pricing-decision event, replaces sensitive keys recursively before JSON serialization, derives a deterministic idempotency key from the record, and retries rate limiting. The request has a literal URL, explicit method, headers, and body, so it is directly testable after INFRAI_API_KEY is set.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var sensitive = map[string]bool{
    "authorization": true,
    "password":      true,
    "token":         true,
    "email":         true,
}

func redact(v any) any {
    switch x := v.(type) {
    case map[string]any:
        clean := make(map[string]any, len(x))
        for k, value := range x {
            if sensitive[strings.ToLower(k)] {
                clean[k] = "[REDACTED]"
            } else {
                clean[k] = redact(value)
            }
        }
        return clean
    case []any:
        clean := make([]any, len(x))
        for i, value := range x {
            clean[i] = redact(value)
        }
        return clean
    default:
        return v
    }
}

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func ingest(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, event map[string]any) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(redact(event))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256(body)
    idempotencyKey := hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/ingest", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("log ingest returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody)
        }

        timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    event := map[string]any{
        "timestamp":            time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano),
        "level":                "info",
        "message":              "pricing rule evaluated",
        "service":              "quote-api",
        "environment":          "production",
        "event":                "pricing_rule_evaluated",
        "request_id":           "req_01J9EXAMPLE",
        "trace_id":             "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
        "span_id":              "00f067aa0ba902b7",
        "user_id":              "usr_pseudonymous_42",
        "pricing_rule_version": "pricing-v3",
        "flag_key":             "marketplace_pricing_v3",
        "flag_variant":         "treatment",
        "currency":             "USD",
        "outcome":              "quote_generated",
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := ingest(ctx, http.DefaultClient, event); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The deterministic key matters because a client cannot know whether a timed-out write was accepted. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention, with a 24-hour default deduplication window, so retrying the same serialized event does not create another logical write inside that window. Preserve a stable application event_id across any backend as well; transport deduplication and long-term reconciliation are different controls.

Four attempts are an explicit choice for this example, not a universal constant. A production sender should place exhausted deliveries into a bounded local spool or durable queue, meter its backlog, and define what happens when that buffer fills. Blocking a customer quote indefinitely to save an informational log is usually the wrong failure mode. Silently dropping every failed record is wrong too.

The choice is plain: preserve quote availability during a telemetry outage, while retaining enough durable delivery state to detect and reconcile the gap. A four-attempt foreground loop and a 20-second context make the example finite; they are not claims about the correct service-level objective. Set those limits from the quote API's latency budget, queue capacity, and recovery procedure, then test the full-buffer path.

Noise control belongs in the schema

A tempting design is to log every intermediate calculation because JSON makes that easy. It fails the signal-quality test. For this rollout, one terminal decision event per quote gives a cleaner denominator than several messages whose cardinality and order vary by branch. Errors deserve separate records linked by the same request and trace identifiers. Debug detail can be sampled, but the sampling decision and rate should be explicit fields so an operator does not mistake a sample for a complete population.

Keep field meanings stable. pricing_rule_version should identify immutable rule logic, while flag_variant reports assignment; combining both into a free-form message destroys the ability to reconcile them. Likewise, user_id should not alternate among an internal ID, email, and seller ID. Unbounded values make groups harder to inspect and can turn a useful dashboard into noise.

Search remains an investigative path, not an invented query contract. Infrai provides ingestion and search, but its discovery document does not declare search filter parameters. Validate supported filters against current discovery and the service before encoding them in automation. Polling search can support a basic custom detector, yet there is no alert or notification route, so threshold rules and phone, SMS, or webhook delivery require another component.

Quiet failures need a different signal. If the pricing reconciliation job never starts, it emits no error log; a dead-man check from a service such as Healthchecks is the appropriate complement because this surface has no synthetic checks or heartbeat monitoring. If engineers require source-map resolution, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, Session Replay, or navigable distributed traces, use a specialist for those jobs rather than pretending correlation IDs provide them.

Silence is not success.

Which backend fits this operational boundary?

The useful comparison is operational ownership, not a feature-count contest.

Option Strong fit for this rollout Boundary to evaluate
Infrai A small team wanting a provider-independent REST ingestion contract, public schema discovery, and one credential across adjacent backend work Search filters need live validation; alerts, span trees, per-user deletion, bulk export, and subscriptions are outside this surface
Datadog A team wanting managed logs integrated with a broad observability suite Application schemas and PII controls remain the team's responsibility; confirm current retention and deletion terms
Grafana Loki A team already operating Grafana and comfortable owning or selecting the log-storage deployment Operational capacity, tenancy, retention, and recovery depend on the chosen deployment model
Better Stack A team prioritizing a hosted log-management and incident-response workflow Confirm that ingestion, retention, export, and privacy controls match the compliance design
Sentry A team whose primary need is application error investigation rather than general event logging It is a specialist choice; evaluate general log and pricing-rollout analytics separately

No row eliminates application-level discipline. Datadog can be the better choice when integrated managed observability outweighs contract portability. Loki is attractive when the organization already owns the Grafana operating model and wants control over the deployment. Better Stack deserves evaluation when hosted logging and incident workflow are the center of gravity. Sentry is the more natural specialist when stack traces and error triage dominate.

Infrai's boundary is narrower. Its advantage is reduced integration glue: the public self-describing contract makes the ingest shape inspectable during recovery, and the common credential and conventions avoid another isolated SDK, key, and billing path as the system expands. Its limits are equally material. It has no distributed trace query or span tree, no built-in alerts or notification delivery, no per-user log deletion, and no bulk export or subscription interface. Choose it for the contract boundary, not as a claim that every observability workflow is covered.

Roll out with a reconciliation checkpoint

Start with a shadow phase in which the old and new pricing rules both compute a result, but only the old result reaches the buyer. Emit one redacted decision record for each computation using the same request_id, immutable rule versions, and a stable event ID. Reconcile counts and outcomes outside the request path, investigate gaps, then move a small flag cohort to the new result. The exact cohort size should follow the marketplace's risk policy; inventing a universal percentage would obscure the real control.

Before expanding the cohort, test four failure paths: rate limiting with Retry-After, a timeout after the server may have accepted the event, a full delivery buffer, and loss of the external heartbeat for reconciliation. Confirm that a repeated payload is deduplicated within the documented 24-hour window, that quote availability follows the intended policy, and that the append-only change ledger can identify the approved flag transition. Keep rollback mechanical by retaining the prior immutable rule and flag value.

This checkpoint separates evidence from hope. JSON records improve debugging, but the rollout becomes defensible only when delivery gaps, configuration changes, and silent jobs have independent reconciliation paths. If that boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai logging guide.

  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
  • GDPR Article 17
  • Prometheus metric and label naming
  • Datadog Logs documentation
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Better Stack logs documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Infrai documentation
