title: Kubernetes Readiness vs Datadog for Node.js Docker Health (Choose 3 Startup Probes)
description:
A pricing rollout in a Node.js Docker app needs two kinds of truth. Kubernetes readiness, liveness, and startup probes must control traffic and restarts, while health monitoring needs metrics and logs showing which pricing rule was evaluated. Confusing those jobs makes incident reconstruction guesswork.

TL;DR: choose Kubernetes startup, readiness, and liveness probes first for container control. Mirror their state changes into logs and metrics, then add Datadog, Prometheus with Grafana, or another evidence backend according to the investigation depth the service needs. For a small gaming SaaS, I would keep the probe contract and event fields stable so the monitoring destination can change without rewriting the application.

The boundary is important: probes can recover a process, but they cannot prove that pricing rule version 17 served a particular request. A monitoring product can retain that evidence, but a remote monitoring dependency should not decide whether a local pod is ready.

What must survive after the pricing incident?

Start the design review with the questions an operator will ask after a flagged pricing rule behaves unexpectedly. Which deployment handled the request? Which rule version and flag decision did it use? Was that pod ready? Did a retry repeat the business mutation, or only repeat telemetry delivery?

Those questions define the evidence contract. A pricing-decision log can carry a UTC timestamp, deployment identity, rule_version, flag_enabled, stable request or order identifier, result, and any available trace_id and span_id. Probe-transition logs should use the same deployment identity and clock convention. Keep customer data out unless retention and deletion obligations are settled; a logging service without per-user deletion may be unsuitable for user-linked records under GDPR Article 17.

The invariant is blunt: health state and business completion are separate claims. A green liveness result does not prove that a scheduled flag rollout occurred, and a successful rollout event does not prove that the serving pod remains healthy.

This is where idempotency belongs in the runbook. The pricing mutation needs a stable transaction key so a retry cannot apply it twice. Telemetry delivery also needs a stable event key because an ambiguous network result may trigger another send. Duplicate evidence is annoying. A duplicate charge is an incident.

How should a Node.js Docker app use Kubernetes readiness, liveness, and startup probes?

Startup should stay false until initialization has completed. Readiness should fall when the instance cannot safely calculate or serve a price. Liveness should fail only when restarting that process is a reasonable repair.

Do not use liveness as a general dependency alarm. If a shared database slows down, killing every Node.js pod can turn one dependency problem into a restart wave. Readiness is normally the safer traffic control for a temporarily unusable dependency, while liveness should remain conservative.

Mirror each transition as a structured event. Increment a counter such as probe_failure_total with a bounded probe label, and maintain a readiness gauge at 0 or 1. Rule versions, order identifiers, and account identifiers do not belong in metric labels; their cardinality grows with the business. Put them in logs.

Three probes. Two metrics. One decision event.

The following transport program sends one prevalidated event to a verified log-ingest route. It deliberately does not invent the request schema: the adapter receives the current JSON body as HEALTH_EVENT_JSON. It checks every response, honors an integer Retry-After on HTTP 429, uses exponential backoff otherwise, and gives each retry the same idempotency key.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    eventID := os.Getenv("EVENT_ID")
    payload := os.Getenv("HEALTH_EVENT_JSON")
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || eventID == "" || payload == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, EVENT_ID, and HEALTH_EVENT_JSON are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodPost,
            baseURL+"/v1/logs/ingest",
            bytes.NewBufferString(payload),
        )
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", eventID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 4 {
            panic(fmt.Errorf("ingest status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
}

This writer stays outside the probe handler. Readiness must remain local and cheap; a logging outage must not remove healthy pods from service. If event delivery needs buffering, put it behind a bounded queue and preserve EVENT_ID at the consumer.

Configure the startup probe against the application's startup endpoint, readiness against its ready endpoint, and liveness against its live endpoint. The names are application choices, so the example does not pretend Kubernetes mandates particular paths. Set periods and failure thresholds from observed initialization and recovery behavior. The startup budget must cover the slowest legitimate boot, readiness should withdraw unsafe instances promptly, and liveness should avoid treating a shared outage as a process defect.

Comparing the evidence backends fairly

Kubernetes remains in every viable design below because none of these products replaces local container control. The actual comparison is about what happens after a signal changes.

Option Strongest fit Evidence available during reconstruction Important boundary
Prometheus with Grafana A team prepared to operate metric collection, dashboards, and alert rules Probe counters, readiness history, and other time series Application logs and outside-in checks need additional systems
Datadog A managed workflow spanning logs, metrics, traces, and synthetic tests Cross-signal investigation in one product It creates broader platform commitment than a small service may require
Better Uptime External reachability and an on-call incident workflow Outside-in checks and an incident timeline It does not replace pricing-decision logs inside the app
Healthchecks.io Scheduled publication or queue work that may fail silently A dead-man signal when an expected check-in is absent It is intentionally narrow, not a general observability backend
Infrai A small service wanting logs and metrics behind one REST contract Searchable logs plus queried metrics, correlated by timestamps and IDs No alert delivery, synthetic checks, distributed trace tree, or per-user log deletion

Prometheus and Grafana are the best choice when the team values control over metric rules and accepts operating the collection path. Datadog is the clearer choice when managed tracing and synthetic monitoring are requirements rather than future possibilities. Better Uptime answers “can a user reach us from outside the cluster?” Healthchecks.io answers the narrower and often missed question: “did the scheduled pricing publication check in?”

Infrai's concrete advantage is one plain REST API with no SDK to install, plus a single API key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. Swapping the vendor behind a capability does not change application code; the contract stays put. Public discovery returns request and response schemas without a key, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That lets a team validate the adapter during build review instead of copying an assumed payload into a rollout runbook. The consolidation is useful here only if the same team genuinely wants one credential lifecycle across multiple backend capabilities.

Its limitations decide the result. It is not suitable when the team needs built-in alert delivery, synthetic checks, or a distributed trace tree; choose Datadog instead for the managed cross-signal case, and choose Healthchecks.io for missed-job detection. With Infrai, alerting requires polling the metrics query and operating the notification path. Cross-service reconstruction relies on timestamps plus trace_id and span_id stored in logs. There is also no source-map processing, crash symbolication, session replay, bulk log export or subscription, or user-scoped log deletion. This trade-off is acceptable only when those are explicit exclusions, not assumptions hidden in the rollout plan.

No row wins every incident.

Why do silent jobs change the choice?

A container can be ready while a pricing publication never begins. That failure emits no request error, and an internal metric may remain flat rather than obviously bad. Kubernetes cannot restart work it never knew was expected.

For that path, add a dead-man check through Healthchecks.io or an equivalent heartbeat product. The job checks in after the publication reaches its defined completion point; absence becomes the signal. If outside users must validate a public pricing endpoint, add Better Uptime or another synthetic checker as a separate outside-in view. These tools complement the three probes because they observe different failure domains.

This distinction also changes alert ownership. Prometheus can evaluate rules, and managed platforms can deliver alerts, but a logs-and-metrics backend with no notification route requires a poller. Someone must own its schedule, deduplication, retry behavior, and escalation target. If that ownership is unclear, the architecture has an unstaffed component.

The rollout gate I would use

Choose probes first when the immediate requirement is safe Kubernetes traffic routing and restart behavior for one Node.js service. Add Prometheus with Grafana if the team already operates that path. Choose Datadog when the incident model spans services and requires managed trace and synthetic views. Use the smaller REST option only when stable instrumentation, public schemas, and a single credential reduce real workflow friction, and when timestamp-based correlation plus a team-owned polling alert loop are sufficient.

Before widening the pricing flag, require an operator to identify the rule version for a request, the pod's readiness at that time, movement in the failure counter, and the publication job's check-in. Then rehearse a retry against a stable transaction key. If any answer requires inference from a green pod alone, hold the rollout.

Stop there.

This design is not enough for a transaction whose primary diagnostic need is causal ordering across several services. Use distributed tracing for that. It also does not cover native crashes that require symbolication or browser failures that require session replay. Probe logs and two metrics are a useful small-system baseline, not a compressed substitute for every observability discipline.

Sources

  • Kubernetes: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes
  • Prometheus: Metric and Label Naming
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Datadog Synthetic Monitoring documentation
  • Better Uptime documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to Erasure

title: Go Profiling in Production: pprof, Flamegraphs and Memory Leaks
description:
Your Go service handles thousands of requests per minute — until it doesn't. Memory climbs steadily, p99 latency spikes, and the first instinct is to add more instances. Before doing that, you need to understand what the code is actually doing. Go's built-in profiling tooling makes this tractable without third-party frameworks or expensive APM subscriptions.

Setting Up pprof in a Running Service

pprof is part of the standard library. Adding it to an existing HTTP service takes four lines:

import (
    "net/http"
    _ "net/http/pprof"
)

func main() {
    // Expose pprof on a separate internal port — never public
    go func() {
        http.ListenAndServe("localhost:6060", nil)
    }()

    // ... rest of your server setup
}

The blank import registers the pprof HTTP handlers automatically. Never expose this on a public port — the CPU profile endpoint can be used to degrade your service deliberately. Bind to localhost or an internal network interface only.

Once the service is running:

go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap

This downloads a heap snapshot and opens an interactive prompt. Type top10 to see the ten functions allocating the most memory. Type web to open a flame graph in your browser (requires Graphviz).

Reading a Flamegraph Without Guessing

Flamegraphs look intimidating until you know one rule: width equals time or allocations spent. The x-axis is not time order — it is sorted alphabetically within each stack frame. A wide box means that function consumes a lot of the profiled resource. The y-axis is the call stack — top is where execution is at sample time, bottom is main.

When investigating a memory leak:

  1. Take a heap profile under normal load: curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap1.prof
  2. Wait 10–15 minutes
  3. Take another snapshot: curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap2.prof
  4. Compare: go tool pprof -diff_base heap1.prof heap2.prof

The diff shows exactly what grew between the two snapshots. If the same function keeps appearing in inuse_objects across successive profiles, that is your leak candidate.

The Most Common Memory Leak Patterns in Go

Go's garbage collector handles most memory automatically, but several patterns slip past it.

Goroutine leaks are the most frequent issue. A goroutine blocked forever on a channel that nobody writes to is unreachable in the traditional sense — but the GC won't collect it because it is still alive on the scheduler. Check goroutine count:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "runtime"
    "time"
    _ "net/http/pprof"
)

func worker(ctx context.Context, ch <-chan struct{}) {
    select {
    case <-ch:
        fmt.Println("got work")
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return // goroutine exits cleanly on cancellation
    }
}

func main() {
    go func() { http.ListenAndServe("localhost:6060", nil) }()

    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
    defer cancel()

    for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
        ch := make(chan struct{})
        go worker(ctx, ch)
        // When cancel() is called, all workers exit
    }

    for {
        fmt.Printf("goroutines: %d\n", runtime.NumGoroutine())
        time.Sleep(5 * time.Second)
    }
}

Check the goroutine profile: go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine. The top output will show goroutines stuck on chan receive. The fix is to always use context.Context for lifecycle management so goroutines have a guaranteed exit path.

Slice header retention is subtler. When you sub-slice a large byte array, the slice holds a reference to the entire underlying array. The whole allocation stays in memory even if you only need a small piece:

// Keeps the full 10MB buffer alive in memory
func extractHeader(data []byte) []byte {
    return data[:16]
}

// Copies only what is needed — the 10MB buffer is eligible for GC
func extractHeaderSafe(data []byte) []byte {
    out := make([]byte, 16)
    copy(out, data[:16])
    return out
}

The heap profile will point to the original make([]byte, 10<<20) allocation site rather than extractHeader, which makes this easy to miss on first inspection.

CPU Profiling for Latency Spikes

For CPU-bound latency issues, collect a 30-second CPU profile:

go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30

In the flame graph, look for unexpected width in functions that should be fast. Common findings:

  • encoding/json.Marshal on hot paths — switch to sonic or jsoniter for 3–5x throughput
  • fmt.Sprintf called thousands of times per second in logging code
  • sync.Mutex.Lock contention showing up as runtime.lock
  • Reflection-heavy code that could be replaced with code generation

For mutex contention specifically, enable the mutex profile fraction before your service starts:

import "runtime"

func init() {
    runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction(1) // record every contention event
}

Then: go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/mutex. This shows which mutexes are hot and the exact call sites where they are acquired.

Running pprof Against a Containerized Service

If your service runs in Docker or Kubernetes, the localhost binding becomes a problem. Two clean options:

Kubernetes port-forward:

kubectl port-forward pod/my-service-abc123 6060:6060

Profile from your local machine at localhost:6060.

Conditional binding via environment variable: gate the pprof listener behind ENABLE_PPROF=1, and only set that variable in staging or when actively investigating production. Never route it through the public ingress.

A useful pattern for performance-critical services is to keep a short operational runbook — including the specific pprof commands for your service — alongside your infrastructure security hardening checklists. Both degrade without maintenance, and both are most valuable when you are under pressure at 2am.

The Takeaway

Go's profiling tools are production-ready and require zero external dependencies. The practical workflow:

  1. Add the pprof import to an internal HTTP listener at startup
  2. Collect heap profiles before and after a suspected leak window
  3. Use diff_base to isolate allocation growth between snapshots
  4. Check goroutine count growth with the goroutine profile
  5. Capture a 30-second CPU profile during a latency event — not after

The hardest part is having the profiles at the right moment. Consider setting up an alert that automatically collects a heap snapshot when RSS memory crosses a threshold. By the time you notice the problem manually and log in, the evidence is often already gone.

I run AYI NEDJIMI Consultants, a cybersecurity consulting firm. We publish free security hardening checklists — PDF and Excel.

title: A 24.6x Latency Gap That Had Almost Nothing to Do With Graph Search Copy
description:
During the performance evaluation of Routavio, a multimodal travel planning and route optimization platform, we encountered an unexpected latency pattern.

The same route computation engine sometimes completed its first search pass in less than one second, while other executions required more than twenty seconds.

The transportation graph contained 24,774 nodes and 228,060 directed edges. It represented flight, rail, coach, and ferry connections obtained from heterogeneous transportation data sources.

Given the computational characteristics of graph traversal, our initial investigation focused on the routing algorithm.

However, the evidence eventually showed that the dominant latency component was not graph search.

It was graph loading.

This article presents the performance investigation, the experimental evidence that distinguished competing explanations, and the architectural modifications introduced to address the problem.

The measurements refer to Routavio's August 2026 pilot implementation, evaluated at repository revision 71e8cd39.

1. The Computational Context

Routavio represents transportation supply as a directed, time-aware graph.

Nodes correspond to locations such as airports, railway stations, coach terminals, and city anchors.

Edges represent transportation connections with attributes including mode, duration, provider, price evidence, and schedule information.

The routing engine performs a budget-bounded, heuristically pruned depth-first search over this network.

Unlike conventional shortest-path implementations operating on a complete static graph, the engine must accommodate incomplete transportation data and connections acquired during search.

The relevant computation pipeline can be summarized as follows:

Computation Request
        |
        v
Graph Loading / Cache Lookup
        |
        v
On-Demand Transport Data Acquisition
        |
        v
Nearby Airport and Station Expansion
        |
        v
Bounded Graph Search
        |
        v
Connection Feasibility Validation
        |
        v
Multicriteria Ranking
        |
        v
Itinerary Persistence
        |
        v
Search Result

The implementation uses PostgreSQL to persist transportation segments and computation state.

An in-memory adjacency structure is constructed from the relational transport data and reused by the worker process.

This architecture avoids introducing a separate graph database, but it introduces a potentially expensive graph materialization stage.

The original performance investigation did not initially distinguish this stage sufficiently from graph traversal.

That distinction became central to explaining the latency variation.

2. Formulating Competing Hypotheses

The performance anomaly was initially attributed to three possible causes.

Hypothesis H1: Algorithmic regression

A recent change to search heuristics might have increased graph traversal work or altered pruning effectiveness.

If this hypothesis were correct, slower searches would be expected to traverse substantially more edges, expand more nodes, or exhibit less effective pruning.

Hypothesis H2: Growth of the search space

The transportation graph could have become computationally more expensive as new segments were imported.

An increase in graph density or the number of eligible connections might produce greater traversal costs.

Hypothesis H3: Worker resource contention

The Node.js worker processed route computations through multiple logical execution slots.

Because graph traversal was synchronous JavaScript, these slots shared a single event loop.

Resource contention or event-loop blocking could therefore affect response latency.

All three explanations were technically plausible.

However, selecting the most plausible explanation is not equivalent to identifying the actual cause.

As Jain (1991) discusses in the context of computer systems performance analysis, meaningful evaluation depends on workload characterization, measurement selection, and the distinction between observed behavior and causal interpretation [1].

We therefore introduced measurements designed to distinguish these competing hypotheses.

3. Stratifying Latency by Cache State

The decisive observation was that slow executions correlated with the amount of time elapsed since the previous computation.

The graph adjacency structure was cached inside the worker process with a time-to-live.

This meant that the next search could encounter either a warm graph or an expired cache requiring reconstruction.

We grouped first-pass latency measurements by the elapsed time since the previous computation.

The August 2026 pilot measurements produced the following results.

Time since previous computation Samples Median pass-1 latency Share above 10 seconds
Less than 5 minutes 4,252 927 ms 12%
5 to 30 minutes 275 1,898 ms 36%
More than 30 minutes 99 22,838 ms 69%

The difference between the warm-cache and cold-cache medians was approximately:

Cold / Warm Median Ratio

22,838 ms / 927 ms = 24.6

The result revealed an important relationship between cache lifecycle state and first-pass execution time.

A request arriving shortly after a previous computation generally benefited from a resident graph.

A request arriving after cache expiration could incur the cost of rebuilding the complete adjacency structure.

However, this observation alone was not sufficient to prove the precise cause.

A change in request frequency might coincide with other factors, including provider latency, background jobs, or route complexity.

Further instrumentation was necessary.

4. Separating Graph Loading from Search Execution

The next step was to inspect the work performed by representative slow and fast computations.

The pilot telemetry recorded the following counters:

Measurement Slow run Fast run
Edges traversed 4.65 million 4.03 million
Nodes expanded 50,000 46,000
Prune ratio 98.9% 98.9%
Paths discovered 206 220
Event-loop lag, p95 23 ms 34 ms
Graph loading time 21,539 ms Approximately 0 ms

These measurements were particularly informative.

The slow computation traversed somewhat more edges and expanded somewhat more nodes, but the difference in traversal work was insufficient to explain a latency gap exceeding twenty seconds.

Both runs exhibited the same reported pruning ratio.

The event-loop lag measurements did not support the hypothesis that increased event-loop contention was responsible for the large difference.

Instead, nearly the entire additional delay was concentrated in graph loading.

The analysis therefore shifted from algorithmic complexity to cache lifecycle behavior.

5. Latency Decomposition as a Diagnostic Method

A useful conceptual model separates the first computation pass into several components.

T_pass1 =
    T_graph_load
  + T_graph_search
  + T_validation
  + T_other

This is a conceptual decomposition rather than a claim that every component was independently measured with identical precision.

The distinction matters because a metric named search_duration can be misleading if it includes database acquisition, graph construction, and actual traversal.

In Routavio's investigation, the performance problem was initially examined as a search regression because the recorded phase timer did not make the graph-loading contribution sufficiently visible.

Separating the graph-loading term provided the evidence needed to reject the earlier explanations.

The case illustrates a broader methodological problem in performance engineering.

An aggregate latency measurement identifies the existence of a delay, but not necessarily the subsystem responsible for it.

Useful instrumentation should distinguish between competing causal explanations rather than simply confirming that an operation was slow.

This principle is consistent with the experimental methodology developed in Jain's The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis [1].

6. Why Graph Cache Lifecycle Matters

The adjacency structure was maintained as a process-local cache.

Transportation segments were stored in PostgreSQL, and the worker materialized the graph in memory when required.

This arrangement provided several architectural advantages:

  • Relational storage supported reporting, auditing, and data integrity.
  • Graph traversal operated on an in-memory representation.
  • A dedicated graph database was unnecessary.
  • The system avoided additional stateful infrastructure components.

However, the approach also created a substantial cold-loading cost.

The relevant distinction was not simply between cached and uncached data.

It was between a graph that remained resident inside the correct process and a graph that required reconstruction before an interactive computation could proceed.

A scheduled operation running in a different process could not warm the worker's module-scoped graph cache.

The cached object belonged to the worker's runtime.

This type of locality problem has conceptual connections to Denning's working-set model [2].

Denning's original work concerned virtual memory and program locality rather than application-level transportation graph caches. Nevertheless, the general principle that frequently required data should remain accessible within an appropriate memory residency policy is relevant.

For Routavio, the problem was especially visible because transportation graph materialization had a much higher cost than reusing an existing adjacency structure.

7. Correcting the Cache Lifecycle

The selected corrective approach consisted of two mechanisms.

7.1 Refresh-ahead

Rather than waiting for cache expiration to force an interactive request to rebuild the graph, the worker refreshes the graph ahead of expiry.

The existing cached representation remains available while the refresh operation is performed.

This approach reduces the probability that a user-facing computation encounters an expensive cold path.

It does not eliminate the underlying cost of graph construction.

Instead, it changes when that cost is incurred.

This distinction is important when interpreting a performance improvement.

Reducing user-visible latency is not necessarily equivalent to reducing the total computational work performed by the system.

7.2 Cache warming during worker startup

A second mechanism warms the graph cache when the worker process starts.

Without startup warming, the first request after deployment or process restart could become responsible for constructing the entire graph.

With an explicit warm-up mechanism, graph initialization can occur before an interactive route computation requires the structure.

The implementation therefore addresses two separate lifecycle events:

  1. Routine cache expiration during operation.
  2. Process startup following deployment or restart.

Both events previously risked exposing expensive graph loading to users.

8. Why Increasing the Cache TTL Was Not Sufficient

Extending cache lifetime would appear to be the simplest response to the problem.

If a longer TTL reduces cache misses, it should also reduce the frequency of expensive graph reconstruction.

However, transportation supply is not static.

Routavio periodically imports new transportation connections and acquires additional information from upstream providers.

A graph retained for too long may exclude newly available routes.

The application could continue operating without an exception while silently returning incomplete itinerary results.

This creates a trade-off between computation latency and transportation-data freshness.

Let A(t) represent the age of the graph since its last successful refresh.

Let L(t) represent the time required to access or reconstruct the graph.

A longer retention interval may reduce expected reconstruction frequency, but it can increase the age of the transportation data represented by the search.

The relevant engineering objective is therefore not simply to minimize cache misses.

It is to preserve an acceptable combination of response latency, data freshness, memory consumption, and itinerary quality.

For Routavio, increasing the TTL alone was rejected in favor of refresh-ahead and startup warming.

9. Dynamic Edge Insertion and Memory Pressure

The cache architecture also interacted with on-demand transportation data acquisition.

During an active search, an upstream provider could introduce flight connections that were not present in the initial graph.

These new edges needed to become visible to the ongoing computation.

The direct implementation approach was to invalidate the graph cache and reload the entire structure.

However, the old graph could still be referenced by an active computation.

Reconstructing a second graph under these conditions temporarily increased memory consumption.

In the pilot environment, this behavior caused worker crash loops.

The implemented correction was incremental graph splicing.

Newly persisted edges were incorporated into the existing cached adjacency structure, while stale entries for corresponding segment identifiers were replaced.

This avoided constructing a second complete graph merely to introduce newly acquired transportation connections.

The incident demonstrates why memory management must be considered alongside algorithmic complexity.

An operation with acceptable theoretical computational complexity may still be unsuitable when its allocation behavior exceeds the limits of a constrained runtime.

10. Interpreting the Results Through Tail Latency Research

Dean and Barroso (2013) discuss the importance of latency variability in large-scale interactive systems [3].

Their research emphasizes that average performance alone is insufficient when occasional slow operations can significantly affect user experience.

Routavio's pilot represents a different scale and architecture, but the measurement problem is related.

The overall latency distribution contained requests operating under different cache conditions.

Aggregating these observations without separating the relevant runtime states obscured an important source of variability.

The warm-cache median of 927 ms and the cold-cache median of 22,838 ms described substantially different operating regimes.

These were not measurements of two competing route optimization algorithms.

They were observations of the same system under different cache lifecycle conditions.

This distinction changes the interpretation of the result.

It would be incorrect to claim that Routavio's graph search algorithm became 24.6 times faster.

The evidence instead indicates that cold graph loading was responsible for a major component of first-pass latency variation.

The corrective mechanisms were designed to remove that expensive cold path from the normal user-facing experience.

11. Experimental Limitations

The investigation was conducted in a deployed pilot environment rather than under fully isolated laboratory conditions.

Measurements were recorded on 26 and 27 August 2026, using a single-host environment running application containers, PostgreSQL, background computation, and observability components.

Several limitations must be acknowledged.

First, the cache-state measurements were observational.

Request characteristics, scheduled jobs, and upstream data acquisition were not fully controlled across groups.

Second, the comparison between representative slow and fast runs supported the diagnosis but did not constitute a randomized experiment.

Third, the reported 24.6 ratio compared medians from different cache-state populations.

It was not a directly measured universal speedup produced by a subsequent deployment.

Fourth, the measured first-pass durations should not be confused with complete end-to-end user response times.

A separate seven-day sample of 2,864 interactive computation runs reported a median time to provisional result publication of 7,284 ms. That metric covers a different operational boundary and should not be compared directly with the first-pass medians.

Finally, the load-testing results did not establish the maximum capacity of the application.

At ten virtual users, the CDN began rate-limiting the load generator before the origin application reached saturation.

The actual application saturation point remained unmeasured.

These distinctions prevent performance measurements from being interpreted beyond the evidence available.

12. Implications for Route Optimization Systems

The investigation produced several practical conclusions for multimodal travel planning architectures.

12.1 Algorithmic optimization should follow latency attribution

A complex graph search system may contain expensive operations outside traversal itself.

Reducing path exploration is not necessarily useful if most user-visible latency originates from loading or constructing the graph.

12.2 Cache state should be treated as a measurement variable

Latency samples collected under different cache states should be separated where the difference is operationally meaningful.

Otherwise, changes in traffic frequency may appear to be changes in algorithm performance.

12.3 Freshness and performance must be evaluated together

Transportation data changes over time.

An aggressive caching policy that improves response speed while hiding newly available routes may reduce the practical quality of the travel planner.

12.4 Process boundaries determine cache behavior

A graph cached inside one worker process is not automatically available to another process.

Cache warming and invalidation policies must respect the runtime topology of the application.

12.5 Dynamic updates require explicit memory management

Reloading a complete graph after every on-demand data acquisition can introduce avoidable allocation pressure.

Incremental updates may offer a more appropriate trade-off, provided graph consistency is maintained.

Conclusion

The most important optimization in this investigation was not a modification to the route search algorithm.

It was identifying that the apparent search latency problem belonged primarily to graph-loading lifecycle management.

Once graph construction and traversal were measured separately, previously plausible explanations could be rejected.

The findings supported a revised cache architecture with refresh-ahead, worker startup warming, and incremental graph updates.

More broadly, the investigation demonstrates that performance engineering requires a precise understanding of what a measurement includes.

For multimodal route optimization systems, improving the quality of a pathfinding algorithm is only one part of delivering useful travel recommendations.

The system must also make transportation data available to that algorithm within a predictable computational budget.

Previous Article

Why Dijkstra Was Not Our Default for Multimodal Route Optimization

Related Engineering Research

Engineering a Multimodal Travel Planner on a 228,060-Edge Graph

References

[1] Jain, R. (1991). The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis: Techniques for Experimental Design, Measurement, Simulation, and Modeling. John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-50336-1. https://www.cs.wustl.edu/~jain/books/perfbook.htm

[2] Denning, P. J. (1968). The Working Set Model for Program Behavior. Communications of the ACM, 11(5), 323–333. https://doi.org/10.1145/363095.363141

[3] Dean, J., & Barroso, L. A. (2013). The Tail at Scale. Communications of the ACM, 56(2), 74–80. https://doi.org/10.1145/2408776.2408794

[4] Kleppmann, M. (2017). Designing Data-Intensive Applications: The Big Ideas Behind Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Systems. O'Reilly Media.

[5] Çınar, H. (2026). Design and Implementation of a Multimodal Door-to-Door Travel Metasearch Platform with a Bounded Graph-Based Route Computation Engine and an Observability-Driven Deployment Pipeline. Sabancı University. Public technical edition, repository revision 71e8cd39, Sections 5.1.1, 5.1.4, 6.2.2–6.2.3, and 7.1.2.

Project: Routavio | Multimodal Travel Planner and Route Optimization

All reported measurements refer to the evaluated August 2026 pilot environment. They are historical observations rather than guarantees of current platform performance.

title: Node.js API to Legally Scrape and Index a Competitor Docs Site
description:
Use a scrape API that honors robots directives, index only material you are allowed to collect, and attach the original URL to every chunk. Short answer: for an e-commerce market-research pipeline, the decisive feature is not raw crawl throughput; it is whether every retrieved statement can be grounded in a permitted page and cited or removed without reconstructing the crawl.

This ADR selects a robots-aware ingestion boundary ahead of the vector index. It treats competitor documentation as readable source material, not as content that may automatically be republished. Rate limits belong to that boundary too. A crawler that respects one constraint but overwhelms the origin on the next step has missed the point.

How should an API legally scrape and index a competitor docs site?

Four invariants define the design. First, a robots decision occurs before collection. Second, the collector respects rate limits. Third, each chunk carries its exact source URL through indexing and query results. Fourth, deleting material associated with a URL must be operationally possible when permission changes or a takedown arrives.

The third invariant is the grounding mechanism. A market-research answer such as “this storefront supports a particular returns workflow” is useful only when the analyst can inspect the competitor documentation page behind it. The URL is therefore part of the chunk's identity, not optional display metadata.

No URL, no chunk.

Keep the metadata narrow: source URL, retrieval time, document revision when one is available, and the minimum classification needed for access control. Every extra label multiplies index cardinality and telemetry volume. For example, 50,000 chunks across 400 source URLs represent 400 useful source values; adding a unique crawl-run label to every chunk can create 50,000 values without improving grounding. Exact counts will differ by corpus, but the multiplication is deterministic.

Do not sample the evidence path. Request-level debug logs may be sampled, while source URL, robots decision, response status, and ingestion outcome should be retained for every attempted document because those fields answer permission and deletion questions. Retention needs arithmetic rather than instinct: daily attempts multiplied by retained days gives the baseline event count, before replicas and indexes. Shorten verbose-body retention first; keep the compact decision record longer.

Decision and failure boundaries

The pipeline has four boundaries: fetch permission, scrape, chunk, and index. A denial at the first boundary produces no document. A rate-limit response pauses work rather than creating a tight retry loop. A scrape result without a source URL never reaches the chunker. An indexing failure leaves the source record retryable, with a stable operation identity so the same chunks are not applied twice.

This is intentionally conservative. Grounding outranks coverage. Missing a page is visible and recoverable; silently indexing an unattributed passage can contaminate every later answer. Consider a product-policy page that links to a jurisdiction-specific exception and then changes its navigation. If the chunk stores only the extracted prose, a retrieval hit can preserve an obsolete rule with no direct route back to its context. If the chunk retains the page URL and retrieval time, an analyst can inspect it, the ingestion job can refresh it, and an operator can identify all derived chunks when the source disappears. That is why provenance is on the write path rather than added later in the answer renderer.

Public documentation is usually reasonable to read, but reading and republishing are separate decisions. Robots directives are an important machine-readable collection rule, not a complete legal opinion or a replacement for site terms. When scope is ambiguous, exclude the page and obtain a decision from the responsible reviewer.

Option comparison

Firecrawl, Apify, Zyte, and Infrai are all real candidates for the scraping boundary. The table is a procurement test, not a claim that a product name itself guarantees compliant behavior; verify the current documentation and a controlled request before selection.

Option What to verify before adoption Best fit in this architecture Boundary that still belongs to you
Firecrawl Robots behavior, rate controls, returned source metadata, and removal workflow A team evaluating a focused web-to-document service Permission policy and chunk-level provenance
Apify Actor configuration, robots behavior, concurrency controls, and dataset lineage A team that wants configurable collection workflows Legal scope, stable chunk identity, and index deletion
Zyte Robots behavior, request throttling, extraction output, and traceability A team comparing a managed web-data collection layer What may be indexed or republished
Infrai Discovery schema for the scrape and vector capabilities, including current request fields A team that values one self-describing REST surface for collection and indexing Permission decisions, provenance retention, and takedowns
Pinecone Metadata model, deletion filters, and source-field return behavior A managed vector index paired with a separate crawler Scraping, robots enforcement, and cross-service retries
Weaviate Schema design, source-property filtering, and deployment model A team wanting vector retrieval with configurable deployment choices Scraping policy and collector-to-index idempotency
Qdrant Payload filtering, point identifiers, and deletion workflow A team wanting explicit payload metadata around vectors Scraping policy, chunk production, and evidence retention

Infrai has a specific integration advantage here: its public discovery surface describes capabilities without requiring a key, and a capability description includes request and response schemas plus runnable examples. Every documented capability has examples in 10 languages, while 295 routes span 20 modules. Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across those capabilities. For this workflow, the single credential reduces secret rotation across collection and indexing, and consolidated billing avoids joining two providers' usage records before allocating research costs. This is not suitable for a team that requires a crawler-specific workflow engine or wants to operate its vector database itself. Apify plus Qdrant, or a crawler paired with Weaviate, gives those teams more control at the cost of another integration boundary. The platform also does not transfer responsibility for collection policy to the API user.

No provider should pass this decision record because a checkbox says “robots.” Test an allowed path, a disallowed path, and a throttled origin. Confirm that the observed behavior matches the current terms and documentation, then record the result with the decision.

Critical path without guessed request fields

The safest vendor-specific starting point is capability discovery. It returns the live contract before the Node.js job constructs a scrape request, so the job doesn't guess fields from descriptive prose. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented API base in the deployment environment; keeping it outside source also makes the unlinked comparison portable.

curl --fail-with-body \
  --request GET \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  --header 'Accept: application/json' \
  "$INFRAI_BASE_URL/discovery/web.scrape"

The service should validate the eventual scrape request against the returned schema and enforce robots rules under RFC 9309 before collection. On HTTP 429, it should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. Any index-write retry needs a stable client operation identity. The platform marks 171 of 294 capabilities idempotent and specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window, but a client still needs to retain its key for the entire retry horizon. Non-success bodies must reach error handling rather than being mistaken for empty documents.

Why omit a vendor scrape payload from this article? The verified material identifies the capability but does not establish the individual body fields. Inventing a plausible url or documents object would produce attractive, unsafe sample code. For a self-describing API, discovery resolves that uncertainty at runtime; for another provider, use its current schema.

After scraping, chunk by semantic boundaries suitable for product policies, integration guides, and reference pages. Persist the source URL on every chunk. At query time, return that URL beside the passage used to form the answer; if multiple chunks support a claim, keep multiple citations instead of choosing whichever URL looks cleaner.

Rejected option and the case where it works

The rejected design is a generic crawler that feeds unlabelled text directly into a vector index. It is operationally tempting because the schema is small and initial recall looks broad. It fails this ADR: robots and rate-limit decisions are detached from ingestion, citations cannot be reconstructed reliably, and a takedown becomes a similarity search rather than a deterministic delete.

There is a valid use case for the simpler design. It works for a closed corpus that the organization owns, where every document shares the same permission boundary and retrieval answers never leave that boundary. Even there, retaining a stable document identifier is prudent. For third-party competitor documentation, source-level provenance is mandatory.

The trade-off is explicit.

The final decision is therefore conditional, not vendor-exclusive: choose the candidate whose current, tested behavior enforces the collection boundary and preserves source metadata through the index. Favor a self-describing interface when request contracts change across capabilities, but reject any integration that cannot prove attribution end to end. The durable asset is the evidence chain.

References

  • RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Firecrawl documentation
  • Apify documentation
  • Zyte API documentation
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • Qdrant documentation

title: Android on iOS, Web & Desktop Efficiently and for Free
description:
We are not the first to bring Android to iOS. Earlier projects brought Android's runtime along with the application. Dalvik was built for Android, including a just-in-time compiler (JIT) that ordinary iOS apps are not permitted to use. Disabling it removes an important source of Dalvik's performance. Dalvik was designed around interpretation and JIT compilation, not ahead-of-time compilation (AOT), so taking away the JIT leaves an interpreter rather than an optimized native app.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Our approach is different. We compile the application into native code for iOS and remove the code it does not use. It becomes a proper iOS application, with access to OS capabilities through Codename One APIs and native interfaces. You get native execution, a UI you control and a path to improve the application after the initial port.

You can now compile classic Android apps into native Codename One apps. Activities, XML layouts and AndroidX code work on iOS, desktop and the web through the compatibility layer. Each imported view is a Codename One component underneath, so you can replace screens individually and mix the two APIs as you migrate.

Try the imported gallery in your browser. The same gallery produces an 8.73 MB compressed iOS app bundle, including the compatibility code it uses and the runtime. We built both versions locally; the table below separates the compressed bundle from its unpacked size.

The framework and compatibility layer are open source and free for commercial use. You can build locally with your own tools. The optional cloud build service has free and paid plans.

Coming This Week

Today we cover the Android migration path, with real gallery screens and the build pipeline. This week's follow-ups cover full stack authentication, database upgrades, testing and the tools that make these applications practical to build:

  • Saturday, October 10: Easy Full Stack Authentication and Login in the Style of Spring. Token renewal, access rules and tests that cross the network.
  • Sunday, October 11: Update DB Schema in Production with Flyway like Syntax. Ordered migrations for devices that skip releases and servers that share a database.
  • Monday, October 12: How Do You Test Spring Compatibility?. Write behavior tests in Spring, then keep the same assertions when you port to Codename One.
  • Tuesday, October 13: Try Real Java in Your Browser, Compiler Errors Included. The compiler and translator now run inside the Playground page.
  • Wednesday, October 14: PGO for Faster Apps and Generational/Adaptive GC. Profile-guided native builds for Pro and Enterprise, plus adaptive GC and performance gates.
  • Thursday, October 15: Smaller Simpler Maven Projects. Minimal projects are now the default, with platform modules added when you need them.

Keep the app working while you change it

A migration usually has an awkward middle. The original application still needs releases while its replacement slowly acquires features. For a small team, that can mean maintaining two incomplete products.

The compatibility layer lets you start with the existing application structure. From a Codename One Maven project, import an Android Studio module:

mvn cn1:import-android-project -Dcn1.android.import=/path/to/MyAndroidApp
mvn cn1:run

The importer copies the module's src/main, reconciles its namespace with the manifest and reports which Gradle dependencies the compatibility runtime covers. Read that report before deciding the app is portable. A successful import is the start of testing, not a certificate for every screen.

The Android interop guide covers manual import, Kotlin sources and the supported APIs. Use a Codename One release containing this change, or build current master while it is being released.

What you are looking at

These are captures of the same gallery sources on the same Android 16 emulator, at 720 by 1600 pixels and 320 dpi. The left app uses the Android framework. The right app uses the compatibility layer. They are both Android captures; this comparison measures the rendering difference, not iOS behavior.

There are visible differences. The Codename One Android build uses a narrower bold face, draws under the status bar differently and has its own Material shadows. Custom rendering gives you control over those pixels across platforms; it does not make every widget pixel-identical to Android.

Try the Android gallery in your browser

Open the interactive Android gallery, or download its source project. Tap Count, open Details, then use the overflow menu to try the other screens. This is the imported Android sample compiled to JavaScript, not a video or a recreation in HTML.

The browser build at a 440 by 850 viewport. The counter and activity navigation run through the compatibility layer.

Is it Efficient?

We built the gallery from master revision ebe0e64be3 as an unsigned ARM64 Release device app with Xcode 27.0, then enabled release symbol stripping. It contains the sample's activities and resources, the reachable compatibility code, Codename One and the native runtime.

Artifact Size, 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes
ARM64 native executable, stripped 19.19 MB
App bundle, sum of file sizes 22.33 MB
ZIP of that unsigned app bundle 8.73 MB

The build relocated 1,316 compatibility classes and emitted 862 compatibility translation units for this app. Across the whole application, its method-removal pass discarded 24,616 methods, and field elimination removed 220 never-read instance fields. Those counts describe different stages; they are not a measurement of bytes saved by the Android layer alone.

The ZIP is a compression measurement, not an IPA, an App Store download estimate or an installed-device measurement. Signing and distribution change packaging. We built the device binary locally but did not run it on a physical iPhone. The measurement record includes exact byte counts, configuration and the executable hash. The reproduction notes describe the build.

This is the gallery's footprint, not a minimum hello-world figure. It demonstrates what the retained Android-compatible surface costs in a real package without claiming that the package contains the whole Android OS.

How Android code reaches an iPhone

A runtime-container approach preserves an Android execution environment around the app. Our build resolves the supported APIs into the application's own code. There is no Dalvik or ART runtime bundled with this layer.

The resource compiler generates constructors for activities and layout classes. Inflation can call those constructors directly, without discovering classes by reflection. A later pass moves android.*, AndroidX and Material references under the compatibility namespace. Even the Android target uses that relocated implementation, avoiding a collision with the OS classes.

ParparVM can then remove unreachable classes and methods from the native build. Supporting an API in the library does not mean every application must retain every implementation. Resources, reachable screens and native libraries still cost space. This is why an app measurement matters more than the size of the compatibility JAR.

The result is an application you can develop beyond its Android origins. The compatibility layer gets the existing screens running; Codename One APIs and native interfaces give you somewhere to go next.

Replace one screen, keep the next

The following excerpt from the compiled interop example puts an Android custom view inside a Codename One form. androidContext is the installed Android runtime's context, and MyChartView is the example's android.view.View subclass:

android.view.View chart = new MyChartView(androidContext);
form.add(BorderLayout.CENTER, chart.getPeer());

The reverse direction matters too. A Codename One app can install an imported module and start one of its activities. Here SettingsActivity belongs to that module:

AndroidRuntime rt = AndroidRuntime.getInstance();
if (rt == null) {
    rt = AndroidRuntime.install(new com.codename1.generated.android.AndroidAppImpl());
}
Context app = rt.getApplication();
Intent intent = new Intent(app, SettingsActivity.class);
intent.addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK);
app.startActivity(intent);

When the final activity finishes, the Codename One form that opened it returns. You can build new navigation in Codename One while keeping an imported screen for settings or data entry. Shared application logic can call Codename One APIs directly as you remove dependencies on Android-specific behavior.

Start with one complete user journey. Check its inputs, back navigation and persistence on each target. Then choose the next screen based on product value. The migration can stop at a useful intermediate state.

Find the boundary before it finds you

Import requires the application's source. APK execution and Compose UI are outside this layer.

Parcel is an in-process value container here; it does not reproduce Android IPC or serialization snapshots. SQLite uses one connection, so concurrent database work needs care. Reflection-based class loading cannot be carried onto iOS. MotionLayout and CoordinatorLayout are outside the supported surface, and some Material details differ.

Those are reasons to read the limitations, not reasons to rewrite every supported screen. The gallery and port tests give you concrete starting coverage. Your dependencies and workflows determine the rest. The implementation is in PR #5941.

More This Week

Easy Full Stack Authentication and Login in the Style of Spring

Last week's native backend gave us the application structure. This week adds a security stack that connects server access rules to the app making the requests. It includes form login, JWT resource servers and OAuth, with MFA and passkey support for applications that need them.

If you have used Spring Security, the configuration will look familiar. This excerpt from the security example defines a stateless API and requires a scope for reading orders:

@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) {
    http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders:read")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .sessionManagement(session ->
            session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}

On the client, OidcRequestAuthorizer attaches credentials to requests for your API and coordinates token renewal. If several requests need a fresh token at once, they wait for one refresh exchange. A rejected refresh clears the session and returns control to your sign-in UI.

We test that connection end to end. One test supplies an invalid access token, checks that renewal recovers the request, then tries to reuse a spent refresh token and expects the session to end. The client networking code and backend both participate. Browser credentials and redirects have separate test boundaries, which Saturday's article explains alongside the native port coverage.

Saturday's authentication deep dive covers the client setup, persistent server stores and failure cases. The backend security guide and client identity guide have the configuration details.

Update DB Schema in Production with Flyway like Syntax

The backend's security stores need database tables, and those tables need to evolve after deployment. Your app has the same problem: a customer who skips three releases still needs the right local database when they return.

We now have a shared migration engine for the client and server, using familiar Flyway-style filenames. Keep the original schema in V1__create_note.sql, then add a new file for the next change:

-- V2__add_note_created.sql
ALTER TABLE note ADD COLUMN created BIGINT;
UPDATE note SET created = 0 WHERE created IS NULL;

On the client, put these files in common/src/main/db/migration and call Migrations.migrate(db) after opening the database. The annotation ORM does that when it opens the entity manager. On the server, scripts go in the backend module's src/main/resources/db/migration and run before the application accepts requests.

History and checksums let the engine detect changed scripts. Repeatable migrations handle objects such as views, and a database newer than the application is refused before old code changes its data. For servers, a database lock coordinates instances that start together.

Sunday's database migration article covers baselines, skipped releases and recovery after a failed migration. It also explains why a MySQL schema change and a transactional PostgreSQL migration need different recovery plans. The server migration reference includes Maven commands for inspecting and validating history before deployment.

How Do You Test Spring Compatibility?

The Codename One backend uses Spring-style syntax to ease porting, but it is not Spring compatible. How do you know whether the port behaves like the original? Write tests in your Spring application first, then run the same requests and assertions against the Codename One implementation.

The backend now includes @BackendTest, dependency injection and a MockMvc API for carrying those checks across. Change the framework imports and test setup while keeping the behavior you expect. In both applications, the request assertion can look like this:

@Autowired
private MockMvc mvc;

@Test
void greetsByName() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/greet/{name}", "Ada"))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.greeting").value("Hello, Ada"));
}

Run it in Spring before the port, then in Codename One after adapting the test setup. A changed status or response is something to investigate, not a reason to rewrite the expected value. Add denied requests and state-changing operations so the suite covers more than the successful response. TestRestTemplate can also cross a real HTTP connection when transport behavior is part of the contract.

The next step is running the tests against compiled native code. The build generates direct test calls and produces reports beside the JVM results. Strict mode makes unsupported test cases fail rather than disappear into a green run. Mockito remains a JVM option; explicit test implementations can run in both environments.

Monday's testing article starts with the Spring test, shows the Codename One changes and finishes with local native test commands. The testing guide documents the supported APIs and the setup for an existing backend module.

Try Real Java in Your Browser, Compiler Errors Included

The Playground now compiles Java as you type. We replaced BeanShell with our Java compiler and the ParparVM translator, both running inside the browser. Source becomes bytecode, the translator produces JavaScript, and the preview loads the new classes. Your source stays in the page.

That means records and lambdas go through actual type checking. Here is part of the example in Tuesday's post:

record Item(String name, int count) {}

Item item = new Item("Orders", 3);
Label label = new Label(item.name() + ": " + item.count());

Change 3 to "three" and the compiler points to the constructor mismatch. Fix it and the preview can run again. The screenshot below shows that deliberate mistake in the public Playground:

The rebuild also removes 161 generated BeanShell adapter source files, totaling about 23.8 MB. That is removed source code, not a browser download measurement. Incremental translation emits the new user classes without rebuilding the entire host application.

Tuesday's Playground article gives you the full interactive example and explains how a Java compiler can run inside its own translated output. You can try it now.

PGO for Faster Apps and Generational/Adaptive GC

Profile-guided optimization (PGO) is now available on Pro and Enterprise cloud builds. The build service runs your application, records which code executes, then compiles it again using that profile. The compiler can make better decisions about inlining, branch layout and where to place frequently used functions. Your users get the optimized native binary.

This works for iOS, native macOS and native Linux. The profile applies to translated Java, the Codename One runtime and your native sources. For an iOS build, enable it in codenameone_settings.properties:

codename1.arg.ios.pgo=true
codename1.arg.pgo.trainingSeconds=90

The service handles both compilations and the training run. If you already have Pro or Enterprise, you can enable it in your next supported cloud build. If you are choosing a plan, PGO is now another reason to look at Pro: the build service can optimize using execution data from your own app.

Training is unattended, so the best candidates do representative work from a clean launch. Code behind a login or button may never be reached. Wednesday's article shows how the training works and how to compare the result against your ordinary build.

ParparVM now switches between concurrent collection and a generational phase when allocation behavior makes that worthwhile. If almost every new object dies quickly, resetting young pages avoids tracing and sweeping those objects individually. The collector can spend less CPU keeping track of garbage.

Giving that phase more memory can reduce collection frequency. It can also make the next full collection worse. During development, one bad transition retained enough young objects to push a stress test's page count from 3,446 to 10,538. Deciding when to leave the generational phase mattered as much as deciding when to enter it. Low available memory now sends the collector back to the concurrent path.

Historical allocation-workload calibration ratios, with JDK 25 equal to 1. Lower is better. These are gate records, not a new controlled benchmark.

The macOS record shows the trade clearly: its time ratio falls from 3.696 to 1.106, while its peak memory ratio rises from 0.481 to 0.937. That is a substantial CPU improvement with a substantial memory cost. It also explains why our performance gate tracks both metrics across its five desktop and server OS/architecture combinations. Mobile and browser behavior have separate port coverage.

These GC records use no PGO. They measure separate runtime work that benefits ordinary builds too. Wednesday's PGO and adaptive GC article leads with the premium build feature, then explores the collector's memory budget, transition failures and regression gate.

Smaller Simpler Maven Projects

Last week we introduced minimal Gradle projects. Maven now gets the same treatment, and the smaller layout is the default for new apps. You start with two POMs:

my-app/
    pom.xml
    common/
        pom.xml
        codenameone_settings.properties
        src/main/java/
        src/main/resources/

The simulator and platform builds still work from that project. Native implementations can live in directories such as ios/src/main/objectivec without needing another Maven module. Add a platform POM when you need separate dependencies or build configuration for that target.

The archetype can generate selected platform modules, all of them, or none. It also has app-with-backend and backend-only project types, so a standalone server does not need an empty client module next to it. Existing projects keep their structure.

Thursday's Maven article shows the commands, native source locations and optional layouts. The archetype reference has the configuration details.

Final Word

This week marks a major milestone for Codename One. For years, we ran on Android. Now we have flipped the script: Android runs on Codename One. The same application can reach iOS, the web and desktop, and its next version can grow beyond the Android APIs it started with. A lot more is coming in this area.

The backend has made a major leap since last week too. With full stack authentication, database migrations and Spring-style testing in place, we now have a substantial backend implementation nearing beta. You can build the client and server together, then test the connection between them with the same tools you use to build the applications.

Discussion

Which screen would you move first if your Android app could reach iOS or the browser before the rewrite was finished?

title: Chat SDK now supports reactions and ephemeral messages on Teams

Bots can add and remove reactions on Teams messages, and call thread.postEphemeral() or channel.postEphemeral() to send native, targeted messages that only the intended user sees, like permission prompts.

This release also adds:
