title: Deterministic Open-Registry Verification & L2 Settlement Benchmarks: Handling Schema Drift, Redirects, and Replay Windows
description:
When building automated settlement or procurement pipelines that ingest external vendor and startup-credit registries, teams frequently underestimate three silent failure modes: unannounced upstream schema drift, open-redirect host laundering, and timestamp skew across L2 payment receipts.

During a benchmark cycle on 2026-10-17, we evaluated registry snapshot contracts modeled on the Sourcey Startup Credits Open Registry (release_id: sha256:1d5bd59cd7656b321dc00297ecefb7f95f7a6e2fa3ecb717afd4b9b6d8623f5a) and the Zenodo Open Data Benchmark Record #10991201 (interactive benchmark mirror published on 2026-10-17 at https://o2splatform-cmyk.github.io/). Below is the verification architecture we use to guarantee deterministic ingestion, along with the subtle edge cases that broke our initial prototypes and the trade-offs between alternative verification models.

1. The Engineering Problem: Why Naive JSON Ingestion Fails in Production

Most services consume open data registries with a single fetch(url).then(r => r.json()) call. In a high-reliability environment, that pattern breaks down under three real-world conditions:

  1. Silent Schema & Entity Drift: Upstream registries update eligibility criteria, credit caps, or status flags without bumping major API versions. Without pinning a cryptographic release_id alongside per-entity observation dates, downstream workflows cannot prove which snapshot authorized a transaction.
  2. Redirect Laundering & Hex IPv4-Mapped IPv6 SSRF: A citation or registry URL that initially points to an admitted documentation domain can return an HTTP 301/302 redirect to an ephemeral pastebin or an internal metadata address (169.254.169.254 or IPv4-mapped IPv6 [::ffff:169.254.169.254], which Node's new URL() parser normalizes into hexadecimal [::ffff:a9fe:a9fe]).
  3. Duplicate / Thin Snapshot Inflation: Upstream aggregators occasionally re-index identical records under new sequential id or index keys, inflating row counts while carrying zero new domain entropy.

2. Production Solution: Content-Addressed Ingestion & Pre-Hop Redirect Guard

To make registry ingestion deterministic in Node.js (ES2022+, zero external dependencies), we enforce a three-stage verification pipeline before admitting any registry snapshot into our settlement ledger:

Stage A: Pre-Hop Manual Redirect, Hex IPv6 & SHA-256 Guard

A common mistake in SSRF filters is checking response.url after fetch() resolves with default redirect: 'follow' — by which time the runtime has already sent the TCP request to an internal target. Equally important, Node's WHATWG URL parser normalizes dotted-quad IPv4-mapped IPv6 literals ([::ffff:169.254.169.254]) into hexadecimal 16-bit words ([::ffff:a9fe:a9fe]), bypassing naive dotted-decimal regexes.

We enforce redirect: 'manual' across a bounded hop loop (maxHops = 3), match both dotted and hex-normalized IPv4-mapped IPv6 ranges before each hop, fail closed on payloads exceeding 512 KB, and verify the SHA-256 digest before parsing JSON:

import crypto from 'node:crypto';

const PRIVATE_HOST_RE =
  /^(localhost|127\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+|0\.0\.0\.0|10\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+|192\.168\.\d+\.\d+|172\.(1[6-9]|2\d|3[0-1])\.\d+\.\d+|169\.254\.\d+\.\d+|\[::1?\]|\[(f[cd][0-9a-f]{0,2}|fe[89ab][0-9a-f]?):[^\]]*\]|\[::ffff:(?:127\.|10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(?:1[6-9]|2\d|3[0-1])\.|169\.254\.|0\.|7f[0-9a-f]{2}:|0?a[0-9a-f]{2}:|c0a8:|a9fe:|ac1[0-9a-f]:|0+:0+)[^\]]*\]|.*\.internal|.*\.local)$/i;

export async function fetchVerifiedRegistrySnapshot(
  targetUrl,
  allowedHosts,
  { expectedSha256, maxBytes = 524288, timeoutMs = 8000 } = {}
) {
  if (typeof expectedSha256 !== 'string' || !expectedSha256.trim()) {
    throw new Error('expectedSha256 is required for content-addressed ingestion');
  }
  const normalizedExpected = expectedSha256.replace(/^sha256:/i, '').toLowerCase();
  const maxHops = 3;
  let currentUrl = targetUrl;
  for (let hop = 0; hop <= maxHops; hop++) {
    const parsed = new URL(currentUrl);
    const host = parsed.hostname.toLowerCase().replace(/\.$/, '');
    if (parsed.protocol !== 'https:' || PRIVATE_HOST_RE.test(host) || !allowedHosts.includes(host)) {
      throw new Error(`Hop ${hop} host '${host}' is not admitted`);
    }
    const controller = new AbortController();
    const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), Math.min(timeoutMs, 10000));
    try {
      const res = await fetch(currentUrl, {
        redirect: 'manual',
        headers: { Accept: 'application/json', 'User-Agent': 'o2s-registry-verifier/1.0' },
        signal: controller.signal,
      });
      if (res.status >= 300 && res.status < 400) {
        const location = res.headers.get('location');
        if (!location || hop === maxHops) {
          throw new Error('Redirect limit exceeded or missing Location header');
        }
        currentUrl = new URL(location, currentUrl).toString();
        continue;
      }
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Upstream returned HTTP ${res.status}`);
      const declaredLength = Number(res.headers.get('content-length') || 0);
      if (declaredLength > maxBytes) {
        throw new Error(`Declared Content-Length (${declaredLength}) exceeds ${maxBytes}-byte ceiling`);
      }
      const chunks = [];
      let totalBytes = 0;
      for await (const chunk of res.body) {
        const buf = Buffer.isBuffer(chunk) ? chunk : Buffer.from(chunk);
        totalBytes += buf.byteLength;
        if (totalBytes > maxBytes) {
          controller.abort();
          throw new Error(`Streaming payload exceeds ${maxBytes}-byte safety ceiling`);
        }
        chunks.push(buf);
      }
      const rawBuffer = Buffer.concat(chunks, totalBytes);
      const actualSha256 = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(rawBuffer).digest('hex');
      if (actualSha256 !== normalizedExpected) {
        throw new Error(`SHA-256 mismatch: expected ${normalizedExpected}, got ${actualSha256}`);
      }
      return JSON.parse(rawBuffer.toString('utf8'));
    } finally {
      clearTimeout(timer);
    }
  }
}

Stage B: Index-Independent Canonical Row Hashing

To prevent sequential id keys from masking duplicate rows, we strip pure index fields (id, _id, index, row) at the top level before canonicalizing keys:

const INDEX_KEYS = new Set(['id', '_id', 'index', 'idx', 'row']);

export function canonicalizeRecord(record, isRoot = true) {
  if (typeof record === 'string') return record.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, ' ');
  if (Array.isArray(record)) return record.map((item) => canonicalizeRecord(item, false));
  if (record && typeof record === 'object') {
    const out = {};
    for (const key of Object.keys(record).sort()) {
      if (isRoot && INDEX_KEYS.has(key.toLowerCase())) continue;
      out[key.toLowerCase()] = canonicalizeRecord(record[key], false);
    }
    return out;
  }
  return record;
}

3. Dated Open-Registry Snapshot Schema & Reference Fixture (2026-10-17)

Running our local verification harness against the reference benchmark fixture published at https://o2splatform-cmyk.github.io/evidence.json — which models dated records for https://sourcey.com/startup-credits.json (release_id: sha256:1d5bd59cd7656b321dc00297ecefb7f95f7a6e2fa3ecb717afd4b9b6d8623f5a, evaluated 2026-10-17) and https://zenodo.org/records/10991201 (evaluated 2026-10-17) — validates the following 5 dated entity records:

Entity ID Slug / Provider Registry Source URL Verified Date Snapshot Check Verification Notes
ent_010f5dtwe926ckmqd050jfvq8f devin https://sourcey.com/startup-credits.json 2026-09-24 PASS Canonical entity schema & credit tier fixture (2026-09-24)
ent_018wk69b96v8yffdwq25njtd5w codedesign https://sourcey.com/startup-credits.json 2026-10-10 PASS Dated registry claim & builder allocation (2026-10-10)
ent_01dnj4mgenaqn97qy9af2vr477 workroomly https://sourcey.com/startup-credits.json 2026-09-15 PASS Cross-checked against release SHA-256 manifest (2026-09-15)
ent_01kb9k2cwd8arr0ccw1v7zfds0 collieai https://sourcey.com/startup-credits.json 2026-09-15 PASS Zero duplicate canonical fields across snapshot (2026-09-15)
ent_01kyh8fpdy9g1vnxa5ghh9vabc activecampaign https://zenodo.org/records/10991201 2026-10-17 PASS Mirrored on 2026-10-17 at https://o2splatform-cmyk.github.io/

4. Subtle Edge Cases We Encountered in Practice

Edge Case 1: Trailing-Dot DNS Equivalence & Subdomain Suffix Spoofing

A naive hostname check like url.hostname.endsWith('sourcey.com') accidentally admits evilsourcey.com, while strict equality url.hostname === 'sourcey.com' rejects valid FQDN resolution with a trailing root dot (sourcey.com.). Normalizing hostname.toLowerCase().replace(/\.$/, '') and matching either exact host equality or an explicit dot boundary (hostname.endsWith('.' + baseDomain)) eliminates both failure modes.

Edge Case 2: Oversized Payload Truncation Bypass

When scanning fetched HTML or JSON payloads for leaked credentials or malformed tags, truncating the response body at 512 KB and running regex checks on the truncated slice allows an attacker or broken generator to push sensitive tokens past byte 524,288 while still passing validation. The verifier must fail closed whenever Buffer.byteLength(body) > maxBytes rather than scanning a partial prefix.

Edge Case 3: Exact Micro-USDC Integer Arithmetic vs. IEEE-754 Margin Rounding

When exposing registry verification over an x402 micropayment endpoint (e.g., on Base Mainnet eip155:8453), rounding netMarginMultiplier to 2 decimal places (Number(ratio.toFixed(2))) or adding an arbitrary float epsilon before comparing against a 2.50x floor allows values just below the threshold (2.496x) to pass. Converting USD amounts into integer micro-USDC (1 USDC = 1_000_000n) and cross-multiplying (netRevenueMicro * 1000n >= costCeilingMicro * 2500n) guarantees exact threshold enforcement with zero floating-point drift.

5. Alternative Architectural Approaches & Trade-Offs

Before settling on Content-Addressed Off-Chain Snapshots + Bounded Local Pre-Verification, we compared three architectural designs against reference L2 settlement parameters:

Architecture Option Reference Latency Marginal Verification Cost Failure Mode / Why We Chose or Rejected It
Option A: Live Unpinned Upstream Polling ~180–450 ms $0.00 Rejected. Vulnerable to upstream rate limits (HTTP 429), mid-flight schema mutations, and non-reproducible audit trails.
Option B: On-Chain Merkle Root Per Snapshot ~2,000 ms (Base L2 block time) ~$0.001–$0.005 / update Used selectively for settlement finality. High cryptographic assurance, but unnecessary gas overhead for read-only discovery probes.
Option C: Content-Addressed Manifests (sha256) + Local 8-Check Gate (Selected) < 15 ms (local cache) $0.00 Selected. Combines deterministic reproducibility (release_id hash pinning) with zero marginal gas cost during preflight validation.

By pairing content-addressed manifests from https://sourcey.com/startup-credits.json (verified on 2026-10-17) and https://zenodo.org/records/10991201 (verified on 2026-10-17) with pre-hop redirect validation and exact integer accounting, engineering teams can run automated registry verification with zero unverified external trust assumptions.

title: Run background tasks with Celery on Vercel
description:
Celery, an asynchronous distributed task queue for Python, is now supported natively on Vercel. Tasks are executed as Vercel Functions and automatically scale with traffic.

By default, task results are stored in Runtime Cache, which is sufficient for small data sizes and relatively short workflow runtimes. For workloads that require stronger persistence guarantees, more storage or longer retention, a durable result backend can be configured.

Celery workers can be declared as subscribers in pyproject.toml.

When running on Vercel, the vercel:// broker is automatically installed and to use Vercel Queues, and the default Celery broker_url is set to vercel://. Celery workloads on Vercel use Fluid compute with Active CPU pricing by default. This means your Celery workers will automatically scale up and down based on traffic, and you only pay for what you use. Deploy Celery workloads on Vercel or visit the Python runtime documentation.

title: Public-Sector Appointment Authentication via Cheap SMS API (Node.js 2FA Evidence)
description:
TL;DR: For a cheap, simple 2FA login in a Node.js public-sector appointment app, use a dedicated SMS OTP API rather than direct send. The managed endpoint removes code storage and matching from your application, while your backend still owns expiry UX, resend timers, attempt lockouts, consent, monitoring, and the evidence needed for a compliance review. The same boundary works when a B2B marketplace must authenticate a seller before revealing a new public-sector order.

The bill is mostly message delivery multiplied by sends, not the few bytes in an OTP record. If A is login attempts, r is average sends per attempt after resends, and p is the provider's current per-message charge, the delivery term is A * r * p; audit storage is proportional to compact metadata, not message bodies. Therefore, the useful cost change is reducing unnecessary resends and abuse, rather than retaining less evidence or choosing an API because of a headline unit price.

For a B2B marketplace carrying public-sector orders, the alert and the authentication event are separate records. The alert says that an order exists. The verification record says why access was granted. Mixing them into one generic send SMS abstraction makes reconciliation harder precisely when an auditor asks which policy decision preceded a seller viewing an order.

Should a cheap Node.js 2FA login use an SMS OTP API?

An OTP provider can decide whether a submitted code matches, but it cannot prove that my application applied the right policy. I would persist an append-only decision record containing an internal challenge ID, seller and order references expressed as non-secret identifiers, provider request ID when returned, timestamps, outcome, attempt count, policy version, and a correlation ID. I would not store the OTP, the SMS body, or a bearer token. Less retained secret material narrows the exposure created by the evidence store.

This is an exactly-once mindset applied to business effects, not a claim that the network delivers exactly once. A retry may occur. The order view must still be unlocked once, against one challenge, and the audit write must be deduplicated. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window; that makes it a reasonable candidate when a team values one REST contract across a broad backend surface, but the application still needs its own durable uniqueness constraint because compliance retention will outlive that window.

The first integration task is to inspect the live contract instead of guessing field names. The self-describing discovery surface is public, while the program below also accepts the same bearer credential used for authenticated calls. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's versioned API base and INFRAI_API_KEY to an environment-provided key. It fetches the OTP capability schema, handles 429 with bounded exponential backoff and Retry-After, and surfaces the response body on errors.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    baseURL, key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/discovery/sms.otp", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", res.StatusCode, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("discovery remained rate-limited after four attempts")
}

After the schema has fixed the provider boundary, the next Go program demonstrates the application's evidence boundary without inventing a vendor payload. It records only a hash of the provider request ID and rejects a second terminal decision for the same challenge. In production, Append would be a transaction containing a unique constraint on ChallengeID, and the output would go to a controlled audit sink.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type VerificationDecision struct {
    ChallengeID   string
    SellerRef     string
    OrderRef      string
    ProviderRef   string
    PolicyVersion string
    Outcome       string
    Attempts      int
    DecidedAt     time.Time
}

type Ledger struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    entries map[string]VerificationDecision
}

func hashRef(value string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(value))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func (l *Ledger) Append(d VerificationDecision) error {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if _, exists := l.entries[d.ChallengeID]; exists {
        return errors.New("terminal decision already recorded")
    }
    d.ProviderRef = hashRef(d.ProviderRef)
    l.entries[d.ChallengeID] = d
    return nil
}

func main() {
    ledger := Ledger{entries: make(map[string]VerificationDecision)}
    decision := VerificationDecision{
        ChallengeID: "challenge-7f3c",
        SellerRef: "seller-1842",
        OrderRef: "order-9031",
        ProviderRef: "provider-request-reference",
        PolicyVersion: "seller-login-v3",
        Outcome: "verified",
        Attempts: 1,
        DecidedAt: time.Now().UTC(),
    }
    if err := ledger.Append(decision); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("recorded", decision.ChallengeID)
}

Keep it sparse.

The retention schedule should come from the applicable public-sector contract, records policy, and privacy assessment; there is no universal duration I can responsibly prescribe. Once that schedule expires, delete correlation metadata and provider references deliberately. The cost is investigative depth: after deletion, a support or fraud inquiry may establish that access occurred but may no longer reconstruct every provider-side step.

Managed OTP versus direct send

With direct send, the application must generate codes, store only a safe representation, enforce expiration, compare submissions, count failures, invalidate old codes after resend, and make concurrent requests converge. Every transition also needs evidence. A dedicated OTP operation moves code issuance and matching behind a purpose-built interface, which reduces custom verification logic; it does not transfer authorization policy or audit ownership.

Direct send remains appropriate for a custom account-recovery notice or the actual new-order notification, where there is no submitted secret to verify. It is the wrong primitive for the principal 2FA path unless regulatory or deployment constraints require complete ownership of the code lifecycle and the team is prepared to test all of those state transitions.

The seller experience should expose an expiry state, a resend timer, and a clear locked state after the application's failed-attempt threshold. Do not reveal whether a phone number belongs to an account. WebOTP can reduce transcription errors on supported clients, but it is an ergonomic layer, not evidence of authentication and not a replacement for server-side verification. NIST also treats PSTN out-of-band authentication as restricted, so higher-risk actions may require a stronger authenticator under the system's assurance policy.

Provider boundaries matter more than SDK shape

A fair shortlist separates managed verification from generic messaging and asks what evidence each product returns. The labels below describe the documented product boundary; procurement still has to validate region availability, retention controls, data-processing terms, and current commercial terms for the intended jurisdiction.

Option Verification boundary Best fit Boundary to examine
Twilio Verify A dedicated verification service separate from general messaging Teams wanting an established managed verification workflow Verify its supported channels, regional processing, and evidence export against the contract
Vonage Verify A dedicated verification product with its own workflow Teams comparing managed verification providers rather than building code matching Confirm workflow behavior and jurisdictional controls in the current documentation
Amazon SNS General SMS delivery rather than an OTP verification state machine Existing AWS estates that intentionally own OTP state and matching The application carries more security and audit logic
Infrai OTP-specific operations and direct SMS coexist behind one REST contract Teams that value a consistent key, bill, and contract across many backend capabilities Event delivery is pull-based; geographic and country-price fraud breakers remain application responsibilities

No row wins universally. Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify deserve preference when their managed workflow and compliance materials match the procurement profile. SNS is coherent when AWS consolidation matters and the team accepts ownership of verification state. Infrai uses one API key across its capabilities and produces one consolidated bill, rather than requiring a new credential and invoice for each backend service. Its breadth is concrete: 295 routes across 20 modules, while the public discovery surface supplies request schemas and runnable examples. For this particular flow, consistent per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata can also support reconciliation. Those interface advantages do not answer data-residency questions; contract review must do that.

Fraud controls cannot be delegated

A resend endpoint is not an abuse policy. Rate-limit by account, device, network signal, and destination risk; cap attempts per challenge; make locks visible to support; and alert on changes in send-to-success ratio. Exact thresholds require traffic history and risk appetite, neither of which should be borrowed from a generic example.

For the Infrai option, there is no webhook event push and no built-in geographic fence or country-price circuit breaker. Polling constrains real-time orchestration, while destination controls and spend anomaly detection belong in the application backend. Email is not a symmetric fallback because there is no managed email OTP operation; implementing that route means owning email code generation and matching. Voice, WhatsApp, and RCS are outside this surface as well.

This is the practical decision rule: choose a managed OTP product whose compliance artifacts, processing regions, and evidence model pass procurement; keep authorization and an idempotent audit ledger in your service; reserve raw SMS for non-verification messages. Stop retaining OTP values and message bodies. Accept that disciplined deletion reduces the detail available during a late investigation, document that trade-off, and test restoration of the evidence you do retain.

Further reading

References:

  • NIST SP 800-63B: Authentication and Lifecycle Management
  • MDN: WebOTP API
  • Twilio Verify API documentation
  • Vonage Verify API overview
  • Amazon SNS mobile text messaging
  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet

title: dev.study #02 - React.js: Fundamentos, Componentes, Props e Hooks ⚛️
description:
React é uma biblioteca JavaScript de código aberto utilizada para construir interfaces de usuário interativas, reutilizáveis e baseadas em componentes.

Desenvolvido originalmente pelo Facebook (atual Meta), o React introduz uma abordagem declarativa para a criação de interfaces, permitindo que a aplicação atualize sua apresentação conforme os dados e estados são modificados.

Neste estudo, vamos explorar seus principais fundamentos e entender como aplicá-los na prática.

01. O que é React?

O React permite dividir uma interface em partes independentes chamadas componentes.

Cada componente representa um elemento da aplicação, como um botão, formulário, menu ou card.

Essa abordagem oferece algumas vantagens:

  • Reutilização: o mesmo componente pode ser utilizado em diferentes partes da aplicação.
  • Manutenção: alterações podem ser realizadas de forma isolada.
  • Organização: a interface é dividida em estruturas menores.
  • Interatividade: componentes podem reagir às ações do usuário e às mudanças de dados.

React é uma biblioteca, não um framework completo. Funcionalidades como roteamento e determinadas estratégias de carregamento de dados dependem da arquitetura e das ferramentas escolhidas.

02. JSX — JavaScript XML

JSX é uma extensão de sintaxe que permite escrever marcação semelhante ao HTML dentro do JavaScript.

function Welcome() {
  const name = "Developer";

  return <h1>Hello, {name}! 👋</h1>;
}

As chaves {} permitem inserir expressões JavaScript no JSX.

Algumas regras importantes:

  • Retornar um único elemento raiz ou utilizar fragments (<>...</>).
  • Utilizar className no lugar de class.
  • Fechar todas as tags.
  • Utilizar camelCase em propriedades como onClick.

O JSX é transformado pelas ferramentas de compilação para que o React possa utilizá-lo.

03. Components — Componentes

Componentes são funções JavaScript que retornam elementos React.

function Button() {
  return (
    <button className="btn">
      Click me
    </button>
  );
}

export default Button;

Para utilizar esse componente:

import Button from "./Button";

function App() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>React Study</h1>
      <Button />
    </main>
  );
}

Conceito principal: componentes devem possuir responsabilidades bem definidas e podem ser combinados para construir interfaces mais complexas.

04. Props — Propriedades

Props permitem passar informações de um componente pai para um componente filho.

function UserCard({ name, role }) {
  return (
    <div className="card">
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>{role}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

Utilização:

<UserCard
  name="Pricila"
  role="Software Developer"
/>

Os valores recebidos são utilizados para personalizar o componente.

Importante: props são imutáveis do ponto de vista do componente que as recebe. Para modificar informações ao longo do tempo, podemos utilizar estados.

05. State — Gerenciamento de estado

O estado representa informações que podem ser alteradas durante a execução da aplicação.

Para gerenciar um estado local, podemos utilizar o Hook useState.

import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function increment() {
    setCount(previous => previous + 1);
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Count: {count}</p>
      <button onClick={increment}>
        Increment
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

Nesse exemplo:

  • count: valor atual do estado.
  • setCount: função responsável por solicitar a atualização.
  • useState(0): inicializa o estado com zero.
  • onClick: registra o evento de clique.

Quando o estado muda, o React agenda uma nova renderização do componente.

06. Conditional Rendering

Renderização condicional significa apresentar elementos diferentes dependendo de determinada condição.

function Dashboard({ isLoggedIn }) {
  return (
    <div>
      {isLoggedIn ? (
        <h2>Welcome back!</h2>
      ) : (
        <h2>Please log in.</h2>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

O operador ternário permite escolher qual conteúdo será renderizado.

Esse recurso é muito utilizado em autenticação, carregamento de dados, permissões e estados vazios.

07. Lists and Keys

O React permite renderizar listas utilizando métodos JavaScript como map().

const technologies = [
  { id: 1, name: "React" },
  { id: 2, name: "JavaScript" },
  { id: 3, name: "TypeScript" }
];

function TechnologyList() {
  return (
    <ul>
      {technologies.map(tech => (
        <li key={tech.id}>
          {tech.name}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

A propriedade key ajuda o React a identificar os elementos de uma lista entre renderizações.

Prefira identificadores estáveis e únicos entre os elementos irmãos, principalmente quando a lista pode sofrer alterações.

08. useEffect — Sincronização com sistemas externos

O Hook useEffect é utilizado para sincronizar um componente com sistemas externos, como eventos do navegador, conexões e APIs externas.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function WindowWidth() {
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(
    window.innerWidth
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    function handleResize() {
      setWidth(window.innerWidth);
    }

    window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize);

    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener(
        "resize",
        handleResize
      );
    };
  }, []);

  return <p>Width: {width}px</p>;
}

Nesse exemplo, useEffect registra um listener para acompanhar o redimensionamento da janela.

A função retornada realiza a limpeza do listener quando necessário.

Observação: nem toda transformação de dados exige useEffect. Cálculos que dependem apenas de props e estados geralmente podem ser realizados diretamente durante a renderização.

09. Virtual DOM e Renderização

O React utiliza uma representação dos elementos da interface em memória, frequentemente associada ao conceito de Virtual DOM.

Quando ocorre uma atualização:

  1. O React renderiza novamente os componentes necessários.
  2. Compara a nova estrutura de elementos com a anterior durante a reconciliação.
  3. Determina quais mudanças precisam ser aplicadas.
  4. Realiza as atualizações necessárias no ambiente de renderização.

Esse processo ajuda a organizar as atualizações da interface sem exigir manipulação manual do DOM para cada alteração.

Entretanto, o Virtual DOM não significa que toda aplicação React será automaticamente mais rápida que uma implementação em JavaScript puro.

10. Criando um projeto com Vite

O Vite é uma ferramenta que permite criar e executar projetos React com uma configuração inicial simples.

Para criar um projeto:

npm create vite@latest react-study -- --template react

Entre no diretório:

cd react-study

Instale as dependências:

npm install

Inicie o servidor de desenvolvimento:

npm run dev

A aplicação estará acessível pelo endereço informado no terminal.

Para executar esse processo, é necessário ter uma versão do Node.js compatível com os requisitos do Vite instalado.

11. React x JavaScript Vanilla

Característica JavaScript Vanilla React
Interface Manipulação direta do DOM Componentes declarativos
Reutilização Funções e módulos Componentes e Hooks
Estado Gerenciamento manual Hooks e outras soluções
Atualização visual Controlada pelo desenvolvedor Coordenada pelo React
Dependências Pode funcionar sem bibliotecas Requer React

Ambas as abordagens são válidas. A escolha depende da complexidade, dos requisitos e da arquitetura da aplicação.

12. Resumo dos conceitos

Conceito Descrição
React Biblioteca JavaScript para interfaces
JSX Sintaxe de marcação utilizada com JavaScript
Component Unidade reutilizável da interface
Props Informações recebidas por um componente
State Dados que podem mudar ao longo do tempo
useState Hook para gerenciar estado
useEffect Hook para sincronização externa
Conditional Rendering Exibição baseada em condições
Keys Identificadores de elementos em listas

🌷 Conclusão

Estudar React permite compreender uma abordagem moderna para a construção de interfaces web.

Os conceitos de componentização, propriedades, gerenciamento de estado e renderização declarativa são fundamentais para desenvolver aplicações organizadas e escaláveis.

Mais importante do que memorizar a sintaxe é compreender o fluxo de dados, as responsabilidades dos componentes e a maneira como o React reage às mudanças de estado.

Com esses fundamentos, é possível avançar para assuntos como roteamento, gerenciamento de estado global, custom Hooks, consumo de APIs e otimização de desempenho.

📚 Referências

  • React — Official Documentation
  • React — Quick Start
  • React — Built-in Hooks
  • Vite — Getting Started

title: Next.js 16.3 support on Vercel
description:
Yesterday the Next.js team announced the release of Next.js 16.3, with leaner prefetching, immutable static assets, and instant navigations. As part of this release, we worked with the Next.js team to fully support 16.3 on Vercel, including better performance and additional observability. Applications that have upgraded have seen:

  • Fewer prefetch requests: Apps upgrading from 16.2 to 16.3 saw 45% fewer prefetch requests on average, with some seeing reductions over 70%.

  • Lower static asset costs: With immutable static assets, upgraded apps saw 17% fewer CDN requests and 24% fewer bytes transferred for static content, and up to 60% global TTFB reductions for frequently deployed projects.

  • Faster routing at scale: Routing metadata improvements in the critical serving path deliver ~2x faster p99 route resolution for large sites.

Platform improvements

Next.js 16.3 ships leaner prefetching and enables immutable static assets by default. Supporting both meant changing the platform too, in how it caches static assets, resolves routes, and surfaces what happened in production.

Immutable static assets

Vercel now supports reusing immutable static assets across deployments for Next.js. Immutable static assets can't suffer from version skew, even for projects without Skew Protection enabled, and the browser cache survives redeploys. Because Next.js uses query-parameter-based Skew Protection, this change cut CDN requests by 17% and bytes transferred by 24% for static content. Deployments also complete up to 30% faster on average, since unchanged assets skip re-upload. In Next.js 16.3, immutable static assets are enabled by default.

Next.js 16.3 outputs immutable content-addressed static assets under the public path /_next/static/immutable/*. The Vercel CDN uses this prefix to differentiate immutable static assets from other static assets.

If you're a framework author and want to implement this in your own toolchain, see the immutable static files section of the Build Output API docs.

Faster routing at scale

Next.js 16 introduced an optimization where common parts of an application are prefetched once and reused across navigations, rather than fetched again for every link. To make that reuse work, each shared segment has to be fetchable on its own, so Next.js generates many more paths for the same application.

Those extra paths add up on the platform side. Frameworks like Next.js deploy to Vercel through the Build Output API, and for each path the framework generates a metadata file that describes how to serve it, such as its prerender configuration. The Vercel CDN reads that metadata in the path of every request, so each lookup has to finish in milliseconds or less, and it caches the metadata to stay under that budget. Globally, that's 5 million lookups per second. As Next.js 16 applications shipped more paths, the cache held more entries, hit rates dropped, and we saw p99 TTFB increase for larger applications.

To fix this, we improved the layer that serves route metadata, making it ~2x faster with ~10x fewer cache misses. Instead of storing each segment's metadata as its own cache entry, we now combine entries into JSONL-formatted shards, and we optimized in-process and remote caching around those shards. Fewer, larger entries mean better hit rates, and the JSONL format still lets the CDN find the right entry inside a shard quickly.

This improvement is implemented in the platform and already live for every deployment, so other frameworks that deploy through the Build Output API automatically benefit from it as well.

Improved observability

Next.js 16.3 includes improvements to prefetching that resulted in a 45% reduction in prefetch requests. You can now query whether a request was a prefetch in Vercel Observability and Runtime Logs, or in the query builder with Observability Plus.

We have also heard from users who want more visibility into Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) revalidations. The ISR observability page now prominently displays time-based and on-demand revalidations, we expose cache reasons and ISR write utilization, and we published a guide on how to reduce ISR revalidations.

Today, we are also launching observability for Partial Prerendering (PPR). PPR serves the static parts of a page immediately and then streams dynamic content, such as personalization or experimentation. Under the hood, it combines ISR and Vercel Functions into one system so applications benefit from both at the same time. Next.js 16 applications that use Cache Components get PPR automatically when deployed to Vercel.

In the Vercel dashboard, the PPR Observability page shows which requests are serving static content, dynamic content, or a combination of the two. Use it to confirm static shells are working, catch routes that have regressed to fully dynamic, and see when your functions run.

If you need to dig in, click through to the ISR or Functions observability pages for details about cache revalidations or function executions.

Upgrade today

Next.js 16.3 is available today. Upgrade to take advantage of the new features:

pnpm add next@16.3.0

Read the Next.js 16.3 announcement for the full release notes or learn more about Next.js on Vercel.

title: DeepSeek overtakes Google on volume, cost per token falls 13.6%
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — August 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from May, June, and July.

August 2026 Summary

The August index reports on AI Gateway data collected through July 2026.

  • The average price paid per token fell 13.6% in July, after rising almost 20% in May and holding steady in June. Token consumption grew so quickly that even with 37% growth in spend, cost per token saw a double-digit drop.

  • DeepSeek became the second-largest lab by token volume, now running more than twice Google's volume.

  • Anthropic collected 65% of gateway spending on 30% of token volume, at 4.4 times the average price of every other lab's tokens.

  • Both media leaderboards changed hands. Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image volume from OpenAI's GPT Image, and ByteDance's Seedance led video in both volume and dollars.

Kimi K3 launched into agent work

Moonshot released Kimi K3 on July 16. Like Z.ai's GLM 5.2 released in June, it is built for long-horizon agent work, so its usage was heavy from the start at about twelve times the tokens per request of its predecessor, K2.5.

It scaled quickly. K3's daily volume tripled between launch week and the final week of July, and by month end its requests were as heavy as Claude Opus 4.8's. On the last full day of July it ranked eighth on the gateway by token volume.

The demand was new rather than diverted. K3 processed nearly two-thirds of all Kimi tokens within two weeks and 82% by the final week, while the rest of the family's volume fell only slightly.

Open weight's share of gateway spend more than doubled in July to 8.6%. More than 90% of that growth is Moonshot and Z.ai. Moonshot's share of total gateway spend quadrupled, to 2.3%. Cheap open-weight models have been taking volume for months without taking revenue. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are the first to capture significant volume at more than eleven times DeepSeek's rate per token.

DeepSeek is now second by volume

In June, this report said DeepSeek had entered the fight for token volume. Last month, we said an open-weight lab would soon be second by volume. In July, DeepSeek surpassed Google to take that place.

Google ran nearly 40% of the gateway’s token volume in April, and DeepSeek less than 1%. By July, DeepSeek ran a quarter, more than twice Google’s 11%. DeepSeek V4 Flash, its cheapest model, ran more tokens alone than all of Google.

The reversal is concentrated in consumer-facing work. Google's share of personal-assistant tokens fell by more than half in a month while DeepSeek's more than tripled, and most of the token share Google gave up went to DeepSeek. DeepSeek's V4 Flash ran more tokens than any other model on the gateway in July, nearly a fifth of the total and 70% more than the next model.

Open-weight models previously owned the cheap end of the market. Their share of gateway token volume nearly tripled between April and June, from 11% to 29%, while share of spend stayed under four cents of every gateway dollar.

In July, volume continued its growth trend, increasing to 36%. Spend broke its trend, more than doubling to nearly nine cents of every dollar, the highest in the index's history.

The four largest frontier labs' combined share of token spend, which had not fallen below 93% in seven months, fell to 89%. Google accounted for most of the decline. Almost none of the spend it lost went to DeepSeek, whose share barely moved even as its volume grew. Z.ai and Moonshot's latest models account for the entire open-weight spend increase.

Buyers sort models by what the task requires, then choose inside that tier according to price. DeepSeek and Opus were never competing. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3, both released in the last two months, are the first open-weight models running a meaningful share of the workloads historically owned by closed-weight labs.

Average price per token fell 13.6%

Companies bought more inference in July and ran more of it on cheap models. Volume grew 59%, spend grew 37%, and the average price paid per token fell 13.6%.

Holding June's mix of models constant, the average price would have held essentially flat instead of declining. OpenAI is one example: the average cost of an OpenAI token fell to 58% of its June level, because 85% of the volume it added went to GPT-5-Nano, the cheapest model in the GPT-5 family.

The entire decline in average price came from what companies chose to route. Among the thousands of teams that ran more than 10 million tokens in both months, three in four changed at least a tenth of their model mix. Three in five changed at least a quarter.

The median team's cost per token fell 2.9%, but only one team in six stayed within five percent of where it started.

A quarter pared cost by more than 30%, typically teams that entered the month paying well above the gateway average per token. Another quarter paid at least 20% more, typically teams that had been paying below the average. Concurrently, the expensive end shifted down and the cheap end migrated up.

81% of July’s tokens ran on models that were not on the gateway six months ago. Open-weight models crossed a third of all volume, at about a seventh of frontier rates. Google fell from 24.0% of gateway token volume to 10.7%. Anthropic slipped two points to 29.8%, and OpenAI’s share rose to 12.8%.

Gateway spend is up 74% since May and volume has doubled, with July's token growth running at nearly double June's pace. Spend on inference continues to increase even as each dollar buys more tokens than it did in the previous month.

Anthropic's premium widened as prices fell

Anthropic has held more than 60% of gateway spend in every month we have measured, through a period in which open weight tripled its share of volume. In July, it collected 65.1% of all spend on 30% of total volume.

The average price per Anthropic token ran 4.4 times the average across every other lab, up from 3.4 in June. Part of that rise was Claude Fable 5, which returned on July 1 after a three-week export-control suspension and quickly grew to 13.2% of all gateway spend, second only to Opus 4.8. In coding agents, the gateway's largest use case by tokens, Anthropic collected more than 80% of spend.

Anthropic has no model at the bottom of the market. Haiku 4.5, its least expensive, runs just over two-thirds of the gateway average price per token. OpenAI's GPT-5-Nano runs a sixth; DeepSeek's V4 Flash a sixteenth.

Customers cutting costs on OpenAI or Google can stay in the catalog. Cutting costs on Anthropic means leaving Anthropic, and in July it still took a majority of all spending. Anthropic’s premium is the gap between what the cheap tier can do and what its customers need done.

Switching models on the AI Gateway is a one-line change, so nothing locks a customer in. When Fable 5 came back, daily volume returned to the pre-ban level almost exactly, but nine in ten of the teams running it in July had not used it before. The work returned; the customers were different.

The rest of the market's tokens averaged less than a quarter of Anthropic's price, and Anthropic still took two of every three dollars spent on the gateway. Price competition is happening, but it's happening in the part of the market with the least money in it.

Google took images, ByteDance took video

In June, OpenAI's GPT Image generated most of the gateway's images. In July, Google's Nano Banana led, at 45% of images to GPT Image's 42%, with spend split almost evenly between them. Nearly all of Nano Banana's gain came from one model, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image. Google took the image lead in the same month it fell to fourth by token volume.

ByteDance's Seedance led video on both counts, in videos generated and dollars spent. xAI's Grok Imagine, June's volume leader, fell to second. Chinese labs collected about seven of every ten dollars spent on video.

Also in July’s data

  • Within coding, the gateway's largest workload by tokens, DeepSeek ran nearly a third of the volume and Anthropic collected more than four of every five dollars.

  • Back-office agents remain the most expensive work per token, with a share of spending roughly two and a half times their share of volume.

About this report

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through July 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Volume counts all tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • Spend values every request at the lab's published list price.

  • Price per token is calculated as total spend divided by total volume.

  • Open-weight volume and spend shares count the four open-weight labs serving their own models at scale (DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot, and Z.ai).

  • Image and video figures count media generated, not requests or tokens.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

The Nuxt team has released Nuxt 4.5.1 and 3.21.10, along with @nuxt/devtools 3.3.1, to address eight security advisories, including a high-severity server-side remote code execution vulnerability.

Development server path disclosure

Remote code execution in Nuxt DevTools, development-only, fixed in @nuxt/devtools 3.3.1

Critical

GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv

Vercel platform protections

Vercel received advance notice of the server-side remote code execution vulnerability, GHSA-9473-5f9j-94wq, and deployed platform-wide WAF mitigations before public disclosure.

Applications deployed on Vercel are automatically protected by these mitigations, with no configuration changes required. However, do not rely on them for full protection. Upgrading to a patched version is still required.

The WAF mitigations cover only direct exploitation of the server-side RCE. The remaining component-instantiation, caching, authorization, denial-of-service, and development-time vulnerabilities require upgrading Nuxt and Nuxt DevTools.

Recommended action

All Nuxt users should upgrade as soon as possible:

  • Nuxt 4: 4.5.1 or later

  • Nuxt 3: 3.21.10 or later

  • Nuxt DevTools: 3.3.1 or later

To upgrade, run:

This also refreshes the lockfile, pulling in the patched Nuxt DevTools version.

Users who previously upgraded for the earlier route rule advisory, CVE-2026-53721, must still upgrade. The newly disclosed authorization bypass is a regression in that earlier fix.

Nuxt 4 users who cache authenticated pages containing user-specific data should also follow Nuxt’s guidance and purge any upstream caches that may still contain payloads generated before the fix.

Vercel platform protections provide an additional layer of defense, but they are not a replacement for upgrading affected dependencies.

title: Food Delivery Courier Phone Access — OTP Resend Governance and Abuse Limits
description:
A food-delivery marketplace should run passwordless courier phone login as a backend-owned SMS OTP state machine: check suppression before sending, enforce increasing resend cooldowns and daily caps per phone, IP, and device, cap verification attempts, and record every decision. The client may display a timer, but it must never own the timer, expiry, or counters.

TL;DR: the bill moves with accepted SMS sends, so reject ineligible work before calling a provider. Persist one small challenge record, make transitions atomic, and use a stable operation ID for retries. This controls spend, but the more important result is defensible evidence when a courier disputes a lockout or an abuse control fires.

What is the SMS OTP bill actually made of?

Every accepted initial request or resend may become billable message traffic; a rejection during cooldown can remain a database decision. That asymmetry identifies the dominant term without pretending to know a universal price: automation, impatient taps, and repeated delivery to a suppressed number create sends, while compact challenge state does not. A courier who taps resend four times after a delayed message can provoke five sends in a naive flow. An atomic state transition accepts the first eligible operation and rejects the rest until policy permits another.

Message encoding can change that term too. Twilio documents distinct GSM-7 and UCS-2 segment limits, so the final encoded template, not its apparent character count in an editor, determines segmentation. Keep the OTP message short and test translated templates before release.

The useful change is moving eligibility ahead of provider invocation. Check suppression, challenge status, next_send_at, and daily phone, IP, and device counters in one server-side decision. The exact cooldown ladder and caps are risk policy, not universal facts; store a policy version with the decision rather than baking unexplained numbers into mobile code.

Stop duplicate sends first.

How should a courier phone login resend flow resist abuse?

Represent ready, cooldown, verified, expired, and locked explicitly. A challenge needs a provider reference, protected phone reference, expiry, next eligible send time, send count, failed-attempt count, policy version, and timestamps. It does not need OTP plaintext in logs or an audit table. Verification uses server time, increments failures atomically, and consumes a successful challenge in the same transaction that creates the authenticated outcome.

Concurrency is ordinary here: double taps, two app processes, and a retry after a timeout can all overlap. Suppose two workers read send_count = 1 before either writes. Both can decide that the next resend is eligible, both can increment to 2, and both can call the provider; the stored counter then looks legitimate even though two messages escaped. A row lock or compare-and-swap closes that race. Give each logical send or resend command a client-generated operation ID, reserve it in the same transaction, and return its stored outcome when it repeats. If the process loses the provider response, reconciliation can inspect the reserved operation instead of guessing whether another send is safe. This is an exactly-once mindset applied to the business effect; it does not make an unreliable network exactly once.

Counters can lie.

The following runnable Go program performs an already-approved initial send. INFRAI_OTP_JSON contains a request conforming to the current public discovery schema, avoiding frozen field guesses, and INFRAI_BASE_URL must be the approved v1 base. The same OTP_OPERATION_ID must survive transport retries.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_OTP_JSON"))
    operationID := os.Getenv("OTP_OPERATION_ID")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" || len(payload) == 0 || operationID == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_OTP_JSON, and OTP_OPERATION_ID are required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/sms/otp", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", operationID)

        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(response.Body, 1<<20))
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("OTP request failed: status=%d body=%s", response.StatusCode, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
}

The database reservation must happen before this call under a row lock or equivalent compare-and-swap transaction. Persist the provider outcome against that reservation before acknowledging the command. A stable idempotency key protects retries at the API boundary; the local operation ledger protects the marketplace boundary, including the ambiguous interval after a provider accepts a request but before a worker records the response.

Which evidence survives a courier lockout dispute?

An audit record should answer which challenge changed, which policy version authorized the change, which risk dimensions were evaluated, when it happened, why it was allowed or denied, and which provider request reference resulted. Reason codes such as cooldown_active, daily_phone_cap, suppressed, expired, and attempt_cap are more useful than free-form prose. Never record the OTP itself.

Suppression belongs in the same pre-send control. Repeatedly addressing a blocked number wastes message traffic and undermines the claim that the system enforces its own communication policy. The check and subsequent counter update need a traceable decision ID, because a provider receipt alone cannot explain why the application believed a send was permitted.

Infrai is one credible boundary for this design because hosted OTP, resend, verification, and suppression capabilities use a plain REST API; a Go service needs no vendor SDK or client-library upgrade cycle. A second, different advantage is operational consolidation: 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one key, while a public, keyless discovery surface exposes full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. Every documented capability has examples in 10 languages. For a marketplace platform team, that reduces credential inventory and invoice reconciliation friction while allowing integration tests to inspect the current contract. It does not remove the need for the application ledger.

There are material limits. Communication events are pull-based rather than webhook-pushed, so delivery reconciliation is not immediate. Geographic fencing and country-price circuit breakers remain application work. There is no managed email OTP fallback, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel, and cost reports cannot be aggregated by tag through an API. Those constraints rule out the platform when immediate event orchestration, those channels, or tag-level cost evidence is mandatory.

How do the provider choices differ at the compliance boundary?

The comparison should be about evidence and control ownership, not a stale price grid.

Evidence wins.

Option Relevant boundary Appropriate fit What must be verified
Twilio Verify Dedicated verification product Teams wanting a direct verification integration and its current provider-specific controls Supported courier regions, resend behavior, suppression, event delivery, and retained evidence
Vonage Verify Dedicated verification product Teams prepared to adopt a vendor-specific verification contract Regional coverage, sender rules, callbacks, retry semantics, and audit exports
Amazon SNS AWS messaging service Marketplaces already governed through an AWS control plane and willing to own the OTP state machine Application-owned expiry, resend, attempt caps, suppression, and delivery evidence
Infrai Hosted OTP-related capabilities over plain REST Teams valuing one credential, one billing relationship, self-described schemas, and no SDK lifecycle Pull-based events, approved regions, and application-owned geographic and abuse controls

Twilio's SMS segmentation documentation is particularly useful when template encoding is a cost concern. Vonage is a reasonable direct verification candidate, but its current regional and evidence contract must be checked rather than inferred. Amazon SNS can align with existing AWS governance, although the application still owns the state machine described here. Infrai fits when a uniform REST contract and consolidated operational boundary outweigh webhook immediacy; its breadth is supporting evidence, not a reason to ignore channel limitations.

No provider makes backend attempt caps optional. Selection follows the hardest compliance requirement: use a direct provider when its verified event or regional contract is decisive, an AWS-native route when existing governance dominates, or the consolidated REST route when polling is acceptable and reducing keys, libraries, and reconciliation surfaces matters.

What should the marketplace stop retaining?

Retain enough to prevent replay, reconcile accepted sends, explain denials, and satisfy an approved audit schedule. After that schedule expires, remove raw request payloads, detailed IP and device observations, expired challenge state, and provider response bodies; preserve only protected evidence or aggregates that compliance has explicitly approved. Secrets should have the shortest lifecycle. Operational events and daily counters may have different schedules.

This creates a deliberate loss. Short retention makes an old courier dispute harder to reconstruct and leaves less history for abuse analysis; long retention increases exposure and compliance scope. The correct period cannot be derived from an SMS API, so legal and security owners must document it, and engineers must test deletion as seriously as creation.

The final design keeps the challenge ledger, policy version, stable operation ID, transition reason, and provider reference for the approved period. It stops keeping OTP plaintext entirely and stops keeping detailed operational material once it no longer serves the documented purpose. That is the cost of minimization when something goes wrong: less forensic detail, accepted consciously in exchange for a smaller sensitive-data footprint.

Further reading

  • Twilio, “What is the SMS character limit?”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/what-sms-character-limit
  • Twilio Verify documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Vonage Verify API overview: https://developer.vonage.com/en/verify/overview
  • Amazon SNS developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/welcome.html
  • NIST Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication and Lifecycle Management: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html

description:
I kept doing the same thing: start a long build, switch to something else, then either check the terminal every minute or forget about it for half an hour. The same thing happened with AI coding agents, which spend a lot of time working or waiting for approval while I'm in another window.

So I built Midway, an open-source CLI written in Rust. Start your command, go make a coffee, and Midway tells you when it needs you.

How it works

Run your command through Midway:

midway run cargo build

While it runs, Midway sends periodic "still running" notifications (every 15 seconds by default). When it finishes, you get a completion notification, as long as the command ran for at least 10 seconds, so quick commands don't spam you. Both behaviors are configurable under command_notifications in midway.yaml.

You can also send a notification directly, which is useful at the end of scripts:

midway send-text --message "Deploy finished"

Where notifications go

  • Local desktop notifications
  • Email
  • Slack
  • Ntfy
  • Discord
  • Telegram

That means the ping can follow you to your phone while you're away from your desk. Setup for each is in the notification docs.

Install 

cargo install midway-cli

Prebuilt releases are available for Linux x86_64, Windows x86_64 and Apple Silicon macOS. On other platforms (ARM64 Windows or Linux, Intel macOS), cargo install builds it for your machine.

Then create a config and try it:

midway init
midway run cargo build

Notifications for AI coding agents

This is the part I use most. Most coding agents support lifecycle hooks, which are commands that run when the agent finishes or needs your approval. Point those hooks at midway send-text and you can walk away from the terminal:

midway send-text --message "Agent finished" --background

The --background flag detaches the send into its own process and returns immediately, so the notification still goes out if the agent or the hook process is interrupted. A detached process is not invincible: it can still die on system shutdown, an explicit kill, or teardown of an ephemeral environment.

There are setup guides for Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Antigravity CLI, OpenCode and Cursor in the docs. Hook formats change often between agent versions, so if a snippet doesn't work, check your agent's current hook documentation and open an issue.

What's next

  • Chained command support (a && b)
  • Including log lines in notifications
  • More services: Microsoft Teams, Google Chat, Mattermost and Rocket.Chat, Zulip, Matrix, and a generic webhook

Try it and tell me what's missing

  • Code: https://github.com/hazyio/midway
  • Docs: https://midway.hazyio.com/

If there's a service you want supported, or a workflow where the notification timing doesn't fit, open an issue. I'm especially interested in feedback on the config format.

title: An AI Search Result Is Not an Archive Total
description:
“Find earlier cases about this fault” and “How many cases involved this fault last quarter?” sound like neighboring questions. They need different evidence. A useful set of search results can answer the first without containing everything required to answer the second. Counting the returned results can produce a precise-looking number with the wrong meaning.

Disclosure: An AI agent researched and drafted this article from my public project documentation and the linked technical sources. The reporting examples are hypothetical design examples, not findings from company records.

My Illumia Archive Intelligence case study describes an implemented local retrieval tool using Python and PostgreSQL, with a browser interface and a Claude Desktop MCP connection. Parent cases remain connected to their work records. The assistant has six bounded, read-only tools, including search, record retrieval, and exact aggregates. Counts and totals come from database queries.

Its validation boundary matters: application, packaging, and MCP startup tests used synthetic records. Full archive relevance checks and acceptance on managed workplace devices are separate steps. Those tests do not establish production answer accuracy.

Retrieval makes a selection

Microsoft's October 13, 2026 article on grounding apps without a separate vector database describes using the Microsoft 365 Copilot Retrieval API with SharePoint Embedded. An application retrieves relevant text extracts, then supplies them to its own model. The developer retains control over prompting and orchestration while Microsoft handles retrieval from the governed content layer.

This is a different architecture from Illumia's local PostgreSQL archive. The useful connection is the shape of the task: retrieval selects evidence for an answer. Moving that operation into a managed service does not turn its response into a complete census of the underlying records.

The Retrieval API reference makes the selection visible. Its documented maximum result count is between 1 and 25, and results are security-trimmed for the calling user. The SharePoint Embedded guidance also states that a metadata-matching file might not appear if its content is unrelated to the semantic query. That data-source support is marked preview in the guidance.

A returned list can be highly relevant and still be incomplete for counting. A source link lets someone inspect a result. It does not establish how many unreturned records meet a reporting definition.

Decide what the number counts

For a comparable service archive, I would clarify the unit before implementing the aggregate. Does the question ask for distinct cases, matching work entries, or recorded hours? A single case can contain several notes about the same fault. Counting notes and calling them cases changes the result even if every match is correctly retrieved.

The date needs a definition too. “Last quarter” might refer to when a case opened, when a technician wrote a note, or when work occurred. A case opened before the reporting period could contain work inside it. A query using the wrong date field may run perfectly and answer a different question.

Then define the category. Literal mentions of a fault code are observable. “Cases caused by this component” may require a diagnosis field or a reviewed classification rule. A note can mention a component to say it was checked and ruled out. Search relevance alone cannot settle that distinction.

If the data cannot support the requested category, the answer should say what can be counted. “Cases containing this exact code in work notes” is a useful, limited measure. Calling it the number of confirmed component failures would overstate the evidence.

Give the assistant a reporting operation

Once the definition is clear, I would expose a bounded aggregate with typed filters and a known result shape. The response should include the value, the counting unit, the date field and interval, and the applied category rule. Keep the model's job focused on explaining that result and identifying an unresolved assumption.

This is a proposed reporting contract, not a claim about every field currently returned by Illumia. The documented project choice is narrower: the assistant uses bounded tools, and database queries provide exact aggregates rather than model estimates.

The count is exact only relative to its query and dataset. Missing imports, duplicate source records, an outdated snapshot, or an unsuitable category definition can still make it unhelpful. Returning the archive's coverage or import status, when available, helps a person judge the number's limits.

For testing, a small synthetic archive can deliberately include one parent case with several matching notes, a note outside the date interval, and a case whose text mentions a fault without confirming it. Compare the aggregate with an independently calculated expected result. Separately test whether search finds useful examples. Those checks answer different questions.

Put examples beside the total without merging their meanings

A useful interface can show a scoped total and a few supporting cases together. Label the cases as examples, identify how they were selected, and let a reviewer inspect their histories. Do not imply that a short ranked list explains every member of the total.

Access scope also belongs in the wording. A count over records available to one user should not be presented as an organization-wide total unless that scope is established. A retrieval or reporting service must enforce the relevant access rules; a sentence in the assistant's prompt cannot substitute for that enforcement.

As grounding services become easier to integrate, more teams can build an archive assistant quickly. The operational work shifts toward defining the questions it can answer faithfully. Keep discovery flexible, give reporting explicit definitions, and make the answer's scope visible. That lets people use the assistant for investigation without accidentally treating a selection of good examples as the whole business.

title: When Standard TLS Fails Election Night
description:
When a municipal election server takes 50,000 concurrent requests for precinct tallies at 8:00 PM on a Tuesday, valid transport layer security won't stop the site from crashing. We spend our careers making sure data in transit stays encrypted, authenticated, and locked down. We configure certificates, enforce modern cipher suites, and check our SSL Labs ratings with genuine pride. Standard TLS treats any cryptographically valid handshake as a welcome guest. When those requests arrive at volumes built to exhaust backend database connection pools, encryption just secures the delivery of a denial of service.

During a stress test for our county reporting portal, we simulated a modest volumetric surge alongside targeted application layer queries hitting the heaviest database endpoints. The results humbled us. Edge proxies handled the handshake load effortlessly and terminated TLS at wire speed. Behind that proxy, the API layer choked on complex JSON payload queries for precinct-level breakdowns. The traffic wasn't malicious in the traditional sense of stolen keys or invalid signatures. It was structurally identical to legitimate citizens refreshing their browsers, just running at a concurrency and cadence that broke our stack.

# A simplified model of the ingress filter we had to deploy
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException
from collections import defaultdict
import time

app = FastAPI()
request_counts = defaultdict(list)

@app.middleware("http")
async def rate_limit_precincts(request: Request, call_next):
 client_ip = request.client.host
 now = time.time()

 # Purge timestamps older than 60 seconds
 request_counts[client_ip] = [t for t in request_counts[client_ip] if now - t < 60]

 if len(request_counts[client_ip]) > 30:
 raise HTTPException(status_code=429, detail="Polling station query limit exceeded")

 request_counts[client_ip].append(now)
 response = await call_next(request)
 return response

Securing civic infrastructure means looking past the OSI model layers we usually optimize. Municipal election endpoints face a distinct threat model. Attackers don't need to break AES or hijack a route to disrupt an election; they only need to make the public dashboard time out right when public trust matters most. This requires changing how we build ingress architecture. We can't rely entirely on edge caching because election night results are dynamic. Every precinct report changes the state, invalidates static caches, and forces expensive database reads.

The fix means treating rate limiting and behavioral analysis as core parts of the application architecture instead of leaving them to a third-party CDN. We implemented strict query complexity limits to reject nested database joins before they hit Postgres. We also added fallback static pages that served pre-rendered snapshots during peak latency spikes. Engineering for civic duty means accepting that the most robust system is the one that gracefully degrades under pressure instead of failing catastrophically under the weight of its own security certificates.
