title: Test blank, zero and service overrides in a branded AI workspace
description:
A pricing form can save successfully while the customer journey still behaves differently from what the operator intended. One easy distinction to lose is a blank service markup versus an explicit zero: they represent different configuration states.

This guide is from the Ace Data Cloud team and uses the documented behavior of a white-label Studio. It provides a manual acceptance workflow for the selected site and service. Check the current configuration guide and actual checkout before applying it to a commercial offer.

Start with four separate cases

In the site's Price settings, the site-wide markup is the default. A service-specific markup takes priority when it is explicitly set.

Service configuration Expected markup behavior What the check must distinguish
No service override Inherit the site-wide markup The site default is the applicable setting
An override exists, but its markup field is blank Inherit the site-wide markup A blank field is not an explicit zero
Service markup is 0 Apply no markup for that service No markup does not make the underlying service free
Service markup contains an explicit percentage Use the service percentage Do not apply it on top of the site-wide percentage

Record the configuration state as well as the visible number. If the site-wide markup is also zero, two different states may produce the same price. That observation alone cannot show whether the service is inheriting the default or using an explicit override.

If you need a more distinguishing configuration, use an authorized test site and record its starting settings. Change one relevant setting at a time. Avoid changing a live commercial offer just to make a test easier to observe.

Compare the same customer path

Choose one service and a specific option within it. Enter through the site address customers will actually use, with an appropriate test account. Check the selected option, charging unit, displayed currency and price before moving to the checkout for that same purchase path.

Record the checkout amount and settlement currency separately. A number on a tool page and a number on a checkout page are not comparable until the service, option, quantity, charging unit and currency are aligned. Current offers or discounts can also affect the applicable price.

Keep two results separate:

  • Configuration check: Which setting should apply, and was that state saved?
  • Customer-path check: What price and conditions did the intended customer actually see?

A screenshot of an administrator's form answers only part of the first question. It does not establish checkout behavior, a completed payment, actual usage or an operator reward.

Treat removing an override as another operation

Removing a service override restores its default display settings and makes its markup inherit the site-wide setting. That can affect more than price: an override can also hold the service's custom name, description, ordering or visibility.

Record those values before changing the override. If the task is to clear just the markup field, do not substitute deletion of the whole override. After a deliberate removal, recheck the service's presentation as well as the price.

Keep display controls separate from spending controls

Hiding the top-up entry does not clear an existing balance or stop a customer from buying shared packages through another entry point. Likewise, hiding a tool is a display choice, not proof that API access has been revoked.

Studio branding uses a shared account, balance and package system. A course budget written in a handoff note is an operating agreement unless a real spending limit has also been configured and verified. Describe only the controls you have actually checked.

Copy a compact acceptance record

Use pass, fail or not checked for each result. Keep the record in an authorized location and share only the parts appropriate to the recipient.

Test time and time zone:
Site and intended customer entry:
Test account role or non-secret reference:
Service, selected option and quantity:
Site-wide markup:
Service state: absent / blank / zero / explicit percentage
Expected applicable markup and its basis:
Displayed price, charging unit and currency:
Checkout amount and settlement currency, if checked:
Saved configuration result and customer-path result:
Actual usage or order evidence, if a paid test was necessary:
Open issue, next check and owner:

Inspect the page and purchase path before deciding whether a paid generation is necessary. If it is, confirm the current service price and agree a small test scope first. Record the actual result and usage; do not generate repeatedly just to improve a screenshot. If a submission's outcome is unknown, reconcile the original task before deciding whether another request is needed.

Watch the three markup choices

This 45-second silent recap covers inheritance, explicit zero and a service-specific percentage:

Open the recap on YouTube.

For the current forms and rules, use the Studio capability and pricing guide.

Customer attribution, valid orders and distributable rewards need their own evidence. A successful task does not prove that a reward is payable; refunds and other applicable adjustments can change the records. Consult the customer attribution and earnings guide when checking those outcomes.

title: The library that appointed itself signal handler
description:
A commit had gone into go-tool-base's root command about a month before I noticed it, and it had been quietly breaking things for anything downstream that used the controls module the whole time. I didn't find it. Someone raised it with me, which is not the order I'd have chosen, and it's on me for not spotting it when it went in.

Two right answers, one process

The commit gave the root command a signal-aware execution context: catch SIGINT, cancel the context, let the command wind itself up properly. That's a good change, and an obviously right one. A CLI wants to flush buffered telemetry before it dies, clean up a half-written self-update, and let a long-running command notice it's been asked to stop.

I'd have approved it. I did approve it, apparently (without reading it anything like carefully enough), and the trouble is what was already sitting underneath. go/controls is the supervisor that runs long-lived services and stops them in the right order, which I wrote up in lifecycle management for long-running Go services. And for most of its life it caught SIGINT and SIGTERM itself, by default.

That was also correct! A supervisor sat in a bare main really is the outermost thing in the process, and catching the interrupt to drive a graceful stop is its job. Doing it without being asked is a kindness. Two right decisions, eighteen months apart, and a collision that only exists where they overlap.

Nothing errors, which is the problem

Go will happily let two parts of one process both handle Ctrl-C, because signal.Notify is additive: register a second channel and it doesn't replace the first, it starts posting to both. No error, no warning, no log line saying "you appear to have two of these". Just two shutdown drivers, racing. So a default about process-global state is less a default about your library and more a claim about your position in someone else's process, and the post doesn't arrive telling you when that position has changed.

My own tools had already told me

So I went and looked at what the downstream tools were actually doing, and this is the part that smarted. Two of them had hit this unaided and written essentially the same workaround, with the same reasoning, without ever comparing notes: one had a comment explaining that the framework's root command already installs the handler that cancels the context so a second one would race it, and the other said it drives its stop from context cancellation specifically to avoid a second handler.

Same conclusion, same boilerplate, arrived at independently by two tools I wrote, working around a problem I'd shipped. And a third had never opted out at all. It had been running both handlers the whole time and I hadn't noticed, because from the outside this looks like a slightly chatty shutdown.

When two of your users pay the same tax and a third is silently broken, I think you can put the design principles away. The users had already told me the default was wrong, and they'd gone to the trouble of writing it in the comments (my comments, in my tools, which somehow makes it worse).

The part that actually hurt

Duplicated log lines are the visible symptom, and they're the least of it. controls publishes a contract. When a service's context is done, context.Cause(ctx) tells you why: if it's ErrShutdown, your controller stopped you deliberately, and anything else means something upstream died and you should behave differently. That's how a service decides whether to finish flushing or bail out now.

With two handlers, that becomes a coin flip. WithCancelCause hands you the parent's cause when the parent cancels first, so if the framework's handler wins the race, the controller's own cancel(ErrShutdown) turns up late and does nothing at all.

Same code, same signal, and a different answer depending on which goroutine the scheduler fancied. A published guarantee, broken by scheduling, with no error anywhere in sight. "It worked when I tested it" and "it is correct" have never been the same claim, and this is the gap that lives between them.

Somewhere else in the estate, I'd got it right

What convinced me this was a principle and not a signals quirk is that another module already handled it properly, by default, and had done from day one. go/transport-metrics sets up Prometheus collectors, and its documentation is blunt about it:

The default is a fresh, private registry (never the global prometheus.DefaultRegisterer), so a tool's metrics are self-contained and tests do not collide.

Different process-global, identical reasoning, opposite instinct. Two libraries in one estate touching shared state, one grabbing it by default and one refusing to, and that comparison did more for the argument than anything I could have written in a spec.

The default went the other way round

NewController no longer installs a signal handler at all, and the doc comment explains itself so you don't have to work it out:

It does NOT install an OS signal handler. Signal disposition is process-global state and belongs to whichever layer is outermost, typically the CLI framework or main. Pass WithSignals when the controller genuinely is that outermost layer.

The behaviour still exists, you just have to ask for it, and in a bare main where the supervisor really is the outermost thing it's WithSignals() and you're away. One small thing I got right by accident: the spec ended up raised against controls and not against the framework, because that's the module whose default was wrong. A boring filing decision, but it means the reasoning now lives next to the code it governs instead of in the repo of whoever happened to notice.

And keryx's comment has changed status without changing much text. It used to be a workaround describing what it was avoiding. It now reads as a note citing the decision. Same words, different thing.

The fix I didn't ship

The obvious worry with handing signals to the CLI is whether the service still gets long enough to shut down cleanly if the framework owns the interrupt. I had a whole cooperative-drain protocol specced out for it. Handshakes, acknowledgements, the lot.

Then I went and read three call sites, and found the graceful path already waits. Wait() blocks RunE, which blocks ExecuteContext, so the root command cannot physically reach its exit path until the controller has fully stopped. The problem I'd spent an evening designing around did not exist, and the only real gap was a single force-exit goroutine on the second Ctrl-C, which is a much smaller creature. An entire protocol, specced and binned, on the strength of going and reading the code instead of reasoning about it.

That's the second time in this story that the answer was sitting in a file I'd already written, once in my consumers' comments and once in my own call sites. I should probably read more and design less.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 17 October 2026.

title: Why your AI agent gets fund holdings wrong: the SEC's "Ticker" field isn't a ticker
description:
If you are building an agent or a model on SEC fund-holdings data, it will read a field called IDENTIFIER_TICKER and trust it. Here is what that field actually contains.

If you build fund-ownership data from SEC Form N-PORT, you will read a field called IDENTIFIER_TICKER and treat it as a stock symbol. The SEC's data-set documentation describes it in one word: "Ticker".

The form itself says more. Form N-PORT, Item C.1.e, asks for "at least one" other identifier: an ISIN, or a "Ticker (if ISIN is not available)", or some other identifier. Nothing requires the ticker to be an exchange symbol. It is a fallback.

So we measured what funds actually put there - every quarter the SEC has published, 2019 Q4 to 2026 Q2:

  • 17,361,050 rows carry a ticker.
  • 72% are on common-stock lines, and they look like real tickers: MSFT, AMZN, AAPL.
  • On mortgage-backed lines (676,336 rows) the "tickers" are agency pool-type prefixes: FN 161,550 rows, GN 109,156, FNMA 55,140, FHLMC 45,223.
  • On bond lines (2,312,102 rows) the ticker is the ISSUER's stock symbol, not the bond's: AT&T bonds carry "T" on 86,298 rows.
  • On derivative lines you find futures contract codes (TYZ2, ESZ2) and currency codes (USD, EUR).

Why it matters: FG is a Freddie Mac pool prefix. It is also the NYSE ticker of F&G Annuities & Life. Join N-PORT's ticker field to a ticker list and Freddie Mac mortgage pools turn into holdings of an insurance company. Bond holdings turn into stock holdings. Ownership counts, "smart money" signals and flow features all inherit it - silently.

Two more traps in the same files:

  • Placeholders that look like data: ISSUER_CUSIP is "N/A" on 47.5 million rows, "000000000" on 15.2 million and "999999999" on 210 thousand. ISSUER_LEI is "N/A" on 67.6 million. Count those as filled and your coverage numbers are wrong.
  • The SEC's machine-readable field list ships unchanged with every historical quarter, so a field "defined" there may not exist in older files (the VaR table is listed back to 2019 but only appears from 2022 Q1).

What to do: before trusting any identifier on an N-PORT line, check what kind of holding the line is (the ASSET_CAT field), and treat placeholder values as blank.

What I don't know yet:

  • Whether anyone publishes an open mapping from N-PORT pool prefixes (FN, GN, FG...) to the agency programs they stand for. I could not find one.
  • How much of the bond-line "issuer ticker" habit comes from filers themselves and how much from the software vendors that prepare their filings.

We published the full N-PORT field dictionary - the SEC's definitions with citations, the official code lists, and what is actually in each field - free, under CC BY 4.0: https://alexbocio.github.io/us-gov-data-dictionary/sec_nport.html

Source data: SEC Form N-PORT data sets, 2019 Q4 - 2026 Q2.

If you build fund-ownership data from N-PORT: how do you handle the non-stock lines today - map them, or drop them? And if someone has already solved this better, link it in the comments and I'll credit it in the dictionary.

title: Belady's Anomaly: FIFO vs LRU vs Optimal, Checked in Python
description:
Page replacement questions in GATE CS are mostly counting. You get a reference string, a number of frames and a policy, and you write a row of letters. The idea is easy; the marks go when you lose track of the oldest page late in the paper.

So the useful skill is a method you can run without thinking, plus a way to check yourself on practice problems. I wrote a small Python checker for the second part.

Schoolabe's GATE memory management chapter uses this reference string with 3 frames as its worked example:

1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2

It says to count FIFO carefully with a queue, and it doesn't print the answer. Here are the three policies, then the numbers. The code blocks in this post are one file, in order; paste them together and it runs.

import random
from collections import OrderedDict, deque

def fifo(refs, frames):
    q, mem, faults, trace = deque(), set(), 0, []
    for p in refs:
        if p in mem:
            trace.append("hit")
        else:
            faults += 1
            if len(mem) == frames:
                mem.remove(q.popleft())
            q.append(p)
            mem.add(p)
            trace.append("F")
    return faults, trace

def lru(refs, frames):
    mem, faults, trace = OrderedDict(), 0, []
    for p in refs:
        if p in mem:
            mem.move_to_end(p)
            trace.append("hit")
        else:
            faults += 1
            if len(mem) == frames:
                mem.popitem(last=False)
            mem[p] = True
            trace.append("F")
    return faults, trace

def opt(refs, frames):
    mem, faults, trace = [], 0, []
    for i, p in enumerate(refs):
        if p in mem:
            trace.append("hit")
            continue
        faults += 1
        trace.append("F")
        if len(mem) < frames:
            mem.append(p)
            continue
        rest = refs[i + 1:]
        # evict the page whose next use is furthest away (or never)
        victim = max(mem, key=lambda x: rest.index(x) if x in rest else float("inf"))
        mem.remove(victim)
        mem.append(p)
    return faults, trace

lesson = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2]
print("Lesson string with 3 frames:", lesson)
for name, policy in (("FIFO", fifo), ("LRU", lru), ("OPT", opt)):
    n, t = policy(lesson, 3)
    print(f"  {name}: {n} faults   {' '.join(t)}")
print("FIFO on the same string with 4 frames:", fifo(lesson, 4)[0], "faults")

Lesson string with 3 frames: [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2]
  FIFO: 7 faults   F F F F F F F hit hit
  LRU: 7 faults   F F F F F F F hit hit
  OPT: 5 faults   F F F F hit hit F hit hit
FIFO on the same string with 4 frames: 7 faults

Check the FIFO row by hand. Pages 1, 2, 3 fill the frames. Page 4 evicts 1, so the next 1 faults and evicts 2, so the next 2 faults and evicts 3. Page 5 evicts 4. Then 1 and 2 are both still in memory and hit. Seven faults.

For the hand trace I write the full frame contents under every reference, not just F or hit. For FIFO I underline the oldest page, and for LRU I rewrite the frames in recency order each time. It is slower, but when you go wrong you can see where.

LRU also gets seven here, so LRU does not always beat FIFO on a given string. Optimal gets five, and that is your floor. It needs the future, so no real system can do it. The chapter calls it the offline lower bound, and if your hand trace beats it, you have miscounted.

The anomaly

The chapter says FIFO can show Belady's anomaly, where more frames give more faults, and calls it a favourite trap. The lesson string above doesn't show it: FIFO with 4 frames also gives 7. The textbook string is the same one extended by three pages, 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5.

belady = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print("Classic string:", belady)
for name, policy in (("FIFO", fifo), ("LRU", lru)):
    for frames in (3, 4):
        print(f"  {name}, {frames} frames: {policy(belady, frames)[0]} faults")

Classic string: [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  FIFO, 3 frames: 9 faults
  FIFO, 4 frames: 10 faults
  LRU, 3 frames: 10 faults
  LRU, 4 frames: 8 faults

FIFO goes from 9 faults to 10 when it gets a fourth frame. The anomaly was described by Belady, Nelson and Shedler in "An anomaly in space-time characteristics of certain programs running in a paging machine", Communications of the ACM 12(6), June 1969, pp. 349-353 (doi 10.1145/363011.363155).

LRU on the same string drops from 10 to 8, as you would expect. The reason is the stack property: the pages LRU holds with k frames are always a subset of what it holds with k+1 frames. FIFO keeps pages by arrival order, not by use, so it has no such property.

How common is this? I guessed "not very" and wanted a number, so I drew random strings of 12 references over pages 1 to 5, with a fixed seed so you can reproduce it, and compared 3 frames against 4.

random.seed(2026)
trials, bad_fifo, bad_lru = 1_000_000, 0, 0
for _ in range(trials):
    refs = [random.randint(1, 5) for _ in range(12)]
    if fifo(refs, 4)[0] > fifo(refs, 3)[0]:
        bad_fifo += 1
    if lru(refs, 4)[0] > lru(refs, 3)[0]:
        bad_lru += 1
print(f"{trials:,} random strings, 12 refs over pages 1-5, 3 frames vs 4:")
print(f"  FIFO faulted more with 4 frames: {bad_fifo}")
print(f"  LRU faulted more with 4 frames:  {bad_lru}")

1,000,000 random strings, 12 refs over pages 1-5, 3 frames vs 4:
  FIFO faulted more with 4 frames: 1
  LRU faulted more with 4 frames:  0

One hit in a million. A first attempt with 100,000 strings found none, so I'd have written "never" if I'd stopped there. A single hit can't pin down a rate, though, so I also counted exhaustively with a small C program: of all 5^12 = 244,140,625 strings of 12 references over five pages, FIFO faults more with 4 frames than with 3 in exactly 120 of them. That is about 1 in 2 million. It also explains why the textbook string looks hand-built. Someone had to go looking for it.

Don't hunt for the anomaly in the trace. Look at the wording: of these three policies only FIFO can fault more with more frames, so a question asking which one can has its answer before you count anything. If the policy is LRU or Optimal, the anomaly can't be the point.

The checker is also good for something duller. Take any previous-year question with a string and a frame count, run all three policies, and compare with your hand trace. Schoolabe's GATE hub says its previous-year questions show questions and options only for now, and tells you to cross-check the official IIT answer key yourself. That is fair advice for any source, this one included.

CLOCK, the chapter's fourth policy, is not covered here.

Written by the Schoolabe team, who build schoolabe.com. The GATE CS section lists free subject tutorials, topic quizzes and previous-year papers.

title: Reading the CVSS 9.8 score of CVE-2026-108474 without overreading it
description:
Reading the CVSS 9.8 score of CVE-2026-108474 without overreading it

Vulnerability overview

CVE-2026-108474 carries a CVSS v3 score of 9.8 and is classified as CWE-89, SQL injection. It affects JetBrains Exposed before 1.5.1, with 1.5.1 as the fixed release. A 9.8 is a strong signal, and it is worth reading precisely rather than treating the decimal as a verdict.

Mechanism and exploitation conditions

The flaw comes from SQL functions in the framework that do not escape string arguments, and it can be triggered without authentication. Those two properties explain the score: no credential barrier and a direct path to a sensitive operation. What the score does not encode is whether untrusted input reaches an affected function in any particular deployment. A service that never forwards external data into those helpers has the vulnerable library without an obvious way to reach the flaw.

Impact

Where the flaw is reachable, impact scales with the database account privileges. Where it is not reachable, the practical risk is lower even though the number is unchanged. The source report notes no confirmed exploitation in the wild and no public proof of concept, so the score reflects potential rather than observed incidents.

Affected products and scope

Exposed before 1.5.1. The same JetBrains October 2026 batch fixed TeamCity issues CVE-2026-106218 (CVSS 8.8, CWE-184) and CVE-2026-106219 (CVSS 6.5, CWE-73), which sit at different points on the same scale.

Exposure context

A ZoomEye query for the TeamCity fingerprint app="JetBrains TeamCity" returned 1,867 assets, describing visible build servers rather than library deployments. A query for vul.cve="CVE-2026-108474" returned zero indexed matches.

Remediation and mitigations

Patch to Exposed 1.5.1 and rebuild. Then convert the score into a decision for your environment: identify services that pass external input into SQL helpers, confirm their call sites bind parameters and check the privileges of their database accounts. The score sets priority; reachability and privilege set the outcome.

References

  • SecurityOnline vulnerability report, 10 October 2026: https://securityonline.info/jetbrains-software-vulnerabilities-teamcity/

title: PostgreSQL 19 Release Date Moved to Nov 19 After AI Review Found Too Many Bugs
description:
PostgreSQL 19 was supposed to be out by now. Postgres 18 shipped on September 25, 2025, and 19 was tracking the same autumn slot. The new PostgreSQL 19 release date is November 19, 2026, and somewhere between eight and ten significant features got ripped out on the way there.

The reason is the part that gets people arguing. Peter Eisentraut, a long-time committer who works at EDB, wrote on October 9 that LLM-assisted code review was at least partly behind the reverts. In his words, review problems "can get found much faster, and then you're staring at a list of like forty defect reports." The Register picked it up with the headline that AI reviewers found more bugs than humans can fix.

As far as I know, this is the first major open source database whose release schedule visibly bent because machine review outpaced the people doing triage. Below is what changed and what I'd do about it if you run Postgres in production.

The new PostgreSQL 19 timeline

From the RC1 announcement and Christophe Pettus's schedule comparison:

Milestone PostgreSQL 18 PostgreSQL 19
Feature freeze April 8, 2025 April 8, 2026
Beta 1 May 8, 2025 June 4, 2026
Beta 4 none September 24, 2026
RC 1 September 4, 2025 October 15, 2026
RC 2 none November 12, 2026
GA September 25, 2025 November 19, 2026 (planned)

RC 2 exists because the November 12 minor release "will include a large number of fixes," and the release team wanted those in 19 before GA. Note the wording: GA happens on November 19 "unless an issue is discovered that requires a delay or an additional release candidate." I wouldn't put that date in a change calendar yet.

What got cut from Postgres 19

The Beta 4 notes list the big reverts:

  • SQL/PGQ property graph queries
  • Online enabling and disabling of data checksums
  • UPDATE/DELETE ... FOR PORTION OF (temporal updates)
  • ALTER TABLE ... MERGE PARTITIONS and SPLIT PARTITIONS
  • pg_get_role_ddl(), pg_get_tablespace_ddl(), pg_get_database_ddl()

Pettus's post adds more that went earlier or quietly: GROUP BY ALL, non-plain pg_dumpall output formats, and the batched foreign-key fast path. That last one is the scary one. Amit Langote's revert commit warned that the bug "can leave a buffered check unperformed, allowing a transaction to commit a permanent foreign key violation without reporting an error."

REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) survived, with its scope trimmed. Pettus's advice on it is the best line in the whole saga: "Use it the way you'd use a 1.0 of anything that rewrites your tables: on something you have a backup of."

What kind of bugs did AI review find?

Two kinds, per Eisentraut. Some features "had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix quickly and during beta." The rest was a long tail of edge cases, each one cheap to fix but collectively eating the beta window.

The numbers that stuck with me come from Pettus. On August 25, Robert Haas started a "scary patch contest" thread on -hackers and had Claude rank v19 patches by post-freeze bug fixes. REPACK came out at 28 fixes, including data loss, online checksums at about 25, FOR PORTION OF at 17, SQL/PGQ at 17, and RI batching at about 16. Noah Misch ran a separate late-August sweep of master with Claude Opus 5.

SQL/PGQ came out over a design problem. As Pettus describes it, prerequisites were only checked at CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH time and could be dropped afterwards. Haas wrote: "To me, this class of problem seems completely unacceptable in a committed feature." A model can flag that pattern. A human still has to decide it's a reason to delete 15,859 lines.

Eisentraut was explicit that this is "not due to 'vibe coding'." Most of these features were written before the tools were much good at review. What changed is that "the effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed."

Were these bugs always in the Postgres you run today?

Partly, yes, and nobody seems keen to say it out loud.

Most reverted code never shipped, so 18 doesn't contain SQL/PGQ bugs. But Pettus notes that a cast-cache invalidation bug, found while testing the RI batching code, turned out to affect 18.6 as well. And the 2026 security load says more: more than forty CVEs fixed by August, 28 of them in the August 13 releases alone, and the 18.6 release notes credit Claude-assisted and OpenAI Codex Security-assisted researchers among the reporters. All of that was sitting in versions people run in production right now.

The Hacker News thread split on exactly this. One camp says the bugs always existed and we're just seeing them earlier. The other says "more bugs than humans can fix" also means more reports than humans can verify. One commenter's anecdote: "out of 82 bugs reported only 6-8 were actually bugs." Nobody budgets for the time it takes to sort through that.

My take: the false-positive argument doesn't fit Postgres. These weren't junk reports. Committers confirmed them, fixed them, or reverted whole features over them. The trouble is that Postgres keeps a fixed annual schedule, and the slow step has moved from finding bugs to fixing them.

Should you stay on PostgreSQL 18?

Yes. I'd have said that even without the delay, and the delay makes it easier.

  • On 18.x: stay. It's supported until November 14, 2030. Apply the November 12 minor release, since the RC 2 note says it carries a large batch of fixes.
  • On 14.x: this one's urgent. Postgres 14 reaches end of life on November 12, 2026, a week before 19 GA. Go to 18, not to a 19 RC.
  • On 15 to 17: no rush. Plan for 18 now, or wait for 19.2 or so.
  • Building something new on 19 features: test RC1 in staging, never in production. The project's own wording is that RC1 is "mostly identical" to GA, not identical.

I'd wait for the first couple of 19 minor releases regardless. Eisentraut expects 19 to be "very robust, after all the additional scrutiny," and he may be right. It's also a release where features were cut weeks before GA, and code that took those features out is new code too.

How to run pg_upgrade checks against 19 now

Testing against 19 now is cheap and turns up the boring incompatibilities early. Do this on a staging copy, not your primary.

First, look for the things the 19 release notes say will break:

-- Pre-19 dumps taken with this off won't load into 19
SHOW standard_conforming_strings;

-- JIT is off by default in 19; check if you rely on it
SHOW jit;

-- MULE_INTERNAL encoding is removed
SELECT datname FROM pg_database
WHERE pg_encoding_to_char(encoding) = 'MULE_INTERNAL';

-- MD5 passwords now log a warning on every login
SELECT rolname FROM pg_authid WHERE rolpassword LIKE 'md5%';

# RADIUS auth is gone in 19
grep -i radius "$PGDATA/pg_hba.conf"

# Not a 19 change, but it bites here: initdb enables data checksums by
# default since 18, and pg_upgrade needs matching settings. "0" here means your old cluster has none.
pg_controldata "$PGDATA" | grep -i checksum

Then a dry run. Install the 19 RC binaries next to 18, init a new cluster (add --no-data-checksums if the old one has none), and run --check, which validates without touching data:

/usr/lib/postgresql/19/bin/initdb -D /var/lib/postgresql/19/main

/usr/lib/postgresql/19/bin/pg_upgrade --check \
  -b /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin \
  -B /usr/lib/postgresql/19/bin \
  -d /var/lib/postgresql/18/main \
  -D /var/lib/postgresql/19/main

Adjust paths for your packaging. On Debian and Ubuntu, postgresql.conf sits in /etc/postgresql/, so you'll need -o/-O to point at the config files. Two new hard blockers in 19 that --check will catch: database, role or tablespace names containing carriage returns or line feeds, and btree_gist indexes on inet/cidr, which per the notes "can exclude rows that should be returned." If you have the second one, you have a correctness bug today, on 18.

After a real test upgrade, raise max_locks_per_transaction if you'd tuned it. The default went from 64 to 128 because lock allocation changed, and the notes say settings "must now be doubled" to keep the same capacity.

What this means for AI code review on your codebase

Postgres has some of the most careful code review in open source. If an LLM-assisted pass can hand committers "like forty" defect reports for features that already got through that review, nobody's codebase is getting a pass. The Postgres team at least had the discipline to revert instead of shipping and patching later.

So: if AI review finds this many bugs in Postgres, what do you think it would find in your codebase? And would your team revert a feature over it, or ship it on schedule and hope?

Sources

  • Peter Eisentraut: The reverts will continue until morale improves
  • PostgreSQL 19 RC 1 Released
  • PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released
  • PostgreSQL 19 release notes
  • PostgreSQL versioning policy
  • Christophe Pettus: 19th Nervous Breakdown
  • The Register: Postgres 19 delayed after AI reviewers find more bugs than humans can fix
  • LWN: Eisentraut: The reverts will continue until morale improves
  • Hacker News discussion

Why Is Keeping Time Correctly So Difficult for Distributed Systems?
description:
Imagine a payment succeeds, but your system records a related database event before the payment itself. The payment service logs the transaction at 10:00:00.120, while the database records the event at 10:00:00.095.

When you inspect the logs, it looks as though the database event happened first. But what if the application logic is correct and the real problem is that the two servers disagree about the current time?

This is one of the more frustrating problems in distributed systems. Timestamps look like reliable facts, yet they can tell a misleading story when events happen across multiple machines.

Developers use timestamps to track transactions, process messages, expire sessions, and resolve database conflicts. Understanding where these timestamps fail is essential when building systems that need to remain reliable under real-world conditions.

1. Every Server Has Its Own Understanding of Time

In a distributed system, each machine maintains its own system clock. Unlike a single computer, where applications generally share the same operating system time source, multiple servers do not have a perfectly shared clock.

Even if two machines synchronize their clocks at startup, their readings can gradually diverge. Their hardware oscillators run at slightly different rates, and environmental conditions can affect their accuracy.

Consider a payment service, a database, and a notification worker running on separate machines. Each records the same sequence of events from its own perspective, potentially producing timestamps that appear inconsistent.

Three related concepts help explain this behavior:

  • Clock offset: The difference between a clock's reading and a reference clock at a particular moment.
  • Clock skew: The difference between two clocks' readings or rates, depending on the context.
  • Clock drift: The change in a clock's timing error over time.

These differences might seem insignificant when measured in milliseconds. However, they become important when application logic relies on timestamps to determine which event happened first.

2. Why Do Computer Clocks Drift?

Computer clocks depend on physical hardware rather than perfect mathematical references. Their oscillators generate signals that operating systems use to maintain time, but those signals are not perfectly stable.

Temperature changes, manufacturing differences, and aging components can cause one clock to run slightly faster or slower than another.

Imagine two clocks synchronized at noon. Clock A gains two milliseconds per second relative to a reference, while Clock B loses one millisecond per second.

After one minute, Clock A is 120 milliseconds ahead of the reference, while Clock B is 60 milliseconds behind it. Their readings now differ by 180 milliseconds.

These figures are illustrative, but the principle is important: small timing errors accumulate. Synchronizing machines once is not enough for long-running systems, so their clocks must be monitored and corrected periodically.

3. The Network Makes Synchronization Even Harder

Suppose Server A wants to determine the current time on Server B. It sends a request, Server B reads its clock, and a response returns to Server A.

Although Server A can measure the total round-trip time, it cannot determine precisely how long the request took in each direction.

For example, the request might take 15 milliseconds to reach Server B, while the response takes 65 milliseconds to return. Assuming that both directions took 40 milliseconds would produce an inaccurate estimate.

Network congestion, routing changes, packet retransmissions, and server load make these delays difficult to predict. Two requests sent seconds apart can experience noticeably different network conditions.

Protocols such as the Network Time Protocol (NTP) address this problem by exchanging timestamps and estimating clock offsets and network delays. They improve synchronization considerably, but they cannot eliminate every source of uncertainty.

4. NTP Helps, but It Cannot Create a Perfect Global Clock

NTP is widely used to synchronize computer clocks against external or internal time references. It considers network delays and measurement variations to estimate differences between clocks.

For many web applications, the remaining timing errors are acceptable. Logging, monitoring, and ordinary business operations generally do not require every server to agree on time with extreme precision.

Other applications have stricter requirements. Financial systems, precision measurements, and tightly coordinated operations may need more accurate synchronization.

Precision Time Protocol (PTP) can provide tighter synchronization in suitably configured environments. However, better synchronization does not automatically guarantee correct event ordering.

The important question is not simply whether the clocks agree. It is whether the application's timing assumptions are strong enough for the decisions it makes.

5. Why Timestamps Cannot Always Tell You What Happened First

Consider an online store with separate order and inventory services. Two customers attempt to purchase the last available item at nearly the same moment.

The inventory service records an update at 10:00:00.120, while the order service records its operation at 10:00:00.105. A naive implementation might conclude that the order operation happened first because its timestamp is earlier.

However, if the order service's clock is running behind the inventory service's clock, that conclusion may be wrong.

This problem extends beyond inventory management. An old profile update might overwrite a newer value, or a database replica might select an unexpected update during conflict resolution.

The underlying issue is that physical timestamps and causal ordering are not the same thing. A timestamp tells you what a particular clock reported, but it does not automatically prove the order in which events occurred across different machines.

When correctness depends on event ordering, applications need mechanisms designed specifically for that purpose.

6. Logical Clocks: Ordering Events Without Relying on Wall-Clock Time

Logical clocks provide another way to track events. Instead of attempting to determine the exact real-world time of every operation, they represent relationships between events.

Lamport clocks, introduced by Leslie Lamport, assign logical timestamps using counters maintained by individual processes. Each process advances its counter when recording events and includes its logical timestamp when sending a message.

When another process receives that message, it updates its counter to a value greater than both its current counter and the timestamp carried by the message.

For example, Service A records an event with logical timestamp 1 and sends a message to Service B. Service B receives the message and advances its counter to 2 before recording a subsequent event with timestamp 3.

This establishes the required causal relationship without depending on synchronized physical clocks.

However, Lamport clocks have a limitation: a smaller logical timestamp does not necessarily prove that one event caused or preceded another. Independent events can occur concurrently.

Vector clocks provide more information about causal relationships, although they require additional metadata. The appropriate choice depends on how much information the application needs about concurrent operations.

7. Physical Clocks, Logical Clocks, and Monotonic Clocks

Not every timing problem requires the same solution. Physical clocks, logical clocks, and monotonic clocks serve different purposes.

  • Physical clocks provide real-world timestamps for transaction records, audit logs, and scheduled operations.
  • Logical clocks help represent event ordering and causal relationships.
  • Monotonic clocks measure elapsed time without being disrupted by adjustments to the wall clock.

Consider a payment service measuring how long a request takes to complete. It needs to calculate a duration, not determine the current date and time.

Using a monotonic clock is a better choice for this task. A wall-clock adjustment should not cause the measured duration to become unexpectedly negative or inaccurate.

This distinction also matters for request timeouts, retry policies, and performance measurements. Using the appropriate clock for each task removes unnecessary dependencies and makes application behavior more predictable.

8. Why Distributed Databases Care So Much About Time

Distributed databases make clock-related problems particularly visible when multiple regions accept updates independently.

Imagine a database replicated across two regions. Region A updates a user's email address, while Region B updates the same user's display name. When the regions exchange their changes, the database must reconcile the updates according to its consistency and conflict-resolution rules.

Some systems use timestamp-based conflict resolution, such as last-write-wins. If two updates conflict, the system selects the one with the later timestamp according to its rules.

But what happens if the clock in Region B is significantly ahead? An older update might appear newer than it actually is, producing an unexpected result.

Not every distributed database resolves conflicts this way. Some use version metadata, transaction ordering, hybrid logical clocks, consensus protocols, or application-level conflict resolution.

The lesson is that database correctness should not depend on the assumption that every machine has a perfectly synchronized clock. Engineers must understand the consistency guarantees their database actually provides.

9. A Subtle Timing Bug in JavaScript

Clock-related problems can also appear in ordinary application code. Consider this JavaScript example:

const start = Date.now();

// Perform some operation.

const elapsed = Date.now() - start;

console.log(`Elapsed: ${elapsed} ms`);

The code looks reasonable because Date.now() returns the current wall-clock time in milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

However, the operating system or time-synchronization mechanisms can adjust the wall clock between the two calls. If the clock moves backward, the calculated duration could even become negative.

In Node.js, process.hrtime.bigint() provides a high-resolution monotonic time source suitable for measuring durations:

const start = process.hrtime.bigint();

// Perform some operation.

const elapsed = process.hrtime.bigint() - start;

console.log(`Elapsed: ${Number(elapsed) / 1e6} ms`);

The difference is measured in nanoseconds and then converted to milliseconds for display. The main advantage is not merely precision; it is that the measurement uses a monotonic clock.

Use wall-clock time when you need to know when something happened. Use monotonic time when you need to know how long it took.

10. How Engineers Build Systems That Handle Time Correctly

The goal is not to make time perfect. It is to ensure that clock uncertainty does not compromise application correctness.

A good starting point is reliable clock synchronization, trustworthy time sources, and monitoring that alerts engineers when synchronization error exceeds acceptable limits.

However, infrastructure alone is not enough. When update ordering matters, applications should use mechanisms such as version numbers, transaction ordering, or explicit causal metadata rather than relying exclusively on timestamps.

Optimistic concurrency control is one practical example. An update must match the version previously read by the client. If another operation has already changed that version, the update can fail instead of silently overwriting newer data.

Distributed leases require similar care. If one worker believes a lease has expired while the previous owner is still running, both workers might attempt to modify the same resource. Depending on the design, fencing tokens can help the resource reject operations from older lease holders.

Testing matters, too. Developers should simulate delayed messages, out-of-order events, concurrent updates, and clock offsets to verify that their applications continue to behave correctly.

A useful question during a design review is: If this timestamp were wrong by 100 milliseconds, would the system still make the correct decision?

The answer may be different for a log entry, an inventory reservation, and a distributed lock. What matters is understanding which operations can tolerate timing errors and which require stronger guarantees.

11. The Bigger Lesson: Distributed Systems Must Account for Uncertainty

The difficulty of distributed time is not simply a hardware problem or an NTP configuration issue. It comes from the nature of distributed computing: machines operate independently, messages experience unpredictable delays, and synchronization measurements remain imperfect.

A timestamp generated on one machine therefore cannot automatically prove the exact ordering of events on another.

Reliable systems address these limitations with a combination of techniques. Physical clocks provide real-world timestamps, monotonic clocks measure durations, logical clocks track event relationships, and versioning or coordination mechanisms enforce stronger guarantees where necessary.

The right choice depends on the operation being performed. A logging system may tolerate small timestamp differences, while an inventory service or distributed lock manager may need stronger protections to prevent incorrect decisions.

Understanding that distinction is more valuable than simply ensuring that every server reports approximately the same time.

Conclusion

Keeping time correctly in distributed systems is difficult because there is no perfectly shared clock and no guarantee that independent machines will agree on the exact moment an event occurred.

NTP reduces clock differences, logical clocks help establish event relationships, monotonic clocks make duration measurements safer, and versioning or coordination protocols protect operations that require stronger guarantees. Each mechanism solves a different part of the problem.

The next time you design a distributed application, look beyond whether all your servers are synchronized. Consider what your application assumes about timestamps, how it determines the order of concurrent operations, and what happens when one machine's clock is significantly ahead of another's.

A reliable distributed system is not one in which every clock is perfect; it is one that continues to behave correctly when clocks are not.
