title: Building an Equipment Checkout System with PostgreSQL, Node.js, and Express
description:
Database design, REST APIs, concurrency control, and practical equipment custody workflows.

Imagine an IT department managing laptops, monitors, and tablets for 200 employees.

Every time a device is issued, someone records the assignment. Every time it is returned, someone updates the equipment register.

That sounds like a simple CRUD application.

But consider what happens when:

  • Two administrators try to assign the same laptop simultaneously.
  • Someone returns equipment that was already marked as returned.
  • An employee leaves, but their assigned devices are difficult to identify.
  • A transaction updates the asset status but fails before saving the checkout record.
  • A device changes hands without preserving its previous assignment history.

These aren't just interface problems. They are data integrity and concurrency problems.

In this tutorial, we'll build the core of an equipment checkout system using PostgreSQL, Node.js, and Express.

By the end, you'll understand how to:

  1. Design a relational model for physical assets and employee custody.
  2. Prevent duplicate active equipment assignments.
  3. Build transactional checkout and return endpoints.
  4. Protect shared assets from concurrent updates.
  5. Record custody events.
  6. Test common failure scenarios.
  7. Identify what must be added before production deployment.

This is a small, executable educational example—not a complete enterprise asset management platform.

1. Understand the Business Problem

An equipment checkout system needs to distinguish between an asset and an assignment.

An asset is a physical item owned or managed by an organization.

For example:

Asset ID Equipment Current status
LAP-101 Dell Latitude laptop Available
LAP-102 MacBook Pro Checked out
MON-201 Dell monitor Maintenance

An assignment describes a period during which a particular employee is responsible for an asset.

For example:

Asset Employee Issued Returned
LAP-101 Alice Oct 1 Oct 10
LAP-101 Bob Oct 12 Not yet returned

Notice that the same laptop can have multiple historical assignments but should have only one active checkout at a time.

That's our most important business rule.

Core workflow 

Register asset
     |
     v
  Available
     |
     | Checkout
     v
 Checked out
     |
     | Return
     v
  Available

Additional states such as maintenance, reservation, retirement, and transfer can be introduced later.

For this tutorial, we'll focus on the checkout/return lifecycle.

2. Define the Database Invariants

Before designing database tables, establish conditions the application must preserve.

Rule 1: Each asset has a unique asset tag.

Rule 2: An asset cannot have multiple active checkout records.

Rule 3: Only available assets may be checked out.

Rule 4: A checkout must reference a valid, active employee.

Rule 5: A return must close the active checkout record.

Rule 6: Asset status and checkout history must be updated together.

Rule 7: Historical custody records should be retained.

Some of these rules can be enforced directly by PostgreSQL constraints. Others require transactions and application-level validation.

Using both layers makes the system more reliable.

3. Create the PostgreSQL Schema

We'll use three primary tables and one simple event table.

The examples use standard PostgreSQL features.

Employees 

CREATE TABLE employees (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    is_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE
);

An employee can become inactive without deleting their historical checkout records.

Assets 

CREATE TABLE assets (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    asset_tag TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    category TEXT NOT NULL,
    serial_number TEXT,

    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available'
        CHECK (
            status IN (
                'available',
                'checked_out',
                'maintenance',
                'retired'
            )
        )
);

The asset_tag uniquely identifies a physical device.

A QR code or barcode can encode that identifier or a URL that resolves to its record.

Importantly, scanning a QR code does not automatically establish custody or continuous location tracking. The business application must explicitly record those activities.

Checkout history 

CREATE TABLE checkouts (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,

    asset_id BIGINT NOT NULL
        REFERENCES assets(id),

    employee_id BIGINT NOT NULL
        REFERENCES employees(id),

    checked_out_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
        DEFAULT NOW(),

    expected_return_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    returned_at TIMESTAMPTZ,

    issued_condition TEXT,
    return_condition TEXT,

    CHECK (
        expected_return_at IS NULL
        OR expected_return_at >= checked_out_at
    ),

    CHECK (
        returned_at IS NULL
        OR returned_at >= checked_out_at
    )
);

We keep historical checkouts instead of deleting them.

An active checkout is defined as:

returned_at IS NULL

Prevent duplicate active checkouts 

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_checkout_per_asset
ON checkouts (asset_id)
WHERE returned_at IS NULL;

This is a PostgreSQL partial unique index.

It enforces a critical invariant at the database level: no more than one active checkout record per asset.

Unlike a simple application-level SELECT check, the unique index still protects data when concurrent requests attempt to insert conflicting records.

PostgreSQL documents partial indexes here:

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html

Record custody events 

CREATE TABLE asset_events (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,

    asset_id BIGINT NOT NULL
        REFERENCES assets(id),

    checkout_id BIGINT
        REFERENCES checkouts(id),

    event_type TEXT NOT NULL
        CHECK (
            event_type IN (
                'CHECKED_OUT',
                'RETURNED'
            )
        ),

    occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
        DEFAULT NOW()
);

This small event table provides an operational history of checkout and return events.

It is not a full security audit log because it does not yet identify the authenticated administrator who performed the action.

A production audit log would typically include a verified actor identity and additional event context.

4. Insert Example Data

Let's create two employees and two assets.

INSERT INTO employees (full_name, email)
VALUES
    ('Alice Carter', 'alice@example.com'),
    ('Bob Smith', 'bob@example.com');

INSERT INTO assets (asset_tag, name, category)
VALUES
    ('LAP-101', 'Dell Latitude', 'Laptop'),
    ('MON-201', 'Dell Monitor', 'Monitor');

These are fictional example records.

Both devices initially have the status available.

5. Set Up Node.js and Express

Start a new Node.js project.

mkdir equipment-checkout-api
cd equipment-checkout-api
npm init -y
npm install express pg dotenv

Add "type": "module" to package.json.

Create a PostgreSQL database, then execute the schema and seed statements above using a PostgreSQL client such as psql.

Create a .env file:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/asset_tracking
PORT=3000

Replace the connection string with one that matches your local PostgreSQL configuration.

Never commit credentials or .env files containing secrets to a public repository.

Database connection

Create db.js:

import "dotenv/config";
import pg from "pg";

export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
});

We use a connection pool for database operations.

However, every statement within a transaction must execute using the same checked-out client.

The node-postgres documentation explicitly requires this.

Reference:

https://node-postgres.com/features/transactions

6. Build the Checkout API

Create server.js.

import express from "express";
import { pool } from "./db.js";

const app = express();

app.use(express.json());

app.post("/api/checkouts", async (req, res) => {
  const { assetId, employeeId } = req.body ?? {};

  if (
    !Number.isSafeInteger(assetId) ||
    assetId <= 0 ||
    !Number.isSafeInteger(employeeId) ||
    employeeId <= 0
  ) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: "Valid assetId and employeeId are required",
    });
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    const assetResult = await client.query(
      `SELECT id, status
       FROM assets
       WHERE id = $1
       FOR UPDATE`,
      [assetId]
    );

    const asset = assetResult.rows[0];

    if (!asset) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");

      return res.status(404).json({
        error: "Asset not found",
      });
    }

    if (asset.status !== "available") {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");

      return res.status(409).json({
        error: "Asset is not available",
      });
    }

    const employeeResult = await client.query(
      `SELECT id
       FROM employees
       WHERE id = $1
         AND is_active = TRUE`,
      [employeeId]
    );

    if (employeeResult.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");

      return res.status(400).json({
        error: "Employee not found or inactive",
      });
    }

    const checkoutResult = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO checkouts (
         asset_id,
         employee_id
       )
       VALUES ($1, $2)
       RETURNING id, asset_id, employee_id,
                 checked_out_at`,
      [assetId, employeeId]
    );

    const checkout = checkoutResult.rows[0];

    await client.query(
      `UPDATE assets
       SET status = 'checked_out'
       WHERE id = $1`,
      [assetId]
    );

    await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO asset_events (
         asset_id,
         checkout_id,
         event_type
       )
       VALUES ($1, $2, 'CHECKED_OUT')`,
      [assetId, checkout.id]
    );

    await client.query("COMMIT");

    return res.status(201).json({
      message: "Equipment checked out",
      checkout,
    });
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");

    console.error("Checkout error:", error);

    if (error.code === "23505") {
      return res.status(409).json({
        error: "Conflicting active assignment",
      });
    }

    return res.status(500).json({
      error: "Checkout failed",
    });
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

Why use a transaction?

A successful checkout changes several records:

  1. The checkout history gains a new active assignment.
  2. The asset status becomes checked_out.
  3. An event is recorded.

These changes must succeed together.

If any statement fails, the transaction rolls back.

This prevents a partially completed checkout from leaving the records inconsistent.

Why use FOR UPDATE? 

SELECT id, status
FROM assets
WHERE id = $1
FOR UPDATE;

The row lock prevents another conflicting transaction from updating or locking the same asset row until the current transaction finishes.

Consider two checkout requests arriving at nearly the same time.

Request A locks LAP-101

Request B waits for LAP-101

Request A creates assignment
Request A commits

Request B reads the updated status

Request B receives HTTP 409

In combination with the partial unique index, this provides strong protection against duplicate active assignments.

The example assumes every custody-modifying operation follows the same transaction and locking conventions.

Reference:

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html

7. Build the Return API

Returning equipment must close its active assignment and update the corresponding asset status.

To reduce lock-order conflicts, we'll locate the checkout's asset, lock the asset first, and then lock the checkout record.

Add this endpoint to server.js:

app.post("/api/checkouts/:id/return", async (req, res) => {
  const checkoutId = Number(req.params.id);

  if (
    !Number.isSafeInteger(checkoutId) ||
    checkoutId <= 0
  ) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: "Invalid checkout ID",
    });
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    const lookup = await client.query(
      `SELECT asset_id
       FROM checkouts
       WHERE id = $1`,
      [checkoutId]
    );

    if (lookup.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");

      return res.status(404).json({
        error: "Checkout not found",
      });
    }

    const assetId = lookup.rows[0].asset_id;

    await client.query(
      `SELECT id
       FROM assets
       WHERE id = $1
       FOR UPDATE`,
      [assetId]
    );

    const checkoutResult = await client.query(
      `SELECT id, returned_at
       FROM checkouts
       WHERE id = $1
       FOR UPDATE`,
      [checkoutId]
    );

    if (
      checkoutResult.rowCount === 0 ||
      checkoutResult.rows[0].returned_at !== null
    ) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");

      return res.status(409).json({
        error: "Checkout is not active",
      });
    }

    const result = await client.query(
      `UPDATE checkouts
       SET returned_at = NOW()
       WHERE id = $1
       RETURNING id, asset_id, employee_id,
                 returned_at`,
      [checkoutId]
    );

    await client.query(
      `UPDATE assets
       SET status = 'available'
       WHERE id = $1`,
      [assetId]
    );

    await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO asset_events (
         asset_id,
         checkout_id,
         event_type
       )
       VALUES ($1, $2, 'RETURNED')`,
      [assetId, checkoutId]
    );

    await client.query("COMMIT");

    return res.json({
      message: "Equipment returned",
      checkout: result.rows[0],
    });
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");

    console.error("Return error:", error);

    return res.status(500).json({
      error: "Return failed",
    });
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

This is a deliberately simple return workflow.

It assumes returned equipment is available for reassignment.

In a real IT department, damaged equipment may need inspection or maintenance before becoming available again.

For that reason, a production system should support condition checks and an appropriate post-return status.

8. Add an Employee Equipment Lookup API

During offboarding, IT needs to identify every device currently assigned to an employee.

Add the following endpoint:

app.get("/api/employees/:id/assets", async (req, res) => {
  const employeeId = Number(req.params.id);

  if (
    !Number.isSafeInteger(employeeId) ||
    employeeId <= 0
  ) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: "Invalid employee ID",
    });
  }

  try {
    const result = await pool.query(
      `SELECT
         a.asset_tag,
         a.name,
         a.category,
         c.id AS checkout_id,
         c.checked_out_at
       FROM checkouts c
       JOIN assets a ON a.id = c.asset_id
       WHERE c.employee_id = $1
         AND c.returned_at IS NULL
       ORDER BY c.checked_out_at DESC`,
      [employeeId]
    );

    return res.json({
      employeeId,
      assets: result.rows,
    });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Asset lookup error:", error);

    return res.status(500).json({
      error: "Unable to fetch assets",
    });
  }
});

This endpoint queries the active checkout records rather than only checking the asset status.

For employee offboarding, that's the relevant source of custody information.

Start the server

Finally, add:

const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000;

app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server running on port ${port}`);
});

Run it:

node server.js

9. Test the Workflow

Let's check out the first laptop to the first employee.

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/checkouts \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"assetId":1,"employeeId":1}'

If the seed data was inserted into a new database in the stated order, this should create an active checkout.

The server should return HTTP 201.

Now repeat the same request.

Because the asset is already checked out, the second request should return HTTP 409.

To retrieve the employee's equipment:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/employees/1/assets

To return the equipment, use the checkout ID from the first successful checkout response:

curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:3000/api/checkouts/1/return

The example above assumes the first generated checkout ID is 1; use the actual returned ID in your environment.

After the return, the asset should be available for another checkout.

Test concurrent requests

The most important concurrency test is to submit two checkout requests for the same available asset at approximately the same time.

Expected behavior:

  • One request succeeds.
  • The other receives a conflict.
  • Only one active checkout exists in the database.

Verify that final condition directly:

SELECT *
FROM checkouts
WHERE asset_id = 1
  AND returned_at IS NULL;

The query should return no more than one row.

The partial unique index provides the database-level guarantee for that condition.

10. What This Example Does—and Doesn't—Guarantee

The example implements:

  • Unique asset identifiers.
  • Historical checkout records.
  • Prevention of duplicate active checkouts.
  • Transactional checkout and return operations.
  • Row locking for asset-level concurrency.
  • Basic checkout and return events.
  • Employee equipment lookup.

It does not implement a complete production system.

Before deployment, several additional components are necessary.

Authentication and authorization

Each request must identify its authenticated user.

An employee should not be able to check out an arbitrary device or retrieve another employee's records without authorization.

Tenant isolation

If multiple organizations use the same application, their assets, employees, and checkout histories must be isolated.

Idempotency

A client may retry a request after a network timeout even if the original operation succeeded.

Production APIs should consider persistent idempotency keys to identify repeated requests safely.

Employee transfers

Transferring equipment should preserve its previous custody period while creating a new assignment.

A transfer workflow should be handled transactionally, with explicit business rules.

Full audit history

A production audit trail should record the authenticated actor, relevant changes, timestamps, and appropriate context.

Operational controls

Real applications also need structured logging, database migrations, monitoring, secure configuration, backup and recovery procedures, and automated integration tests.

A particularly important engineering consideration is that the checkout and return endpoints rely on consistent asset-first locking. Any future transfer or maintenance workflow must coordinate with that strategy.

11. Why These Design Decisions Matter to IT Teams

From a business perspective, these database concepts solve practical problems.

Technical decision Operational benefit
Unique asset tags Consistent equipment identification
Partial unique index Prevents conflicting active assignments
Historical checkouts Preserves previous custody records
Transactions Prevents partially completed handovers
Row locking Protects concurrent equipment assignments
Employee lookup API Supports offboarding and reconciliation
Custody events Provides a foundation for change history

For growing businesses, the most useful equipment management system is not necessarily the one with the longest feature list.

It is one that keeps responsibility and asset records consistent as equipment moves between employees and locations.

12. How This Relates to Real Asset Management Platforms

Building an internal equipment checkout system can be a valuable engineering project.

However, teams also need to consider ongoing maintenance, authorization, auditing, user experience, and the operational effort required to manage equipment at scale.

That is why some organizations evaluate dedicated physical asset management platforms instead of maintaining custom software.

For example, Stackroom focuses on centralized physical asset records, equipment assignments, documented handovers and returns, and audit workflows.

For an operational explanation of the equipment handover process, see:

Equipment Checkout Process Guide — Stackroom

Disclosure: I am associated with Stackroom, a physical asset and equipment management platform.

Conclusion

A reliable equipment checkout system is more than an inventory database.

It needs to preserve custody information, enforce business rules, and remain consistent when operations happen concurrently.

The most important lessons are:

  1. Model assets and checkout periods separately.
  2. Use database constraints for critical invariants.
  3. Wrap multi-step state changes in transactions.
  4. Lock shared asset records consistently.
  5. Retain historical checkout information.
  6. Record custody events.
  7. Test duplicate requests, concurrency, and failure conditions.
  8. Treat authorization and tenant isolation as production requirements.

A good equipment checkout system should answer not only “What equipment do we own?” but also “Who currently has it, and how did that assignment happen?”

Discussion

If you were designing an equipment tracking application, would you store transfers as separate checkout periods or introduce a dedicated transfer entity?

What trade-offs would influence your decision?

Technical references

  • PostgreSQL — Partial Indexes
  • PostgreSQL — Explicit Locking
  • node-postgres — Transactions
  • Express — Error Handling

title: What is an AI agent cloud? A practical definition
description:
The core idea

An AI agent cloud is not a new type of server. It is a set of services that let you write a small program that talks to an event source, does some computation, and then publishes a result. The platform gives that program a sandbox, a persistent identity, and the ability to talk to other services on your behalf. The agent is the unit of deployment, the unit of scaling, and the unit of billing.

When we built the platform we started from the same problem that most teams face: they want to run an AI-powered bot that watches a queue, processes a document, or answers a question, but they do not want to manage the underlying infrastructure. The answer we found was to expose a simple runtime that hides the complexity of containers, networking, and key management. That runtime is what we call the AI agent cloud.

What an agent looks like

An agent is a container image that follows a small contract. The contract is a single entry point that receives an event payload, runs a loop, and writes back to an output channel. The image can bundle any binary, any language runtime, or any model file. The only requirement is that the agent can start quickly, stay idle until it receives work, and shut down when it is not needed.

The platform supplies the following to every agent:

  • Compute - a CPU share and a memory quota that are metered per second. The platform scales the number of instances up or down automatically based on the event queue depth.
  • Storage - a temporary file system that is reset on each start, and a persistent volume for logs that can be queried from the dashboard.
  • Networking - a private VPC that isolates the agent from the public internet, with a single ingress point that the platform uses to deliver events.
  • Identity - a vault that holds the agent’s API keys and secrets. The keys are scoped to the agent and cannot be accessed by other agents or by the platform itself.
  • Observability - metrics, logs, and traces that are automatically collected and sent to the platform’s monitoring stack.

When you deploy an agent you do not need to write any Terraform or Kubernetes manifests. You simply push the image to the registry, declare a name, and the platform creates a deployment that lives in its own namespace. The platform then watches the event source you specify - a queue, a webhook, or a scheduled trigger - and starts the agent when a new event arrives.

How the platform runs an agent

The platform’s runtime is built on a lightweight orchestration layer that sits on top of our dedicated infrastructure. When an event arrives, the runtime does the following:

  1. Pulls the image from the registry and verifies its signature.
  2. Starts the container in a sandbox that limits CPU, memory, and network access.
  3. Injects the event payload into the container’s standard input or a file.
  4. Monitors the container’s health and restarts it if it crashes.
  5. Collects the output from the container and publishes it to the target channel.
  6. Parks the container when it becomes idle, freeing resources for other agents.

Because the runtime is stateful only for the duration of a single event, it can scale to thousands of agents without a proportional increase in resource usage. The platform also keeps a small cache of the most recent image layers so that the next start is fast. In practice, the average start time is under 200 milliseconds for most agents.

Security and key ownership

Security is a first-class concern in an AI agent cloud. Every agent runs in its own sandbox that is isolated from other agents and from the host. The sandbox is implemented with Linux namespaces and seccomp filters that restrict system calls. The platform also enforces a strict network policy that allows outbound traffic only to the services the agent explicitly declares.

Key ownership is handled by a vault that is integrated into the runtime. When you create an agent you can attach a set of API keys. The platform stores those keys in a key-management service that encrypts them at rest and only gives the agent process access to the keys it needs. The keys are never exposed in logs or in the container image. If an agent is compromised, the attacker only has access to the keys that were attached to that agent, not to the keys of other agents or to the platform itself.

We wrote a dedicated post on this topic, “Key ownership for agent API keys.” It explains the vault architecture and the best practices for rotating keys. If you want to dive deeper, you can read that post for more detail.

Scaling and cost

Because the platform starts an agent only when there is work, the cost model is per-second billing. Compute is metered in 1-second increments, and the platform does not charge for idle time. The only time you pay for a running agent is when it is actively processing an event. This is a direct contrast to the traditional VM model where you pay for the whole instance regardless of usage.

The platform also supports autoscaling at the cluster level. If you have many agents that all listen to the same queue, the platform can spin up additional instances of the queue consumer and distribute the load. The scaling decisions are based on event queue depth, latency targets, and the number of active instances. The platform exposes these metrics in the dashboard, so you can see how many instances are running and how long each event takes to process.

The free tier of the platform gives you a small amount of compute and storage that is ideal for experimentation. It includes a limited number of concurrent agent instances and a small event

title: Replacing a no-op confirm with a promise means every exit now owes somebody an answer
description:
Munchable's confirm dialogs used to be Alert.alert. On react-native-web that export is literally class Alert { static alert() {} }, so every confirmation in the browser build did nothing at all: sign out, delete account, the report flow. I wrote that one up already. The replacement is a small store plus a host component, and it works on all three platforms.

This post is about the bug the replacement is capable of, which has the same symptom as the one it fixed.

A promise is a debt

The API that replaced Alert.alert is an awaitable:

const ok = await confirm({
  title: 'Delete your account?',
  message: '...',
  confirmLabel: 'Delete',
  destructive: true,
});
if (!ok) return;

There are six of these in the app and six plain showAlert calls. The awaitable form is what makes the call sites readable, and it is also the whole problem: confirm() resolves from inside an action handler. If a dialog goes away without running one of its handlers, the await never finishes. The screen does not crash and nothing is logged. A button was pressed and nothing happened, which is exactly the failure this module was written to delete.

So the store's contract is not "show a dialog". It is: one dialog at a time, and every request is settled exactly once.

Five ways a dialog ends, and all of them settle

  • A button. select(index) clears current and then runs that action's handler.
  • The backdrop, or hardware back. dismiss() runs the cancel action's handler, so a backdrop tap behaves exactly like tapping Cancel rather than being a third outcome.
  • Eviction. Opening a second dialog replaces the first, so the first's cancel handler runs as it goes: 
show: (request) => {
  // Settle the dialog being replaced before it is gone, so its awaiting
  // caller is released instead of being left pending forever.
  const evicted = cancelOf(get().current);
  set({ current: request });
  evicted?.();
},
  • Unmount. The host settles anything still open as it tears down. Closing the screen that raised a confirm would otherwise leave that await pending for the rest of the session, with no dialog on screen to resolve it.

Because every one of those paths can reach the cancel handler, the handler has to be able to run twice without being believed twice:

let settled = false;
const answer = (value: boolean) => {
  if (settled) return;
  settled = true;
  resolve(value);
};

confirm() resolving false for cancel, dismissal and eviction alike is what makes if (!(await confirm(...))) return correct at every call site, and what makes it safe to put the await inside a try/finally that clears a busy flag. The flag is not defensive programming for its own sake. It is the thing that lets five independent exits share one cancel handler.

The registry exists because UIKit says no

The second half of the module is stranger, and it is iOS specific.

A react-native <Modal> presents from its nearest view controller. Munchable's capture, menu and paywall screens are declared presentation: 'modal', so when one of them is open, the root view controller is already presenting something. A dialog host mounted only at the app root would be asking that controller to present a second time, and UIKit refuses. The visible result was the two buttons on the result screen doing nothing, which is the same no-op symptom again, arriving by a third route.

The fix is that hosts register themselves and only the innermost one renders:

hosts: number[],              // mount order
// ...
const isActive = hosts[hosts.length - 1] === id;

Mount order means the last entry is the host nearest the screen the user is looking at. The root host stays mounted as the fallback for ordinary screens. The capture screen mounts three, one in each of its render branches, because the branch that is rendering is the one whose tree the dialog has to appear in.

Two of the sheet screens, menu and paywall, currently mount no host of their own. Neither raises a dialog today, which is precisely why the degradation matters: a modal screen that forgets to mount a host gets a dialog that may not appear, rather than a crash or a hang. That is a deliberately boring failure mode for a mistake that is easy to make, and I would rather have it than a cleverer arrangement that fails interestingly.

The unmount path has to respect the same ordering:

const wasActive = state.hosts[state.hosts.length - 1] === id;
unregisterHost(id);
if (wasActive && state.current) state.dismiss();

Only the host that was actually rendering the dialog settles it on the way out. Without that check, a background host unmounting would cancel a dialog the user is currently looking at.

One rendering detail that cost two attempts

The modal's visible prop flips off the moment current becomes null, but the fade-out takes a few hundred milliseconds. Reading the title, message and buttons straight from current therefore blanked all three for the length of the animation, and faded an empty card over the backdrop on the app's most consequential confirmations. The host keeps the last request in a ref and renders current ?? lastRequest.current, so the dialog that is leaving still has words in it.

Reduced motion is honoured by jumping the entrance to its end state rather than by skipping the dialog, and the card animates opacity plus a translate rather than a scale, so a message that wraps to four lines is the same size on the first frame as on the last.

Seeing it

The browser build is at app.munchable.app, which is the same code as the phone app. Sign in and the confirmations you meet there, including the two destructive ones in Profile, are this store rather than the operating system's dialogs. What those two destructive buttons actually do is written up on the privacy page: an export, and a deletion that mostly happens on the device because that is where the sensitive data already lives.

title: The leaderboard move in our product demo is a swap between two frozen arrays, and its 20 second timer lasts 10
description:
Our landing page runs three animated mocks of the product: a host view in a laptop frame and two phone views. No video, no screen recording, just components and a module-scope fixture.

I went back into that fixture recently for an unrelated reason and found that almost none of it does what the screen appears to be doing. None of it is a bug. All of it is the kind of thing worth knowing before you build one of these.

The clock

The host mock shows a countdown. It starts at 20 and goes to 0, with an s after it:

const timer = Math.max(0, TIME_LIMIT - elapsed)
// …
{`${timer}s`}

TIME_LIMIT is 20. elapsed increments by 1 on an interval:

const t = setInterval(() => {
  setElapsed(p => (p >= TIME_LIMIT ? TIME_LIMIT : p + 1))
}, 500) // faster for demo

Five hundred milliseconds. So the label counts down twenty seconds and twenty seconds take ten.

The comment is honest and the decision is right: nobody is going to watch a marketing page for twenty seconds to see one question close. The part I would not have predicted is that it is completely invisible. I had looked at that section a dozen times without noticing that the seconds were not seconds, because there is nothing on screen to compare it to. Once you know, you can count along with it, and it is obviously wrong, and it still does not matter.

The player mock has its own identical interval, in a different component, with no shared clock between them. They start on different mounts and different phase changes, so on the live page the two countdowns are simply never on the same number, which is the correct outcome: three mocks that pivot on the same beat read as one animation, and three that do not read as three things happening.

The "live" standings are two constants

The host mock's leaderboard reorders itself when a question closes. That is the thing the product actually does, and it is the thing the mock most needs to show.

Here is the whole mechanism:

const POST_Q4_SCORES = INITIAL_SCORES
  .map(e => ({ ...e, score: e.score + (Q4_POINTS[e.name] ?? 0) }))
  .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
  .map((e, i) => ({ ...e, rank: i + 1 }))

That runs once, at module load, before anything is on screen. And the render is:

{(hostPhase === "results" ? POST_Q4_SCORES : INITIAL_SCORES).map(entry => …)}

Two arrays and a ternary. The scoreboard does not recompute, does not accumulate, and does not depend on which question the loop happens to be showing. Question seven produces the identical reshuffle to question four, because there is only one reshuffle in the file.

What the arithmetic produces, once:

before after
1. The Brainwaves 3840 1. The Brainwaves 5180
2. Quiz Khalifa 3510 2. Quiz Khalifa 4690
3. Newton Johns 3200 3. Trivia Pursuit 3840
4. Trivia Pursuit 2890 4. The Know-It-Alls 3530
5. The Know-It-Alls 2650 5. Newton Johns 3200
6. Smarty Pints 2420 6. Smarty Pints 3140
7. Brain Freeze 2180 7. Quiz on My Face 2600
8. Quiz on My Face 1950 8. Brain Freeze 2180

Five of the eight rows move. The top two never do, which is deliberate: a demo where the leader changes reads as a different product claim than the one we make, and a demo where nothing moves shows nothing at all. Two tables score zero on the question, which is what pushes the middle around, and both of them fall. That is the whole dramatic content of the animation and it is eight lines of fixture.

The same two constants drive the third mock, the player's own phone, including the "you moved up" moment. Nothing in any of the three is computed from anything a visitor does.

The counter that looks like events

Above the leaderboard, the host view shows how many tables have answered. It increments as the countdown runs, which is the single most convincing detail in the whole section.

const TABLE_ANSWER_TIMES = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 13, 16, 19]

const answered = hostPhase === "results"
  ? TOTAL_TABLES
  : TABLE_ANSWER_TIMES.filter(s => s <= elapsed).length

Eight tables, eight fixed moments, and the counter is a filter over the clock rather than a queue of anything. The gaps widen towards the end (two, then three) because real rooms do that, and the last table answers at 19 of 20 so the question looks like it is going to time out and then does not. Somebody thought about this for longer than the code suggests.

The part I would change 

const myEntry = POST_Q4_SCORES.find(e => e.name === MY_TABLE)!

MY_TABLE is the string "Table 3, The Brainwaves", declared at the top of the file. POST_Q4_SCORES derives from INITIAL_SCORES, where that same string is typed again. Q4_POINTS is an object keyed by those strings, so it is typed a third time. The lookup is by string equality, and the non-null assertion says "this will be found".

It will be found right up until somebody renames a team in one of the three places and not the others, at which point myEntry is undefined, the ! has told TypeScript not to worry, and the landing page throws during render. A fixture is exactly where that mistake gets made, because fixtures are where you go to change a name to something funnier.

The fix is to key the fixture on an id and derive the display name, or to index the array and let the index be the source of truth. Either is five minutes. Neither has been done, which is why it is in this post.

One small thing that made me laugh

Three of the eight fake teams are real entries from our team name generator: Quiz Khalifa, Smarty Pints and Brain Freeze are all in that pool of 110. A fourth, Trivia Pursuit, is the pool's "Trivia Pursuits" with the s removed, which I assume was a typo and which now looks like a deliberate joke about a team that is only pursuing one thing.

Nobody wired those together. Somebody needed eight plausible pub quiz team names, and the person who needed them had recently written a hundred and ten of them.

Go and watch it

The three mocks are on pub-trivia.app, roughly one screen down. Count the countdown against a real clock and you will see the double speed; watch the leaderboard twice and you will see the same five rows move in the same order. Then look at the live leaderboard page, which is the feature the mock is standing in for and is the thing that actually recomputes.

title: Comment les réseaux DePIN gèrent-ils la vérification physique du matériel déployé (Proof of Physical Work) ?
description:
Rédigé avec l’aide de l’IA

Guide pédagogique crypto

Comprendre « Comment les réseaux DePIN gèrent-ils la vérification physique du matériel déployé (Proof of Physical Work) ? » avec des explications précises, des exemples et des sources vérifiables.

Mis à jour le 17/10/2026

Définition : de quoi parle-t-on ?

Les réseaux DePIN (Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks) sont conçus pour décentraliser la gestion d’infrastructures physiques telles que les stations météo, les relais IoT ou les serveurs edge. Contrairement aux chaînes de blocs traditionnelles qui vérifient uniquement des transactions numériques, ces réseaux intègrent un mécanisme appelé preuve de travail physique. Celui‑ci associe un jeton numérique à un appareil réel, garantissant que le matériel exploité est bien présent, opérationnel et respectueux des règles établies.

À quoi cela sert-il ?

La preuve de travail physique vise à sécuriser la confiance dans les réseaux DePIN. Elle permet aux participants de confirmer que le matériel déployé est réellement en place et fonctionne comme annoncé, ce qui est essentiel pour les services qui dépendent de la disponibilité géographique et de la performance des équipements. En imposant des vérifications physiques, les réseaux réduisent les risques de fraude, améliorent la qualité du service et facilitent la rémunération équitable des opérateurs.

Comment cela fonctionne, étape par étape

  • Déploiement du matériel et inscription Dans un premier temps, le propriétaire du dispositif scanne un code QR unique, qui localise l’équipement et l’enregistre dans le registre distribué. Cette action crée un identifiant numérique lié à l’adresse physique du matériel.

  • Collecte de données de performance Une fois l’appareil activé, des capteurs mesurent en continu la température, la vitesse d’horloge et la consommation énergétique. Ces mesures sont transmises à la blockchain sous forme de paquets cryptés, assurant l’intégrité des données.

  • Vérification indépendante et audit Des vérificateurs tiers, souvent des réseaux de drones ou des caméras autonomes, comparent les données transmises avec des lectures physiques sur place. Si les valeurs concordent, un nonce est ajouté au registre, attestant de la présence réelle du matériel.

  • Rémunération basée sur la preuve Une fois la preuve validée, le protocole distribue des jetons proportionnellement aux heures de fonctionnement et à la qualité mesurée. Ce système incite les opérateurs à maintenir le matériel en bon état et à répondre aux exigences de service.

Exemple concret (scénario fictif)

Imaginons un réseau DePIN de stations météo décentralisées. Un contributeur, Alice, installe une station dans une zone rurale. Pour valider son matériel, elle soumet des données GPS, des photos et des relevés météorologiques. Le réseau utilise un mécanisme de vérification multi-étapes : d'abord, un traitement groupé des données vérifie la cohérence des informations. Ensuite, des nœuds vérificateurs valident la géolocalisation via des satellites. Enfin, un consensus est atteint par vote des participants. Si la station est approuvée, Alice reçoit des jetons en récompense. Un jour, une anomalie est détectée : les données de température divergent des stations voisines. Le réseau déclenche une vérification physique aléatoire. Alice doit fournir une nouvelle preuve, sinon ses jetons sont gelés. Cette approche garantit l'intégrité du réseau tout en incitant les contributeurs à maintenir leur matériel.

Différences et cas d’utilisation

Preuve de travail physique vs. Preuve d'enjeuLa preuve de travail physique exige une vérification matérielle concrète, comme des données GPS ou des capteurs, tandis que la preuve d'enjeu repose sur la possession de jetons pour valider des transactions. La première est adaptée aux réseaux DePIN car elle lie la récompense à une présence physique, alors que la seconde privilégie l'investissement financier.Vérification centralisée vs. DécentraliséeUne vérification centralisée dépend d'une autorité unique pour valider le matériel, ce qui crée un point de défaillance. En revanche, une vérification décentralisée utilise un réseau de participants pour confirmer les données, réduisant les risques de fraude et augmentant la résilience du système.Preuve statique vs. DynamiqueUne preuve statique, comme une photo, peut être falsifiée ou réutilisée. Une preuve dynamique, telle que des données en temps réel ou des capteurs, garantit une vérification continue. Les réseaux DePIN privilégient cette approche pour s'assurer que le matériel reste opérationnel et bien localisé.

Avantages et intérêts possibles

  • Les réseaux DePIN qui utilisent une preuve de travail physique permettent de lier directement la récompense à la présence réelle d’un dispositif, ce qui décourage les acteurs malveillants qui ne pourraient simuler leur participation sans déployer effectivement le matériel requis.

  • En outre, la vérification périodique du fonctionnement du matériel via des capteurs ou des attestations cryptographiques crée un incitatif économique à maintenir les équipements en bon état, améliorant ainsi la fiabilité globale du service rendu aux utilisateurs du réseau.

Inconvénients et limites

  • La mise en œuvre d’une preuve de travail physique exige souvent l’installation de capteurs supplémentaires ou de modules de télémétrie, ce qui augmente le coût initial et la complexité de déploiement pour les petits opérateurs qui pourraient être écartés du réseau.

  • De plus, la dépendance à des mesures physiques externes introduit des points de failure liés à l’environnement (intempéries, vandalisme ou pannes de connectivité) qui peuvent entraîner des pénalités injustes ou des périodes d’indisponibilité non imputables à la mauvaise foi du participant.

Risques réels à connaître

  • La fraude matérielle est un risque majeur : des participants malveillants peuvent simuler la présence d'appareils ou falsifier des données pour obtenir des récompenses indues, compromettant l'intégrité du réseau.

  • Les pannes ou la dégradation du matériel peuvent entraîner une perte de revenus pour les contributeurs, surtout si le réseau ne prévoit pas de mécanismes de compensation ou de maintenance proactive.

  • La centralisation des fournisseurs de matériel peut créer des goulots d'étranglement, augmentant les coûts et limitant l'accès, ce qui va à l'encontre des principes décentralisés des réseaux DePIN.

  • Les attaques de sybil, où un acteur contrôle de multiples identités pour manipuler le réseau, sont plus faciles à exécuter si la vérification physique n'est pas suffisamment robuste.

Comment vérifier concrètement

  • Vérifier l'authenticité des appareils via des signatures matérielles ou des certificats uniques peut aider à prévenir la fraude, mais cela nécessite une infrastructure de suivi fiable.

  • Des audits périodiques par des tiers indépendants peuvent confirmer la présence et le bon fonctionnement des appareils, bien que cela ajoute des coûts et des complexités logistiques.

  • L'utilisation de capteurs intégrés pour surveiller l'état du matériel en temps réel permet une détection rapide des anomalies, mais elle dépend de la qualité et de la sécurité des capteurs.

  • Les mécanismes de réputation ou de pénalités pour les participants malhonnêtes peuvent dissuader les comportements frauduleux, mais ils doivent être équitables et transparents pour éviter les abus.

  • La décentralisation de la vérification via des nœuds multiples réduit les risques de manipulation, mais elle exige une coordination et une synchronisation complexes entre les participants.

Pour aller plus loin

Ces références officielles permettent de recouper les règles et les mises en garde ; elles ne valident pas un projet particulier.

  • AMF — informations et prévention pour les épargnants

  • Définition : Double vérification

  • Débuter en crypto

  • Checklist avant transfert

  • Assistant anti-arnaque

FAQ

Comment la preuve de travail physique diffère-t-elle de la preuve d'enjeu ?La preuve de travail physique vérifie l'existence et le fonctionnement d'un matériel réel, contrairement à la preuve d'enjeu qui se base sur la possession de jetons. Elle exige une validation tangible, souvent via des capteurs ou des signatures numériques, assurant que l'appareil est actif et conforme aux règles du réseau DePIN.

Quels défis pose la vérification décentralisée du matériel ?La vérification décentralisée nécessite un consensus entre les participants, ce qui peut ralentir le processus. De plus, la fiabilité des données dépend de la qualité des capteurs et de la sincérité des contributeurs. Une fraude ou une défaillance technique peut compromettre l'intégrité du réseau.

Pourquoi la preuve dynamique est-elle essentielle dans les réseaux DePIN ?Une preuve dynamique permet une vérification continue de l'état du matériel, contrairement à une preuve statique qui ne garantit qu'un état ponctuel. Cela assure que les appareils restent opérationnels et conformes, même en cas de changements ou de dégradations, renforçant ainsi la confiance dans le réseau.

title: How to Reduce AWS NAT Gateway Costs Without Breaking Outbound Traffic
description:
Start with the traffic path, not the gateway count

A NAT Gateway bill can look disproportionate to the size of your application. A small web service might pull large container images, download packages repeatedly, or move backups through the same outbound path. Reducing compute spend will not necessarily reduce those bytes.

The useful question is: which traffic needs this path, and what would it cost to move that traffic elsewhere? This guide gives you a review you can run before changing production routing. It is narrower than a general AWS bill audit.

Separate the charges before proposing a saving

AWS charges for NAT Gateway availability hours and processed data. Other transfer charges can also apply. Check the rates for your Region and architecture in the AWS NAT Gateway pricing guidance, rather than copying a price from an old tutorial.

Create a small worksheet with one row per gateway and billing period:

  • Owner, environment and Region.
  • Availability hours and their cost.
  • Processed gigabytes and their cost.
  • Associated transfer charges you can identify.
  • Private subnets and applications using the gateway.
  • Proposed replacement path, its running cost and its owner.

Keep credits, discounts and taxes separate. Otherwise a promotional credit disappearing can look like an architectural regression, and a discount can make a poor design look efficient.

Do not add several recommendations for the same traffic together. Moving an S3 download to an endpoint and eliminating that download are competing ways to avoid the same bytes, not two independent savings.

Find the route that the workload actually uses

Start with a read-only inventory. These commands list gateways and route tables in a Region; they do not change your network:

aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --region YOUR_REGION \
  --query 'NatGateways[].{Id:NatGatewayId,Subnet:SubnetId,State:State}'

aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region YOUR_REGION \
  --query 'RouteTables[].{Id:RouteTableId,Associations:Associations,Routes:Routes}'

Match each application subnet to its effective route table, including the VPC main table where there is no explicit association. A diagram from last year is not sufficient evidence. Capture the current route, the intended change and the route you would restore if the test fails.

Use the metrics and network logs already available to investigate major traffic producers. If additional logging is necessary, scope its retention and collection cost first. You do not need to collect every packet indefinitely to decide whether image downloads dominate a development environment's egress.

Evaluate endpoints one service at a time

For supported S3 and DynamoDB access, a gateway endpoint can provide a path without a NAT device. AWS does not charge separately for gateway endpoints. They are associated with selected route tables, so creating one alone does not prove every workload uses it. Check the gateway endpoint documentation for Region, routing and access-policy constraints.

For an interface endpoint, calculate its hourly and data-processing costs across the Availability Zones you need. An endpoint is not automatically cheaper just because its traffic avoids NAT.

A useful comparison is:

net monthly reduction =
  NAT processing charges actually avoided
  + other transfer charges actually avoided
  - new endpoint charges
  - other new recurring charges

For illustration, if an alternative avoids $120 of processing charges but adds $45 of endpoint charges, the gross recurring reduction is $75 before engineering time and other changes. Those are invented worksheet inputs, not AWS rates or a savings promise. Leave NAT availability charges in the baseline if the gateway must remain for other traffic.

Do not exchange resilience for an unexplained discount

Centralizing outbound traffic may reduce gateway hours while changing failure dependencies and transfer costs. Putting a gateway closer to workloads may improve the traffic path while increasing the number of gateways you pay for. Evaluate both the total bill and the failure model.

Likewise, an instance you operate yourself has patching, capacity and recovery work attached. Include that work before calling it a cheaper replacement. A small difference in infrastructure charges can disappear during the first avoidable incident.

Roll out a route change with an acceptance checklist

Choose a non-production workload with representative traffic. Record a baseline, then make one routing or endpoint-policy change through your normal infrastructure review process.

Test the application's ordinary requests, artifact downloads, scheduled jobs, deployment process and recovery path. Check access-denied errors as well as latency and timeouts. A health endpoint can stay green while a nightly export is broken.

Compare similar workload periods after the change. Record actual bytes, costs and errors, rather than declaring success because an endpoint exists. Keep a named rollback owner and the previous configuration until the acceptance window closes.

What to bring to a cost review

Bring an approximate monthly spend, the relevant billing categories and a simple description of the traffic path. Keep credentials, account identifiers and raw customer data out of an introductory booking form.

If you want a second opinion, the free 15-minute AWS cost review is a starting point. We discuss the information you share and send a short recap of areas to investigate. Detailed account analysis and implementation are scoped separately, and the review does not guarantee savings.
