title: Digital Marketing Metrics Made Simple: A Practical Guide to Advertising Calculators
description:
Digital marketing gives businesses many ways to reach their audiences, attract visitors, and generate sales. However, running a campaign is only one part of the process. Understanding its performance is equally important.

Marketers regularly work with impressions, clicks, conversions, advertising costs, and revenue. Without the right calculations, these numbers can be difficult to interpret. This is where digital marketing calculators become useful.

In this guide, we will explore important advertising metrics, explain how to calculate them, and show how marketers can use the results to make better decisions.

Why Are Marketing Calculators Important?

Marketing calculators help turn raw campaign data into meaningful performance indicators. Instead of manually applying formulas every time, marketers can enter their numbers and quickly understand what those numbers mean.

These tools are useful for freelancers, marketing agencies, website owners, ecommerce businesses, content creators, and anyone learning digital advertising.

A reliable advertising calculator can help you compare campaigns, monitor spending, evaluate profitability, and identify opportunities for improvement.

  1. CPM Calculator: Understanding Advertising Costs

CPM stands for cost per mille, or the cost of one thousand ad impressions. It is commonly used in display advertising, video campaigns, and other impression-based advertising models.

Formula:

CPM = (Total Ad Spend ÷ Total Impressions) × 1,000

For example, if you spend $200 to generate 50,000 impressions, your CPM is $4.

A CPM Calculator makes this calculation easier and helps advertisers compare the cost of reaching audiences across different campaigns.

  1. CTR Calculator: Measuring Click-Through Rate

Click-through rate (CTR) measures the percentage of impressions that result in clicks.

Formula:

CTR = (Total Clicks ÷ Total Impressions) × 100

If an advertisement receives 300 clicks from 15,000 impressions, its CTR is 2%.

A CTR Calculator helps marketers evaluate whether their advertisements encourage people to engage. Creative design, audience targeting, messaging, and placement can all influence this metric.

  1. CPA Calculator: Tracking Acquisition Costs

Cost per acquisition (CPA) measures how much a business spends to generate a desired action, such as a purchase, registration, or qualified lead.

Formula:

CPA = Total Campaign Cost ÷ Total Acquisitions

For example, spending $600 to generate 30 acquisitions results in a CPA of $20.

A CPA Calculator helps businesses understand the cost of acquiring customers or leads and evaluate whether their campaigns are meeting their targets.

  1. ROAS Calculator: Evaluating Advertising Revenue

Return on ad spend (ROAS) measures the revenue generated for every unit of advertising expenditure.

Formula:

ROAS = Revenue Attributed to Ads ÷ Advertising Spend

If a campaign generates $2,000 in attributed revenue from $500 in advertising spend, its ROAS is 4x, or 400%.

A ROAS Calculator helps advertisers compare campaign performance and assess how effectively their advertising generates revenue. Remember that ROAS does not account for every business expense, so a strong ROAS does not automatically mean a campaign is profitable.

  1. ROI Calculator: Looking Beyond Ad Spend

Return on investment (ROI) measures the return relative to the investment made. Unlike ROAS, ROI can account for additional costs when calculating profit.

Formula:

ROI = (Net Profit ÷ Total Investment) × 100

Suppose a campaign generates $3,000 in revenue and incurs $2,000 in total costs. Its net profit is $1,000, giving an ROI of 50%.

An ROI Calculator helps businesses evaluate whether their marketing activities deliver sufficient returns after relevant expenses.

  1. RPM Calculator: Measuring Website Monetization

Revenue per mille (RPM) measures estimated revenue per 1,000 units of traffic or content consumption, depending on the metric being used.

For publishers, page RPM commonly measures revenue per 1,000 pageviews.

Formula:

Page RPM = (Estimated Revenue ÷ Total Pageviews) × 1,000

If a website earns $120 from 30,000 pageviews, its page RPM is $4.

A page RPM Calculator helps bloggers, publishers, and website owners compare monetization performance across different periods or sections of a website.

  1. LTV Calculator: Estimating Customer Lifetime Value

Customer lifetime value (LTV) estimates the value a customer generates throughout their relationship with a business.

The appropriate formula depends on the business model. For a simple subscription business, one estimate is:

LTV = Average Revenue per Customer per Period × Gross Margin × Average Customer Lifetime in Periods

For example, a customer generating $40 in monthly revenue, with a 75% gross margin and an average lifetime of 12 months, has an estimated gross-profit LTV of $360.

An LTV Calculator helps businesses understand long-term customer value and make more informed acquisition and retention decisions.

  1. CAC Calculator: Calculating Customer Acquisition Cost

Customer acquisition cost (CAC) measures the average cost of acquiring a new customer.

Formula:

CAC = Total Acquisition Costs ÷ Number of New Customers Acquired

If a business spends $1,500 on sales and marketing and acquires 50 new customers, its CAC is $30.

A CAC Calculator can help businesses compare acquisition costs across channels and evaluate whether their customer growth strategy is sustainable.

  1. Conversion Rate Calculator: Measuring Desired Actions

Conversion rate measures the percentage of visitors or users who complete a desired action.

Formula:

Conversion Rate = (Number of Conversions ÷ Total Visitors or Eligible Sessions) × 100

If 80 out of 2,000 visitors complete a purchase, the conversion rate is 4%.

A Conversion Rate Calculator helps marketers assess landing pages, sales funnels, signup forms, and advertising campaigns. Always use a consistent denominator when comparing results.

  1. Ad Frequency Calculator: Understanding Audience Exposure

Ad frequency describes how often people see an advertisement on average.

Formula:

Average Ad Frequency = Total Impressions ÷ Unique Reach

For example, 40,000 impressions delivered to 10,000 unique people produce an average frequency of 4.

An ad frequency calculator can help marketers understand audience exposure and investigate whether repeated impressions are contributing to results or creating advertising fatigue. The ideal frequency depends on the campaign, audience, platform, and objective. https://adcalculatorhub.com/

Choosing the Right Digital Marketing Calculator

Different campaigns require different measurements. Awareness campaigns often focus on CPM and reach, while performance campaigns may prioritize CTR, CPA, and conversion rate. Ecommerce businesses frequently compare ROAS with ROI, while publishers monitor page RPM.

Growth teams can combine CAC and LTV to understand customer economics.

Using several marketing calculators together provides a more complete picture than relying on a single metric. For example, a campaign may achieve an excellent CTR but still produce few sales. Reviewing its conversion rate and CPA can help reveal where improvements are needed.

Explore Practical Advertising Calculation Tools

If you want to calculate these metrics without repeatedly working through formulas, Ad Calculator Hub provides free online tools for common advertising, marketing, and monetization calculations.

You can explore its CPM Calculator, CTR Calculator, CPA Calculator, ROAS Calculator, ROI Calculator, RPM Calculator, LTV Calculator, CAC Calculator, and Conversion Rate Calculator.

Whether you are searching for a digital marketing calculator, marketing calculators, an ad calculator, an advertising calculator, a page RPM calculator, or calculator ads resources, choosing tools with clear formulas can make performance analysis easier. You may also encounter names such as AdRateHub when researching advertising tools; compare each resource based on its functionality and accuracy.

title: Why DeepSeek’s Flash 1017 Lets You Run a 1 M‑Token AI on One GPU – The Future of On‑Prem LLMs
description:
DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 1017 – Why the “million‑token” LLM finally feels affordable

The Lead

“A 1 M‑token context used to cost a data‑center the price of a small‑car loan.”

When DeepSeek unveiled v4.1‑Flash 1017 on September 17, 2026, the headline sparked more than a few skeptical comments on Hacker News. The claim sounded almost mythical: a 284‑billion‑parameter transformer that can remember an entire novel‑length document and fit into the memory budget of a single A100 GPU.

Two weeks later, the model’s public API, the accompanying arXiv paper (2609.19969), and a handful of early‑stage deployments proved the hype wrong. Flash 1017 does not rewrite the physics of transformer scaling, but it re‑engineers the memory bottleneck that has held back long‑context applications for years. The result? A model that delivers near‑state‑of‑the‑art reasoning while slashing both compute cost and hardware footprint.

Below, I break down the technical underpinnings, benchmark results, and real‑world use cases that make Flash 1017 the most compelling “middle‑ground” LLM on the market today.

The Case Study: One‑Shot Legal Review on a Single A100

Imagine a midsize law firm that wants to run an internal “contract‑assistant” without sending confidential PDFs to a cloud provider. The firm’s hardware budget includes a single NVIDIA A100‑40GB GPU.

Step 1 – Load the model

Using DeepSeek’s open‑source “Harness” runtime, the team loads the Flash‑13B sub‑model (the activated slice of the 284 B‑parameter network). The loading step consumes ~12 GB of VRAM, leaving 28 GB for KV‑cache.

Step 2 – Ingest the contract

The assistant reads a 300‑page commercial lease (≈ 750 k tokens). Because Flash 1017 compresses the KV‑cache to 0.12 GB per k tokens, the entire document fits comfortably:

KV‑cache size = 750 k × 0.12 GB/k ≈ 90 GB → compressed to ~10 GB after the hybrid sparse‑plus‑quantized pipeline, well within the remaining GPU memory.

Step 3 – Query

The lawyer asks, “What termination clauses could the landlord invoke under a force‑majeure event?” The model generates a concise answer in ≈ 2 s (256‑token chunk) while still retaining the full lease context for follow‑up questions.

Result

The firm processes a full‑document review in under a minute, pays $0.001 per 1 k generated tokens, and keeps all data on‑prem. No multi‑GPU cluster, no external API latency, and no compromise on accuracy (the model scores 71.2 % on MMLU, comparable to GPT‑4‑Turbo).

This scenario illustrates the core value proposition of Flash 1017: million‑token context + GPU‑friendly memory enables on‑premise, single‑GPU deployments that were previously impossible.

The Meat: Hard Numbers and Technical Deep‑Dive

1. Architecture at a Glance

Component Description
Total parameters 284 B (sparse Mixture‑of‑Experts)
Activated parameters per token 13 B (Flash‑13B)
KV‑cache compression Hybrid Sparse + Quantized Attention (HSQ‑A)
Context length 1 M tokens (full model)
Inference engine DeepSeek “Harness” runtime + optional TensorRT‑accelerated kernels

DeepSeek engineers built HSQ‑A by fusing two ideas that appeared separately in 2024 papers: (1) sparse attention maps that prune low‑impact keys, and (2) FP8 quantization of the remaining values. The pipeline first identifies a 15 % “high‑impact” subset of keys using a lightweight scoring network, then stores those keys in FP8 format while discarding the rest. The net effect reduces the per‑token cache from the typical 0.8 GB/k (for a dense 70 B model) to 0.12 GB/k, an 85 % compression ratio.

2. Benchmark Overview

Metric DeepSeek V4.1‑Flash 1017 DeepSeek V4‑Pro (49 B) OpenAI GPT‑4‑Turbo Meta Llama‑3‑70B
Activated parameters 13 B 49 B 100 B (est.) 70 B
Context length 1 M tokens 1 M tokens (sparse) 128 k tokens 64 k tokens
KV‑cache footprint 0.12 GB/k 0.25 GB/k 0.30 GB/k 0.28 GB/k
Throughput (tokens/s) – 1 A100 45 (13 B sub‑model) 28 38 32
Zero‑shot MMLU (dev) 71.2 % 73.5 % 71.8 % 68.4 %
LongBench QA (top‑5) 68.9 % 66.1 % 62.3 % 60.7 %
Power per 1 M‑token 0.42 kWh 0.62 kWh 0.55 kWh 0.58 kWh
Speculative decoding speed‑up 2.3× 1.9× 2.0× 1.7×

Key takeaway: Flash 1017 outpaces GPT‑4‑Turbo on raw throughput while staying within 0.6 % of its accuracy on standard reasoning benchmarks.

3. Cost Model

Free tier: 100 k tokens/month → perfect for academic prototyping.

Pay‑as‑you‑go: $0.001 per 1 k generated tokens → 30 % cheaper than DeepSeek’s V4‑Pro tier.

Assuming a 10 M‑token monthly workload (typical for a small‑to‑mid enterprise chatbot), the bill lands at $10—well below the $15‑$20 range many SaaS LLM providers charge for comparable throughput.

4. Speculative Decoding Synergy

Flash 1017 doubles as a draft model for larger MoE systems. In a mixed‑precision pipeline, Flash‑13B generates a provisional token sequence, after which the full 284 B model validates or revises each token. The arXiv “SpecDec‑Hybrid” paper (2608.03447) reports a 2.3× wall‑clock speedup on a 4‑GPU node, cutting latency for long‑form generation from 12 s to ~5 s for a 2 k‑token output.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

Risk Why it matters Mitigation
Cache‑compression artifacts Aggressive pruning may drop subtle long‑range dependencies, especially in code or formal logic. Run a secondary “verification pass” with the full‑model MoE on critical sections; DeepSeek already provides an API flag (verify=true).
Hardware lock‑in DeepSeek’s “Harness” runtime optimizes for A100‑class GPUs; performance drops on older GPUs. Use the FP8‑quantized CPU path for batch‑size ≤ 4; expect ~2 s latency per 256‑token chunk—acceptable for non‑real‑time workloads.
Pricing volatility Pay‑as‑you‑go rates could rise if demand spikes. Negotiate enterprise licences with on‑prem KV‑cache licensing; the model’s weight file remains free under an Apache‑2.0 license.
Ecosystem maturity Tooling for 1 M‑token prompts still evolves (e.g., tokenizers, streaming APIs). Leverage DeepSeek’s open‑source “Search‑API‑Flash” wrapper, which streams tokens and automatically manages cache eviction.

None of these issues invalidate Flash 1017’s core advantage, but they shape the adoption curve. Early adopters who pair the model with robust token‑management pipelines reap the biggest gains.

The Outlook: Where Long‑Context LLMs Go Next

  1. Unified knowledge graphs – By feeding an entire corporate knowledge base (1 M + tokens) into a single prompt, enterprises can replace multi‑step retrieval pipelines with a single inference pass. The compression technique that powers Flash 1017 will likely become a standard layer in future open‑source frameworks (e.g., Hugging Face’s “kv‑compress” module).

  2. Autonomous agents with multi‑day memory – Reinforcement‑learning‑from‑human‑feedback (RLHF) agents currently reset after a few thousand tokens. Flash 1017’s million‑token window lets an agent retain the full history of a planning episode, opening research avenues in supply‑chain optimization and long‑horizon scientific discovery.

  3. On‑premise generative AI for regulated industries – Financial services, healthcare, and legal sectors demand data residency. Flash 1017’s single‑GPU footprint satisfies both compliance and cost constraints, nudging these sectors away from “black‑box” SaaS offerings.

  4. Hybrid MoE ecosystems – The speculative decoding benchmark proves that a small, fast “draft” model can coexist with a gigantic “review” model. Expect to see more modular pipelines where Flash‑13B acts as the front‑line, while a 1 T‑parameter specialist refines outputs for niche domains (e.g., scientific literature synthesis).

Closing Thoughts

DeepSeek’s v4.1‑Flash 1017 does not overturn transformer theory; it sidesteps the memory wall that has hamstrung long‑context LLMs for the past three years. By compressing the KV‑cache by 85 %, activating only a 13 B slice per token, and exposing a low‑cost API, Flash 1017 delivers a practical, affordable path to million‑token reasoning.

The model’s benchmark performance proves the engineering trade‑offs are sound: throughput surpasses GPT‑4‑Turbo, power consumption drops by a third, and accuracy remains within a hair’s breadth of the flagship V4‑Pro. Real‑world pilots—legal‑tech firms, enterprise search platforms, and autonomous‑agent labs—already showcase tangible productivity gains.

If the AI community can keep refining compression pipelines, we may soon see 10 M‑token contexts running on a single GPU, turning today’s “large‑context” projects into tomorrow’s standard workflow. Flash 1017 marks the first solid step on that road.

title: AWS IAM mistakes teams keep making
description:
Most AWS security incidents do not start with an exotic exploit. They start with an over-broad policy, a key that was never rotated or a role that trusts more than it should, each created because it was the fastest way to make something work. Here are the IAM mistakes that recur most often, what to do instead, and how to check that the fix held.

1. Wildcards in actions and resources 

{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" }

That is administrator access. Less obvious variants are s3:* on every bucket, or ec2:* for a pipeline that only starts and stops instances. Name the actions and narrow the resource:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/uploads/*"
}

Object-level actions such as s3:GetObject apply to the object ARN (bucket/prefix/*), while s3:ListBucket applies to the bucket ARN - mixing these up is a common reason a "tight" policy fails and someone swaps in a wildcard. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from CloudTrail activity; test it, and don't treat the first working policy as the final one.

2. Long-lived access keys

A leaked key keeps working until someone notices. Prefer temporary credentials:

  • Workloads on AWS: instance profiles, ECS task roles, or a Kubernetes service account mapped to a role.
  • CI/CD: OpenID Connect federation (sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity) - no stored key.
  • People: federated sign-in through IAM Identity Center.

Audit what's left with aws iam generate-credential-report and aws iam get-credential-report.

3. Loose trust policies

Trusting arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root trusts the whole account. Name the specific role instead, use sts:ExternalId for third parties, and for GitHub Actions OIDC roles always restrict the sub claim:

"Condition": {
  "StringEquals": {
    "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
    "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main"
  }
}

4. Unrestricted iam:PassRole

iam:PassRole on "Resource": "*" lets a user hand compute a more powerful role than their own. Restrict it to specific role ARNs and add the iam:PassedToService condition. Treat iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachUserPolicy and iam:PutRolePolicy the same way.

5. No guardrails above individual policies

Permissions boundaries cap what a role's policies can grant; SCPs cap whole accounts; an explicit deny anywhere wins. Effective permissions are the intersection.

6. Shared users and unused identities

Shared logins destroy auditability. Use last-accessed data or Access Analyzer's unused-access findings to remove old users, roles and keys. The root user: MFA, no access keys, rarely used.

7. Skipping MFA and visibility

Require MFA (passkeys or security keys where you can), keep CloudTrail logs somewhere workload roles can't delete, and review Access Analyzer findings.

A quick audit for this week

  • Find policies with "Action": "*" or "Resource": "*" and justify each.
  • Generate a credential report; delete or rotate old keys.
  • Read the trust policy of every role assumable from outside the account.
  • List who holds iam:PassRole and IAM-write permissions.
  • Move one CI pipeline from a stored key to OIDC.

Want to see how well this sticks? I put together a free 10-question AWS skills check - scenario questions with an explanation for every answer, no sign-up: braintally.com/technical-assessments/aws/check

Originally published on BrainTally.

title: Reserve image space on your landing page so the button does not jump: a layout shift check
description:
You open a landing page on your phone, start to tap "Get started", and the button jumps down because an image above it finished loading. That is a layout shift, and the usual cause on a marketing page is an image with no reserved space.

What the sources say

web.dev's guidance on optimizing Cumulative Layout Shift says to always include width and height size attributes on image and video elements. The alternative is to reserve the space with CSS aspect-ratio or something similar. That lets the browser allocate the right amount of space while the image is still loading.

web.dev also gives the target: a good CLS score is 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads, and anything above 0.25 is poor. A shift score is the share of the viewport that moved multiplied by how far it moved, so a hero image pushing the whole page down counts a lot.

The check

  1. Find the images above the fold: hero, logo strip, screenshots.
  2. Make sure each <img> has width and height set to the file's real pixel size, for example <img src="hero.png" alt="..." width="1200" height="800">.
  3. Keep your CSS responsive with img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }. The attributes give the browser the ratio, and CSS still controls the display size.
  4. For embeds and video, use aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 on the container so the space exists before the content does.
  5. Throttle the network in browser dev tools, reload, and watch whether any text or button moves while images arrive.

What this does not cover

Missing image sizes are one cause of layout shift. Web fonts swapping, banners injected late, and ads can also move content. This is a quick check, not a full performance audit, and your real score depends on your own pages and visitors.

Source: web.dev, Optimize Cumulative Layout Shift and web.dev, Cumulative Layout Shift

title: 🔥 30 Days of Frontend — Day 5: React DevTools Profiler
description:
When a React application starts feeling slow, one of the first things developers often do is reach for useMemo, useCallback, or React.memo.

We've all seen this pattern:

  • A component renders more often than expected.
  • The UI feels sluggish when interacting with a page.
  • A large list becomes noticeably slower as more items are added.
  • Updating one piece of state seems to trigger work across an entire component tree.

The natural reaction is to start memoizing components and functions.

But here's the problem: you might be optimizing code that isn't responsible for the slowdown in the first place.

React performance optimization should start with understanding what is happening, not guessing what might be happening.

That's where the React DevTools Profiler becomes useful.

1. What Is the React DevTools Profiler?

React DevTools is a browser extension that helps developers inspect React component trees, props, state, and other component-related information.

It includes two particularly useful panels:

  • Components: Inspect the component hierarchy, props, state, and component details.
  • Profiler: Record rendering activity and investigate how React updated the component tree.

The Profiler helps you understand the rendering work associated with a particular interaction.

For example, imagine you're working on an e-commerce application with a product grid containing hundreds of products.

When a user changes a filter, several things might happen:

  • The parent component updates.
  • The product list renders again.
  • Individual product cards render.
  • Sorting or filtering calculations run.
  • Some components render even though their visible data hasn't changed.

Some of this work might be necessary. Some might be avoidable.

Instead of assuming which component is responsible, you can record the interaction and inspect the results.

The goal isn't to eliminate every render. It's to understand whether the work is necessary and whether it affects the user experience.

2. Understanding How React Rendering Relates to Profiling

Before opening the Profiler, it's worth understanding what it actually measures.

A React update generally involves two important phases.

The render phase

During the render phase, React calls components as needed to determine what the next UI should look like.

This phase includes calculating the next React element tree and determining the changes required.

A component rendering doesn't automatically mean that the browser DOM will change.

For example:

function Counter({ count }) {
  console.log("Counter rendered");

  return <p>Count: {count}</p>;
}

Whenever React calls Counter, the component function executes and returns a React element describing the UI.

React may then determine that the resulting output doesn't require a DOM mutation.

A render is not the same thing as a DOM update.

This distinction is important because developers sometimes interpret every component render as expensive browser work.

The commit phase

After React finishes the necessary render work, it can commit the changes to the host environment, such as updating the DOM in a browser.

The Profiler helps you investigate rendering activity, but its measurements shouldn't be interpreted as a complete measurement of every part of browser performance.

For example, a page can have relatively inexpensive React rendering but still feel slow because of:

  • Expensive JavaScript outside React.
  • Large amounts of DOM layout or painting.
  • Long-running event handlers.
  • Network delays.
  • Large images or other resources.
  • Main-thread work that blocks user interactions.

This is why the React Profiler is one tool in a broader performance investigation, not a replacement for the browser's Performance panel.

3. What Can You Learn From the Profiler?

When you record a profiling session, the Profiler provides several useful ways to understand React's work.

A. Which components rendered?

The Profiler helps you identify the components involved in an update.

Suppose your component tree looks like this:

App
├── Header
├── SearchBar
├── FilterSidebar
└── ProductGrid
    ├── ProductCard
    ├── ProductCard
    ├── ProductCard
    └── ...

When the user types into the search field, you might discover that SearchBar, ProductGrid, and many ProductCard instances rendered.

That doesn't automatically mean all those renders are unnecessary.

You need to understand why they rendered and whether the work was expensive.

The component tree gives you a starting point for that investigation.

B. How often did components render?

Repeated rendering can be perfectly normal.

For example, typing into a controlled input typically updates state as the user types:

function SearchBar() {
  const [query, setQuery] = React.useState("");

  return (
    <input
      value={query}
      onChange={(event) => {
        setQuery(event.target.value);
      }}
      placeholder="Search products..."
    />
  );
}

Each keystroke can trigger an update.

That's expected behavior.

The more interesting question is what else happens during those updates.

If typing into the search field also triggers expensive calculations or unnecessary rendering across a large product grid, the Profiler can help you investigate that work.

Render frequency is a clue, not a performance verdict.

C. What caused a component to render?

This is one of the most useful parts of profiling.

A component might render because:

  • Its state changed.
  • Its parent rendered.
  • Its props changed.
  • Its context value changed.
  • An external store or another subscription triggered an update.

The exact cause depends on the component and the update mechanism.

For example:

function ProductPage() {
  const [query, setQuery] = React.useState("");
  const [selectedCategory, setSelectedCategory] =
    React.useState("all");

  return (
    <>
      <SearchInput
        value={query}
        onChange={setQuery}
      />

      <CategoryFilter
        value={selectedCategory}
        onChange={setSelectedCategory}
      />

      <ProductGrid query={query} />
    </>
  );
}

When selectedCategory changes, ProductPage renders again.

Because ProductGrid is a child of ProductPage, React may also render ProductGrid, even though its query prop hasn't changed.

That can be a candidate for optimization, but it isn't automatically a problem. First, determine whether the work is expensive enough to matter.

Also, remember that React DevTools' ability to display detailed render reasons depends on the React version, development tooling, and available settings. Don't assume every render will always have a definitive explanation displayed.

4. How to Use React DevTools Profiler: A Step-by-Step Workflow

Let's turn this into a practical workflow.

Step 1: Reproduce the actual performance problem

Start with the user interaction that feels slow.

Examples include:

  • Typing into a search field.
  • Changing a product filter.
  • Switching tabs.
  • Expanding a large navigation menu.
  • Updating a dashboard with multiple charts.
  • Scrolling through a long list.

Avoid profiling random interactions without a clear question.

A useful starting question might be:

Why does changing a product filter cause so much rendering work?

This gives you a specific behavior to investigate.

Step 2: Open React DevTools

Install React Developer Tools for your browser if you haven't already.

Open your application, launch the browser's developer tools, and locate the Profiler tab.

Make sure you're profiling the application and interaction you want to investigate.

For realistic performance measurements, prefer a production build or a profiling-enabled production build where appropriate. Development mode can introduce extra overhead, and Strict Mode may intentionally invoke rendering-related logic more than once to help reveal bugs.

Development profiling is still valuable for understanding component behavior, but don't assume its timings represent production performance.

Step 3: Start recording

In the Profiler tab, start a recording.

Then perform the exact interaction that causes the slowdown.

For example:

  1. Start recording.
  2. Type a search query.
  3. Change a category filter.
  4. Wait for the UI to settle.
  5. Stop recording.

Keep the recording focused.

Step 4: Inspect the recorded commits

The Profiler organizes recorded updates into commits.

A commit represents a point at which React applied an update to the host environment

Select a commit related to your interaction, then inspect the available visualization and component details.

Look for patterns such as:

  • A large subtree rendering during a small interaction.
  • An expensive component repeatedly appearing in relevant commits.
  • Components rendering even though their inputs appear unchanged.
  • Expensive calculations associated with frequently occurring updates.

Don't immediately optimize the component with the largest-looking bar. First establish what the measurement represents and whether that component is related to the user-visible problem.

Step 5: Make one targeted change

Change one thing at a time whenever possible.

If you simultaneously add React.memo, introduce several useMemo calls, restructure the component tree, and change how state is managed, you won't know which change made the difference.

A focused experiment makes the results easier to interpret.

Step 6: Profile again

Repeat the same interaction under comparable conditions.

Compare:

  • Actual rendering duration.
  • Which components rendered.
  • How much of the subtree participated in the update.
  • Whether the interaction feels more responsive.
  • Whether the optimization introduced additional complexity or bugs.

If the measured React work decreased but the interaction still feels slow, investigate other parts of the performance pipeline.

An optimization isn't complete until you've verified its effect.

The React DevTools Profiler helps turn vague performance complaints into concrete questions about rendering behavior.

Instead of asking:

"Why is React so slow?"

Start by asking:

"Where is my application actually spending time, and what evidence do I have?"

That shift—from guessing to measuring—is what makes performance optimization more systematic.

title: Give your eve agent a browser
description:
Your eve agent can now navigate the web like a human with agent-browser.

The @agent-browser/eve extension gives any eve agent a full set of browser tools: navigate pages, read content, click, fill forms, take screenshots, and inspect console and network activity. Everything runs inside the agent's sandbox.

Install the extension:

Then mount it under agent/extensions/:

Your agent gets namespaced tools like browser__navigate, browser__snapshot, browser__click, browser__fill, and browser__screenshot. Snapshot refs such as [ref=e12] become @e12 selectors, so the agent can inspect a page, then act on exactly what it saw.

The extension includes:

  • Sandbox isolation: Chromium and agent-browser run in the eve sandbox, not your app. Pre-install them in your sandbox template so sessions start warm, or let the extension install them on first use.

  • Domain allowlist: Restrict navigation and subresources with allowedDomains, and control output size, screenshot handling, proxy use, and session naming through extension options.

  • Credential protection: Cookie, storage, and saved-auth-state commands are never exposed to the model. Use eve extension overrides to disable tools, require approvals, or add app-specific guarded tools.

title: AsyncLocalStorage vs Scope.REQUEST in NestJS: Fixing a Multi-Tenant Data Leak Without Killing Performance
description:
A while ago in a high-scale multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform, we ran a high-concurrency benchmark before launching an enterprise data portal.

Everything looked solid on paper — modular NestJS architecture, TypeScript type safety, PostgreSQL connection pooling tuned.

Then we saw something that gave every backend engineer in the room chills:

Under concurrent load, Tenant A's dashboard occasionally displayed cached data belonging to Tenant B.

In a multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform handling sensitive enterprise metrics, cross-tenant data leakage is a tier-0 catastrophe.

Here is the exact autopsy of how default NestJS scoping caused the leak, why the classic Scope.REQUEST fix nearly cratered our API performance, and how we solved it cleanly using Node.js AsyncLocalStorage.

1. The Root Cause: The Singleton Trap

By default in NestJS, every provider is a Singleton.

NestJS instantiates your service once during application bootstrap. Every incoming HTTP request shares the exact same class instance.

In our codebase, a developer had created a TenantContextService to hold the currently authenticated tenant:

// DANGEROUS: Singleton service storing request-specific state
@Injectable()
export class TenantContextService {
  private tenantId: string;

  setTenantId(id: string) {
    this.tenantId = id;
  }

  getTenantId(): string {
    return this.tenantId;
  }
}

In a sequential test environment, this works fine. Request 1 sets the ID, queries the DB, finishes.

But Node.js is an event-driven, single-threaded asynchronous runtime.

When Request 1 (Tenant A) awaits a slow database query, the event loop picks up Request 2 (Tenant B). Request 2 overwrites this.tenantId = 'tenant_b'.

When Request 1 resumes execution after its await, this.getTenantId() now returns 'tenant_b'.

Tenant A just queried Tenant B's data.

2. The Naive Fix: Scope.REQUEST (And Why It Almost Killed Us)

The official NestJS documentation mentions that if a service needs request-specific data, you can make it Request-scoped:

// DANGEROUS AT SCALE: Request-scoped provider
@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })
export class TenantContextService {
  private tenantId: string;
  // ...
}

While this isolates the state per HTTP request, it triggers a massive cascading effect across your entire dependency injection tree:

  1. Bubble-Up Effect: Any Singleton service that injects TenantContextService automatically becomes Request-scoped.
  2. Object Creation Overhead: If your controller injects 5 services that cascade into Request scope, NestJS must instantiate hundreds of class instances for every single incoming HTTP request.
  3. Garbage Collection Pressure: Under 1,000 requests per second, V8 garbage collection spikes trying to clean up thousands of short-lived transient objects.
  4. Latency Degradation: In our load tests, p99 API latency jumped from 35ms to over 210ms, and memory usage tripled.

Scope.REQUEST traded a data leak for severe latency and CPU starvation. We needed a better way.

3. The Real Solution: Node.js AsyncLocalStorage

Node.js introduced AsyncLocalStorage (ALS) in the async_hooks module to allow storing data throughout the lifetime of a web request across asynchronous continuations — without passing it as function arguments and without instantiating new service classes.

In NestJS, the battle-tested library nestjs-cls wraps AsyncLocalStorage into an idiomatic, blazing-fast module.

Here is the exact architecture we implemented:

Step 1: Register the CLS Module 

// app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ClsModule } from 'nestjs-cls';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ClsModule.forRoot({
      global: true,
      middleware: {
        mount: true, // Automatically creates ALS context per request
        setup: (cls, req) => {
          // Extract tenant ID from JWT or header cleanly
          const tenantId = req.headers['x-tenant-id'] || req.user?.tenantId;
          cls.set('TENANT_ID', tenantId);
        },
      },
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

Step 2: Access Tenant Context Inside Any Singleton Service

Notice that UserRepository remains a standard, high-performance Singleton:

// user.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ClsService } from 'nestjs-cls';

@Injectable()
export class UserRepository {
  constructor(
    private readonly cls: ClsService,
    private readonly db: DatabaseService,
  ) {}

  async findUsers() {
    // Isolated per request via AsyncLocalStorage
    const currentTenantId = this.cls.get<string>('TENANT_ID');

    return this.db.query(
      `SELECT * FROM users WHERE tenant_id = $1`,
      [currentTenantId],
    );
  }
}

The Performance Difference:

  • Services remain Singletons: Initialized once at startup.
  • Zero GC spikes: V8 does not allocate or deallocate class trees per request.
  • Strict tenant boundary: No cross-contamination between concurrent asynchronous promises.
  • Latency: Dropped right back down to 34ms (p99) under heavy load.

4. The Failing Test That Protects Us in CI

To ensure this bug could never silently re-enter our codebase, we wrote a concurrent stress test using Promise.all:

it('should maintain strict tenant isolation under concurrent load', async () => {
  const runRequest = async (tenantId: string) => {
    return request(app.getHttpServer())
      .get('/api/v1/users')
      .set('x-tenant-id', tenantId);
  };

  // Fire 100 simultaneous requests interleaved across 2 tenants
  const requests = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) => 
    runRequest(i % 2 === 0 ? 'tenant_alpha' : 'tenant_beta')
  );

  const responses = await Promise.all(requests);

  responses.forEach((res, index) => {
    const expectedTenant = index % 2 === 0 ? 'tenant_alpha' : 'tenant_beta';
    expect(res.body.tenantId).toBe(expectedTenant);
  });
});

If any service accidentally mutates a shared state, this test fails in CI before code ever touches staging.

Summary Cheat Sheet

Feature Singleton Scope Scope.REQUEST AsyncLocalStorage (CLS)
Instance Creation Once at boot Every single request Once at boot
Memory Footprint Extremely Low High (GC pressure) Extremely Low
Tenant Isolation Leaks state Safe Safe
Performance Impact Blazing fast 3x-5x latency hit Negligible (~1ms)
Production Ready For stateless code Rarely recommended Industry Standard

Enjoyed this breakdown?

title: I Gave an EC2 Instance Zero Internet and It Still Uploaded to S3
description:
The challenge

The client's requirement fit in one sentence:

The private backend must talk to Amazon S3 without ever touching the public internet.

The environment had two VPCs:

  • A custom VPC with a private EC2 instance. It had no Internet Gateway and no NAT Gateway.
  • A default VPC with a public-facing EC2 instance acting as a bastion (jump host).

The plan was to SSH into the bastion, hop to the private machine, and run aws s3 cp from there while keeping every packet on the AWS network. That took five pieces working together: VPC Peering, route tables, security groups, an IAM role and an S3 Gateway Endpoint.

![Full architecture: default VPC with bastion, custom VPC with private EC2, peering link, IAM role and S3 Gateway Endpoint]

The diagram above is the whole design. The rest of this post builds it one layer at a time and shows where each layer can fail.

The roadblocks

1. There was no road out.
With no IGW and no NAT, the private subnet has no default route. Any call to the S3 public endpoint just hangs until it times out.

2. Peering is easy to create and easy to get wrong.
A VPC Peering connection (pcx-...) is only a handshake. Traffic flows only when both route tables point at it. My first ping test looked like this:

$ ping 172.31.22.46
8 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 7274ms

A common cause of this is a one-sided route. The request reaches the target, but the reply has no route back, so ping reports nothing received.

3. Locking down security groups without locking yourself out.
Both instances started with 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH and ICMP, and the console warns about this for good reason. Replacing those rules with /32 entries means one typo can cut off your own access, so the order of changes matters.

4. Credentials.
Running aws configure and pasting access keys onto an EC2 instance is exactly what a secure design should avoid.

The implementation

Step 1: Create and accept the VPC Peering connection

Request the connection from one VPC and accept it from the other. It is not active until accepted, and that step is easy to forget.

Step 2: Build symmetric route tables

This was the fix for the 100% packet loss. Each side needs a route to the other:

Route table Destination Target
Custom VPC (private route table) Default VPC CIDR pcx-xxxxxxxx
Default VPC (main route table) Custom VPC CIDR pcx-xxxxxxxx

Edit the route table that is actually associated with the subnet. Across two VPCs there are several route tables, including main tables with no explicit associations, so it is easy to edit the wrong one.

Step 3: Harden security groups to a /32 micro-perimeter

Each instance accepts SSH (22) and ICMP only from the other instance's exact private IP:

  • Private instance SG: allow from <bastion-private-ip>/32
  • Bastion SG: allow from <private-instance-ip>/32

Do this after peering and routing are confirmed working, and keep one SSH session open while you change the rules. Use private IPs here. Traffic across the peering connection arrives from the peer's private address, not its public one.

Step 4: Attach an IAM role instead of access keys

Create an IAM role for EC2 with S3 permissions and attach it to the private instance as an instance profile. The AWS CLI picks up temporary credentials from the instance metadata service automatically, so there is nothing to leak.

I used AmazonS3FullAccess to validate the architecture. For production, scope it down:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-BUCKET"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-BUCKET/*"
    }
  ]
}

Step 5: Deploy an S3 Gateway Endpoint

In VPC console > Endpoints, search for the S3 service and choose the Gateway type: com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3. Associate it with the private subnet's route table.

AWS adds a route that sends S3 traffic (via a managed prefix list) to the endpoint, so S3 requests stay on the AWS network. The bucket must be in the same Region as the endpoint.

Where a request can fail, hop by hop

Each hop has its own checks and its own symptom. This map helped me debug faster than guessing:

![Hop-by-hop map from laptop to S3 showing the checks that must pass at each hop and the symptom when one fails]

A short rule of thumb:

  • Timeout or 100% packet loss means a network problem: peering, routes or security groups.
  • AccessDenied (403) means an identity problem: the role policy or bucket policy.
  • Unable to locate credentials means no IAM role is attached to the instance.

The outcome

Once the routes were symmetric, the same ping that had failed worked immediately:

$ ping 172.31.22.46
64 bytes from 172.31.22.46: icmp_seq=1 ttl=127 time=0.877 ms
64 bytes from 172.31.22.46: icmp_seq=2 ttl=127 time=0.508 ms
...
6 packets transmitted, 6 received, 0% packet loss
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.490/0.564/0.877/0.139 ms

![Before and after ping: 100% packet loss with one-sided routes versus 0% packet loss with symmetric routes]

Sub-millisecond latency and 0% packet loss confirmed the peering was healthy. Then the real test, from the private instance:

$ aws s3 ls
2026-10-17 08:02:05 your-bucket-name

$ echo 'this is my first private machine upload' > test.txt
$ aws s3 cp test.txt s3://your-bucket-name/
upload: ./test.txt to s3://your-bucket-name/test.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://your-bucket-name/
2026-10-17 08:04:59         75 test.txt

The CLI listed buckets and uploaded the file. Authentication came from the IAM role, and the request was routed through the Gateway Endpoint.

What the design delivers:

  • No static credentials anywhere. Temporary role credentials only.
  • A tiny attack surface. SSH and ICMP are allowed only between two exact private IPs.
  • A private S3 path. Traffic to S3 stays on the AWS network instead of crossing the public internet.
  • Lower cost. Gateway Endpoints for S3 carry no additional endpoint charge, unlike Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink), which bill hourly and per GB.

Debugging checklist

Work through these in order. A failure early in the chain hides everything after it:

![Six-step checklist table with what to verify, the symptom if wrong, and the fix]

  1. Is the peering connection Active (accepted)?
  2. Do both route tables have the peer CIDR pointing at pcx-?
  3. Is each route table associated with the right subnet?
  4. Do the security groups allow the peer's private IP as /32?
  5. Is the Gateway Endpoint attached to the private route table, in the bucket's Region?
  6. Does the instance have an IAM role whose policy allows the S3 actions you call?

Final thoughts

Most "it doesn't work" moments in AWS networking come down to routes and security groups. With peering, creating the connection is the easy part, and the route tables on both sides are what make it work. When something fails silently, check both directions before blaming the service.

Have you run into cross-VPC routing problems like this?

Tell me in the comments: do you use peering, Transit Gateway, or PrivateLink for this kind of setup?

title: Postgres 19 Reverted 8 to 10 Features and Now Targets Nov 19. Was AI Review the Cause?
description:
• Book: AI Agents Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

"About 8 to 10 significant features, depending on how you count, have been reverted" from PostgreSQL 19, committer Peter Eisentraut wrote on October 9. One reason he gives is LLM-assisted code review, which finds defects much faster than before, "meaning that the effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed."

The schedule moved too. PostgreSQL 19 was originally slated for late September or early October, The Register reported on October 16. The project's RC1 announcement on October 15 now plans general availability for November 19, 2026, "unless an issue is discovered that requires a delay or an additional release candidate."

The line about review became the headline. Other people who work on Postgres read the same revert history and came to a different answer. If a bot reviews your pull requests, the disagreement is about your queue too.

What left PostgreSQL 19, and what stayed

On September 16, a Snowflake engineering post by developer advocate Elizabeth Garrett Christensen counted 53 PG19 reverts since beta began and listed the bigger user-facing features among them. Some of the larger ones:

  • SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ)
  • ALTER TABLE ... MERGE/SPLIT PARTITION(S)
  • UPDATE/DELETE ... FOR PORTION OF
  • GROUP BY ALL
  • online data checksums

The Register reports that SQL/PGQ, part of the SQL standard since 2023, came out over unresolved issues, and that Tom Lane said in September he would "be willing to bet dinner" that shipping it in v19 would produce post-release bugs that couldn't be fixed until v20.

What stays: Eisentraut names REPACK CONCURRENTLY, logical replication of sequences and pg_plan_advice as notable features still in 19. The RC1 notes list fixes since Beta 4 for REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) and pg_plan_advice, plus parallel autovacuum and COPY (query) TO ... (FORMAT json). Eisentraut expects many of the reverted features to return, which means PostgreSQL 20 at the earliest.


Several of PostgreSQL 19's biggest features came out of the branch before RC1. The release still stands on the ones that stayed.

The case that AI review moved the bar

Eisentraut's post doesn't name a tool or a model. It talks about LLM-assisted code review in general, and his argument is about timing. Review now catches architectural defects that are hard to fix during beta, plus a long tail of smaller edge-case issues, and "there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these." He's explicit that the situation "is not due to 'vibe coding'", since the affected code predates that practice.

He gives a second reason in the same post. Because of what he calls the "Vulnpocalypse," many senior developers were busy with security fixes from roughly April to August, instead of beta testing and review.

Snowflake's September post put AI closer to the center: "AI has to be part of the story for why we're in this situation." It also noted that "PostgreSQL currently has no official AI contribution policy, though one is expected soon."

The case that it was late human review

Tomas Vondra, another committer, went through the mailing-list threads behind 12 reverts dated May 20 to September 16 and checked, for each one, whether AI had found the problem. His summary: "only 4 came out at 'probably AI' or 'AI'." Christophe Pettus, a PostgreSQL consultant, points out that Vondra's per-revert verdicts are stingier than that headline: one scored AI, one possibly AI, two probably not.

Vondra's explanation is a review backlog. He plots commits whose subject starts with "Revert" by day of the development cycle: feature freeze sits around day 275, releases usually land around day 480, and the PG19 reverts spike around day 430. On why review came so late, he points at security work: "Last year we had maybe 5 CVEs, this year we're already at 44." He calls that "one of the primary reasons for the lower review activity during the stabilization period."

Pettus's verdict: "The reverts were not AI finding unfixable bugs." AI did show up, through senior contributors and in public threads. Vondra's post mentions reviews done with Opus 4.8 and Opus 5, and Claude use in a couple of threads. Pettus writes that Noah Misch dismissed three of the four findings in the commit he reviewed with a model, and that the revert came from Misch's own design judgment. His line for it: "The filtering is the review."

Both camps describe the same mechanism: review came late, and when it came, it found more than the project could fix before release. They disagree on how much of that a model found.


A finding is cheap to produce. Someone still has to read it, decide, and own the answer.

What to take from it if your team runs AI review

You probably don't maintain a database, but you may have a review bot on every pull request now. Three things carry over.

Run the expensive review before merge. Eisentraut's point is that the quality bar moved after features were committed. A finding on an open PR costs a comment. The same finding after the code has merged can cost a revert.

Budget for triage. "A fixed overhead to dealing with each" applies to your team too. A reviewer that produces more findings than people can read just lengthens the queue.

Keep a human as the owner of every verdict. Pettus wants PostgreSQL to write down the shape other projects' AI policies already share: "Assisted use is fine. AI as the contributor is not. The human reviews and owns the result." One of the rules he proposes is shorter still: "Own every point you post." Misch throwing out three of four model findings is that rule at work.

What to do about your Postgres upgrade

If you planned a PostgreSQL 19 upgrade for October, move it. The project's beta testing page says beta and release candidate releases "are not meant for use in production systems," and Snowflake's September post recommended PostgreSQL 18 as the safe upgrade target for now.

RC1 is a good time to test, though. Point pg_upgrade --check at a copy of your data and a freshly initialized 19 cluster, using the 19 pg_upgrade binary from $NEW_BIN. It checks the clusters for compatibility without changing any data:

pg_upgrade --check \
  --old-bindir "$OLD_BIN" \
  --new-bindir "$NEW_BIN" \
  --old-datadir "$OLD_DATA" \
  --new-datadir "$NEW_DATA"

Then read the PostgreSQL 19 release notes against the list above. If your plan counted on GROUP BY ALL, SQL/PGQ or the partition merge and split commands, take them out of the 19 plan. The wiki's beta testing guide explains how to report what you find, and the open items list shows what is still being fixed.

Does your team's AI reviewer produce more findings than anyone reads? Tell me in the comments.

If this was useful

A review bot on every PR is an agent with a human approval step, and this story is what happens when that step falls behind. The AI Agents Pocket Guide covers the patterns for giving agents autonomy with guardrails, including where the human stays in charge of the result. I also build Hermes IDE, a source-available desktop app where you review each coding agent's changes turn by turn before you land them (GitHub), so weigh that mention accordingly.

title: Static Single Assignment in Go: From Compiler IR to Taint Analysis
description:
Subtitle: A 1988 compiler optimization turns out to be the cleanest way to trace untrusted data through Go.

When you write this:

x := 1
x = x + 1
x = x * 2

you have written one name, x, that holds three different values at three different moments. That is convenient for humans and miserable for machines. Any tool that wants to reason about x must first answer a question your code never asked: which x do you mean, at this line?

Static Single Assignment (SSA) form is the answer. In SSA, every variable is assigned exactly once. The same program becomes:

x1 := 1
x2 := x1 + 1
x3 := x2 * 2

Three names, three values, no ambiguity. Each definition has exactly one use-site chain, and each use has exactly one definition. The data-flow graph of the program becomes explicit instead of implied.

This is not a new idea. SSA was developed at IBM in the 1980s; Rosen, Wegman, and Zadeck named it and introduced Φ-functions in their 1988 paper "Global Value Numbers and Redundant Computations." It made numerous compiler optimizations easier — constant folding, dead-code elimination, global value numbering — because when you look at a use of a variable, there is only one place where that variable may have received a value. SSA became the default internal representation for LLVM, GCC, and most production compilers.

Go adopted it too. The Go 1.7 release notes describe a new compiler back end based on SSA that "generates more compact, more efficient code" with optimizations like bounds check elimination and common subexpression elimination. The Go compiler's own SSA package documents the core idea plainly: "a value is defined exactly once, but it may be used any number of times."

The part that matters for this article is the side effect. A representation that makes data flow explicit for an optimizer also makes data flow explicit for an auditor. If you want to know whether a value that came from an HTTP request can reach a SQL query, SSA has already done the hard part: it has told you, unambiguously, which value is which.

Go exposes this representation directly. The golang.org/x/tools/go/ssa package builds an SSA IR for arbitrary Go packages, and its documentation states that "the level of abstraction of the SSA form is intentionally close to the source language to facilitate construction of source analysis tools." It is the same machinery that powers go vet, staticcheck, gopls, and gosec. You do not need to be writing a compiler to use it. You need to be writing a question about data flow.

This article is about one such question, and about a small tool that answers it.

The Guard That Only Looks Like a Guard

Here is the shape of a whole class of security bugs, in four lines:

name := r.FormValue("name")   // attacker-controlled
q := "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
db.Query(q)                   // injection

The data enters at a source (FormValue), travels through the program, and exits at a sink (db.Query). If nothing in between removes the danger, you have a vulnerability. This is taint analysis: mark the untrusted values, propagate the mark, and complain if a marked value reaches a dangerous place.

The naive version of this is a grep. The naive version is also wrong, in both directions:

  • It misses flows that pass through helper functions, string concatenation, or a struct field.
  • It invents flows that a guard already neutralized, because a regex cannot tell whether SanitizeHTML(name) actually sanitizes anything.

That second failure is the interesting one. Consider:

func ValidateAndEscape(s string) string {
    if len(s) > 100 {
        return ""
    }
    return s // ← returns the input unchanged
}

The name promises validation and escaping. The body does neither. A human reviewer skimming a call site sees ValidateAndEscape(name) and moves on. A regex-based scanner sees a function call and either flags it (noisy) or trusts it (dangerous). Neither one reads the body.

A tool that reads the body can tell the difference. And SSA is what makes reading the body tractable.

Picatz's write-up on static taint analysis for Go makes the same point from the other direction: SSA provides "the foundation for performing taint analysis," transforming the program into a value graph where each node is a value or instruction, then into a call graph where edges are calls — the structure you need to identify data flow from source to sink.

Five Steps From Source to Sink

The project is a single Go module called leakcheck. It does five things:

  1. Loads a set of Go packages and builds SSA for each.
  2. Classifies every project function that looks like a guard into one of eight classes.
  3. Walks the SSA instructions, propagating taint from sources to sinks.
  4. Probes every sink rule's argument index against the callee's real declared signature.
  5. Runs the whole thing twice — once trusting guards, once treating every guard as a no-op — and reports the difference.

That last step is the point of the whole exercise. The delta between the two passes is the set of flows that are silent only because someone wrote a reassuring function name.

Loading and building SSA

The entry point is the standard packages + ssa pairing:

cfg := &packages.Config{Mode: packages.LoadAllSyntax, Dir: dir}
pkgs, err := packages.Load(cfg, patterns...)

prog := ssa.NewProgram(fset, ssa.SanityCheckFunctions)
for _, p := range pkgs {
    ssapkg := prog.CreatePackage(p.Types, p.Syntax, p.TypesInfo, false)
    ssapkg.Build()
}

ssa.NewProgram gives you a container; CreatePackage turns a type-checked package into SSA; Build() does the actual translation. After that, every function body is a list of basic blocks, and every basic block is a list of instructions.

The instruction walk

The core of the analysis is a switch over instruction types. This is where SSA earns its keep — the cases are few and each one is unambiguous:

switch v := instr.(type) {
case *ssa.Call:
    return a.stepCall(f, v, v.Common(), state)
case *ssa.Defer:
    return a.stepCall(f, v, v.Common(), state)
case *ssa.Go:
    return a.stepCall(f, v, v.Common(), state)
case *ssa.BinOp:
    // taint flows from either operand to the result
case *ssa.Store:
    // taint flows from the value into the address
case *ssa.FieldAddr:
    // taint flows from the struct into the field
}

Three things are worth noticing.

First, Call, Defer, and Go share a shape. All three carry a *ssa.CallCommon, which holds the callee, the arguments, and the receiver. A deferred call and a goroutine-launched call are the same data-flow event as a direct call, just scheduled differently. One helper handles all three.

Second, BinOp is where string concatenation lives. "SELECT ... " + name is a BinOp with a + token. Taint flows from either operand to the result. This is the single most common propagation step in real injection bugs, and in SSA it is one case in a switch.

Third, Store and FieldAddr are why SSA beats the AST here. If taint enters a struct field and is read back three functions later, the AST gives you a syntax tree with no edges between the write and the read. SSA gives you a value graph where the field address is a node and the store is an edge into it.

The guard classifier

This is the part that does something a regex cannot. Every project function is inspected and sorted into one of eight classes:

Class Cuts taint? Meaning
effective yes Delegates to a recognized sanitizer and does nothing else
constant yes Takes no input, so it cannot forward taint
non-forwarding yes Returns only error/bool; the input never comes back out
passthrough no Returns its argument unchanged
rewrites no Transforms the input without calling a recognized sanitizer
conditional no Branches on the input; the analyzer cannot correlate branch with sink
unknown no No rule matched

The classification is decided by the SSA body, not the name. SanitizeHTML is effective because it calls a known escaper and does nothing else. ValidateAndEscape is conditional because it branches. CleanInput is passthrough because it returns its argument. IsSafePath is non-forwarding because it returns a bool and the string never leaves.

Only three of the eight classes cut taint. That ratio is the finding.

The argument-layout probe

Every sink rule names an argument index. os.Open is index 0. db.Query is index 1 (the query string, after the receiver). Header.Set is index 2.

Those indices are guesses about someone else's function signature. And there is a genuine trap here, because Go's SSA representation is asymmetric about receivers:

  • A static method call puts the receiver in Args[0], so Header.Set(key, value) has the value at index 2.
  • An invoke-mode call (through an interface) puts the receiver in CallCommon.Value and excludes it from Args, so the indices shift by one.

A tool that assumes one convention will silently mis-index half its rules. So leakcheck measures instead of assuming: for every sink rule, it looks up the callee's declared signature and checks that the named index exists and has a plausible type.

if idx >= len(sig.Params()) {
    // rule is out of range for this callee — report it
}

The probe prints a table and exits non-zero if anything is suspicious. It is the difference between a confidently wrong report and a report you can check.

The two-pass delta

The whole analysis runs twice. Pass 2 is byte-identical except for one flag:

guardsNoop = true

With that flag set, every project guard is treated as a no-op — taint flows straight through it. The difference between the two passes is the set of flows that a guard is currently suppressing.

If that number is zero, your guards are decorative. If it is large, your guards are load-bearing and you should look at exactly which ones.

Nine Seconds, Ten Findings

Here is the actual output, formatted as if from a Linux machine:

cheikh@dev:~/ssa-taint$ go run .
==============================================================================
  LEAKCHECK — SSA taint analysis for Go
==============================================================================

TIMING
  load + SSA build           8.6312159s
  guard classification       534.2515ms
  summary fixpoint           4.9699ms
  pass 1 (guards trusted)    0s
  pass 2 (guards no-op)      0s
  layout probe               0s
  total                      9.1704373s

PROGRAM
  packages analysed          2
  functions                  80
  SSA instructions           3011
  guards classified          14
  callees indexed            17035
  summaries that taint       19

FINDINGS (pass 1 — guards trusted) — 10
  #   SEVERITY KIND                FUNCTION                       ARG   ORIGIN
  1   HIGH     sql-injection       corpus.H01Query                1     request.form
  2   HIGH     sql-injection       corpus.H02EnvQuery             1     environment
  3   HIGH     path-traversal      corpus.H05Open                 0     request.form
  4   HIGH     ssrf                corpus.H06Fetch                0     request.form
  5   HIGH     path-traversal      corpus.H10TwoHop               0     request.form
  6   HIGH     path-traversal      corpus.H11OneHop               0     request.form

CAVEATS
  - Sanitizers are not checked against sink kind. url.QueryEscape stops taint at a SQL sink, which is wrong. This is planted false negative FN-1.
