title: Screenshot Every Page of a Website from Its Sitemap with One Node.js Script
description:
You're about to relaunch a site and someone asks for a screenshot of every page as it stands today. Or a client wants to sign off 140 pages of copy, or legal wants a dated record of what the pricing page said. Doing it by hand means opening each URL, waiting for the lazy images, closing the cookie banner and saving the file under a name you'll still understand next month. Two minutes a page adds up to most of a working day for a 200-page site.

So I wrote one Node.js script that reads the sitemap, captures every page at desktop and mobile widths in real Chrome, and leaves a folder of named PNGs, a CSV manifest and a contact sheet. Last run: 38 full-page captures in 35 seconds, no failures.

Disclosure: I run HTML to Image, and the script uses its Screenshot API for the captures. This is a cross-post of the full guide on the HTML to Image blog, which is the canonical version and goes further into webhooks, costs and compliance archives.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18 or later, for the built-in fetch.
  • An HTML to Image API key. The free credits are enough to try this on a handful of pages.
  • A site with a sitemap, or a text file of URLs from a crawl. 
npm install @html2img/client
export HTML2IMG_API_KEY=your_api_key

Step 1: Find the sitemap

Most sites declare their sitemap in robots.txt, so check there first:

curl -s https://example.com/robots.txt | grep -i '^sitemap:'

If nothing comes back, try /sitemap.xml, then /sitemap_index.xml (Yoast and Rank Math on WordPress), then /wp-sitemap.xml (WordPress core since 5.5). Big sites use a sitemap index that points at child sitemaps, some of them gzipped. The script follows all of that, so you only ever pass the top-level URL.

One caveat: a sitemap is the list the CMS chooses to publish. Orphaned landing pages and anything marked noindex won't be in it. For a migration archive, cross-check against a crawl and feed the script a text file instead.

Step 2: The script

Save this as capture-site.mjs. It's long-ish because it handles the boring parts properly: sitemap indexes, .gz files, duplicates, a credit check before spending anything, four captures at a time, retries for errors that can recover, and the reports at the end.

// capture-site.mjs
// node capture-site.mjs https://example.com/sitemap.xml [--dry-run]
// node capture-site.mjs urls.txt
import { mkdir, readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { gunzipSync } from 'node:zlib';
import {
  Html2img,
  InsufficientCreditsError,
  TimeoutError,
  ServerError,
  ConnectionError,
} from '@html2img/client';

const SOURCE = process.argv[2];
const DRY_RUN = process.argv.includes('--dry-run');
const OUT = 'shots';
const CONCURRENCY = 4;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3;

// One credit per page per variant.
const VARIANTS = [
  { name: 'desktop', width: 1440 },
  { name: 'mobile', width: 390 },
  // { name: 'pdf', format: 'pdf' }, // A4 document with a real text layer
];

// Sent with every capture.
const CAPTURE = {
  fullpage: true,
  css: `#onetrust-banner-sdk, .onetrust-pc-dark-filter, #CybotCookiebotDialog,
        .qc-cmp2-container, .osano-cm-window, #cookie-law-info-bar,
        .intercom-frame, #crisp-chatbox { display: none !important; }`,
};

const SKIP = /\.(pdf|jpe?g|png|gif|webp|svg|zip|mp4|xml)$/i;
const apiKey = process.env.HTML2IMG_API_KEY;
const client = DRY_RUN ? null : new Html2img(apiKey);

// 1. Every <loc> in a sitemap, following sitemap indexes and .gz files.
async function readSitemap(url, seen = new Set()) {
  if (seen.has(url)) return [];
  seen.add(url);
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${url} returned ${res.status}`);
  let body = Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer());
  if (body[0] === 0x1f && body[1] === 0x8b) body = gunzipSync(body);
  const xml = body.toString('utf8');
  const locs = [...xml.matchAll(/<loc>\s*(?:<!\[CDATA\[)?(.*?)(?:\]\]>)?\s*<\/loc>/gs)]
    .map((m) => m[1].replace(/&(amp|apos|quot|lt|gt);/g, (_, e) =>
      ({ amp: '&', apos: "'", quot: '"', lt: '<', gt: '>' })[e]));
  if (!/<sitemapindex[\s>]/.test(xml)) return locs;
  const children = await Promise.all(locs.map((loc) => readSitemap(loc, seen)));
  return children.flat();
}

// 2. Same site only, no files, no duplicates.
const bare = (host) => host.replace(/^www\./, '');
function toPages(urls, onlyHost) {
  const pages = new Set();
  for (const raw of urls) {
    let u;
    try { u = new URL(raw.trim()); } catch { continue; } // header rows, blanks
    if (onlyHost && bare(u.hostname) !== bare(onlyHost)) continue;
    if (SKIP.test(u.pathname)) continue;
    u.hash = '';
    pages.add(u.href);
  }
  return [...pages];
}

// "/blog/launch-notes/" -> "blog__launch-notes"
let multiSite = false;
function fileName(page) {
  const { hostname, pathname, search } = new URL(page);
  const slug = (pathname + search)
    .replace(/^\/+|\/+$/g, '')
    .split('/')
    .map((part) => part.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/gi, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, ''))
    .join('__')
    .toLowerCase()
    .slice(0, 150) || 'home';
  return multiSite ? `${bare(hostname)}__${slug}` : slug;
}

async function creditsLeft() {
  const res = await fetch('https://app.html2img.com/api/me', {
    headers: { 'X-API-Key': apiKey },
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Key check failed with ${res.status}`);
  return (await res.json()).credits_remaining;
}

const retryable = (err) =>
  err instanceof TimeoutError ||
  err instanceof ServerError ||
  err instanceof ConnectionError ||
  err.errorCode === 'page_load_timeout';

// 3. One capture, retried on errors that are worth a second attempt.
async function capture({ page, variant }) {
  const { name, ...options } = variant;
  const ext = options.format === 'pdf' ? 'pdf' : 'png';
  const row = { page, variant: name, status: 'failed', file: '', image_url: '', error: '' };
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
    try {
      const shot = await client.screenshot({ url: page, ...CAPTURE, ...options });
      row.image_url = shot.url;
      const img = await fetch(shot.url);
      if (!img.ok) throw new Error(`download returned ${img.status}`);
      row.file = `${name}/${fileName(page)}.${ext}`;
      await writeFile(`${OUT}/${row.file}`, Buffer.from(await img.arrayBuffer()));
      return { ...row, status: 'ok', error: '' };
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof InsufficientCreditsError) throw err;
      row.error = err.errorCode ?? err.message;
      if (!retryable(err) || attempt === MAX_ATTEMPTS) return row;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 3000 * attempt));
    }
  }
}

// 4. A fixed number of captures in flight at once.
async function runAll(jobs) {
  const rows = [];
  let next = 0;
  let stopped = false;
  async function lane() {
    while (!stopped && next < jobs.length) {
      const job = jobs[next++];
      try {
        const row = await capture(job);
        rows.push(row);
        console.log(`${rows.length}/${jobs.length} ${row.status} ${row.variant} ${job.page}`);
      } catch (err) {
        if (!stopped) console.error(`Stopping early: ${err.message}`);
        stopped = true;
      }
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: CONCURRENCY }, lane));
  return rows;
}

// 5. A manifest for spreadsheets and an index.html for people.
async function writeReports(rows) {
  const cols = ['page', 'variant', 'status', 'file', 'image_url', 'error'];
  const cell = (v) => `"${String(v).replaceAll('"', '""')}"`;
  const csv = [cols, ...rows.map((r) => cols.map((c) => r[c]))]
    .map((line) => line.map(cell).join(','))
    .join('\n');
  await writeFile(`${OUT}/manifest.csv`, csv);

  const esc = (s) => s.replace(/[&<>"]/g, (c) => `&#${c.charCodeAt(0)};`);
  const cards = rows
    .filter((r) => r.status === 'ok' && r.file.endsWith('.png'))
    .map((r) => `<a href="${esc(r.file)}"><img src="${esc(r.file)}" loading="lazy"><span>${r.variant} · ${esc(r.page)}</span></a>`)
    .join('\n');
  await writeFile(`${OUT}/index.html`, `<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Site capture</title>
<style>body{font:14px system-ui;margin:24px;display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(240px,1fr));gap:20px}
a{color:#334155;text-decoration:none}img{width:100%;height:320px;object-fit:cover;object-position:top;border:1px solid #e2e6ec;border-radius:8px}
span{display:block;margin-top:6px;word-break:break-all}</style>\n${cards}`);
}

const fromSitemap = /^https?:\/\//.test(SOURCE);
const urls = fromSitemap
  ? await readSitemap(SOURCE)
  : (await readFile(SOURCE, 'utf8')).split(/\r?\n/);
const pages = toPages(urls, fromSitemap ? new URL(SOURCE).hostname : null);
multiSite = new Set(pages.map((page) => bare(new URL(page).hostname))).size > 1;

if (DRY_RUN) {
  console.log(pages.join('\n'));
  process.exit(0);
}

const jobs = pages.flatMap((page) => VARIANTS.map((variant) => ({ page, variant })));
const credits = await creditsLeft();
console.log(`${pages.length} pages x ${VARIANTS.length} variants = ${jobs.length} credits. Balance: ${credits}.`);
if (credits < jobs.length) {
  console.error('Not enough credits for the whole run. Trim the list or top up first.');
  process.exit(1);
}

for (const { name } of VARIANTS) await mkdir(`${OUT}/${name}`, { recursive: true });
const rows = await runAll(jobs);
await writeReports(rows);

const failed = rows.filter((r) => r.status !== 'ok').length;
const skipped = jobs.length - rows.length;
console.log(`Saved ${rows.length - failed}, failed ${failed}, skipped ${skipped}. Open ${OUT}/index.html`);

The css string is doing quiet but important work. The renderer arrives as a first-time visitor with no cookies, so every page shows its consent banner. Injecting display: none !important for the common consent providers and chat widgets takes them out before the shot. If a site uses something else, find the banner's ID in dev tools and add it.

Step 3: Dry run first, then capture

--dry-run prints the URLs the script would capture. It doesn't need a key and spends nothing, so use it to filter out tag archives, paginated listings and anything else you don't need a picture of:

node capture-site.mjs https://html2img.com/sitemap.xml --dry-run | grep '/tools/' > urls.txt
node capture-site.mjs urls.txt

That's the real run I mentioned at the top, against the free tools section of my own site:

19 pages x 2 variants = 38 credits. Balance: 100.
1/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/docs/mcp/tools/
2/38 ok mobile https://html2img.com/docs/mcp/tools/
3/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/tools/
4/38 ok mobile https://html2img.com/tools/
...
38/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/tools/youtube-thumbnail/
Saved 38, failed 0, skipped 0. Open shots/index.html

Spot the first line. My lazy grep also matched /docs/mcp/tools/, which I never meant to include. That's exactly why the dry run exists: grep '^https://html2img.com/tools/' would have kept it out.

The desktop captures came back 1,440 pixels wide and between 3,737 and 10,016 pixels tall. Here's the index.html the run produced, each card cropped to the top of its page:

What the script does when things go wrong

Not every page cooperates, so the retry logic only retries what a second attempt can fix:

  • 504 timeouts, 500s, slow-loading sites and dropped connections get two more attempts, 3 then 6 seconds apart.
  • Dead links, SSL failures and sites that block automated visitors (url_not_found, url_unreachable, connection_refused) are logged in manifest.csv and skipped.
  • Running out of credits stops every lane, still writes the reports, and tells you how many captures were skipped.

To re-run only the failures, pull them out of the manifest and run them in a fresh folder so the first run's reports stay intact:

awk -F'","' '$3 == "failed" { print substr($1, 2) }' shots/manifest.csv | sort -u > retry.txt
mkdir retry && cd retry && node ../capture-site.mjs ../retry.txt

Keep CONCURRENCY low for sites you don't own. Every capture is a real page load against somebody's production server.

A few limits worth planning around

  • Public pages only. The renderer has no cookies or headers, so anything behind a login captures as the sign-in page.
  • Infinite scroll has no bottom. Cap the feed with injected CSS such as main.feed { max-height: 12000px; overflow: hidden; }.
  • Closed accordions stay closed. Nobody clicks during a capture, so open hidden panels with CSS if they matter.
  • One credit per page per width. Desktop plus mobile doubles the cost, and the PDF variant adds a third.

Where I'd use this

Before a migration, so you have the old site on disk the day the DNS switches. For client sign-off, where one contact sheet beats 200 links. And for compliance, where the commented-out pdf variant gives you searchable A4 documents in a dated folder.

The full guide on the HTML to Image blog also covers handing long captures to a webhook instead of waiting on them, a bash version for short URL lists, and what a full-site capture costs at different sizes.

How are you archiving sites before a relaunch at the moment? Browser extension, Screaming Frog, something homegrown? Let me know in the comments.

title: How much GPU energy does fp16 save? Measured on a Tesla T4
description:
How much GPU energy does fp16 actually save over fp32? Spec sheets give TDP and peak FLOPS, not joules per job, so I measured it on a Tesla T4 using the GPU's own NVML energy counter.

The job 

import sys, torch
dtype = {"fp16": torch.float16, "fp32": torch.float32}[sys.argv[1]]
a = torch.randn(8192, 8192, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
for _ in range(100):
    b = a @ a
torch.cuda.synchronize()

fp16 and fp32 runs alternate (so temperature and clock drift hit both sides), 5 measured runs each, medians reported, Mann-Whitney test between the two.

Results: the whole job

Setup fp16 fp32 GPU energy saved
No cooling between runs 475 J, 8.6 s 2.53 kJ, 39.7 s 81.2%
Every run starts at ≤65 °C 426 J, 7.8 s 2.21 kJ, 33.8 s 80.8%
≤65 °C + 3 warm-up runs 413 J, 8.4 s 2.50 kJ, 40.1 s 83.5%
Same, a second session 392 J, 7.9 s 2.29 kJ, 36.1 s 82.9%

p = 0.008 every time: every fp16 run beat every fp32 run.

Results: just the matmuls

Measuring inside the process, without Python start-up and CUDA set-up, 20 matmuls took about 73 J and 1.1 s in fp16 against about 486 J and 7.4 s in fp32: roughly 85% less GPU energy and 6.6× faster.

import torch, joules
with joules.Session(gpus=[0]) as s:
    with s.phase("fp16") as p:
        ...  # your code
print(p.energy_j, p.duration_s)

Why the gap is so large

The T4 is Turing: fp16 matmuls run on the tensor cores, but there is no TF32, so fp32 runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. Energy is power × time, so most of the saving comes from finishing sooner. fp32 also sat throttled 93% of the time at the T4's 70 W cap, against about 60% for fp16.

On an A100, H100 or L4, fp32 matmuls can use TF32, so expect a much smaller gap there. Measure it rather than assume it.

Run it yourself 

pip install -U landauer-gap
joules compare --names fp16,fp32 --baseline fp32 --runs 5 --warmup 3 --cool-to 65 --gpus 0 \
  "python3 bench.py fp16" "python3 bench.py fp32"

Full write-up with power and throttling tables: https://wattops.dev/blog/fp16-vs-fp32-gpu-energy-t4

Disclosure: I built joules, the open-source CLI used here.

title: Sovereign Private Clouds Anchor Data Control in Regulated Markets
description:
Qatar Launch Signals Rising Demand for Localized Control

The recent announcement by Meeza and Microsoft to deliver a sovereign private cloud environment in Qatar provides a clear illustration of how organizations increasingly require their data to remain physically and legally within national borders. This deployment allows Qatari entities to leverage Microsoft’s Azure stack while ensuring that customer data, metadata, and control-plane operations stay inside the country’s jurisdiction. By establishing this capability, the partnership directly addresses scenarios where cross-border data flows risk violating local laws on data residency, government access requests, or sector-specific compliance obligations. The move underscores a growing recognition that global hyperscale platforms must be adapted to meet sovereign requirements rather than forcing organizations to choose between modern cloud capabilities and regulatory adherence.

Regulated industries in Qatar and similar markets face immediate operational consequences from this development. Financial institutions handling customer accounts, payment data, and transaction records can now pursue cloud modernization without exposing information to foreign legal processes. Healthcare providers managing patient records and clinical systems gain a pathway to advanced analytics and AI workloads while satisfying strict confidentiality mandates. Government agencies responsible for citizen services and critical infrastructure can migrate workloads to a controlled environment that limits external administrative access. These sectors no longer need to maintain entirely separate on-premises infrastructure or accept the latency and cost penalties of fully disconnected systems; instead, they can adopt private-cloud architectures that embed sovereignty controls at the infrastructure layer.

The Core Tension Between Global Scale and National Oversight

This Qatar initiative also highlights the deeper friction between the efficiencies of global cloud platforms and the imperative of local sovereignty. Public-cloud services deliver rapid elasticity, continuous innovation, and consolidated security tooling that individual organizations struggle to replicate. Yet these benefits rest on architectures where data may traverse multiple jurisdictions, be subject to provider-wide operational processes, and potentially fall under extraterritorial legal authorities. Sovereign private-cloud models attempt to reconcile the two by preserving the software and operational familiarity of hyperscale providers while enforcing data locality, key management inside the country, and restricted access for foreign personnel. The result is an environment that retains much of the convenience of public cloud while satisfying regulators who prioritize jurisdictional control over data.

Enterprises evaluating such offerings must weigh trade-offs in performance, cost, and operational responsibility. Sovereign deployments often involve dedicated hardware footprints and localized support teams, which can limit the instantaneous scalability associated with multi-tenant public regions. At the same time, they reduce the compliance overhead of mapping every data flow against evolving national regulations. The Meeza-Microsoft arrangement in Qatar demonstrates how these considerations are moving from theoretical discussions into concrete procurement decisions, prompting organizations across the Gulf and beyond to reassess their cloud strategies in light of both technological opportunity and sovereign obligation.

Azure Local in Established Facilities Creates Sovereign Foundations

The Meeza Microsoft partnership centers on delivering a sovereign private cloud solution purpose-built for Qatar through the deployment of Azure Local inside Meeza’s already operational data centers. Rather than commissioning new construction projects that would require extended permitting, environmental assessments, and capital outlays, the two organizations have integrated Microsoft’s Azure Local software stack directly into Meeza’s existing facilities in Doha. This approach allows Qatar-based organizations to run Azure-consistent workloads on infrastructure that already meets local physical-security standards, power redundancy requirements, and network connectivity mandates, thereby accelerating time-to-value while satisfying data-residency and operational-control expectations set by Qatari regulators.

Azure Local functions as a fully managed extension of the Azure control plane that runs on-premises, enabling customers to consume familiar services such as virtual machines, container orchestration, and storage accounts without routing traffic outside national borders. By placing these capabilities inside Meeza’s pre-built halls, the partnership sidesteps the multi-year timelines typically associated with greenfield sovereign-cloud builds. Existing cooling infrastructure, UPS systems, and fiber connectivity are leveraged immediately, while Meeza’s on-site engineering teams continue to handle day-to-day facility operations using the same processes they have refined over years of managing enterprise workloads for government and financial-sector clients in Qatar.

Operational familiarity is preserved because Azure Local exposes the same portal, APIs, and identity framework that customers already use in the public Azure cloud. Meeza staff therefore require only targeted training on the localized hardware configuration rather than wholesale retraining on new management tools. This continuity reduces the risk of configuration drift and accelerates adoption among local IT teams that must maintain compliance with Qatar’s data-protection and cybersecurity directives. At the same time, Microsoft retains responsibility for software updates, security patching, and capacity planning, ensuring that the sovereign environment receives the same level of engineering rigor applied to Azure regions worldwide.

The model also supports incremental scaling: additional Azure Local nodes can be added within the same facility footprint as demand grows, without triggering new real-estate acquisition cycles. Organizations in sectors such as energy, healthcare, and public administration can therefore migrate sensitive workloads in phases while continuing to rely on Meeza’s proven physical-security posture and 24/7 monitoring. By anchoring the sovereign cloud in Qatar’s established data center real estate established data center real estate, the partnership demonstrates how existing infrastructure can be transformed into a compliant, Azure-native platform without the delays or cost premiums of purpose-built facilities.

Ultimately, the decision to deploy Azure Local inside Meeza’s current sites underscores a pragmatic pathway toward digital sovereignty that balances regulatory compliance, speed of deployment, and operational continuity. Qatar’s public and private sectors gain access to a production-grade sovereign cloud that inherits Azure’s global innovation cadence while keeping every byte of customer data and every control-plane transaction within the country’s borders and under local operational oversight.

Data Residency Requirements Drive Infrastructure Choices

Sovereign private cloud deployments, such as the one launched by Meeza and Microsoft in Qatar, place both compute resources and storage arrays inside national borders to satisfy strict data residency mandates. Qatar’s regulatory framework, particularly for government, financial services, and critical infrastructure operators, requires that certain categories of sensitive information never leave the country. By housing the physical servers and associated networking equipment within Qatari data centers, these platforms eliminate the possibility of inadvertent or deliberate cross-border data movement that could violate local statutes. The architecture ensures that every virtual machine, database instance, and object storage bucket operates on hardware located on Qatari soil, creating a verifiable boundary that regulators can inspect and audit without relying on foreign jurisdiction assurances.

Running production workloads entirely within the sovereign environment changes day-to-day operational procedures. Administrators no longer configure data pipelines that route traffic through international gateways; instead, all processing occurs on local clusters connected by domestic fiber links. This setup removes the need for data export controls or transfer impact assessments that typically accompany multi-region cloud strategies. Workload orchestration tools are configured with strict locality policies, so even automated backup or disaster-recovery jobs remain inside the same national facility. As a result, compliance teams can demonstrate continuous adherence to residency rules through simple physical-location attestations rather than complex legal opinions about data flows across multiple countries.

Latency and Policy Implications of In-Country Operations

The absence of cross-border transfers produces measurable improvements in application performance. Round-trip times between user devices in Doha and the sovereign cloud instances drop to single-digit milliseconds, supporting real-time analytics, high-frequency trading platforms, and citizen-facing digital services that would otherwise suffer from transcontinental delays. Network architects can also implement fine-grained access policies at the physical layer, such as mandatory use of locally issued encryption keys and role-based controls enforced by Qatari identity providers. These controls align directly with national cybersecurity directives and reduce the attack surface that would exist if traffic traversed foreign networks or relied on overseas key-management services.

Organizations evaluating sovereign options frequently combine them with specialized colocation services to extend capacity while preserving the same residency guarantees. This hybrid model allows additional racks to be added under the same regulatory umbrella, maintaining consistent latency profiles and unified access governance across all workloads. Because every component remains physically inside Qatar, incident-response teams can apply forensic tools and legal holds without navigating mutual legal assistance treaties or foreign data-protection authorities. The resulting operational environment therefore delivers both regulatory certainty and technical performance advantages that conventional public-cloud regions cannot replicate when residency constraints are non-negotiable.

Regulatory Compliance Becomes Built-In Rather Than Bolted-On

Placing Azure Local instances inside Meeza-operated facilities in Qatar embeds regulatory compliance into the core infrastructure rather than requiring organizations to layer additional controls onto externally hosted environments. Because the physical hardware resides entirely within Qatari data centers, every byte of customer data processed by the sovereign private cloud remains subject to local jurisdiction from the moment it is created. This architecture directly supports adherence to Qatar’s national data protection requirements, which mandate that certain categories of information never leave the country’s borders. Organizations no longer need to negotiate complex cross-border data transfer mechanisms or obtain repeated approvals for routine operations, since the default location of all workloads satisfies residency obligations by design.

Sector-specific regulators benefit equally from the localized deployment. Financial institutions subject to Qatar Central Bank oversight can maintain transaction records and customer profiles on infrastructure that meets the bank’s expectations for in-country processing and audit accessibility. Similarly, healthcare providers handling sensitive patient information align with Ministry of Public Health guidelines without introducing latency or additional gateways that would arise when routing data to distant cloud regions. Government agencies gain the ability to run classified or restricted workloads on a platform that combines Microsoft’s enterprise-grade logical controls with Meeza’s locally managed physical security perimeter, creating a single point of accountability that simplifies inspection and certification processes.

The decisive advantage lies in the co-location of physical and logical control layers within the same facility. Physical access policies, environmental monitoring, and hardware lifecycle management are administered by Meeza personnel on Qatari soil, while Microsoft’s Azure Local software stack delivers consistent identity, encryption, and network segmentation capabilities. When these two layers operate together under one roof, compliance teams can execute unified audits that examine both the tangible data center environment and the software-defined policies in a single visit. Requests from regulators for data location verification or forensic imaging can be fulfilled rapidly because the relevant systems are not separated by thousands of kilometers or multiple legal jurisdictions.

In contrast, reliance on distant cloud providers often forces organizations to maintain parallel compliance programs. Data may reside in regions governed by foreign laws, requiring additional contractual safeguards, encryption key management outside the provider’s control, and periodic legal opinions confirming that no unintended disclosure pathways exist. These measures add operational overhead and introduce points of failure whenever regulations evolve. The Meeza-Microsoft sovereign private cloud eliminates that friction by ensuring that both the physical substrate and the logical orchestration remain inside Qatar, allowing compliance to become an inherent property of the platform instead of a perpetual retrofit exercise.

This integrated model also streamlines incident response and regulatory reporting. When a security event occurs, local teams can isolate affected hardware immediately while Microsoft’s centralized monitoring continues to provide visibility into logical activity, all without crossing international borders that might trigger additional notification requirements. Over time, the reduced complexity translates into more predictable audit cycles and clearer alignment between technical controls and the expectations of Qatari authorities across multiple industries.

Enterprise Control Expands in Hybrid Sovereign Environments

Sovereign private clouds such as the Meeza and Microsoft deployment in Qatar introduce layered operational demands that require enterprises to retain granular oversight of compute allocation, policy enforcement, and maintenance schedules without sacrificing the benefits of hybrid connectivity. In these environments, organizations must configure resource pools so that virtual machines and containers remain under direct enterprise command while still permitting selective data flows to regional or global hubs. This setup demands tooling that maps every workload instance to defined ownership boundaries, ensuring that compute decisions—such as scaling thresholds or placement constraints—originate from the enterprise’s own control plane rather than being delegated entirely to the sovereign provider.

Security policy management grows more intricate when regulatory sovereignty rules intersect with corporate standards. Enterprises typically establish a master policy repository that propagates rules on encryption key handling, access logging, and threat detection signatures into the sovereign instance, yet they must also permit local administrators to apply jurisdiction-specific overrides. The result is a dual-layer model in which baseline controls remain synchronized across the hybrid estate while Qatar-specific requirements, including data localization mandates and audit trail formats, are enforced at the edge. Continuous validation through automated compliance scans prevents drift, allowing security teams to detect when a local exception inadvertently weakens broader zero-trust architecture.

Update and Patch Governance

Update cycles present a further operational challenge because sovereign clouds often restrict or delay vendor-driven patches to satisfy national review processes. Enterprises therefore implement staged rollout pipelines that first validate patches in non-sovereign test environments, then push approved updates through enterprise-managed orchestration tools into the Qatar instance. This approach preserves local autonomy over timing while maintaining consistency in vulnerability posture across the hybrid footprint. Logging every patch decision in a centralized repository further enables audit teams to demonstrate that update governance never relinquishes enterprise accountability.

Achieving the right equilibrium between local autonomy and hybrid integration requires deliberate architectural choices. Workload classification frameworks help teams decide which applications can operate with full sovereign isolation and which benefit from shared identity, monitoring, or analytics services. By anchoring these decisions in explicit risk and performance criteria, organizations avoid both over-isolation that fragments operations and excessive centralization that violates sovereignty commitments. Organizations seeking deeper insights into these frameworks can explore resources from global cloud data initiatives that outline governance patterns for multi-jurisdiction estates. Ultimately, success hinges on maintaining unified visibility dashboards that surface both sovereign-specific metrics and enterprise-wide key performance indicators, allowing decision makers to adjust controls in real time without compromising either regulatory compliance or operational coherence.

AI Workloads and Localization Needs Accelerate Adoption

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence workloads is placing unprecedented demands on cloud infrastructure, particularly in regions where data residency requirements intersect with the need for extreme computational scale. Training and inference for large language models, computer vision systems, and real-time analytics engines require clusters of high-end GPUs or specialized accelerators, along with low-latency access to massive datasets. When these datasets include personally identifiable information, financial records, or critical infrastructure telemetry, organizations face strict rules that prevent unrestricted movement of data across borders. Sovereign private cloud environments address this tension by delivering hyperscale performance inside national boundaries, allowing AI pipelines to run at full speed while keeping every byte under local jurisdictional control.

Performance Without Compromise

Modern AI workloads exhibit bursty, data-intensive patterns that public cloud regions outside a country cannot always satisfy under localization mandates. A sovereign deployment supplies the same GPU-accelerated instances, high-bandwidth networking fabrics, and managed AI services found in global commercial clouds, yet confines storage and processing to facilities operated under the host nation’s legal framework. This architecture eliminates the latency penalties and compliance friction that arise when data must be anonymized or tokenized before crossing borders. Organizations can therefore maintain continuous model retraining cycles on fresh, jurisdictionally compliant datasets without redesigning their entire data architecture.

Regulatory pressure is expected to intensify. Future legislation in the Gulf and elsewhere is likely to expand the definition of “critical data,” impose mandatory residency for AI training logs, and require auditable proof that no foreign entity can access raw inputs. Sovereign clouds position adopters to absorb these changes with minimal operational disruption. Because the underlying platform already mirrors mainstream cloud APIs and security controls, teams retain access to the latest model registries, MLOps tooling, and managed Kubernetes services while satisfying new audit and reporting obligations from day one.

Strategic Positioning for Regulated Sectors

Financial institutions, healthcare providers, and government agencies in Qatar are early beneficiaries. These entities generate high volumes of sensitive data that must remain inside the country yet require advanced analytics to detect fraud, personalize care, or optimize logistics. By running AI workloads inside the Meeza-Microsoft sovereign environment, they avoid the trade-off between regulatory adherence and technological capability. Model development proceeds on the same familiar stack used globally, while data never leaves the sovereign boundary. This dual assurance accelerates pilot projects into production and reduces the risk of future re-architecture when oversight frameworks tighten further.

Practical Steps for Evaluating Sovereign Cloud Partners

Enterprises evaluating sovereign private cloud options must begin by examining the physical and operational integrity of proposed facilities. Key questions include whether the data centers hold internationally recognized certifications such as ISO 27001 for information security management, ISO 27701 for privacy, and SOC 2 Type II reports that demonstrate ongoing controls over security, availability, and confidentiality. Additional scrutiny should focus on local regulatory alignment, including adherence to Qatar’s data protection frameworks and any sector-specific mandates for financial or government workloads. Operators should request evidence of independent audits covering environmental controls, redundant power systems with N+1 or 2N configurations, and biometric access layered with 24/7 on-site security personnel. These certifications provide measurable assurance that data remains within national borders while meeting the operational resilience standards required for mission-critical applications.

Integration Paths and Technical Compatibility

Next, organizations need to probe integration capabilities with existing technology stacks. Practical questions center on native support for hybrid connectivity through dedicated ExpressRoute or equivalent private links, compatibility with established virtualization platforms, and the availability of automated migration tooling that preserves encryption keys and identity federation. Enterprises should determine whether the provider offers pre-validated reference architectures for common workloads such as ERP systems, analytics platforms, and container orchestration environments. Equally important is clarity on latency guarantees between on-premises sites and the sovereign facility, measured in milliseconds, along with options for direct peering with regional internet exchanges. These details determine how quickly workloads can move without re-architecture and whether multi-cloud strategies remain feasible over time.

Long-Term Support Models and Operational Governance

Long-term viability hinges on clearly defined support structures. Decision makers should ask about service-level agreements that specify recovery time and recovery point objectives, the composition of local engineering teams available for on-site intervention, and escalation paths that include named technical account managers. Further questions must address software update cadences, capacity expansion lead times measured in weeks rather than months, and training programs that enable internal staff to manage sovereign resources independently. Governance considerations include data access request procedures, incident notification timelines, and contractual provisions for technology refresh cycles that align with hardware depreciation schedules. These elements collectively reduce the risk of service disruption or vendor lock-in as business requirements evolve.

When assessing multiple providers, enterprises benefit from structured evaluation frameworks that score responses across weighted criteria such as certification depth, integration speed, and support responsiveness. Pilot projects limited to non-production workloads can validate claims around performance and compliance before full-scale commitments. By systematically addressing these operational dimensions, organizations can select sovereign cloud partners that deliver both regulatory compliance and sustained technical excellence. For enterprises seeking robust Global Cloud Data infrastructure services, engage directly with their specialized team to begin a tailored assessment.

How Global Cloud Data infrastructure services Helps

Teams navigating the issues above don't have to solve them from scratch. Global Cloud Data infrastructure services was built for exactly this kind of operational challenge, giving teams a practical path forward without reinventing the wheel in-house.

title: Bevy instancing: drawing 639,000 units with one draw call per mesh
description:
Originally published at tensorust.com.

TL;DR: Bevy already instances meshes for you when entities share a mesh and a material. Past a few thousand moving units, we stopped making them entities at all: units live in a plain Vec, each frame builds one 48-byte instance per unit, and a custom render command draws each mesh once. In LAWN WAR that holds 639,000 live units at 25 fps on an RTX 4070, and the thing that finally slows it down is not the GPU or the draw calls. It's the CPU loop that builds the instance lists.

Short answer first, since that's what you searched for. Bevy has two kinds of instancing. The automatic kind: if many entities use the same Handle<Mesh> and the same material, Bevy batches them into instanced draws on its own (the custom_shader_instancing example says so in its first lines). For a few thousand objects, use that and stop reading.

The manual kind is that same example: you skip entities per object, hand the GPU a buffer of per-instance data, and issue one draw call that renders the mesh N times. That's what you want when you have hundreds of thousands of things that move every frame. Below is the version that runs LAWN WAR, with the real code, the numbers we measured on October 16, 2026, and the traps.


One frame of LAWN WAR with 600,000 plants and about 38,700 zombies alive. Timings from LW_LOG, Oct 16 2026, 9:11 PM ET, RTX 4070.

What is LAWN WAR, and why did it need this?

LAWN WAR is a Rust game on Bevy 0.19.1: an endless plants-versus-zombies war in first and third person, where both armies keep growing until the field is a sea of units. It was built on October 2 and 3, 2026, mostly by a coding agent working from Matthew's design notes, and the source is public on GitLab. The design doc asks for "hundreds of thousands of units per side". Every one of them walks, attacks, burns, dies and tumbles through the air when something explodes.

The first playable build did it the normal ECS way. Each zombie slot was an entity with a Mesh3d, a material, a Transform and a Visibility, and a system copied positions from the simulation into those transforms every frame. Here's the spawn, from the first commit (src/horde.rs, Oct 2, 2:58 PM):

h.entities = (0..h.cap)
    .map(|i| {
        commands
            .spawn((
                Mesh3d(mesh.clone()),
                MeshMaterial3d(fx.vertex.clone()),
                Transform::from_xyz(0.0, -50.0, 0.0),
                Visibility::Hidden,
                NotShadowCaster,
                ZombieSlot(i as u32),
            ))
            .id()
    })
    .collect();

The two stress screenshots we kept from that build show 974 zombies on the field at 36 fps and 916 at 8 fps. We never profiled that version properly, so I won't pin the blame on one Bevy system. What matters is the decision it forced: 2 hours and 10 minutes later the whole thing was rewritten around custom instancing, and units stopped being entities.


The first build, one ECS entity per zombie: 974 zombies on the field at 36 fps (QA screenshot, Oct 2 2026, 3:37 PM ET).

Step 1: why aren't the units entities?

An entity is a great home for a player, a camera or a boss. For 600,000 identical soldiers it's overhead you pay on every frame: change detection, transform propagation, visibility checks, extraction to the render world. So each army is just a flat Vec of plain Copy structs, allocated once at full capacity, with a free list for recycled slots (src/war.rs):

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)]
pub struct Unit {
    pub pos: Vec2,
    pub vel: Vec2,
    pub y: f32,
    pub hp: f32,
    // ... 12 more f32 status fields (burn, chill, tox, corpse timer...)
    pub kind: u8,
    pub strain: u8,
    // ... mark, elite, jumped, died_now ...
    pub alive: bool,
    /// Left the battle window: free the slot without a death.
    pub gone: bool,
}

pub struct Army {
    pub units: Vec<Unit>,
    pub free: Vec<u32>,
    /// One past the highest slot ever used: every loop stops here, not at capacity.
    pub hw: usize,
    // ...
}

That hw field (a high-water mark) is a small thing that matters a lot. The default cap is 600,000 per army, but early waves only use a few hundred slots. Every loop runs over units[..hw], so a skirmish never pays for the empty 599,000.

The simulation runs over those slices in parallel with rayon, and finds neighbours through a grid rebuilt every frame with a counting sort: count units per 2 m cell, turn the counts into start offsets, then drop each unit index into its slot. No hashing, no per-cell Vec, two flat arrays. Both armies rebuild at once:

rayon::join(
    || a0.grid.rebuild(origin, size, &a0.units[..a0.hw]),
    || a1.grid.rebuild(origin, size, &a1.units[..a1.hw]),
);

Step 2: what goes into one instance?

Each visible unit becomes 48 bytes: three vec4s the vertex shader reads as extra vertex attributes. Position and facing, then scale, animation phase and kind, then tint and glow. bytemuck's Pod lets us cast the whole list to bytes for free (src/inst.rs):

#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Pod, Zeroable, Default, Debug)]
pub struct Inst {
    /// world xyz, yaw
    pub a: [f32; 4],
    /// scale, phase, anim kind, extra
    pub b: [f32; 4],
    /// tint rgb, emissive (0 = lit)
    pub c: [f32; 4],
}

Notice what's missing: a full 4x4 transform matrix (64 bytes on its own) and any bone data. Units only turn around the vertical axis, so yaw is one float, and the shader builds the rotation. Keeping the instance this small matters at scale. At 562,727 instances a frame, the list is about 27 MB, and at 25 fps that's roughly 680 MB a second going to the GPU.

Step 3: how do you build 600,000 instances fast?

This is the function the chart further down is about. It walks each army in chunks of 8,192 on all cores, skips what the camera can't see, picks a level of detail (LOD) by distance, picks an animation frame, and sorts each unit into a per-mesh list (src/war.rs, render(), trimmed):

let lists: Vec<Vec<Inst>> = a.units[..a.hw]
    .par_chunks(8192)
    .map(|chunk| {
        let mut local: Vec<Vec<Inst>> = vec![Vec::new(); nb];
        for u in chunk {
            if !u.alive && u.corpse <= 0.0 {
                continue;
            }
            let p = Vec3::new(u.pos.x, u.y, u.pos.y);
            let to = p - cp;
            let d2 = to.length_squared();
            // Behind the camera: skip (with a margin for big things nearby).
            if d2 > 400.0 && to.dot(cf) < -0.15 * d2.sqrt() {
                continue;
            }
            let lod = if d2 < 40.0 * 40.0 { 0 } else if d2 < 120.0 * 120.0 { 1 } else { 2 };
            // ... tint for burning/frozen/toxic, elite scale, animation frame ...
            local[idx].push(Inst::new(p, yaw, scale, phase, an, extra, tint, glow));
        }
        local
    })
    .reduce(|| vec![Vec::new(); nb], |mut a, mut b| {
        for (x, y) in a.iter_mut().zip(b.iter_mut()) {
            if x.is_empty() { std::mem::swap(x, y); } else { x.append(y); }
        }
        a
    });

A few choices in there are worth stealing. The culling is one dot product, not a full frustum test: anything more than about 20 m away and behind the camera is dropped, and the GPU clips the rest. The LOD cut-offs are 40 m and 120 m. And each rayon task fills its own lists, so there are no locks; the reduce step just glues them together, swapping instead of copying when one side is empty.

The zombies' walk, attack and death animations come from Kenney's CC0 graveyard kit. Instead of skinning on the GPU, each clip is baked into separate meshes (8 walk frames, 4 attack frames, 1 death pose), and a unit picks its frame from its own phase. Every frame is just another mesh with its own instance list.

Step 4: how does the list reach the render world without a copy?

Bevy renders in a separate "render world" and copies (extracts) what it needs from the main world every frame. Copying 27 MB twice a frame would be silly, so the lists are wrapped in an Arc. Extraction clones the pointer, not the data (src/inst.rs):

#[derive(Component, Clone)]
pub struct InstanceData(pub Arc<Vec<Inst>>);

fn flush(mut commands: Commands, mut b: ResMut<Batches>, mut q: Query<&mut InstanceData>) {
    for (id, (mesh, list)) in b.lists.iter_mut() {
        let data = Arc::new(std::mem::replace(list, Vec::with_capacity(list.capacity())));
        match b.entities.get(id).copied() {
            Some(e) => { if let Ok(mut d) = q.get_mut(e) { d.0 = data; } }
            None => { /* first time this mesh appears: spawn ONE entity for it,
                         with NoFrustumCulling, holding InstanceData(data) */ }
        }
    }
}

So there's still an entity, but one per mesh, not one per unit. That entity gets NoFrustumCulling, because Bevy would otherwise cull the whole batch based on the mesh's own bounds at the origin. The measured cost of this step at 639,000 units: 0.08 ms a frame.

Step 5: why not make a new GPU buffer every frame?

Bevy's example creates a fresh buffer with create_buffer_with_data for every batch, every frame. That's fine for a demo. For lists that are millions of instances long, it's a GPU allocation per mesh per frame. LAWN WAR keeps each buffer and rewrites it in place with Queue::write_buffer, and only reallocates when the list outgrows it, with 50% headroom:

match existing {
    Some(mut b) if b.cap >= n => {
        if n > 0 {
            queue.write_buffer(&b.buffer, 0, bytes);
        }
        b.len = n;
    }
    _ => {
        let cap = (n * 3 / 2).max(1024);
        let buffer = device.create_buffer(&BufferDescriptor {
            label: Some("lawnwar instances"),
            size: (cap * size_of::<Inst>()) as u64,
            usage: BufferUsages::VERTEX | BufferUsages::COPY_DST,
            mapped_at_creation: false,
        });
        queue.write_buffer(&buffer, 0, bytes);
        commands.entity(entity).insert(InstanceBuffer { buffer, cap, len: n });
    }
}

Step 6: what does the draw call look like?

The pipeline is Bevy's normal mesh pipeline with one extra vertex buffer bolted on. Its step mode is VertexStepMode::Instance, which means the GPU advances through it once per instance instead of once per vertex:

d.vertex.buffers.push(VertexBufferLayout {
    array_stride: size_of::<Inst>() as u64,
    step_mode: VertexStepMode::Instance,
    attributes: vec![
        VertexAttribute { format: VertexFormat::Float32x4, offset: 0, shader_location: 8 },
        VertexAttribute { format: VertexFormat::Float32x4, offset: f4, shader_location: 9 },
        VertexAttribute { format: VertexFormat::Float32x4, offset: f4 * 2, shader_location: 10 },
    ],
});

And the draw is a single draw_indexed whose instance range is the whole list: pass.draw_indexed(islice.range.start..(islice.range.start + count), vslice.range.start as i32, 0..ib.len as u32). One call, however many units use that mesh. If you want the concept explained from scratch in raw wgpu, the Learn Wgpu instancing chapter is the clearest walkthrough I know.

Step 7: who animates 600,000 zombies?

The GPU does. The CPU writes a phase and an animation kind; the WGSL vertex shader turns that into motion. Here's the zombie shamble from src/inst.wgsl:

if anim == 1u {
    // Zombie shamble: lean forward, rock side to side, lunge when attacking.
    let gait = sin(t * 4.5 + ph * 7.0);
    let lean = -0.12 - extra * 0.6;
    p = rz(rx(p, lean), gait * 0.12);
    n = rz(rx(n, lean), gait * 0.12);
    p.y = p.y + abs(gait) * 0.05;
}

Plants sway harder toward the top and recoil when they fire, corpses lie flat, debris tumbles, and lightning bolts are a unit cube stretched between two points. Smoke is the clever bit: there's no alpha blending at all. A negative "emissive" value means see-through, and the fragment shader throws away a share of pixels using a 4x4 Bayer pattern. No sorting of half a million transparent things, ever.


The 600,000 cap run, Oct 16 2026, 9:12 PM ET: 600K plants and 38.4K zombies alive, 26 fps in the corner. Bot-driven QA screenshot, unedited.

So what does it cost at 639,000 units?

We measured it tonight. The game has a QA mode that launches straight into a war, plays itself with a bot and prints timings every 2 seconds (LW_LOG=1, using Bevy's RenderDiagnosticsPlugin for GPU time). Five runs on Oct 16, 2026, 9:11 to 9:17 PM ET, same wave (28), same stage (30), only the army cap changing. The shipped build, 1600x900 window, RTX 4070, i7-13700KF. Each number is the average of 16 to 21 samples after the first 12 seconds.

  • 5,568 units: 50 fps. Most of the 186,000 instances are explosion particles, not units.
  • 27,934 units: 61 fps, CPU 9.17 ms, GPU 10.56 ms.
  • 115,217 units: 49 fps, CPU 11.31 ms, GPU 15.60 ms.
  • 277,469 units: 40 fps, CPU 19.17 ms, GPU 20.19 ms.
  • 638,734 units: 25 fps (23 to 28), CPU 34.82 ms, GPU 35.08 ms, 562,727 instances a frame.

The 115,000 run lines up with what the design doc recorded on Oct 2 ("~110k units 9-13 ms CPU and 10-14 ms GPU"), on a different graphics backend, which is a nice sanity check.


Per-system CPU time per frame, five runs with different army caps, Oct 16 2026, 9:11 to 9:17 PM ET. Source: LW_LOG spans, averaged over 16 to 21 samples per run.

The surprise is in the per-system breakdown. Going from 28,000 to 639,000 units (23 times more), think(), the whole two-army simulation, went from 1.13 ms to 10.09 ms. That's under 9 times the cost, thanks to the counting-sort grid. render(), the loop from Step 3 that only builds instance lists, went from 0.69 ms to 18.85 ms, 27 times the cost. At full size, building the lists costs more CPU time than simulating the war.

Nothing in the timings pointed at the draw calls. The GPU did get slower as the war grew, but steadily, and it finished at 35.08 ms, neck and neck with the CPU.


Whole-frame CPU vs GPU time, same five runs. The smallest run has the most GPU time per unit because 173,000 explosion particles dominate it.

What broke along the way?

  • Meshes without vertex colours crash the pipeline. The shader reads @location(5) color. A Bevy primitive like Sphere or Cuboid has no colour attribute, so the pipeline fails validation at location 5. The fix is a three-line helper, inst::white(), that adds white vertex colours to every primitive before it's instanced.
  • Slot recycling needs its own flag. An early version marked "free this slot" with a magic hit-point value. Late-game damage numbers got big enough to blow straight through it (the HUD in the screenshot above shows 45.8 trillion HP). Now units that leave the battle window set gone = true and go back on the free list without counting as a death.
  • Shader compile time on DirectX 12. On Oct 2 this PC had no Vulkan adapter, Bevy used DX12, and the shader compiler (FXC) took about 40 seconds per launch. The faster DXC compiler broke the particle crate, bevy_hanabi, so the game hides the wait behind a loading screen. Tonight's runs, on a newer NVIDIA driver (617.42), picked Vulkan instead. Check which backend your log line says before you blame your code.
  • Parallel QA launches lie. Running two copies at once slowed shader compile for both and skewed the screenshots' timing. Measure one at a time, which is how the five runs above were done.

What would I try next?

The chart says the next win is in Step 3, not in rendering tricks. My bet, untested so far: keep the instance lists alive between frames and only rewrite units that moved, or skip the CPU list entirely and do the culling and LOD pick in a compute shader that writes straight into the instance buffer. That's the "GPU-driven" direction, and Bevy's own renderer has been heading there for its built-in meshes since 0.16. Either could plausibly take 10+ ms off the frame. If someone has done the compute-shader version in Bevy, I'd genuinely like to see the numbers.

Do this in your project

  1. Start with Bevy's automatic instancing. Same mesh handle, same material handle. Only go custom when entity count, not triangles, is what hurts.
  2. Keep mass objects as data. A Vec of Copy structs, a free list and a high-water mark. Entities for the few things that need them.
  3. Shrink the instance. Pack position plus yaw instead of a 4x4 matrix. 48 bytes instead of 64+ adds up at half a million.
  4. Build lists in parallel with private buffers. par_chunks, one Vec per mesh per task, merge at the end. No locks.
  5. Hand off with an Arc, and add NoFrustumCulling to the one entity per mesh.
  6. Reuse GPU buffers. write_buffer into a buffer with headroom; reallocate only on growth.
  7. Animate in the vertex shader, and dither instead of alpha-blending when you have huge counts of transparent things.
  8. Log per-system timings from day one. Without the spans, we'd have guessed "too many draw calls" and optimized the wrong thing.

If you're building in Rust, the write-up on rendering Chinese, Japanese and Korean text in our own Rust game engine covers the other engine, and the geodesic live wallpaper is another GPU-in-Rust side quest. LAWN WAR itself was written with coding agents; what broke running 20 of them on one PC is the story of how that works without melting the machine.

Our other Rust game, O'BLOCK, a sneaker-flipping sim where you haggle from a $300 shoebox to a billion, is free on Steam, out October 20. Wishlist it here.

What's the biggest unit count you've pushed through Bevy, and what fell over first: the CPU, the GPU, or you?

title: Our creator avatars expire after a few days, and the whole of instrumentation.ts exists to silence them
description:
Nakodo shows brands a list of creators from YouTube, Instagram and TikTok, and every row has a round picture next to it. That picture is the single most failure prone thing on the page, for a reason that has nothing to do with our code: Instagram and TikTok sign their avatar URLs, and the signature is good for a few days.

We store a creator for weeks. So a creator found a fortnight ago, shown to a brand today, has an avatar URL that now answers 403 and will never work again.

This post is about the four places that fact reaches.

1. The fallback has to be a design decision, not an empty box

When there is no avatar, or the one we have has expired, the circle is hatched:

if (!src || failed === src) {
  return <div className={cn(box, "hatch")} style={{ width: px, height: px }} aria-hidden="true" />;
}

hatch is one utility, used across the whole app for exactly one meaning:

/* Hatching always means "locked" or "not yet observed", and always comes with text. */
@utility hatch {
  background-image: repeating-linear-gradient(45deg, var(--hatch) 0 1px, transparent 1px 4px);
}

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .hatch {
    background-image: none;
    border: 1px dashed CanvasText;
  }
}

A background image disappears entirely in forced colours mode, so there is a dashed border waiting there instead. You can see the hatched circle without signing in: the sample entries on our home page use it, because a sample creator has no picture to show.

The aria-hidden matters too. An avatar is decoration next to a name that is already text; a screen reader announcing "image" here is noise, and an alt text saying the creator's name would announce it twice.

2. onError does not fire for an image that already failed

This was the bug that sent me reading the HTML spec. The obvious handler is fine when the image loads and then fails:

onError={() => setFailed(src)}

But server rendered HTML means the browser often starts the request before React hydrates. If it finishes failing first, the error event has already been dispatched, React attaches its listener afterwards, and nothing ever calls your handler. You get a broken image icon and no state change.

The fix is in the ref callback, which runs on an element that already exists:

ref={(img) => {
  // One that failed before the page came to life never fires onError.
  if (img?.complete) img.decode().catch(() => setFailed(src));
}}

complete is true for both "loaded" and "finished failing", so it is not the test on its own. decode() is: it resolves if the browser has a usable image and rejects with an EncodingError if it does not. Two lines, and they cover the case the event handler structurally cannot.

3. Two kinds of picture, two code paths, one allowlist

Creator avatars come from a known set of hosts, so they go through Next's optimiser:

images: {
  remotePatterns: [
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "yt3.ggpht.com" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "yt3.googleusercontent.com" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "i.ytimg.com" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "**.tiktokcdn.com" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "**.tiktokcdn-eu.com" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "**.tiktokcdn-us.com" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "**.cdninstagram.com" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "**.fbcdn.net" },
    { protocol: "https", hostname: "platform-lookaside.fbsbx.com" },
  ],
}

Nine entries, and the list is a security boundary rather than a convenience: /_next/image fetches whatever URL you hand it, from our server, so an unconstrained remotePatterns is an open proxy with our egress bill attached.

The second kind of picture is a business's own icon, taken from its website, and a business can be on any domain on the internet. There is no allowlist that could cover that, so those bypass the optimiser entirely:

// eslint-disable-next-line @next/next/no-img-element
<img
  src={src}
  alt=""
  loading="lazy"
  referrerPolicy="no-referrer"
  onError={() => setFailed(src)}
  ref={(img) => { if (img?.complete) img.decode().catch(() => setFailed(src)); }}
/>

referrerPolicy="no-referrer" is the part I would not skip. Without it, every brand looking through a list of local businesses sends that business's web server a referrer header naming the page of our app they were on. A plain <img> is also the one case where disabling the lint rule is right rather than lazy, which is why the line above it says so.

4. One optimised size for four display sizes

The avatar component takes a size name, and the sizes are 28, 36, 48 and 72 pixels. The naive implementation asks the optimiser for each of them, and then one creator who appears in a list, a detail header and a conversation is three resize operations and three cache entries.

So the request is always the same:

// Every size asks the optimiser for the same picture, 64px across (128 on a
// sharp screen), so a creator's avatar is resized and billed once rather than
// once per size it's shown at. The largest, 72px, is barely softer for it.
const OPTIMISED_PX = 64;

<Image width={64} height={64}> with a CSS size applied through style means Next generates a srcset of 64 and 128 (both are in the default imageSizes), and the 72px avatar is drawing a 128px image, which is fine. The only visible cost is that the largest size is very slightly soft on a 1x screen.

The cache TTL is the other half of that:

// An avatar's address changes when the picture does (Instagram and TikTok
// sign theirs afresh on each read), so a resized one is kept for a week
// rather than resized again every 4 hours.
minimumCacheTTL: 7 * 24 * 60 * 60,

Next 16 raised the default from 60 seconds to 4 hours, which is a sensible default for images whose URL stays put while the bytes change. Ours is the opposite: the URL is a fresh signed one every time the picture changes, so re-fetching the old URL on a timer can only ever produce the same bytes or a 403. A week is the useful number, and it has a ceiling we do not get to pick: YouTube's API terms let us keep their data for 30 days, so any cache we hold has to be comfortably inside that. Our retention rules are public, and the image cache is quietly part of them.

Also in that config block, and doing nothing at all:

qualities: [75],

That is Next 16's default now, spelled out. It stays because the next person to read the file should see which quality the optimiser is allowed to produce without having to know a version specific default.

5. And then the logs

With all of the above, an expired avatar is handled correctly: the request fails, the component falls back to a hatched circle, the user sees a tidy list. The only thing left is that the optimiser logs every refused upstream fetch as an error, and in production, with a list of creators gathered over several weeks, that is a lot of error lines for an outcome that is both expected and already handled.

The entire contents of src/instrumentation.ts:

// Instagram and TikTok sign their avatar links for a few days, so a creator
// kept from an earlier search can have one that now answers 403. The avatar
// falls back to its hatched circle, but Next's image optimiser still logs
// every refused fetch as an error. Those lines are dropped; everything else
// goes through untouched.
export function register() {
  if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME !== "nodejs") return;
  const error = console.error.bind(console);
  console.error = (...args: unknown[]) => {
    if (args.some((arg) => typeof arg === "string" && arg.includes("upstream image response failed for"))) return;
    error(...args);
  };
}

Thirteen lines, one of which is a guard so it does not run in the edge runtime, and the rest of which is a monkey patch of console.error matched on a substring of someone else's log message.

I am not going to pretend this is elegant. It is a string match against a message from a dependency, which means a Next release that rewords the message turns the filter off silently. The alternatives I considered were worse:

  • Turn the log off. There is no option for it; the optimiser's logging is not configurable.
  • Check the URL before rendering. That is a server round trip per avatar to discover something we will discover anyway when the browser asks.
  • Delete expired avatar URLs on a schedule. Expiry is not visible in the URL, so this means fetching every stored avatar to see which ones still work: a lot of requests to someone else's CDN, every day, to pre-compute a fallback that already costs nothing.
  • Leave the noise in. This was the status quo, and the actual cost of it is that a real error in a list of hundreds of fake ones does not get noticed.

The last one is the argument. A log line that is always there is not information, and it trains you to skim exactly the output you keep around for the day something breaks. Dropping it on a brittle substring match is a trade I will take, and the comment above it is written for the person who has to notice when it stops working.

What generalises

The pattern underneath all five sections is: a resource you do not own can expire without telling you, and every layer has to agree on what that looks like. The component shows the fallback, the hydration path catches the case the event misses, the config stops the cache from outliving the thing it caches, and the log filter stops the handled case from looking like an incident.

If you want the non code version of why a creator sticks around in our database long enough for this to happen at all, how Nakodo works has a section on what is kept and for how long, and the privacy notice lists it field by field.
