title: A 7-Step AWS and Azure Cloud Cost Checklist (With CLI Commands)
description:
Cloud bills grow quietly. A test server stays on. A disk is left behind. Nobody owns the bill.

This post is a simple FinOps checklist. FinOps simply means managing cloud costs on purpose, as a shared habit. It works for AWS and Microsoft Azure. Do the steps in order. Each step makes the next one easier.

In this guide, CloudSkill Consulting LLC walks you through seven steps. First you see your costs. Then you label them with tags, remove waste and resize servers. After that you commit to steady use, set alerts, and review every month.

Figure 1. The seven steps, in the order you should do them.

Step 1: Turn on cost views

You can't fix what you can't see.

  • AWS: Open Cost Explorer in the Billing and Cost Management console. Look at cost by service and by account.
  • Azure: Open Cost Management, then Cost analysis. Look at cost by resource group and by service.

Pick one view. Save it. You will use it every month.

Step 2: Tag everything

Tags tell you who owns a resource and why it exists. Start with three keys:

Tag key Example value Why it helps
owner data-platform You know who to ask
env dev, test, prod You can find non-prod waste fast
project billing-api You can split the bill by project

Two things people miss:

  • AWS: User-defined tags do not show up in cost reports until you activate them as cost allocation tags in the Billing console.
  • Azure: Use Azure Policy to require tags on new resources. Then untagged resources can't sneak in.

Keep the same tag keys on both clouds. Same spelling. Same case.

Figure 2. Three tag keys to start with, and the one extra step each cloud needs.

Step 3: Find idle resources

This is often the fastest win. Look for things you pay for but don't use.

Unattached disks and unused public IPs on AWS. A volume in the available state is not attached to any instance. An Elastic IP with no association is not in use, and AWS charges for public IPv4 addresses.

# AWS: list unattached EBS volumes in the current region
aws ec2 describe-volumes \
  --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query "Volumes[].{ID:VolumeId,SizeGiB:Size,Type:VolumeType,AZ:AvailabilityZone}" \
  --output table

# AWS: list Elastic IPs that are not associated with anything
aws ec2 describe-addresses \
  --query "Addresses[?AssociationId==null].{IP:PublicIp,AllocationId:AllocationId}" \
  --output table

# AWS: run the volume check in every enabled region
for r in $(aws ec2 describe-regions --query "Regions[].RegionName" --output text); do
  echo "== $r"
  aws ec2 describe-volumes --region "$r" \
    --filters Name=status,Values=available \
    --query "Volumes[].VolumeId" --output text
done

Unattached managed disks on Azure. When a managed disk is not attached to a VM, its managedBy property is null.

# Azure: list unattached managed disks in the current subscription
az disk list \
  --query '[?managedBy==`null`].{Name:name,RG:resourceGroup,SizeGB:diskSizeGb}' \
  -o table

Azure CLI options can change between versions, so check the Azure CLI docs for your version before you run these.

Before you delete anything:

  1. Check the tags. Ask the owner.
  2. Take a snapshot if the data might matter (aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id <id> on AWS).
  3. Then delete (aws ec2 delete-volume --volume-id <id> on AWS, az disk delete --ids <id> --yes on Azure).

Deleting a disk is permanent. Go slow here.

Figure 3. How to spot idle disks and IPs, and the safe order for removing them.

Also look for VMs that are on all night and all weekend in dev and test. Azure VMs have a built-in auto-shutdown setting. On AWS, you can use the Instance Scheduler on AWS solution or a simple scheduled job.

Step 4: Rightsize

Rightsize means picking a smaller server that still does the job. Many servers are bigger than they need to be. Both clouds will tell you which ones.

  • AWS Compute Optimizer looks at usage and suggests better instance sizes. You need to opt in first.
  • Azure Advisor has a Cost category with rightsizing and shutdown advice. 
# AWS: see rightsizing findings (after you opt in to Compute Optimizer)
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations \
  --query "instanceRecommendations[].{Instance:instanceArn,Finding:finding}"

# Azure: list cost recommendations from Azure Advisor
az advisor recommendation list --category Cost -o table

Change one thing at a time. Watch performance for a week. Then move on.

Step 5: Commit for steady use

Some workloads run 24/7 and will keep running. For those, a commitment is usually cheaper than on-demand pricing.

  • AWS: Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, with 1-year or 3-year terms.
  • Azure: Azure Reservations and the Azure savings plan for compute, also with 1-year or 3-year terms.

Simple rule: rightsize first, then commit. If you commit to a server that is too big, you lock in the waste.

Figure 4. Steps 4 and 5 work together: rightsize first, then commit.

Step 6: Set budgets and alerts

A budget will not fix waste. But it tells you early when something goes wrong.

  • AWS Budgets: Create a monthly cost budget. Add alerts at levels you choose, for example when actual or forecast spend crosses part of the budget.
  • Azure Cost Management budgets: Create a budget at the subscription or resource group level. Add alert conditions and email recipients. You can also connect an action group (a set of actions Azure runs when an alert fires).

Note: by default, alerts only notify people. They do not stop resources. Make sure a real person reads them.

Figure 5. A budget alert warns a person early. By default, it does not stop anything.

Step 7: Review every month

Put a short meeting on the calendar. Same day each month. Use the saved view from Step 1.

Ask four questions:

  1. What went up, and why?
  2. Are there new untagged resources?
  3. Are there new idle disks or IPs?
  4. Do our commitments still match our steady usage?

That's it. Small, boring, and it works.

Quick copy-paste checklist

  • [ ] Cost Explorer and Cost Management views saved
  • [ ] owner, env, project tags on everything (and activated on AWS)
  • [ ] Unattached disks and unused IPs reviewed
  • [ ] Non-prod VMs shut down at night
  • [ ] Rightsizing advice reviewed (Compute Optimizer, Azure Advisor)
  • [ ] Commitments only for steady, right-sized workloads
  • [ ] Budgets and alerts set, with a named owner
  • [ ] Monthly review on the calendar

About the author: CloudSkill Consulting LLC is a cloud consulting firm in Omaha, Nebraska, founded in September 2024. We work on AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, with a focus on cost control (FinOps), multi-cloud planning and migration. We also provide technical and IT services across the USA. If this checklist helped, you can find more at cloudskillconsulting.com.

title: What an Executor Needs Before It Can Test Production
description:
The quality of a check is set by the inputs, not by the executor.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer working mostly in PHP/Symfony and Go, currently carving a live PHP monolith into Go services.

A lot of that work is checking production: does the extracted service behave there the way the piece it replaced did. Most of those checks are handed to an executor - person or program, the rules below hold either way.

Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov. This is the assignment I write today, price attached - maybe you write yours better, and I'd like to hear how.

The thesis

The quality of a production check is decided by the completeness of the assignment, not by the intelligence of whoever executes it.

Everything below is a consequence of that one line.

What one line of the assignment was worth

I ran a sweep across a vertical of 276 configurations: does each one have a result, and if not, where does the path stop. 184 came back empty - against the assignment I had written, that was 184 problems.

Then one condition entered the assignment: a configuration's schedule can be of a type that produces no tasks of this kind at all. With that line the same 184 became normal - the setup was doing what it was configured to do.

One line changed 67% of the picture, and no care from the executor would have found it. The fact is not a field, not a status, not a counter - it lives in how the domain works, and it enters a check only if someone writes it into the assignment first.

One line of the assignment, 276 configurations
the same sweep, read against the assignment before and after that line

without the line
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
│ 184  empty result - filed as a defect        │ 92  has a result      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

with the line
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
│ 184  empty - the schedule makes no such task │ 92  has a result      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

67% of the picture changed, and no care from the executor would have
found it. The fact is not a field, not a status, not a counter.

That is the whole argument. What follows is the list I now write before any check starts.

The ten inputs

1. The surface, and a ban on every other one

Name the one entry point the check goes through, and state that every other one is off limits. A system in migration has more than one front door, and results measured through two of them are not comparable.

Without this line the executor picks whichever door answers, and the report silently mixes two systems.

2. How to authenticate, with secrets living only in the environment

State the authentication scheme and where credentials come from: the environment, never the assignment, an artefact or a commit.

This is not only hygiene - an executor that has to improvise credentials improvises something that works once and cannot be repeated.

3. The exact shape of every request

Path, method, every parameter with its range, every body field - the literal shape, not "call the listing endpoint".

Anything left open gets interpreted plausibly, and a plausible-but-different request produces numbers that look comparable and are not.

4. How each link is measured, and what counts as the fact

For every link in the chain, say which single value is the fact: this field, this header, this counter. One number per link, read cheaply.

Two people measuring "does this have data" in two different ways will disagree forever, and neither will be wrong.

5. The domain conditions that no read returns

Provider coverage. Schedule types. What each task status actually means. No endpoint exposes any of it.

This is the line that was worth 67% of my picture, and the one most likely to be missing - it is the only one that cannot be discovered by reading the system.

6. What counts as a normal empty

Say which empties are expected outcomes and which are defects, and how to tell them apart.

An executor with no such rule counts every empty as a finding.

7. Where the artefacts go, and in what form

One folder per run, one file per probe, written as the run goes, not assembled at the end.

Left unspecified, the report becomes the only record - and a report is a summary of evidence, not the evidence.

8. The rule for writing in production

Snapshot, act, restore, a unique probe marker, and a confirmation by reading again.

This one gets its own section below.

9. The shape of the verdict, and the duty to separate "not checked" from "passed"

State the vocabulary of the verdict and require that unchecked cases be reported as unchecked.

Left unstated, "not checked" quietly becomes "nothing found", which reads as "passed" to everyone downstream.

10. An explicit ban on concluding from one field without a control case

Every conclusion needs a control beside the suspect: an object where the thing is known to work, read the same way, in the same run.

I put this in writing because I broke it myself, twice.

Ten inputs, written before the first request
the executor fills every one of these itself if the assignment leaves it out

    01  one surface, every other one banned
    02  auth scheme, secrets only from the environment
    03  the exact shape of every request
    04  one measured fact per link
 ▶  05  the domain conditions no read returns
        not exposed by any read - this one line moved 67% of the picture
    06  what counts as a normal empty
    07  artefacts: one folder per run, one file per probe
    08  snapshot, act, restore, verify
    09  verdict format: not checked ≠ passed
    10  no conclusion without a control case

Nine of them can be checked against the system. The fifth cannot - it is
a hand-written record of the world outside.

Why the normal empty gets its own line

If a system answers "no data" with an error, every mass run looks like a catastrophe. Two thirds of the objects come back as not found, the genuine failures sit inside that pile, and every run starts by clearing the noise away.

A normal empty is a success with zeros in it. Note where that requirement lands: on the system, not on whoever is checking it. Writing "treat two thirds of the answers as noise" into an assignment is a workaround for a contract that should have said so itself.

Why the write rule is not up for discussion

Any write executed against production follows one shape:

snapshot  →  act  →  restore  →  verify by reading again

Every object touched carries a unique probe marker, so anything left behind is identifiable as mine and removable without guessing. Restore is not done when the restore call returns - it is done when a fresh read shows the original state again.

A check that leaves the polygon different from how it found it is not a check. It is a change, and whoever runs anything there next inherits it. Without the marker, cleanup depends on memory - the one part of a run nobody can audit.

Every write executed against production

┌──────────┐   ┌─────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ snapshot │──▶│ act │──▶│ restore │──▶│ verify by reading again │
└──────────┘   └─────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────────────────────┘
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                              │
                              ▼
        every touched object carries a unique probe marker
   so anything left behind is identifiable as mine and removable
                        without guessing

What happens when these are missing

The executor does not stop. It fills the gaps itself, plausibly. A missing input does not produce an obviously broken report - it produces a coherent, confidently worded, wrong one, with nothing marking which parts came from the system and which from a guess.

My own example, and not a flattering one: my first conclusion from a sweep was that a set of objects would not rebuild at all. They had failed on time, back to back. The objects were fine - the failure belonged to the pace I was driving the endpoint at, and one at a time with a pause they came back almost entirely clean. That distinction is the next part.

My assignment did not contain rule 10. Without it, one run and no control was enough to file a defect against a service that had lost nothing.

What it costs

The inputs are assembled by hand, up front, before any checking starts. On a vertical of this size that is several hours whose only output is a document.

On a one-off check that is pure overhead: if the question is asked once and never again, writing the ten inputs takes longer than answering it badly and answering it again. The trade pays when the check gets repeated - by the second run the assignment exists, while the guesswork would be re-invented from scratch.

The other part of the price: the fifth input has no owner inside the system. It is a hand-written record of how the world outside works, and it goes stale silently.

The part that generalises

A fast executor amplifies whatever is in the assignment, holes included. Complete inputs get a complete answer sooner; a gap gets a confident wrong answer sooner, and the confidence reads identically in both.

The advantage goes to whoever can make correctness visible from the assignment itself, rather than from a second run and a comparison.

This is my list right now, on one vertical, in a system halfway through a migration, price included.

So: maybe you do this better, and your assignments already carry the domain conditions in a form that stays current. Maybe you have been through this and found which of the ten you can drop without paying for it. Maybe you see it differently and think an executor should be trusted to work the conditions out for itself.

How is this solved on your side, and what broke there?

Testing production with an executor - Part 1.

Next: a failure on time, checked twice - once in a stream and once one at a time with a pause - and how to tell a property of the object from a property of the pace.

title: Stop AI NullPointerExceptions: Compile-Time Zero-NPE Java with JSpecify, NullAway, and Claude Code
description:
Stop AI NullPointerExceptions: Compile-Time Zero-NPE Java with JSpecify, NullAway, and Claude Code

AI agents generate Java at blistering speeds, but LLMs still hallucinate null safety by littering codebases with redundant null-checks instead of enforcing structural invariants. If your agentic workflow in 2026 isn't hard-gated by strict compile-time diagnostics, you are simply automating the generation of production NullPointerExceptions.

Why Most Developers Get This Wrong

  • Relying on fragmented annotations: LLMs mix JSR-305, SpotBugs, and JetBrains annotations indiscriminately, breaking static analysis across modular boundaries.
  • Overusing Optional<T>: Models default to wrapping internal domain fields and method parameters in Optional, degrading memory efficiency and polluting domain models.
  • Treating the LLM as a typist, not a compiler loop: Developers still manually review AI-generated diffs instead of forcing the agent to resolve raw AST compiler errors autonomously.

The Right Way

Make non-null the default and wire deterministic compiler errors into Claude Code's execution loop.

  • Enforce standard JSpecify (org.jspecify:jspecify:1.0.0) across your codebase to give LLMs a single, unambiguous annotation grammar.
  • Mark entire packages with @NullMarked, forcing the compiler to treat every unannotated type as strictly non-null.
  • Wire Uber's NullAway into Error Prone with TreatWarningsAsErrors enabled to fail builds immediately upon any contract violation.
  • Run Claude Code CLI inside a closed feedback loop (claude "fix NullAway errors after running ./gradlew compileJava"), allowing the agent to self-correct based on exact line-and-column diagnostic outputs.

I built javalld.com while prepping for senior roles — complete LLD problems with execution traces, not just theory.

Show Me The Code 

// package-info.java: @org.jspecify.annotations.NullMarked
package com.payment.core;

import org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable;

public final class SettlementService {
    // NullAway halts compilation if order is null, or if nullable ledger is dereferenced unsafely
    public Receipt settle(Order order, @Nullable AuditLedger ledger) {
        String txId = order.transactionId(); // Guaranteed non-null by @NullMarked
        long auditCode = (ledger != null) ? ledger.record(txId) : 0L; 
        return new Receipt(txId, auditCode);
    }
}

Key Takeaways

  • Standardize on JSpecify: Stop letting AI guess between checker frameworks; standardize on @NullMarked and @Nullable.
  • Fast diagnostics win: NullAway adds single-digit millisecond overhead to compilation, making it fast enough for real-time agent loops.
  • Close the agent loop: Feed raw javac and NullAway errors directly back into Claude Code so it fixes its own nullability violations before code ever hits git.

title: Your retry logic has never seen a real 429. Here is how to test it with a local fault-injecting mock
description:
Most LLM client code has a retry branch that has never actually run. The provider returns 200 in every test, so the 429, 500 and timeout paths sit untested until production hits them at 3am.

The fix is cheap: point your client at a local server that fails on a schedule you control.

The idea

Run a tiny HTTP server on localhost that mimics a chat-completions endpoint. Give it a failure schedule, for example:

[
  {"status": 429, "retry_after": 2},
  {"status": 500},
  {"status": "timeout"},
  {"status": 200}
]

Each incoming request consumes the next step. Your client sees a 429 with a Retry-After header, then a 500, then a hang, then a good response.

What to assert

  1. Retry-After is honored. The second attempt should not fire before the header says it can.
  2. There is a time budget. The loop gives up after N seconds, not after infinity.
  3. Timeouts are set. A hung request raises instead of blocking forever.
  4. Non-retryable errors fail fast. A 400 should not be retried.
  5. Backoff has jitter. Two clients should not retry in lockstep.

A minimal version 

import json, sys, time
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

SCHEDULE = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
step = {"i": 0}

class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        s = SCHEDULE[min(step["i"], len(SCHEDULE) - 1)]
        step["i"] += 1
        if s["status"] == "timeout":
            time.sleep(60)
            return
        self.send_response(s["status"])
        if "retry_after" in s:
            self.send_header("Retry-After", str(s["retry_after"]))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b'{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"ok"}}]}')

HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 9797), H).serve_forever()

Point your client's base URL at http://127.0.0.1:9797 and run your normal code path.

If you want it packaged

I bundled a slightly more complete version (schedule file, README, examples) as a pay-what-you-want download, minimum $1: https://renevibe76.gumroad.com/l/sargxm

The snippet above is enough to get started on your own, though. The point is to see your retry code run at least once before production does it for you.

title: AI Gateway logs now have a dedicated page
description:
AI Gateway now has a dedicated Logs page listing every request your team sends through the gateway, newest first, with cost, token counts, duration, and the model, provider, and region that served it. Open any request to see how it was routed. It's available at the team scope and per project.

Filter and search

Filter by provider, model, modality, credentials, or status, or search by model, provider, or request ID to jump straight to one request. You can also export the current view as CSV or JSON, with your filters applied.

Drill into a request

Click any row to open its details next to the list: total cost, a token breakdown across input, output, reasoning, and cache reads and writes, duration, time to first token, and whether Zero Data Retention and region restrictions were applied.

The fallback path lists every provider attempt for the request in order. Each attempt shows the model, provider, status code, credentials, and how long it took, and failed attempts include the reason, such as a provider timeout or an exhausted routing budget.

title: Give every agent in Herdr its own Vercel Sandbox
description:
Terminal coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode can now each run in their own isolated Vercel Sandbox, orchestrated from Herdr, a tmux-style manager that runs them side by side in panes. Nothing an agent runs or edits touches your machine.

When you start an agent, the plugin uploads your project files into a new Sandbox, installs the agent there, and opens a pane connected to it.

The pane works like a local terminal; you type to the agent and watch it work. But it lives in the Sandbox, not on your machine, so you can run several agents at once without slowing anything down.

Everything the plugin does is machine-readable. Each action returns its results as JSON, so whatever you can do from a pane, like starting an agent, checking its state, or applying its changes, a script or another agent can do too.

A few safeguards are built in. The plugin shows every file before the first upload, returns remote changes as a Git patch you apply only when you choose, and requires a human to type DELETE to permanently remove a Sandbox.

Claude Code (2.1.220), Codex (0.146.0), and OpenCode (1.18.9) are all verified and available by default.

To get started, install the plugin:

Run vercel link in the repository you want the agent to work on, then start an agent from Herdr's action menu.

Starting takes two invocations. The first is a dry run: it lists every file it would upload and creates nothing. Run it again, and the plugin creates the Sandbox and opens the agent in a pane. To pull the agent's work back to your machine, run the apply action and its changes arrive as a Git patch.

Usage is billed at standard Sandbox rates. Learn more in the documentation.

title: I ran my text-to-SQL access control on a benchmark I didn't write
description:
Every number I had published for schemagate came from my own tests. This month a SIGMOD'27 paper released a public benchmark for exactly the problem schemagate exists for: Benchmarking Text-to-SQL under Role-Based Access Control. So I ran it.

The test

Each question comes with a role and a list of the columns that role may read. If the answer needs a column the role can't see, the right reply is "Sorry, I cannot answer." The authors score it with their own evaluator. I didn't change a line of it.

Their main finding is uncomfortable for tools like mine. If you just hide the restricted columns, models still answer. They patch something together from the columns that are left. On BIRD, their best "hide the schema" setup still answered 27% of the questions it should have refused.

What schemagate does differently

Three things happen for every question:

  1. The role's policy becomes visibility. The model never sees a hidden table or column, not even its name.
  2. One line tells the model that its view is partial, without saying what is missing. If the question needs data it can't see, it should refuse instead of improvising.
  3. Every query passes a scope check before it runs. SQL that touches anything outside the policy is refused.

Results

Same model as the paper's best BIRD run (Claude Sonnet 4.5), five trials, the authors' scoring:

AC-F1 answered when it should refuse SQL that read forbidden data
BIRD, schemagate 90.1 5.4% 0
BIRD, paper's best 88.1 7.4% not reported
Spider, schemagate 93.0 5.1% 0
Spider, paper with the same model 93.0 4.6% not reported
Spider, paper's best (DeepSeek V3.2-Reasoning) 95.9 2.0% not reported

On BIRD it beats the best of the paper's thirteen models. On Spider it ties the same model and is behind the paper's best Spider result (95.9, DeepSeek V3.2-Reasoning). In neither did any query read data the role wasn't allowed to see. The scope check makes that a guarantee rather than a measured rate.

And the paper's best setup shows the model the whole schema plus the policy. schemagate gets these numbers without the model ever seeing what is restricted.

What each piece is worth

Taking the scope check out doubled the bad answers on BIRD (5.4% to 11.3%). The one-line notice was tested on 100 questions: 16% bad answers without it, 5% with it.

One surprise: giving the model BIRD's column descriptions made things worse. Better notes on the visible columns helped it find workarounds for questions it should have refused.

The honest caveats

  • I chose the notice's wording on 100 BIRD questions that are part of the test set. Spider played no part in any choice, so it's the cleaner of the two results.
  • One model, where the paper tested thirteen.
  • My BIRD databases are the 2024 release; the paper used the 2025 one.

The notice ships on by default in schemagate 1.6.0. To reproduce the runs: benchmarks/rbac_text2sql.py, plus the evaluator's reports in benchmarks/results/rbac/.

pip install schemagate · GitHub

title: February 29 Needs a Policy Parameter, Not a Hidden Exception
description:
As of 2026-10-15

A birthday reminder fails on February 29, so a developer catches the exception and substitutes February 28. The program now runs. But the patch has also chosen a policy about when somebody's anniversary occurs in a non-leap year. That choice belongs in the feature's contract, where users and tests can see it.

We build the free age calculator at agecalc.fyi. Its English FAQ explicitly says that it uses March 1 for February 29 birthdays in non-leap years. That visible rule is the starting point here. We will implement two possible reminder conventions, without treating either one as a universal legal rule.

Keep the birthday unchanged

Someone born on February 29 should retain February 29 in the source record. Do not “repair” their date of birth to make a yearly scheduler simpler. A date of birth describes an event that happened; an anniversary date is a value derived for a particular target year.

The Gregorian leap-year rule makes years divisible by four leap years, except century years unless divisible by 400. Thus 2000 is a leap year, while 2100 is not. For application code, Python already supplies calendar.isleap; datetime.date validates calendar dates. Their behavior is documented in the Python calendar module and date API.

Source birthday Target year February 28 policy March 1 policy
2000-02-29 2027 2027-02-28 2027-03-01
2000-02-29 2028 2028-02-29 2028-02-29
2000-02-29 2100 2100-02-28 2100-03-01
2000-05-12 2027 2027-05-12 2027-05-12

The policy changes only the missing-date case. A normal birthday should not move, and a leap-year February 29 should remain February 29. Those are good invariants because they prevent a narrowly intended workaround from becoming a general month-end adjustment.

An executable policy, with boundary tests

Save this as birthdays.py and run python3 birthdays.py. It uses only the standard library. anniversary returns a date; completed_years computes a whole-year age under the same explicit convention. The latter is a calendar model, not an eligibility determination for a contract or public service.

from calendar import isleap
from datetime import date
import unittest


def anniversary(born, year, policy):
    if policy not in ("feb28", "mar1"):
        raise ValueError("Unknown leap-day policy")
    if born.month == 2 and born.day == 29 and not isleap(year):
        month, day = (2, 28) if policy == "feb28" else (3, 1)
        return date(year, month, day)
    return date(year, born.month, born.day)


def completed_years(born, as_of, policy):
    if as_of < born:
        raise ValueError("Reference date precedes birth")
    boundary = anniversary(born, as_of.year, policy)
    return as_of.year - born.year - int(as_of < boundary)


class BirthdayTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_non_leap_boundaries(self):
        born = date(2000, 2, 29)
        cases = [
            (date(2027, 2, 27), "feb28", 26),
            (date(2027, 2, 28), "feb28", 27),
            (date(2027, 2, 28), "mar1", 26),
            (date(2027, 3, 1), "mar1", 27),
        ]
        for as_of, policy, expected in cases:
            with self.subTest(as_of=as_of, policy=policy):
                self.assertEqual(completed_years(born, as_of, policy),
                                 expected)

    def test_centuries_and_ordinary_dates(self):
        born = date(2000, 2, 29)
        self.assertTrue(isleap(2000))
        self.assertFalse(isleap(2100))
        for policy in ("feb28", "mar1"):
            self.assertEqual(anniversary(born, 2028, policy),
                             date(2028, 2, 29))
            self.assertEqual(anniversary(date(2000, 5, 12), 2027, policy),
                             date(2027, 5, 12))
        self.assertEqual(anniversary(born, 2100, "mar1"),
                         date(2100, 3, 1))

    def test_rejected_inputs(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            date(2027, 2, 29)
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            anniversary(date(2000, 2, 29), 2027, "rollover")
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            completed_years(date(2000, 2, 29), date(1999, 1, 1), "mar1")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

For February 28, 2027, the year subtraction is 2027 - 2000 = 27. Under the March 1 policy the anniversary has not arrived, so subtract one and obtain 26. Under the February 28 policy it has arrived, so the result remains 27. The disagreement is exactly the declared policy, not an arithmetic error.

Do not hide the choice in exception handling

A broad except ValueError that substitutes the end of February can swallow unrelated input problems. An impossible source date, an unsupported year and a missing anniversary are different cases. Validate the source date first, then handle the known February 29 branch deliberately.

The function also rejects unknown policy strings even for ordinary birthdays. That catches misspellings immediately instead of letting them survive until the next leap-day record reaches production. A typed enum can serve the same purpose in a larger application.

Reminders and age displays need a shared contract

If the profile says a person is still 26 but the birthday banner says they turned 27 today, inspect whether two features used different conventions. Store the policy near the feature configuration and pass it to both calculations. Include it in bug reports alongside the birth date and reference date, using synthetic dates where possible.

For legal age gates, get the applicable rule and jurisdiction separately. Do not infer those requirements from a birthday-party reminder, a general calculator or a developer's default. The functions above deliberately do not contain a country table.

The web calculator also exposes a reference-date field. That is useful for inspecting a boundary without waiting for it to occur: compare the day before, the chosen anniversary and the day after. An executable test should use fixed dates for the same reason. A test that depends on today's date can pass for months while missing the only boundary that matters.

FAQ

Why not add 365 days to find the next birthday?

That advances a duration. It does not preserve a month and day across leap years.

Is February 28 always wrong?

No. It is one explicit anniversary convention. This calculator's displayed rule uses March 1 instead.

Should I change the stored birth date?

No. Keep the original valid date and derive each year's anniversary separately.

Does this calculate months and days too?

No. The example returns anniversaries and completed years only. Month-and-day decomposition needs its own documented convention.

The age calculator is free to use without signing up.

Inspect an age at a chosen reference date

title: AI Agent Autonomy Levels: A Small TypeScript Approval Gate
description:
An agent with a delete tool and a loose prompt can read “clean up my old entries” as permission. Nothing malfunctions. The message allows that reading and the tool allows the action. What's missing is a rule about when the tool may run.

This post continues my series on building agents. The previous one covered MCP.

What autonomy is

An agent's autonomy is how much it may do on its own before a human has to approve, review or step in. It is a policy your code enforces, not a trait of the model.

A scale from Level 0 to Level 4

No standard defines these levels. This is my own working scale.

Level Meaning
0 No tools. A plain chatbot
1 Read-only tools
2 Writes, each approved by a human
3 Routine writes run alone inside limits, irreversible actions still ask
4 Full autonomy, rarely justified

A level belongs to a tool, not to the whole agent. The same agent can run reads at Level 4 and deletes at Level 2.

Sort tools by what a mistake costs

A read tool changes nothing. A write tool changes something you can undo. An irreversible tool can't be taken back: deleting data, sending a message, moving money. The class comes from the cost of a wrong call, not the tool's name.

flowchart TD
    A[Model requests a tool] --> B{Tool risk class}
    B -->|read| C[Run it]
    B -->|write| D{Autonomy level}
    B -->|irreversible| E{Autonomy level}
    D -->|1| F[Refuse]
    D -->|2| G[Ask a human]
    D -->|3 or 4| C
    E -->|1| F
    E -->|2 or 3| G
    E -->|4| C
    G -->|approved| C
    G -->|declined| I[Send an error result to the model]
    F --> I
    C --> H[Send the result to the model]

The policy in code

Run it with AUTONOMY=2 npx tsx agent/autonomy.ts and change the value to compare levels.

// agent/autonomy.ts
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
import { createInterface } from 'node:readline/promises';

const client = new Anthropic();
const rl = createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout });

type Risk = 'read' | 'write' | 'irreversible';
type Decision = 'allow' | 'ask' | 'deny';

const LEVEL = Number(process.env.AUTONOMY ?? 2);

const expenses = [{ id: 1, item: 'tea', amount: 40 }];
let nextId = 2;

const risks: Record<string, Risk> = {
  get_total: 'read',
  add_expense: 'write',
  delete_expense: 'irreversible',
};

function decide(level: number, risk: Risk): Decision {
  if (risk === 'read') return 'allow';
  if (level <= 1) return 'deny';
  if (level >= 4) return 'allow';
  if (risk === 'write' && level === 3) return 'allow';
  return 'ask';
}

const tools: Anthropic.Tool[] = [
  {
    name: 'get_total',
    description: 'Return the exact sum of every expense recorded so far. Use this whenever the user asks for a total.',
    input_schema: { type: 'object', properties: {} },
  },
  {
    name: 'add_expense',
    description: 'Record one expense. Use it whenever the user says they spent money.',
    input_schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: { item: { type: 'string' }, amount: { type: 'number' } },
      required: ['item', 'amount'],
    },
  },
  {
    name: 'delete_expense',
    description: 'Permanently delete one expense by its id. Use it only when the user names the expense to remove.',
    input_schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: { id: { type: 'number' } },
      required: ['id'],
    },
  },
];

function execute(name: string, input: Record<string, unknown>): unknown {
  if (name === 'get_total') return { total: expenses.reduce((sum, e) => sum + e.amount, 0) };
  if (name === 'add_expense') {
    const expense = { id: nextId++, item: String(input.item), amount: Number(input.amount) };
    expenses.push(expense);
    return expense;
  }
  if (name === 'delete_expense') {
    const index = expenses.findIndex((e) => e.id === Number(input.id));
    if (index === -1) return { error: 'no such expense' };
    expenses.splice(index, 1);
    return { ok: true };
  }
  return { error: 'unknown tool' };
}

async function approve(name: string, input: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<boolean> {
  const answer = await rl.question(`Allow ${name} ${JSON.stringify(input)}? (y/n) `);
  return answer.trim().toLowerCase() === 'y';
}

async function guarded(name: string, input: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown> {
  const decision = decide(LEVEL, risks[name] ?? 'irreversible');
  console.log(`[${decision}] ${name}`);
  if (decision === 'deny') return { error: 'not permitted at this autonomy level' };
  if (decision === 'ask' && !(await approve(name, input))) return { error: 'the user declined this action' };
  return execute(name, input);
}

async function runAgent(userText: string): Promise<string> {
  const messages: Anthropic.MessageParam[] = [{ role: 'user', content: userText }];

  for (let step = 0; step < 6; step++) {
    const response = await client.messages.create({
      model: 'claude-sonnet-5',
      max_tokens: 500,
      tools,
      messages,
    });

    messages.push({ role: 'assistant', content: response.content });

    if (response.stop_reason !== 'tool_use') {
      return response.content.flatMap((b) => (b.type === 'text' ? [b.text] : [])).join('');
    }

    const results: Anthropic.ToolResultBlockParam[] = [];
    for (const block of response.content) {
      if (block.type === 'tool_use') {
        const output = await guarded(block.name, block.input as Record<string, unknown>);
        results.push({ type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: block.id, content: JSON.stringify(output) });
      }
    }
    messages.push({ role: 'user', content: results });
  }

  return 'Stopped: step limit reached';
}

runAgent('Add 300 for groceries, then delete expense 1.')
  .then(console.log)
  .finally(() => rl.close());

A tool missing from risks falls back to irreversible, so anything you forget to classify gets the strictest treatment. Denials and declined approvals go back as error results, not exceptions, so the model can explain what happened.

What I noticed rereading my own series code

The system prompt template in my prompt-engineering post says “Never delete or change a past expense unless the user explicitly asks to.” The agent in that post has no delete tool. The line guards an action the agent can't take. The tracker from the components post writes with no approval and only a six-step cap, which was a Level 3 decision I never named. That is why the gate here lives in code next to execute, with the prompt line as a second layer.

Common mistakes

  • Keeping the rule only in the prompt.
  • Classifying tools by name instead of by what a wrong call costs.
  • No default for unclassified tools. Fail closed.
  • Raising the level for the whole agent instead of one tool at a time.
  • Running approvals in parallel. Keep anything that waits on a person sequential.
  • Treating a decline as a crash instead of returning it as a tool result.

Read the full version

I write each post in English and Bangla. The full version is on my blog: How Autonomous Should an AI Agent Be?

Which of your agent's tools would you never let run without asking?

title: Introducing the new v0 API
description:
Today we're introducing the new v0 API: programmatic, headless access to v0's app-building agent. Send a prompt and v0 generates an app, starts a dev server in a Vercel Sandbox, and gives you a preview URL you can embed in your own UI.

Each chat is an isolated workspace for one app, where v0 can read, edit, and run the files. Follow-up messages continue from the current state. v0 verifies the code running in the Sandbox, so it can catch and fix errors in your app in real time.

The new API is now generally available.

How it works

Create a chat from a prompt, stream its work, and render the live preview, all from your own interface. First, install the v0 SDK.

Then, create a chat. Send a prompt, and v0 generates your app.

Send follow-up messages to the same chat to keep building. Each one continues from the current state.

Then embed the app.

A prompt goes in, a running app comes out. v0 operates the Sandbox, dev server, and preview behind it. When you're ready, deploy to Vercel in one API call. v0 manages the whole pipeline.

What this unlocks

The new API lets you run v0's app builder inside your own product or pipeline. This opens use cases like:

  • A white-labeled app builder: Your users describe an app and get one back.

  • Automated app changes: Trigger v0 from a script, CI job, or webhook to generate a new app or update an existing one.

  • A build tool for your agents: An agent hands back a working app instead of a code snippet.

Below, we break down the API primitives behind this workflow.

Start with a chat

Each chat holds the state for one app, and a repo or Vercel project can have many. Keep each chat's ID and send its follow-up messages to that chat. Metadata lets you group chats by customer, workspace, app, or any key you already use.

Learn more about messages.

Stream the trace

Your interface needs to show what happens between sending a request and seeing the updated preview.

Every message includes ordered parts: text, thinking, file reads and edits, searches, bash commands, tool calls, and agent actions. The same object can drive a one-line status, a changed-files view, or the full trace.

Usage is returned with chat and message responses, so you can account for the work when it finishes.

Choose sync, async, or streaming

Chat creation and messages support synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming responses. Use sync when the caller needs the completed response. Use async to queue the work and receive updates via webhook or poll for v0's response later. Stream the request to render v0's work as it happens.

Work from existing code

You can also create a chat from a repository, ZIP archive, or set of files.

Render the dev server preview

Each chat gets a short-lived preview token. Fetch it from a server route and proxy browser requests through it, so your v0 API key never reaches the browser. When a preview is ready, traffic forwards to it; while the Sandbox spins up, requests fall back to a loading route. Point an iframe at your proxy route and cache the preview details until they expire.

Read more about Accessing Previews in the docs.

Bring your own tools and design systems

Turn on specific MCP servers for a chat, or use the defaults.

Design Systems 2.0 saves a design system as a skill. Include it in a request to load its components, tokens, setup, and starter app.

You can pass up to three skills per request, from team or user memory, skills.sh, or the connected repo, or let the agent pull them in for you.

Use v0 from agents

If you're building an agent, give it v0 as a tool. When the agent needs to produce a working app, it calls v0, and gets back a running preview or deployment to hand to the user. Your agent stays in charge of everything else.

There are three ways to connect it:

MCP

Connect the v0 MCP server to an IDE, desktop assistant, or agent runtime that supports MCP.

The first connection starts an OAuth flow. The MCP server exposes tools for creating chats, listing chats, getting chat details, listing and sending messages, resolving pending tasks, and getting preview URLs.

AI SDK

For TypeScript agents built with AI SDK, use @v0-sdk/ai-tools to expose v0's API operations as tools in the agent's own loop.

The agent decides when to create or continue a chat. Your AI SDK run keeps control of the orchestration and final response.

eve

For eve agents, add an OpenAPI connection file. eve turns the allowed operations into tools and attaches the API key at execution time, out of model context.

Connect a Vercel project

Create a Vercel project for the chat, then manage its environment variables, integrations, and settings through the Vercel API. Your apps get Vercel's security and observability by default.

When you're ready to ship, deploy the chat to Vercel.

Migrate your chats

Chats from the previous version of the v0 API don’t run on the new one, so carry them forward. Pick the version you want to keep, download it as a ZIP, and create a new chat from that ZIP. Store the old identifiers in the new chat’s metadata if you need traceability.

The migration guide covers the full mapping. The main changes:

  • Use https://api.v0.dev/v2 for new requests.

  • The chat holds current app state, and messages hold its history.

  • Replace version workflows with chat file workflows, and v0 Project organization with chat metadata.

  • Use vercelProjectId plus the Vercel API for project operations.

  • Render message parts, not only final text.

Get started

Create an API key in v0 settings and install the SDK.

Or, scaffold a full app.

Read the documentation and migration guide.
