title: # From AI Prototype to Production: A Practical Guide to Deploying, Scaling, and Operating AI Systems
description:
By Ahmed Adawy

Your AI application works on your machine. Your API returns responses. Your model integration looks promising. Your tests pass.

Then production introduces a different set of problems.

Dependencies behave differently across environments. Deployments become fragile. API latency increases under load. Secrets end up in the wrong place. Logs reveal too little when something breaks. A service that worked perfectly during development becomes difficult to monitor, secure, and maintain.

This is where AI engineering becomes production engineering.

Building an AI-powered application is only one part of the job. Operating it reliably requires a broader understanding of software architecture, deployment automation, infrastructure, observability, security, and performance.

That is the engineering problem behind my book:

The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate.

Read the book on Leanpub:
https://leanpub.com/theaiengineervolumeiideployscaleoperate

The Missing Step Between Building AI and Operating AI

Modern AI development makes it relatively easy to connect a Python application to an LLM, expose an API, generate embeddings, or build a semantic search pipeline.

But a working demonstration is not the same as a dependable production system.

Consider an AI document-processing service. Its basic workflow might look like this:

  1. Accept a document through an API.
  2. Validate the input.
  3. Extract and normalize the text.
  4. Generate embeddings or call an AI model.
  5. Store the results.
  6. Return a response to the client.

That workflow describes functionality, but it does not answer the operational questions.

What happens if the model provider times out? How does the application recover from a failed deployment? Where are credentials stored? How do you detect rising latency? Can the service handle concurrent requests? How do you prevent a database connection pool from becoming a bottleneck? How can you reproduce a production failure locally?

These are not secondary concerns. They determine whether an AI application can be operated reliably.

1. Docker: Make the Runtime Reproducible

An application depends on more than its source code. It also depends on a Python version, system libraries, installed packages, configuration, and runtime assumptions.

Docker helps package an application and its dependencies into a reproducible container image.

For a Python API built with FastAPI, a basic Dockerfile might look like this:

FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

This example assumes that requirements.txt exists and that the application exposes a FastAPI instance named app in app/main.py.

Build the image:

docker build -t ai-document-service .

Run the container:

docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ai-document-service

The API should now be reachable at http://localhost:8000, assuming the application starts successfully.

This is a starting point, not a complete production security configuration. A production image should also consider a non-root user, dependency pinning, image scanning, secret management, and an appropriate build context.

The objective is to reduce environmental surprises and make the application easier to build, test, and deploy consistently.

2. CI/CD: Turn Deployment Into a Repeatable Process

Manual deployment creates opportunities for inconsistent steps, forgotten checks, and configuration mistakes.

A continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline can automate the path from a code change to a deployable artifact.

A typical workflow looks like this:

Developer Push
      |
      v
Automated Tests
      |
      v
Static Checks
      |
      v
Build Container Image
      |
      v
Security and Artifact Checks
      |
      v
Deploy to Target Environment
      |
      v
Health Verification

The precise stages depend on the project, but the principle remains the same: make important deployment steps explicit and repeatable.

For an AI application, automated checks can cover request validation, authentication, document processing, database behavior, model-client error handling, and API contracts.

Not every test should call a live LLM. Many application tests can use deterministic fake clients to avoid unnecessary cost, network dependencies, and unpredictable model output.

A reliable pipeline should tell you not only that a deployment command completed, but also whether the deployed application is healthy enough to serve requests.

3. Cloud Deployment: Design for the Actual Runtime

Deploying an application to the cloud is not simply a matter of uploading code.

You need to understand the runtime environment, network access, configuration, storage, process management, health checks, and failure behavior.

An AI application might depend on:

  • A FastAPI service for HTTP requests.
  • A relational database for application records.
  • Object storage for uploaded documents.
  • An embedding service or vector database for semantic retrieval.
  • An external LLM provider.
  • Background workers for long-running tasks.

Each dependency creates an operational boundary.

If the model provider becomes slow, should the API wait indefinitely? If document ingestion takes several minutes, should it run inside the original HTTP request? If a deployment restarts the application, what happens to queued work?

These questions influence architecture before the first production incident occurs.

4. Kubernetes: Understand Orchestration Before Adding Complexity

Kubernetes provides mechanisms for deploying and managing containerized workloads, including scheduling, service discovery, health-based restarts, and scaling.

However, Kubernetes is not automatically the right choice for every AI application.

A small service may be easier and cheaper to operate on a managed application platform. A larger system with multiple services, more demanding availability requirements, and established infrastructure practices may benefit from orchestration.

The important engineering skill is understanding the trade-offs.

Before adopting Kubernetes, identify the operational problem you are solving. Then evaluate deployment complexity, resource requirements, observability, scaling behavior, team experience, and ongoing maintenance.

Infrastructure should serve the application rather than become an objective in itself.

5. Observability: Make Failures Investigable

When an AI application fails, a single message saying “Internal Server Error” rarely provides enough information to identify the cause.

Useful observability combines several sources of evidence:

Logs help explain what happened during a request.

Metrics reveal trends such as latency, request volume, error rates, memory consumption, and resource saturation.

Traces help follow a request across services and identify where time is being spent.

AI applications also benefit from measuring model-specific behavior, including provider latency, token usage, timeout frequency, retry counts, and retrieval performance.

For example, a slow response could originate from database access, embedding generation, a remote model call, or a queue that is falling behind. Without useful measurements, those possibilities are difficult to distinguish.

Operational logs must be designed carefully. Avoid recording API keys, access tokens, private documents, or unnecessary personal information. Diagnostic detail should improve investigation without exposing sensitive data.

6. Production Security: Protect the Entire AI Workflow

AI security is not limited to the model itself.

A production system may expose API endpoints, process untrusted files, store confidential information, communicate with external providers, and execute background jobs.

Security therefore needs to be considered across the complete application.

Important areas include:

  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Secret and credential management.
  • Input validation and request-size limits.
  • Dependency and container-image security.
  • Database permissions and secure connections.
  • Rate limiting and abuse prevention.
  • Safe handling of uploaded documents.
  • Appropriate retention and protection of sensitive data.
  • Monitoring for suspicious access and unexpected usage.

An application can produce correct AI outputs and still be insecure if its API exposes data, its credentials are mishandled, or its resource limits are poorly designed.

Security is an architectural responsibility, not a final checklist added just before launch.

7. Scaling and Performance: Measure Before Optimizing

Scaling an AI application involves more than adding servers.

Performance may be limited by database queries, connection pools, synchronous operations, network latency, large request payloads, embedding generation, model-provider limits, or inefficient background processing.

Different bottlenecks require different solutions.

Caching can reduce repeated work when the cached result remains valid. Background jobs can move long-running operations outside the request-response path. Database indexing can improve query performance. Batching may improve throughput when the underlying service supports it. Concurrency controls can help protect limited resources.

But every optimization introduces trade-offs.

Caching creates invalidation questions. Retries can amplify traffic during an outage. Larger batches can increase memory use and response latency. More workers can overwhelm a database or external API.

A sound performance process starts with measurements, identifies the actual bottleneck, applies a targeted change, and measures the result again.

8. Architecture and Production Readiness

A maintainable AI system separates responsibilities instead of placing every operation in one large request handler.

For example:

API Layer
    |
    v
Application Services
    |
    +---- Document Processing
    |
    +---- Embedding and Retrieval
    |
    +---- Model Integration
    |
    +---- Persistence
    |
    +---- Background Jobs
    |
    v
Infrastructure and External Services

The boundaries do not have to correspond to separate microservices. They can begin as modules inside a single application.

The goal is to make responsibilities clear, dependencies explicit, and important behavior testable.

A production-readiness review should ask whether the system can be deployed repeatedly, configured safely, monitored effectively, recovered after failure, and maintained without relying on undocumented manual steps.

What This Book Covers

The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate. focuses on the engineering practices that take AI applications beyond the prototype stage.

The book covers:

  • Docker and containerization.
  • Linux and production operations.
  • Git, GitHub, and engineering workflows.
  • Continuous integration and continuous deployment.
  • Cloud deployment and infrastructure.
  • Kubernetes and cloud-native operations.
  • Observability, logging, and monitoring.
  • Production security.
  • Scaling and performance engineering.
  • AI engineering architecture patterns.
  • Production-readiness reviews.
  • A final engineering challenge and reference materials.

The material is organized around the progression from deployment fundamentals to operating and evaluating a more complete production system.

This volume is intended for Python developers, backend engineers, AI engineers, and software developers who want to understand what happens after an AI application works locally.

It is also useful for engineers who want a more structured way to think about deployment decisions, operational failure modes, and the trade-offs involved in running real-world AI systems.

The Goal Is Not Just to Make It Work

A successful prototype proves that an idea can work.

A production system must also be deployable, observable, secure, recoverable, and maintainable.

That difference is where much of the real engineering begins.

If you are building AI applications and want to strengthen the engineering practices around deployment, infrastructure, monitoring, security, and scaling, explore the book here:

The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate.

https://leanpub.com/theaiengineervolumeiideployscaleoperate

Author: Ahmed Adawy

Build beyond the prototype. Understand the system. Operate it with confidence.

Topics

AI Engineering, Production AI, Python, FastAPI, Docker, CI/CD, Kubernetes, Cloud Deployment, MLOps, Observability, AI Infrastructure, Distributed Systems, Software Architecture, DevOps, Performance Engineering

title: Low-Cost SMS Alert Service Explained — 4 Go Boundaries for Passwordless Backup Account Notifications
description:
TL;DR: Choose an SMS service for passwordless backup alerts and account notifications only after it can produce the evidence your edtech system must retain. For a generated learner report sent as an email attachment, keep four records separate: consent or another approved processing basis, authentication challenge state, report-email state, and SMS delivery observations. Compare Twilio, Vonage, and Telnyx with the same evidence request and controlled test; do not infer compliance, delivery, or security from a low advertised message price.

This is an architecture decision record for a developer portal serving US and EU users. The decision is to own the compliance ledger and treat each communications provider as a replaceable source of observations. That rule sounds conservative because it is: GDPR Article 7 assigns the controller the burden of demonstrating consent when consent is relied upon, while the OWASP Forgot Password guidance requires controls around reset tokens and advises against changing the account before a valid token is presented. A transport receipt answers neither obligation by itself.

How should a low-cost SMS alert service handle passwordless backup account notifications?

Start with reconstruction, not transmission. Given one internal event ID, an authorized reviewer should be able to establish why a recipient was contacted, which channel was requested, which policy applied at that time, whether the report email and the SMS alert diverged, and what later observations arrived. The reviewer should not need raw one-time codes, the learner report, or a phone number copied through routine worker logs.

Four evidence boundaries follow:

  1. Authority: record the purpose, policy version, recipient reference, region classification, and the evidence supporting the chosen processing basis. If consent is the basis, its withdrawal must be as easy to account for as its grant; Article 7 also says consent must be distinguishable, intelligible, and given in clear language.
  2. Authentication: record challenge creation, expiry, attempt outcomes, and consumption without retaining the plaintext code. OWASP says tokens or codes should be generated with a cryptographically secure algorithm, be sufficiently long, be stored securely, be single-use, and expire after an appropriate period.
  3. Document delivery: record report generation, integrity checking, attachment creation, and mail handoff as a lifecycle independent of SMS. The SMS should say that a report is available, not contain report data.
  4. Transport observation: append provider acceptance, callbacks, terminal status, and reconciliation outcomes. Acceptance is evidence of an accepted request. It is not proof that the intended person read the message.

This ordering prevents a common modeling error: one sent Boolean cannot describe four systems with different failure boundaries. A report may be generated while attachment creation fails. An email may be handed off while an SMS request is rejected. A delayed SMS observation may appear after the authentication challenge has expired. None of those facts should overwrite another.

Short records matter.

Compare evidence, not brochure categories

The requested comparison names Twilio, Vonage, and Telnyx, but the supplied facts do not support declaring a universal winner. Their applicable contracts, configured processing locations, sender-registration paths, retention controls, webhook security mechanisms, and status vocabularies must be reviewed in their current documentation and then tested under the same workload. Those are objective differences to capture; they are not safe to assume from a brand name.

Use one dated matrix for all three candidates:

Candidate Contract and data evidence Authentication evidence Delivery and export evidence Decision state
Twilio Record the applicable terms, subprocessors, configured region, retention, and deletion procedure Verify current webhook authentication guidance and whether application-owned expiry, one-time use, and attempt limits remain enforceable Test stable correlation, duplicate events, late events, and export availability Pass, fail, or unresolved per deployment
Vonage Request the same artifacts for the same US/EU scope Run the same challenge-state and callback tests Reconcile the same controlled message corpus against internal IDs Pass, fail, or unresolved per deployment
Telnyx Request the same artifacts for the same US/EU scope Apply the identical security acceptance criteria Measure evidence completeness with the identical reconciliation rules Pass, fail, or unresolved per deployment

The table is intentionally asymmetric in only one respect: each provider will return its own artifacts and observations. The questions do not change. A candidate fails the compliance-evidence gate when an accountable owner cannot retrieve a required artifact, a control cannot be enforced, or a test result cannot be reconciled; an unresolved answer stays unresolved instead of becoming a favorable score.

Cost enters after that gate. Compare total operational cost for the actual destination mix and sender configuration, including failed attempts, registration work, evidence retention, support, and reconciliation labor. Public unit prices are too narrow to support the architectural decision, and they change independently of the evidence obligations.

No price repairs a missing audit trail.

Model the ledger before writing the adapter

The critical path begins when the application commits an immutable intent. It does not begin with an SDK call. The minimal Go example below creates no provider-specific contract, stores no report content, and refuses to pretend that a repeated business event is new work. A production AppendIntent implementation must enforce uniqueness on EventID; an existing ID with a different digest is a collision requiring investigation, while an identical record is an idempotent replay.

package evidence

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Intent struct {
    EventID       string
    RecipientRef  string
    Purpose       string
    PolicyVersion string
    PayloadDigest string
    ExpiresAt     time.Time
}

type Observation struct {
    EventID    string
    ExternalID string
    Kind       string
    ObservedAt time.Time
}

type Ledger interface {
    AppendIntent(context.Context, Intent) (created bool, err error)
    AppendObservation(context.Context, Observation) error
}

type Transport interface {
    Send(context.Context, string, string, string) (string, error)
}

type Service struct {
    ledger    Ledger
    transport Transport
    now       func() time.Time
}

func (s Service) SendReportAlert(
    ctx context.Context,
    eventID string,
    recipientRef string,
    phoneToken string,
    policyVersion string,
) error {
    if eventID == "" || recipientRef == "" || policyVersion == "" {
        return errors.New("missing evidence identity")
    }

    body := "Your learner report is ready. Sign in to the portal to view it."
    digest := sha256.Sum256([]byte(body))
    intent := Intent{
        EventID:       eventID,
        RecipientRef:  recipientRef,
        Purpose:       "report_ready",
        PolicyVersion: policyVersion,
        PayloadDigest: hex.EncodeToString(digest[:]),
        ExpiresAt:     s.now().Add(15 * time.Minute),
    }

    created, err := s.ledger.AppendIntent(ctx, intent)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !created {
        return nil
    }

    externalID, err := s.transport.Send(ctx, eventID, phoneToken, body)
    if err != nil {
        return s.ledger.AppendObservation(ctx, Observation{
            EventID: eventID, Kind: "request_failed", ObservedAt: s.now(),
        })
    }

    return s.ledger.AppendObservation(ctx, Observation{
        EventID: eventID, ExternalID: externalID,
        Kind: "request_accepted", ObservedAt: s.now(),
    })
}

The 15-minute value is an application policy in this example, not a universal recommendation or a provider guarantee. Record the policy version so a future reviewer can distinguish a code defect from a deliberate policy change. The phoneToken is an opaque reference resolved inside the adapter, which narrows exposure in queue payloads; it does not remove the controller's duties for the underlying personal data. Similarly, SHA-256 supplies a comparison digest here, not encryption or authorization.

There is an uncomfortable edge at the external boundary. If a provider accepts the request and the process loses its connection before recording the returned ID, a retry can create a second message unless that transport supports and honors the application's idempotency key. The ledger must preserve the ambiguous outcome. Exactly-once business intent is enforceable in the application database; exactly-once handset delivery is not a claim this design makes.

Operate it as a reconciliation system

Testing should interrogate evidence completeness. Replay the same callback twice. Deliver a later status before an earlier status. Submit an unknown external ID. Expire a challenge before a late delivery observation arrives. Confirm that routine logs expose neither the one-time code nor contact data, and verify that report-email events can be reconstructed without joining them to SMS payloads.

Deployment proceeds by destination class and sender configuration because one route does not establish another route's behavior. Canary traffic should use synthetic accounts and should validate correlation, redaction, and callback handling before real account notifications move. The useful operational signals are aging intents, unmatched external IDs, duplicate observations, expired challenges followed by delivery, and divergence between the report-email lifecycle and its optional alert. Raw send count is an activity measure, not evidence of correctness.

Retention deserves an explicit schedule. Keep the minimum fields needed for the stated purpose and legal basis, restrict access, and document deletion behavior; do not preserve authentication secrets merely because audit records are valuable. GDPR Article 7 supplies specific consent conditions, but it does not convert every communication purpose into consent, so the organization's legal owner must identify and document the applicable basis rather than letting application code guess.

The rejected shortcut still has one valid home

The rejected option is a synchronous controller that generates the report, attaches it to email, sends the message, sends an SMS, and returns one success value. It resembles a transaction while spanning systems that do not share the application's database commit. A retry can duplicate one channel, and suppressing the retry can lose the other; worse, the single result erases which obligation was actually satisfied.

That shortcut remains valid for a local template preview using sink transports, synthetic recipients, and no assertion about delivery. It gives a developer quick visual feedback without becoming an evidence model.

For production, the report-ready state and an outbox record should commit in one database transaction, while separate workers advance email and SMS observations with bounded retries and reviewable dead letters. SMS should remain a backup channel rather than the only recovery route, since the OWASP guidance explicitly recommends a consistent forgot-password process, side-channel delivery of reset material, single-use expiry, and protection against excessive submissions. The final decision packet should contain the four-boundary data model, the dated three-candidate matrix, test evidence, named control owners, and unresolved risks. That packet is the product of the comparison. The provider is one replaceable dependency inside it.

This design has limitations. Its audit quality depends on disciplined policy versioning, access control, retention work, reconciliation ownership, and review of ambiguous outcomes; a small team that cannot operate those controls should choose an independently assessed managed authentication system for the passwordless flow and keep report email separate. The trade-off is direct control over evidence in exchange for database, queue, privacy, and on-call responsibilities. It also remains unsuitable wherever SMS cannot be an acceptable backup factor under the organization's security assessment.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-7-gdpr/

title: Stress-test a card with longer content before adding breakpoints
description:
A card that fits “Design” may fail when its title becomes “Website design for international service businesses.”

Before adding another breakpoint, change the content. Longer headings, translated labels and a missing image can reveal assumptions that resizing the viewport alone will miss.

Start with a deliberately fragile component

Paste this into a static HTML preview or a local file:

<style>
  * { box-sizing: border-box; }
  body { margin: 0; padding: 16px; font: 16px/1.5 system-ui; }
  .card { width: 420px; border: 1px solid #777; padding: 20px; }
  h2 { margin-block: 0 12px; }
</style>
<article class="card">
  <h2>Design</h2>
  <p>A practical service for your next website project.</p>
  <a href="#">Read more</a>
</article>

At a 375px viewport, the page has only 343px after its two 16px gutters. A 420px card cannot fit. This follows from the example's dimensions; it is not a new measured test result.

A smaller font would hide the wrong problem. The card itself is wider than the available space.

Fix the constraint you found

Replace the card rule:

.card {
  inline-size: 100%;
  max-inline-size: 420px;
  border: 1px solid #777;
  padding: 20px;
}

Then test a long title and a longer link label. Avoid a fixed card height unless the design has a clear reason for one and an explicit strategy for overflowing content.

The width change makes this example fit the available inline space. It does not prove that a larger component with images or nested grids has no other problems.

Compare the same content at three widths

I use 375, 768 and 1200px as a quick comparison set. At each width, inspect:

  • Whether anything extends beyond the content area.
  • Whether text overlaps or clips, even without a horizontal scrollbar.
  • Whether longer labels wrap in a useful way.
  • Whether hiding an image leaves an awkward gap or removes needed information.

These are starting points. Your project may need narrower or intermediate checks too.

Keep automated overflow results in their lane

On 17 October 2026, the built-in example in my Responsive Content Tester was checked with its Long translation preset. It rendered all three comparison widths and reported no horizontal overflow at any of them.

That result applies to that example. It says nothing about the deliberately fragile card above until you run it, and it does not certify clipping, readability or accessibility.

Try content variations

I maintain the free Responsive Content Tester. Paste HTML with inline CSS, apply the longer-content preset, compare Original and With tests, then run the three-width comparison.

The preview blocks scripts and external files and does not fetch a live website URL. It is useful for a static layout experiment, not for reproducing an application's complete runtime or testing another browser engine.

After the experiment, apply the relevant change in your actual project and test the saved page again. The preview helps identify a question; the real page provides the final context.

Disclosure: I maintain the linked tool or kit. This article was prepared with AI assistance. Practical checks are identified separately from illustrative examples; verify the result in your own project.

title: Turborepo and Vercel Remote Cache now support OpenID Connect (OIDC)
description:
You can now exchange OIDC tokens from CI/CD workflows, including GitHub workflows, for short-lived Turborepo access tokens.

These tokens grant access to Vercel's Remote Cache, and are a more secure alternative to long-lived Personal Access Tokens (PATs). OIDC tokens are short-lived, only grant access to Vercel Remote Cache, and are associated with your Vercel team, rather than a specific team member.

We recommend all customers migrate their CI/CD workflows from PATs to OIDC.

Get started by adding a Turborepo OIDC policy under Settings → Build and Deployment → OIDC Policies for CLI Access and learn more in the documentation.

Read more

title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

title: A footer saying "generated by AI" is not a machine-readable mark
description:
Article 50 of the EU AI Act asks two different things about synthetic content, and only one of them is a wording problem. A sentence under an image telling the reader it was generated by AI discharges the duty to disclose. It embeds nothing in the file, and 50(2) wants a mark inside the content, detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Compliance checklists tend to collapse both into one row ("AI content is labelled"), and that row is true and useless at once.

We hit this while building disclosurekit, a package that works out which parts of Article 50 apply to a system, says what a notice has to contain and where it has to appear, and keeps the record. It does not write the notice and it does not mark content. The second disclaimer is the one worth dwelling on, because a library that quietly let wording stand in for a watermark would be worse than no library at all. It would hand you a green assessment for a system that is not marking anything.

The duty with no wording

The article is short. Five duties, one table: who owes it, when it bites, what has to happen, what can excuse it. The 50(2) row reads like this. The provider owes it, it bites when the system generates or manipulates synthetic audio, image, video or text, and what has to happen is that a machine-readable mark is embedded in the content. It is excused by assistive standard editing that does not substantially alter the input, or by authorised law enforcement. Nothing in that row mentions a sentence, a footer, a tooltip or a header. No wording can satisfy it, because the obligation is about the artefact and not about the reader.

The 50(4) deep-fake row sits immediately below it and works the other way round: the whole duty is to disclose, and a sentence is exactly how you do that. So one image pipeline can owe both duties at once, and exactly one of them closes by writing something.

That asymmetry is the thing to model. In disclosurekit it is a field on the requirement, derived from whether the measure has any wording elements at all:

function requirementsOf(assessment: Assessment): readonly Requirement[] {
  return measures(assessment).map((measure) => {
    const spec = REQUIRED[measure];
    return {
      measure,
      obligations: assessment.applies
        .filter((applied) => applied.obligation.measure === measure)
        .map((applied) => applied.obligation.id),
      elements: spec.elements.map((id) => ELEMENTS[id]),
      placement: spec.placement,
      satisfiedByText: spec.elements.length > 0,
    };
  });
}

REQUIRED["mark-machine-readable"] has an empty elements list, so satisfiedByText comes back false and there is no element for a caller to write wording against. Its placement does not point at a page or a response either, it says the mark goes inside the content. A pipeline that generates images of real places owes both rows, and the requirements come back in that order:

const profile: SystemProfile = { role: "both", generatesSyntheticContent: true, deepfake: true };

requirements(profile).map((r) => r.measure);
// ["mark-machine-readable", "disclose-artificial-content"]

const [marking] = requirements(profile);
marking.satisfiedByText; // false
marking.elements;        // []
marking.placement.where; // inside the content

Once the distinction is a boolean on a row rather than a paragraph in a policy document, the rest follows mechanically.

What the notice is, and what reading it does not accomplish

disclose() takes the profile and the caller's wording and returns the disclosure. The statement is the caller's words. We take the view that a package cannot write a sentence in a language it has not read, and that the only failure a library can honestly catch is a blank. So element wording is trimmed, anything empty raises IncompleteDisclosure naming each Element.must, so the error tells you what the missing sentence was supposed to get across. What survives is deduped and joined in element order:

  const machineReadable: Record<string, string> = {};
  if (obligations.length > 0) {
    machineReadable[DISCLOSURE_HEADER] = obligations.join(", ");
  }

  return {
    statement: [...new Set(elements.map(wording))].join(" "),
    elements,
    obligations,
    unmetByStatement: required.filter((r) => !r.satisfiedByText).map((r) => r.measure),
    machineReadable,
    notes,
    locale: notice.locale,
  };

Two fields on that object carry the whole argument of this post. statement is what the person reads. unmetByStatement is the list of measures that reading it does not accomplish. For the image pipeline above the statement is one sentence and unmetByStatement is ["mark-machine-readable"]. The AI-Disclosure header names both obligations, art50-2, art50-4-deepfake, and it is only set when something actually applies, so a system that owes nothing does not advertise a header claiming it owes nothing.

The second field is not an error. It is not a warning either. It is part of the normal, successful return value of a function that just built a perfectly valid notice. The notice is correct, it is simply not the whole duty, and the type refuses to let you forget that by making the gap a value you have to look at.

A marker that admits it is not a marker

The package ships a Marker interface and one implementation, UnmarkedContent:

const result = await new UnmarkedContent().mark({ content: pixels, mediaType: "image/png" });
result.marked; // false
result.method;  // "none"

It returns marked: false, method "none", and a detail saying Article 50(2) is not met. That is the honest default for a package that is not in the business of re-encoding files. Embedding a detectable mark is a format and provenance problem, so it belongs wherever the bytes are produced, not in a wrapper that only ever sees a finished Response and cannot touch the inside of a PNG without decoding and re-encoding it. What the wrapper can do is refuse to pretend. A default marker returning marked: true with method "footer" would probably be the most damaging line of code in the repository.

The gap goes into the record, not into a ticket

The reason to compute unmetByStatement at all is that somebody will ask about it months later, by which time the footer will have been reworded twice and the pipeline replaced. So recordDecision writes it into the evidence log next to everything else that went into the decision:

  return log.append("assessment", {
    inputs: inputsOf(profile),
    applies: assessment.applies.map(({ obligation, note }) => ({ ... })),
    excluded: assessment.excluded.map(({ obligation, because }) => ({ ... })),
    needsReview: assessment.needsReview.map(({ obligation, question }) => ({ ... })),
    unmetByStatement: disclosure?.unmetByStatement,
    elements: disclosure?.elements,
    statement: disclosure?.statement,
    locale: disclosure?.locale,
  });

The entry is written to be legible on its own. It repeats each obligation's article and summary rather than only its id, keeps the reason for every exemption and the text of every unanswered question, and records an input nobody answered as "not stated" rather than as a false on the operator's behalf. Entries are hash-chained, verify() walks the chain, and toJSONL() exports one canonical record per line. Those are the same bytes that were hashed, so a line can be checked where it lies, and the file greps with tools that have never heard of the package.

The result is a record that says, in one place: these duties applied, this is what we told people, in these words, in this locale, and this duty was not covered by saying it. That is a much better artefact than a green checkmark, because it reads the same whether or not anyone got round to wiring up a marker.

Where the failure lands

withDisclosure builds the notice once, at wrap time, and records the decision at the same moment:

export function withDisclosure(
  handler: Handler,
  profile: SystemProfile,
  options: MiddlewareOptions = {},
): Handler {
  const disclosure = disclose(profile, options);
  if (options.log) recordDecision(options.log, profile, disclosure);
  ...

So a profile with wording missing for a required element throws where the service starts up, not in front of a user mid-request. The same holds for an unanswered question. An input given as "unknown" sends the obligation to needsReview, and disclose() refuses to build a notice while a question is open. A service that cannot say what it owes does not boot.

What it costs to run

Almost nothing per request. The assessment and the notice are computed once per wrapped handler. Per response the middleware copies headers, sets the disclosure header, optionally injects the statement into a JSON body under a key you name explicitly, and appends one log line recording the path, method, obligations, statement and locale. Bodies are otherwise untouched, since silently reshaping a service's response is the kind of surprise that gets a library deleted.

The real cost is the one the library makes visible. If your pipeline owes 50(2), you still have to mark the bytes, and no amount of good wording moves that line. What the model buys you is that the gap has a name, a place in the return value, and a line in the record, instead of living in the space between a footer and a checklist, where nobody is looking.

Originally published on shipmindlabs.com — where we write about payment systems, infrastructure and marketplace backends.

title: iMessage support for eve agents
description:
eve agents can now connect to iMessage through the new Photon channel.

The channel keeps each iMessage conversation in one eve session, verifies incoming webhooks, and marks accepted messages as read.

If more messages arrive while the agent is replying, they steer the in-progress reply instead of each getting a separate answer. The onMessage hook filters which messages the agent handles and adds context to a turn.

Run eve add channel/photon-imessage to add the channel. iMessage delivery runs through Photon, so the command sets up a Photon project, registers your phone number, and scaffolds the channel:

eve uses Vercel Connect to create the connector and configure Photon's webhook. On hosts without Connect support, choose Use portable credentials during setup and the channel reads its credentials from environment variables instead.

Read the Photon channel docs to get started, or deploy an agent from a template.
