title: Cross-Tab and Cross-Browser Communication
description:
Cross-Tab and Cross-Browser Communication

A practical guide to communication between tabs, windows, iframes, and workers in one browser instance, plus communication across browser instances and devices.

Table of Contents

  1. Start With the Communication Boundary
  2. What the Browser Provides by Default
  3. BroadcastChannel
  4. The localStorage Storage Event
  5. window.postMessage and MessageChannel
  6. SharedWorker
  7. Service Worker as a Relay
  8. IndexedDB and Web Locks
  9. A Production Cross-Tab Event Bus
  10. Common Cross Tab Use Cases
  11. Leader Election and Single Owner Work
  12. Cross Browser Instances and Devices
  13. Server Mediated Real Time Architecture
  14. Reliability, Ordering and Replay
  15. Security and Privacy
  16. Decision Guide
  17. Testing and Observability
  18. Interview Questions and Answers

1. Start With the Communication Boundary

Before choosing an API, identify which contexts must communicate.

Same JavaScript context
  └─ components/modules in one page

Related browsing contexts
  ├─ parent ↔ iframe
  ├─ opener ↔ popup
  └─ page ↔ dedicated worker

Same origin + same browser instance
  ├─ Chrome Tab 1 ↔ Chrome Tab 2
  ├─ Chrome Window 1 ↔ Chrome Window 2
  ├─ SharedWorker clients
  └─ Service Worker clients

Outside that browser instance
  ├─ Chrome instance ↔ Firefox instance
  ├─ browser ↔ desktop/mobile app
  └─ device A ↔ device B

The most important distinction

For this guide, a browser instance means one running browser environment containing its tabs and windows. For example, Chrome Tab 1 and Chrome Tab 2 belong to the same Chrome instance.

The practical boundary is usually:

Same origin + same browser instance

Tabs inside that boundary can use browser-native communication. A different browser instance or device needs a shared external system—normally your backend.

Scope matrix

Contexts Direct browser communication? Typical option
Components in one page Yes In-memory event bus or state store
Parent and known iframe/popup Yes postMessage
Chrome Tab 1 and Tab 2 on the same origin Yes BroadcastChannel, storage, SharedWorker
Two Chrome windows on the same origin in one browser instance Yes BroadcastChannel, storage, SharedWorker
Different origins Restricted postMessage for related windows; otherwise backend
Chrome instance and Firefox instance No direct local channel Backend
Two separate browser instances No direct local channel Backend
Different devices No direct local channel Backend

Example: Chrome Tab 1 and Tab 2

Suppose both tabs are open in the same Chrome instance:

Tab 1: https://shop.example.com/products
Tab 2: https://shop.example.com/cart

Both URLs have the same origin:

protocol: https
host:     shop.example.com
port:     443 (the default HTTPS port)

Tab 1 can notify Tab 2 when an item is added to the cart.

Tab 1:

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('shop-events');

channel.postMessage({
  type: 'cart:item-added',
  productId: 'P-100',
});

Tab 2:

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('shop-events');

channel.addEventListener('message', event => {
  if (event.data.type === 'cart:item-added') {
    refreshCart();
  }
});

This works because both pages use the same origin and open a channel with the same name, shop-events.

It would not work directly if Tab 2 used https://admin.example.com, because that is a different origin.

Example: two Chrome windows

The same rule applies when the pages are in separate Chrome windows:

Chrome Window 1: https://shop.example.com/dashboard
Chrome Window 2: https://shop.example.com/orders

The pages can still use the same BroadcastChannel. Moving a tab into another Chrome window does not change its origin or prevent browser-managed communication.

For example, Window 1 can announce a logout:

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('auth-events');
channel.postMessage({ type: 'auth:logged-out' });

Window 2 listens for it:

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('auth-events');

channel.addEventListener('message', event => {
  if (event.data.type === 'auth:logged-out') {
    window.location.assign('/login');
  }
});

The important rule is not whether the pages are displayed as tabs or separate windows. They can communicate when they are in the same browser instance, use the same origin, and use the same channel name.

Back to Top

2. What the Browser Provides by Default

No library is required for the browser's core communication APIs.

API Scope Message or shared state? Durable? Best use
BroadcastChannel Same origin in one browser instance Message No General cross-tab events
storage event Same origin using localStorage Change notification Value persists Compatibility fallback, simple signals
window.postMessage Related windows/iframes Message No Popup/iframe communication
MessageChannel Two contexts with transferred ports Message No Private point-to-point channel
SharedWorker Same-origin tabs supported by the browser Shared process/state + ports Worker lifetime only One socket or shared in-memory coordinator
Service Worker Controlled pages for one origin Message/relay Worker is event-driven Page coordination plus network/offline logic
IndexedDB Same origin in one browser instance Shared durable storage Yes Shared source of truth
Web Locks Same origin in one browser instance Coordination, not messaging Lock lifetime only Ensure one tab performs a task

Browser support is part of the design

Support and lifecycle behavior vary, especially for SharedWorker, service workers, and background throttling. Build capability detection and choose an explicit fallback rather than assuming every API exists.

const capabilities = {
  broadcastChannel: 'BroadcastChannel' in globalThis,
  sharedWorker: 'SharedWorker' in globalThis,
  serviceWorker: 'serviceWorker' in navigator,
  webLocks: 'locks' in navigator,
  indexedDB: 'indexedDB' in globalThis,
};

Back to Top

3. BroadcastChannel

BroadcastChannel is the simplest general-purpose API for same-origin cross-tab messaging.

Tab A ─┐
Tab B ─┼── channel: "app-events"
Tab C ─┘

Basic example 

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('app-events');

channel.addEventListener('message', event => {
  console.log('Received:', event.data);
});

channel.postMessage({
  type: 'cart:item-added',
  payload: { productId: 'P-100', quantity: 1 },
});

// When this tab no longer needs the channel:
channel.close();

What it gives you

  • One-to-many delivery to listening contexts
  • Structured-clone payloads, not JSON-only strings
  • No need to know which tabs exist
  • No mutation of persistent browser storage
  • Simple lifecycle and small API surface

What it does not give you

  • Durable history or replay
  • Delivery acknowledgement
  • Guaranteed delivery to sleeping, frozen, or closed tabs
  • Cross-origin communication
  • Communication across separate browser instances
  • A central owner for shared state or one shared WebSocket

Delivery semantics

Treat it as best-effort notification:

  1. Update the authoritative state.
  2. Broadcast that something changed.
  3. Receivers re-read or reconcile the source of truth.

For example, send cart:invalidated rather than assuming a full cart snapshot reached every tab.

Back to Top

4. The localStorage Storage Event

Changing localStorage in one tab produces a storage event in other same-origin tabs.

const EVENT_KEY = 'app:cross-tab-event';

window.addEventListener('storage', event => {
  if (event.key !== EVENT_KEY || event.newValue === null) return;

  const message = JSON.parse(event.newValue);
  console.log('Received:', message);
});

function publish(message) {
  localStorage.setItem(
    EVENT_KEY,
    JSON.stringify({
      ...message,
      id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      sentAt: Date.now(),
    })
  );

  localStorage.removeItem(EVENT_KEY);
}

Important behavior

  • The tab that calls setItem does not receive its own storage event.
  • Values are strings, so serialization is required.
  • localStorage operations are synchronous and can block the main thread.
  • Storage can be unavailable or restricted.
  • Reusing an identical value may not produce the change behavior you expect; include a unique ID.

When to use it

  • Compatibility fallback when BroadcastChannel is unavailable
  • Low-frequency signals such as logout, theme changes, or cache invalidation
  • Cases where the persisted value itself is useful

When not to use it

  • High-frequency events
  • Large payloads
  • Streaming updates
  • Secrets or authentication tokens
  • A queue requiring reliable delivery

Back to Top

5. window.postMessage and MessageChannel

window.postMessage

Use postMessage when contexts have a direct relationship:

  • Parent page and iframe
  • Window and popup opened with window.open
  • Embedded micro frontend and host shell 
const popup = window.open('/payment', 'payment-window');

popup?.postMessage(
  { type: 'payment:start', orderId: 'O-100' },
  'https://app.example.com'
);

Receiver:

window.addEventListener('message', event => {
  if (event.origin !== 'https://app.example.com') return;
  if (event.source !== window.opener) return;

  const message = event.data;
  if (message?.type === 'payment:start') {
    startPayment(message.orderId);
  }
});

Never use '*' as targetOrigin for sensitive messages. Validate origin, source, message type, and payload.

MessageChannel

MessageChannel creates two connected ports. Transfer one port to another context to establish a private point-to-point channel.

const channel = new MessageChannel();

channel.port1.onmessage = event => {
  console.log('Reply:', event.data);
};

iframe.contentWindow?.postMessage(
  { type: 'connect' },
  'https://app.example.com',
  [channel.port2]
);

channel.port1.postMessage({ type: 'ping' });

This is useful when a host wants to give one embedded context a dedicated communication port instead of sharing all traffic on window.

Limitation

Unrelated tabs do not automatically have references to each other. Use BroadcastChannel, a worker relay, or the backend for discovery and communication between arbitrary tabs.

Back to Top

6. SharedWorker

A SharedWorker is one worker context shared by multiple same-origin tabs or windows.

Tab A ── MessagePort ─┐
Tab B ── MessagePort ─┼── SharedWorker ── one WebSocket ── Server
Tab C ── MessagePort ─┘

Shared worker 

// shared-connection-worker.js
const ports = new Set();
let socket;

function broadcast(message) {
  for (const port of ports) {
    port.postMessage(message);
  }
}

function ensureSocket() {
  if (socket && socket.readyState <= WebSocket.OPEN) return;

  socket = new WebSocket('wss://api.example.com/events');
  socket.addEventListener('message', event => {
    broadcast({
      type: 'server:event',
      payload: JSON.parse(event.data),
    });
  });
}

self.addEventListener('connect', event => {
  const [port] = event.ports;
  ports.add(port);
  port.start();
  ensureSocket();

  port.addEventListener('message', messageEvent => {
    if (messageEvent.data?.type === 'disconnect') {
      ports.delete(port);
      port.close();
    }
  });
});

Tab 

const worker = new SharedWorker('/shared-connection-worker.js', {
  name: 'app-connection',
});

worker.port.start();
worker.port.addEventListener('message', event => {
  handleServerEvent(event.data);
});

window.addEventListener('pagehide', () => {
  worker.port.postMessage({ type: 'disconnect' });
  worker.port.close();
});

Best uses

  • One WebSocket shared by all tabs
  • Shared in-memory state
  • Request deduplication
  • One centralized coordinator
  • Cross-tab work distribution

Trade-offs

  • Support and lifecycle behavior must be verified for target browsers.
  • The worker can terminate when no clients remain.
  • It is not a durable data store.
  • Authentication refresh and reconnect logic still need careful design.
  • A broken worker can affect every connected tab.

Back to Top

7. Service Worker as a Relay

A service worker can find controlled windows and relay messages.

Service worker 

self.addEventListener('message', async event => {
  const clients = await self.clients.matchAll({
    type: 'window',
    includeUncontrolled: false,
  });

  for (const client of clients) {
    if (client.id === event.source?.id) continue;
    client.postMessage(event.data);
  }
});

Page 

navigator.serviceWorker.addEventListener('message', event => {
  handleCrossTabMessage(event.data);
});

async function publish(message) {
  const registration = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
  registration.active?.postMessage(message);
}

Best uses

  • Coordination already tied to offline/network behavior
  • Push notification fan-out to open pages
  • Cache invalidation after background sync
  • Messaging between controlled pages and the service worker

Important lifecycle rule

A service worker is event-driven and can be stopped between events. Do not treat its global variables as durable shared state. Store durable state in IndexedDB and use messages as signals.

Newly opened pages may not be controlled until navigation or clients.claim() is used during activation.

Back to Top

8. IndexedDB and Web Locks

These APIs solve coordination problems rather than replacing a message bus.

IndexedDB as shared durable state

All same-origin tabs in the same browser instance can read the same IndexedDB database.

Good pattern:

Tab A writes durable record to IndexedDB
  -> Tab A broadcasts { type: "record:changed", id: "R-100" }
  -> Tab B receives the signal
  -> Tab B reads the current record from IndexedDB

This avoids sending large payloads and lets a tab recover after missing a transient message.

Handle versionchange so old tabs close stale database connections during schema upgrades:

database.addEventListener('versionchange', () => {
  database.close();
  showReloadRequired();
});

Web Locks for single-owner work

The Web Locks API ensures that only one same-origin context holds a named lock at a time.

async function tryBecomeSyncLeader(signal) {
  return navigator.locks.request(
    'background-sync-leader',
    { ifAvailable: true, signal },
    async lock => {
      if (!lock) return false;

      await runSyncLoop(signal);
      return true;
    }
  );
}

The lock remains held until the callback's promise settles.

Use Web Locks for:

  • One tab performs polling
  • One tab refreshes a shared cache
  • One tab processes an IndexedDB queue
  • Avoiding concurrent migrations

Web Locks do not send results to other tabs. Pair them with BroadcastChannel or shared storage.

Back to Top

9. A Production Cross-Tab Event Bus

A wrapper gives the application one contract with a BroadcastChannel primary path and storage fallback.

type EventMap = {
  'auth:logged-out': { reason: string };
  'cart:invalidated': { cartId: string };
  'theme:changed': { theme: 'light' | 'dark' };
};

type Envelope<K extends keyof EventMap = keyof EventMap> = {
  id: string;
  sourceId: string;
  type: K;
  version: 1;
  sentAt: number;
  payload: EventMap[K];
};

class CrossTabBus {
  #sourceId = crypto.randomUUID();
  #storageKey: string;
  #channel?: BroadcastChannel;
  #handlers = new Map<keyof EventMap, Set<(payload: never) => void>>();

  constructor(name: string) {
    this.#storageKey = `cross-tab:${name}`;

    if ('BroadcastChannel' in globalThis) {
      this.#channel = new BroadcastChannel(name);
      this.#channel.addEventListener('message', event => {
        this.#receive(event.data);
      });
    } else {
      window.addEventListener('storage', this.#onStorage);
    }
  }

  publish<K extends keyof EventMap>(type: K, payload: EventMap[K]) {
    const envelope: Envelope<K> = {
      id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      sourceId: this.#sourceId,
      type,
      version: 1,
      sentAt: Date.now(),
      payload,
    };

    // BroadcastChannel and storage events do not deliver to the sender.
    this.#receive(envelope);

    if (this.#channel) {
      this.#channel.postMessage(envelope);
      return;
    }

    localStorage.setItem(this.#storageKey, JSON.stringify(envelope));
    localStorage.removeItem(this.#storageKey);
  }

  subscribe<K extends keyof EventMap>(
    type: K,
    handler: (payload: EventMap[K]) => void
  ) {
    const handlers = this.#handlers.get(type) ?? new Set();
    handlers.add(handler as (payload: never) => void);
    this.#handlers.set(type, handlers);

    return () => handlers.delete(handler as (payload: never) => void);
  }

  close() {
    this.#channel?.close();
    window.removeEventListener('storage', this.#onStorage);
    this.#handlers.clear();
  }

  #onStorage = (event: StorageEvent) => {
    if (event.key !== this.#storageKey || event.newValue === null) return;
    this.#receive(JSON.parse(event.newValue));
  };

  #receive(envelope: Envelope) {
    if (!this.#isValid(envelope)) return;

    const handlers = this.#handlers.get(envelope.type);
    for (const handler of handlers ?? []) {
      handler(envelope.payload as never);
    }
  }

  #isValid(value: unknown): value is Envelope {
    if (typeof value !== 'object' || value === null) return false;
    const candidate = value as Partial<Envelope>;

    return (
      typeof candidate.id === 'string' &&
      typeof candidate.sourceId === 'string' &&
      typeof candidate.type === 'string' &&
      candidate.version === 1 &&
      typeof candidate.sentAt === 'number'
    );
  }
}

Production additions

  • Deduplicate recent message IDs.
  • Expire messages older than an allowed clock-skew window.
  • Validate each payload with a runtime schema.
  • Add event-version migration rules.
  • Record publish/receive/drop metrics.
  • Do not send secrets.
  • Use invalidation events when the payload can be re-read.

Back to Top

10. Common Cross-Tab Use Cases

10.1 Logout across tabs in one browser instance 

bus.subscribe('auth:logged-out', () => {
  clearInMemoryAuthState();
  router.navigate('/login');
});

async function logout() {
  await api.logout();
  clearInMemoryAuthState();
  bus.publish('auth:logged-out', { reason: 'user-requested' });
  router.navigate('/login');
}

The server must still invalidate the session. A cross-tab event improves UX but is not the security boundary.

10.2 Theme and preference sync

Persist the preference, then broadcast its new version.

function setTheme(theme) {
  localStorage.setItem('theme', theme);
  bus.publish('theme:changed', { theme });
}

10.3 Cache invalidation 

bus.subscribe('cart:invalidated', ({ cartId }) => {
  queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['cart', cartId] });
});

Invalidation is safer than treating transient messages as the only copy of state.

10.4 Prevent duplicate notifications

Elect one owner to show system notifications while every tab can still update its visible UI.

10.5 Draft coordination

Store drafts in IndexedDB and broadcast document version changes. If two tabs edit simultaneously, use version checks, conflict resolution, or a collaborative protocol rather than last-write-wins by accident.

10.6 Single background poller

One tab holds a Web Lock and polls the server. It writes results to IndexedDB and broadcasts invalidations to other tabs.

Back to Top

11. Leader Election and Single-Owner Work

Leader election is useful when only one tab should:

  • Poll the server
  • Maintain a connection
  • Process an offline queue
  • Display a system notification
  • Refresh shared data

Prefer a platform coordinator

Use, in order:

  1. SharedWorker when one shared runtime/connection is the design
  2. Web Locks when one tab should temporarily own a task
  3. A backend lease when ownership must span browser instances or devices

Why a localStorage lease is risky

A naive lease uses read-modify-write operations:

Tab A reads "no leader"
Tab B reads "no leader"
Tab A writes "A is leader"
Tab B writes "B is leader"
Both believe they won

localStorage does not provide a compare-and-swap transaction. A timestamp lease can reduce collisions but cannot provide strong distributed-lock guarantees.

Leases need fencing

For critical server-side work, issue a monotonically increasing fencing token:

leader A gets token 41
leader A pauses
leader B gets token 42
server rejects later writes carrying stale token 41

Do not rely on a browser tab as the exclusive owner of financially or operationally critical work. Put correctness on the server.

Back to Top

12. Cross-Browser Instances and Devices

What “cross-browser” can mean

Scenario Browser-local APIs work?
Chrome Tab 1 and Tab 2 in the same Chrome instance Yes
Two Chrome windows in the same Chrome instance Yes
Chrome instance and Firefox instance No
Two separate browser instances No
Browser and mobile app No
Laptop and phone No

Browser-local APIs connect tabs and windows inside one browser instance. They do not create a direct channel to another browser instance. For example, a Chrome instance cannot open a BroadcastChannel directly to a Firefox instance.

The shared meeting point

Use infrastructure both clients can reach:

Chrome tab ──┐
Firefox tab ─┼── HTTPS / WebSocket / SSE ── Backend ── shared state/event broker
Mobile app ──┘

Possible transports:

  • WebSocket for bidirectional real-time messaging
  • SSE for server-to-client streams
  • Short or long polling as fallback
  • Push notifications for background delivery
  • WebRTC for peer-to-peer data after server-based signaling

WebRTC does not remove the need for discovery, authentication, signaling, and usually a relay fallback.

Back to Top

13. Server-Mediated Real-Time Architecture

Reference architecture 

Browser instance/device A
        |
        | WebSocket + authenticated session
        v
Connection Gateway
        |
        +── Presence/connection registry
        |
        +── Event broker ── durable event store
        |
        +── Authorization service
        |
        v
Connection Gateway
        |
        v
Browser instance/device B

Connection identity

Model at least:

  • userId
  • sessionId
  • deviceId
  • connectionId
  • Optional tabId

One user can have many active connections. Route events to the intended scope:

user scope     -> every session/device for the user
session scope  -> tabs sharing one login session
device scope   -> one device
connection     -> one socket/tab

Example event 

{
  "id": "evt_01J...",
  "type": "cart.updated",
  "version": 2,
  "sequence": 1842,
  "occurredAt": "2026-10-17T10:00:00Z",
  "scope": {
    "userId": "U-100"
  },
  "payload": {
    "cartId": "C-900",
    "revision": 17
  }
}

Client flow

  1. Authenticate the connection.
  2. Subscribe only to authorized scopes.
  3. Receive an event with ID, version, and sequence.
  4. Deduplicate by event ID.
  5. Detect sequence gaps.
  6. Re-fetch authoritative state or request replay.
  7. Apply the update.
  8. Persist the last processed cursor if required.

Back to Top

14. Reliability, Ordering and Replay

Local browser channels

BroadcastChannel, storage, and worker messages are useful notifications, but do not treat them as a durable event log.

Tabs can:

  • Open after an event was sent
  • Sleep or freeze
  • Crash
  • Miss a transient message
  • Process events at different times

Reliable-state pattern 

Authoritative state: server or IndexedDB
Transient message: "state changed"
Recovery: read current version/snapshot

Event envelope

Include:

  • Unique message ID
  • Source context ID
  • Event type
  • Schema version
  • Timestamp
  • Entity revision or sequence
  • Payload

Ordering

Do not assume unrelated publishers create one global order.

Use:

  • Per-entity revisions
  • Per-stream sequence numbers
  • Server-assigned order where required
  • Conflict-resolution rules

Deduplication

Maintain a bounded set of recent event IDs:

class RecentIds {
  #ids = new Map();

  constructor(maxSize = 1_000) {
    this.maxSize = maxSize;
  }

  has(id) {
    return this.#ids.has(id);
  }

  add(id) {
    this.#ids.set(id, true);
    while (this.#ids.size > this.maxSize) {
      this.#ids.delete(this.#ids.keys().next().value);
    }
  }
}

Reconnection

After reconnect:

  1. Send the last processed cursor.
  2. Replay missed events when supported.
  3. If replay is unavailable or the gap is too large, fetch a fresh snapshot.
  4. Resume live events from the new cursor.

Back to Top

15. Security and Privacy

Same origin is not the same as trusted

An XSS vulnerability in any same-origin tab can publish and receive the same cross-tab messages. Browser-local messaging does not protect against compromised code running under the origin.

Security rules

  • Validate every message type and payload at runtime.
  • Never put access tokens, refresh tokens, passwords, or sensitive personal data in cross-tab messages.
  • Treat channel names as identifiers, not secrets.
  • Validate event.origin and event.source for postMessage.
  • Use exact targetOrigin, not '*', for sensitive communication.
  • Authorize every server-side subscription and event.
  • Apply CSP, Trusted Types, and XSS defenses.
  • Minimize payloads and broadcast invalidations where possible.

Logout

Cross-tab logout is a UX optimization:

server revokes session/token
  -> initiating tab clears local state
  -> initiating tab broadcasts logout
  -> other tabs clear UI state

Other tabs must not remain authorized merely because a message was missed. The server remains authoritative.

Back to Top

16. Decision Guide 

Which contexts must communicate?
  |
  +-- Same page/components
  |     -> in-memory state store/event bus
  |
  +-- Parent ↔ iframe or opener ↔ popup
  |     -> postMessage; MessageChannel for a dedicated port
  |
  +-- Arbitrary same-origin tabs
  |     |
  |     +-- Simple events
  |     |     -> BroadcastChannel
  |     |
  |     +-- Compatibility fallback
  |     |     -> storage event
  |     |
  |     +-- One shared socket/state owner
  |     |     -> SharedWorker
  |     |
  |     +-- Network/offline/push coordination
  |     |     -> Service Worker + IndexedDB
  |     |
  |     +-- Exactly one tab performs a task
  |           -> Web Locks + BroadcastChannel
  |
  +-- Different browser instances/devices
        |
        +-- Bidirectional real time
        |     -> WebSocket + backend broker
        |
        +-- Server-to-client only
        |     -> SSE
        |
        +-- Real time not required
              -> polling or normal API refresh

Comparison summary

Requirement Recommended starting point
Logout/theme/cart sync across tabs BroadcastChannel
Old-browser fallback for small events storage event
Popup or iframe integration postMessage
One WebSocket for all tabs SharedWorker
Push/offline/cache coordination Service Worker
Durable local shared state IndexedDB
One tab performs polling Web Locks
Chrome-to-Firefox communication Backend WebSocket/SSE
Cross-device sync Backend durable state + real-time delivery

Back to Top

17. Testing and Observability

Test matrix

Test at least:

  • Two same-origin tabs
  • A tab opened after previous events were sent
  • Sender tab closing during publish
  • Receiver sleeping/backgrounded
  • Browser refresh and reconnect
  • A separate browser instance
  • Chrome and Firefox
  • Offline then reconnect
  • Duplicate and out-of-order server events

Playwright multi-page example 

test('logout propagates to another tab', async ({ context }) => {
  const firstTab = await context.newPage();
  const secondTab = await context.newPage();

  await firstTab.goto('/dashboard');
  await secondTab.goto('/dashboard');

  await firstTab.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log out' }).click();

  await expect(secondTab).toHaveURL(/\\/login$/);
});

Useful metrics

  • Messages published/received/dropped by transport
  • Schema-validation failures
  • Active tabs/ports per SharedWorker
  • Leader changes and lease duration
  • WebSocket reconnect count
  • Sequence gaps and replay requests
  • Time from server event to tab application
  • Fallback usage by browser/version

Logging

Include messageId, sourceId, event type, schema version, and entity revision. Do not log sensitive payloads.

Back to Top

18. Interview Questions and Answers

How do two tabs communicate by default?

For arbitrary same-origin tabs, start with BroadcastChannel. Use the storage event as a simple compatibility fallback. Related windows or iframes can use postMessage.

Can BroadcastChannel communicate between Chrome and Firefox?

No. They are separate browser instances. Both clients must connect to shared backend infrastructure such as WebSocket, SSE, or polling.

Can Tab 1 and Tab 2 in the same Chrome instance use BroadcastChannel?

Yes, when both tabs use the same origin. Create a BroadcastChannel with the same channel name in each tab.

How do you share one WebSocket across tabs?

Use a SharedWorker as the connection owner and connect each tab through a MessagePort. If SharedWorker is not available, elect one tab as leader or allow one connection per tab and manage the extra server load.

Is the storage event a message queue?

No. It is a notification that storage changed. It has no acknowledgement, replay, or durable queue semantics, and the writing tab does not receive its own event.

How do you prevent duplicate work across tabs?

Use Web Locks for same-origin tab coordination, a SharedWorker as a central owner, or a server-issued lease with fencing when correctness must span browsers or devices.

What happens if a tab misses an event?

Transient events should point to an authoritative source of truth. The tab re-reads IndexedDB or server state, or reconnects with a cursor and requests replay.

How do you secure cross-tab communication?

Validate payloads, avoid secrets, close channels on teardown, and remember that any same-origin XSS can access the channel. For postMessage, validate both origin and source. For backend events, authenticate and authorize every subscription.

What is the difference between coordination and communication?

Communication transfers information. Coordination decides who may perform an action. BroadcastChannel communicates; Web Locks coordinates. Production designs often use both.

Summary

Use the smallest mechanism that matches the real boundary:

  1. postMessage for related windows and iframes.
  2. BroadcastChannel for simple same-origin cross-tab events.
  3. storage events as a low-frequency fallback.
  4. SharedWorker for shared in-memory state or one connection.
  5. Service Worker for network, push, and offline coordination.
  6. IndexedDB for durable local state.
  7. Web Locks for one-owner work.
  8. Backend WebSocket, SSE, or polling across browser instances and devices.

Browser-local messages are transient. Keep important state in an authoritative store, validate every message, and design for sleeping tabs, missed events, reconnection, deduplication, and versioning.

Back to Top

title: 89 of 190 reviewer subagents graded their own model's work. A PreToolUse hook has blocked 7 since; one walked around it
description:
We want the subagent that grades our Claude Code agent's work to run on a different model family from the session that wrote it. For five weeks that rule lived in a sentence of our instructions and one line of an agent file, and when we finally counted, 89 of 190 reviewer launches had run on the main session's own model. A PreToolUse hook now blocks those launches. It has blocked 7 real ones, and one of them was relaunched around it 15 seconds later. Below is how the hook decides, what it blocked, what it can't see, and the reviews we deliberately put back on one model.

All times below are UTC.

Why the grader shouldn't share the writer's model

Our agent drafts a lot of text that other people read: replies to comments, pages, design notes. Before any of it goes out, a subagent we call deep-reviewer grades it against a written rubric. The reviewer gets the draft and the rubric, not the conversation that produced the draft, so it can't simply agree with reasoning it never saw.

Hiding the drafting history covers one kind of shared blind spot. The other kind lives in the model. If the writer is a model that tends to see a loosely related aside as a natural connection, a grader built the same way will tend to see it that way too, and the rubric line meant to catch it passes. So since 2026-08-19 our written rule has been that the reviewer runs on a different model from the main session. The agent file said model: opus, and the rule assumed the main session would be on a model from another family by default.

That assumption was the whole mechanism. Nothing checked it.

How we found out, and how far back it went

On 2026-09-26 one of our direct-message replies pulled in a measurement of ours that had little to do with what the other person was talking about, and the tone review passed the connection. Around the same time a reviewer, partway through another review, compared its own transcript with the agent file and reported that it was running on the same model as the main session. We put three options to the owner: move the reviewer to a model from another family, move it to a cheaper model, or redefine the rule as "a reviewer that hasn't seen the drafting history" and drop the model requirement. The owner chose a variant of the first: Opus by default, the other family whenever the main session itself is on Opus, and a mechanism instead of a reminder.

Our diagnosis at the time was that the opus alias had started pointing at a newer Opus version, the one the main session was already using. While writing this article we reread the subagent docs and found a rule that gives the same result wherever the alias points. In the docs' words, a family alias such as opus "resolves to the main conversation's model instead of the version the alias points to" when "the main conversation's model belongs to that family". Every main session that launched a reviewer from 2026-09-23 on ran on Opus, so our records can't tell the two explanations apart. Both lead to the same conclusion: from an Opus main session, asking for opus cannot get you a different model.

For this article we counted. On our machine, Claude Code keeps a transcript for every subagent run in a folder next to the session's own transcript, plus a small .meta.json file that names the agent type and the description the run was launched with. Our oldest surviving transcripts start on 2026-09-13. We matched each deep-reviewer launch to the run it produced, read the model name on the reviewer's own answers, and compared it with the main session's model at the moment of the launch.

Before the hook, 190 launches matched a run. In 101, the main session was on another family and the reviewer on Opus, which is what the rule intended. In the other 89, the reviewer was not just in the main session's family but on its exact model: 24 on 2026-09-13 and 09-16, when the main session ran an earlier Opus version, and 65 between 09-23 and 09-27 on claude-opus-5-5. The problem we noticed on 09-26 had already happened on 2026-09-13, the oldest day the transcripts reach back to. Nobody saw it then, because a verdict file looks the same whichever model wrote it.

How the hook decides

The hook is a shell script, scripts/hooks/require-cross-model-reviewer.sh, registered in .claude/settings.json as a PreToolUse hook with the matcher Agent|Task. It went in on 2026-09-27 at 10:08. Claude Code hands a command hook a JSON object on stdin, and that object includes transcript_path, the path to the session's transcript, along with the tool's input. For the Agent tool, the input carries subagent_type, description and an optional model.

The script lets every launch through unless subagent_type is deep-reviewer. For a reviewer launch, it reads the last 400 lines of the main transcript, keeps the assistant entries, skips the ones marked <synthetic>, and takes the last model name it finds. Here is the decision, with the Japanese error messages translated and shortened:

main_model="$(tail -n 400 "$transcript_path" |
    jq -rR 'fromjson? | select(.type == "assistant") | .message.model // empty' 2>/dev/null |
    grep -v '^<synthetic>$' | tail -n 1 || true)"

if [ -z "$main_model" ]; then
    exit 0
fi

case "$main_model" in
*opus*)
    if [ "$requested_model" != "fable" ]; then
        echo "Main is ${main_model} (Opus): launch deep-reviewer with model: \"fable\"" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    ;;
*)
    if [ -n "$requested_model" ] && [ "$requested_model" != "opus" ]; then
        echo "Main is ${main_model}: launch deep-reviewer with no model or model: \"opus\"" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    ;;
esac
exit 0

For PreToolUse, exit code 2 blocks the tool call, and Claude receives the stderr text as the reason. In six of the seven real blocks below, the session read the message and relaunched the reviewer with the model it named. When the hook can't read a model from the transcript, it lets the launch through. We chose that on purpose: we didn't want a block that nothing in the session could satisfy.

The family test is a substring match on opus. When the main session runs anything else, the hook accepts the reviewer's default (opus) and blocks any other explicit model.

What it blocked

Between the hook going in and 19:00 on 2026-10-13, our sessions made 851 Agent calls. 596 of them launched deep-reviewer, and every one of those came from a main session running on Opus, so the non-Opus branch has only ever run in the test file.

The hook blocked 8 launches. The first was ours: about a minute before the commit, the session launched a reviewer with no model on purpose, to see the hook stop it. The other 7 were real:

  • Five at 13:38–13:39 on 09-27. A pull-request review fanned out to five reviewers at once, all launched without a model. Each was relaunched with model: "fable" within a minute.
  • One at 04:07 on 09-30, launched with model: "opus". It was relaunched with fable 24 seconds later.
  • One at 17:29 on 10-12, also with model: "opus". Fifteen seconds later the same review was launched again, this time as general-purpose, still with model: "opus".

The hook ignores general-purpose, so that review ran on claude-opus-5-5, the main session's model. The transcript doesn't record why the session made that choice. What it does record is that the session changed the one field the hook keys on, and got a review on the writer's own model. The 66 reviewer launches outside reply review that did get through all ran on the other family, according to their own transcripts.

Under six hours later, we put the most common review back on one model

The hook went in at 10:08. At 15:54 the same day, a second commit carved out reply reviews, the reviews we run far more often than any other. The owner's reasoning, paraphrased: tone criteria are vague by nature, so verdicts will drift between runs and that is acceptable; for now every reply review should run on the same Opus model, even when Opus wrote the reply, and each reply should get at least two reviewers instead of one.

So the hook has a second branch, checked first. A launch whose description starts with the Japanese for "reply review" must be a deep-reviewer, and its model must be unset or opus, whatever the main session runs. From that commit until 19:00 on 2026-10-13, 526 reply-review runs could be matched to their transcripts, and every one ran on claude-opus-5-5, the same model as the main session that wrote the replies. For the review we run most, writer and grader share a model by decision, not by accident.

What replaced model diversity there is a second opinion. Each reply goes to at least two reviewers who don't see each other's verdicts. A rubric criterion both pass is fine, a criterion both fail sends the reply back, and a split criterion is decided by the main session re-checking only that criterion and writing down why.

Checking who actually wrote a verdict

Two reviewers only help if both verdicts really came from reviewers. The main session could write a verdict file itself, or tidy one up afterwards, and the file would look the same. So the same commit added src/marketing/reply-reviewer-provenance.ts, which the tools that count reply verdicts call for every verdict file. For each file it looks through the subagent transcripts that changed after the file did, finds the run that wrote that path with the Write tool, and checks four things: the run's .meta.json says deep-reviewer, its description starts with the reply-review marker, every model name in its transcript is claude-opus-5-5, and the last content it wrote equals what is on disk now (compared as JSON, so whitespace doesn't matter). If any check fails, the verdict isn't counted. If the transcripts can't be found at all, it says so and stops. That is the opposite choice from the hook, which lets the launch through when it can't tell; here a wrong guess only delays a reply.

This is the part that sees what the hook can't: the model that actually answered, not the one that was asked for.

Our local error log, which isn't committed, has 4 runs where this check refused a verdict: on 09-30, 10-04, 10-05 and 10-13. All four gave the same reason: the content had changed after the reviewer wrote it. We traced each one. In all four, the reviewer itself had written the file with Write and then fixed a detail with Edit. The check reads only Write calls, so the reviewer's own correction looked like someone else's edit. Each time, the main session asked the same reviewer to rewrite the file in a single Write, and the round went through. None of the four was about a wrong model, a wrong agent type, or a file the main session wrote. So far the strictest check we have has caught only honest mistakes, which is what we would see if nothing went wrong, and also what we would see if it were looking in the wrong place.

What the hook cannot see

The model that actually runs. The hook checks the requested value. The subagent docs list ways the running model can differ from the request: a mod's spawn hook can replace the per-invocation model, an organization's model allowlist can substitute another one, and the family-alias rule quoted above maps opus onto the main session's model. For reviews other than replies, nothing compares the requested model with the one that answered. The counts in this article are the first time we did, with a one-off script.

Other agent types. The 10-12 relaunch is one case. After the hook went in, nine launches, that one included, ran as general-purpose with model: "opus" and had "review" in their description. Whether those should have been on another family is a policy question the hook can't answer, because it has no idea which launches are reviews.

A transcript that lags or is missing. The hooks docs say the transcript is written asynchronously and may not yet include the current turn's latest messages when a hook fires. The hook takes the last model it finds, so a model switch earlier in the same turn could leave it judging against the old one. If no model can be read, the launch goes through.

Its own failure. We haven't set onFailure on this hook. Per the docs, a command hook that exits with any code other than 0 or 2, or fails to start, is a non-blocking error and the tool call proceeds; "onFailure": "block" changes that. The script runs with set -e, so if jq were missing it would exit with an ordinary error code and every reviewer launch would go through.

Whether another family catches more. We have one case, and it doesn't settle anything. The direct-message reply that started all this passed its same-model review on 09-26, and that reviewer's transcript adds a twist: the draft it passed was a rewrite it had suggested itself in an earlier round, which it pointed out in its own report. On 09-27 at 10:58 we re-graded the same text with a reviewer from the other family, on the rubric as it was committed then, and it passed every criterion again. The rubric simply had no line for it. Shortly after, we tested a rubric revision that added two criteria, "answers the other person's point" and "doesn't change the subject", against recorded replies including that one. Two reviewers from the other family flagged it under the new criteria. Later that day, on a slightly revised rubric, two claude-opus-5-5 reviewers still held the reply back, but under an older criterion, and passed it on both new ones. After the subject-change criterion was reworded more concretely, two more claude-opus-5-5 reviewers flagged it there. One reply, four rubric versions, eight reviewers: the clearest effect in it is the rubric's wording, not the model. The middle step fits "same model, same blind spot", and it fits "the wording was still too vague" just as well.

What we'd like to know

  • Do you run reviewer agents on a different model from the writer? If you do, have you seen the other model catch something the writer's own model passed, on the same rubric?
  • Do you block or rewrite? A PreToolUse hook can also return updatedInput and change the model itself. We block so the session sees the reason, and the 10-12 case shows the cost: a blocked session can pick a route the hook doesn't watch.
  • Do you check afterwards which model answered, or do you trust the launch parameters?
  • For fuzzy calls like tone, would you rather have two reviewers on the writer's model or one reviewer from another family?

If you have measured whether a reviewer from another model family catches more than one from the writer's own family, or decided it isn't worth enforcing, we'd like to read how you got there in the comments below. We'll answer each one there.

title: Enterprise RAG Has a Blindspot Nobody Measures: We Fixed It with a Temporal Claim Graph on FalkorDB
description:
Enterprise RAG Has a Blindspot Nobody Measures: We Fixed It with a Temporal Claim Graph on FalkorDB

Enterprise knowledge is not a bag of facts. It is time-bound assertions.

Here is a failure mode that almost every production RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline encounters:

An employee asks: "What is our tier-1 enterprise discount threshold?"

The retriever searches across 500,000 internal documents.

It finds a Confluence page from 2022 that says: "Discounts apply at $100k."

The BM25 score is sky-high. The embedding cosine similarity is 0.94.

The retriever ranks it #1 or #2 in context.

The LLM reads it and responds with complete confidence: "Our discount threshold is $100k."

The document is highly relevant. It is also completely false.

Six months later, VP Finance signed an update: "Effective Q3 2023, the enterprise discount threshold is increased to $250k, superseding all previous guidelines."

Eight other internal documents still quote the old $100k price. If your agent uses majority voting, outdated documents win 8 to 1. If your retriever uses vector similarity, the old document matches the query phrasing better than the revision memo.

The model didn't hallucinate. It faithfully summarized the evidence it was given.

To fix this, we built Canon: a temporal truth layer for enterprise AI powered by FalkorDB. Canon sits directly between retrieval and generation, transforming documents into a temporal claim graph that decides which evidence is still valid before the language model ever sees it.

The Core Primitive: The Temporal Cut

Instead of treating an enterprise corpus as an unorganized bucket of text chunks, Canon structures claims into a temporal graph.

       [2022 Confluence Doc]
                │
         (asserts: $100k)
                │
                ▼
        (:Proposition {state: "SUPERSEDED"})
                ▲
                │ [:SUPERSEDES]
                │
        (:CanonEvent {provenance: "Memo Q3 2023", t: 1690848000})
                │
                ▼
        (:Proposition {state: "VALID", value: "$250k"})

When an enterprise query arrives, Canon executes the Temporal Cut:

  1. Retrieve candidate documents using standard high-recall retrieval (BM25 or dense embeddings).
  2. Graph Traversal: Inspect the propositions asserted by the retrieved candidates in FalkorDB.
  3. Identify Superseded Evidence: Any proposition that has an incoming [:SUPERSEDES] relation from a later, valid CanonEvent is marked invalid.
  4. Cut Out Expired Documents: Remove the invalidated documents from the prompt window.
  5. Backfill: Pull the next best candidate from the original retrieval ranking so the model still receives a full context window. 
BM25 Candidates:   [Doc A (Rank 1), Doc B (Rank 2), Doc C (Rank 3), Doc D (Rank 4)]
                          │
FalkorDB Check:    [Doc B asserts Proposition_129, which was SUPERSEDED by Event_42]
                          │
Temporal Cut:      [Doc B REMOVED]
                          │
Backfill:          [Doc A (Rank 1), Doc C (Rank 3), Doc D (Rank 4), Doc E (Rank 5)]

The beauty of this architecture is division of responsibility: Your retriever decides what is relevant. The FalkorDB graph decides what is still true.

Why FalkorDB Is the Engine (Not Just a Store)

Temporal graph traversal at query time cannot add 200ms of latency to an LLM pipeline. The graph resolution must happen in single-digit milliseconds before prompt serialization.

We chose FalkorDB as our core graph engine for three specific reasons:

1. Blazing Fast Traversal (<3ms)

FalkorDB's GraphBLAS sparse-matrix representation and in-memory execution mean multi-hop reachability queries resolve in 2 to 4 milliseconds. In an interactive agentic loop, this overhead is practically invisible.

2. Expressive Cypher for Temporal Lineage

Every claim transition in Canon is reified as a CanonEvent node with exact evidence byte spans, timestamps, and attribution edges.

To check if any retrieved proposition is superseded or contested, Canon runs a single Cypher query:

MATCH (p:Proposition)-[:ASSERTED_IN]->(a:Assertion)-[:SOURCED_FROM]->(art:Artifact)
WHERE art.id IN $retrieved_doc_ids
OPTIONAL MATCH (newer_event:CanonEvent)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(p)
RETURN art.id AS doc_id, 
       p.id AS prop_id, 
       p.status AS status, 
       count(newer_event) > 0 AS is_superseded,
       newer_event.evidence_span AS superseding_evidence

If is_superseded is true, the document is cut instantly.

3. Entity & Alias Resolution (Company Brain)

Enterprise documents refer to the same people, teams, and products by dozens of names ("T. Farhan", "Toufiq", "VP Eng", "Head of Engineering").

In FalkorDB, we store 1,488 nodes and 1,661 relationships, including 985 Person nodes and 300 Alias nodes connected via [:RESOLVES_TO] edges. When a user asks what someone decided before an update, FalkorDB resolves all aliases and traverses their historical assertions seamlessly.

The Benchmark: 511,958 Documents, Zero Prompt Cheats

We didn't test on a toy synthetic toy set. We evaluated Canon against Enterprise RAG-Bench, consisting of 511,958 real enterprise documents (a 4.03 GB corpus database) with official human-labeled conflict questions.

Every test ran under strict constraints:

  • Exactly the same model
  • Exactly the same prompt
  • Exactly the same BM25 retriever
  • Exactly the same 10-document context budget
Metric Standard RAG Baseline Canon (FalkorDB) Delta
Benchmark Correctness 70.0% 82.5% +12.5%
Superseded Docs in Context 14 / 20 1 / 20 -93% reduction
Current Gold Doc Recovered 20 / 20 20 / 20 100% recall
Weaker Model Correctness 75.0% 80.0% +5.0%
Non-Conflict Context Preservation 480 / 480 471 / 480 98.1% byte-identical
Harm to Non-Conflicting Contexts - 0 harmed Zero regression

The Negative Control

To prove the +12.5% correctness wasn't merely an artifact of having fewer words in context, we ran a negative control: randomly cutting the same number of documents.

Result: The random control scored exactly 70.0% (identical to baseline).

The entire performance gain comes from knowing precisely which document to cut.

Live Verification & Database Restart

An enterprise graph must survive real-world operational conditions. We built an automated test harness (scripts/verify/verify_falkordb.py) that executes 7 live checks against FalkorDB:

  1. Connection & Schema Verification: Validates 20 claim keys, 19 resolved transitions, and 1 contested case.
  2. Active vs Contested Integrity: Ensures contested claims are flagged honestly rather than forced into an incorrect resolution.
  3. Temporal Cut Verification: Verifies that superseded documents are cleanly filtered and backfills are verified against the raw corpus.
  4. Adversarial Supersession: Injects conflicting claims and confirms explicit supersession syntax always wins over repetition count.
  5. Database Restart Persistence: The test issues a docker restart to the FalkorDB container in the middle of execution. Once FalkorDB boots back up, it re-queries the graph: all state, relationships, and claim keys remain 100% intact.

All 7 checks pass, and our unit test suite runs 71/71 passing tests across graph operations, retrieval, and API serialization.

Try It Yourself in 4 Commands

The repository is open-source and completely reproducible:

# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/toufiqfarhan0/falkor-hack.git
cd falkor-hack

# 2. Start FalkorDB in Docker
docker compose up -d

# 3. Install dependencies & run test suite
uv sync
uv run pytest

# 4. Run the live FalkorDB verification suite
uv run python scripts/verify/verify_falkordb.py

To run the full stack with the interactive UI:

# Start backend API (Port 8000)
uv run uvicorn canon_api.app:app --port 8000

# Start Next.js frontend (Port 3000)
pnpm --dir apps/web dev

Visit http://localhost:3000 to inspect the live dashboard, explore the /cut visualizer, and test queries in real time.

What We Learned

  1. RAG without temporal graphs is fundamentally fragile: As enterprise codebases and document repositories grow, the probability that the most similar document is outdated approaches certainty.
  2. Graph databases belong in the inference path: FalkorDB isn't just an offline database for knowledge dumps—it is fast enough to act as an inline query gate during active generation.
  3. Honest systems abstain on ambiguity: When two active documents conflict without an explicit supersession clause, Canon does not guess or hallucinate—it surfaces the conflict as contested, preserving both historical context and present truth.

Built for the FalkorDB Hackathon 2026.

Repository: github.com/farhan0-code/graph-hack

Demo Video: https://youtu.be/eIrE17qlf7Q

title: BackupManager: Sistema de Gestión y Recuperación de Respaldos en PostgreSQL
description:
Introducción

En el curso de Base de Datos II desarrollé BackupManager, una aplicación web orientada a la gestión de respaldos y recuperación de información almacenada en PostgreSQL.

El objetivo de este trabajo fue implementar una solución que permitiera realizar respaldos reales de una base de datos, verificar la integridad de los archivos generados y comprobar que la información pudiera recuperarse correctamente.

Para desarrollar el sistema utilicé Python con FastAPI, PostgreSQL y diferentes servicios en la nube. Además, incorporé herramientas de automatización para que los procesos de respaldo y despliegue pudieran ejecutarse sin depender únicamente de una operación manual.

Durante el desarrollo pude comprobar el funcionamiento de la aplicación tanto en un entorno local como desde Internet, utilizando una base de datos alojada en Neon y un servicio web publicado en Render.

1. Tecnologías utilizadas

Para la implementación de BackupManager seleccioné herramientas que permitieran desarrollar una aplicación web, conectar una base de datos PostgreSQL en la nube y automatizar las operaciones de respaldo.

Tabla 1. Tecnologías utilizadas en BackupManager

Tecnología Función en el proyecto
Python Lenguaje de programación utilizado en el backend
FastAPI Desarrollo de la API y lógica del sistema
PostgreSQL 18 Almacenamiento y gestión de la información
SQLAlchemy Comunicación entre Python y PostgreSQL
Neon Alojamiento de PostgreSQL en la nube
Render Despliegue público de la aplicación web
Docker Preparación del entorno de ejecución
GitHub Repositorio público del código fuente
GitHub Actions Automatización de respaldos, pruebas y despliegues

La arquitectura utilizada permite separar la aplicación de la base de datos. Mientras Render ejecuta el backend y la interfaz web, Neon se encarga de almacenar la información de manera independiente.

Esta separación permite acceder al sistema desde Internet sin necesidad de mantener encendida la computadora utilizada durante el desarrollo.

El código fuente y la aplicación se encuentran disponibles en los siguientes enlaces:

Repositorio GitHub: BackupManager - Código fuente

Aplicación desplegada: BackupManager - Aplicación web

2. Funcionamiento general del sistema

BackupManager cuenta con una interfaz web organizada en cuatro apartados principales: Resumen, Registros, Respaldos e Historial.

Cada apartado permite acceder a las diferentes funcionalidades implementadas para administrar información y realizar operaciones de respaldo.

En la sección Resumen se presenta el estado general de la aplicación, incluyendo el motor de base de datos utilizado, la cantidad de registros existentes y los respaldos completos que han sido generados.

Figura 1. Panel principal y estado general de BackupManager.

En la Figura 1 se observa el panel principal del sistema, donde se presenta información sobre su funcionamiento. La interfaz muestra la conexión activa con PostgreSQL, ocho registros almacenados y un respaldo completo generado. También se encuentran disponibles las opciones para crear nuevas copias de seguridad y consultar el historial de operaciones.

2.1. Gestión de registros

En el módulo de registros se pueden agregar, consultar, modificar y eliminar datos. Estas operaciones permiten trabajar con información almacenada directamente en PostgreSQL.

Para comprobar la conexión con la base de datos, ingresé ocho registros de prueba desde BackupManager. Posteriormente, accedí al panel de Neon y consulté la tabla records para verificar que la información se hubiera almacenado correctamente.

Los datos registrados contenían información relacionada con servidores, estaciones de trabajo y dispositivos de red.

Figura 2. Registros almacenados en PostgreSQL mediante Neon.

En la Figura 2 se visualiza la información almacenada en la tabla records de PostgreSQL. Se pueden observar los identificadores de cada registro, sus nombres, categorías, cantidades y fechas de creación. Esta comprobación permitió confirmar que los datos ingresados desde BackupManager se encontraban almacenados correctamente en la base de datos alojada en Neon.

2.2. Estructura de la base de datos

La aplicación utiliza diferentes tablas para administrar los registros y mantener información relacionada con las operaciones realizadas.

Tabla 2. Tablas principales de BackupManager

Tabla Descripción
records Almacena los registros administrados desde la aplicación
audit_events Registra información relacionada con las operaciones realizadas
full_backups Almacena los metadatos de los respaldos completos generados

Estas tablas permiten separar los datos principales del sistema de la información relacionada con su administración y los respaldos.

3. Estrategias de respaldo de bases de datos

Un respaldo o backup consiste en conservar una copia de la información para que pueda recuperarse ante una eliminación accidental, un fallo del sistema o cualquier situación que comprometa la disponibilidad de los datos.

Contar con una estrategia de respaldo es importante porque permite reducir el impacto de estos incidentes y facilita la recuperación de la información.

Existen diferentes tipos de respaldos, entre los cuales destacan los completos, incrementales y diferenciales.

Tabla 3. Comparación de estrategias de respaldo

Estrategia Características Estado en BackupManager
Completo Conserva el esquema y los datos de la base de datos Implementado con pg_dump
Parcial Conserva información específica de una tabla Implementado mediante JSON
Incremental Respalda los cambios posteriores a una copia anterior No implementado
Diferencial Respalda los cambios desde el último respaldo completo No implementado

En esta versión de BackupManager se implementaron dos modalidades: la exportación parcial de registros en JSON y el respaldo lógico completo de PostgreSQL.

3.1. Respaldo parcial en formato JSON

Esta función permite exportar la información de la tabla records y conservarla en un archivo JSON.

Su principal utilidad es recuperar un conjunto específico de registros sin necesidad de restaurar todas las tablas de la base de datos.

La aplicación permite generar y descargar estos archivos. También incorpora una operación de restauración parcial, mediante la cual se puede recuperar el contenido de la tabla respaldada.

Esta modalidad es adecuada para trabajar con conjuntos pequeños de información, aunque no reemplaza un respaldo completo de PostgreSQL.

3.2. Respaldo completo de PostgreSQL

Para implementar los respaldos completos se utilizó pg_dump, una herramienta de PostgreSQL que permite realizar exportaciones lógicas del esquema y los datos de una base de datos.

El comando básico utilizado sigue la siguiente estructura:

pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner --no-acl --file=respaldo.dump

La opción --format=custom genera un archivo de respaldo en formato personalizado, que posteriormente puede procesarse mediante pg_restore.

Durante la prueba de recuperación se utilizaron las opciones --no-owner y --no-acl de pg_restore para evitar restablecer los propietarios y privilegios originales. Esto facilitó la restauración del respaldo en una base de datos temporal e independiente.

En BackupManager, los parámetros de conexión se obtienen mediante variables de entorno privadas para evitar almacenar las credenciales directamente en el código fuente.

Durante las pruebas ejecuté la generación de un respaldo desde la aplicación y obtuve un archivo .dump de aproximadamente 6.2 KB.

El archivo se generó correctamente y pudo descargarse desde la interfaz web.

Figura 3. Generación y registro de un respaldo completo de PostgreSQL.

En la Figura 3 se observa el módulo de respaldos de BackupManager, donde se encuentra registrado el archivo generado mediante pg_dump. El sistema muestra información sobre el identificador del respaldo, su fecha de creación y su tamaño. Además, permite descargar el archivo y verificar su integridad mediante las funciones disponibles en la interfaz.

3.3. Verificación de integridad

Después de generar el respaldo, utilicé la opción Verificar, implementada en BackupManager.

Esta función realiza dos comprobaciones principales.

La primera consiste en calcular el valor SHA-256 del archivo y compararlo con el registrado cuando se creó el respaldo. Esto permite detectar si su contenido ha cambiado.

La segunda comprobación utiliza pg_restore --list para verificar que PostgreSQL pueda reconocer la estructura interna del archivo.

Durante las pruebas, ambas comprobaciones finalizaron correctamente.

Sin embargo, la verificación de integridad no garantiza por sí sola que los datos puedan recuperarse. Por esta razón, también fue necesario implementar una prueba de restauración.

4. Automatización de respaldos con GitHub Actions

Una de las funcionalidades principales de BackupManager es la automatización de los respaldos mediante GitHub Actions.

Para implementar este procedimiento configuré un archivo YAML dentro de la carpeta .github/workflows del repositorio.

El workflow permite ejecutar respaldos manualmente y también dispone de una programación diaria.

El proceso está organizado en diferentes etapas, desde la conexión con la base de datos hasta el almacenamiento del archivo cifrado.

Tabla 4. Etapas del proceso automatizado de respaldo

Etapa Operación realizada
1. Conexión Acceso a PostgreSQL alojado en Neon
2. Exportación Generación del respaldo mediante pg_dump
3. Restauración Recuperación del respaldo utilizando pg_restore
4. Comprobación Consulta de la tabla restaurada
5. Cifrado Protección del archivo mediante AES-256
6. Almacenamiento Conservación del artefacto cifrado durante siete días

4.1. Prueba de restauración

Para comprobar la recuperación de la información, el workflow utiliza una base PostgreSQL temporal e independiente.

En este entorno se ejecuta pg_restore, lo que permite reconstruir el contenido del respaldo sin modificar los datos de la base de producción.

Después de realizar la restauración, el proceso consulta la tabla records para verificar que está disponible y que puede obtenerse su cantidad de registros.

La ejecución finalizó correctamente, lo que permitió comprobar que el archivo generado pudo restaurarse en el entorno de prueba.

Figura 4. Ejecución satisfactoria del respaldo automatizado y la prueba de restauración.

En la Figura 4 se muestra el resultado de la ejecución del workflow configurado en GitHub Actions. El proceso finalizó con estado Success, después de completar las operaciones de generación del respaldo, restauración en PostgreSQL y cifrado del archivo. Esta evidencia confirma que el procedimiento de recuperación pudo ejecutarse correctamente en un entorno independiente.

Evidencia del proceso:

Ver ejecución del respaldo y restauración en GitHub Actions

4.2. Cifrado de los archivos de respaldo

Después de realizar la restauración de prueba, el workflow cifra el archivo generado utilizando AES-256-CBC con derivación de clave mediante PBKDF2.

Esta operación agrega una medida de protección para evitar que el contenido del respaldo quede almacenado directamente como un archivo sin cifrar.

Posteriormente, el archivo cifrado se conserva como artefacto en GitHub Actions durante siete días.

Aunque este procedimiento permite demostrar el almacenamiento temporal de respaldos, en un entorno de producción sería necesario utilizar un servicio de almacenamiento externo con políticas de seguridad y conservación más completas.

5. Despliegue de BackupManager en la nube

Para publicar BackupManager utilicé Render, conectándolo con el repositorio público del proyecto en GitHub.

Previamente configuré una base PostgreSQL en Neon y comprobé su conexión desde la aplicación ejecutada localmente.

Una vez verificado el funcionamiento, preparé el despliegue mediante Docker y configuré las variables de entorno necesarias para conectar la aplicación con PostgreSQL.

Durante el procedimiento fue necesario actualizar las herramientas cliente de PostgreSQL a la versión 18, debido a que inicialmente algunos archivos estaban configurados para una versión anterior.

Después de completar la configuración, BackupManager quedó disponible desde una dirección pública.

5.1. Automatización del despliegue

Además del respaldo automático, configuré un segundo workflow en GitHub Actions para ejecutar las pruebas del backend y solicitar nuevos despliegues en Render.

El procedimiento comienza cuando se envían cambios a la rama principal del repositorio o cuando se ejecuta manualmente.

Primero se instalan las dependencias y se realizan las pruebas automatizadas de la aplicación.

Si estas pruebas finalizan correctamente, GitHub Actions utiliza un deploy hook para solicitar la actualización del servicio en Render.

De esta manera, los cambios enviados al repositorio pueden pasar por un proceso de comprobación antes de solicitar su publicación.

Figura 5. Ejecución correcta del proceso automatizado de pruebas y despliegue.

En la Figura 5 se observa el resultado del workflow encargado de ejecutar las pruebas del backend y solicitar el despliegue de BackupManager en Render. El proceso finalizó correctamente, lo que permitió comprobar la integración entre el repositorio de GitHub, las pruebas automatizadas y el mecanismo de despliegue configurado para la aplicación.

Evidencia del proceso:

Ver ejecución de CI y despliegue en GitHub Actions

6. Pruebas y resultados obtenidos

Después de completar el desarrollo y la configuración de los servicios, realicé diferentes pruebas para comprobar el funcionamiento de BackupManager.

Estas incluyeron la conexión con PostgreSQL, el almacenamiento de registros, la generación de respaldos, la verificación de integridad y la recuperación automatizada.

Tabla 5. Resultados de las pruebas funcionales

Prueba realizada Resultado
Conexión de FastAPI con PostgreSQL en Neon Correcto
Registro de información desde BackupManager Correcto
Comprobación de ocho registros en Neon Correcto
Generación de respaldo completo .dump Correcto
Descarga del archivo de respaldo Correcto
Verificación de integridad SHA-256 Correcto
Restauración en una base PostgreSQL temporal Correcto
Ejecución automatizada del respaldo Correcto
Pruebas automatizadas del backend Correcto
Solicitud de despliegue mediante GitHub Actions Correcto
Publicación de BackupManager en Render Correcto

Los resultados permitieron comprobar que la aplicación trabaja con una base de datos PostgreSQL real y que las operaciones de respaldo y recuperación pueden ejecutarse satisfactoriamente.

Una de las pruebas más importantes fue la restauración automatizada, debido a que permitió verificar el contenido del respaldo en una base temporal sin afectar la información original.

6.1. Limitaciones identificadas

Aunque el sistema cumple con las funcionalidades principales de esta práctica, existen algunos aspectos que podrían mejorarse.

Uno de ellos es el almacenamiento de los respaldos. En el plan gratuito de Render, los archivos guardados localmente no tienen persistencia garantizada después de reinicios o nuevos despliegues.

Por esta razón, los respaldos deben conservarse fuera del servidor. En esta implementación se utilizó GitHub Actions para almacenar temporalmente copias cifradas.

Para una implementación de mayor alcance sería conveniente incorporar almacenamiento externo permanente, políticas de retención, monitoreo de errores y mecanismos de recuperación a un punto específico en el tiempo.

6.2. Demostración audiovisual de BackupManager

Como evidencia complementaria del proyecto, se elaboró un video de demostración donde se presenta la arquitectura, el desarrollo y el funcionamiento de BackupManager.

En la presentación se explica la integración de FastAPI con PostgreSQL en Neon, la generación de respaldos, la verificación de integridad, las pruebas de restauración, la automatización mediante GitHub Actions y el despliegue en Render.

La exposición fue desarrollada por Juan Carlos Calderón Rodríguez y Franco Mango Puma, integrantes del proyecto del curso de Base de Datos II.

Enlace al video: Demostración de BackupManager en YouTube

7. Conclusiones

El desarrollo de BackupManager me permitió aplicar conceptos relacionados con la protección y recuperación de bases de datos mediante el uso de PostgreSQL.

Durante el trabajo pude comprobar que generar una copia de seguridad no es suficiente para garantizar la recuperación de información. También resulta necesario verificar la integridad de los archivos y realizar pruebas de restauración.

Otro aspecto importante fue la automatización. Mediante GitHub Actions fue posible ejecutar procesos de respaldo y comprobación de manera programada, reduciendo la necesidad de intervención manual.

Además, la integración de FastAPI, Neon y Render permitió publicar una aplicación funcional que trabaja con una base de datos PostgreSQL alojada en la nube.

Finalmente, BackupManager constituye una implementación práctica de respaldo, verificación y recuperación de datos. Aunque todavía puede ampliarse con otras estrategias y mecanismos de almacenamiento, permitió comprobar el funcionamiento de herramientas reales utilizadas en la administración de bases de datos.

Referencias

  • PostgreSQL Global Development Group. pg_dump — PostgreSQL 18. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/app-pgdump.html
  • PostgreSQL Global Development Group. pg_restore — PostgreSQL 18. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/app-pgrestore.html
  • GitHub. GitHub Actions Documentation. https://docs.github.com/en/actions
  • Neon. Neon Documentation. https://neon.com/docs
  • Render. Render Documentation. https://render.com/docs
