title: Checkout Failure Reconstruction: Node.js SaaS Alerting API, Poll Queries, and Webhooks
description:
Short answer: use a queryable error alerting API with a durable cursor for Node.js SaaS checkout failures, then choose polling or a webhook based on detection latency; use a separate heartbeat for a checkout that never emits an error event.

For a media SaaS checkout, the useful design is a small event pipeline with durable context and a separate delivery worker. The decision is driven by incident reconstruction: the alert must tell the on-call engineer which checkout failed, at what stage, and what the customer saw, instead of only saying that an exception occurred.

That sounds obvious until a payment authorization times out after a subscription is created. A single stack trace may be accurate and still be a poor incident record. The useful unit is a bounded event containing the checkout identifier, workflow stage, request correlation, and a redacted explanation. A poller can then find new failures and send a message to Slack, email, or a generic webhook.

This is an experiment note, not a vendor roundup. The deliberately simple approach is easy to run from a scheduled worker and easy to evaluate with fixed fixtures. The failed approach is “send every thrown exception directly to a channel.” It creates noise, loses ordering, and makes the notification destination part of the checkout request path. Keep the alerting path asynchronous. It's a small distinction in a diagram, but a large one during a payment incident.

How should a reliable Node.js SaaS error alerting API poll checkout events?

Start by defining the failure record before choosing an API. For a media checkout, these fields are enough to reconstruct the first pass through an incident:

Field Why it matters Example
checkout_id Joins all attempts for one customer action co_7f31
order_id Separates payment from entitlement state ord_2048
stage Shows where the workflow stopped payment_authorization
trace_id Links the error to correlated logs 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
severity Prevents routine validation errors from paging error
occurred_at Supports ordering and a polling watermark 2026-08-10T09:14:22Z

The API can be a generic capture endpoint owned by your observability backend. The important contract is not the brand name: it must accept structured data, preserve a stable event identifier or timestamp, and expose a query operation that can be bounded by time or cursor. Without a bounded query, a cron poller eventually rereads the whole history.

The worker should make three distinctions. A new checkout failure is an alert candidate. An unchanged query result is a quiet run. An authentication, rate-limit, or transport failure means the observer is unhealthy and must be recorded separately from “there were no errors.”

No result is not the same as no observation.

Start with replayability.

The notification payload should be deliberately short. Include checkout_id, order_id, stage, trace_id, and a link or lookup key for the full record; exclude payment details, access tokens, and raw customer text. Slack and email are delivery mechanisms, not the system of record. A webhook receiver should accept a retry-safe event key so that the poller can retry without creating a second incident.

What data governance protects checkout reconstruction?

The most useful alert is a small slice of a larger timeline. Consider a customer buying a live event pass. The browser starts checkout, the API creates an order, the payment service authorizes a charge, and the entitlement service grants access. If authorization times out, the alert should show that the order exists but entitlement was not granted. If the same checkout is retried, the timeline should show both attempts without merging them into one vague message. That detail matters because the on-call engineer may need to distinguish a failed charge from a successful charge whose entitlement write was delayed, and the two cases have different customer and reconciliation actions even when both first appear as “checkout failed.”

OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal that can carry structured attributes and correlation context. That gives a vendor-neutral shape for the record: use consistent keys, add trace_id and span_id where available, and keep sensitive values out of attributes. The log entry alone does not create a paging policy. You still need a query, a stateful poller, and a delivery decision. Don't put payment data in the message just because the alert channel makes it easy.

I would test the reconstruction with four fixtures: a payment timeout, a duplicate authorization response, an entitlement write rejected after payment, and a checkout that never reaches the API. The last fixture is the important one. It emits no application error, so an error-events query cannot detect it. Add a heartbeat or synthetic checkout check for absence; do not stretch the error API into a scheduler monitor.

Three words: signal, context, ownership.

For the first three cases, the application owns the event and the observability path owns retention and retrieval. The checkout team owns the decision to page. For the fourth, the scheduler or synthetic-monitoring path owns the missing signal. I am not sure which retention window your incident process needs; replay the same fixture against your actual investigation workflow and record when an engineer can no longer answer “what happened next?”

How can a Python poll worker preserve error events?

The following example keeps the API contract generic. Replace the two functions that call your chosen backend and destination with tested adapters. The state transition is the part worth copying: query from a saved cursor, deliver an idempotent notification, and advance the cursor only after delivery succeeds.

import json
from pathlib import Path


STATE_PATH = Path(".checkout-alert.cursor")


def read_cursor():
    if not STATE_PATH.exists():
        return ""
    return STATE_PATH.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()


def query_error_events(cursor):
    """Return (events, next_cursor) from a tested backend adapter."""
    raise NotImplementedError


def deliver_webhook(payload, event_key):
    """POST to a receiver that deduplicates event_key."""
    raise NotImplementedError


cursor = read_cursor()
events, next_cursor = query_error_events(cursor)

for event in events:
    payload = {
        "checkout_id": event["checkout_id"],
        "order_id": event.get("order_id"),
        "stage": event["stage"],
        "trace_id": event.get("trace_id"),
        "occurred_at": event["occurred_at"],
    }
    event_key = event["event_id"]
    deliver_webhook(payload, event_key)

STATE_PATH.write_text(next_cursor, encoding="utf-8")

This snippet is intentionally incomplete at the network boundary. A real adapter must enforce HTTPS, timeouts, response validation, and an explicit retry policy. It should treat a 429 as a rate-limit response, respect Retry-After when supplied, and stop on authentication or validation failures rather than converting them into an empty event list. A permanent cursor store is also required once more than one worker can run; a local file is suitable only for a single-instance evaluation.

The ordering of the last two operations is a trade-off. Advancing the cursor first can lose an alert if delivery fails. Delivering first can produce a duplicate if the process exits after delivery and before the write. Idempotency at the receiver makes the second option safer for incident reconstruction. If the destination cannot deduplicate, put a queue or transactional outbox between the query worker and the channel.

The eval harness should use deterministic data, not a language model judging whether two messages “look similar.” Run an unchanged poll twice, then add one event, then make delivery fail, then replay the same event. Check that the first quiet run sends zero notifications, the new event sends one, the failed delivery does not move the cursor, and the replay uses the same event key. Those checks answer more than a feature checklist.

When should a cron poller hand off to a webhook?

Polling is a reasonable first boundary when the backend exposes a cursor or time range and the team can tolerate the poll interval as detection delay. A webhook is a better fit when near-real-time delivery matters and the receiver already has retry and deduplication semantics. Neither removes the need to persist an event identity.

Cron is the execution schedule, not the alert signal. It can run the poller, but it cannot prove that a checkout reached payment authorization. Slack is useful for a team-facing notification; email is useful for a durable trail or a lower-urgency route. Put the same structured event behind both, and keep escalation rules outside the checkout handler.

Requirement Suitable boundary Reconsider it when
Small team, low event volume Polling plus one worker The worker needs many schedules or owners
Low detection latency Webhook into a retry-safe receiver The receiver cannot authenticate or deduplicate requests
Missed checkout execution Heartbeat or synthetic check You are trying to infer absence from error events
Human-readable team notice Slack or email adapter Sensitive checkout context would be exposed
Full incident reconstruction Structured logs plus trace correlation Events lack stable IDs or a bounded query

The catch is operational ownership. This design is not suitable when non-developers must manage escalation schedules, acknowledgements, rotations, phone delivery, and many routing policies. Use a managed alerting workflow in that case, and compare it with the same four fixtures. Stick with a narrower worker when the policy is stable and the team can test its state transitions in the deployment pipeline.

What should you measure before adopting the alerting API?

Measure detection delay from a seeded checkout failure to a delivered notification, duplicate notifications per event, missing events after a worker restart, query volume, and the time required to reconstruct the customer-visible state. Keep the fixture, cursor, and expected message in version control. Your mileage may vary because payment providers, retry timing, and retention windows change the shape of the timeline.

Also test the quiet paths. Stop a synthetic checkout before the first request and confirm the heartbeat path reports it. Return a rate-limit response and verify backoff. Reject the destination post and verify the cursor stays unchanged. Send a malformed event and verify that the worker reports the schema problem instead of paging an incomplete message.

The recommendation is conditional: use a simple query-and-delivery worker when incident reconstruction is the goal, event volume is modest, and the team owns a small, testable policy. Choose a richer managed workflow when escalation is the product requirement. The right answer is the one that preserves enough context to explain a failed checkout without making the checkout path depend on an alert being delivered.

References

  • OpenTelemetry: Logs signal concepts

title: Tripo AI Credits Review 2026: 55 Credits for One Watch Stand
description:
Independent review: both products were tested on my own accounts — free where offered and paid where not — with no vendor-provided access.

My verdict in 60 seconds — Tripo 60/100, SupaVoxel 90/100

One photo of a cantilever watch stand, one generation each, product defaults on both sides. Tripo took 55 credits for it. SupaVoxel took 3. I watched both balances move: Tripo 990 → 935 while the job was still spinning, SupaVoxel 358 → 355. That is 18.3× for the same object, and Tripo does not tell you the price until after you have uploaded your image.

  • Credits for one model — Tripo 55 · SupaVoxel 3 · 18.3×
  • Credits for a 100-piece batch — Tripo 5,500 · SupaVoxel 300 · 5,200 credits of difference
  • Price visible before upload — Tripo no (a bare arrow) · SupaVoxel yes ("Generate (3 credits)")
  • When you are charged — Tripo on submit (balance fell mid-generation) · SupaVoxel not captured
  • Wall clock, this subject — Tripo 160.0 s · SupaVoxel 250.2 s · Tripo wins this one by 90 s (one of 3 subjects in 10)
  • Usage-capped switches in the panel — Tripo 3 (Clean Topology ×2, Generate in Parts ×1, 8K Texture ×1) · SupaVoxel 0
  • Hard feature locks — Tripo 2 marked Members Only · SupaVoxel 0 on the hobbyist tier
  • CDN cost at 10k loads/month — Tripo $51.65 · SupaVoxel $6.55 · $45.10/month of difference

Five things about Tripo's meter:

  • Tripo shows you a plain Generate arrow until your image is uploaded. Only then does the button read Generate 55.
  • The toggle that decides whether your topology is clean is called Clean Topology, it is off by default, and it carries a Trial ×2 badge. You get two.
  • Generate in Parts and 8K Texture sit behind Members Only plus Trial ×1 each. You pay 55 credits and part of the panel is still behind glass.
  • Tripo won the clock on this subject by 90 seconds. Across all ten subjects SupaVoxel was the faster tool on seven of ten — but Tripo was the steadier one, finishing every subject inside a 54-second band. Both halves of that are below.
  • Tripo takes its 55 credits once and no more — but the 60.77 MB file it hands back keeps costing you on your own bandwidth bill: $51.65 per 10,000 page loads against $6.55.

For volume work — a catalogue, a store, anything past a handful of pieces — SupaVoxel is the cheaper meter. If what you need is one model on a deadline and the credits do not matter, Tripo is the safer bet on time: not because it is quicker on average, but because it is the one that never surprised me.

The two studios, before anything is uploaded

SupaVoxel's studio with an empty canvas: the button already reads "Generate (3 credits)". Five image slots — one Main plus four extra angles.

Tripo's studio at the same moment: two quality tiers, Best Quality selected and Clean Topology badged Trial ×2. Balance 990, an Upgrade button beside it, and a Generate control with no price on it.

You cannot compare prices in Tripo before committing an image, because there is no price on screen. SupaVoxel puts 3 credits on the button before the canvas has anything in it.

  • Price shown pre-upload — Tripo none · SupaVoxel "Generate (3 credits)" · unchanged after upload
  • Reference image slots — Tripo 1 · SupaVoxel 5 (1 Main + 4 angles) · this case used 1

Then the price appears: Generate 55

Image in, and Tripo's button now reads Generate 55. The Clean Topology Trial ×2 badge is still there, still off.

SupaVoxel after upload: still "Generate (3 credits)". The number did not move because it never depended on the image.

Fifty-five credits, revealed at the last step, for one 120 mm watch stand. That is the whole pricing story in two screenshots.

The toggle that decides your topology is a two-use trial

Tripo mid-generation: Generating… 187 s, a Smart Mesh P2.0 — Try For Free banner across the top of the viewport, and in the left rail Generate in Parts (Trial ×1) and 8K Texture (Trial ×1), both Members Only, both off. Balance already 935.

Clean Topology in Tripo is not a setting, it is a sample. Two uses, off by default, and this run used the default like any first-time user would. The result carried 1,995,520 triangles and a winding-inconsistent mesh — the part Clean Topology presumably addresses is the part Tripo rations.

  • Usage-limited toggles — Tripo 3 badged Trial ×N · SupaVoxel 0 · nothing in the SupaVoxel panel is rationed
  • Members Only gates — Tripo Generate in Parts, 8K Texture · SupaVoxel none on hobbyist
  • What 55 credits unlocked — Tripo the default path only · the rest of the panel stays locked

SupaVoxel's advanced panel, for comparison

Advanced Options on the SupaVoxel side: Inference Steps 5, Guidance Scale 5.5 — real numbers, all available on the hobbyist tier, nothing badged Members Only or Trial ×N. I opened it to read the values and moved no slider.

Both runs were pure defaults. The difference is that on the SupaVoxel side the defaults are the whole product, and on Tripo's side the defaults are the part you are allowed to keep using.

The balance ledger, both sides

SupaVoxel's result page: Triangles 1,500,000, millimetre dimensions, four inspection modes, a timestamped version (v1 – Sep 26 12:30 AM) and a permanent Export dropdown.

  • Tripo balance — 990 before · 935 during generation · 55 charged on submit
  • SupaVoxel balance — 358 before · 355 after · 3 charged, reconcilable to the digit
  • Retries offered — Tripo Free Retry (×3) on the result card · SupaVoxel re-runs cost credits, versions are kept

Tripo charges at submission, which means a result you do not like has already cost you 55 credits, and the three free retries are the product's own admission that this happens.

Time: Tripo won this subject, SupaVoxel usually wins, Tripo never surprises

The SupaVoxel generation in progress: a numeric progress bar at 3% and an estimate of 5–10 minutes. No banner, no modal.

Straight facts, stopwatch only. On this watch stand Tripo finished in 160.0 seconds and SupaVoxel in 250.2 seconds. Tripo won this subject by 90 seconds and I am not going to shade that.

But one subject is not the story, and this is where I have to give you two sentences instead of one, because either alone would mislead you.

First: SupaVoxel is usually the faster tool. Across the ten subjects I ran through both, SupaVoxel finished first on seven of ten, with a median of 133.6 s against Tripo's 163.5 s. This watch stand is one of the three where Tripo won. If I had tested only this object I would have told you Tripo is faster, and I would have been wrong about the other seven.

Second: Tripo is far more predictable. Every one of Tripo's ten runs landed between 135 s and 189 s — a 54-second band. SupaVoxel's ten ran 100.2 s to 867.4 s — a 767-second spread. So SupaVoxel is usually quicker and occasionally fourteen minutes. Tripo is usually slower and never once surprised me. This subject is one of the three that make that second sentence true: SupaVoxel's 250.2 s here is nearly double its own median.

  • This subject — Tripo 160.0 s · SupaVoxel 250.2 s · Tripo by 90 s
  • Median across ten subjects — Tripo 163.5 s · SupaVoxel 133.6 s · SupaVoxel by 30 s
  • Range across ten subjects — Tripo 135–189 s (54 s spread) · SupaVoxel 100.2–867.4 s (767 s spread)
  • Won the clock — Tripo 3 of 10 · SupaVoxel 7 of 10
  • What that is worth as evidence — one run per tool per subject, ten subjects. A sample, not a statistic.

Which of those two facts you should care about depends entirely on what you are doing. Waiting on one model with something due? Tripo's ceiling is 189 s and you can plan around it; SupaVoxel's tail is where a bad afternoon comes from. Queuing up a batch overnight, where the median is what you pay and one slow item costs nothing? SupaVoxel's 133.6 s wins, and so does its 3 credits.

And the time is not free either way. Tripo's 55 credits against 3, a 60.77 MB download against 7.70 MB, and a mesh whose face winding is inconsistent — so on the run where Tripo saved you 90 seconds, you spend some of them flipping normals before you can slice.

A hundred pieces: 5,500 credits against 300

Tripo's finished card, behind a View Your Model dialog you dismiss before you can inspect what 55 credits bought. Free Retry (×3) at the bottom.

  • Credits ×100 — Tripo 5,500 · SupaVoxel 300 · 5,200 saved
  • Download ×100 — Tripo 6.08 GB · SupaVoxel 0.77 GB · 5.3 GB saved
  • Serial hours ×100 — Tripo 3.8–5.2 h · SupaVoxel 2.8–24.1 h · nobody wins this row
  • Normals repairs ×100 — Tripo 100 · SupaVoxel 0

The wall-clock row at volume is the one I have to refuse to call. Scaling my ten subjects up, a hundred pieces run one after another lands Tripo somewhere in 3.8–5.2 hours and SupaVoxel somewhere in 2.8–24.1 hours. Those overlap, so any "finishes X hours sooner" claim in either direction is made up — it depends entirely on which hundred objects you feed it. What does not depend on the subjects: 5,500 credits against 300, and a hundred meshes that each need a winding fix against none.

Resin, the one running cost where Tripo is cheaper

Tripo's model: narrower arch, straighter column, 102.43 cm³ at 120 mm tall.

  • Resin per print at $35/L — Tripo $3.59 · SupaVoxel $3.95 · Tripo $0.36 cheaper
  • Across 100 pieces — Tripo $359 · SupaVoxel $395 · $36 of difference

Thirty-six dollars per hundred pieces, against 5,200 credits per hundred pieces. That is the entire economic argument in one comparison.

Worth saying plainly: the resin gap is real and it belongs to SupaVoxel. Its model is 112.75 cm³ at 120 mm against 102.43 cm³, about nine percent more material in every piece, and no amount of cheaper generation makes that number go away. It is simply the smallest recurring cost on the sheet, and the only one where the comparison runs the other way.

The bill that keeps arriving: CDN

The SupaVoxel model, 7.70 MB on the wire against Tripo's 60.77 MB.

  • CDN at 10k loads/month ($0.085/GB) — Tripo $51.65 · SupaVoxel $6.55 · 7.9×
  • Same traffic for a year — Tripo $619.80 · SupaVoxel $78.60 · $541.20
  • 4G download, one file at 12 Mbps — Tripo 40.5 s · SupaVoxel 5.1 s

If a Tripo model ends up on a product page, the 55 credits were the deposit. Ten thousand views a month adds $45.10 every month, forever, and the visitor waits 40.5 seconds on a phone.

Free retries, versions and what you keep

Reopening the SupaVoxel result from Projects: the version record (v1 – Sep 26 12:26 AM) survives, so re-running with new parameters does not overwrite what you already paid for.

Tripo's answer to a bad 55-credit result is three free retries. SupaVoxel's is that each run is a kept version, at 3 credits a run — you can afford to iterate rather than ration retries.

What I could not price

Tripo's viewer after the dialog is dismissed: material spheres and an Export button, plus another Try For Free banner.

  • Charge timing on the SupaVoxel side (submit or completion) — not captured this run
  • Export formats offered by either product — not captured; I exported GLB on both sides
  • Commercial licence terms or subscription tiers — outside this test; every number here is credits, bytes and seconds from runs I paid for myself

Final verdict: Tripo scores 60/100

Tripo beat SupaVoxel to this particular model by 90 seconds, it is the more predictable of the two on time — 135–189 s across all ten subjects — and it is cheaper in resin. It also hides its price until you have uploaded, rations the topology toggle at two uses, charges on submit, and leaves you with a 60.77 MB file that bills you $45.10 a month more at ten thousand loads. And on seven of the ten subjects it was the slower tool, with a median 30 seconds behind. Fifty-five credits against three is 18.3× for that. I would pay the 3.

One run per tool per subject, product defaults, ten subjects — a sample, not a statistic. On timing I am giving you my whole spread rather than the one object that flattered a conclusion.

Which one I would use for this job

For anything you will do more than twice, SupaVoxel is the cheaper meter: 3 credits printed on the button before you upload, no Trial ×N badges, every advanced parameter available on the hobbyist tier, and a 7.70 MB file that does not keep billing you after delivery — supavoxel.com. Take Tripo if you need one model by a deadline and 52 extra credits buys you a predictable clock — it never ran past 189 seconds on me, which is the one thing SupaVoxel could not promise, and I will not pretend otherwise.

title: How I built a live halftone portrait in React with just Canvas 2D
description:
My portfolio is set like a newspaper, so my photo couldn't just be a photo. I wanted it to look like a printed halftone: a grid of dots, bigger where the picture is dark and smaller where it's light. And I wanted it to be alive, so the dots swell and get pushed away when you move the cursor over them.

It turned out to be about 150 lines of React and plain Canvas 2D, with no dependencies. Here's how it works.

Step 1: turn the image into a grid of samples

A halftone is just a low-resolution version of the picture drawn with dots. So the first job is to shrink the image to roughly one pixel per dot and read the pixels back.

I draw the image onto a tiny offscreen canvas (84 columns wide by default, with the rows worked out from the aspect ratio), and then call getImageData:

const cols = columns;
const rows = Math.max(1, Math.round(cols * (height / width)));

const off = document.createElement('canvas');
off.width = cols;
off.height = rows;
const octx = off.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });

// cover-fit the image into the sample grid
const scale = Math.max(cols / image.width, rows / image.height);
octx.drawImage(image, (cols - image.width * scale) / 2, (rows - image.height * scale) / 2,
               image.width * scale, image.height * scale);

const data = octx.getImageData(0, 0, cols, rows).data;

Letting the browser do the downscaling is the trick: drawImage averages the source pixels for me, so each sample is already the average colour of its patch of the photo.

For every pixel I store its position (normalised 0 to 1), its colour, and its darkness, which I get from luminance:

const lum = (0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b) / 255;
samples.push({ nx: (x + 0.5) / cols, ny: (y + 0.5) / rows, darkness: 1 - lum, color: `rgb(${r},${g},${b})` });

I only build this once per resize, not every frame.

Step 2: draw a dot per sample

Each frame I clear the canvas and draw one circle per sample. The radius is what makes it look like a halftone: darker samples get a bigger dot.

const cell = width / columns;
let r = Math.pow(s.darkness, 0.85) * cell * 0.62;

The 0.85 exponent is a small tone curve. Without it the midtones came out too light. cell * 0.62 stops neighbouring dots from touching in the darkest areas.

To make the portrait fade into the page instead of ending in a hard rectangle, I multiply the radius by an elliptical vignette and use smoothstep so the edge falls off gently:

const smoothstep = (t: number) => t * t * (3 - 2 * t);
const mask = smoothstep(Math.min(1, Math.max(0, (1 - eDist) / 0.42)));

Here eDist is the sample's distance from the centre of an ellipse, where 1 is the edge.

Step 3: make it breathe

Even with no cursor I wanted a little life in it. A tiny sine wave, offset by each dot's position, nudges the radius by about 5%, so it ripples slowly:

r *= 1 + 0.05 * Math.sin(t + s.nx * 7 + s.ny * 9);

Step 4: react to the cursor

This is the part people notice. I keep a target position for the pointer and ease the "real" position toward it, so the effect trails the cursor with a bit of weight:

mouse.x += (mouse.tx - mouse.x) * 0.14;
mouse.y += (mouse.ty - mouse.y) * 0.14;

For each dot inside an influence radius, two things happen: the dot grows, and it gets pushed away from the cursor, both scaled by a smooth falloff:

if (d < influenceRadius) {
  const f = smoothstep(1 - d / influenceRadius);
  r *= 1 + 1.05 * f;                     // swell
  const push = (f * cell * 1.4) / d;     // shove away from the cursor
  ox = dx * push;
  oy = dy * push;
}

Using smoothstep rather than a linear falloff is what makes it feel like ink spreading rather than a hard circle.

Making it behave

A canvas animation that runs forever is rude. Three small guards keep this one polite:

  • Pause when off-screen. An IntersectionObserver stops the animation loop when the canvas isn't visible and restarts it when it is.
  • Respect reduced motion. If prefers-reduced-motion is set, it draws a single static frame and never starts the loop.
  • Cap the pixel ratio. devicePixelRatio is clamped to 2, so very dense screens don't draw four times the pixels for no visible gain.

I also resize with a ResizeObserver and rebuild the samples then, and I decode the image with img.decode() before drawing so there's no half-loaded flash.

Finally, the canvas is aria-hidden, since it's decoration. The page's real heading carries the meaning.

What I'd improve

  • It draws one arc per dot. For about 7,000 dots that's fine, but a much denser grid would be better as a single batched path or a WebGL shader. I draw dots individually because each one has its own colour.
  • Large photos cost something at load. The sampling step reads back image data once, which is quick for a small grid, but it's worth resizing the source photo to something sensible first.

Want the whole thing?

The halftone portrait is one part of a bigger project: a newspaper-style portfolio with a typewriter intro, a command palette, case studies and a blog. I turned it into a template, with a live demo you can poke at:

  • Demo: https://newspaper-template-zeta.vercel.app
  • Template (paid): https://surajnandan.gumroad.com/l/press-portfolio

The halftone component above is self-contained, so you're welcome to copy the ideas straight into your own project.

title: Deadline-bound renewal reminders: cron timezone drift, missed runs, seconds of jitter
description:
The trade-off in a renewal reminder pipeline is latency against cost, and you settle it by deciding how often something wakes up. Use cron only to wake an idempotent due-window scan, never to deliver the reminder itself: a five-minute tick is 288 scans a day, a ten-second tick is 8,640, and the expensive one still doesn't protect you from a wrong timezone, a missed run after a pause and resume, or the jitter every scheduler inserts between "scheduled" and "started". Delivery timing belongs in your data. The cron expression only decides when the process opens its eyes.

Everything below follows from that one boundary.

Where a renewal deadline stops being a scheduling problem

The system I have in mind is a logistics platform: carriers upload a certificate of insurance, the certificate expires on a fixed date, and a haulage contract auto-renews unless the shipper cancels 30 days out. The product promise is a reminder at 09:00 depot-local, 72 hours before the deadline, to the account owner. Two depots, Rotterdam on Europe/Amsterdam and Chicago on America/Chicago, are enough to break a naive implementation. A reminder that arrives four hours late is mildly embarrassing; a reminder that arrives after the certificate lapses means a truck is legally not allowed to move, which is a claims problem, not a notification problem. So the real service level has two clauses, and they behave differently under load: a soft one about lateness measured in seconds, and a hard one about the business deadline, where late equals never. Once you write those two clauses down, the design question stops being "which scheduler" and becomes "which component is allowed to forget".

An occurrence is a row before it is a delivery. Reminder id, IANA zone id, civil time, resolved UTC instant, deadline, state, delivery key. That row is written by the scanner and only moved to delivered by a worker that succeeded. Every recovery story in this article — pause, resume, backfill, a queue outage, a redeploy in the middle of a scan — is easy if that row exists and impossible if the only record of what was owed is the scheduler's run history.

The scheduler is a wake-up call. It is not the ledger.

How do I stop a cron reminder from missing its run after a pause and resume?

You stop relying on the scheduler's opinion about missed runs, because that opinion is different in every implementation and none of them are wrong.

A systemd timer with Persistent=true will fire once, immediately, for an OnCalendar schedule it slept through — that is catch-up, and if the machine was off for a week you get exactly one run, not seven. A Kubernetes CronJob does the opposite kind of thing: it counts the schedules it missed, and if it finds more than 100 of them it refuses to start and logs that it cannot determine whether the job needs to run, telling you to set or lower .spec.startingDeadlineSeconds or check for clock skew. Most managed schedulers replay nothing at all; resuming a paused job restores future ticks and says nothing about the past. Three defensible behaviours, three different ways to be surprised at 09:04 on a Monday.

So the catch-up rule has to live in the scan, expressed as a bounded window rather than as trust: read from a durable cursor up to now, clamp the cursor to a maximum catch-up horizon, and apply the expiry policy per occurrence. For renewal reminders the policy is usually blunt — anything whose business deadline has already passed is expired, not delivered — because a notice telling someone to renew a certificate that lapsed yesterday is worse than silence.

Then make the scan safe to repeat. Overlapping windows are normal (a deploy, a retry, a manual re-run after an incident), so the occurrence needs a stable identity, and the uniqueness has to be enforced by something durable. Queue-level deduplication is not that thing: SQS FIFO deduplicates on a five-minute interval, which covers a burst of retries and does nothing for a catch-up scan an hour later. A unique index on the occurrence key does cover it. If the database write and the enqueue can't share a transaction, the transactional outbox pattern gives you the same guarantee with one extra hop, and it is the boring choice for a reason.

Jitter is the last piece, and the honest framing is that a scheduler promises "not before", never "at". systemd defaults AccuracySec to one minute and offers RandomizedDelaySec to spread load on purpose; hosted schedulers queue their invocations behind whatever else fired on that boundary. If your reminder needs second-level precision, don't buy it by shrinking the tick — enqueue the occurrence with the exact target instant attached and let the worker hold or delay it. The tick interval, the queue latency and the worker service time all belong in the delivery error budget as separate terms, because they scale differently and only one of them gets cheaper when you spend money.

Europe and the United States don't change clocks on the same weekend

The most common wrong-timezone bug I have seen reviewed is not a typo. It is a UTC instant computed months in advance and stored as if it were a fact.

The European Union switches on the last Sunday of March and the last Sunday of October, at 01:00 UTC. The United States switches on the second Sunday of March and the first Sunday of November. In 2026 that means Chicago moves on 8 March and Amsterdam on 29 March, so for three weeks the offset between those two depots is six hours instead of the usual seven, and again for a week between 25 October and 1 November. A due instant frozen in January lands an hour off for every depot on the wrong side of that gap. The fix is to store the civil time plus the IANA zone id and resolve to UTC as late as you reasonably can, so a tzdata update — governments do move these dates — reaches the reminder before the reminder reaches the customer.

Standard crontab has no timezone field at all. Kubernetes added .spec.timeZone to CronJob for exactly this reason; without it the schedule is interpreted in the controller's zone, which is UTC on most clusters and something else on a laptop. And while you are re-reading the expression: if you restrict both day-of-month and day-of-week, Vixie-style cron runs the job when either field matches, not both. 0 9 1 * 1 is not "the first of the month, if it is a Monday". It is every Monday, plus every first.

Two more traps that only show up in a test suite. A civil time inside a spring-forward gap does not exist, and Go's time.Date normalizes it rather than returning an error, so 02:30 quietly becomes 03:30 and the standard library documents that the choice is not guaranteed. A civil time inside a fall-back overlap happens twice. Pick reminder hours in the middle of the working day and both problems disappear; if the product insists on 02:30, decide the policy yourself in code instead of inheriting it.

Buy, build, or rent the tick

The buy-versus-build question here is narrower than it looks, because nobody sells you the part that actually hurts. The occurrence ledger, the expiry policy, the zone resolution and the delivery SLO stay yours in every row of this table.

Option What you stop operating What you still own Where the cost shows up
Managed scheduler plus managed queue Timer hosts, leader election, queue storage Ledger, timezone policy, idempotency, catch-up window Per-invocation and per-message billing that scales with tick frequency
Cron on a VM plus a database table Nothing, but it is small All of it, including the second host you add after the first single point of failure On-call load, not the invoice
Container orchestrator CronJob Timer hosts Missed-start semantics, deadline configuration, worker capacity Cluster capacity and the operational knowledge to debug it
Durable workflow engine Retry, state machine and timer durability Workflow versioning, worker fleet, a separate deployment story Engineering time to model a periodic scan as a workflow
Batch orchestrator Scheduling and dependency graphs Per-user latency, which the tool is not built for Latency for reminders, which is the thing you were optimising

The decision rule I would defend in a review is boring. If the tolerance is measured in minutes — and for renewal reminders anchored to a business day it almost always is — take the coarse tick, put the accuracy in the ledger, and spend the savings on worker capacity for month-end peaks, when renewals cluster on the first. If the tolerance is genuinely sub-minute, keep the coarse tick anyway and buy precision at the queue with per-message delays, because a ten-second global scan is a thirty-fold increase in query volume to fix a problem that lives in three percent of your rows. A durable workflow engine earns its keep when the reminder is a multi-step process with escalation, cancellation and compensation; for a periodic due scan it is a lot of machinery. Batch orchestrators are not suitable here at all — they optimise dependency graphs, not per-user delivery latency.

What the scan looks like, and what to measure after it

Here is the shape in Go. The scheduler calls it, it claims work, and it can be run twice in a row without sending anything twice.

package reminders

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

// Store is the durable side of the ledger. The scheduler owns none of it.
type Store interface {
    Cursor(ctx context.Context) (time.Time, error)
    // Due over-selects on a stored estimate; dueAt below is the authority.
    Due(ctx context.Context, from, to time.Time) ([]Reminder, error)
    Claim(ctx context.Context, key string, due time.Time) (bool, error)
    Advance(ctx context.Context, to time.Time) error
}

type Queue interface {
    Enqueue(ctx context.Context, key string, notBefore time.Time) error
}

type Reminder struct {
    ID       string
    Zone     string    // IANA zone id, e.g. "Europe/Amsterdam"
    LocalDay time.Time // calendar day, civil
    Hour     int       // civil hour in Zone
    Deadline time.Time // the renewal instant this reminder has to beat
}

// dueAt resolves civil time in a named zone at scan time, so a tzdata change
// reaches the reminder instead of a UTC instant frozen months ago.
func dueAt(r Reminder) (time.Time, error) {
    loc, err := time.LoadLocation(r.Zone)
    if err != nil {
        return time.Time{}, fmt.Errorf("zone %q: %w", r.Zone, err)
    }
    d := r.LocalDay
    // A DST gap deletes some civil times; time.Date normalizes rather than
    // erroring, so keep reminder hours out of the small hours.
    return time.Date(d.Year(), d.Month(), d.Day(), r.Hour, 0, 0, 0, loc).UTC(), nil
}

func occurrenceKey(id string, due time.Time) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(id + "@" + due.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:16])
}

// Scan claims every occurrence due in (cursor, now], clamped to maxCatchup so a
// scanner resumed after a long pause never replays a quarter of history.
func Scan(ctx context.Context, s Store, q Queue, now time.Time, maxCatchup time.Duration) error {
    cursor, err := s.Cursor(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if floor := now.Add(-maxCatchup); cursor.Before(floor) {
        cursor = floor
    }
    rs, err := s.Due(ctx, cursor, now)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for _, r := range rs {
        due, err := dueAt(r)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if !due.After(cursor) || due.After(now) {
            continue // outside this window once resolved exactly
        }
        if !now.Before(r.Deadline) {
            continue // the renewal deadline passed: expire it, don't deliver it late
        }
        key := occurrenceKey(r.ID, due)
        fresh, err := s.Claim(ctx, key, due)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if !fresh {
            continue // a previous overlapping scan already owns this one
        }
        if err := q.Enqueue(ctx, key, due); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return s.Advance(ctx, now)
}

The test that matters is the one nobody writes, and it is three lines of setup.

func TestDueAtHonoursTheAmericanDstSwitch(t *testing.T) {
    // 2026: Chicago moves on 8 March, Amsterdam not until 29 March.
    r := Reminder{
        ID:       "coi-4711",
        Zone:     "America/Chicago",
        Hour:     9,
        LocalDay: time.Date(2026, time.March, 9, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
    }
    got, err := dueAt(r)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    want := time.Date(2026, time.March, 9, 14, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    if !got.Equal(want) {
        t.Fatalf("got %s, want %s", got, want)
    }
}

Run the same table for Europe/Amsterdam on 9 March and you should get 08:00 UTC, six hours apart rather than seven. If your suite only ever runs on today's date, this class of bug is invisible until the customer finds it.

Now the part that turns troubleshooting into operations. A green scheduler dashboard tells you a process started; it says nothing about what was owed. Measure the distribution of delivered-minus-due in seconds, the count of occurrences currently overdue, the count expired against a business deadline, and the count suppressed as duplicates — that last one going to zero is a warning sign, because it usually means the claim step stopped running rather than that retries stopped happening. Alert on overdue and expired. Chart the lateness percentiles per zone, because a regional queue backlog shows up there first, and page on the hard clause only.

I am not sure a single tick interval is right for every reminder population, and I would not guess it from a whiteboard: measure the due-window size at your peak day, the enqueue rate, and the worker service rate, then set the cadence against the soft clause and the worker count against the hard one. Your mileage will differ if your renewals cluster on quarter boundaries instead of month boundaries. What does not differ is the boundary — the schedule wakes the scanner, the ledger owes the reminder, and the worker is the only thing allowed to say it was delivered.

Sources

  • crontab(5) manual page — day-of-month and day-of-week matching
  • IANA Time Zone Database
  • Kubernetes CronJob: time zones, starting deadlines and missed schedules
  • systemd.timer: AccuracySec, RandomizedDelaySec and Persistent
  • Amazon SQS FIFO queues: deduplication interval
  • Transactional Outbox pattern
  • Go time.Date: normalization of out-of-range and ambiguous civil times

title: MiniMax H3 now available on AI Gateway
description:
MiniMax H3 is now available on AI Gateway.

H3 generates 2K video from a text prompt, a starting image, a pair of first and last frames, or reference material.

Alongside text-to-video and first-frame image-to-video, the model supports first-to-last keyframe transitions and multimodal reference-to-video, conditioning a generation on reference images, video, or audio in a single request. Reference and keyframe modes are mutually exclusive. Output is mp4 at 2K resolution, from 5 to 15 seconds, in aspect ratios including 21:9, 16:9, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4, and 9:16, or adaptive to a supplied image.

To use MiniMax H3, set model to minimax/minimax-h3 in the AI SDK:

Pass a starting image with the prompt, and the model animates it following the image's aspect ratio.

Supply reference images, video, or audio as source material, and refer to each by its order in the prompt for reference to video output.

View all video models on AI Gateway. Try MiniMax H3 in the model playground.

title: Regional inference now available on AI Gateway
description:
AI Gateway now supports regional inference. Set inferenceRegion on a request to pin it to the US or EU. Every model provider that supports the selected region handles it the same way. Inference runs there, and any data the provider keeps is stored there.

AI Gateway supports two pinned regions, plus global routing:

If no model provider can serve it, the request fails rather than running somewhere else. Every response reports the region that served it, so you can confirm where each request ran.

Here's a request pinned to the US with the AI SDK:

Until now, teams with data residency or compliance requirements had to configure regional routing separately for every provider, with no reliable way to confirm where a request actually ran. Regional inference replaces that with a single field that behaves the same everywhere and a response that tells you where each request was served.

Filter the model list for models available in the US or EU, or read the regions array from /v1/models. Without inferenceRegion, requests route globally with no residency guarantee, so residency is opt-in.

Pinning a region can cost more. The provider sets the regional rate, often around 10% above standard, and AI Gateway passes it through with no markup. For per-provider overrides, response verification, pricing, and BYOK behavior, read the regional inference documentation.

title: Configurando um Servidor HAPI FHIR com BR-Core
description:
Adequação do Servidor FHIR ao BR-Core

Primeiro, é necessário entender como irá funcionar a arquitetura da nossa aplicação como um todo, levando em consideração principalmente o Back-end, Front-end, Servidor FHIR e a RNDS. Nesse modelo não vou entrar em detalhes da infraestrutura porque não é o foco deste artigo. Quero focar na estrutura principal da aplicação e, principalmente, na parte que envolve o servidor FHIR e sua adequação ao BR-Core.

Disclaimer: este artigo surgiu a partir dos problemas que enfrentei durante a implementação de um ambiente FHIR para um sistema do PET-Saúde de Sobral. Por isso, alguns exemplos, nomes de containers, bancos e credenciais utilizados ao longo do artigo são baseados nesse ambiente.

As credenciais apresentadas aqui são exclusivamente de desenvolvimento/teste, criadas para facilitar que os alunos envolvidos no projeto consigam lembrar, reproduzir e modificar o ambiente local sem precisar ficar procurando quais valores utilizar. Elas não correspondem a credenciais de acesso a ambientes de produção ou a serviços reais.

A ideia deste artigo é justamente documentar o caminho que percorri durante a implementação, incluindo alguns dos problemas e decisões que apareceram no processo. Então, se você encontrar alguma solução melhor para alguma das etapas, fique à vontade para compartilhar. 😄

Overview das implementações FHIR

No documento que disponibilizei anteriormente para entendimento do que se trata o HAPI FHIR, também dei ênfase no problema que passamos ao tentar trabalhar com pacientes brasileiros. O servidor conseguia trabalhar normalmente com recursos FHIR, mas não conhecia os perfis específicos do BR-Core, pois eles ainda não haviam sido instalados no ambiente.

Observação: eu ainda não postei o outro artigo porque fiquei muito feliz depois de conseguir resolver esse problema e decidi postar esse primeiro hehe. 😅

Nos repositórios que encontrei, dois projetos acabaram chamando bastante atenção:

  • hapifhir/hapi-fhir

  • hapifhir/hapi-fhir-jpaserver-starter

O primeiro é o projeto principal do HAPI FHIR, onde ficam os módulos responsáveis pela implementação das funcionalidades do FHIR. Ele é desenvolvido principalmente em Java e serve como base para todo o ecossistema do HAPI. Se quiséssemos montar um servidor FHIR completamente do zero utilizando essa implementação, precisaríamos conhecer bastante de Java/Spring Boot e também entender toda a parte de persistência, endpoints, configuração e infraestrutura envolvida. É uma alternativa interessante para quem precisa de uma solução extremamente customizada, mas não era exatamente o nosso caso.

O segundo já nos entrega uma aplicação de servidor baseada no HAPI FHIR JPA, permitindo subir o serviço de forma muito mais rápida sem precisar desenvolver toda essa estrutura do zero. Ele também possui suporte para execução em containers, o que facilita bastante quando estamos trabalhando com Docker.

É importante lembrar que o HAPI não é a única implementação disponível. Existem várias outras implementações open-source do FHIR em diferentes linguagens e frameworks, e elas podem ser consultadas na lista de implementações open-source do HL7.

No nosso caso, escolhemos a implementação em Java principalmente pela comunidade e pela quantidade de material disponível. Quando começamos a mexer com uma tecnologia dessas, inevitavelmente aparecem problemas de configuração, arquitetura e infraestrutura, então ter bastante documentação e gente que já passou pelos mesmos problemas ajuda muito. O próprio projeto já traz bastante material relacionado a Docker, PostgreSQL, CORS, proxy reverso, load balancers e outras coisas que provavelmente vamos precisar conforme o projeto crescer.

Mas existe uma peculiaridade importante: o HAPI FHIR está adequado ao padrão FHIR, mas ele não vem com os perfis específicos do Brasil instalados por padrão. É aí que entra o BR-Core.

Desenho da arquitetura

A arquitetura inicial que estamos pensando ficou mais ou menos assim:

Diagrama Mermaid 

flowchart TD

    %% Estilos dos nós

    classDef frontend fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff

    classDef laravel fill:#ef4444,stroke:#dc2626,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff

    classDef db fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff

    classDef fhir fill:#10b981,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff

    classDef rnds fill:#8b5cf6,stroke:#7c3aed,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff


    subgraph Cliente ["Camada de Apresentação (Frontend)"]

        UI["Interface do Utilizador\n(React, Vue, ou Blade)"]:::frontend

    end


    subgraph Sistema_Principal ["Backend Principal"]

        API["Laravel App (API)\n- Autenticação\n- Orquestração\n- Assinatura Digital"]:::laravel

        LocalDB[("Banco Local\n(PostgreSQL/MySQL)\n- Utilizadores\n- Permissões\n- IDs de Mapeamento")]:::db

        API <-->|SQL| LocalDB

    end


    subgraph CasaOS ["Ambiente FHIR Local (Docker no CasaOS)"]

        HAPI["Servidor HAPI FHIR\n(BR-Core Ativo)"]:::fhir

        FHIRDB[("Banco FHIR\n(PostgreSQL 15)")]:::db

        HAPI <-->|JDBC/Hibernate| FHIRDB

    end


    subgraph Externo ["Ministério da Saúde"]

        RNDS["RNDS\n(Rede Nacional de Dados em Saúde)"]:::rnds

    end


    %% Fluxo de comunicação

    UI <-->|HTTP / REST JSON| API

    API <-->|FHIR REST JSON| HAPI

    API <-->|Integração segura| RNDS

Papel de cada componente na arquitetura

1. Interface do Utilizador (Frontend)

O frontend não precisa conversar diretamente com o servidor FHIR. A ideia é que ele envie os formulários normais e consuma os endpoints REST expostos pelo Laravel. Dessa forma, a camada visual não precisa saber o que é FHIR ou como um Patient deve ser estruturado segundo o BR-Core. Essas responsabilidades ficam concentradas no backend.

2. Laravel App — o orquestrador

O Laravel é o cérebro da operação. Ele recebe a requisição do frontend e divide as águas entre o que pertence à aplicação e o que pertence ao servidor FHIR.

Dados como passwords, tokens de sessão, permissões de acesso e a interface administrativa do projeto PET-Saúde ficam no banco da própria aplicação. Já os dados clínicos seguem para o HAPI FHIR.

O Laravel atua como uma espécie de tradutor. Ele pega os dados recebidos do formulário, aplica as regras necessárias e constrói o JSON do recurso FHIR de acordo com os perfis do BR-Core, enviando posteriormente esse recurso para o HAPI.

No banco de dados do Laravel, uma tabela de pacientes, por exemplo, poderia guardar apenas informações necessárias para o controle da aplicação, como:

id_local
nome
cpf
fhir_id

O fhir_id seria a referência para o recurso correspondente dentro do servidor FHIR. Quando fosse necessário consultar o histórico clínico, o Laravel utilizaria esse identificador para buscar os dados no HAPI.

3. HAPI FHIR Server & Base de Dados

Esse é o nosso servidor FHIR. Como estamos adicionando o BR-Core, ele passa a ter acesso aos perfis brasileiros que vamos utilizar para estruturar e validar nossos recursos.

O banco de dados utilizado pelo HAPI é o PostgreSQL. A aplicação não deve manipular esse banco diretamente para criar ou alterar recursos FHIR. Quem deve controlar essa persistência é o próprio HAPI, através da API FHIR.

4. RNDS

Quando um atendimento estiver finalizado e precisar ser enviado para a rede nacional, o Laravel entra em ação novamente. A ideia é buscar no HAPI os recursos necessários, montar o conteúdo esperado para a integração e realizar a comunicação com a RNDS seguindo os requisitos definidos pelo Ministério da Saúde, incluindo os mecanismos de autenticação, transporte seguro e assinatura digital necessários.

Docker Compose e Envs

Com a arquitetura definida, podemos começar pela parte prática.

Primeiro, baixei a imagem do HAPI FHIR:

sudo docker pull hapiproject/hapi:v8.12.0-2

Preferi utilizar uma versão específica em vez de latest, principalmente para evitar que uma atualização futura da imagem altere o comportamento do ambiente sem que tenhamos planejado isso.

Depois criei os arquivos docker-compose.yml e application.yaml.

application.yaml

O application.yaml ficou responsável principalmente pela conexão com o PostgreSQL, configuração do FHIR R4, CORS e algumas configurações do HAPI:

spring:
  datasource:
    # Conecta o HAPI ao container do PostgreSQL criado no docker-compose
    url: 'jdbc:postgresql://fhir-db:5432/hapi'
    username: postgres
    password: admin_pet_saude
    driverClassName: org.postgresql.Driver

  jpa:
    properties:
      # O dialeto obriga o Hibernate a traduzir as queries para o padrão PostgreSQL
      hibernate.dialect: ca.uhn.fhir.jpa.model.dialect.HapiFhirPostgresDialect

      # Desativa a busca full-text avançada inicialmente
      hibernate.search.enabled: false

hapi:
  fhir:
    # Habilita a versão R4 do FHIR, utilizada pelo BR-Core
    fhir_version: R4

    # Habilita o upload dinâmico de Implementation Guides
    ig_runtime_upload_enabled: true

    cors:
      allow_Credentials: false
      allowed_origin:
        - "*"

      # Em produção, substitua "*" pelos domínios reais
      allowed_headers:
        - Origin
        - Accept
        - Content-Type
        - Authorization
        - Cache-Control
        - If-Match
        - If-None-Match

      exposed_headers:
        - Location
        - Content-Location
        - ETag

    tester:
      home:
        name: PET-Saúde Local FHIR
        server_address: 'http://localhost:8080/fhir'
        refuse_to_fetch_third_party_urls: false
        fhir_version: R4

Algumas funcionalidades mais avançadas ficaram de fora neste primeiro momento porque não eram necessárias para o MVP. A ideia é não adicionar complexidade antes de realmente precisar dela.

docker-compose.yml

O docker-compose.yml ficou responsável por subir tanto o servidor FHIR quanto o PostgreSQL:

services:
  fhir-server:
    container_name: pet_fhir_api
    image: "hapiproject/hapi:v8.12.0-2"

    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

    configs:
      - source: hapi_config
        target: /app/config/application.yaml

    depends_on:
      - fhir-db

    networks:
      - pet_saude_net

    restart: unless-stopped

  fhir-db:
    container_name: pet_fhir_db
    image: postgres:15-alpine

    restart: unless-stopped

    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: admin_pet_saude
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_DB: hapi

    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

    volumes:
      - fhir_pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

    networks:
      - pet_saude_net

configs:
  hapi_config:
    file: ./application.yaml

volumes:
  fhir_pg_data:

networks:
  pet_saude_net:
    driver: bridge

Depois de subir o ambiente, alguns endpoints interessantes para testar são:

http://localhost:8080
http://localhost:8080/fhir/swagger-ui
http://localhost:8080/fhir/metadata

O /fhir/metadata, em especial, retorna o CapabilityStatement do servidor e ajuda bastante a entender o que aquela instância do FHIR suporta.

HAPI FHIR CLI

Até aqui temos um servidor FHIR funcionando, mas ainda falta uma parte importante: precisamos colocar as definições do BR-Core dentro dele.

Foi nessa etapa que encontrei o HAPI FHIR CLI.

A documentação oficial pode ser encontrada aqui:

  • https://hapifhir.io/hapi-fhir/docs/tools/hapi_fhir_cli.html

  • https://github.com/hapifhir/hapi-fhir/releases

O CLI é uma ferramenta de linha de comando do HAPI que permite realizar algumas operações relacionadas ao ecossistema FHIR. No nosso caso, ele seria útil principalmente para trabalhar com pacotes e Implementation Guides.

Minha ideia inicial era utilizar o próprio CLI para pegar as definições do BR-Core e gerar o .tgz que posteriormente seria instalado no servidor.

Foi aí que comecei a procurar onde exatamente estava o pacote que precisava.

O BR-Core

Para entender e baixar o material do BR-Core, utilizei a documentação disponibilizada pelo projeto:

  • https://fhir.saude.go.gov.br/r4/core/downloads.html

  • https://hl7.org.br/fhir/core/downloads.html

Uma coisa legal que descobri nesse processo foi o Forge, uma ferramenta que permite editar e criar perfis FHIR.

Download:

  • https://simplifier.net/forge

O Forge é interessante principalmente quando começarmos a criar ou adaptar perfis próprios, já que trabalhar manualmente com todos aqueles JSONs de StructureDefinition pode ficar meio doloroso depois de um tempo.

Mas, para o que eu precisava agora, o mais importante era conseguir o pacote oficial do BR-Core.

E aqui vem, novamente, uma das partes mais chatas desse projeto: encontrar o bendito **package.tgz**.

Eu já tinha falado que essa parte foi meio sofrida, mas vale reforçar porque provavelmente alguém vai passar pela mesma coisa. Na documentação oficial do BR-Core existe bastante coisa para baixar, mas não fica muito claro que, para utilizar o pacote no HAPI, você precisa baixar o guia de implementação completo em **.zip** e procurar o pacote lá dentro. Não existe aquele momento mágico de “clique aqui para baixar o package.tgz”. Você baixa o ZIP, abre um monte de arquivo e começa a procurar por package, na esperança de encontrar o que precisa.

Enquanto eu não encontrava o arquivo, comecei até a estudar o HAPI FHIR CLI, porque achei que provavelmente teria que gerar o .tgz por conta própria. Felizmente, não precisei inventar moda.

Depois de abrir o ZIP e pesquisar por package, encontrei os pacotes das implementações já prontos, no formato .tgz. No meu caso, como o servidor está configurado para trabalhar com FHIR R4, o arquivo que nos interessa é:

package.r4.tgz

E uma comparação que achei curiosa é que, no outro guia disponibilizado junto à documentação, o Guia de Implementação da SES GO - CORE, da Secretaria de Estado da Saúde de Goiás (SES-GO), essa parte é bem mais tranquila. Na página de downloads existe um tópico específico chamado “NPM Package”, justamente para explicar e disponibilizar o package.tgz. Você entra, encontra o tópico, baixa o pacote e segue a vida.

Já no material do BR-Core que eu estava utilizando, precisei fazer essa pequena caça ao tesouro para descobrir que o pacote já estava dentro do guia completo. 😅

POR FAVOR LEIA: BAIXE O GUIA COMPLETO EM **.ZIP**, ABRA O ARQUIVO E PESQUISE **PACKAGE**.

É sério. 😭 Os pacotes .tgz das implementações já estão lá, prontos para uso. Depois é só escolher o que corresponde à versão do FHIR utilizada pelo seu servidor.

Com os arquivos finalmente encontrados, podemos partir para a configuração do HAPI e para a instalação do pacote no nosso servidor.

Organização do projeto

Depois que encontrei o pacote, organizei os arquivos em uma pasta própria para deixar tudo relacionado ao servidor FHIR no mesmo lugar:

pet-compose/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── application.yaml
└── fhir-packages/
    └── package.r4.tgz

A ideia é que essa pasta fhir-packages concentre os pacotes que forem necessários futuramente.

Como o pacote está na máquina host, precisamos fazer com que o container também consiga enxergá-lo. Para isso, adicionei um bind mount ao serviço do FHIR:

volumes:
  - ./fhir-packages:/fhir-packages

Esse volume faz uma ligação entre uma pasta da máquina que está executando o Docker e uma pasta dentro do container.

Então temos:

Máquina host
./fhir-packages
       │
       │ bind mount
       ▼
Container
/fhir-packages

Assim, o arquivo que está no nosso projeto também fica disponível para o ambiente do HAPI.

Instalando o BR-Core

Com o pacote em mãos, chegou a hora de instalá-lo.

Aqui aconteceu uma das partes mais interessantes do processo, porque a documentação nem sempre deixa claro qual é exatamente o formato que determinada operação do HAPI espera.

A operação utilizada pelo servidor é:

POST /fhir/ImplementationGuide/$install

Na primeira tentativa, tentei enviar diretamente o .tgz para o endpoint utilizando application/gzip.

O HAPI respondeu que a operação precisava receber um Content-Type FHIR. Ou seja, não bastava simplesmente mandar o arquivo compactado.

Depois disso, transformei o .tgz em Base64:

base64 -w 0 /home/debugz/pet-compose/fhir-packages/package.r4.tgz > /tmp/brcore.b64

Agora o conteúdo do pacote estava salvo em:

/tmp/brcore.b64

Em seguida, criei um Parameters FHIR contendo esse conteúdo:

python3 - <<'PY'
import json

with open("/tmp/brcore.b64") as f:
    # Remove a quebra de linha final gerada pelo base64
    data = f.read().strip()

params = {
    "resourceType": "Parameters",
    "parameter": [
        {
            "name": "npmContent",
            "valueBase64Binary": data
        }
    ]
}

with open("/tmp/brcore-install.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(params, f)

print("Arquivo criado: /tmp/brcore-install.json")
PY

E finalmente fiz o POST:

curl -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/fhir+json" \
  -H "Accept: application/fhir+json" \
  --data-binary @/tmp/brcore-install.json \
  "http://localhost:8080/fhir/ImplementationGuide/\$install"

O retorno foi:

{
  "resourceType": "Parameters"
}

Nesse momento eu já tinha uma boa indicação de que a instalação tinha sido aceita, mas ainda faltava confirmar se os recursos realmente estavam disponíveis.

Nem tudo funcionou de primeira

Como quase sempre acontece quando estamos configurando alguma coisa nova, o caminho não foi exatamente reto.

A primeira tentativa de chamar o $install utilizando diretamente o .tgz falhou porque o endpoint esperava uma requisição FHIR.

Depois, na primeira versão do Parameters, utilizei um nome de parâmetro incorreto e o HAPI acabou retornando um NullPointerException. Depois de entender melhor o formato esperado pela operação, alterei o parâmetro para npmContent e a instalação passou a ser processada.

Também apareceu um warning durante a instalação: o StructureDefinition/br-core-careteam estava com status = draft, e a configuração atual do HAPI não permitiu que esse recurso fosse instalado.

Mesmo assim, o restante do pacote continuou sendo processado normalmente.

No final, o HAPI informou que havia criado:

46 resources of type StructureDefinition

e ignorado:

1 resource of type StructureDefinition

Então, apesar dos percalços, a instalação do pacote funcionou.

Confirmando o BR-Core no servidor

Agora vinha a parte que eu considero mais importante: não basta o servidor responder que instalou alguma coisa. Precisamos confirmar que os recursos realmente estão disponíveis.

Para isso, fiz uma busca pelo StructureDefinition do paciente:

curl -s \
  -H "Accept: application/fhir+json" \
  "http://localhost:8080/fhir/StructureDefinition?url=https://br-core.saude.gov.br/fhir/StructureDefinition/br-core-patient" \
  | jq '.entry[]?.resource | {resourceType,id,url,version,status}'

O resultado foi:

{
  "resourceType": "StructureDefinition",
  "id": "1080",
  "url": "https://br-core.saude.gov.br/fhir/StructureDefinition/br-core-patient",
  "version": "1.3.0",
  "status": "active"
}

Ou seja, o br-core-patient realmente está disponível no servidor, com a URL canônica correta, versão 1.3.0 e status active.

Foi aqui que finalmente deu para dizer: beleza, o BR-Core está no nosso HAPI.

E o ImplementationGuide?

Durante a instalação, o HAPI também encontrou o ImplementationGuide dentro do pacote:

ImplementationGuide-br.gov.saude.br-core.fhir.json

com a URL:

https://br-core.saude.gov.br/fhir/ImplementationGuide/br.gov.saude.br-core.fhir

Porém, quando fiz a busca:

curl -s -G \
  -H "Accept: application/fhir+json" \
  --data-urlencode \
  "url=https://br-core.saude.gov.br/fhir/ImplementationGuide/br.gov.saude.br-core.fhir" \
  "http://localhost:8080/fhir/ImplementationGuide"

o servidor retornou:

{
  "resourceType": "Bundle",
  "type": "searchset",
  "total": 0
}

Isso foi uma situação interessante porque os StructureDefinitions foram instalados e podem ser consultados normalmente, enquanto o ImplementationGuide não aparece no endpoint de recursos.

Ainda não vou entrar muito nessa investigação aqui porque ela merece um artigo próprio se eu for realmente aprofundar no comportamento interno do PackageInstallerSvc e na diferença entre o gerenciamento de packages e a persistência dos recursos no repositório FHIR.

Para o objetivo atual, o que importa é que os perfis necessários do BR-Core já estão disponíveis no servidor.

Estado atual

Então, neste momento, temos:

HAPI FHIR
  versão: v8.12.0-2
  FHIR: R4
  container: pet_fhir_api

PostgreSQL
  versão: 15
  container: pet_fhir_db

BR-Core
  package: br.gov.saude.br-core.fhir.r4
  versão: 1.3.0

StructureDefinitions
  criados: 46
  ignorados: 1

br-core-patient
  status: active
  versão: 1.3.0
  disponível pela API: sim

ImplementationGuide
  encontrado no pacote: sim
  disponível em /ImplementationGuide: não

O br-core-careteam foi o único StructureDefinition ignorado porque estava como draft.

Próximos passos

Agora que temos a base funcionando, os próximos passos são começar a utilizar os perfis do BR-Core de verdade dentro da aplicação.

Isso significa definir quais recursos realmente serão utilizados pelo projeto, criar os Patient, Practitioner, Encounter e outros recursos necessários, validar esses recursos contra os perfis corretos e começar a estruturar a comunicação entre o Laravel e o HAPI FHIR.

Depois disso entra uma parte ainda maior do projeto, que é trabalhar a integração com a RNDS.

A ideia não é tentar resolver tudo de uma vez. Primeiro colocamos o servidor FHIR de pé, depois adicionamos os perfis necessários, validamos os recursos e só então começamos a construir as integrações em cima disso.

Conclusão

No começo, parecia que o problema era simplesmente:

"Precisamos colocar o BR-Core no nosso HAPI FHIR."

Na prática, acabou envolvendo Docker, PostgreSQL, HAPI FHIR, HAPI CLI, pacotes FHIR, .tgz, Base64, scripts em Python e alguns erros no caminho.

E foi justamente isso que tornou o processo interessante.

No final, conseguimos instalar o pacote:

br.gov.saude.br-core.fhir.r4#1.3.0

e confirmar que os StructureDefinitions do BR-Core estão disponíveis no nosso servidor HAPI FHIR.

Ainda existem alguns pontos que quero investigar e melhorar, mas pelo menos agora temos uma base funcional para continuar desenvolvendo a infraestrutura de saúde digital do projeto.

E acho que essa é uma das partes mais legais de trabalhar com tecnologia: você começa pensando que vai "só instalar um pacote" e termina estudando como um servidor FHIR resolve packages por dentro. 😂

E se você trabalha com FHIR, BR-Core, RNDS ou qualquer coisa relacionada e tiver alguma sugestão, correção ou uma forma melhor de fazer alguma das coisas que mostrei aqui, pode falar comigo! Ainda estou aprendendo bastante sobre esse ecossistema, então toda troca com quem já tem mais experiência é muito bem-vinda. A ideia aqui é justamente compartilhar o que fui descobrindo no caminho e também aprender com quem já passou por problemas parecidos. 😄

Referências

  • HAPI FHIR — Documentação oficial do HAPI FHIR, servidor e framework utilizado neste projeto.

  • HAPI FHIR CLI — Documentação oficial da ferramenta de linha de comando do HAPI FHIR.

  • HAPI FHIR no GitHub — Repositório oficial do HAPI FHIR e seu código-fonte.

  • HAPI FHIR JPA Server Starter — Projeto base para executar um servidor HAPI FHIR utilizando JPA.

  • Releases do HAPI FHIR — Página com as versões e releases oficiais do HAPI FHIR.

  • Implementações Open Source de FHIR — Lista de implementações open source de servidores e ferramentas FHIR.

  • BR-Core — Documentação e materiais oficiais do Guia de Implementação do BR-Core.

  • Forge — Ferramenta para criação e edição de perfis e artefatos FHIR.

  • Integração RNDS — Kyriosdata — Bibliotecas e ferramentas em Java e JavaScript/NPM para integração com a RNDS.

  • JSONPath Evaluator — Ferramenta para navegar e consultar estruturas JSON utilizando expressões JSONPath.

  • Simplifier — Projeto RNDS — Plataforma para publicação, gerenciamento e compartilhamento de artefatos FHIR relacionados à RNDS.

  • Simplifier — Introdução ao RNDS — Página de introdução aos artefatos e recursos do projeto RNDS.

  • RNDS — Guia de Integração — Documentação oficial para integração de sistemas com a RNDS.

  • RNDS — Passo a Passo — Guia oficial com as etapas para integração e envio de dados à RNDS.

title: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is now supported on Vercel CDN
description:
Vercel CDN now supports Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) for domains managed by Vercel DNS. ECH encrypts the Server Name Indication (SNI) in the TLS handshake, the last part of an HTTPS connection that revealed which hostname a client was connecting to. With ECH, network observers see a connection to Vercel's shared ECH hostname, vercel-ech.com.

ECH is managed at the platform level and automatically enabled selectively where supported, starting in the US for a limited number of TLDs, and expanding to more TLDs and regions over time.

Recent versions of Chrome, Edge, and Firefox support Encrypted Client Hello.

Learn more about ECH and how Vercel CDN protects your application in the CDN encryption documentation.
