title: Everything hackable will get hacked
description:
Over the past year, AI models have become much more capable of performing cybersecurity work. These changes are reshaping both the threats facing the web and the tools available to defend it. Right now, defenders have an advantage because they can use stronger models for defensive work than the open-weight models broadly available for offensive research. But this advantage will not always last. The gap will soon close.

I have both good news and bad news, neither of which is yet widely understood in the community.

  • Bad news: Near-frontier open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today. Kimi K3 is an Opus 4.X-class model with no relevant cybersecurity safeguards.

  • Good news: You do not need to wait for “Mythos access” or OpenAI’s cyber program to begin defensive cybersecurity work. Frontier models, with the notable exception of Fable 5, will perform defensive cybersecurity tasks today.

The uncertainty around Mythos 5's release seems to have created a kind of paralysis among defenders, many of whom are underutilizing the powerful tools available to them today. This post aims to give readers insight into how we're thinking about AI-enabled defensive cybersecurity at Vercel and why we think teams should be moving with more urgency.

The OpenAI/Hugging Face security incident

This YouTube video from OpenAI researchers on the widely reported security incident involving Hugging Face is an absolute must-watch for anyone concerned with cybersecurity. It clarifies that there were two separate security incidents exploiting vulnerabilities that will be found in most computer systems.

The gist is that models working on an OpenAI training run found 0-day vulnerabilities that allowed them to bypass egress internet restrictions, enabling communication between models and access to the broader internet. Once internet access was established, broader exploitation occurred.

Open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today

Open-weight model capabilities have been top of mind in the AI community lately, but it is less widely understood that Kimi K3, a popular open-weight model, has no effective safeguards against offensive cybersecurity work.

On DeepSec Bench, which measures application-code vulnerability discovery, it ranks highest among the open-weight models we evaluated, roughly matching Sonnet 5 and outperforming Opus 4.8.

I tasked Kimi K3 with trying to break out of Vercel Sandbox, and while it did not successfully escape, it mapped the guest-kernel attack surface, followed possible privilege escalation paths, built a VM environment to reproduce its ideas, and implemented and ran a fuzzer.

These are some excerpts from that research, beginning with an analysis of the guest-kernel attack surface.

The model followed that lead into candidate privilege escalation paths and considered what guest-kernel control could mean for a microVM escape.

When paths still needed testing, Kimi built a VM environment for reproductions and wrote a stateful fuzzer for the device path it was investigating.

While none of this produced an escape from Vercel Sandbox, it did show Kimi conducting an investigation on its own, and given the right vulnerable surface, this would lead to a successful exploit.

Frontier models can help defenders today

Much of the community assumed that meaningful security review would require access to Mythos-class models and therefore held off on using the models already available to them.

But that assumption has never been true. All the frontier models that we evaluated, with the notable exception of Fable 5, can perform defensive cybersecurity work today and have been able to do so throughout the year so far.

The rough heuristic I have observed is that models with safeguards will still make hypotheses about security vulnerabilities when they have access to source code, apparently because access to proprietary source code typically suggests a defensive use case. Attackers can also obtain source code, but I think source-code access is a reasonable working signal of defensive intent.

I personally discovered this in March, when I first heard about cyber variants and was also seeing AI code reviews find security issues in my own code. That made me wonder, “If code review can find issues in a diff, can I also run it across an entire codebase?” It turns out the answer was yes. From that experiment, I created deepsec, an open-source security harness for performing security analysis at scale across large codebases.

The temporary defensive advantage

Right now, OpenAI’s Sol 5.6 on XHigh is the best model for cybersecurity defense. It is much smarter than Kimi K3, the best available open-weight model without safeguards against offensive work. As defender, you have the better tool at your disposal, but you have to use it.

A full deepsec review will help you improve the security posture of your codebase by surfacing vulnerability hypotheses for you to investigate. In my experience, it is especially good at finding IDORs, XSS, and SSRF. The Hugging Face incident shows what this kind of application-level research looks like from the other side, since the models kept searching after an SSRF attempt was blocked and eventually found successful routes through file disclosure and template injection.

deepsec is open source and can run entirely in your own infrastructure with inference providers controlled by you. Vercel has no financial gain from you using it. It is really worth trying on your own source code.

Once the run finishes, review every finding yourself and compare the results with what your current security process already catches.

Continuous defense

AI model capabilities will continue to improve, and I expect open-weight models to catch up with Sol’s current performance on application-code vulnerability discovery even as frontier models advance again. We need to prepare for that cycle by continuously improving how we find and fix vulnerabilities as the models progress.

At Vercel, we run full deepsec reviews across mission-critical repositories every quarter and whenever a stronger model becomes available, in addition to automated security reviews on every pull request.

Those full reviews cost tens of thousands of dollars, which we consider a relatively small expense compared with what we spend on our HackerOne program or the opportunity cost of a security incident.

We have connected deepsec output to Vercel software factories for automated vulnerability processing and will share more about this work soon. As these reviews produce more findings, automatically managing them becomes the next frontier.

What Vercel is doing

As an immediate measure, we made the full egress firewall in Vercel Sandbox available on the Hobby plan, giving everyone access to the same network controls.

We are also working to launch a dedicated HackerOne program focused on finding zero-day vulnerabilities in Vercel Sandbox and the egress firewall. We want to redirect offensive model capabilities toward defensive work, so the program will cover AI costs for researchers who use AI Gateway and submit a vulnerability report that is accepted.

We also plan to extend deepsec to use the offensive capabilities of open-weight models and cyber variants of frontier models when triaging the vulnerability hypotheses it identifies.

Defenders can already use stronger models than those broadly available for offensive work. Teams should use that advantage now and continue reviewing their systems as the gap closes.

Takeaways

  • The cybersecurity threat from AI models is real.

  • Everybody can improve their defensive posture with tools like deepsec today.

  • Doing this is urgent, and the practice should continue as models improve.

title: NodeSchool Learn on your own
description:
When it comes to learning a new technology or understanding the features of a language, we always look for tutorials on the internet that teach us its concepts. That's why today I want to talk to you about NodeSchool.io, an initiative that aims to teach these topics through self-guided workshops.

Node School is a community that helps you gain skills in Node.js and JavaScript in an interactive format. All their tutorials are Open Source and start with simple exercises that gradually increase in difficulty as you progress. To complete the Node School modules, you should have an intermediate knowledge of JavaScript. Otherwise, I recommend reading a couple of tutorials or doing the javascripting workshop that you can find within Node School. When you feel comfortable with the language, you will be ready to start.

Getting Started with Node School

To start with the workshops provided by Node School, you need to have Node.JS installed on your computer. You can download the installers from their official page and follow the wizard (personally, I like to install Node via NVM). The lessons run in the terminal and work on Linux, Mac, and Windows. Let's see how to work with these lessons.

Installing a Lesson or Workshop

It is recommended to create a directory on your computer with the name of the workshop and access it from the terminal. Then we will install the workshop via NPM.

$ mkdir learnyounode
$ cd learnyounode
$ npm install -g learnyounode
$ learnyounode

After running the learnyounode command, we will have a list of exercises to complete in the console. Let's see now how to work on these exercises in the best way.

Completing an Exercise

When we select an exercise, in this case, "Hello World," we will have a screen similar to the one shown below, where we will see the exercise description and some tips and resources to learn more about the content.

The exercise recommends creating a file with a .js extension (I particularly like to name this file with the name of the exercise). In this case, I will create a file called helloworld.js where we will write the solution. To verify that our solution to the exercise is correct, we must run the command learnyounode verify helloworld.js.

$ touch helloworld.js
$ learnyounode verify helloworld.js

If our solution is correct, Node School will indicate it with a similar screen. If it fails, it will tell us where we went wrong.

Finally, if we run the learnyounode command again, Node School will indicate that we have completed the previous exercise.

I hope this short guide helps you start your self-learning journey. Until next time.

I hope this has been useful and/or taught you something new!

@khriztianmoreno 🚀

title: Vercel WAF for Blob is now in beta
description:
The Vercel WAF can now protect a Vercel Blob store. The same rules that guard your deployments (deny, challenge, rate limit) now apply to blob traffic with no changes to your code, blob URLs, or @vercel/blob.

Every blob is already served through Vercel's CDN, so protection is a switch on the store, not a new proxy. Stop scrapers, geo-restrict downloads, rate limit expensive assets, or block abusive IPs before a byte is served.

Rules evaluate at the edge, matching on IP, country, path, and more:

  • Deny returns a 403 and stops the request early, so no data transfer is incurred.

  • Challenge serves the standard browser challenge, and a request that fails it is blocked.

  • Rate limit returns a 429 when a client exceeds your limit.

  • Redirect and log behave as they do for deployment traffic.

The OWASP Core Ruleset is not supported, since it targets dynamic application traffic, not object delivery.

Protecting a store

Setup is a single switch in the dashboard:

  • Open your Blob store, select Settings, then Protect your store.

  • Vercel connects it to a shared vercel-blob-default-project on your team. You author its rules with the standard rule builder, and they take effect immediately.

  • One rule set covers every protected store, so rules can't be scoped per store.

During the beta, setup is dashboard-only, and challenges need a browser to solve, so server-side @vercel/blob requests matching a challenge rule are blocked. Use challenge rules for browser traffic.

Vercel WAF for Blob is available in beta on all plans. See the documentation for the full setup.

title: Keeping a browser timer accurate in background tabs (what I learned building ClockAura)
description:
I run ClockAura, a free site of online timers: countdowns, a Pomodoro timer, a stopwatch, interval timers for the gym. The first versions had the bug I suspect every browser timer has at some point: start a countdown, switch to another tab, and it rings late. Sometimes minutes late.

The bug wasn't in one line of code. It came from an assumption: that the browser keeps running your code at the same pace when nobody is looking. It doesn't. This post covers what I changed and why. The code snippets are lightly trimmed from the real hook that runs every countdown on the site.

The naive version

My first countdown looked like most tutorials:

// Don't do this
const id = setInterval(() => {
  setRemaining((r) => r - 1000);
}, 1000);

Two separate things are wrong here.

First, setInterval(fn, 1000) doesn't promise a call every 1000 ms. It promises at least 1000 ms between calls. Every late call adds a little drift, and subtracting a fixed 1000 bakes that drift into the result. Over a 25-minute Pomodoro you can lose whole seconds even in a foreground tab.

Second, background tabs. Chrome limits timers in hidden tabs to roughly one wake-up per second, and after a page has been hidden for a few minutes it can batch chained timers much more aggressively, down to about once a minute. Firefox and Safari have their own versions of this. A countdown that counts ticks is at the mercy of how many ticks the browser lets you have.

Rule 1: store the end, not the remaining

The fix most people land on, and the one that matters most: when the timer starts, compute the moment it should end, and from then on derive everything from that moment.

useEffect(() => {
  if (running) {
    targetRef.current = performance.now() + remaining;
    liveRef.current = true;
    rafRef.current = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    armBackup();
  }
  // cleanup cancels the frame and the timeout
}, [running, tick]);

Each tick then asks "how far are we from the end?" instead of "subtract one more second":

const tick = useCallback(() => {
  if (!liveRef.current) return;
  const left = Math.max(0, targetRef.current - performance.now());
  setRemaining(left);
  if (left <= 0) { /* finish: see Rule 3 */ return; }
  rafRef.current = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}, []);

A late tick no longer causes drift. If a frame arrives 300 ms late, the display jumps 300 ms and is correct again. Nothing accumulates.

I use performance.now() here, not Date.now(). performance.now() is monotonic: it doesn't move when the user's clock syncs with a time server or when someone changes the system time. Date.now() can jump backwards or forwards, and a countdown that gains five minutes because Windows corrected the clock is a fun bug report to read.

There is one place where I do use Date.now(): when a running timer is saved to localStorage so it can be resumed after a reload. performance.now() restarts at zero on every page load, so it can't be stored. The saved record keeps a wall-clock endsAt, and the page turns it back into a duration when you come back:

const left = t.endsAt ? t.endsAt - Date.now() : t.left;

Rule 2: don't trust requestAnimationFrame to finish the job

I moved the display loop to requestAnimationFrame because it lines up with the screen refresh and makes the digits look smooth. The catch: browsers pause rAF entirely in hidden tabs. Not slow it down. Pause it.

With a rAF-only loop, the end-timestamp math is still correct, but nothing runs the check. So the timer "finishes" the moment you switch back to the tab, which might be ten minutes after it should have rung. That was most of the late-alarm reports.

The fix is a second, much simpler mechanism: one setTimeout aimed straight at the end time.

const armBackup = useCallback(() => {
  clearTimeout(backupRef.current);
  if (!liveRef.current) return;
  const left = targetRef.current - performance.now();
  backupRef.current = setTimeout(() => {
    if (!liveRef.current) return;
    if (targetRef.current - performance.now() <= 0) tick();
    else armBackup();
  }, Math.max(0, left) + 15);
}, [tick]);

A few details that took me more than one try:

  • One long timeout, not a ticking one. Background throttling hits chained timers hardest: timers that schedule timers, again and again. A single timeout set for 25 minutes is about the friendliest thing you can ask a throttled tab for. At worst it gets lined up with the next one-second boundary, which is fine for a kitchen timer and a Pomodoro.
  • The +15 ms. Timer callbacks and performance.now() don't share an exact clock, and performance.now() is deliberately coarsened for security reasons. Without the padding, the timeout sometimes fired a hair before the target, saw 2 ms left, and had to re-arm. The padding makes the common case a single wake-up.
  • Re-arm if early. If it does fire early anyway, it schedules itself again for the real remainder instead of giving up or ringing early.

When the user adds a minute with the +1 button, the end moves, so the backup has to move too:

const addMs = useCallback((deltaMs) => {
  setRemaining((prev) => {
    const next = Math.max(0, prev + deltaMs);
    targetRef.current += next - prev;
    return next;
  });
  setTimeout(armBackup, 0); // end time moved: re-aim the backstop
}, [armBackup]);

The setTimeout(armBackup, 0) is there because the state updater runs later than you might expect. Re-arming on the next turn means the backup reads the updated target.

Rule 3: two ways to finish means two ways to ring twice

Once both rAF and setTimeout can end the timer, you have a race. Come back to the tab at exactly the wrong moment and both fire within a few milliseconds. The user hears the alarm twice and the "focus minutes" stat would count the session twice.

The guard is one ref that both paths check, and the finishing path flips it first, before doing anything else:

if (left <= 0) {
  liveRef.current = false;          // close the door first
  clearTimeout(backupRef.current);  // cancel the other path
  cancelAnimationFrame(rafRef.current);
  setRunning(false);
  onDoneRef.current();              // ring exactly once
  return;
}

It has to be a ref, not state. State updates are batched and applied on the next render, so two callbacks in the same turn would both read the old running === true. A ref is just a mutable box, and the second caller sees false immediately.

onDone lives in a ref for a related reason: the page passes a fresh callback on every render, and I didn't want tick to be recreated 60 times a second because of it.

Rule 4: keep the screen on, but only when it matters

A lot of timers end up on a projector or a TV: classroom timers, workout timers across the room. Nothing kills that faster than the laptop dimming its screen at minute nine.

The Screen Wake Lock API fixes it in a few lines, with two catches. The lock is released automatically whenever the page is hidden, and it's not re-acquired when you come back. So the hook listens for visibilitychange and asks again:

const onVisible = () => {
  if (active && document.visibilityState === 'visible' && !lockRef.current) acquire();
};
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', onVisible);

The other catch is about scope. The lock is held while a timer runs or while the page is full screen, and released otherwise. A wake lock that stays on after the timer ends drains a laptop battery for nothing.

Rule 5: the service worker must never serve an old timer

Timers are the kind of page people open with bad Wi-Fi: in a gym basement, a classroom, a kitchen. So the site has a service worker that caches the core timer pages after the first visit, and they open offline.

The thing I was most nervous about was the opposite problem: shipping a fix and having half my users stuck on the cached old page. The rules I settled on:

  • HTML is network-first. The cached copy is only used if the network fails, or on a repeat visit when the network hasn't answered within 700 ms.
  • Hashed assets are cache-first. /assets/index-a1b2c3d4.js never changes content, so caching it forever is safe.
  • The cache name includes the build id. Every deploy creates a new cache and the activate handler deletes the others, so a cached page always matches the scripts cached with it. 
const VERSION = '__BUILD_ID__';           // replaced at build time
const CACHE = `clockaura-${VERSION}`;

self.addEventListener('activate', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil((async () => {
    const keys = await caches.keys();
    await Promise.all(keys.filter((k) => k !== CACHE).map((k) => caches.delete(k)));
    await self.clients.claim();
  })());
});

The service worker has nothing to do with timing accuracy, but it's part of the same promise: when you press Start, the timer works, whatever the tab or the network is doing.

One gap I found while writing this

The tab title ("04:59 · Countdown") and the little progress ring in the favicon were updated from the same render loop as the digits, and that loop is driven by rAF. In a background tab the ending was reliable, thanks to the backup timeout, but the title could sit still until you looked at the tab again. Ironically, a background tab is exactly when you'd look at the title. The fix is a one-second interval that only runs while document.hidden is true and only updates the title. Background throttling allows one wake-up per second, and that's all a title needs.

The short version

If you're building anything that counts down in a browser:

  1. Store the end time and derive the remaining time from it. Never subtract fixed ticks.
  2. Use performance.now() inside a page and Date.now() only for anything you save.
  3. Drive the display with rAF, but back up the finish with one setTimeout aimed at the end.
  4. Guard the finish with a ref so it can only happen once.
  5. Re-acquire the wake lock on visibilitychange.

If you want to see it all working, start a Pomodoro timer, switch to another tab, and wait for the bell. Or open a link timer like clockaura.com/t/25m, which starts a 25-minute countdown straight from the URL.

I'm happy to answer questions in the comments, especially if you've found a browser where this still rings late.

Build Pages Without Starting from Scratch

Creating every section manually can take time, especially when building marketing pages or product websites. Ready-to-use blocks give you a starting point and help you assemble layouts faster.

Design Visually

Try it here: builder.shadcnspace.com

Shadcn Space also offers a growing collection of shadcn blocks and components to help you build modern interfaces for React and Next.js projects.

What Should We Build Next?

We are always looking for ways to make the development workflow better.

Your feedback can help shape what we build next for shadcn ecosystem.

title: I almost pasted my AWS key into ChatGPT, so I built a goblin to stop me
description:
LeakGoblin is a free, local-only CLI that scans and redacts API keys, tokens and passwords before you paste text into AI tools. Here's why I built it and how it works.

Scan locally. Redact sensitive-looking values. Review before sharing.

It was a boring Tuesday. I was debugging a failing deploy, so I did what I do a dozen times a day: I selected a wall of terminal output, copied it, and switched to an AI chat window.

My finger was already on Enter when I noticed line 14 of the log. It was an AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, sitting there in plain text, followed by the secret right below it.

I didn't send it. But I sat there for a moment thinking about all the times I might not have noticed.

That moment is why I built LeakGoblin 🛡️, a small open-source CLI that checks your text for secrets before it leaves your machine. This post covers why the problem is getting worse, how the tool works, the design decisions I made, and where it falls short.

Why AI tools make this worse

Leaking secrets by copy-paste isn't new. People have pasted credentials into Stack Overflow questions and GitHub issues for years. But AI tools changed the volume and the habit:

  • We paste far more context. Asking an assistant to debug something usually means pasting the whole stack trace, the config file, the Dockerfile and the relevant .env lines, because more context gets better answers.
  • It's conversational and low-friction. A chat box feels private. It doesn't feel like publishing, so we don't get the pause we'd get before posting publicly.
  • Agents read files directly. Coding agents and assistants can pull files into their context on their own. Whatever is in those files goes with them.
  • We rely on remembering to check. Every paste is a chance to forget, and "I'll be careful" is not a security control.

The usual answer is "never put secrets in your code or logs," and that's right. But real projects have .env files, verbose logs, connection strings in error messages, and tokens in curl commands you copied from a tutorial. The goal isn't perfection. It's a safety net at the exact moment of the paste.

What LeakGoblin does

It does two main jobs, scan and sanitize, plus a repo mode.

Install 

# Try it without installing
npx leakgoblin --help

# Or install globally (Node >= 20)
npm install -g leakgoblin

1. Scan text from stdin 

cat prompt.txt | leakgoblin scan --stdin

Output looks like this (secrets are always masked):

⚠️  The goblin found 2 suspicious tokens!

  <stdin>
    [CRITICAL] Private Key Block (confidence: high) L1:1
      → -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- [REDACTED]
    [HIGH] AWS Access Key (confidence: high) L2:10
      → apiKey = [REDACTED]

Each finding includes the type, line number, severity and confidence, plus a masked snippet. It never prints the full secret.

2. Sanitize stdin

This is the one I use most. Instead of just telling you what it found, it gives you a safe copy:

cat prompt.txt | leakgoblin sanitize --stdin

Input:

api_key = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"
password = "s3cr3tP@ssw0rd"

Output:

api_key = "[REDACTED:API_KEY:aws_access_key]"
password = "[REDACTED:PASSWORD:password_assignment]"

Surrounding text and line breaks are preserved, so the AI still gets the context it needs (the structure of your config, the shape of the error) without the actual credentials. The placeholder tells you what kind of secret was removed, which helps when you're reviewing the result.

A workflow that works well for me is to pipe straight into the clipboard, review, then paste:

cat prompt.txt | leakgoblin sanitize --stdin | pbcopy   # macOS
cat prompt.txt | leakgoblin sanitize --stdin | xclip -selection clipboard   # Linux

3. Scan a repository 

leakgoblin scan .
leakgoblin scan ./src
leakgoblin scan . --format json > leakgoblin-report.json

It skips the usual noise (.git, node_modules, dist, build, .next, coverage), plus large and binary files. --verbose shows what was skipped, and --exclude adds your own patterns.

4. Use it in CI 

leakgoblin scan . --quiet
echo $?

The exit codes are simple:

Code Meaning
0 No secrets found
1 Secrets found
2 Error (bad path, invalid config, input too large, etc.)

So a pipeline step can fail the build on a finding:

leakgoblin scan . --quiet
if [ $? -eq 1 ]; then echo "Secrets detected!"; exit 1; fi

How detection works

The part I thought about most is what to flag and how to say how sure you are.

Signatures first

The core of LeakGoblin is a set of format-specific signatures, patterns for credentials that have a recognizable shape:

Category Examples
Private keys -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
Cloud credentials AWS AKIA..., aws_secret_access_key
API keys GitHub ghp_..., Stripe sk_live_..., Slack xoxb-..., Google AIza..., OpenAI-style sk-...
Bearer tokens / JWTs Bearer ..., eyJ...
Passwords password = "...", secret: ...
Connection strings mongodb://user:pass@host, postgres://...
Env vars GITHUB_API_KEY=..., *_SECRET=...

When a string starts with AKIA and has the right length and character set, that's a strong signal. Findings like that are marked high confidence. Looser patterns, like generic password = ... assignments or JWT-looking strings, are medium.

Then a labeled heuristic

Not every secret has a neat prefix. For those, LeakGoblin also has a heuristic for long, high-entropy strings. These are the random-looking blobs that might be a token, or might be a hash, a UUID or a build ID.

I deliberately made two choices here:

  1. Heuristic findings are labeled confidence: low and severity: low. They're never mixed in with signature matches as if they were equally certain.
  2. You control the noise. If the heuristic is too chatty for your codebase, raise confidenceThreshold to medium in your config and it goes quiet.

Why not "flag everything"?

It's tempting to make a secret scanner paranoid. Flag every long string, every base64 blob, every hex value. The tool then feels thorough, but it fails in practice.

If a scanner cries wolf constantly, people stop reading its output. Then they add it to an ignore list, or stop running it. A tool that gets disabled protects nobody. So the design goal is that when LeakGoblin says "critical, high confidence," you believe it, and when it says "low, heuristic," you know to look but not panic.

Customizing it

If your company has its own token format, add a rule in leakgoblin.config.json:

{
  "version": 1,
  "severityThreshold": "low",
  "confidenceThreshold": "low",
  "maxFileSizeMB": 5,
  "customPatterns": [
    {
      "id": "internal_token",
      "pattern": "INTERNAL_[A-Z0-9_]{16,}",
      "description": "Internal token format",
      "category": "api_key",
      "severity": "high",
      "confidence": "medium"
    }
  ],
  "allowlist": {
    "patterns": ["^AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE$"]
  }
}

The allowlist is for approved test fixtures like AWS's documented example key, so they don't trigger every run. Use it carefully.

Design decisions I care about

1. It never prints the full secret

This sounds obvious, but a secret scanner that echoes secrets into your terminal, your CI logs or its JSON report becomes a new leak path.

Every finding is masked in text output. In JSON output, the raw match fields are stripped. The tool is built so that its own output is safe to look at, share in a bug report, or save as a CI artifact.

2. Fully local, with no telemetry

LeakGoblin makes no network requests during scan or sanitize. There's no upload, no account and no phoning home. For a tool whose whole purpose is keeping sensitive data from leaving your machine, anything else would be absurd.

That also keeps the trust model simple. You can read the source and confirm it.

3. Boring, predictable exit codes

0, 1, 2. That's it. It works in a shell script, a GitHub Action, a pre-push hook or a Makefile without parsing anything.

4. Synthetic test data only

All the tests use canary values like AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE, never real credentials. If you report a false positive or a missed format, please do the same and send a synthetic example of the shape, never a real secret.

Honest limitations

I'd rather you hear this from me than discover it later:

  • It's a best-effort filter, not a guarantee. It uses signatures plus conservative heuristics, and it can't identify every possible secret. Always review the sanitized output before sharing it.
  • Novel or obfuscated formats can be missed. If a provider changes its token format, or a secret is split or encoded, the scanner may not catch it. Custom patterns help.
  • The heuristic is only a hint. Low-confidence findings can be false positives.
  • It's not a secrets manager. It doesn't replace a vault, encrypted env files or proper rotation. If a real secret does leak, rotate it no matter what any scanner said.
  • It assumes you trust your machine. It doesn't protect against a compromised OS.
  • It's not a compliance certification.

It also isn't trying to replace tools like gitleaks or trufflehog, which are built for scanning git history and org-wide repos. LeakGoblin targets a narrower moment: the clipboard on its way to an AI chat or an issue tracker.

Roadmap, and a call for contributors

LeakGoblin is MIT licensed and free to use. Here's what's planned next, and where I'd love help:

  • [ ] More provider tokens (Azure, GCP, npm and others) with high-confidence signatures
  • [ ] SARIF output for GitHub Code Scanning
  • [ ] --fix as an explicit opt-in that writes sanitized files
  • [ ] Pre-commit hook example
  • [ ] VS Code extension using the same engine
  • [ ] Better .env and Docker secret detection

The easiest way to contribute is adding a detection rule for a token format you know well. CONTRIBUTING.md walks through it. Reporting a false positive or a missed secret format with a synthetic example is just as valuable.

Try it 

npx leakgoblin --help
echo "test AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE" | npx leakgoblin scan --stdin
  • 📦 npm
  • 💻 GitHub

If it saves you from one bad paste, a ⭐ on the repo helps other developers find it. And I'd really like to hear: how do you keep secrets out of your AI chats today? Tell me in the comments, along with any token formats you want covered.

The goblin is watching. Stay vigilant. 🛡️
