title: Your Agent's RENAME COLUMN Breaks Every Old Pod. Expand-Contract in 4 Steps
description:
• Book: Database Playbook
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You ask a coding agent to rename users.name to full_name. It updates the model, fixes every query, and writes a migration with one line in it: ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;. The diff is tidy and the tests pass, because the tests run against one version of the code. Production runs two.

A Kubernetes Deployment rolls out by scaling the new ReplicaSet up while it scales the old one down, and both maxUnavailable and maxSurge default to 25%. For the length of the rollout, old Pods and new Pods serve traffic side by side. Your migration runs once, just before or somewhere inside that window. Every old Pod still alive after the rename sends SELECT name ... to a table that no longer has a name column.

Why one RENAME breaks the rollout

There are two separate failures packed into that one line.

The first is the code-schema mismatch. Run the rename before the new code and the old Pods fail. Ship the code first and the new Pods fail until the migration lands. No ordering makes both versions happy, which is why the strong_migrations README puts it bluntly: "Renaming a column that's in use will cause errors in your application." The Squawk linter has a renaming-column rule for the same reason.

The second is the lock. A rename touches no data; the Postgres docs say "there is no effect on the stored data." But ALTER TABLE takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock "unless explicitly noted," and that mode conflicts with every other lock mode, including the ACCESS SHARE lock a plain SELECT takes. If a long transaction is holding the table, the rename waits. While it waits, as Xata's write-up on the lock queue explains, every later statement that needs a lock on that table queues behind it. The table is blocked for reads and writes until the rename finishes or gives up.

The fix is old. Danilo Sato described it as Parallel Change in 2014: expand the interface to support old and new, migrate the clients, then contract back to only the new. For a column rename in Postgres, that is four steps.


During a rolling deploy, two versions of your code share one schema.

The lab: one table, two app versions

Start a throwaway Postgres 18 and seed a table:

docker run -d --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw postgres:18
# wait a few seconds for it to accept connections
docker exec -i pg psql -U postgres <<'SQL'
CREATE TABLE users (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO users (name)
SELECT 'user ' || g FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g;
SQL

The "app" is two files, one per image version. Each does what a request handler would do: write a row, read it back.

-- old_app.sql: what the old image runs
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Old Pod Writer');
SELECT id, name FROM users ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1;

-- new_app.sql: what the new image runs
INSERT INTO users (full_name) VALUES ('New Pod Writer');
SELECT id, full_name FROM users ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1;

Run either one with docker exec -i pg psql -U postgres < old_app.sql. Right now old_app.sql works and new_app.sql fails. Apply the agent's rename and the result flips: old_app.sql fails with a column-does-not-exist error. That flip is your rolling deploy. Rename the column back to name before you go on.

You can also watch the lock queue. Open three terminals with docker exec -it pg psql -U postgres:

  1. Terminal A: BEGIN; SELECT count(*) FROM users; and leave the transaction open.
  2. Terminal B: ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name; hangs, waiting for A.
  3. Terminal C: SELECT id FROM users LIMIT 1; hangs too, queued behind B.

Cancel B with Ctrl-C and C returns at once. Now run SET lock_timeout = '2s'; in B and try the rename again. B gives up after two seconds with a lock-timeout error instead of holding everyone hostage. lock_timeout "applies separately to each lock acquisition attempt," and it is the setting every migration below starts with. Roll back A when you're done.

Step 1: expand without a long lock

The first deploy is a migration only. No application code changes. It adds the new column and a trigger that keeps the two columns in sync, whichever one a writer touches.

-- 001_expand.sql (deploy 1, app code unchanged)
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
SET statement_timeout = '10s';
BEGIN;
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text;

CREATE FUNCTION users_sync_name() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
    NEW.full_name := coalesce(NEW.full_name, NEW.name);
    NEW.name := coalesce(NEW.name, NEW.full_name);
  ELSIF NEW.name IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.name THEN
    NEW.full_name := NEW.name;
  ELSIF NEW.full_name IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.full_name THEN
    NEW.name := NEW.full_name;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;

CREATE TRIGGER users_sync_name
  BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON users
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION users_sync_name();
COMMIT;

Apply it with docker exec -i pg psql -U postgres -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 < 001_expand.sql. If the lock wait times out, psql exits with status 3, the transaction rolls back, and you run it again: two seconds lost, instead of every query on the table stuck behind your ALTER.

Three details make this safe. Adding a column with no default gives existing rows NULL, and the ALTER TABLE page says "in neither case is a rewrite of the table required," so the exclusive lock is held only briefly. The trigger is a BEFORE row trigger, so it fills name before the NOT NULL check runs, which is what lets new_app.sql insert without naming the old column. And the UPDATE branch copies in one direction only, from whichever column changed, so a writer on either version never has its value overwritten by the other column.

Run both app files now. Both succeed, and the last two rows have name and full_name filled. Old and new code can live together, which is the whole point of the expand step.

Step 2: backfill in batches that give up fast

The 200,000 seed rows still have full_name empty. Don't fix that with one UPDATE users SET full_name = name. On a big table that is one long transaction holding row locks on every row, and strong_migrations names the three keys to doing it safely: "batching, throttling, and running it outside a transaction."

One batch, keyed on the primary key so each batch starts where the last one stopped:

-- backfill.sql: one batch of 1,000 rows
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
SET statement_timeout = '30s';
WITH batch AS (
  SELECT id FROM users
  WHERE id > :last
  ORDER BY id
  LIMIT 1000
), upd AS (
  UPDATE users u
  SET full_name = u.name
  FROM batch b
  WHERE u.id = b.id AND u.full_name IS NULL
)
SELECT coalesce(max(id), 0) FROM batch;

The upd step has no RETURNING and nothing reads it, and it still runs: Postgres executes data-modifying statements in WITH "exactly once, and always to completion." The query prints the last id it handled, or 0 when nothing is left.

A short loop drives it. psql runs in autocommit mode, so each batch is its own transaction:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backfill.sh: run after deploy 1, before deploy 2
last=0
while :; do
  next=$(docker exec -i pg psql -U postgres -qtA \
    -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -v last="$last" < backfill.sql) \
    || { echo "batch failed, retrying"; sleep 1; continue; }
  [ "$next" -eq 0 ] && break
  echo "backfilled through id $next"
  last=$next
  sleep 0.2
done

Size the batch so each one finishes far below the 30-second statement_timeout. When a batch hits a timeout, it rolls back on its own and the loop retries the same range. Then check that nothing drifted:

SELECT count(*) FROM users
WHERE full_name IS DISTINCT FROM name;

That count has to be zero before you go on.


Expand, migrate, contract: the schema gets wider before it gets narrower.

Steps 3 and 4: switch, then contract

Step 3 is a normal code deploy (deploy 2): the image that runs new_app.sql, reading and writing only full_name. During that rollout, old Pods still write name and the trigger copies it across. New Pods write full_name and the trigger copies it back, so an old Pod reading name still sees rows the new Pods wrote. Until step 4, rolling back to the old image loses nothing.

If the column should be NOT NULL, Postgres 18 lets you add that without a long lock. The ALTER TABLE docs allow NOT VALID on not-null constraints, and validation runs as a separate statement:

SET lock_timeout = '2s';
SET statement_timeout = '15min';
ALTER TABLE users
  ADD CONSTRAINT users_full_name_nn NOT NULL full_name NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE users VALIDATE CONSTRAINT users_full_name_nn;

The statement_timeout is longer than the 10 seconds used elsewhere because VALIDATE scans the whole table. It only takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock while it does, so reads and writes keep going.

Step 4 waits until no released code reads name and you are past the point where you would roll back. Then it removes the old column in its own deploy:

-- 002_contract.sql (deploy 3, nothing reads name)
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
SET statement_timeout = '10s';
BEGIN;
DROP TRIGGER users_sync_name ON users;
DROP FUNCTION users_sync_name();
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name;
COMMIT;

DROP COLUMN is quick too. Per the same page, Postgres "does not physically remove the column"; it makes the column invisible to SQL, and the space comes back on the next table rewrite. One catch: some ORMs cache the column list at boot. strong_migrations notes that Active Record "caches database columns at runtime," so on Rails you add the column to ignored_columns and deploy that before you run the drop.

The rule to give your agent

The agent wrote the one-liner because nothing told it about the second version of the code. Tell it. Claude Code loads path-scoped rules from .claude/rules/ when it works on matching files, so this file only shows up when the agent touches a migration:

---
paths:
  - "migrations/**/*.sql"
---

# Postgres migration rules

- Never RENAME COLUMN or RENAME TABLE on a table the
  running app reads. Propose expand-contract instead.
- Expand migration: ADD COLUMN (nullable, no volatile
  default) plus a BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE trigger
  that keeps the old and new columns in sync.
- Backfill is a separate batched script keyed on the
  primary key, never part of the migration.
- Every migration file starts with SET lock_timeout
  and SET statement_timeout.
- DROP COLUMN goes in its own migration, in a later
  deploy, after no released code reads the column.
- When asked for a rename, write out the 4-step plan
  and put only step 1 in this change.

Other coding agents in the repo read AGENTS.md, so copy the bullets there too. Claude Code keeps loading .claude/rules/ either way, and the same docs page covers when it reads AGENTS.md at all.

A rule file is advice. The docs say so directly: Claude "treats them as context, not enforced configuration." So back it with a check that does not care who wrote the SQL. Run squawk 'migrations/*.sql' in CI, or the squawk-action on pull requests. Its renaming-column rule catches the one-liner, and require-lock-timeout and require-statement-timeout catch a migration that forgot its timeouts. It will also flag the drops in step 4, which is fine: that is the one migration a human should read before it ships.

If you want the expand-contract bookkeeping automated, pgroll does the add-column, backfill and sync-trigger work for you and serves old and new schema versions through views at the same time. Knowing the four steps by hand is still what lets you review what it, or your agent, is about to run.

If this was useful

The four steps here are what a schema change costs once a store has live traffic and more than one version of your code talking to it. I wrote the Database Playbook for the decision that comes before all of this: which store to pick for a system, knowing you will be changing its schema under real load for years. If this post made you look harder at your own migrations, the book is the wider version of that look.

title: A Free Random Color Generator I Built for Designers and Developers
description:
Colors are one of those things that seem simple until you need one. "Just pick a nice blue" sounds easy, and then you spend forty minutes cycling through a color picker, squinting at slightly different shades of the same blue, and going in circles. I have lost more hours to this than I care to admit, which is why I eventually built myself a random color generator and put it on my site for anyone to use.

This post is about what the tool does, how I built it, and the real use cases where a random color button beats a color picker.

What the tool does

The idea is deliberately simple. You open the page, you click generate, and you get a random color with its HEX, RGB, and HSL values. Each value has a copy button, so the hex code goes straight into your CSS or your design tool without any typing (and without typos in hex codes, which have bitten me more than once).

But single colors are only the start. The generator can also build full palettes: complementary pairs, analogous sets, and multi-color palettes you can use as a starting point for a design. Palettes are where the random approach really pays off, because humans tend to keep picking variations of the same colors they already like. Randomness forces you out of that rut.

How I built it (the technical bit)

The core is small, and that is the point. A random color is just three random numbers between 0 and 255 for red, green, and blue. The interesting parts are the conversions and the palette math.

HEX, RGB, and HSL are just three ways to write the same color. HEX is what CSS and most design tools want. RGB is intuitive for developers (it maps directly to screen pixels). HSL is the one designers usually reason in, because hue, saturation, and lightness map to how we actually think about color: "make it a bit more saturated" or "make it a touch darker."

Palette generation is where it gets fun. The color wheel math is straightforward:

  • Complementary: take the hue and add 180 degrees. Instant contrast pair.
  • Analogous: take hues 30 degrees on either side of the base. Calm, harmonious sets.
  • Triadic: three hues 120 degrees apart. Bold and balanced.
  • Random multi-color: pick several hues and you have a starting point for something playful.

All of this runs in the browser with plain JavaScript. No server round trip, no tracking, no account. Colors generate instantly because there is nothing to wait for.

Use cases where this actually helps

CSS and frontend work. You need a background color for a hero section, a badge, or a dashboard chart series. Instead of opening a picker and deliberating, generate a few options and pick one. Chart series are a great use case: generate five colors, and you instantly have a distinct set.

Branding and logo exploration. When a client or a side project has no brand colors yet, random palettes are a fast way to explore directions you would never have considered. I find it breaks the "everything I make is blue and gray" habit.

Game development. Procedural color assignment is everywhere in games: enemy variants, player colors, loot rarity tiers, particle effects. A random color button is a quick way to test how a palette feels before you commit it to code.

Design system stress testing. If you maintain a design system or a component library, random colors are a great way to sanity-check contrast. Generate colors, drop them into your components, and check whether your text remains readable. It catches assumptions you did not know you had made.

Art and creative coding. Generative art thrives on randomness. A random palette as a constraint ("build this piece with only these five colors") is a classic creative exercise, and starting from a random seed keeps it honest.

Why random beats deliberate (sometimes)

There is a real psychological reason this works. When you pick colors deliberately, you keep making the same choices. Your taste is consistent, which sounds good but means your work converges on a narrow band of what you already like. Randomness injects options from outside your taste. You do not have to use the random color as-is. It is a starting point: generate, react, adjust. The generation is cheap, so generate a lot.

Try it

If you want a no-signup, free random color generator with HEX, RGB, and HSL values, copy buttons, and palette generation, I built one here: Random Color Generator. It works on desktop and mobile, everything runs in your browser, and nothing is stored anywhere.

Next time you catch yourself fiddling with a color picker for the tenth minute, try the random button instead. You might be surprised how often the third or fourth generated color is the one you keep.

title: That’s Not the Green I Meant”: A Colour Preview and Quote Tool for Crochet Sellers
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Submission 💸

What I Built

I started my crochet business only recently. Within a few weeks of meeting other crochet artists, I noticed we were all losing sleep over the same three problems.

  1. “Same thing, but in different colours.” A customer sends a reference photo and wants it in other colours. Often they aren’t sure which shade they mean. “Green” could be light green, sage or even olive. We agree in words, and the finished piece arrives weeks later. Sometimes it isn’t what they pictured. Nobody did anything wrong; we just never looked at the same picture.

  2. Pricing something that doesn’t exist yet. To price a piece I need to know how many grams of yarn it will use and how many hours it will take. I only know that after it’s made, but the customer wants a number today. So we guess, and most of us guess low.

  3. Keeping track. Which orders have I agreed to? Which one is due in two days? If I accept one more, does another go late? Spread across chat threads, that is a lot to hold in your head.

So I built KARSAZ Stitch Desk, a small web app that handles all three. The seller goes through five steps:

  • Upload the customer’s reference photo and paste their message.
  • Say whether they want a colour change.
  • Pick the parts of the photo to recolour (petals, leaves, body, trim) and choose the colours, so the customer sees their order before any yarn is cut.
  • Enter the size or age, quantity, deadline and any extra changes.
  • Get a price, a ready date, a before-and-after picture, a reply message to send, and a quote card the customer can keep.

Every quote can be logged as an order. The Orders tab shows what is agreed, what is overdue and what is at risk of being late, and each seller sets their own yarn cost, hourly rate and markup in the Prices tab.

Demo

Watch the video:

Try it yourself:

karsaz.tech

Upload a photo of a crochet item on the New order tab. To see the Orders and Prices tabs, create a test account on the Account tab.

An honest note: the live site runs on a small server, and Gemma photo reading and Smart selection need more memory than it has. I run those on my own computer in the video. On the live site you choose the item by hand and colour parts with automatic colouring or hand-drawn shapes.

One order, start to finish

Here’s a real order going through the app. A customer sends a photo of a star baby cocoon and asks for it for a 1-year-old by 18 October. These screenshots were taken on my own computer, where Gemma and Smart selection run.

Step 1: Photo in

A custom order starts the way it does in real life: a reference photo and a message. The seller uploads the photo and pastes in whatever the customer wrote, such as “Want this for a 1 year old in mint green”. The message is optional, because many customers just send a picture.


On my own computer, Gemma reads the photo and the message to work out which item it is and what the customer asked for. It only identifies. It never produces a price or a date.

Step 2: Do they want a colour change?

This step is a single question: does the customer want the item in different colours, or exactly as in the photo? If not, the app skips the colour work and goes straight to the details. If yes, it opens the colour screen. It is quick on purpose, because many orders are “exactly this one, please”.

Step 3: Choose the colours

This is the step that solves “that’s not the green I meant”. The customer sees their order in the new colours before any yarn is cut. The seller can colour everything at once or one part at a time.

Option A:

One tap with a palette. The app suggests palettes made for this kind of item. For a baby cocoon: soft pastel, sunny morning, lavender dream and more. One tap colours every part.

Option B:

Part by part. Clicking a part of the photo, here the hood, selects it. The highlighted area is what will change. Then the seller taps a colour.

If “green” isn’t specific enough, “Any other colour” opens a picker with an exact hex code.


The new colour keeps the photo’s own light and shadow, so it still looks like crocheted yarn rather than a flat paint fill.


The customer can see this before any yarn is cut. I picked deliberately loud colours to show that each part is handled separately.

When the selection isn’t perfect. The “Fine-tune” panel lets the seller add area, remove area or draw a shape by hand. The quick-fix buttons (“Colour spilling outside”, “Old colour left at the edge”) adjust the last part. Fixing a rough edge takes a click, not a restart.

Step 4: Size, deadline and details

Now the practical details. The seller confirms the item, then enters the size or age, the quantity, the customer’s deadline and any extra changes, such as “add ears”. Extra changes add a small amount to the hours, and the app uses all of this to calculate the quote. This is the only typing the seller has to do.

Step 5: Price, ready date and reply

One button, “Create quote and reply”, and everything comes together on one screen: before and after side by side, the price, the grams and hours, and an estimate of yarn per colour.


The part I’m proudest of is the deadline check. The customer wanted this by 18 October. The app tells the seller that the earliest realistic date is 26 October, and explains why: about 7 days of crocheting at 3 hours a day, with only 1 day left. It then drafts a reply with the size in cm, the price and an honest date. The seller can copy it and edit it.


From here the seller presses “Log this order” or “Make quote card”. The quote card turns the quote into a single image with the shop logo, the customer’s name, before and after side by side, the price and the ready date. It’s easy to send in a chat, and it replaces a long message of numbers.

After the five steps: keeping track

Orders: Logged quotes go into the Orders tab. The seller moves each one from Quoted to Pending to In progress to Done, and only Pending and In progress count toward the workload check.

Prices: Every quote comes from numbers the seller sets: yarn cost, hourly rate, markup, rounding and hours per day. Change them once and every future quote follows. My numbers are defaults. Each seller uses their own.

Account: Guests can make quotes and previews. An account keeps orders and prices in a private space.

Code

sunbal822 / KARSAZ_Stitch_Desk

KARSAZ Stitch Desk

An order assistant for a crochet business. Upload a customer's reference photo and message, pick the colours on the photo, and get a price, a ready date, a before/after preview, a reply draft and a quote card you can send.

What it does

  1. Photo and message – upload the customer's photo and paste what they wrote.
  2. Colour change? – say whether the customer wants different colours.
  3. Pick the colours – click each part of the photo and choose its colour (palettes, swatches or a colour picker).
  4. Size, deadline, details – age or size, quantity, due date, extra changes.
  5. Quote – price, ready date, before/after picture, a reply you can copy, and a downloadable quote card.

Other tabs:

  • Orders – search and filter your orders, change status (Quoted, Pending, In progress, Done, Cancelled), see counts and the month's booked value. Overdue and at-risk orders are flagged.
  • Prices –…
View on GitHub

A quick map of the project:
  • app.py is the web app, with the five steps and the Orders, Prices and Account tabs.
  • quote.py holds the pricing and ready-date formulas.
  • pipeline.py turns a request into a quote and a reply message.
  • extract.py reads the photo and message with Gemma.
  • recolor_v5.py does the part-by-part recolouring.
  • orders.py and accounts.py handle the order log, deadline checks and sign-in.

How I Built It

Open models do the seeing and the reading. The hardest part of a custom order is turning a reference photo and a vague message into something clear. Three open models do that work:

  • Gemma 3 (4B), running locally through Ollama, looks at the photo and reads the customer’s message to work out which item it is and what they asked for.
  • ISNet cuts the item out of its background, so the app can find its parts.
  • Segment Anything lets the seller click a part of the photo and get its exact outline.

I gave the models the jobs they are good at, seeing and reading. Prices, weights and dates come from plain Python, so a small model on a laptop is enough, and its mistakes can never reach a customer’s quote.

Job Open piece
Reading the photo and the customer’s message Gemma 3 (4B) through Ollama, running locally
Cutting the item out of its background ISNet (isnet-general-use) through rembg
Click-to-select on a part of the photo Segment Anything through rembg (optional, local)
Recolouring OpenCV, NumPy and Pillow
The app Gradio
The order log An ordinary Excel file written with openpyxl
Hosting Render, with a persistent disk

Three design decisions are worth explaining.

  • Colours come only from the customer’s words. The model’s guess at colours is thrown away. A small parser reads the message (“red flower and green leaves”) and ties each colour to the part it names. If the customer wrote no colours, there are none. Nothing is guessed, so the preview can’t drift from what the customer asked for.

  • A quote is a formula, not a guess. Each catalogue item has yarn grams, hours and a number of colours. The quote scales them by size, adds a small increase for every extra change the customer asks for, and then applies the seller’s own rates. Here is the default tulip:

Part Working Result
Yarn 80 g × Rs 225 per 100 g Rs 180
Labour 5 hours × Rs 50 Rs 250
Extra colour 1 extra × Rs 20 Rs 20
Cost Rs 450
Price Rs 450 × 1.4 markup, rounded to the nearest Rs 50 Rs 650
Ready date 5 hours ÷ 3 hours a day, rounded up, plus 2 spare days about 4 days

For wearables, the age in months scales the yarn and hours along a size chart, and the reply shows the matching height and chest in centimetres.

  • The deadline check counts work you have already agreed. The ready date isn’t today plus hours. It starts after your agreed orders. When a new order would push another one past its date, the app says so in plain words, and the Orders tab flags overdue and at-risk jobs. It works through jobs earliest deadline first, which is how a human would plan the week.

Recolouring that still looks like yarn. A flat colour fill looks like paint. The “natural lighting finish” keeps the photo’s own light and shadow on the new colour, so the preview looks like real yarn. Parts can be found three ways: automatically by grouping the item’s pixels by colour, by clicking with Smart selection, or by drawing the corners of a shape by hand. A hand-drawn edge follows the drawn line exactly.

What went wrong.

The first version only worked on my laptop, with one set of orders. Making it multi-user meant giving each account its own folder for orders and prices, with passwords hashed using PBKDF2.
My first deploy ran out of memory on the smallest paid server. The cause wasn’t the model I expected: even with Smart selection off, cutting the item out of its background loads a second model. I turned Smart selection off by default on the website and gave the server more memory.

What’s next: a password reset, remembering the sign-in after a page refresh, and a repeat-order shortcut for returning customers.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Privacy: A customer’s reference photo and message are personal. Run locally, they never leave the seller’s computer. (The hosted demo does upload photos to its server; the local version is the private one.)
  • Cost: Margins on handmade work are thin. There are no per-photo fees for background removal or for reading a message. A small model on a laptop costs electricity.
  • Swappable: The model is one line, MODEL = "gemma3:4b" in extract.py. A seller with a stronger machine can try a bigger one.
  • Fixable: When the app picks a wrong part of a photo, I can read the code and fix it.

My First User

I wanted someone who actually sells crochet to try it. A friend of mine runs her own crochet business and asked to stay anonymous. She became the first person outside my laptop to use Karsaz Stitch Desk.

She had a real customer who wanted a white tulip in a different colour. Normally that means guessing, crocheting, or hours of scrolling on Pinterest, and hoping the customer likes it. Instead she uploaded the photo and tried pink, light blue and purple. Eventually she landed on lilac with green leaves.

Then she wanted to see how far it could actually go. So she uploaded a child frok to see how it goes. This is the result.

Then to take it up a notch she uploaded a bunny and recoloured the ears, arms and legs separately.

I asked what she'd pay. Nothing yet, because this was a trial. But she said she'd consider a monthly subscription if it costs less than Adobe-type tools, mainly to keep her crochet work in one place.

She also found a weakness. With very blurry or very dark photos, the Segment Anything selection picks objects poorly. It finds roughly the right thing, but not cleanly. The next step is a warning when a photo is too blurry or dark.

It's one seller and one trial, so I'm not calling it proof. But for a tool I built for my own business, it was a good first real test.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 (4B) runs through Ollama on the seller’s own computer, reading the customer’s reference photo and message locally.

  • Best Use of Render: Render hosts the live app at karsaz.tech and deploys it automatically from GitHub. A persistent disk keeps each seller’s accounts, orders and prices safe, and Render runs the ISNet background-cutting step. Gemma and Smart selection run on my own computer.

  • Best Use of a .tech Domain: Karsaz_Stitch_Desk is live at https://karsaz.tech, so anyone can open it and try it without installing anything. The .tech domain gives the project a short, memorable address that fits what it is: a tool built for sellers, with the app served from Render under that name.

  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: The narration for the demo video was generated with ElevenLabs. I wrote the script myself and used an ElevenLabs voice to deliver it, which let me produce a clear, consistent walkthrough of the full flow, from the customer’s photo and message to the seller’s order.

Next time a customer says “that’s not the green I meant,” I want it to be before the first stitch, not after the last.

title: Top 8 Azure Cloud Services Every Java Developer Should Know
description:
Top 8 Azure Cloud Services Every Java Developer Should Know

Azure offers hundreds of services, and most of them will never matter to a typical Java team. A small set covers the majority of enterprise workloads: running the application, storing data, handling messages, managing secrets, and seeing what happens in production. This article walks through eight services that appear again and again in Java architectures on Azure, explains what each one is for, and shows how a Spring Boot application uses several of them together.

The services are grouped by the job they do in a system: where code runs, where data lives, how components communicate, and how you operate them safely. Code examples use the official Azure SDK for Java, which follows a consistent pattern: a builder creates a client, and the client authenticates with DefaultAzureCredential, which works locally with your developer login and in Azure with a managed identity.

1. Azure App Service

App Service is a managed platform for web applications and APIs. You deploy a Spring Boot JAR or WAR, and Azure handles the operating system, patching, load balancing, TLS certificates, and scaling. For many Java teams, it is the simplest production target: no containers to build, no cluster to manage.

App Service supports deployment slots, which let you deploy a new version to a staging slot, verify it, and swap it into production with minimal downtime. It also integrates with managed identities, so the application can call other Azure services without storing credentials.

Use App Service when you have one or a few web services with straightforward scaling needs and your team prefers to focus on application code rather than platform operations.

2. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

AKS is managed Kubernetes. When you have many services, custom networking needs, sidecars, or a platform team that already standardizes on Kubernetes, AKS gives you the control you need without operating the control plane yourself. Azure manages the API server and upgrades, while you manage node pools, deployments, and ingress.

AKS is powerful, and it brings real operational responsibility. Many teams adopt it too early. A good rule is to choose AKS when your workload genuinely needs Kubernetes features, not because microservices sound like they require it.

For smaller container workloads that do not need full Kubernetes, Azure Container Apps offers a simpler serverless container platform built on Kubernetes concepts, and is worth evaluating first.

3. Azure Functions

Azure Functions runs small units of code triggered by events: an HTTP request, a message on a queue, a file uploaded to storage, a timer. You pay for execution rather than for idle servers, and scaling happens automatically.

Java support is available through the Azure Functions Java worker and annotations such as @HttpTrigger. A minimal HTTP function looks like this:

import com.microsoft.azure.functions.*;
import com.microsoft.azure.functions.annotation.*;

public class InvoiceFunctions {

    @FunctionName("getInvoiceStatus")
    public HttpResponseMessage run(
            @HttpTrigger(name = "req", methods = {HttpMethod.GET},
                    authLevel = AuthorizationLevel.FUNCTION,
                    route = "invoices/{id}") HttpRequestMessage<java.util.Optional<String>> request,
            @BindingName("id") String id,
            final ExecutionContext context) {

        context.getLogger().info("Checking status for invoice " + id);
        return request.createResponseBuilder(HttpStatus.OK)
                .body("{\"id\":\"" + id + "\",\"status\":\"PAID\"}")
                .build();
    }
}

Functions work well for event-driven integration, scheduled jobs, and lightweight APIs. Keep in mind that Java functions have cold-start characteristics, so latency-sensitive endpoints may need a premium plan or a different host.

4. Azure Cosmos DB

Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model database with single-digit millisecond latency at the 99th percentile, according to Microsoft's published service-level targets for reads and writes within a region. It offers several APIs, including NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, and Table. For Java, the NoSQL API with the azure-cosmos SDK is the most common choice.

Cosmos DB works best when you design around partition keys from the start. Choosing a poor partition key creates hot partitions, which limit throughput no matter how many resources you buy. Consistency levels are another decision point: strong consistency protects correctness, while session consistency is usually the default balance for user-facing applications.

import com.azure.cosmos.CosmosClient;
import com.azure.cosmos.CosmosClientBuilder;
import com.azure.cosmos.CosmosContainer;
import com.azure.identity.DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder;

public class CosmosSetup {

    public static CosmosContainer orders(String endpoint, String databaseName, String containerName) {
        CosmosClient client = new CosmosClientBuilder()
                .endpoint(endpoint)
                .credential(new DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder().build())
                .buildClient();

        return client.getDatabase(databaseName).getContainer(containerName);
    }
}

Using DefaultAzureCredential here means no account keys are stored in configuration files, which is a good default for any service that supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication.

5. Azure Database for PostgreSQL (Flexible Server)

Many Java applications are relational at heart, and PostgreSQL is a popular choice. Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server provides a managed PostgreSQL instance with automated backups, high availability options, maintenance windows, and monitoring. You still write standard JDBC or JPA code, and Spring Boot connects with its usual configuration.

A practical setting for Spring Boot is to store the connection details in configuration, and let Azure handle the lifecycle of the server. Enable zone-redundant high availability for production workloads that cannot tolerate long outages, and enforce SSL connections in the connection string.

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://myserver.postgres.database.azure.com:5432/orders?sslmode=require
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate

For passwordless access, Azure also supports Microsoft Entra authentication with managed identities, which removes the password from configuration entirely. That is worth adopting once your team is comfortable with the setup.

6. Azure Service Bus

Service Bus is a managed enterprise messaging service with queues and topics. It guarantees delivery with at-least-once semantics, supports sessions for ordered processing, dead-letter queues for messages that cannot be processed, and scheduled delivery. It is the right tool when you need reliable asynchronous communication between services, especially for business workflows where losing a message is unacceptable.

Sending a message from Java uses the azure-messaging-servicebus SDK:

import com.azure.identity.DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder;
import com.azure.messaging.servicebus.ServiceBusClientBuilder;
import com.azure.messaging.servicebus.ServiceBusMessage;
import com.azure.messaging.servicebus.ServiceBusSenderClient;

public class OrderPublisher {

    private final ServiceBusSenderClient sender;

    public OrderPublisher(String namespace) {
        this.sender = new ServiceBusClientBuilder()
                .fullyQualifiedNamespace(namespace + ".servicebus.windows.net")
                .credential(new DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder().build())
                .sender()
                .queueName("orders")
                .buildClient();
    }

    public void publish(String orderId, String payloadJson) {
        ServiceBusMessage message = new ServiceBusMessage(payloadJson);
        message.setMessageId(orderId);      // enables duplicate detection when configured
        message.setSubject("OrderPlaced");
        sender.sendMessage(message);
    }
}

Because delivery is at least once, consumers must be idempotent. Setting a message ID and enabling duplicate detection on the queue catches many accidental duplicates on the send side, but the consumer still needs to handle redelivery safely.

7. Azure Key Vault

Key Vault stores secrets, keys, and certificates, and controls access to them with Microsoft Entra ID. It removes secrets from source code, configuration files, and container images. It also provides audit logs of who accessed what, and supports rotation.

With Spring Cloud Azure, a Spring Boot application can load secrets from Key Vault as properties, which keeps application code clean. Alternatively, the SDK gives direct access:

import com.azure.identity.DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder;
import com.azure.security.keyvault.secrets.SecretClient;
import com.azure.security.keyvault.secrets.SecretClientBuilder;

public class SecretReader {

    private final SecretClient client;

    public SecretReader(String vaultUrl) {
        this.client = new SecretClientBuilder()
                .vaultUrl(vaultUrl)
                .credential(new DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder().build())
                .buildClient();
    }

    public String read(String name) {
        return client.getSecret(name).getValue();
    }
}

Grant the application's managed identity only the permissions it needs, such as "get" on specific secrets, rather than broad access to the whole vault. Least privilege applies to secrets as much as to code.

8. Azure Monitor and Application Insights

Production systems fail in ways that are hard to predict. Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs across your resources, and Application Insights adds application-level telemetry: request rates, dependency calls, exceptions, and distributed traces. For Java, the simplest start is the Application Insights Java agent, which instruments common frameworks such as Spring Boot, JDBC, and HTTP clients without code changes.

Attaching the agent requires only a JVM argument and a connection string:

java -javaagent:/opt/agents/applicationinsights-agent.jar \
     -jar orders-service.jar

The connection string is set through an environment variable or configuration, not hard-coded. Once telemetry flows, build alerts on the signals that matter to users, such as failed requests, slow dependencies, and rising queue depth in Service Bus. Dashboards are useful, but alerts that wake the right person are what keep incidents short.

How the services fit together

A common Java architecture on Azure looks like this. A Spring Boot service runs on App Service or AKS and handles HTTP requests. It stores transactional data in PostgreSQL and product catalog documents in Cosmos DB. When an order is placed, it publishes an event to Service Bus. An Azure Function consumes that event to send a notification. Secrets such as database passwords and API keys are read from Key Vault through managed identities. Application Insights traces a request from the HTTP call through the database query and the message publication.

Notice what the design avoids: no shared credentials in code, no direct coupling between the order service and the notification logic, and full visibility into what happened. Each service does one job, and the platform handles the undifferentiated work.

Common mistakes

  • Storing connection strings and keys in source control. Use managed identities and Key Vault from the start. Retrofitting this later is painful.
  • Choosing AKS by default. Many workloads run more simply on App Service or Container Apps.
  • Ignoring partition keys in Cosmos DB. A poor choice is expensive to fix after data has grown.
  • Assuming messages arrive once. Design consumers to tolerate duplicates.
  • Skipping observability until production. Enable telemetry in the first deployment, not the first incident.

A roadmap for adopting Azure as a Java team

Weeks 1 to 2: Deploy one existing Spring Boot service to App Service with a managed identity. Move its secrets to Key Vault and confirm the application starts without any stored credentials.

Weeks 3 to 4: Enable Application Insights with the Java agent, and build a dashboard and alerts for error rate and latency. Move the database to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with Entra authentication if it is not already there.

Weeks 5 to 6: Introduce Service Bus for one asynchronous workflow, with idempotent consumers and a dead-letter monitoring process. Add an Azure Function for one event-driven task.

Weeks 7 and beyond: Evaluate whether any workload truly needs AKS or Cosmos DB, based on measured requirements rather than preference, and adopt them where the case is clear.

Key takeaways

  • App Service is the simplest path for Java web services; choose AKS only when you need Kubernetes features.
  • Azure Functions suits event-driven and lightweight workloads, with attention to cold starts.
  • Cosmos DB rewards careful partition key design and a deliberate consistency choice.
  • PostgreSQL Flexible Server gives you a managed relational database that works with standard JDBC and JPA.
  • Service Bus provides reliable messaging, and consumers must be idempotent.
  • Key Vault and managed identities remove secrets from code and configuration.
  • Application Insights with the Java agent gives you production visibility with minimal code changes.

Azure is broad, but a Java team can be productive with a focused set of services. Start with the ones that solve a problem you have today, apply security and observability from the first deployment, and expand only when the requirements call for it.

title: How to Add Payments to an App You Built With AI (Without It Breaking)
description:
You built an app with Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. It works, and people like it. Now you want to charge for it, so you type "add payments" into your agent, and a few minutes later there's a checkout button. It feels done.

It usually isn't. I'm Deepak, a solo developer in Hyderabad, and I've spent a lot of time wiring payments into apps built with AI agents. The checkout button is the easy part. The bugs hide in what happens after someone pays, and they don't show up in a demo. They show up when your first real customer emails you asking why they can't get in.

This is the guide I wish I'd had: how the money moves, the five mistakes I keep seeing, how to check for each before launch, and how to choose between Polar and Stripe. You don't need to read any code to follow it.

How the money actually moves

Here's the whole flow in plain words:

  1. A customer clicks "Upgrade" in your app.
  2. Your app sends them to a checkout page run by the payment company (Polar or Stripe). They type their card details there, not in your app. That's a good thing: you never touch card numbers.
  3. The payment goes through, and the customer is sent back to your app's "thank you" page.
  4. Separately, behind the scenes, the payment company sends your app a short message: "this person just paid for Pro." Developers call this a webhook. I'll just call it the payment message.
  5. Your app reads that message, checks that it's real, and writes down in your database: "this person has Pro."
  6. Every time that person opens a paid page, your app checks what it wrote down before letting them in.

The key idea: the thank-you page proves nothing. Anyone can visit a thank-you page. The payment message in step 4 is what should unlock things. Similar messages later tell your app when someone cancels, gets a refund, or their card stops working. Almost every bug I see lives in steps 4 to 6.

The five things that go wrong (and how to check each one)

1. The customer pays, but stays locked out

What happens: checkout works and the money arrives, but the app never updates the customer's account. Usually the payment message never reaches the app, or it arrives and gets ignored. Sometimes the app can't match the payment to the right person, for example when they used a different email at checkout.

How to check: in test mode, sign up as a brand-new user, pay with a test card, and see whether the paid features unlock without you touching anything. Then log out, log back in, and check they're still unlocked. If you ever have to fix someone's account by hand, it's broken. Also open your payment company's dashboard: it shows whether its messages to your app were delivered or failed.

2. Cancelled users keep the paid features

What happens: someone cancels, but your app never takes access away. There's a sneakier version too: payment messages can arrive late and out of order. An old "this person is active" message shows up after the "cancelled" one, and your app happily gives access back.

How to check: in test mode, subscribe and then cancel. Access should last until the end of the period they paid for, and then stop. Not right away, and not never. Do the same with a refund. Then ask your agent: "If an older payment message arrives after a newer one, does the app ignore it?"

3. Fake payment messages unlock premium

What happens: your app has a public address where it listens for payment messages. If it doesn't check that each message really came from Polar or Stripe, anyone who finds that address can send a fake "this person paid" message and get premium for free. Payment companies stamp every message with a secret so your app can tell it's genuine, but AI agents sometimes skip that check, or get it wrong and then "fix" it by switching the check off.

How to check: ask your agent to send a made-up "payment succeeded" message to your app without the secret stamp. Your app must reject it. If it unlocks anything, stop and fix that before launch. While you're there, make sure the secret is stored in your app's settings, not pasted into the code.

4. The AI invents payment features that don't exist

What happens: payment companies update their tools often, and AI agents learned from older versions. So the agent confidently writes something that looks right but uses options that were renamed, removed, or never existed. The worst case is when it fails quietly and you only find out when a real payment doesn't unlock anything.

How to check: tell your agent to follow only the payment company's official docs for the version your app actually uses, and to tell you which doc page each step came from. Then run the full flow in test mode, from clicking "Upgrade" to seeing paid features unlock. "It builds without errors" is not the same as "it works."

5. The billing page breaks for free users

What happens: you add a "Manage billing" button so customers can update their card or cancel. A free user clicks it, and because they've never paid, the payment company has no record of them, so the page shows an error.

How to check: log in as a free user who has never paid and click everything billing-related. Either hide "Manage billing" from people who never paid, or show them a friendly "You're on the free plan" message instead.

One bonus check if you have more than one plan: buy the cheapest one and make sure it never unlocks the features of a more expensive one.

A simple pre-launch checklist

Run through this in test mode before you switch to real money. It doesn't take long, and it heads off the "I paid, why can't I get in?" emails.

  • A brand-new user pays with a test card, and paid features unlock on their own.
  • They log out and back in, and features are still unlocked.
  • They cancel, and access ends at the end of the period they paid for.
  • They get a refund, and access goes away.
  • A fake payment message without the secret stamp is rejected.
  • A free user opens the billing page, and nothing breaks.
  • The cheapest plan never unlocks a more expensive plan.
  • Your payment dashboard shows messages to your app as delivered, not failing.
  • Your secret keys live in your app's settings, not in the code.
  • Terms, Privacy and Refund pages exist and are linked from your site. Payment companies often ask for them.
  • After going live, you make one real purchase yourself with a real card, check that it unlocks, then refund it.

That last one matters. Test mode and live mode use separate keys and settings, and it's easy to update one and forget the other.

Polar or Stripe, in plain terms

Both are solid. The biggest practical difference is who deals with sales tax.

Polar is what's called a merchant of record. In plain words, Polar is the seller on paper: it collects and pays sales tax and VAT in the countries your customers buy from, then pays you out. For a solo maker selling worldwide, that removes a pile of paperwork. The trade-off is a higher fee per sale than Stripe's basic rate, so check their current pricing.

Stripe processes the payment, but you are the seller, so tax is your job. Stripe has a tax add-on that can work out and collect the right amount, but registering and filing is still on you. In return you get more control, which suits you if you already have a Stripe account or need something specific.

My rule of thumb: if you're solo, selling a digital product or subscription to people in many countries, and you don't want to think about tax, start with Polar. If you already use Stripe or have a business set up to handle tax, use Stripe. Either way, before you build anything, check that the one you pick can pay out to your country. And if tax questions worry you, a short chat with an accountant is worth it.

The checks above apply to both: the bugs are about how your app reacts to payments, not which company handles them.

Where ShipToPaid fits

I hit every one of these problems myself while building a real app, so I turned the fixes into written instructions, called skills, that Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can follow. That's ShipToPaid. Instead of hoping your agent remembers to check the secret stamp or ignore late messages, you type a plain request like "/add-paywall add payments to my app," and it follows tested steps with those traps already written down. A launch audit then walks through a checklist like the one above.

If you want to see how it works first, there's a free lite pack on GitHub with three skills: Polar checkout, Polar payment messages, and a short launch check. The full pack adds Stripe, access that follows payments, a customer billing page, credits, license keys, five ready-made commands and a working Next.js starter app. Every skill is a plain file you can read and change.

You don't need either one to use this guide. Run the checklist in test mode, fix whatever fails, and your first paying customer will get exactly what they paid for. That's the whole goal.

This post first appeared on the ShipToPaid blog.

title: How to Humanize AI Text Without Losing the Content: A Diff-Based Review Workflow
description:
Any rewrite tool, whether it's a humanizer, a paraphraser or "ChatGPT, make this sound natural," has the same failure mode: it improves the voice and quietly changes the meaning. A version number becomes "the latest version." "Must" becomes "should." A three-step process becomes two.

For docs, release notes, support macros or anything technical, that's a bug. Here's the workflow I use to humanize AI-drafted text and prove nothing important changed, using tools you already have: git diff, Python's difflib and a short checklist.

The core idea: treat prose like code

You'd never merge a refactor without reviewing the diff. A humanizing pass is a refactor of prose: same behaviour (meaning), different implementation (wording). So:

  1. Commit the original.
  2. Run the rewrite.
  3. Review the diff with the questions that matter.

Step 1: Put the original under version control 

mkdir humanize-review && cd humanize-review
git init
cp ~/drafts/release-notes.md .
git add release-notes.md
git commit -m "AI draft, before humanizing"

Now any change shows up in review.

Step 2: Humanize in small sections

Rewriting a whole document in one pass gives the tool more room to drift. Work section by section, ideally a few hundred words at a time. Keep headings, code blocks and tables out of the rewrite. Those should never change.

I use UnAIMyText for this step because it rewrites at the sentence level and is designed to keep meaning while changing rhythm and phrasing. The free tier takes up to 500 words per input, which fits the section-by-section approach. The workflow below works with any tool, including your own LLM prompt.

Paste the result back over the section in the file.

Step 3: Review a word-level diff

Line diffs are useless for prose because one edit marks a whole paragraph as changed. Use word-level diffs instead:

git diff --word-diff=color

--word-diff is documented in the git diff reference. It shows insertions and deletions inline, so you can see exactly which words moved.

Step 4: Automatically flag the dangerous changes

Some tokens should almost never change in a humanizing pass: numbers, versions, code identifiers, URLs, product names and modal verbs like must, never and only. A small script can catch them.

# check_meaning.py
import re, sys, difflib

PROTECTED = re.compile(
    r"\b\d[\d.,:%]*\b"          # numbers, versions, times, percentages
    r"|`[^`]+`"                 # inline code
    r"|https?://\S+"            # URLs
    r"|\b(must|never|only|always|required|not)\b",  # meaning-critical words
    re.IGNORECASE,
)

def tokens(text):
    return [m.group(0).lower() for m in PROTECTED.finditer(text)]

before = open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8").read()
after = open(sys.argv[2], encoding="utf-8").read()

diff = list(difflib.ndiff(tokens(before), tokens(after)))
changes = [d for d in diff if d.startswith(("- ", "+ "))]

if changes:
    print("Protected tokens changed:")
    for c in changes:
        print("  ", c)
    sys.exit(1)
print("No protected tokens changed.")

Run it against the committed version:

git show HEAD:release-notes.md > /tmp/before.md
python check_meaning.py /tmp/before.md release-notes.md

difflib.ndiff comes from Python's standard library (difflib docs), so there's nothing to install. A non-zero exit code means you need to look at that section again.

Step 5: Human review with four questions

The script catches the mechanical stuff. For the rest, read the word diff and ask:

  1. Did any claim get stronger or weaker? "Fixes" vs "should fix" is a meaning change.
  2. Did any step disappear or merge? Count the steps before and after.
  3. Did any qualifier move? "Only on Linux" becoming "on Linux" changes who's affected.
  4. Did anything new appear? Tools sometimes add a friendly example that isn't true.

Revert those hunks by hand. Keep the rhythm and phrasing improvements.

Step 6: Commit with a message that explains the pass 

git commit -am "Humanize release notes: rhythm and phrasing only, protected tokens unchanged"

If someone questions a sentence later, you have both versions and the reasoning.

What usually changes (and is fine)

  • Openers like "Additionally" and "Furthermore" get dropped.
  • Long, uniform sentences get split.
  • Filler intensifiers ("robust," "seamless") disappear.
  • Passive constructions become active.

What usually changes (and isn't fine)

  • Numbers get rounded or turned into words.
  • Hedges are added to definite statements, or removed from uncertain ones.
  • Lists lose an item.
  • Product or feature names get "naturalised" into generic terms.

Tune the protected list for your content

The regex above is a starting point. Adjust it to what carries meaning in your docs:

  • API and CLI docs: add flag patterns like --[a-z-]+ and HTTP verbs such as GET, POST and DELETE.
  • Legal or policy text: add "may," "shall," "unless" and "except," where one word changes an obligation.
  • Release notes: add your product and feature names so they don't get swapped for generic terms.
  • Support macros: add plan names, prices and time limits like "within 30 days."

Keep the list short enough that a failure means something. If the script flags every run, people stop reading its output. Start with numbers, code and a few modal verbs, then add patterns only when a real regression slips through. Over time the list becomes a record of the mistakes your rewrite step has actually made, which is the most useful kind of check.

Make it a habit

For a team, put check_meaning.py in a pre-commit hook for your docs/ folder. Anyone can humanize AI drafts however they like. The hook just makes sure the facts survive.

Takeaway

Humanizing is safe when you can see exactly what changed. Commit first, rewrite in sections, review a word-level diff, and let a ten-line script guard the tokens that carry meaning. The voice gets better and the content stays the same.

title: Why Clicking "Retry" Is Safe Sometimes, and Dangerous Other Times
description:
You've done this before: you're transferring money on a banking app, the screen freezes for a second, and you don't know if it went through. What do you do?

Most people's gut instinct is to click again. "Maybe it didn't send the first time." And most of the time, that's completely fine.

But every now and then, you've heard the horror story someone clicked twice, and the money left their account twice. That's not bad luck. That's a real gap in how the system was built, and it's worth understanding why it happens, because it applies to way more than banking apps.

Why retrying feels safe

When you ask an app to do something check your balance, search for a product, load a page and it fails or hangs, retrying is harmless. You can ask "what's my balance" a hundred times, and nothing changes because of it. You're just asking, not doing.

This is why most systems are built to automatically retry when something goes wrong. A request times out, the system quietly tries again in the background, and you never even notice. This is good design, most of the time.

Why retrying isn't always safe

The trouble starts with actions that actually do something send money, place an order, submit a form. Here's the part people miss:

A failure doesn't always mean the action didn't happen. Sometimes it means you just didn't hear back.

Think about it step by step:

  1. You tap "send money."
  2. The request reaches the bank. The bank actually sends the money.
  3. On the way back, the "success" message gets lost bad network, server hiccup, whatever.
  4. Your screen just... freezes. From where you're sitting, it looks exactly like the request never went through.

If the system (or you) retries at this point, assuming step 2 never happened, you just sent the money a second time. The action did happen. You just never got told.

This is the actual gap not carelessness, not bad luck. It's the simple fact that "I didn't get a reply" and "it didn't happen" are two different things, and a plain retry can't tell them apart.

The fix: give every action a fingerprint

The real fix isn't "don't retry." Retrying is still the right instinct you just need a way for the system to recognize "wait, I've already done this one" before it does it again.

The common way to do this: attach a unique ID to the action itself, generated once, before you even send it the first time. Something like a random code you create on your side and attach to the request "this is attempt number xyz123 of send-money."

Now, if the same request arrives twice (because of a retry), the receiving system checks: "have I already processed xyz123?" If yes, it just replies "already done, here's what happened" instead of doing it again. If no, it processes it normally.

This one idea has a name in tech idempotency which sounds complicated but just means: doing something once, or doing it five times by accident, gives you the exact same end result.

A simple way to picture it: imagine writing your name on a form versus adding a rupee to a piggy bank. Writing your name five times doesn't change anything same name, same result, every time. Dropping a rupee in five times gives you five rupees. The first is naturally "idempotent." The second isn't, unless you specifically design it to be for example, by numbering each rupee and refusing to accept the same number twice.

The simple rule to remember

Before adding automatic retries anywhere, ask one question:

"If this exact same action runs twice by accident, is that okay?"

  • Checking something, reading something, searching something? Almost always yes retry freely.
  • Sending money, placing an order, submitting something that changes real data? Not automatically you need that fingerprint check first.

The takeaway

Retries are one of the most useful tools for making a system feel reliable most failures really are just temporary blips, and quietly trying again is the right call. But retries are not a free upgrade you can bolt onto anything without thinking. The moment an action does something instead of just asking something, you owe it a way to recognize its own repeats otherwise, "just retry" quietly turns a small network hiccup into a real, hard-to-undo mistake.

title: Centralizing Error Capture Across HTTP, Cron, and Workers (With Trust Boundaries)
description:
A production error pipeline is only useful if its data boundary is acceptable. TL;DR: centralize NestJS HTTP exceptions with a global filter, send worker and cron failures through the same small adapter, and keep process-level handlers for failures that escape both paths. Then choose the backend only after checking region, retention, deletion, and processor terms. A single capture path improves signal quality; it does not transfer those obligations away from the app owner.

This is the practical choice for a small SaaS because three failure paths become one reviewable boundary. The tempting first pass is to instrument controllers and job callbacks separately. It looks simple, but it creates inconsistent context and lets scheduled work fail quietly. Centralization wins here, provided the payload is deliberately narrow.

How should a NestJS error tracking filter capture exceptions?

Capture enough to group and debug a failure: the execution surface, exception name, a scrubbed message, time, and an internal correlation identifier. Do not make entire request bodies, authorization headers, prompts, worker payloads, or customer records the default. More context raises diagnostic signal until it becomes duplicated sensitive data and cardinality noise.

That trade-off matters in an AI agent loop. A failed tool call may sit beside a prompt, model output, token accounting, and vendor metadata. Error tracking needs the exception and correlation ID; latency and cost belong in purpose-built measurements. Joining them by an internal identifier keeps the error event small without losing the path back to operational evidence. Prometheus gives the same broad warning from the metrics side: every unique label combination creates another time series, so unbounded identifiers should not become labels.

Infrai is one reasonable capture backend when a solo team wants a plain REST boundary instead of another SDK. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so integration starts by reading one capability rather than learning a proprietary client. The supporting benefit is operational and distinct from schema discovery: 295 routes across 20 modules use one key for multiple backend capabilities and produce one consolidated bill. For a small team already measuring agent-loop latency and cost, one API key can serve this error boundary and adjacent services instead of adding another secret-rotation path, another vendor credential, and another invoice reconciliation step. It won't improve the exception itself, but it removes work around the exception pipeline.

Infrai consolidates those capabilities under a single key, a single wallet, and a single bill. In this workflow, that is credential consolidation rather than an error-tracking feature; it reduces the number of secrets and vendor accounts the operator has to control.

Fewer moving parts matter.

Teams that want a compact, self-describing REST capture boundary should try Infrai for centralized NestJS error ingestion, because discovery makes the contract inspectable before any application data crosses it. It does not replace the specialist that owns alert delivery, heartbeat monitoring, tracing, replay, symbolication, or contractual data guarantees.

A focused NestJS capture adapter

Keep vendor fields outside the exception filter. The adapter below is intentionally typed around an application-owned event, which makes redaction testable and permits a backend change without rewriting every execution surface. The HTTP filter, worker, and cron paths all call the same function.

import {
  ArgumentsHost,
  Catch,
  ExceptionFilter,
  HttpException,
} from "@nestjs/common";

type ErrorSurface = "http" | "worker" | "cron" | "process";

type SafeErrorEvent = {
  surface: ErrorSurface;
  name: string;
  message: string;
  occurredAt: string;
  correlationId?: string;
};

type Capture = (event: SafeErrorEvent) => Promise<void>;

type DiscoveryManifest = {
  version: string;
  generated_at: string;
  capabilities: Array<{
    id: string;
    method: string;
    path: string;
    available: boolean;
  }>;
};

async function readInfraiManifest(attempt = 0): Promise<DiscoveryManifest> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return readInfraiManifest(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  return (await response.json()) as DiscoveryManifest;
}

function toSafeEvent(
  error: unknown,
  surface: ErrorSurface,
  correlationId?: string,
): SafeErrorEvent {
  const value = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error("Unknown failure");

  return {
    surface,
    name: value.name,
    message: value.message.slice(0, 500),
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    correlationId,
  };
}

@Catch()
export class GlobalErrorFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  constructor(private readonly capture: Capture) {}

  async catch(error: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost): Promise<void> {
    const http = host.switchToHttp();
    const request = http.getRequest<{ headers: Record<string, string | undefined> }>();
    const response = http.getResponse<{
      status: (code: number) => { json: (body: unknown) => void };
    }>();
    const status = error instanceof HttpException ? error.getStatus() : 500;

    await this.capture(
      toSafeEvent(error, "http", request.headers["x-request-id"]),
    );
    response.status(status).json({ statusCode: status });
  }
}

export async function runWorkerJob(capture: Capture): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await Promise.reject(new Error("Worker task failed"));
  } catch (error) {
    await capture(toSafeEvent(error, "worker"));
    throw error;
  }
}

export async function runCronJob(capture: Capture): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await Promise.reject(new Error("Scheduled task failed"));
  } catch (error) {
    await capture(toSafeEvent(error, "cron"));
    throw error;
  }
}

export function installProcessHandlers(capture: Capture): void {
  process.on("uncaughtException", (error: Error) => {
    void capture(toSafeEvent(error, "process"));
  });
  process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason: unknown) => {
    void capture(toSafeEvent(reason, "process"));
  });
}

export async function verifyCaptureContract(): Promise<void> {
  const manifest = await readInfraiManifest();
  const capture = manifest.capabilities.find(
    (capability) =>
      capability.method === "POST" &&
      capability.path === "/v1/errors/capture" &&
      capability.available,
  );
  if (!capture) throw new Error("Error capture capability is unavailable");
}

Call verifyCaptureContract during an integration check, then use the capability-specific schema and TypeScript example returned by discovery to implement the concrete Capture; this avoids fabricating request fields or pinning an undocumented payload. Register the filter globally and wrap each worker and scheduled entry point. A production process handler also needs an explicit shutdown policy after capture; continuing after an uncaught exception can leave state uncertain. Keep that lifecycle decision separate from the reporting adapter. This sequence is deliberately less convenient than pasting a guessed POST body. It is also the point of a self-describing API: the executable integration follows the current machine-readable contract.

One subtle trap remains. A try/catch can report a job that throws, but it cannot report a job that never starts. That gap is structural, not an exception-filter bug.

Silence has no stack trace.

The trust-boundary checklist changes the vendor decision

Before sending even the narrow event above, draw the processor chain. Record the application region, ingestion region, downstream processors, retention duration, deletion mechanism, and which party can access stored payloads. Require evidence for each cell. An unspecified value is not a promise.

Infrai's observability surface does not provide a per-user log deletion interface, while retention and cold-storage configuration are not exposed. Do not route personal data there on the assumption that it can later be erased by user identifier. Keep direct identifiers out of the event, use an internal correlation ID, and retain the identifying join only inside the system whose deletion controls you own. A specialist provider is the better choice when configurable residency, contractual retention, per-user deletion, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Session Replay, or a distributed span tree is mandatory.

The boundary also extends beyond storage. Notification delivery is a separate processor relationship, as are paging, SMS, and webhooks. Infrai has no native notification routing, so an app can poll recent unresolved groups and feed its own alert path. That is workable for a small queue and explicit polling budget. It is a poor fit when mature escalation policies are the requirement.

How do the real alternatives compare?

Do not collapse error trackers and uptime monitors into one category. They answer different failure questions, and the data they receive differs.

Option Evaluate it for Boundary or limitation to verify
Sentry Specialist application error tracking Verify region, retention, deletion, replay, and source-map settings against the exact plan and deployment choice.
Datadog A broader observability stack where errors must correlate with other telemetry The wider telemetry footprint can increase both processor scope and noise; define which payloads and tags are allowed.
Bugsnag Specialist error monitoring with an application-focused workflow Confirm data-location and deletion terms, and test how grouping behaves on the app's real exception mix.
Infrai A small REST ingestion boundary with public schema discovery and no required vendor SDK Bring separate alert routing; it has no heartbeat, span-tree query, replay, or source-map symbolication.
Healthchecks Detecting scheduled work that did not run It complements exception capture; it is not the store for HTTP and worker exception detail.

This is not a universal ranking. Sentry or Bugsnag deserves the first trial when deep error-investigation features drive the decision. Datadog makes more sense when one established platform already owns telemetry correlation and its data boundary is approved. Healthchecks closes the negative-space problem: a missed ping reveals silence that no exception pipeline can observe.

For Infrai, the unusual advantage is inspectability. Public discovery returns the contract and runnable examples before a key is used. Still, discovery of an API schema does not establish residency, retention, deletion, or processor commitments. Those require separate, current evidence.

Measure this before copying the design

Start with signal quality, not event volume. Over a representative release, inspect the ratio of actionable groups to noisy duplicates, the fraction of HTTP, worker, cron, and process failures carrying a correlation ID, capture-path latency, dropped reports, and the time from a new unresolved group to an operator seeing it. For an agent loop, measure token cost and model latency separately, then verify that the correlation ID joins those records without copying prompts into error payloads.

Also run two blunt tests: stop a scheduled job without throwing, and request deletion for a test user. The first proves whether heartbeat coverage exists. The second proves whether the full processor chain can satisfy the deletion path instead of merely documenting one.

No magic here.

The chosen design is useful because its boundary is small enough to reason about. Centralize capture, minimize the payload, preserve correlation, and let specialist systems handle the guarantees they actually provide. If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai discovery documentation and inspect the live capability contract before wiring the adapter.

  • https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/task-scheduling
  • https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#event-uncaughtexception
  • https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#event-unhandledrejection
  • https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/
  • https://docs.sentry.io/
  • https://docs.datadoghq.com/
  • https://docs.bugsnag.com/
  • https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery
