title: Vercel Passport is now generally available
description:
Vercel Passport is now generally available.

Passport allows you to protect your Vercel deployments with your own identity provider. Visitors authenticate through Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or any OIDC provider before viewing a protected deployment, and Vercel forwards a signed identity token to the deployment so application code can build on who the visitor is.

Read visitor identity in application code

The getIdentity() helper in @vercel/passport reads the Vercel request context and returns the authenticated visitor. Vercel strips client-supplied values for the x-vercel-oidc-passport-token header and injects the verified token after Passport validates the session, so the identity your code receives is already verified.

The subject field is a stable identifier for the visitor, scoped to your team and the Vercel Connect application that links Passport to your identity provider, and externalSubject is the visitor's ID in the provider itself. The helper returns null only when a request arrives without a Passport session, because unauthenticated browser visitors are redirected to the identity provider before they ever reach your code.

In local development, getIdentity() returns a configurable development identity, so the same code path works without a real identity provider.

Authorize with groups from your identity provider

The signed Passport token can now carry additional identity claims from your provider, such as group membership. Request the groups scope and allowlist the claim in the Vercel Connect application that Passport uses, then read it from the identity payload:

The additional identity scopes documentation covers provider configuration, including a full Okta walkthrough.

Verify identity in downstream services

Forward the Passport token from your application to another backend as a bearer token and verify it there with verifyIdentity(), available in @vercel/passport 1.0.0 and later. The helper checks the token signature, the Passport claims, and that the token came from the expected project and environment:

Services outside JavaScript can verify the token as a standard JWT with the published JWKS. Learn more in the verify identity documentation.

Monitor Passport access

Every successful Passport authentication records a passport-access-granted event in both the Activity Log and Audit Logs, identifying the visitor and recording the protected hostname and project. The Activity Log view is already filtered to Passport access.

Bypass Passport for automated traffic

Protection Bypass for Automation now applies to Passport. Webhooks, cron jobs, and CI runs that already send a bypass secret in the x-vercel-protection-bypass header or query parameter keep working when you turn Passport on. Because Passport runs in Vercel's network before your deployment's routes and proxy functions, the secret has to be part of the original request rather than added by your own middleware. A bypassed request has no signed-in visitor, so getIdentity() returns null.

Bypass Passport with Trusted Sources

Trusted Sources offers the same bypass without a shared secret. Protected deployments accept short-lived OIDC tokens from the Vercel projects and external services you authorize, which is how the workflow that triggers eve from Slack reaches a Passport-protected deployment.

Protect custom environments

Passport now supports custom environments, so deployments in an environment like staging or qa get the same identity provider sign-in as your preview and production deployments.

Get started

Vercel Passport is available on the Enterprise plan. New guides cover identity provider setup, token claims, local development, forwarding identity between backends, and bypassing Passport for automation.

Set up Passport with your identity provider in the Passport documentation, or configure it programmatically through the Vercel API.

title: Expiring Video Session Recording Links for Customer Support Explained
description:
In Node.js, store each completed customer-support video session recording in a private bucket you control, then put playback behind a short-lived presigned link. Do not pass a recording vendor's permanent URL to an agent or customer.

TL;DR: create the video room with scoped participant tokens, copy the completed recording into your own bucket, and presign each playback request after authorization. Keep recording completion in a durable queue; use the realtime channel only to tell connected clients that playback is ready. A publish is not a substitute for a job that must eventually run.

That split is the practical result. It preserves your retention policy and access control, while an expired link limits the useful lifetime of a copied URL. Recordings also grow faster than the rest of this feature, so scheduled deletion belongs in the first release, not a later cleanup sprint.

How should Node.js store a video session recording behind a private link?

A vendor URL couples playback access to the room provider's storage and retention model. Even if the URL is difficult to guess, difficulty is not an authorization decision. A presigned URL is different: the application first decides that this support agent may view this ticket, then creates a link with a narrow lifetime.

The bucket should remain private or signed-only. Never add public-read, and never attach your backend's provider authorization header when the browser follows a presigned URL. The signature in that URL is already the temporary credential.

Keep it private.

There are two clocks to choose. Link expiry should cover a normal playback session without becoming a reusable bookmark. Object retention should follow the support case and compliance policy. They solve different problems. Thirty minutes for a link and 30 days for an object might be reasonable inputs for one business, but they are not universal defaults; decide them explicitly and test deletion.

The minimal Express implementation

This example accepts a completed recording from a trusted internal worker, writes it to a private S3-compatible bucket, and issues an expiring playback URL only after an application authorization hook succeeds. It uses a random object key rather than customer-supplied path text. The upload is idempotent for a given recordingId, so a retried completion job overwrites the same object instead of producing duplicates.

Before wiring an Infrai room or storage call, the following small program reads its live capability contract. This is the useful part of a self-describing API: the integration begins with the actual method, path, JSON Schema, billing information, and runnable examples instead of a guessed SDK call. The discovery surface is public, but the sample still reads the same key used by the RTC, queue, realtime, and storage calls so the handoff has one credential boundary.

type Capability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  params: unknown;
  idempotent: boolean;
};

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");
}

async function discover(id: string, attempt = 0): Promise<Capability> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/discovery/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return discover(id, attempt + 1);
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json() as Promise<Capability>;
}

const roomCreate = await discover("rtc.room.create");
console.log({
  method: roomCreate.method,
  path: roomCreate.path,
  requestSchema: roomCreate.params,
  idempotent: roomCreate.idempotent,
});

Use the returned method, path, and schema to build the room request rather than deriving a path from prose. The same pattern exposes the queue and realtime contracts. This avoids pretending that a made-up field is runnable code.

import express, { type Request } from "express";
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import {
  GetObjectCommand,
  PutObjectCommand,
  S3Client,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { getSignedUrl } from "@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner";

const bucket = required("RECORDINGS_BUCKET");
const region = required("AWS_REGION");
const s3 = new S3Client({ region });
const app = express();

app.use(express.raw({ type: "video/*", limit: "2gb" }));

function required(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Missing ${name}`);
  return value;
}

function safeId(value: string): string {
  if (!/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$/.test(value)) {
    throw new Error("Invalid identifier");
  }
  return value;
}

function objectKey(ticketId: string, recordingId: string): string {
  return `support/${safeId(ticketId)}/${safeId(recordingId)}.webm`;
}

async function canViewRecording(req: Request, ticketId: string): Promise<boolean> {
  // Replace with the same ticket-membership check used by the support console.
  return req.header("x-demo-ticket") === ticketId;
}

app.put("/internal/recordings/:ticketId/:recordingId", async (req, res) => {
  if (!Buffer.isBuffer(req.body) || req.body.length === 0) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "A video body is required" });
  }

  try {
    const Key = objectKey(req.params.ticketId, req.params.recordingId);
    await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
      Bucket: bucket,
      Key,
      Body: req.body,
      ContentType: req.header("content-type") ?? "video/webm",
      ServerSideEncryption: "AES256",
      Metadata: { checksum: crypto.createHash("sha256").update(req.body).digest("hex") },
    }));
    return res.status(201).json({ recordingId: req.params.recordingId });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
    return res.status(502).json({ error: "Recording storage failed" });
  }
});

app.post("/tickets/:ticketId/recordings/:recordingId/playback", async (req, res) => {
  try {
    if (!(await canViewRecording(req, req.params.ticketId))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: "Forbidden" });
    }

    const command = new GetObjectCommand({
      Bucket: bucket,
      Key: objectKey(req.params.ticketId, req.params.recordingId),
    });
    const url = await getSignedUrl(s3, command, { expiresIn: 900 });
    res.setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store");
    return res.json({ url, expiresInSeconds: 900 });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
    return res.status(502).json({ error: "Playback link creation failed" });
  }
});

app.listen(3000);

The demo header is deliberately a replaceable seam, not production authentication. The important ordering is fixed: authorize first, sign second. Also configure a bucket lifecycle rule for deletion; an application cron job is easier to forget and harder to audit.

For large recordings, stream or use multipart upload instead of buffering two gigabytes in the Express process. The buffer keeps this sample readable, but it sets the wrong memory profile for production unless an upstream proxy enforces a much smaller limit.

Delivery guarantees belong outside the socket

Recording completion is a state transition. A connected support console benefits from a realtime notification, but an offline console must not make the completion disappear. Put a small message such as { ticketId, recordingId, status: "ready" } on a durable queue after storage succeeds. A worker can then publish to the ticket's realtime channel and record notification delivery idempotently. Standard queues are at-least-once, so use recordingId as the consumer's deduplication key.

This creates a clear fan-out rule: the queue owns eventual work; the socket owns low-latency presentation. Slow or disconnected subscribers can refetch ticket state after reconnecting, while fast clients get the update immediately. Imagine the upload finishing at 14:03 while the assigned agent's laptop is asleep: the queued recordingId remains work to perform, and the console later reconciles from ticket state. If the worker receives that message twice, its deduplication record turns the second delivery into a no-op. A bare socket publish provides neither property. No recording bytes belong in either path.

Infrai is one option when reducing integration surface matters. Its public discovery response describes capability paths, request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so adding room creation, scoped RTC tokens, a queue, and realtime publishing starts from one machine-readable contract. The queue and socket share one API key and base URL. A Pusher plus Amazon SQS alternative requires two signups, two credential sets, and application glue that maps queued events to channel publishes. The trade-off is concentration: separate services let a team select and replace each delivery component independently.

Pusher is a focused managed-channel choice with broad client support. Ably is worth evaluating when its realtime messaging model matches the delivery semantics you need. PubNub also targets managed publish-and-subscribe applications. Socket.IO gives a Node.js team more direct control over the server layer, but the team then owns its operation and still needs a durable queue. These products do not erase the queue-versus-socket distinction; compare their documented guarantees against the exact offline workflow.

One missed event is enough.

Do not infer stronger delivery from a shared credential. Keep the queue-to-publish worker idempotent, acknowledge a job only after the publish attempt finishes, and make the client reconcile against durable ticket state. Short code is useful. Ambiguous ownership is not.

Choosing the storage and video boundary

The best choice depends on what you want to own:

Option Useful fit Boundary to account for
Amazon S3 Teams already using AWS IAM, lifecycle rules, and SQS More AWS policy and credential configuration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object storage near a Cloudflare delivery stack Verify the S3 features your implementation relies on
Google Cloud Storage Teams centered on Google Cloud IAM and signed URLs The signing setup differs from the S3 SDK example
Mux A managed video pipeline where processing and playback matter more than owning raw storage mechanics Keep your application authorization and retention contract explicit
Infrai One self-describing API surface for RTC, queues, realtime, and storage A broader shared abstraction is less component-specific than direct vendor SDKs

These are not interchangeable purchases. S3, R2, and Cloud Storage are primarily object-storage choices. Mux moves further into video processing and playback. Infrai spans backend capabilities behind one contract. For a small team, I would choose the narrowest boundary that removes work I do not want to maintain, then keep the object key and authorization model portable.

The room token should be scoped to the room and participant role. It grants call access, not recording access. Playback still passes through the ticket authorization check, even for somebody who joined the original call.

What to measure before copying this design

Measure the completed-recording size distribution, upload duration, queue age, duplicate completion count, notification lag, presign failures, playback starts after link expiry, and deletion lag. Percentiles matter more than a single average because one long support call can dominate memory and transfer time.

Run three failure drills. Disconnect the agent before completion, deliver the queue message twice, and request playback after both link expiry and object deletion. The expected outcomes are boring: state appears after reconnect, duplicate work changes nothing, the expired link fails, and the deleted recording stays gone.

That is the design worth shipping: private storage under your policy, temporary access after authorization, durable completion work, and realtime fan-out as an optimization. Everything else is vendor selection.

  • Mux secure video playback documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation

  • PubNub message reliability documentation

title: Safe Voice Commands for My Home Automation Server
description:
Introduction

Running a home‑automation server from my garage in Pompano Beach has been a hobby that turned into a daily workhorse for Dream Futures Tech. I wanted to control lights, the coffee maker, and the garage door with my voice, but I also needed to make sure that a stray phrase or a mis‑heard command didn’t trigger something dangerous. The solution I landed on is simple: filter everything through a whitelist regular expression before handing the text to a language model. In this article I walk through the exact steps I took, the code I wrote, and the pitfalls I avoided.

The Problem

Voice assistants are great, but they are also black boxes. When you feed raw speech‑to‑text output into a large language model (LLM) you hand it free reign to interpret anything it sees. A mis‑recognition like “turn off the oven” becoming “turn off the oven door” could be harmless, but “unlock the front door” misheard as “unlock the front store” could expose a business. I needed a deterministic gate that only allowed commands I explicitly approved.

Why Regex First?

A regular expression is deterministic, fast, and easy to audit. By defining a whitelist of patterns that represent the actions I actually want to perform, I can reject everything else outright. This gives me three benefits:

  1. Safety – No surprise commands slip through.
  2. Performance – The regex check runs in a few microseconds, far cheaper than an API call.
  3. Transparency – The list of allowed phrases lives in source control, so any change is tracked.

Building the Whitelist

I kept the whitelist in a JSON file so I could edit it without touching code. Each entry contains a pattern and a short description.

[
  {"pattern": "^turn on (the )?lights?$", "action": "lights_on"},
  {"pattern": "^turn off (the )?lights?$", "action": "lights_off"},
  {"pattern": "^open (the )?garage door$", "action": "garage_open"},
  {"pattern": "^close (the )?garage door$", "action": "garage_close"},
  {"pattern": "^brew coffee$", "action": "coffee_start"}
]

The patterns are deliberately simple – I avoid optional words and wildcards that could broaden the match unintentionally. When the server receives a transcription from the microphone, it iterates over the list and picks the first match.

Integrating the LLM

Even with a whitelist, I still want the LLM to handle variations like “please turn the lights on” or “could you open the garage door?”. The trick is to run the regex first, and only if it fails do I fall back to the LLM with a very narrow prompt that asks for a command only from the allowed set.

const fetch = require('node-fetch');
const whitelist = require('./whitelist.json');

function matchWhitelist(text) {
  for (const entry of whitelist) {
    const re = new RegExp(entry.pattern, 'i');
    if (re.test(text)) return entry.action;
  }
  return null;
}

async function askLLM(text) {
  const prompt = `You are a voice‑command parser for a home automation system. Only respond with one of the following keywords: ${whitelist.map(e=>e.action).join(', ')}. If the request does not match any, reply with "unknown".
User: ${text}`;
  const response = await fetch('https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json'
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({model: 'gpt-4o-mini', messages: [{role: 'user', content: prompt}], temperature: 0})
  });
  const data = await response.json();
  return data.choices[0].message.content.trim();
}

async function handleCommand(transcript) {
  let action = matchWhitelist(transcript);
  if (!action) {
    action = await askLLM(transcript);
  }
  if (action && action !== 'unknown') {
    // dispatch to the hardware controller
    console.log('Executing:', action);
    // e.g., send MQTT message or call a local script
  } else {
    console.warn('Command rejected:', transcript);
  }
}

Key points:

  • Temperature 0 forces deterministic output from the LLM.
  • The prompt explicitly limits the LLM’s vocabulary, reducing hallucination risk.
  • If the LLM still returns "unknown", the command is dropped.

Putting It All Together

My server runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 with Node.js 20. I use the speech-to-text library from the local microphone to get a raw string, then feed it into handleCommand. The flow looks like this:

  1. Capture audio → speech‑to‑text.
  2. Run matchWhitelist. If a match, execute immediately.
  3. If no match, call askLLM with the constrained prompt.
  4. Execute the returned action or log a rejection.

Because the whitelist check happens first, most everyday commands (lights, garage) are processed locally without any network latency. Only the occasional polite phrasing hits the LLM, and even then the response is bounded.

Lessons Learned

  • Keep the whitelist tight. Adding a new pattern should be a deliberate code change, not a casual addition.
  • Log rejections. I store every rejected transcript in a SQLite table; reviewing them helped me spot common mis‑recognitions and expand the whitelist safely.
  • Rate‑limit the LLM. I set a per‑minute cap (10 calls) to avoid surprise bills if the microphone picks up background chatter.
  • Test with real speech. Synthetic text works, but the acoustic environment in my garage introduced quirks that only field testing revealed.

Conclusion

By front‑loading a deterministic regex whitelist and only falling back to a language model when needed, I got a voice‑controlled automation system that feels responsive and, more importantly, safe. The pattern is portable: any small business that wants voice control—whether it’s a local bakery turning on the oven or a plumbing shop opening a service door—can adopt the same two‑layer approach.

I build sites and automations for small businesses at dreamfuturestech.com.

title: Independent Liveness Proof for Missed Cron Job Runs and Heartbeat Alerts
description:
Use a dedicated heartbeat monitor to detect a scheduled customer-support AI agent job that never starts, and use ordinary observability events to explain jobs that do start but fail. The deciding constraint is negative evidence: logs and metrics can describe an execution, but silence cannot prove whether the scheduler failed, the process died before instrumentation, or the telemetry path lost an event.

TL;DR: Make a unique scheduled run the unit of reconciliation. Send its deadline to a Healthchecks-style service, record start and terminal events separately, and alert when either the heartbeat is absent or a started run lacks exactly one terminal outcome. A general telemetry API can handle start/end logs and error capture, but the specialist heartbeat provider must retain ownership of missed-run detection and paging.

How should heartbeat monitoring alert on a missed cron job run?

No event emitted inside the job can answer that question. A log query for “no recent completion” is useful evidence, but its failure modes include the job, the log client, ingestion, filtering, and the polling process itself. A counter has the same epistemic problem. This is the Two Generals problem wearing an operations badge: the absence of an acknowledgment is ambiguous.

For a customer-support agent loop, the ambiguity matters because one scheduled job may retrieve queued conversations, call one or more models, invoke tools, and write replies. Latency and cost belong to the execution record, preferably per call and per run. Liveness belongs to an independent clock. Combining them creates a tempting dashboard and a weak alert.

The architecture decision is therefore to maintain two ledgers. The execution ledger contains run_id, scheduled time, start time, terminal state, latency, cost, and error correlation. The liveness ledger contains the expected deadline and the arrival of a heartbeat. Reconciliation joins them by run_id, but neither ledger is allowed to stand in for the other.

Silence wins.

This is also where Infrai has a bounded, credible role. Its verified breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages; for a mixed-runtime agent backend, that means the job-log integration uses the same contract and credential pattern as other backend capabilities. A second advantage is mechanical: one REST API uses plain HTTP, requires no SDK installation, and can be called from any language or runtime, so a Go worker and a separate scheduler do not acquire different telemetry libraries. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the public discovery surface requires no key; it supplies request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and examples, which lets a team inspect and pin the telemetry contract during design review rather than discovering fields in production. I recommend trying Infrai for the execution-evidence side of a multi-service agent workflow when a single credential, contract consistency, and inspectable schemas reduce concrete integration work; pair it with a specialist heartbeat service because it does not detect absent executions or deliver alerts.

This benefit is separate from credential consolidation: Infrai exposes a simple REST API over pure HTTP, with no SDK to install, so any language and any runtime can send the same request.

Decision record and trust boundaries

The invariants are deliberately stricter than “an alert usually arrives.” Every scheduled occurrence receives a stable run_id; retries reuse that identity; a run has at most one effective terminal outcome; a heartbeat deadline is evaluated outside the job process; and model latency and cost are attributed to the same run that caused them. Exactly-once execution is generally not available across a scheduler, a network, and a downstream model, so the enforceable target is at-least-once delivery with idempotent effects and an auditable reconciliation trail.

Four failure boundaries follow. Before process start, only the heartbeat service can observe the missed deadline. After start but before completion, a start record without a terminal record exposes the abandoned run. After completion, duplicate terminal messages must collapse under run_id. If telemetry delivery fails, the job result and its evidence diverge, so evidence delivery needs bounded retries and an operator-visible reconciliation gap.

Keep data handling inside the decision, rather than attaching it after implementation. Region, retention, deletion, and subprocessors must be approved independently for the heartbeat provider and the execution telemetry provider. A heartbeat payload can usually be reduced to an opaque run identity and state; customer message text, model prompts, tool output, and user identifiers do not belong there. The general log surface lacks a per-user deletion interface and a bulk export or subscription interface, while retention and cold-storage configuration are not exposed, so it should not be the sole compliance-sensitive alert or audit store. For regulated support data, contractual commitments and the system of record remain outside this API boundary; NIST SP 800-66r2 is a useful reminder that technical telemetry does not replace documented risk analysis and controls.

Option Missed-run signal Execution diagnosis Trust-boundary consequence Best fit
Healthchecks.io Dedicated absent-ping monitoring Limited compared with an event store Receives a minimal run identity and timing signal Simple cron and scheduled-job liveness
Cronitor Dedicated job monitoring Separate monitoring surface Adds a specialist processor that must pass region, retention, deletion, and notification review Teams wanting scheduled-job monitoring as a distinct product
Better Stack Heartbeat monitoring in a broader operations product Can sit beside other operational signals Consolidation may reduce consoles, but processor scope still needs review Teams already standardizing operational response there
Sentry Error capture is strong when code runs and reports Error-centric diagnosis Application context may be richer and therefore more sensitive Exceptions and failed executions, not proof of a never-started job
Infrai plus a heartbeat specialist Specialist owns absence; Infrai does not Start/end logs and error capture under a consistent REST contract Two deliberately narrow processors; Infrai log deletion/export limits remain relevant Agent backends that value broad API consistency and accept split liveness ownership

The table is not a feature-score exercise. Healthchecks.io, Cronitor, and Better Stack should be evaluated against the actual deployment regions, retention controls, deletion procedure, subprocessors, and alert transports in their current contracts and documentation. Sentry is the better comparison for captured failures. The broader API is a reasonable execution-evidence adapter when its one-key surface removes integration work, but a specialist is the better choice for the one signal that matters most here: nothing happened.

The limitation is explicit: Infrai is not suitable as the primary missed-run monitor or as the sole compliance audit store. Choose Healthchecks.io, Cronitor, or Better Stack for absence detection, and choose Sentry when error diagnosis is the dominant requirement. This trade-off is intentional.

Critical path in Go

The job should establish a stable run identity before doing work. The following runnable program records start and end events through the verified log-ingest route. It explicitly sets the HTTP method, authenticates from the environment, checks non-success responses, and honors Retry-After on HTTP 429 with exponential fallback. The same run_id appears in both records, which makes a retry reconcilable; the heartbeat ping remains a separate call owned by the selected specialist and is intentionally not fabricated here.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type logEvent struct {
    Level   string                 `json:"level"`
    Message string                 `json:"message"`
    Fields  map[string]interface{} `json:"fields"`
}

func ingest(client *http.Client, key string, event logEvent) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(event)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/ingest", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("log ingest returned %s: %s", resp.Status, responseBody)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("log ingest remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    runID := os.Getenv("RUN_ID")
    if key == "" || runID == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY and RUN_ID are required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    started := time.Now().UTC()
    if err := ingest(client, key, logEvent{
        Level: "info", Message: "support agent run started",
        Fields: map[string]interface{}{"run_id": runID, "scheduled_at": started.Format(time.RFC3339)},
    }); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    // Run the idempotent support-agent workload here. Customer content stays out of telemetry.
    if err := ingest(client, key, logEvent{
        Level: "info", Message: "support agent run completed",
        Fields: map[string]interface{}{"run_id": runID, "latency_ms": time.Since(started).Milliseconds()},
    }); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

One detail is easy to miss: repeated start or completion logs are not harmful only because reconciliation treats run_id plus state as a uniqueness key. The log endpoint is evidence transport, not the transaction coordinator. Any reply-writing side effect needs its own idempotency key and durable state transition. Consider a retry after the model has produced an answer but before the scheduler records success: the second attempt may legitimately repeat telemetry, yet it must discover the committed reply by run_id rather than send another response to the customer. The audit record should preserve both attempts and the single effective outcome. That is the useful meaning of an exactly-once mindset here; claiming exactly-once transport would obscure the real guarantee.

Cost measurement follows the same boundary. Attach per-call cost and latency to the execution ledger when the runtime supplies them, then aggregate by run_id; never infer a missing run from a zero-cost interval. Zero could mean an empty queue, a cached path, a failed measurement, or no execution. Ambiguous zeros do not page well.

Rejected design and when it is still valid

The rejected design polls recent logs or metrics and alerts when no completion appears. It is attractive because it avoids another provider and can work for low-consequence internal maintenance, especially when an independent poller already exists and the team accepts delayed, best-effort detection. It can also provide a useful secondary reconciliation query.

Keep it secondary.

It is weaker as the primary control. The API does not support an alert or notification route, its log-search and metric-query filtering parameters are not declared in discovery, and the polling stack shares the operational domain of the job it watches. There is no distributed trace query or span tree either; trace and span identifiers can correlate logs, but they do not create a liveness guarantee. Do not promote a telemetry query into a heartbeat contract merely because both can draw a green chart.

The specialist boundary has a valid rejection case too. If policy cannot approve that provider's region, retention, deletion, or subprocessors, do not send it customer data and do not assume an AI runtime supplies the missing contractual guarantee. Self-hosting a minimal heartbeat receiver may then be justified, provided its clock, storage, alert delivery, redundancy, and audit trail are operated as a separate control plane. That is a larger commitment than a periodic query.

The final acceptance test is plain: stop the scheduler before the process starts. The heartbeat system must alert without receiving any application event. Then force a failure after start; the execution telemetry must preserve a correlated error or missing-terminal record. Finally, replay the same run_id; downstream replies must not duplicate, and the audit view must show why. Three tests, three different guarantees.

References

  • Infrai API documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Cronitor documentation
  • Better Stack heartbeat documentation
  • Sentry cron monitoring documentation
  • NIST SP 800-66r2: Implementing the HIPAA Security Rule

If this split trust boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation for the execution-evidence contract, then complete a separate data-processing and alert-path review for the heartbeat provider.

title: Your XML Parser Opened a File Because the Document Asked It To
description:
The feature was an import.

Suppliers upload a product feed
as XML,
and the screen shows a preview.

Name.
Price.
Description.

A tester sent a feed
with four extra lines at the top.

The preview came back
and the description field
held the contents
of a configuration file
from the server's disk.

Nobody had written code
to read that file.

The parser did it,
because the document asked.

XML has a part
most of us never use on purpose.

The document type declaration.

It can define entities,
named pieces of text,
and an entity can be external,
which means its text lives
somewhere else.

At a file path.

At a URL.

So the feed declared an entity
pointing at a file on the server,
then used that entity
inside the description.

The parser did what the standard says.

It went and fetched the text
and put it in place.

Then your code
showed the description,
as it always does.

That is XXE,
an XML external entity attack.

It is old,
and it is still on the OWASP lists
because the defaults keep it alive.

In Java,
the standard DocumentBuilderFactory
resolves external entities
unless you tell it not to.

Use the same trick
with a URL inside the entity,
and your server
makes requests for the attacker,
from inside your network.

It is not only feeds.

An SVG is XML.

A Word document is a zip of XML.

A SAML response is XML.

Anywhere you parse a document
someone else wrote,
the document gets a say
in what your parser does.

So take the say away.

Turn off document type declarations
entirely,
the disallow doctype feature in Java,
which is what the OWASP cheat sheet
recommends first.

If you really need them,
turn off external entities
and external DTD loading,
one setting at a time,
and test each one.

Put the safe factory
in one helper,
and make it the only way
the codebase builds a parser.

Then write the test
with the four extra lines
and keep it forever.

The parser was not broken.

It was obedient.

To whoever wrote the file.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: How to Build Ultra-Fast WordPress Sites in 2026: The Essential Developer Stack
description:
Every web developer knows the struggle: a client wants a visually stunning website with sliders, custom forms, and dynamic animations, but they also demand a 95+ score on Google PageSpeed Insights.

WordPress can easily get bloated if you stack plugins blindly. However, with the right modern developer stack, you can achieve lightning-fast loading speeds, clean database queries, and modular designs.

Here is the 5-tool developer stack we use to build high-performance client sites in 2026:

1. The Lightweight Foundation: Astra Pro

A fast website starts with clean theme architecture. Unlike heavy legacy themes packed with thousands of unused stylesheets, a lightweight theme like Astra Pro loads in less than 0.5 seconds with vanilla JavaScript. It gives you deep styling controls, sticky headers, and mega menus without adding DOM bloat.

2. High-Speed Visual Building: Elementor Pro

While visual builders have a reputation for slowing down sites, Elementor Pro in recent updates has introduced optimized asset loading and container-based flexbox layouts. When configured properly with nested containers and font preloading, you can build custom client landing pages 3x faster without sacrificing performance.

3. Structured Data Architecture: Advanced Custom Fields (ACF Pro)

For developers building dynamic websites, directories, or SaaS blogs, relying solely on standard post types is inefficient. ACF Pro lets you model custom metadata, flexible content blocks, and relationship fields with minimal database queries.

4. Enterprise-Grade Caching: WP Rocket

Caching is non-negotiable for Core Web Vitals. A dedicated performance tool like WP Rocket automates:

  • Removing unused CSS (RUCSS)
  • Delaying non-essential JavaScript execution until user interaction
  • Native lazy loading for media assets
  • Preloading cache files and DNS queries

5. WooCommerce Conversion Stack

If you are developing eCommerce stores, default WooCommerce cart and checkout funnels often experience high drop-off rates. Implementing streamlined checkout extensions and Ajax-based add-to-cart plugins keeps page latency below 1 second.

title: New setup page after domain checkout
description:

Registration can take a few minutes. Each setup action unlocks as soon as the domain is ready. If registration fails, the page shows what went wrong and the status of your refund.

title: Share Vercel Container Registry repositories across teams
description:
Vercel Container Registry now lets you share a repository with other Vercel teams to grant read access to its images.

Sharing is read-only and covers the whole repository. Recipients can pull and use every image, but cannot push, delete, or re-share. You can also share a repository with your own team. Each repository can be shared with up to 100 teams.

Share from the project dashboard under Images → repository → Settings → Repository Sharing, or with the Vercel CLI:

# Share a repository with a team vercel vcr permissions my-repository add other-team # List teams with access vercel vcr permissions my-repository ls # Revoke a team's access vercel vcr permissions my-repository rm other-team # Remove all shared access vercel vcr permissions my-repository clear

Shared images can be used in Vercel Sandbox, accepting a team-scoped image reference in Sandbox.create() :

import { Sandbox } from '@vercel/sandbox'; const sandbox = await Sandbox.create({ image: 'other-team/their-project/shared-repository:latest', });

Repository sharing is available on all plans. Update the Vercel CLI to v58.3.0 or later with npm i -g vercel@latest to get started and see the Vercel Container Registry documentation to learn more.

title: CheckMate: An AI-Powered Chess Game Built with Java
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

I built CheckMate, a Java-based chess game that lets players enjoy chess against an AI opponent through a graphical user interface.

CheckMate is designed for chess enthusiasts, students, and beginners who want to practise chess, enjoy a single-player experience, and challenge themselves against a computer opponent.

The idea is to make chess accessible and enjoyable while providing a project that developers can explore, learn from, and extend.

For students and casual players, CheckMate can provide a convenient way to practise without needing another person to play with. In the future, features such as difficulty levels, game analysis, and move suggestions could make it even more useful.

Demo

GitHub Repository: CheckMate – Java Chess Game

Here is a preview of the project:

Code

Explore the source code on GitHub:

♟️ CheckMate – View Source Code

The project contains components for chessboard management, move handling, and gameplay. The repository is available for developers who want to study the implementation, learn from the code, or contribute improvements.

How I Built It

I developed CheckMate using Java, separating the chess gameplay logic from the graphical interface.

The main components include:

  • Java: The programming language used to build the application.
  • Graphical User Interface: Provides the interface through which players interact with the chessboard.
  • Chess Engine: Handles board representation, piece movements, and chess rules.
  • AI Opponent: Enables players to compete against the computer.
  • GitHub: Hosts the source code and provides a foundation for further development.

The AI opponent is a key part of the project because it makes single-player chess possible. The specific algorithm and decision-making process can be explained further by referencing the actual AI implementation in the source code.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation makes it easier for developers to learn from existing projects, share ideas, and build upon one another's work.

With CheckMate, other developers can explore the chess engine, experiment with AI strategies, improve the interface, and contribute new features. The project can also help students learn about Java, game development, algorithms, and AI-assisted gameplay.

An openly accessible codebase encourages collaboration and gives learners a practical example they can build upon instead of starting from scratch.

My goal is to continue improving CheckMate and make it a useful learning project for the chess and open-source communities.

title: DPIA for AI Systems: When and How to Run One
description:
Originally published at https://charz.ai/blog/dpia-for-ai-systems by Char-Z AI.

This article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed for factual accuracy. AI-origin labeling applies under Article 50 of the EU AI Act.

What a DPIA Is and Why AI Triggers It

A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is a structured assessment of how a processing operation affects individuals' privacy and data-protection rights. Under GDPR Article 35, a DPIA is required where processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms (European Commission, 2016).

AI systems trigger DPIAs more often than traditional processing because their characteristics — automated decision-making, profiling, processing special-category data at scale, and opaque decision logic — match the Article 35 high-risk indicators. If your AI system makes consequential decisions about people, uses their data in ways they cannot easily understand, or handles sensitive data at significant scale, a DPIA is likely required before you deploy it.

The EU AI Act extends this obligation for high-risk AI by requiring an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights as part of its documentation duties (European Commission, 2024). A well-run DPIA serves both.

When a DPIA Is Required (Indicators)

Run a DPIA when processing is likely high risk. Common AI triggers:

  • Systematic and extensive evaluation of individuals, including profiling, that produces decisions with legal or similarly significant effects

  • Large-scale processing of special-category (sensitive) data, such as health or biometric data

  • Large-scale, systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area (e.g., camera-based systems)

  • Innovative use or application of new technologies where the impact is not yet well understood

  • Combining, comparing, or matching data across datasets (which AI systems commonly do)

What a DPIA Must Cover

A complete DPIA describes:

  • The processing — a systematic description of the operations and purposes.

  • Necessity and proportionality — why the AI processing is necessary and proportionate to the purpose.

  • Risks to individuals — the impact on rights and freedoms of the processing.

  • Mitigations — measures to address the risks, including safeguards, security, and mechanisms to protect individual rights.

  • Consultation — where required, the views of data subjects or a supervisory authority.

Running One Efficiently for AI

Start with a screening.

Run a quick Article 35 threshold screening before a full DPIA. Many AI systems fail the "likely high risk" test and need only a lighter analysis. Screening avoids over-assessing low-risk tools.

Reuse the data-flow map.

A current data-flow map of the AI system (what data enters, where it goes, who sees it) supplies most of the DPIA's processing description (see our data-flow mapping guide).

Involve the right people.

Include the system owner, the data-protection function, and — for consequential AI decisions — a human-oversight design that the DPIA records.

Consult where required.

GDPR requires consulting the supervisory authority before processing where a DPIA indicates high risk that mitigations cannot reduce to an acceptable level (European Commission, 2016).

Keeping It Current

A DPIA is a snapshot. Re-run or update it when the AI system materially changes — a new data source, a changed purpose, expanded profiling, or a new vendor. Tying DPIA re-runs into your system's change triggers (the same ones that re-score your risk register) keeps them from going stale.

DPIA vs. Risk Register

They are complementary. The risk register tracks risks operationally over time; the DPIA is a focused, documented assessment required before high-risk processing begins. Run the DPIA at the right gate, then maintain the register. Both support the governance picture that frameworks like the NIST AI RMF describe (NIST, 2023).

Sources

European Commission. (2016). Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation. *Official Journal of the European Union*.
European Commission. (2024). Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council. *Official Journal of the European Union*. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689
NIST. (2023). *Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)*. National Institute of Standards and Technology. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1
