title: How to select multiple columns based on a condition in SQL?
description:
ERROR 1241 (21000): Operand should contain 1 column(s).

This error often appears when you try to make a SQL CASE expression return multiple columns at once. If you're asking "how to select multiple columns based on a condition in sql?", the first thing to understand is the difference between filtering rows and changing which column values appear in your results. Both are possible, but they require different SQL techniques.

Quick answer: To select multiple columns based on a condition, list the required columns in SELECT and filter matching rows using WHERE. If individual column values should change depending on a condition, use separate CASE expressions for each output column. If the actual number or names of returned columns must change, use separate queries or safely constructed dynamic SQL.

Here's how to implement each approach in MySQL without running into confusing syntax errors.

1. Create a sample table to understand conditional column selection

We'll use an employee table throughout this tutorial.

Imagine you're building an employee management dashboard. Your database stores employee names, departments, salaries, and employment status.

You want to answer questions such as:

  • Show the names and salaries of active sales employees.
  • Display different salary columns depending on the department.
  • Return salary totals for active and inactive employees.
  • Change the columns displayed when someone selects a different report.

Start by creating a temporary table.

Open MySQL Workbench, phpMyAdmin, or your preferred MySQL client and execute:

DROP TEMPORARY TABLE IF EXISTS demo_employees;

CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE demo_employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    department VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    annual_salary DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(12) NOT NULL
);

Now insert some sample records:

INSERT INTO demo_employees
    (employee_id, full_name, department, annual_salary, status)
VALUES
    (1, 'Ana', 'Sales', 54000.00, 'active'),
    (2, 'Ben', 'Support', 47000.00, 'active'),
    (3, 'Cara', 'Sales', 62000.00, 'inactive'),
    (4, 'Deepak', 'Engineering', 78000.00, 'active'),
    (5, 'Ema', 'Sales', 51000.00, 'active'),
    (6, 'Farah', 'Support', 50000.00, 'inactive');

Confirm that the records exist:

SELECT * FROM demo_employees
ORDER BY employee_id;

You should see six employees across three departments.

We're using a temporary table so the exercise doesn't modify an existing application table. Run all the SQL examples using the same database connection, because MySQL temporary tables disappear when their connection closes.

If you're testing through PHP and the connection fails before your query runs, check the mysqli_connect host parameter explained. Connection problems and SQL syntax problems need different fixes.

2. Select multiple columns using a WHERE condition

This is the simplest solution, and it's usually all you need.

Suppose your dashboard should show only active employees from the Sales department.

You need three output columns:

  • Employee ID
  • Employee name
  • Annual salary

The condition belongs in WHERE, not inside the column list.

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    annual_salary
FROM demo_employees
WHERE department = 'Sales'
  AND status = 'active'
ORDER BY employee_id;

Expected result:

employee_id full_name annual_salary
1 Ana 54000.00
5 Ema 51000.00

Notice what SQL does here.

SELECT decides which columns appear in the result.

WHERE decides which rows qualify.

These are independent parts of the query. You can return five columns while filtering by a sixth column, even if that sixth column isn't displayed.

For example:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    annual_salary
FROM demo_employees
WHERE status = 'active';

The query filters using status, but doesn't include status in the returned columns.

That's perfectly valid.

Select columns using multiple conditions

You can combine conditions with AND, OR, or IN.

For employees belonging to either Sales or Support:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    department
FROM demo_employees
WHERE department IN ('Sales', 'Support')
  AND status = 'active'
ORDER BY employee_id;

Expected employee IDs: 1, 2, and 5.

You could write the same department condition using OR, but IN is easier to read when you're checking one column against several values.

One mistake I frequently recommend checking for is missing parentheses when mixing AND and OR.

This query may return unexpected results:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    department,
    status
FROM demo_employees
WHERE department = 'Sales'
   OR department = 'Support'
  AND status = 'active';

SQL evaluates AND before OR.

So inactive Sales employees can still appear.

If you want active employees from either department, write:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    department,
    status
FROM demo_employees
WHERE (department = 'Sales'
       OR department = 'Support')
  AND status = 'active';

Better still, use the earlier IN example.

3. How to select multiple columns based on a condition in SQL?

Sometimes filtering rows isn't the real requirement.

You want to return every employee, but show different values depending on their department.

For example:

  • Sales employees should have their salary in sales_salary.
  • Support employees should have their salary in support_salary.
  • Everyone else should have NULL in those columns.

This is where CASE becomes useful.

Use a separate CASE expression for each column 

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,

    CASE
        WHEN department = 'Sales'
        THEN annual_salary
        ELSE NULL
    END AS sales_salary,

    CASE
        WHEN department = 'Support'
        THEN annual_salary
        ELSE NULL
    END AS support_salary

FROM demo_employees
ORDER BY employee_id;

Expected result:

employee_id full_name sales_salary support_salary
1 Ana 54000.00 NULL
2 Ben NULL 47000.00
3 Cara 62000.00 NULL
4 Deepak NULL NULL
5 Ema 51000.00 NULL
6 Farah NULL 50000.00

All six employees appear because there's no WHERE condition.

However, each calculated column displays a salary only when its condition matches.

There's an important detail here: Cara and Farah are inactive, but their salaries still appear because these conditions only check the department.

If inactive employees shouldn't have a salary displayed, extend each condition.

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,

    CASE
        WHEN department = 'Sales'
         AND status = 'active'
        THEN annual_salary
        ELSE NULL
    END AS sales_salary,

    CASE
        WHEN department = 'Support'
         AND status = 'active'
        THEN annual_salary
        ELSE NULL
    END AS support_salary

FROM demo_employees
ORDER BY employee_id;

Now inactive employees receive NULL in both salary columns.

Keep in mind that conditional display isn't a security control. Database permissions and application authorization must still protect sensitive salary data.

Why one CASE cannot return two columns

Here's a common incorrect attempt:

SELECT
    employee_id,

    CASE
        WHEN department = 'Sales'
        THEN (full_name, annual_salary)
        ELSE (department, status)
    END AS details

FROM demo_employees;

This produces an error similar to:

ERROR 1241 (21000): Operand should contain 1 column(s)

The problem isn't the condition.

It's the attempt to return two values from a single CASE expression.

A CASE expression produces one result value. It doesn't expand into multiple output columns.

The correct approach is to use separate expressions:

SELECT
    employee_id,

    CASE
        WHEN department = 'Sales'
        THEN full_name
        ELSE department
    END AS display_label,

    CASE
        WHEN department = 'Sales'
        THEN annual_salary
        ELSE NULL
    END AS display_salary

FROM demo_employees;

Each CASE produces one column.

You can also use MySQL's IF() function for simpler conditions:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    IF(
        department = 'Sales',
        annual_salary,
        NULL
    ) AS sales_salary
FROM demo_employees;

IF() works for a basic true-or-false decision.

I prefer CASE when several conditions are involved because it's easier to extend and is also standard SQL.

The MySQL documentation for CASE expressions explains the supported syntax.

4. Select multiple columns with different WHERE conditions

Another situation is filtering rows based on different combinations of column values.

Suppose the business rule is:

Return active Sales employees, plus Support employees whose annual salary is at least 50000.

The query is:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    department,
    annual_salary,
    status
FROM demo_employees
WHERE
    (department = 'Sales'
     AND status = 'active')

    OR

    (department = 'Support'
     AND annual_salary >= 50000)

ORDER BY employee_id;

Expected matching employees:

employee_id full_name department
1 Ana Sales
5 Ema Sales
6 Farah Support

Farah appears even though her status is inactive.

Why?

Because the Support condition checks the salary, not the employment status.

This is intentional for the example, but it's exactly the kind of mistake that can cause incorrect reports in a real application.

If both groups must be active, apply the active condition to the entire expression:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    department,
    annual_salary
FROM demo_employees
WHERE status = 'active'
  AND (
        department = 'Sales'
        OR (
            department = 'Support'
            AND annual_salary >= 50000
        )
      )
ORDER BY employee_id;

Now Farah is excluded.

Don't confuse WHERE with CASE

The distinction is simple.

Use WHERE when a condition should remove entire rows.

Use CASE when a condition should change a value in the returned row.

You can combine both:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,

    CASE
        WHEN annual_salary >= 60000
        THEN 'High salary'
        ELSE 'Standard salary'
    END AS salary_category

FROM demo_employees
WHERE status = 'active'
ORDER BY employee_id;

Only active employees appear, and each employee receives a calculated salary category.

This pattern is useful for administrative dashboards and filtered reports.

5. Select conditional totals across multiple columns

Sometimes you don't need individual employee records.

You want a report containing several calculated columns based on conditions.

For example, show each department with:

  • Total number of employees.
  • Number of active employees.
  • Number of inactive employees.
  • Combined salary of active employees.

You can build this using conditional aggregation.

SELECT
    department,

    COUNT(*) AS total_employees,

    SUM(
        CASE
            WHEN status = 'active'
            THEN 1
            ELSE 0
        END
    ) AS active_employees,

    SUM(
        CASE
            WHEN status = 'inactive'
            THEN 1
            ELSE 0
        END
    ) AS inactive_employees,

    SUM(
        CASE
            WHEN status = 'active'
            THEN annual_salary
            ELSE 0
        END
    ) AS active_salary_total

FROM demo_employees
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department;

Expected result:

department total_employees active_employees inactive_employees active_salary_total
Engineering 1 1 0 78000.00
Sales 3 2 1 105000.00
Support 2 1 1 47000.00

Here's how this works.

GROUP BY department creates one result row for each department.

COUNT(*) counts all employees in that department.

Each SUM(CASE ...) evaluates a condition for individual rows and adds the matching values.

For the active employee count:

SUM(
    CASE
        WHEN status = 'active'
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
    END
)

A matching employee contributes 1.

A non-matching employee contributes 0.

For the salary total, the same approach adds salary amounts instead.

Why WHERE can break conditional totals

Don't add:

WHERE status = 'active'

to the aggregation query if you still need inactive employee counts.

That condition removes inactive rows before the grouping and aggregation happen.

Your inactive count would always be zero.

Keep both types of records available and let the individual CASE expressions handle the conditions.

There's another small detail.

Using ELSE 0 makes the total zero when a department has no matching employees. Without ELSE, the expression returns NULL for non-matching records, and SUM() may return NULL if every input is NULL.

That difference matters when your result feeds a chart or financial report.

6. Select different column names dynamically in MySQL

What if your requirement is more specific?

You want the SQL query itself to return different columns depending on a selected report.

For example:

Directory report:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    department
FROM demo_employees;

Payroll report:

SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    annual_salary
FROM demo_employees;

These queries have different output structures.

A normal CASE expression cannot switch the entire SELECT column list.

You need separate SQL statements or dynamic SQL.

Build a safe dynamic SELECT statement

MySQL supports prepared statements using PREPARE and EXECUTE.

For this example, we'll allow only predefined column lists.

SET @view = 'payroll';

SET @columns = CASE
    WHEN @view = 'payroll'
        THEN 'employee_id, full_name, annual_salary'

    WHEN @view = 'directory'
        THEN 'employee_id, full_name, department'

    ELSE 'employee_id, full_name'
END;

SET @sql = CONCAT(
    'SELECT ',
    @columns,
    ' FROM demo_employees',
    ' WHERE status = ?',
    ' ORDER BY employee_id'
);

SET @status = 'active';

PREPARE employee_stmt FROM @sql;

EXECUTE employee_stmt USING @status;

DEALLOCATE PREPARE employee_stmt;

With @view = 'payroll', the result contains employee IDs, names, and salaries.

Change the variable to:

SET @view = 'directory';

Then rerun the remaining statements.

You'll receive employee IDs, names, and departments instead.

This works because the complete SQL statement is built before MySQL prepares it.

The column list is selected from fixed, trusted alternatives.

Never concatenate an unchecked user-supplied column name directly into SQL.

Prepared statement placeholders such as ? work for values, not SQL identifiers or entire column lists.

If users can choose columns, map their choices to a list of permitted identifiers first.

For most applications, I would keep a small set of predefined queries rather than construct complicated SQL strings. It's easier to review and much harder to misuse.

7. Apply conditional column selection in Laravel

If you're using Laravel, the Query Builder makes ordinary column selection straightforward.

Suppose your actual database contains a permanent employees table with the columns used in our example.

To get active Sales employees:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

$employees = DB::table('employees')
    ->select(
        'employee_id',
        'full_name',
        'annual_salary'
    )
    ->where('department', 'Sales')
    ->where('status', 'active')
    ->orderBy('employee_id')
    ->get();

This is the Laravel equivalent of our second step.

Choose different columns for different reports

You can select the column list in PHP before building the query.

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

$reportType = 'payroll';

$allowedColumns = [
    'directory' => [
        'employee_id',
        'full_name',
        'department',
    ],
    'payroll' => [
        'employee_id',
        'full_name',
        'annual_salary',
    ],
];

$columns = $allowedColumns[$reportType]
    ?? $allowedColumns['directory'];

$employees = DB::table('employees')
    ->select($columns)
    ->where('status', 'active')
    ->orderBy('employee_id')
    ->get();

The important part is the $allowedColumns mapping.

Your application chooses a known column list rather than accepting arbitrary SQL identifiers from a request.

For calculated columns, Laravel can also use raw SQL expressions with bound values.

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

$department = 'Sales';

$employees = DB::table('employees')
    ->select('employee_id', 'full_name')
    ->selectRaw(
        'CASE
            WHEN department = ?
            THEN annual_salary
            ELSE NULL
         END AS selected_salary',
        [$department]
    )
    ->orderBy('employee_id')
    ->get();

Here, Laravel binds the department value safely.

Don't interpolate untrusted values directly into selectRaw().

And remember that the earlier demo_employees table was temporary. The Laravel examples assume you've created a normal application table with the corresponding fields.

What if the columns come from different tables?

That's a different problem.

Suppose names are stored in employees, but salaries are stored in employee_salaries.

You'll need a JOIN to combine those records.

For a related example, see how to JOIN a second table in CodeIgniter Query Builder.

The principle is the same in Laravel or plain MySQL: a join combines related tables, while WHERE and CASE handle the conditions.

Verify the results before using the query in production

Before adding your final SQL to a controller or report, check the row counts and the actual result values.

Start with:

SELECT
    department,
    status,
    COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM demo_employees
GROUP BY department, status
ORDER BY department, status;

This tells you how many records exist for each department and status combination.

Now test the basic filter:

SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS matching_employees
FROM demo_employees
WHERE department = 'Sales'
  AND status = 'active';

Expected result:

matching_employees
------------------
2

Next, check a conditional calculation:

SELECT
    SUM(
        CASE
            WHEN department = 'Sales'
             AND status = 'active'
            THEN 1
            ELSE 0
        END
    ) AS active_sales_count
FROM demo_employees;

Expected result:

active_sales_count
------------------
2

Both methods should agree.

If they don't, inspect the conditions rather than immediately changing the SQL structure.

I'd also check these issues before blaming CASE:

  • NULL comparisons: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, not = NULL.
  • Unexpected duplicate rows: Look for joins that match multiple records.
  • Incorrect data types: Confirm that the values being compared use compatible types.
  • Missing columns: Run SHOW COLUMNS FROM demo_employees; to inspect the table.
  • Incorrect column aliases: An alias defined in SELECT generally cannot be referenced directly in the same query's WHERE clause.

If a query runs but returns zero records, temporarily remove the WHERE clause and add conditions back one at a time.

That's usually more useful than rewriting the whole query.

If the query is slow on a large production table, use:

EXPLAIN
SELECT
    employee_id,
    full_name,
    annual_salary
FROM demo_employees
WHERE department = 'Sales'
  AND status = 'active';

EXPLAIN shows how MySQL plans to read the table.

For a real, persistent table, check whether indexes support your frequently used filters. Don't automatically add an index for every column, because indexes also cost storage and make writes more expensive.

For a second set of eyes on a production query, you can also check HeadsNTail services.

FAQ

Can I select multiple columns using one CASE statement in SQL?

Not using a single CASE expression in a normal SELECT list. Each CASE expression produces one result value, so you'll need a separate expression for every conditional output column. If you want to change the actual set of output columns, use separate queries or dynamic SQL.

How do I select multiple columns with multiple WHERE conditions?

List the columns after SELECT, then combine your filters using AND, OR, or IN. Use parentheses to make the intended logic clear when mixing AND and OR. Remember that WHERE filters rows, not individual column values.

What's the difference between CASE and IF in MySQL?

Both allow conditional values to be returned in a query. IF() takes a condition and two possible results, while CASE can express multiple conditions more clearly. CASE is standard SQL, making it a better choice when portability matters.

Can SQL dynamically select column names based on user input?

Yes, but the column list must be decided before the SQL statement is prepared and executed. You can choose between predefined queries in your application or construct a statement using validated identifiers. Parameter placeholders cannot replace column names.

Can I use WHERE and CASE together in the same SELECT query?

Yes. WHERE removes rows that don't match your filter, while CASE calculates conditional values for rows that remain. Using both is common in reporting queries where you need to filter employees and calculate different output values based on their departments or statuses.

Next, apply these patterns to a small copy of your real data. Once you understand the difference between filtering rows, calculating conditional values, and switching column lists, the question "how to select multiple columns based on a condition in sql?" becomes much easier to solve.

Originally published at headsntail.com.

title: crates.io download count: 80% of ours arrived with a new version
description:
Originally published at tensorust.com.

TL;DR: On October 17, 2026 I pulled every daily download number crates.io has for my 69 Rust crates. Over 89 days they logged 3,676 downloads, and 80.1% of them landed on the day a new version went up or the day after. A new version collects about 13 downloads in its first 24 hours no matter what is in it, then flatlines. Outside crates that depend on any of the 69: zero. The number that actually tells you whether people use your crate is the quiet-day baseline, and for us it was 339 downloads, about 3.8 a day.

Short answer for the search. The crates.io download count is the number of times the crate's .crate file was fetched from the crates.io CDN, counted from the CDN's request logs (crates.io moved to log-based counting in March 2024). Since October 29, 2025 only requests that look like they came from cargo (or send no user agent at all) are counted. It is not a count of users, installs or projects. One developer's CI that runs cargo build on a clean machine 30 times a day adds 30 downloads a day; one person who installs your crate once and keeps it in their local cache adds one, ever.

So what is actually inside a small crate's number? Below is a fresh measurement on a real portfolio, the script that pulls it (copy it and run it on your own crates), and how to read your own chart without lying to yourself in either direction.


Every daily download for all 69 crates, colored by kind of day. crates.io API, pulled Oct 17 2026, 7:10 AM ET. Bar height is square-root scaled so quiet days stay visible.

Where the 69 crates came from

Some context, because the shape of the data comes straight from how these crates were published. I maintain a pile of Rust libraries and tools: fin-primitives (trading building blocks), tokio-prompt-orchestrator (an LLM proxy with dedup and a circuit breaker), proof-engine (an OpenGL game engine), and CoreScout, an MCP server split into a workspace of 33 crates.

They went out in three bursts: 51 versions in March 2026, 116 in September and 68 in October, 235 versions in total. The October burst was one big release run on October 4, after a pass where AI coding agents upgraded every crate and I published everything at the end in one go. That single day matters a lot later.

All-time total when I pulled it at 7:10 AM ET on October 17: 4,815 downloads. The crates.io "recent downloads" figure (last 90 days) was 3,677. My goal for these crates is 100,000, so the honest question is how much of the 4,815 is people.

Pull the numbers yourself in 40 lines

crates.io has a public JSON API. It isn't formally versioned, but it's what the website itself calls, and the data access policy asks for two things: at most one request per second, and a User-Agent that says who you are. Three endpoints give you everything:

  • /api/v1/crates?user_id=N: every crate a user owns, with all-time and 90-day totals.
  • /api/v1/crates/<name>/downloads: daily downloads for the last 90 days, split by version (older versions are lumped into extra_downloads).
  • /api/v1/crates/<name>/reverse_dependencies: which published crates depend on this one.

This is the script I ran this morning (pull.py, trimmed only of the JSON field picking). It stops dead on a 429 instead of retrying, because a polite scraper doesn't argue with a rate limit:

UA = "tensorust-deepdive-research (contact: hello@tensorust.com)"
last = [0.0]

def get(path):
    wait = 1.05 - (time.time() - last[0])   # stay under 1 request/second
    if wait > 0:
        time.sleep(wait)
    last[0] = time.time()
    req = urllib.request.Request("https://crates.io" + path, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as r:
            return json.load(r)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        if e.code == 429:
            print("429 - stopping"); sys.exit(2)
        raise

user = get("/api/v1/users/mattbusel")["user"]
crates = get(f"/api/v1/crates?user_id={user['id']}&per_page=100")["crates"]
for c in crates:
    n = c["name"]
    dl = get(f"/api/v1/crates/{n}/downloads")
    vers = get(f"/api/v1/crates/{n}/versions?per_page=100")
    rev = get(f"/api/v1/crates/{n}/reverse_dependencies?per_page=100")
    # ... store dl["version_downloads"], dl["meta"]["extra_downloads"], versions, rev

69 crates times three calls, one per second, took about three and a half minutes. Then a second pass of 69 calls to map version ids to version numbers and publish times, because the downloads endpoint labels each row with a numeric version id, not "2.15.0".


Real output from pull.py and the analysis scripts, Oct 17 2026, 7:10 to 7:16 AM ET.

If you have more than a few hundred crates (or you want every crate on the registry), don't hammer the API: crates.io publishes a database dump every 24 hours (static.crates.io/db-dump.tar.gz) that includes the per-day, per-version download table for the last 90 days.

What the crates.io page shows you

Here's the bottom of the fin-primitives page, which is my most-downloaded crate. Look at the chart before reading the numbers: a low wiggle of 0 to 3 a day through the summer, then tall spikes in the last week of September and the first week of October, each spike a different color. Each color is a version.


The real crates.io page for fin-primitives, captured Oct 17 2026. Each colored spike is a new version.

That chart is honest, but it's per crate. With 69 crates you can't eyeball 69 charts, so I classified every crate-day in the 90-day window into three buckets.

The three kinds of download day

The rule is simple and fully mechanical:

  1. Publish window: that crate published a version on this UTC day or the day before.
  2. Sweep day: no publish, but at least half of all my crates that existed got downloaded on the same day.
  3. Quiet: everything else.

The core of the classifier, from analyze.py:

for n, c in C.items():
    for v in c['downloads']['version_downloads'] + c['downloads']['meta']['extra_downloads']:
        d = dt.date.fromisoformat(v['date'])
        if any(0 <= (d - p).days <= 1 for p in pub[n]):
            cat[v['date']][0] += v['downloads']      # publish window
        elif v['date'] in sweeps:
            cat[v['date']][1] += v['downloads']      # sweep day
        else:
            cat[v['date']][2] += v['downloads']      # quiet

And the result over July 20 to October 16, 2026 (89 full UTC days, 3,676 downloads):


All 69 crates, Jul 20 to Oct 16 2026 (UTC days), classified by the script in this article.

2,945 downloads (80.1%) came in a publish window. 392 (10.7%) came on six sweep days. 339 (9.2%) were quiet-day downloads. The biggest single day was October 4, the release run: 68 versions published, 1,195 downloads.

Put another way: if I had never published those September and October versions, the 90-day number would have been somewhere around 730, not 3,676.

A new version gets about 13 downloads, then nothing

To see what a publish is worth on its own, I took every version published inside the window with at least a week of data after it (181 versions) and lined up its downloads by days since publish.


181 versions published Jul 20 to Oct 9 2026, each with at least a week of data. 86.9% of first-week downloads land on day 0 or 1.

Mean downloads on day 0: 13.45 (median 10). Day 1: 1.21. Day 2: 0.02. 86.9% of a version's first-week downloads arrive on day 0 or day 1. The smallest day-0-plus-day-1 total for any version was 8, the largest 66, the median 12.

The floor is the tell. Across all 235 versions ever published, the lowest all-time count for a single version is 9. The median is 18. I have 19 crates that have only ever had one version, including internal plumbing crates like corescout-cli and corescout-lineage that nobody outside this project has a reason to know about. Their all-time totals run from 10 to 28, median 15. Something fetches every new version within hours of publish, whether or not a human ever reads the README.

What is that something? The data can't say. My guess, and it's a guess: registry mirrors and build farms that follow the crates.io index and fetch new versions as they appear, plus security and license scanners. The 2025 user-agent filter was written to drop mirrors, so whatever survives it is either cargo itself or a client that sends no user agent. docs.rs also builds documentation for every new version automatically; I couldn't confirm from public docs whether its fetch is counted, so I'm not claiming it is.

The consequence is very practical: on crates.io, the number of versions you publish predicts your downloads better than anything about the code. Across my 69 crates, the correlation between version count and all-time downloads is 0.82. That's why fin-primitives (13 versions) leads and my genuinely more interesting crates trail it.

Sweep days: when every crate gets hit at once

The second bucket surprised me more. On October 9 nothing was published, yet all 69 crates got downloaded on the same day, 184 downloads in total. October 13: 56 of 69 crates, mostly one download each. That's not a person. A person installs one tool and its dependency tree, not a stats crate, a trading crate, a game engine and a TFT advisor in the same afternoon.


Sweep days in the crates.io data, one square per crate that existed that day. Nothing was published on any of them.

Six days in the window match the pattern: August 3 (17 of 17 crates that existed then), September 29, October 5, 9, 13 and 15. Some of the later ones lean toward the CoreScout family: on October 6 and 15 the top crates were corescout-core, corescout-mirror and corescout-memory, which is exactly what you'd see if something resolved the dependency tree of a CoreScout binary. That brings up the multiplier nobody mentions.

Workspaces multiply the count

CoreScout is a Cargo workspace, and when you publish a workspace to crates.io, every member becomes its own crate. Here's the real root Cargo.toml (excerpt):

corescout-core = { version = "1.2.0", path = "crates/core" }
corescout-mirror = { version = "1.2.0", path = "crates/mirror" }
corescout-substrate = { version = "1.2.0", path = "crates/substrate" }
corescout-memory = { version = "1.2.0", path = "crates/memory" }
corescout-represent = { version = "1.2.0", path = "crates/represent" }
corescout-science = { version = "1.2.0", path = "crates/science" }

corescout-core has 25 dependents, all of them its own siblings. By the reverse-dependency data, corescout-mcp has 16 of my other crates somewhere in its dependency tree, so one cargo install corescout-mcp on a clean machine should show up as up to 17 downloads spread over 17 crate pages. Across all 69 crates, the reverse-dependency API lists 178 dependent versions, and every one of them is mine.

That's the cruel bit. The crates with the most dependents look the most "used" (11 crates with five or more dependents had a median of 6 quiet downloads; the 25 crates with no dependents had a median of zero in 89 days) and it's entirely my own wiring.

The quiet baseline: the only number that means people

Strip the publish windows and the sweeps and you're left with 339 downloads in 89 days, about 3.8 a day across all 69 crates. That's the closest thing to "someone, somewhere, built with my code today." It isn't zero, and it's been rising: the portfolio averaged 1.7 quiet downloads a day in late July, 3.4 in August, 2.8 in September and 8.1 in the first half of October (with far more crates, so treat October with care).

One crate does most of the work. fin-primitives alone is 128 of the 339 quiet downloads (38%), one or two on most days since July, long before this autumn's release pile. My bet is that a handful of people or one CI pipeline builds against it regularly. That's a real signal, and it's exactly what a "publish-day bots" dismissal would throw away along with the noise.

And the number that settles every argument: external reverse dependencies, 0. No published crate outside my own uses any of the 69. The ecosyste.ms crates.io index is a good second source for this, since it also tracks repositories that depend on a crate without publishing one.

Do this with your own crates

  • Read your number as three numbers. Publish-window, sweep and quiet. Run the classifier above (or just look at the per-version colors on your crate page); only the quiet line is about users.
  • Expect about 10 to 15 downloads per version for free. If a brand-new crate shows 12 downloads on day one, nobody has found it yet, and that's fine. If it shows 12 on a random Tuesday three weeks later, somebody probably has.
  • Don't release to pump the count. It works (we just measured it working), which is exactly why the count can't be trusted as a popularity number, and why anyone evaluating your crate will look at dependents and recent activity instead.
  • Count dependents, not downloads. crates.io's Dependents tab, the reverse-dependency API and GitHub's "Used by" are where real adoption shows. One crate in someone else's dependency tree is worth more than a thousand publish-day fetches, because every one of their CI runs downloads yours too, forever.
  • Know that a workspace inflates by its width. Splitting one tool into 30 crates makes every install look like 30 downloads. Report the binary crate's number if you want an honest headline.
  • Re-pull on a schedule. The API only keeps 90 days of daily data per crate. If you want a trend, save the JSON every month; once a day falls out of the window, the per-day split is gone for good.

The numbers, all of them

Measure (crates.io API, pulled Oct 17 2026, 7:10 AM ET) Value
Crates / versions 69 / 235
All-time downloads 4,815
Downloads Jul 20 to Oct 16 (89 days) 3,676
In a publish window 2,945 (80.1%)
On sweep days 392 (10.7%)
Quiet 339 (9.2%), 3.8/day
Downloads per new version, day 0 (mean / median) 13.45 / 10
Share of first-week downloads on day 0 or 1 86.9%
Lowest all-time count of any version 9
Correlation, versions vs downloads 0.82
External reverse dependencies 0

For the record, this isn't a "downloads are fake" post. The counting rules are public and reasonable, and the quiet baseline is real and growing. It's a "know which part of the number you're looking at" post. The next milestone I care about isn't 10,000 downloads, it's the first crate with an outside dependent. I'll pull this again in 30 days and publish the diff.

If you maintain crates: what does your quiet-day baseline look like next to your total? I'd genuinely like to know whether 80% publish-window is normal for small crates or whether my release habits made it worse.

More from the same projects: the semantic cache inside tokio-prompt-orchestrator, running 20 coding agents on one PC (the agents that upgraded these crates), and Bevy instancing at 639,000 units.

Publishing is not distribution. The agent team that pulled this data also runs distribution for products: see the offer.

title: My webhook catcher needed a way to say "I got it" differently — and learned idempotency is a sender's problem
description:
I built a webhook catcher for integration testing: throw a POST at an ephemeral URL, read the events back later. Simple. Then I pointed a real payment provider's test mode at it and watched my event log fill up with 14 identical "payment succeeded" events for one click.

The catcher was doing its job — storing everything that arrived. The problem was upstream: the sender's retry policy. My first instinct was to dedupe on my side. That's the wrong lesson. You can't dedupe reliably at the receiver because you don't know the sender's idempotency key convention, and two genuinely different events can look identical (same payload, same second, same source IP during a re-deploy).

What I actually changed: my catcher now exposes each event with a stable id, the raw headers, and the arrival timestamp — and I stop trying to be smart about "the same" event. If I'm testing a retry storm, I want to see the storm. If I'm testing a single delivery, I assert on event count and let the sender's idempotency header be the contract, not my storage.

The config gotcha that bit me: my catcher answered 200 to every retry, including malformed payloads. A sender that treats 200 as "done, never retry" will silently swallow its own bugs. Now it returns 4xx for payloads it can't parse, and the retry behavior I'm testing is the sender's, not mine.

Any agent wiring up Stripe/GitHub/internal hooks can use this directly — create a hook, get a URL that lives 24h, read events back with headers intact. It's at https://x402.freeq.one/tools/webhook_catch.html

The honest takeaway: a webhook receiver's job is to be a faithful witness, not a filter. The moment you start deciding what "counts" as an event, you've built a second system that lies differently than the first.

title: Building Medirescue-AI: Revolutionizing Emergency Healthcare with FalkorDB Knowledge Graphs
description:
Building Medirescue-AI: Revolutionizing Emergency Healthcare with FalkorDB Knowledge Graphs

When a medical emergency strikes, every single second matters. Yet, one of the biggest bottlenecks in emergency response isn't the speed of the vehicle—it's the friction in data coordination. Ambulances, dispatchers, and hospitals often operate in silos, making it difficult to instantly match a patient's specific emergency needs with the right facility.
To solve this critical problem, I built Medirescue-AI: An Intelligent Emergency Hospital & Ambulance Tracking System.

The Problem: The Chaos of Emergency Coordination

During critical healthcare events, emergency responders face a fragmented data ecosystem. Finding the optimal hospital requires cross-referencing multiple variables simultaneously:
• Patient symptoms and immediate medical needs.
• Real-time location and traffic constraints.
• Hospital capacities, specializations, and available emergency resources.
Traditional relational databases struggle to handle these highly interconnected, rapidly changing data networks efficiently. To map out a dynamic network of patients, ambulances, symptoms, and medical facilities, we need a system designed from the ground up to understand relationships.

The Solution: Enter Medirescue-AI

Medirescue-AI is an AI-powered emergency healthcare platform that seamlessly bridges the gap between ambulances, hospitals, and emergency medical facilities.
At its core, the platform dynamically identifies the most appropriate medical facilities for a patient based on their exact medical needs and the current operational status of surrounding facilities. By visualizing the physical and logical connections between emergency resources, Medirescue-AI aims to dramatically minimize the time spent searching for appropriate care, ultimately saving lives.

The Tech Stack: Solving Complex Problems with FalkorDB

To map and traverse these complex, multi-layered connections in real-time, FalkorDB was implemented as our primary graph database.
Because FalkorDB is built for low latency and high-throughput relationship queries, it provided the split-second performance necessary for real-time emergency routing. Here is how we used FalkorDB to solve our core technical challenges:
• Medical Entity Mapping: We structured complex medical relationships within the graph, linking specific patient symptoms directly to potential conditions and required medical specializations.
• Dynamic Proximity Routing: We mapped real-time patient and ambulance locations directly to the nearest, most optimal emergency response units, helping prevent hospital overcrowding and reducing transit times.
• Structured First-Aid Knowledge Graphs: The database manages an interconnected knowledge base of first-aid procedures. This allows the system to surface instant care instructions based on the mapped symptoms while the ambulance is en route.

Key Learnings & Future Outlook

Building Medirescue-AI highlighted the immense power of graph databases in solving real-world, high-stakes problems. Moving away from standard tabular structures allowed us to query deep relationships—like “Find a hospital within 5 miles that has an open ICU bed AND an available neurologist right now”—in milliseconds.
In the future, I plan to integrate deeper predictive AI models directly with the FalkorDB knowledge graph to anticipate emergency resource shortages before they even happen

title: PostgreSQL 19 Slips to November as AI Code Review Finds Bugs Faster Than Humans Can Fix Them
description:
PostgreSQL 19 Slips to November as AI Code Review Finds Bugs Faster Than Humans Can Fix Them

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed PostgreSQL 19, pushing general availability from the original late-September/early-October target to around November 19, 2026 — and the culprit, remarkably, is not sloppy engineering. It is the opposite: AI-assisted code review has become so effective that it is finding problems faster than the volunteer-driven project can fix them.

According to a detailed account from leading PostgreSQL committer Peter Eisentraut, VP at support and consultancy firm EDB, the release team has reverted somewhere between eight and ten significant features from PostgreSQL 19, deferring them to PostgreSQL 20. While some of those reverts stem from genuine architectural defects that could not be patched "quickly and during beta," Eisentraut attributes a substantial share of the disruption to something new: LLM-assisted code review raising the project's effective quality standards mid-cycle, on patches that were written before the tooling became powerful enough to catch their flaws.

A list of forty defect reports nobody had time for

The mechanics of the delay are almost mundane. During the extended beta window, LLM-assisted review surfaced roughly forty defect reports — a long tail of "relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases" that in previous release cycles would likely have trickled out as post-release bug fixes over the following five years. As Eisentraut put it: "With LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you're staring at a list of forty defect reports."

Every one of those reports still needs a human committer to read it, confirm it is real, write a fix, test it, and get it reviewed under PostgreSQL's commit policies. "Even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time," Eisentraut explained. Forty tickets at even modest triage cost per item adds up to days or weeks of committer attention that a project operating on an annual release clock simply did not have before the planned freeze.

The result is an unusual situation for one of the world's most widely deployed open source databases: a release that is late not because the tooling failed, but because it worked.

SQL/PGQ and the biggest casualties

The highest-profile feature pulled from PostgreSQL 19 is support for SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), the SQL-standard syntax added in 2023 for querying graph-style relationships between nodes and edges over relational data. Its implementation was removed over unresolved issues, after veteran contributor Tom Lane warned: "At this point I'd be willing to bet dinner that if we ship it in v19 there will be post-release bug discoveries that are unfixable until v20."

Eisentraut was careful to head off the obvious hot take. The reverts, he stressed, are not the result of "vibe coding" — AI-generated patches — because those techniques were not available when most of the affected features were originally written. The affected code predates the current wave of AI review tooling; what changed is the scrutiny applied to it after the fact.

What still ships

Despite the cuts, PostgreSQL 19 is still expected to be what Eisentraut calls "a great release." The headline survivor is REPACK CONCURRENTLY, which reclaims disk space without the heavy table locking that VACUUM FULL requires — a long-requested win for large production deployments. The project shipped Release Candidate 1 on October 15, with a second release candidate scheduled for November 12 ahead of the November 19 GA date.

There is a knock-on effect for PostgreSQL 20, too. Just a few months ago, developers expected PG 20 to be a quiet, bug-fix-oriented release. Now it is likely to absorb the reverted features from PG 19, making it unusually feature-rich.

Why this matters beyond Postgres

The PostgreSQL episode is worth watching even if you never run the database, because it is a preview of a problem every serious software project is about to face. AI reviewers do not just accelerate finding bugs — they accelerate the accumulation of work. When a tool can surface in an afternoon the edge cases that would previously have taken five years of production incidents to discover, the bottleneck shifts decisively from detection to remediation.

For enterprises, the practical guidance is straightforward. Teams that budgeted Q4 2026 migration windows around the original October target now have a tighter runway into the November-December change freeze. Managed PostgreSQL providers will push their rollout timelines back accordingly. And those waiting specifically for SQL/PGQ graph queries will need to wait for PostgreSQL 20.

There is also a security dimension to this trend. PostgreSQL historically averaged a couple of CVEs per release cycle; the August 2026 patch release for PostgreSQL 18 shipped fixes for 28. The same AI-assisted tooling that is disrupting release schedules is also dramatically expanding the number of known vulnerabilities being found and fixed — a net positive, even if it makes release calendars messier.

The irony is hard to miss: PostgreSQL 19 will ship later than planned, but precisely because of that, it will likely arrive as a cleaner, better-audited baseline than the version that would have gone out on the original schedule. In an industry still arguing about whether AI makes software better or worse, Postgres just offered a data point on the uncomfortable middle: AI makes software better, but slower — at least until the humans catch up.

title: Building a Real-Time Quant Trading Terminal in the Browser (Without React Frame Drops)
description:
The Problem with High-Frequency Data in React
If you have ever hooked a raw WebSocket stream into standard React state (useState and useEffect), you already know the nightmare.

When you are streaming financial market data — like Binance Level-2 order book depth ladders or sub-millisecond trade tickers — market updates can easily hit 200 to 500 events per second.

If every incoming message triggers a React state update, the browser's main thread chokes immediately:

Frames drop from 60 FPS down to a choppy 14 FPS.
Memory usage spikes aggressively due to continuous garbage collection.
User interactions, like clicking tabs, zooming charts, or dragging panels, become painfully sluggish.
Professional proprietary trading firms solve this with hardware-accelerated desktop apps or expensive $24,000/year Bloomberg Terminals.

I wanted to challenge that assumption: Can we engineer an institutional-grade quantitative trading workstation that runs 100% inside a web browser with silky smooth 60 FPS performance?

That was the engineering motivation behind Lumen OS.

What is Lumen OS?
Lumen OS is a Bloomberg-style modular trading workstation designed for proprietary quantitative traders. It brings all essential market intelligence into a synchronized 12-tile master cockpit:

Live L2 Depth Orderbook: Visualizing institutional buy and sell walls in real time.
Liquidity Heatmaps: Spotting hidden liquidity clusters across order books.
Cross-Asset Correlation Matrix: Calculating real-time Pearson correlations across BTC, ETH, Gold, S&P 500, and the US Dollar Index (DXY).
Macro Telemetry: Ingesting live US Treasury Yield Curves (2Y, 10Y, 30Y) and Federal Reserve FOMC interest rate probabilities.
Strategy Backtester & VaR Journal: Real-time Value-at-Risk, Sharpe Ratio, and drawdown metrics.
Tactical Sound Synthesizer: Low-latency procedural audio cues powered by the Web Audio API.
Here are the key architectural patterns I implemented to eliminate browser bottlenecks.

  1. Bypassing React Reconciliation for High-Velocity Feeds The biggest mistake when building real-time dashboards in React is treating high-frequency streaming data like standard UI state.

The Tradeoff:

Standard UI elements (tab switches, modal dialogs, profile settings) belong in standard React state.
Fast-moving market feeds (price ladders, bid/ask spreads, tick streams) must bypass React reconciliation completely.
The Ring Buffer & RAF Loop Pattern: Instead of calling setState on every single incoming WebSocket frame:

Incoming WebSocket packets are pushed into an in-memory queue (Ring Buffer) with zero React overhead.
A decoupled requestAnimationFrame (RAF) loop polls the buffer and paints updates directly to the DOM or Canvas elements.
This guarantees that the browser only renders as fast as the monitor can display (60Hz or 120Hz), regardless of whether 50 or 5,000 WebSocket packets arrive in that split second.

  1. Local-First Zero-Latency Architecture In active trading, network jitter can ruin execution. Lumen OS follows a strict local-first philosophy:

0ms UI Interaction: All active telemetry, trade journals, risk metrics, and interface states are held in local memory and synchronized to browser storage.
Background Persistence: Data is synced asynchronously with a Neon Serverless PostgreSQL database. If the network drops or experiences packet loss, the UI never blocks, hangs, or freezes.
Direct Edge WebSockets: Feeds stream directly from exchange edge endpoints to the client without passing through an intermediary bottleneck server.

  1. Hardening the Perimeter with Cloudflare Zero Trust Because a proprietary trading terminal involves custom quant algorithms and private journal entries, standard JWT authentication on open endpoints was insufficient.

Lumen OS isolates its proxy backends behind Cloudflare Zero Trust Access:

Enforces mutual Service Token verification (CF-Access-Client-Id and CF-Access-Client-Secret).
Blocks unauthorized internet scrapers and automated probes before traffic ever touches application code.

  1. Reducing Visual Fatigue with Web Audio API Traders stare at dense numbers across 12 tiles for hours. To prevent visual burnout, I integrated a custom procedural audio synthesizer using the native browser Web Audio API:

Smooth micro-tonal sine waves notify traders when large institutional bid walls are filled.
Distinct audio frequencies sound on volatility breakouts or stop-loss hits.
Zero audio assets (MP3/WAV) to download — every tone is synthesized procedurally in real time with sub-5ms audio latency.
Key Lessons Learned
Virtual DOM has its limits: React is fantastic for complex component trees, but high-frequency data feeds demand direct DOM or RAF throttling.
Local-first makes web apps feel native: When you stop waiting on server roundtrips for every UI state toggle, the web feels as responsive as desktop software.
Sound is an underutilized UI dimension: In data-dense applications, subtle audio cues reduce cognitive load significantly.

Lumen OS is part of my digital laboratory where I build and ship production systems across AI, quant finance, and developer tools.

title: Sorting your Polar policies before you pick an Oso alternative
description:
I am on the marketing team at Permit. A lot of teams are re-reading their Oso setup this month, and sorting the Polar policies tends to get skipped at the start.

Oso Cloud was acquired by Tiny, with the deal closing on Oct 1, and Oso says Cloud will continue to operate as usual. Most of the Oso team joined Temporal. Nothing in that announcement means a team has to move today.

If you are planning a move, export your Polar policies first and sort each rule before you evaluate vendors. Role grants inside a resource block are RBAC. A role that comes from a relation is ReBAC, for example a repo reader who inherits from an org member, and copying that rule across also means syncing the relationship data behind it. Conditions on user or resource attributes are ABAC. For those you need to decide whether the attributes get synced ahead of time or sent with each check.

List filtering deserves its own line in the inventory. A single check and a query for every document a user can read do not fail in the same way.

We published a longer mapping with Permit code examples for each pattern: https://www.permit.io/blog/migrate-from-oso-to-permit?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=oso-migration

Whatever target you pick, run the old and new systems side by side for a while and log where they disagree. Cut over after the disagreements reach zero.

title: Understanding AI System Design: Beyond a Simple LLM API Call
description:
I'm starting a journey to understand how production-grade AI systems are designed, built, scaled, and maintained.

My goal isn't just to integrate an LLM API into an application. I want to understand the engineering decisions behind reliable AI products.

Let's start with a fundamental question:

What does it actually take to build an AI system?

1. An LLM API call is not a complete AI system

Calling an LLM API can generate a response, but production applications need much more:

  • Authentication and authorization
  • Data retrieval and context management
  • Rate limiting and cost control
  • Timeouts, retries, and error handling
  • Evaluation and output validation
  • Monitoring, security, and scalability

An LLM is one component of a larger software architecture.

2. Our first design problem

Imagine building an AI knowledge assistant for a company with 100,000 internal documents.

Employees should be able to ask questions such as:

"What is our enterprise refund policy?"

The system should retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer grounded in those documents, and provide citations.

It must also ensure employees cannot access information they aren't authorized to see.

3. A high-level architecture

Our initial design contains these components:

Client → Go API Backend → Retrieval Service → AI Orchestration → LLM Provider

The supporting infrastructure includes:

  • PostgreSQL: users, document metadata, permissions, and application records.
  • Vector search: retrieval of semantically relevant document chunks.
  • Object storage: original uploaded documents.
  • Message queue: asynchronous document processing.
  • Background workers: text extraction, chunking, and embedding generation.
  • Redis: selected caching and rate-limiting workloads.

These are initial technology choices, not universal requirements. The final architecture depends on workload, scale, cost, and operational constraints.

4. Where does RAG fit?

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) allows an application to retrieve relevant external information and provide it to an LLM as context.

A typical workflow looks like this:

  1. A user submits a question.
  2. The backend authenticates the user.
  3. The retrieval layer searches relevant, authorized document chunks.
  4. The orchestration layer builds a prompt containing the question and retrieved context.
  5. The LLM generates an answer.
  6. The backend validates the response and returns it with source references.

RAG can improve grounding, but it doesn't guarantee correctness. Poor retrieval, outdated documents, and misleading source material can still produce incorrect answers.

5. Production challenges worth thinking about

A working prototype is only the beginning.

Latency: How do we keep retrieval and generation fast enough for interactive use?

Cost: How do we control token consumption and avoid unnecessary model calls?

Security: How do we enforce document-level permissions before context reaches the model?

Reliability: What happens when the model provider times out or becomes unavailable?

Quality: How do we measure retrieval relevance and answer correctness instead of relying on a few manual tests?

These questions turn AI integration into system design.

6. What I'm exploring next

I'll investigate each component, implement practical examples, and document the architectural trade-offs as I learn.

The next topic is RAG: how document ingestion, chunking, embeddings, and retrieval work together—and why simply connecting an LLM to a database isn't enough.

This is the beginning of a hands-on AI system design series focused on practical backend engineering.

Question for other developers: When designing an AI knowledge assistant, would you prioritize retrieval accuracy, response latency, or cost first? Why?

title: 94% Faster Reads! How I Optimized the ShopEase Backend
description:
ShopEase: Optimizing Backend Performance with Redis, Hibernate & MySQL

Overview

As part of my ShopEase e-commerce project, I worked on improving backend performance by optimizing the catalog and order data pipelines. The goal was to reduce read latency, eliminate inefficient database queries, improve connection management, and make data retrieval more efficient.

Key Optimizations

1. Redis Cache-Aside

Implemented a Redis Cache-Aside layer for catalog and order pipelines, along with automated cache invalidation to keep cached data consistent with updates.

Reported result: Read latency reduced from 1.88 seconds to 110 milliseconds — a 94% reduction.

2. Hibernate N+1 Query Optimization

Resolved Hibernate N+1 query bottlenecks using JOIN FETCH, allowing related data to be retrieved more efficiently and reducing unnecessary database round trips.

3. HikariCP Connection Pool Tuning

Optimized HikariCP connection pool settings to improve database connection management and resource utilization.

4. MySQL Composite B-Tree Indexes

Introduced composite B-Tree indexes to improve query execution efficiency and reduce unnecessary row scans.

Reported result: MySQL query row-scans reduced by 95%.

Technology Stack

  • Language: Java
  • Backend: Spring Boot, Hibernate, Spring Data JPA
  • Database: MySQL
  • Caching: Redis
  • Connection Pooling: HikariCP
  • Query Optimization: JOIN FETCH and composite B-Tree indexes

What I Learned

This optimization work reinforced that backend performance depends on multiple layers working together. Caching reduces repeated database reads, efficient ORM queries help avoid unnecessary round trips, connection pooling improves resource management, and indexing makes data retrieval more efficient.

Conclusion

Improving ShopEase was not just about adding features; it was also about making existing functionality faster and more efficient. These optimizations strengthened my practical understanding of Java backend development, database performance tuning, caching strategies, and scalable application design.

Engineered a multi-tier performance optimization for catalog and order pipelines: implemented a Redis Cache-Aside layer cutting read latency by 94% (1.88s → 110ms) with automated cache invalidation, resolved Hibernate N+1 query bottlenecks via JOIN FETCH, tuned HikariCP connection pooling, and introduced composite B-Tree indexes reducing MySQL query row-scans by 95%.

About ShopEase
ShopEase is a full-stack e-commerce application built with Java, Spring Boot, MySQL, and Redis. It focuses on secure shopping, efficient data management, and high-performance backend architecture.

title: Stop Letting Your Group Bot Only Reply: Route Every Event to Its Own Agent
description:
Scenario

A new member joins and the bot says nothing. A friend request arrives and it sits there. The bot is pulled into another group and does nothing there either — and that is usually not the adapter's fault: only messages can travel down the current path.

In 4.10 a bot had a single entry point: use_pipeline_name, use_pipeline_uuid and pipeline_routing_rules (measured 2026-10-16 on a live v4.10.11 instance), and its rules could only filter launcher_type, launcher_id, message_content and message_has_element (source src/langbot/pkg/persistence/alembic/versions/0009_migrate_event_bindings.py:35-52). A QQ group bot should answer questions by day, welcome new members and hand friend requests to a human; on 4.10 you could only split messages across pipelines.

How it works in 4.11

4.11 replaces "bot → one pipeline" with "bot → event bindings". Each binding answers three questions: which event, under which conditions, to whom.

Data model (new in 4.11). Bindings live in new JSON columns on the bots table: event_bindings and plugin_processors (source src/langbot/pkg/entity/persistence/bot.py:55-56). There is no separate routing table; the three legacy columns are dropped by 0011_drop_legacy_bot_routing.py. One binding carries (official docs docs/event-based-agents/04-event-routing.md:69-73, plus order at runtime):

  • event_pattern — the event type: exact match, namespace.*, or the global * (source src/langbot/pkg/platform/botmgr.py:152-159).
  • filters — conditions on chat_type, chat_id, message_text, message_element_types; operators include eq, neq, contains, not_contains, starts_with, regex; all of them must hold.
  • target_type + target_uuid — pipeline, agent or discard (in the UI: Pipeline / Agent / Discard).
  • priority — higher wins; enabled — false eliminates the row.
  • order — list position, written from the array index on save (source src/langbot/pkg/api/http/service/bot.py:257); dragging a row edits it.

Arbitration. An event ends up with exactly one response target. Disabled bindings are dropped, the event type is matched, the target is checked, filters are evaluated, and survivors are sorted by (priority, -order) descending — first wins (source botmgr.py:274-345, collect :330, sort :335; official docs 04-event-routing.md:115-119). Losers are recorded as lower_priority, so dragging a row up and raising its priority mean the same thing.

Event naming (new in 4.11). Event types are {namespace}.{action} strings (official docs docs/event-based-agents/01-event-system.md:5), e.g. message.received, group.member_joined, friend.request_received, feedback.received. Platform events use platform.{adapter}.{action} (:447-451). Support depends on the adapter and platform — check the support matrix first.

Separate 4.10 from what is new. Adapters are unchanged: http_bot.py is byte-identical between v4.10.11 and v4.11.0 (27,029 bytes), and 4.10 already shipped aiocqhttp, kook and wecombot. What is new is the event-binding data model and routing mechanism — adapters emit events, bindings pick the handler. A legacy adapter declaring no supported_events only emits message.received (source EventBindingsEditor.tsx). Support depends on the adapter and platform — check the support matrix first.

Upgrading is not a blank slate. 0009_migrate_event_bindings.py turns use_pipeline_uuid into one binding and each pipeline_routing_rules entry into another (launcher_type→chat_type, launcher_id→chat_id, message_content→message_text, message_has_element→message_element_types, eq→contains, neq→not_contains; source :38-52). Bindings keep the same pipeline UUID; no agent or Runner configuration is created. That migration has an empty downgrade (source :133, not reversible), and 0035_pipeline_received_only.py later narrows message.* to message.received.

Hands-on steps

Start a fresh 4.11 instance (container name and data directory are yours to change):

docker network create lang7-411
docker run -d --name lang7-411-core --network lang7-411 \
  -e BOX__ENABLED=false -e SPACE__DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true -p 15400:5300 \
  -v "$PWD/deploy/411/data:/app/data" rockchin/langbot:v4.11.0

The first boot runs the migrations first. Open http://127.0.0.1:15400 and sign in as admin@langbot.local (the password is a local demo value — replace it). Then:

  1. Create or select a bot (the demo uses the generic HTTP adapter).
  2. On the bot detail page, find the Event Routing card — it decides which processor gets an incoming event.
  3. A new bot already has a message.received route pointing at a pipeline. The supported-events header groups events by what the adapter declares (here: Messages · 1).

  1. Click Add behavior and pick a preset (reply to messages, welcome new members, ...), or use Add route to fill in event and target yourself.
  2. On the new route row, pick the event and processor: the picker offers existing pipelines and agents, or Create new processor. The screenshot below shows the row added but not yet saved.

  1. Expand Trigger conditions for filters: chat type, chat ID, message text, message elements — all must hold.
  2. Drag rows to reorder (order), change weights with Priority, switch a route off with Enabled.
  3. After saving, run Check routing (a dry run) before live traffic.

An upgraded instance needs no manual re-wiring: copy the 4.10.11 data directory, point the same docker run at it, and legacy rules land as bindings through the mapping above. The field map is in pipeline-migration-config-map.zh-CN.md.

Verify

Three ways, fastest first:

  1. Check routing in the card: pick an event type, run one synthetic dispatch, and it lists every binding's outcome — matched / delivered / discarded — or why it lost: event_pattern_mismatch, filters_mismatch, lower_priority, processor_incompatible (a pipeline pointed at a non-message event). Dry run and real dispatch share one matcher (source botmgr.py:361, diagnose_eba_event_binding).
  2. Match records: recent matches held in the bot's memory. Cleared on restart — use the operation log for long-lived checks.
  3. Look at the database: sqlite3 deploy/411/data/langbot.db "select name, event_bindings from bots". A migrated binding (measured 2026-10-16): {"event_pattern":"message.received","target_type":"pipeline","target_uuid":"2e59bbf9-…","filters":[],"priority":0,"enabled":true,"description":"Migrated from default pipeline binding","order":0}. While the pipeline behind target_uuid exists, the route works.

Limits and caveats

  • One response target per event. Bindings arbitrate rather than run in parallel: if two match, only the first runs.
  • A pipeline target only accepts message.received. Any other event fails as processor_incompatible — "Pipeline targets only support message events" (source botmgr.py:162, :315-317). To greet someone on join, target an agent or plugin event processor.
  • Wildcards were narrowed. Legacy message.* bindings were rewritten to message.received by 0035. Hand-written message.* still matches those events, but a pipeline target fails the target check.
  • Adapters and events are not one-to-one. Support depends on the adapter and platform — check the support matrix first. The official table (docs/event-based-agents/01-event-system.md:453-476) calls itself a preliminary assessment: confirm per platform before relying on an event and treat anything unconfirmed as unverified.
  • Plugin event processors are a second, parallel channel. The plugin-processors section at the card's bottom takes no part in arbitration: it receives plugin-declared events independently of the routes above (source botmgr.py:285 skips those rows, :1012 reads plugin_processors separately). A plugin subscribing to an event is not your bot handling it.
  • Migration is a one-way door. The binding conversion has no downgrade and 0011 drops the old columns; Runner configuration migration is a separate, user-confirmed API. Back up the data directory first.

Summary and next steps

Upgrading from 4.10? Read the field map first: pipeline-migration-config-map.zh-CN.md. See the v4.11.0 release page for this version's scope and the official 01-event-system.md for event types and fields. Next up: Runner plugins — installing one from the marketplace and selecting it in a pipeline.

title: Three of Five Founder Mailboxes Rejected first.last, the Layout Everyone Defaults To
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali, and the other half of my week goes into Apify Actors. One of them is narrow on purpose: you give it a LinkedIn profile URL, it gives you back the person's name, title, current company, location — and their work e-mail address with the mailbox checked over SMTP.

The part that looks like the hard problem is finding the address. It isn't. Writing first.last@domain.com takes one line of code, and that is exactly what most of this category ships, with a label like deliverable next to it. The hard problem is the one that appears the moment you actually ask a mail server whether the thing you just wrote down exists: you only get a couple of questions, so the order you ask them in is the product.

Here is what that costs, measured on nine runs between 10 and 17 October 2026 across six public profiles of founders and executives (builds 0.1.32 to 0.1.41).

The ranked guess was wrong more often than it was right

Every one of the six people got the same treatment: read the public profile, resolve the company to a domain, build candidate addresses in the company's own layout, then check mailboxes over SMTP — at most two per person — and keep the first one the server confirms.

Person Domain Check 1 (ranked first) Check 2 Delivered
Bill Gates gatesfoundation.org bill.gates@ → safe — bill.gates@
Garry Tan ycombinator.com garry.tan@ → safe — garry.tan@
Satya Nadella microsoft.com satya.nadella@ → invalid satya@ → safe satya@
Rand Fishkin sparktoro.com rand.fishkin@ → invalid rand@ → safe rand@
Jeff Weiner nextplayventures.com jeff.weiner@ → invalid jeff@ → safe jeff@
Patrick Collison stripe.com patrick.collison@ → catch_all patrick.collison@arcinstitute.org → catch_all nothing

Five of the six ended with a mailbox the server confirmed. In three of those five the highest-ranked candidate came back invalid — not "unconfirmed", not "probably", but a mail server actively saying there is no such mailbox. The address that worked was the plain first name.

Six people is not a statistical law about corporate mail, and I'm not going to dress it up as one. It is, however, a direct cost argument. If your highest-ranked candidate fails 60% of the time on the kind of person people actually pay to reach, then a tool with no mailbox check hands out three wrong addresses in five with a confident label on each, and a tool with a mailbox check spends 60% of its check budget on check 1.

Why the default led in all six cases

The Actor's first choice of layout is not supposed to be a default. It's supposed to be evidence:

// The whole product rests on one observation: a company that publishes any personal
// address on its own website has told you the rule for all of them. jane.doe@acme.com
// on the team page means the sales director is firstname.lastname too.

If the company site publishes j.diaz@acme.com and m.kent@acme.com, you don't guess — you've been told the layout, and you write the one address you were asked for in it. That path works, and I wrote about the evidence side of it separately. It just didn't fire once in this batch. All six rows came back with patternEvidenceCount: 0 and emailPatternSource: "default": gatesfoundation.org, microsoft.com, stripe.com, ycombinator.com, sparktoro.com and nextplayventures.com publish no personal address a crawler can read. Big companies route you to a contact form; two-person funds have a hello@.

With nothing to learn from, the ranked prior takes over, and the prior is this list:

export const PATTERNS = [
    'first.last', 'first', 'flast', 'firstlast', 'first_last', 'firstl', 'f.last',
    'last.first', 'lastfirst', 'first-last', 'last', 'fl',
];

first.last is roughly half of corporate mail, so it leads. But look at who rejected it: the CEO who joined in 1992, the founder of a two-person company, a founding partner of his own fund. People who were employee number small tend to hold the short mailbox, and the short mailbox is first@. The population you want from LinkedIn — founders, partners, heads of things — is enriched in exactly the people for whom the most common layout is the wrong one.

The budget is two checks, and that's the whole design 

const REOON_MAX_CHECKS = 2;
…
const pool = candidatesFor(first, last, company.domain, company.pattern || 'first.last', …);
const order = [...(onSite ? [onSite] : []), ...pool.filter((c) => c.email !== onSite?.email)];
v = await verifyFirst(order.map((c) => c.email), { maxChecks: REOON_MAX_CHECKS });

Two, not ten, for two unglamorous reasons. Each check is a paid API call, and the Actor charges per found e-mail — so checks that find nothing come out of my margin, not the buyer's bill. And hammering one domain with ten mailbox probes per person is how a verification provider's IPs stop being trusted by that domain's mail server.

Which means the ranking is not a nicety. With a budget of two, "the right layout is third in my list" and "I have no address for this person" are the same outcome. The three saves above all happened on check 2. There is no check 3.

That also explains a field people ask about. alternatives in every row is not padding — it's the rest of the ranked list that never got measured, labelled as such, so a buyer whose first address bounces has somewhere to go:

"email": "satya@microsoft.com",
"emailPattern": "first",
"confidence": "verified",
"emailStatus": "mailbox-verified",
"emailVerification": { "provider": "reoon", "status": "safe", "score": 98, "checks": 2,
  "tried": [ { "email": "satya.nadella@microsoft.com", "status": "invalid" },
             { "email": "satya@microsoft.com", "status": "safe" } ] },
"alternatives": [ { "email": "satya.nadella@microsoft.com", "pattern": "first.last" },
                  { "email": "snadella@microsoft.com", "pattern": "flast" } ]

Where no amount of check budget helps

stripe.com answered catch_all to patrick.collison@stripe.com in all six runs it appeared in, with a score of 75 against the 98 a confirmed mailbox gets. A catch-all server accepts every address you offer it, including ones you invent, so nothing can be confirmed there — not by me, not by any vendor, no matter what their UI says. The remaining check rolled to the person's other current company from the profile, arcinstitute.org, which is also catch-all. Two checks spent, nothing learned:

"email": null,
"emailGuess": "patrick.collison@stripe.com",
"emailCatchAll": true,
"emailStatus": "catch-all",
"summary": "Not delivered as an e-mail: the mail server of stripe.com accepts any address
            (catch-all), so no mailbox can be confirmed there; best unverified guess
            patrick.collison@stripe.com is in \"emailGuess\". This row was not charged."

The guess still ships, in a differently-named field, free. If you're building this yourself, that split is the only honest shape I've found: one field for "a server confirmed this", a different field for "this is my best construction", and never the same field for both.

The failure that only shows up when you run the same thing twice

One run out of nine broke the pattern. On 13 October, microsoft.com answered unknown to satya.nadella@microsoft.com after a single check — no score, no verdict — where the eight other runs got a flat invalid on that same address. The row came back free, no e-mail, status mailbox-unknown.

That's the right outcome for billing and the wrong one for the buyer, and it exposes a limit I'd rather print than hide: because the run stopped at unknown instead of invalid, it never reached satya@, and emailGuess was filled with satya.nadella@microsoft.com — the exact address eight other runs proved does not exist. Nothing in a single row is wrong. The row simply can't know what a different run knew. If you're consuming SMTP verdicts in a pipeline, treat unknown as "ask again tomorrow", never as "no mailbox", and keep your own memory of addresses that came back invalid across runs.

Calling it 

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~linkedin-email-finder/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"profileUrls":["https://www.linkedin.com/in/satyanadella",
                      "https://www.linkedin.com/in/patrickcollison",
                      "https://www.linkedin.com/in/williamhgates"]}'

Those three profiles took 14.6 seconds end to end in the 17 October run these numbers come from, and about $0.0006 of platform compute; the price is per e-mail found, and the two catch-all and unknown rows above cost nothing. It's LinkedIn Email Finder on Apify if you want the rows rather than the reasoning.

Where it doesn't fit: there's no login, so the roughly one profile in five that LinkedIn hides from anonymous readers needs an unblocking route and sometimes still doesn't open. If your target list is all large-enterprise domains, expect a pile of catch-all rows and plan on guesses. If you already have a name and a company domain and no LinkedIn URL, the profile read is wasted work — the name-plus-domain path is a different Actor. And if your list is twenty people, reading twenty company websites by hand will beat any of this.

What I'd keep even if you never run it: a mailbox check turns e-mail finding from a text-formatting exercise into a search problem with a budget. Spend the budget on the layout the company told you about. When it hasn't told you anything, know that your prior is tuned for the median employee, and the people you're looking for aren't median.
