title: A cancer drug is a classifier. My body is the dataset.
description:
I'm a data scientist with stage IV cancer. I build an AI tool that matches patients to clinical trials — but the model I can't stop thinking about isn't in my code. It's the drug in my arm.

A cancer treatment is a classifier. Not as a metaphor — literally. Every dose of chemo, every round of radiation, every targeted drug makes the same binary call, billions of times over: this cell — kill it, or spare it? The ground truth is malignant or healthy. The whole fight is a classification problem, and my body is the dataset it runs on.

Once you see it that way, the confusion matrix stops being a diagram and becomes a diagnosis.

I'm not the first to see it. In 2014 a group of researchers formalized exactly this — cancer drugs as classifiers — into a framework for designing more selective drugs, treating a therapy as a (suboptimal) classifier that tells malignant cells from healthy ones by their molecular profiles (Lawlor et al., PLOS ONE 2014). They modeled the classifier from the outside, to build better ones. I've spent two years living inside its test set — and the view from in here is different.

The four cells — and they're literal cells

True positive — a cancer cell killed. The therapeutic effect. The tumor shrinks. This is the only cell anyone is rooting for.

False positive — a healthy cell killed. This is toxicity. Every false positive has a name: the hair, the crashed blood counts, the mouth sores, the neuropathy in my feet. Side effects aren't a separate thing from the treatment — they are its false-positive rate, made flesh. Not all of it is a cell struck dead; some is healthy tissue damaged, a nerve misfiring, an immune system thrown off balance. But it's the same error at root — the drug acting where it shouldn't, and the body paying for it.

False negative — a cancer cell that survived. The ones that got away. And here is what makes this the most unforgiving classifier I know: it can take just one false negative — a single surviving cell with the capacity to seed new growth — to rebuild the entire tumor. Miss that one positive and, months later, it quietly undoes all the true positives you were so proud of. And the cell that survives needn't be one that was always going to: under the drug's pressure, cells can acquire resistance they didn't start with — so what grows back is often a harder problem to classify than the one you began with.

True negative — a healthy cell, correctly left alone. The silent majority — most of me, on a good day. Nobody celebrates a true negative, but they're the reason I can walk around between infusions.

The metrics are the whole history of oncology

Oncologists don't say precision and recall. But that's what a century of cancer drugs has been chasing.

When the goal is a cure, recall has to be almost perfect. Of all the cancer cells, what fraction did you kill? In most machine-learning problems you can live with 0.9. Here, 0.9999 can still lose — because the 0.0001 that survived is alive and dividing. Cancer is the classification problem where a handful of missed positives regrow into the whole thing. That's why treatment is so brutal: you're not trying to be mostly right, you're trying not to miss a single one.

And no single systemic drug gets there. A drug in the bloodstream reaches everywhere and kills imperfectly — broad coverage, mediocre recall. So a cure, when it's possible, is an ensemble: induction chemo shrinks the tumor to cut the burden, then surgery or radiation takes the bulk with near-perfect recall inside its field, and systemic therapy mops up whatever slipped the net. Each classifier covers another's blind spot. You stack them because not one of them, alone, clears the last cell.

Precision is the part your body pays for — a different question from recall. Not what fraction of the cancer you killed, but: of all the cells you killed, what fraction were actually cancer? Chemotherapy is a catastrophically low-precision classifier. Its decision rule is barely a rule at all — "kill whatever's dividing fast" — so its false positives are precisely your fast-dividing healthy tissues: the gut lining (nausea), the hair follicles (baldness), the bone marrow (the blood counts that crash). The side-effect profile is just a readout of a crude decision boundary.

And the two trade off — that tradeoff is cancer treatment. Push the dose higher to raise recall — kill more cancer, at least until the dose-response flattens — and precision falls: more healthy cells die, more toxicity, until the false positives start threatening to kill the patient themselves. The maximum tolerated dose an oncologist reaches for is, exactly, how far you can trade precision for recall before the false positives turn lethal. Chemo asks you to poison your whole body a little to be more sure you got the cancer.

So the entire arc of better cancer drugs is a campaign to raise precision without surrendering recall — to sharpen the boundary so it catches cancer and spares the healthy. Targeted therapies pick a mutation only the cancer carries. Antibody-drug conjugates — the class of the drug in my arm — bolt a targeting antibody onto a chemotherapy warhead: a feature engineered to lower the false-positive rate by carrying the poison closer to the cancer. Closer, not exclusively — the payload still leaks in transit, the target still sits on some healthy cells, and the neuropathy in my feet is proof the false positives never hit zero. A sharper boundary, not a perfect one. A tumor-specific target is nothing but a feature with real area under the ROC curve — one that separates malignant from healthy cleanly. Most targets don't, quite; they're shared with some normal tissue, and that leftover overlap has a clinical name too: on-target, off-tumor toxicity. False positives from an imperfect feature.

Immunotherapy retrains the classifier itself. Cancer survives partly by looking like self — fooling the immune system's own classifier into labeling it "healthy." Checkpoint inhibitors take the brakes off that classifier. And when the retrained immune system starts over-calling — attacking healthy tissue it now flags as foreign — you get colitis, pneumonitis, thyroiditis: autoimmune side effects that are, exactly, the immune classifier's false positives.

And all of it runs on the worst class balance imaginable — which is exactly what makes precision so merciless. Cancer cells are a vanishing fraction of the cells in a body. So a drug can be highly specific — spare the overwhelming majority of healthy cells, hold its false-positive rate low — and still kill more healthy cells than cancer ones in sheer count, simply because the healthy cells so enormously outnumber the targets. High specificity, low precision: that's the signature of a rare positive class, and it's why even a fairly selective drug can feel like it's poisoning your whole body. Put that beside a false-negative cost that's existential and a false-positive cost paid in your own tissue, and I don't know a harder classification problem.

A worked example: the drug in my arm

Put the drug I'm actually on through this lens. Becotatug vedotin is an antibody-drug conjugate: an antibody that recognizes EGFR — a protein my cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, carries at high levels — welded to a cytotoxic warhead called MMAE. MMAE (monomethyl auristatin E) is a microtubule poison: it jams the scaffolding a cell has to build in order to divide, and it's so potent that it would be far too toxic to put into a vein on its own. That toxicity is the point: the antibody is what makes an otherwise-unusable warhead usable, by carrying it only where it's wanted.

And "where it's wanted" isn't a single feature. For the drug to kill a cell, several things all have to be true at once: EGFR on the surface for the antibody to grab, the whole conjugate pulled inside and digested to free the MMAE, the cell dividing when the poison lands, and no pump spitting the drug back out. The real feature is that conjunction — EGFR and internalizing and dividing and not-effluxing, all ANDed together — and that's exactly why it's selective: almost no healthy cell checks every box, so the false positives fall. It's also where resistance hides, because a cell escapes by failing any single clause — shed the antigen, go dormant, or learn to efflux the drug.

Its Phase 3 trial pitted it against the conventional alternative: standard chemotherapy, the doctor's choice of capecitabine or docetaxel — drugs whose decision rule is essentially "attack whatever divides fast." Docetaxel, in fact, goes after the very machinery MMAE does — the microtubules a cell needs to divide — just in mirror image. The warhead wasn't exotic; what changed was the aim: a sharp feature against a crude one.

In classifier terms, the result is exactly what the sharper feature should buy. Against chemotherapy, becotatug vedotin produced about two and a half times the response rate (30.2% vs 11.5%), roughly doubled the time before the cancer regrew (median progression-free survival 5.8 vs 2.8 months; hazard ratio 0.63), and trended toward longer survival at the interim look (17.1 vs 12.0 months; hazard ratio 0.73, not yet conclusive) — all in patients whose disease had already slipped past two or more prior lines of treatment (ASCO 2025, abstract LBA6005). It didn't win with a more violent poison — its warhead is a cytotoxic like the others. It won with a better boundary: a feature, EGFR, that tells my kind of cancer cell from my healthy ones more cleanly than "divides fast" ever could.

That's the whole thesis in a single trial — and worth stating precisely. Those numbers describe a population, not a prophecy. A median is a fact about a few hundred strangers; what the drug is doing inside me I read off scans and side effects, not off a survival curve. But the reason it's the drug in my arm at all is that, across that population, a sharper feature beat the doctor's best crude one.

The objective function changes when it spreads

Everything above assumes you're playing for a cure — driving recall toward one, because a single survivor regrows the tumor. That's curative intent: early-stage disease, the adjuvant setting, the places where gone is still on the table.

I'm not in that setting. My cancer is metastatic — it spread. For some people even that leaves a narrow path to cure: oligometastatic disease, a few deposits you can still ablate one by one. But mine is widespread, and there the arithmetic changes — not because the drugs got weaker but because the ensemble lost its best member. Surgery and radiation reach near-perfect recall inside a field; they can't touch disease seeded microscopically through the whole body. Take the local step away and only the broad, imperfect systemic classifiers are left — and alone, they don't reach one. Recall of 1.0 isn't a target I keep missing; for disease spread like mine, it's no longer the one I'm realistically playing for. Durable control is.

So the objective function changed. I'm not trying to classify every cell correctly, once. I'm running a control problem — hold the tumor burden down, keep the false positives (the toxicity I'll carry for as long as this lasts) livable, and keep the classifier running as long as the math allows. The false negatives I've stopped trying to zero out. I've conceded them; the fight now is over what they're allowed to do, and how much of me it costs to hold them there.

A curative patient is solving a one-shot classification: miss nothing. I'm solving something closer to control — keep a system in a tolerable state, over time. A different loss function entirely. And in mine, a false positive I'll carry for years can weigh more than a false negative I've already made my peace with.

Every new line of treatment is the next split in the tree

A classifier doesn't have to be a single decision. String them together and you get a decision tree: a sequence of splits, each one working only on the data that survived the split before it. That's what lines of treatment are. First-line therapy makes its cut; the cancer that comes back is, by definition, the subset of cells that landed in that drug's false-negative region — the ones it couldn't separate out. So when I choose a next line, I'm choosing the next split in the tree, and it only ever operates on the survivors.

Which quietly dictates a rule every oncologist already follows: don't reach for a drug whose boundary looks like the last one's. A split highly correlated with one you've already made buys almost no information — the cells it could have carved off are already gone, and what's left is precisely the part that kind of feature can't touch. That's cross-resistance, stated in the language of trees: near-zero conditional gain. It's why the next line usually changes mechanism rather than reloading a cousin of the drug that just failed, and why we stack combinations — several splits at once, each covering the cells the others miss — always weighed against what each new cut costs in healthy tissue.

But two things break the tidy picture, and both are why this is the hardest version of the problem. The first: the data isn't fixed. Every split I make changes the distribution. It kills the sensitive cells and leaves behind — enriches — the resistant ones. I'm not fitting one tree to a frozen dataset; I'm splitting a population that reshapes itself, adversarially, in answer to every cut. Each line selects for the clone that beats it. Changing mechanism is the counter-move — a fresh feature the survivors haven't been selected against, which buys back some of the lost ground. How much depends on how independent the new mechanism is: swap one cytotoxic for a close cousin and the survivors' general hardiness — drug efflux, dormancy, a defused self-destruct — carries straight over; hand the killing to something that works on entirely different rules, like the immune system, and the reset can be far deeper. What moves that floor is the overlap between the new mechanism and the ones the tumor has already beaten — not the number of lines you've been through. Overlap keeps it high; a mechanism independent enough can push it back down. It's never guaranteed to be one-way: the right switch can leave the tumor more vulnerable, not less.

The second is that I'm choosing these splits almost blind. In a real decision tree you know every feature value and every label, so you can compute which split gains the most. I can't. I don't fully know which features my tumor is even carrying — the molecular readout is partial, and a snapshot ages. The response odds are borrowed from trial populations that aren't me. So I'm not maximizing information gain; I'm maximizing expected information gain under deep uncertainty — and sometimes choosing a line not because it's the likeliest to work, but because it will tell me something about what I'm fighting. Explore versus exploit, played for the highest stakes there are.

Where it breaks: I can't see the matrix

Here's the part that keeps me up.

You never get to see this confusion matrix. You can't count the cells.

The whole four-box reality is inferred from two blurry shadows. Recall, I read off a scan — a tumor that shrank means a lot of true positives, roughly, in aggregate. Precision, I read off myself — how sick I feel is the false-positive rate, translated into symptoms. And the cell I most need to know is the one I can't see at all: the false negative. The single cancer cell that survived the last infusion and is, as I write this, quietly dividing. Minimal-residual-disease tests are a smudged attempt to glimpse that false-negative rate — did any escape? — and even they can't see one cell.

So the classifier runs across billions of cells in my body; I'm told its approximate recall months later, in a radiology report, and its precision continuously, in how I feel. The confusion matrix that decides how long I live is computed in the dark, and I only ever see its shadows on the wall.

The best classifier may not exist yet

Here's what makes control worth it. The set of classifiers I get to choose from isn't fixed. Every year, oncology ships better ones — drugs with sharper features, mechanisms that didn't exist when I was diagnosed. The drug in my arm now wasn't on the table for me when I started. The frontier — the best boundary anyone can yet draw between my cancer and me — keeps moving outward, slowly and unevenly, but it moves.

So for a metastatic patient, control isn't only holding a tolerable state for its own sake. It's buying time against that moving frontier — staying in the game long enough for a better classifier to arrive. The loss function isn't just "keep the tumor down"; it's "keep the tumor down until the tooling improves." Every month held is a month closer to a feature sharp enough to change the math. It's a bet, not a promise — the better drug may not come in time — but it's the bet the whole strategy rests on.

And you don't wait for it passively. The better classifier might already exist — in a trial that hasn't reached my clinic, in a drug class my oncologist hasn't reached for, in a study running in another country. So part of the job, the part I can actually control, is searching: scanning that frontier, continuously, for a boundary sharper than the ones I've already been offered. It's a discipline of its own — most of what you find won't fit, and a trial is a candidate, not a cure — but when the classifiers you've got are failing, looking is the move with the most upside left. It's not a coincidence that searching for a better one is the thing I decided to build.

The name of the thing

I find it steadying anyway — the way it's steadying to know the name of the thing trying to kill you. My treatment isn't a mystery or a punishment. It's a classifier working the worst class imbalance there is, paying for its false positives in my own healthy cells. Side effects are its precision problem. Recurrence is its recall problem. And with cure no longer the realistic goal for disease spread like mine, mine isn't trying to win the classification outright — only to keep it running, tolerably, for as long as the math allows. "Precision oncology" is the long campaign to sharpen the boundary enough to buy more of that.

Every cancer drug is a classifier. My body is the dataset. And the one cell that matters most — the one that got away — is the one neither of us can see.

Meet Pip. Pip is the study companion inside Stride, a free learning app I built for Maths, Python and Java.

👉 Try it now: stride.crooli.com

No account. No sign-up. No paywall. Open it and start learning.

Why I made it

Most learning sites want an email address before you've learnt anything, then bury you in streak guilt and quizzes that punish you for not knowing something yet. I wanted the opposite: a calm place where "I'm not sure" is a perfectly good answer.

How it works

  1. Pick a subject. Maths, Python or Java.
  2. Take a six-question starting check. It doesn't matter how well you do. It only decides which lessons you need, and "I'm not sure" is always allowed.
  3. Follow your personal path. Lessons are small steps: learn an idea, explore it, modify it, then apply it.
  4. Watch evidence build, not a score. Each topic moves from introduced to practised to used independently. Answers after hints or retries never count as independent, so the progress you see is honest.

Java goes all the way to 26 topics, from your first program to tested applications and engineering projects, with a downloadable Maven/JUnit starter that has deliberately failing tests for you to fix.

Say hi to Pip

Pip lives in the corner of every page and has opinions about your code (kind ones). Pip can:

  • give hints instead of handing over answers
  • explain error messages in plain language in the Playground
  • nudge you when it's time to back up your progress
  • chat about lessons, what to practise next, or how Stride works

There's a full-screen chat at stride.crooli.com/chat. Ask Pip who made Stride. Pip knows. 😉

Other things in the box

  • Playground: write and run code in many languages at stride.crooli.com/playground
  • Focus timer: 15, 25 or 50 minute sessions with breaks, if you like them
  • Your data stays yours: progress lives in your browser. Move it between devices with a progress code, or turn on optional sync that's encrypted on your device before it's stored
  • Accessible by default: reduced-motion is respected, including Pip's animations

Under the hood

For the curious: Stride is a build-less, framework-less static site made of plain ES modules, with zero npm dependencies. Pip's character is an SVG driven by small spring animations, and its hints and error explanations are deterministic rather than AI-generated. Only the optional chat uses an AI model. Code runs through the public Wandbox API, so nothing executes on my server.

Where to use it

🌱 stride.crooli.com, free, in any modern browser, on desktop or phone.

If you try it, I'd love to hear what you think. Which subject did you pick, and did Pip say anything that made you smile? Let me know in the comments. 💚

title: Stamping a Company Seal on Excel Invoices: No Private Storage, a Lying resize(), and Three Coordinate Systems
description:
The task

In our internal business system, I built a feature that stamps a company seal (the square kaku-in used on Japanese business documents) onto invoices, quotes, and purchase orders. The documents are Excel templates filled with data and converted to PDF via LibreOffice. The requirements:

  • Never distribute the seal image by itself — no public URL, no image-serving API. It may only be seen stamped on a document
  • Per-document ON/OFF toggle
  • Once a document is finalized, replacing the seal later must not change it — but copying the image per document is forbidden
  • Position it relative to the issuer block, slightly overlapping the address; same physical size across all three templates

"Just paste one image," I thought. I then got stuck in three different layers: infrastructure, the library, and the coordinate systems.

Problem 1: there was no private storage

My first idea was the existing S3 bucket that stores attachments and logos. Then I read its bucket policy:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*"
}

Principal: * with s3:GetObject — anyone who knows the key can read the object. No matter how careful the application code is, putting the seal there breaks the "never distribute" requirement at the storage layer.

The seal is a PNG of a few dozen KB, so I stored it in a PostgreSQL bytea column instead. If you never build a GET endpoint for the image, a public URL cannot exist by construction. The only consumer is the document renderer.

The seemingly contradictory pair "no copies, yet finalized documents are immutable" was solved by an append-only design:

  • Replacing the seal inserts a new row and repoints the company's "current seal" reference
  • Deleting the seal keeps the row and only cuts the reference
  • Finalizing a document snapshots the seal's row ID onto the document

Finalized documents keep pointing at the old row, so later changes never touch them. There is always exactly one copy of each image.

As a bonus finding, finalized PDFs were also sitting in that same public bucket under guessable keys. That was out of scope for this feature, so I filed it as an infrastructure task (prefix-level deny in the bucket policy) and handed it over.

Problem 2: POI's resize() trusts the font

Next, placing the image. With Apache POI I anchored the picture at the right edge of column F in the issuer block, set the anchor's dx, and called Picture.resize(scale). The seal ended up in the middle of the cell.

The cause is inside resize(): it re-derives the horizontal offset by estimating cell widths from font metrics. The template uses MS PGothic, and the estimate came out at roughly 60% of the real column width — so my carefully computed dx was overwritten based on a wrong premise.

The fix was to drop resize() entirely and compute all four corners of the twoCellAnchor (from/to col, row, dx, dy, in EMUs) myself:

XSSFClientAnchor anchor = new XSSFClientAnchor(
    fromDx, fromDy, toDx, toDy,
    fromCol, fromRow, toCol, toRow);
anchor.setAnchorType(ClientAnchor.AnchorType.MOVE_DONT_RESIZE);
Picture pic = drawing.createPicture(anchor, pictureIdx);

Row heights read back accurately from the template, so vertically I just accumulate rows until the required height is reached. I also set the shape's xfrm off/ext to the same values. Convenience methods hide their assumptions — here, the font.

Problem 3: there were three coordinate systems

The PDF output was still off in position and size. It turned out three separate layers transform coordinates, each modified at a different stage:

1. Cell width in "characters". Before PDF conversion, our pipeline enlarges fonts by 6pt and shrinks cell widths (which Excel stores in character units) proportionally to preserve the layout — e.g. 45.66 chars → 29.5 chars. Computing pixels from the shrunken value gives you a too-narrow cell. I multiply the font ratio back in first.

2. Print scale. The templates print at 61%, so 66 px on the sheet is 10 mm on paper. A kaku-in is conventionally 18–21 mm, which back-calculates to a ~110 px square on the sheet.

3. Millimeters on paper. The only layer anyone actually cares about. Luckily all three templates use the same 61% scale, so equal sheet pixels automatically satisfied the "same size everywhere" requirement.

Characters on the sheet, pixels on the sheet, millimeters on paper: ignore any one of the three and it looks right on screen and wrong on paper.

Verification: what ships on paper must be checked on paper

Unit-test templates are empty sheets, so they can't tell you what the paper will look like. I rendered 12 documents (3 real templates × long/short address × ON/OFF) with a dummy seal PNG, converted them with local LibreOffice, and cropped the top of each PDF to a PNG for eyeballing:

libreoffice --headless --convert-to pdf out/*.xlsx
pdftoppm -png -r 100 -y 0 -H 350 out/invoice.pdf check/invoice

All three "not yet" verdicts (not overlapping the address yet, too big, etc.) came from those images. The harness was deleted, not committed; what stayed in the repo were six unit tests: ON puts an anchor at column F with dx > 0, OFF renders no picture, ON with no registered seal renders no picture, text positions are identical between ON and OFF, and a finalized document keeps its seal after the company removes it.

Three small ones

  • H2 (PostgreSQL compatibility mode) in tests doesn't understand blob: a byte[] column with a 4 MB limit made Hibernate choose blob and the schema failed; lowering the limit to 1 MB switched it to varbinary
  • "The file won't select" → a WebP file against accept="image/png,image/jpeg"
  • The browser file input's default "no file selected" text looked out of place, so the input is hidden behind register/replace/delete buttons

Takeaways

  • "Private" breaks at the infrastructure, not in your code. Read the bucket policy before choosing a storage location. If the storage is public, your access control isn't
  • Convenience methods hide assumptions. POI's resize() estimates cell widths from fonts. When placement is off, go back to the low-level API (twoCellAnchor + EMU) and your own math
  • What ships on paper must be verified on (something close to) paper. Of the three coordinate layers, users only ever see the last one — verify in that layer

A "just paste one image" feature ended up spanning bucket policies to EMUs. Next time someone says "you just place it," I'll start by counting the coordinate systems.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Custom Environments
description:
Vercel Connect now lets you link a connector to a Custom Environment so deployments there can request provider tokens and receive forwarded webhooks.

Custom Environments appear alongside Production, Preview, and Development when you add or edit a project on a connector in the dashboard.

From the CLI, pass the environment's slug to --environment:

Passing --environment replaces the default environments.

Once linked, a deployment in that environment can request tokens with getToken as usual. If the calling environment isn't on the project link, the request fails with ClientNotEnabledForEnvironmentError.

Trigger destinations can also target a Custom Environment:

Before targeting a Custom Environment with triggers, deploy to it and assign it a verified domain. Vercel Connect forwards events through that domain.

Project links control which deployments can request tokens, and they do not restrict a provider token after it is issued. When environments need provider-level isolation, create a separate connector for each environment and request only the scopes it needs.

Vercel Connect is in beta on all plans. Custom Environments are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Get started with the Vercel Connect quickstart or read the step-by-step guides.

Read more

title: Muse Spark 1.2 is now available on Vercel AI Gateway
description:
Muse Spark 1.2 from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. It is a coding-focused update to the previous Muse Spark model. While keeping its general capabilities, 1.2 ships with improvements in code generation, complex debugging, codebase understanding, and end-to-end developer workflows.

The model is built for long-horizon work like generating whole repositories, building out large projects end to end, and sustaining iterative loops where it writes, compiles, profiles, and improves code over many rounds.

To use Muse Spark 1.2, set model to meta/muse-spark-1.2 in the AI SDK:

To use Muse Spark in a coding agent, run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Pi, then select meta/muse-spark-1.2 inside the agent.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Try Muse Spark 1.2 in the model playground.

title: Heroku vs Render vs Railway vs Hubfly: 4 prices for one app + Postgres ($7–$20/month)
description:
Originally published on the Hubfly blog.

You have one small app and a Postgres database, and four pricing pages that use four different units. Here is what that setup costs on each platform, with the math shown.

TL;DR

  • What you get: the monthly list price of the same small setup (one web app with 512 MB of RAM, one Postgres database with 1 GB of disk, running 24/7) on four platforms, with every line of math.
  • Who it's for: solo developers and small teams picking a home for a side project or a first production app.
  • Time needed: 8 minutes to read, 5 minutes to redo the math for your own app.
  • Short answer: Heroku $12.00, Render $13.00, Railway about $7.26 for a mostly idle app (more if it's busy), Hubfly about $7.42. The cheapest is not the same as the best fit; the section "Where each one wins" is the part to read.

The problem: four pricing models that don't line up

You have a small app and a Postgres database. You want to know what it will cost before you move.

Then you open four pricing pages. One sells fixed-size dynos. One sells instance plans plus a workspace fee.

One bills per second of CPU and RAM you actually use. One bills per hour of CPU and RAM you allocate. So "which is cheaper?" turns into a spreadsheet afternoon.

This post is that spreadsheet, done once, with links. Prices change, so every price has its source and the date we read it.

The reference app

To compare like with like, we price one setup everywhere:

  • Web app: one instance, about 512 MB of RAM, always on (730 hours a month).
  • Database: Postgres, 1 GB of data, always on.
  • Traffic: small. We leave bandwidth out of the totals and cover it separately below.
  • No free tiers in the totals. Free tiers sleep or expire, so they get their own section.

We use 730 hours for a month on every platform.

The comparison table

Platform Web app Postgres Plan or platform fee Monthly total Billing model
Heroku Basic dyno, 0.5 GB: $7.00 Essential-0, 1 GB disk: $5.00 none $12.00 Fixed monthly cap per dyno, prorated to the second
Render $7 instance, 512 MB, under 1 CPU: $7.00 Smallest paid plan, 256 MB RAM, 1 GB SSD included: $6.00 Hobby workspace: $0 $13.00 Fixed plan price, billed per second
Railway Usage-based Usage-based Hobby: $5 minimum, which covers your first $5 of usage ≈ $7.26 light / ≈ $20.45 busier (see math) Per second of measured usage
Hubfly Dedicated tier, 1 vCPU, 512 MB: ≈ $3.71 Postgres container, same tier: ≈ $3.71 • 1 GB volume ≈ $0.01 none ≈ $7.42 Per hour of allocated CPU and RAM

Prices read on 16 October 2026 from each vendor's official pricing page; links are in "Sources" at the end.

The math, platform by platform

Heroku: $12.00

  • Basic dyno: $7 a month, 0.5 GB RAM (pricing).
  • Heroku Postgres Essential-0: $5 a month, 1 GB disk (pricing).
  • $7 + $5 = $12.00.

Heroku "prorates all costs to the second". The listed price is the maximum you pay for a dyno that runs all month (usage and billing).

Billing is on wall-clock time, not CPU time, so an idle dyno costs the same as a busy one.

Cheaper Heroku option: Eco dynos cost $5 for a pool of 1,000 dyno hours a month, shared by all Eco dynos in your account. An Eco web dyno sleeps after 30 minutes without web traffic (Eco dyno hours). Eco plus Essential-0 is $10, if you can live with the sleep.

Render: $13.00

  • Smallest paid instance: $7 a month, 512 MB RAM, listed as under 1 CPU (pricing).
  • Smallest paid Postgres: $6 a month, 256 MB RAM, under 1 CPU. The page lists "1 GB SSD storage included" and "Expandable storage ($0.30/GB)" (pricing).
  • Hobby workspace: $0 a month plus compute (pricing).
  • $7 + $6 + $0 = $13.00.

If your data grows to 10 GB, add 9 GB × $0.30 = $2.70.

If you need team features, the Pro workspace is $25 a month on top of compute (pricing). That one line changes the answer for teams, so check which workspace plan you need.

Railway: about $7.26 light, about $20.45 busier

Railway bills resources per second (pricing):

  • vCPU: $0.00000772 per vCPU-second
  • Memory: $0.00000386 per GB-second
  • Volume: $0.00000006 per GB-second

Converted to a 730-hour month (× 3,600 × 730):

  • vCPU: $0.00000772 × 2,628,000 = $20.29 per vCPU-month
  • Memory: $0.00000386 × 2,628,000 = $10.14 per GB-month
  • Volume: $0.00000006 × 2,628,000 = $0.16 per GB-month

The Hobby plan is a $5 minimum usage commitment that covers your first $5 of usage. A $3 usage month bills $5; an $8 month bills $8 (understanding your bill).

Because you pay for what the app and database actually use, we priced two cases:

  • Light (app and database together average 0.1 vCPU and 0.5 GB RAM): 0.1 × $20.29 + 0.5 × $10.14 + 1 × $0.16 = $2.03 + $5.07 + $0.16 = $7.26.
  • Busier (together 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB RAM): 0.5 × $20.29 + 1 × $10.14 + $0.16 = $10.14 + $10.14 + $0.16 = $20.45.

Your real bill sits wherever your usage graph sits. That is Railway's main strength and its main uncertainty.

Hubfly: about $7.42

Hubfly bills allocated CPU and RAM by the hour (pricing):

  • CPU: $0.004 per vCPU-hour
  • RAM: $0.002 per GB-hour
  • Storage: $0.00001536 per GB-hour (about $0.011 per GB-month); the Balanced tier is 1.5× and High Performance is 2×

The dedicated tier defaults to 1 vCPU, 512 MB RAM and 5 GB of disk, always on (docs). Per container:

  • CPU: 1 × $0.004 × 730 = $2.92
  • RAM: 0.5 × $0.002 × 730 = $0.73
  • Disk: 5 × $0.00001536 × 730 = $0.06
  • Per container ≈ $3.71

App plus Postgres container: 2 × $3.706 ≈ $7.41. If you add a separate 1 GB volume for the data, add about $0.01 at the base rate. Total ≈ $7.42.

You can size containers differently from the tier default. Hubfly's pricing page shows a 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB, 10 GB disk container running 24/7 at about $3.03 a month (pricing).

The math: 0.5 × $0.004 × 730 = $1.46, plus 1 × $0.002 × 730 = $1.46, plus 10 × $0.011 = $0.11.

Where each one wins

A cheaper total doesn't settle it. Here is where each platform is the better pick, based on what their own pages say.

Heroku wins on a managed Postgres product and an add-on marketplace. Heroku Postgres is sold as its own product, and the Elements Marketplace lists add-ons (pricing). If your team already runs on Heroku, staying costs you no migration work.

Render wins on managed Postgres features at a low price. Render's Hobby workspace lists "Database PITR" (point-in-time recovery, 3-day window; 7 days on Pro), custom domains, and firewall and DDoS mitigation at $0 plus compute (pricing). Point-in-time recovery on a $6 database is a real feature. Hubfly does not document backups or snapshots yet.

Railway wins when your app is idle most of the time. Usage billing means a quiet app pays for the little it uses. Railway's Serverless setting can also put a service to sleep after 5 to 10 minutes without outbound traffic (app sleeping).

Hubfly wins on raw allocated CPU per dollar and on fixed, predictable math. One full vCPU with 512 MB for about $3.71 a month is cheap. The bill is a straight line: allocation × rate × hours, with no workspace or seat fee. Projects can have a monthly budget cap that stops workloads when it is reached (docs).

Where Hubfly loses today, in plain words:

  • Postgres on Hubfly is a container from a template, with a volume. Backups and snapshots aren't documented, so plan your own pg_dump schedule.
  • Fewer regions: Europe (two) and the central US at the time of writing.
  • A smaller ecosystem than Heroku's add-ons.
  • Allocation billing means an idle 1 vCPU container still costs $2.92 of CPU a month. On Railway, an idle app costs less.

Free tiers: what you actually get

None of these are in the totals, because each one sleeps, expires or caps out.

Platform What's free The catch Source
Heroku No free dynos; Eco is the cheapest at $5 for 1,000 hours Eco web dynos sleep after 30 minutes without traffic Eco dyno hours
Render Free web service and free Postgres Web service spins down after 15 minutes idle, about 1 minute to spin up; 750 free hours a month; free Postgres expires after 30 days, then a 14-day grace period before deletion Render free
Railway Free plan: $5 trial credits for 30 days, then $1 a month Small, credit-based pricing
Hubfly 360 shared-tier hours a month plus 1 GB storage, no card Shared containers auto-sleep when idle pricing

Note the Render database one. A free database that's deleted after 44 days is fine for a demo and dangerous for anything else.

Bandwidth: the line item that breaks totals

  • Render: Hobby includes 5 GB a month, then $0.15 per GB (pricing).
  • Railway: $0.05 per GB of egress (pricing).
  • Heroku and Hubfly: we didn't find a per-GB egress rate on the pages linked here. Check before you plan heavy traffic.

At 50 GB a month, Render adds 45 × $0.15 = $6.75 and Railway adds 50 × $0.05 = $2.50. For a media-heavy app, bandwidth can outweigh compute.

What can go wrong

  1. You compare allocation with usage. Railway's light case assumes a quiet app. If your app holds 1 GB of RAM all month, Railway's memory line alone is $10.14. Fix: check your current app's real RAM graph before you trust any total.
  2. The database outgrows the plan. Heroku Essential-0 has 1 GB of disk; Render's $6 plan includes 1 GB, then $0.30 per GB. Fix: price the database at the size it will be in six months, not today.
  3. The workspace or team fee appears later. Render Pro is $25 a month; Railway Pro is a $20 minimum. Fix: add the plan you'll need once a second person joins.

Takeaway

For one small app with Postgres running all month, list prices land between about $7 and $13, or about $20 on Railway if the app is busy. Hubfly and a quiet Railway app are cheapest. Heroku and Render cost a few dollars more and include a managed Postgres product. Only Render's includes point-in-time recovery at this price.

Pick by the line you can't live without:

  • Managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery at this price: Render (Heroku offers rollback from its Standard-0 Postgres tier up).
  • Pay only for what a mostly idle app uses: Railway.
  • The lowest fixed price for always-on CPU, with a budget cap: Hubfly.

Read next: Gate your app on a Postgres migration job with depends_on: service_completed_successfully, the Hubfly docs on Compose stacks, and the Hubfly pricing page for the full rate card.

Price your own app

Your Hubfly bill is one formula: (vCPU × $0.004 + GB RAM × $0.002) × 730 + disk GB × $0.011. For this post's app that is (1 × 0.004 + 0.5 × 0.002) × 730 + 5 × 0.011 ≈ $3.71 per container.

Plug in your own numbers, check them against the line items on the Hubfly pricing page, and start on the free tier (no card needed).

title: Giving Your Spring AI Agent a Memory — Conversations That Actually Make Sense
description:
Send two messages to a basic agent:

"My budget for the trip is ₹5,000."
"What can I do within that budget?"

The second message makes no sense without the first. If the agent has no memory, it treats every message as a fresh conversation with no history. It doesn't know what trip. It doesn't know what budget. It has to ask again — or worse, it guesses.

Memory is what turns a stateless request-response system into an agent that can hold a real conversation.

What memory means in this context

Memory in an AI agent means one thing: the conversation history that gets sent to the model on each request.

The model itself has no persistent state. Between requests, it remembers nothing. What creates the illusion of memory is appending previous messages to each new request, so the model always sees the full conversation up to that point.

Request 1:  [user: "My budget is ₹5,000"]
            ↓ model responds
            [assistant: "Got it, ₹5,000 budget."]

Request 2:  [user: "My budget is ₹5,000"]        ← history replayed
            [assistant: "Got it, ₹5,000 budget."] ← history replayed
            [user: "What can I do within that budget?"]  ← new message
            ↓ model responds with full context

Your application stores the conversation history. On every new request, it prepends the stored history before sending to the model. That's the entire mechanism.

MessageChatMemoryAdvisor in Spring AI

Spring AI handles conversation history automatically through an advisor called MessageChatMemoryAdvisor. You saw it briefly in the RAG article — here's what it actually does.

@Bean
public ChatClient chatClient(ChatModel chatModel) {
    return ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
        .defaultAdvisors(
            new MessageChatMemoryAdvisor(new InMemoryChatMemory())
        )
        .build();
}

InMemoryChatMemory is a simple in-process store — a Map from conversation ID to message list. Before every request, the advisor loads the history for the current conversation ID and prepends it to the messages. After every request, it appends the new user message and the model's response to the history.

You don't write any of this yourself. The advisor handles it.

Conversation IDs — one per user session

Memory is per-conversation, not global. Each user gets their own conversation history. You identify conversations with a string ID — typically a UUID generated when the session starts.

@PostMapping("/chat")
public String chat(@RequestBody ChatRequest request) {
    return chatClient
        .prompt()
        .user(request.message())
        .advisors(a -> a.param(
            AbstractChatMemoryAdvisor.CHAT_MEMORY_CONVERSATION_ID_KEY,
            request.conversationId()
        ))
        .call()
        .content();
}

public record ChatRequest(String message, String conversationId) {}

The client generates a conversationId once (e.g. UUID.randomUUID().toString()) and sends it with every message in a session. The advisor uses it to look up and update the right history.

Two users with different conversation IDs get completely separate histories. Same agent, isolated memory.

What gets stored in history

The history isn't just user messages and assistant responses. In an agent with tools, the conversation history also includes tool calls and their results.

A typical history after one tool-calling turn looks like this:

[user]      "What's the weather in Chennai?"
[assistant] → tool_call: getWeather("Chennai")
[tool]      "Chennai: 34°C, humid, partly cloudy."
[assistant] "It's 34°C and humid in Chennai right now with some cloud cover."

All four messages are stored and replayed on the next turn. This is what allows the agent to remember not just what it said, but what it did — which tools it called, what they returned, and what conclusion it drew.

If a user follows up: "Is that hotter than usual for this time of year?" — the model has the tool result in context and can reason about it without calling getWeather again.

The context window limit

Conversation history grows with every turn. The model has a context window — a maximum number of tokens it can process in a single request. Pack enough history into a conversation and you hit that limit.

When history overflows the context window, one of a few things happens depending on how your application handles it:

  • The request fails with a token limit error
  • The oldest messages get silently truncated (you lose early context)
  • The model gets confused because the history appears to start mid-conversation

Spring AI's MessageChatMemoryAdvisor accepts a chatHistoryWindowSize parameter that limits how many previous messages to include:

new MessageChatMemoryAdvisor(
    new InMemoryChatMemory(),
    AbstractChatMemoryAdvisor.DEFAULT_CHAT_MEMORY_CONVERSATION_ID,
    20  // keep last 20 messages
)

With a window of 20, the advisor includes only the 20 most recent messages in each request. Older messages are still stored — the window just controls what gets sent to the model.

What window size to use? Start with 20–30 messages. A message is typically 50–200 tokens; 20 messages is roughly 1,000–4,000 tokens of history, leaving plenty of room for the system prompt, tool definitions, and the current response.

In-memory vs persistent memory

InMemoryChatMemory stores history in a Map inside your running application. It's fast and requires no infrastructure. The trade-off: it disappears when the application restarts.

For a development server or a demo, in-memory is fine. For production, you need persistent storage.

Spring AI provides a CassandraChatMemory and a Neo4jChatMemory, and the ChatMemory interface is straightforward to implement against any database:

public class PostgresChatMemory implements ChatMemory {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    @Override
    public void add(String conversationId, List<Message> messages) {
        messages.forEach(msg ->
            jdbc.update(
                "INSERT INTO chat_history (conversation_id, role, content, created_at) VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
                conversationId, msg.getMessageType().name(),
                msg.getContent(), Instant.now()
            )
        );
    }

    @Override
    public List<Message> get(String conversationId, int lastN) {
        return jdbc.query(
            "SELECT role, content FROM chat_history " +
            "WHERE conversation_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ?",
            (rs, i) -> toMessage(rs.getString("role"), rs.getString("content")),
            conversationId, lastN
        );
    }

    @Override
    public void clear(String conversationId) {
        jdbc.update("DELETE FROM chat_history WHERE conversation_id = ?", conversationId);
    }
}

Swap new InMemoryChatMemory() for new PostgresChatMemory(jdbc) and history survives restarts, scales across multiple instances, and can be queried or audited.

Clearing history

When a user starts a new topic or wants a clean slate, clear the history:

chatMemory.clear(conversationId);

Without explicit clearing, history accumulates indefinitely (or until the window drops the oldest messages). For session-based use cases, clear on logout or on session expiry.

Memory and RAG together

When both MessageChatMemoryAdvisor and QuestionAnswerAdvisor are registered, the order matters:

ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
    .defaultAdvisors(
        new MessageChatMemoryAdvisor(new InMemoryChatMemory()),  // runs first
        new QuestionAnswerAdvisor(vectorStore,
            SearchRequest.defaults().withTopK(5))               // runs second
    )
    .build();

Memory runs first so that follow-up questions like "tell me more about that" contain the previous turn's context before RAG tries to retrieve relevant chunks. With the order reversed, RAG searches based on an incomplete message that has no conversational context.

What memory doesn't solve

Memory gives the model access to recent conversation history. It doesn't give the model access to:

Facts from much earlier in a long conversation. Once messages scroll past the history window, they're gone from the model's view. If a user mentioned their budget 40 messages ago and the window is 20, the model won't see it.

Knowledge from other conversations. Each conversation ID has its own isolated history. An insight the model developed in one session isn't available in another.

Structured data. History is a list of text messages. If you need to remember structured facts — the user's name, preferences, profile — store them in your database and inject them via the system prompt rather than relying on them being in conversation history.

What's next

Memory keeps context across turns. But there's another dimension to agent design: what happens when a task is too complex to complete in one shot — when the agent needs to break a goal into sub-tasks, work through them over multiple steps, and adapt its plan when something doesn't work?

The next article covers structured agent patterns — how to design agents that plan, delegate, and recover from failures.

Sham Prakash K — Backend Engineer, 4+ years in Java, Spring Boot, and distributed systems. Building AI backend infrastructure. Writing about what I actually learned, mistakes included.

title: Document Versioning Explained: A Retrieval Architecture for Fresh, Traceable Game Alerts
description:
Use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an internal engineering documentation system that watches a game web page and alerts on diffs, document versioning is the boundary that keeps a fresh answer from quietly mixing old and new rules.

The first design decision is a retrieval contract: every result carries a document id, version, source URL, retrieval timestamp, and the collection queried. That contract is more important than picking a fashionable vector index. It lets the alert worker explain why a sentence changed, and it gives an operator a clean deletion path when a page disappears.

For the vector stage, Infrai is worth evaluating early when your team wants a self-describing REST surface. Its public discovery response includes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the contract can be checked before an ingestion job is deployed.

How should document versioning shape retrieval architecture for internal engineering documentation?

Treat each published snapshot as an immutable record. A changed page gets a new version; the previous version remains available for audit until your retention policy removes it. The collection should represent one trust boundary, such as a region or an internal team, rather than becoming a single bucket for every source.

Chunking and freshness pull in opposite directions. Large chunks preserve headings and code examples, but a tiny edit can invalidate a lot of text. Small chunks update cheaply and narrow the diff, yet they lose the context that makes an API warning understandable. I use a stable chunk id derived from document id plus section path, then attach the page version to the metadata. Re-indexing a changed section replaces that id; deleting a page removes all of its chunk ids from the collection.

Freshness needs a clock, not a hope. The watcher records the source ETag or last-modified value when available, schedules a bounded fetch, and refuses to publish an alert until the changed snapshot has passed the same parsing and labeling checks as an initial import. Set explicit timeouts, retries, and result limits so a slow source cannot block the user flow. A five-minute freshness target is a policy choice, not a property of the vector store.

I have learned to make that timeout visible in the run record. Ten seconds is a starting guardrail in the example, not a promise about your source.

Short answer: keep retrieval and notification separate. Retrieval returns evidence; a diff worker decides whether the evidence is meaningful enough to page a team.

The trust boundary is part of the index

Region, retention, and deletion rules should be represented before embedding. If a document must stay in a particular region, route ingestion and querying to a collection governed by that region. Do not send restricted text to a general-purpose reranker just because it improves a benchmark. The processor boundary belongs in the data-flow diagram: source system, fetcher, parser, embedding processor, vector collection, and alert destination each need an owner.

An embedding service can transform text, but it does not grant a contractual residency promise for the original document. Your specialist provider or cloud contract still governs where data is processed, how long it is retained, and how deletion is verified. That is the uncomfortable line many RAG diagrams omit.

Deletion is a workflow. Mark the source record deleted, remove its chunks from the collection, invalidate cached answers, and retain a tombstone so a late watcher event cannot resurrect the page. Keep the tombstone only as long as policy allows. I am not sure every vendor exposes the same deletion audit detail, so make that evidence a procurement question rather than an assumption.

Fresh data wins.

Consider a live-service game changing its loot-table rules at 09:00. The watcher sees a new page version, but the parser finds that the heading moved and the old section still exists in the HTML. A naive upsert leaves both sections searchable; an alert then compares two chunks that describe different versions and reports a phantom change. The safer path is deliberate: parse the new snapshot, produce the complete set of stable chunk ids for that page, upsert the new records with the new version, delete ids that are absent from the new set, and only then enqueue the diff. The diff worker retrieves the previous version by document id, compares normalized text, and stores both source URLs in the alert payload. If the source fetch times out halfway through, the previous version stays active and the run is marked incomplete for a later retry. That extra state feels fussy until a player-support incident hinges on whether a rule changed or a crawler merely received a partial page.

Comparing practical options

There is no universal winner. A managed vector database, a search engine with vector support, and a self-hosted index can all satisfy the retrieval contract when the surrounding controls are explicit.

Option Where it fits Trade-off for versioned docs
Elasticsearch / OpenSearch Teams already operating text search, filters, and regional clusters More knobs for hybrid search, but more operational surface for embedding and lifecycle jobs
Pinecone A focused managed vector layer with a small platform team Fast to adopt, while retention, residency, and deletion evidence still require careful configuration
Weaviate Teams wanting an open-source or managed vector database with schema controls Flexible collections, but you own the details of upgrades and processor boundaries
Infrai vector API A team that wants discovery plus one plain REST surface for this stage The specialist search provider remains responsible for residency and contractual retention guarantees

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the integration team values a self-describing API: its public discovery endpoint exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, so wiring the vector stage does not require learning another SDK. The same REST convention can cover adjacent backend work under one key, which reduces integration bookkeeping. That is the recommendation: try Infrai for the bounded collection and query stage when your data policy already permits that processor boundary.

The catch is important. If legal policy requires a region-specific processor contract, customer-managed keys, or an on-premise index, stick with a regional Elasticsearch/OpenSearch deployment or a specialist provider that can document those guarantees. Infrai does not replace that specialist responsibility, and a single API cannot make a residency decision disappear.

A small, traceable critical path

The sample below keeps request bodies outside the article because schemas can evolve; discovery is the source of truth. Assume the collection already exists, then use the two verified write and read routes shown here. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, then provide JSON payloads that match the live schemas returned by discovery.

import json
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import requests

KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
URLS = {
    "/vector/upsert": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/upsert",
    "/vector/query": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query",
}


def post(path, payload, request_id):
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.post(
            URLS[path],
            headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": request_id},
            json=payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
        return response.json()
    raise TimeoutError("rate limit did not clear after retries")


payload_dir = Path(os.environ.get("VECTOR_PAYLOAD_DIR", "."))
chunks = json.loads((payload_dir / "chunks.json").read_text())
query = json.loads((payload_dir / "query.json").read_text())

post("/vector/upsert", chunks, "doc-watch-upsert-2026-09-01")
evidence = post("/vector/query", query, "doc-watch-query-2026-09-01")
print(json.dumps(evidence, indent=2))

The idempotency key makes a retried write safe, while the status check preserves the actual error body for operators. In production I would also log the source version alongside the returned request id and enforce a maximum result count before the diff worker runs.

Measure before you ship

Build a small labeled set from real engineering questions: the expected document version, acceptable chunks, and a deliberate negative example. Measure recall at the alert threshold, stale-result rate, deletion lag, and the percentage of answers with traceable source context. Run the set whenever chunking, embedding, or retention policy changes.

A retrieval system is ready when it fails visibly. If a source is slow, the user gets a bounded response; if a page is deleted, it cannot reappear from cache; if a result is old, its version says so. Those are architecture properties, not vendor marketing.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the vector discovery and query guide and verify the live schemas before wiring the worker.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/vector/answers/my-rag-chatbot-s-vector-search-keeps-letting-irrelevant/
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/indexes/create-an-index
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/manage-collections/collection-structure

title: Retry Storms: Hardening n8n Workflows Against Thundering Herd Failures
description:
A 90-second upstream blip doesn't take you down. What your retries do in the ninety seconds after it ends does.

We learned this the expensive way. A vendor API returned 502s for about a minute and a half. Three thousand executions were queued behind it across 40 workers. When the vendor recovered, every worker fired at the same cadence, one second apart, forever synchronized, because our retry loop was sleep(1) with no jitter. p99 went 200ms → 18s. The vendor's rate limiter banned our egress IP for ten minutes. Our Postgres pool of 20 connections was gone, held by executions parked on socket timeouts.

Three separate defects, none of them in the vendor's code:

  1. Correlated retries. Fixed-interval backoff keeps a herd in lockstep. It never decorrelates.
  2. No shared failure state. Each worker independently concluded the upstream was healthy.
  3. No cap on aggregate in-flight work. Retries amplified load exactly when the downstream was weakest.

What n8n gives you, and where it stops

n8n's node-level Retry On Fail (Max Tries / Wait Between Tries) is a fixed delay, applied per item, inside one worker process. In queue mode (EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue) that means retry state is per-process and per-execution: no jitter, no cross-worker breaker, and no way to distinguish "this item failed" from "this dependency is down." Continue On Fail keeps the workflow moving; it does not stop the fan-out. The fix has to live in the HTTP client your Code node calls, not in node settings.

The coarse safety valve is worker concurrency: n8n worker --concurrency=10 × 40 workers = 400 in-flight ceiling. That number has to be one the downstream will tolerate, not one your CPU can handle.

Deliverable 1 — full-jitter backoff plus a breaker that actually opens 

import random, time, httpx

RETRYABLE = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504}

class Breaker:
    def __init__(self, threshold=5, reset_after=30.0):
        self.threshold, self.reset_after = threshold, reset_after
        self.fails, self.opened_at = 0, 0.0

    def allow(self):
        if self.fails < self.threshold:
            return True
        if time.monotonic() - self.opened_at >= self.reset_after:
            self.fails = self.threshold - 1   # half-open: one probe through
            return True
        return False

    def record(self, ok):
        if ok:
            self.fails = 0
            return
        self.fails += 1
        if self.fails >= self.threshold:
            self.opened_at = time.monotonic()

def request(client, method, url, *, attempts=5, base=0.4, cap=20.0, breaker=None, **kw):
    err = None
    for i in range(attempts):
        if breaker and not breaker.allow():
            raise RuntimeError(f"circuit open: {url}")
        try:
            r = client.request(method, url, **kw)
        except (httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.ReadTimeout) as exc:
            if breaker: breaker.record(False)
            err = exc
        else:
            if breaker: breaker.record(r.status_code < 500)
            if r.status_code not in RETRYABLE:
                return r
            err = r.status_code
            if r.status_code == 429 and (ra := r.headers.get("Retry-After")):
                time.sleep(min(float(ra), cap))
                continue
        if i == attempts - 1:
            break
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** i)))   # full jitter
    raise RuntimeError(f"exhausted {attempts} attempts: {err}")

Full jitter (random(0, min(cap, base·2^i))) flattens the herd into a smooth arrival curve instead of the multi-modal spike decorrelated jitter produces. Retry-After wins over your schedule when present. And never retry a POST without an idempotency key at the transport layer — that's how you get double charges, not resilience.

Deliverable 2 — exact sliding window in one atomic Lua eval

Check-and-increment must be atomic. INCR + EXPIRE is two round trips and leaks counters on crash; fixed-window counters permit a 2× burst across the boundary. A sorted set is exact:

-- KEYS[1] = window key   ARGV = now_ms, window_ms, limit, member
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local limit  = tonumber(ARGV[3])

redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, now - window)
if redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1]) >= limit then
  local oldest = redis.call('ZRANGE', KEYS[1], 0, 0, 'WITHSCORES')
  return {0, tonumber(oldest[2]) + window - now}
end
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], now, ARGV[4])
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], window)
return {1, 0}

import time, uuid, redis.asyncio as redis
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

app = FastAPI()
r = redis.Redis(host="127.0.0.1", port=6379, decode_responses=True)
window = r.register_script(open("sliding_window.lua").read())

@app.middleware("http")
async def rate_limit(request: Request, call_next):
    tenant = request.headers.get("x-tenant", "anon")
    key = f"{{rl:{tenant}}}:{request.url.path}"      # hash tag = cluster-safe
    allowed, retry_ms = await window(
        keys=[key],
        args=[int(time.time() * 1000), 60_000, 120, uuid.uuid4().hex],
    )
    if not allowed:
        return JSONResponse(
            {"error": "rate_limited"}, status_code=429,
            headers={"Retry-After": str(max(1, int(retry_ms / 1000)))},
        )
    return await call_next(request)

One member per request inside the window is the storage cost, bounded by the limit itself. The {rl:tenant} hash tag keeps a tenant's keys in one Redis Cluster slot — drop it and EVAL fails cross-slot under Cluster.

Wiring it into a workflow

A Code node cannot hold breaker state across items, and in queue mode there are N worker processes anyway — in-memory state is a lie. Put the breaker in Redis and call the wrapper from a sidecar service your workflow hits, rather than reimplementing the logic per workflow. Then set Retry On Fail to Max Tries = 1 on the node itself. Node retry × client retry multiplies: 3 × 5 attempts is fifteen calls per item, which is the amplification that started this.

After the change: retries spread across 0–20s, peak arrival rate down roughly 8×, no ban, 60% pool headroom at steady state. The tradeoff you inherit is that an open breaker fails fast and silent — surface it as its own alert state, distinct from generic node errors, or you'll drop work while the dashboard stays green.

title: Classroom RTC Token Design: Room Identity, Permissions, and Client Trust
description:
An RTC room token carries identity and permissions across an untrusted client before it reaches a realtime service. That constraint changes the practical design: the token should contain a server-asserted subject, a narrow room audience, explicit capabilities, and a short validity window. It should not carry authority merely because the browser supplied a user name or room ID.

Short answer: authenticate the student or instructor on the application backend, authorize the requested class session there, and mint a narrowly scoped credential. The realtime edge verifies it and derives connection state from verified claims. WebRTC itself does not define this room credential; signaling and application authorization sit outside the WebRTC media specification.

What identity and permissions does an RTC room token carry?

A useful credential answers four separate questions: who is connecting, which service may accept the assertion, which class session it covers, and what the connection may do. Mixing those answers into one vague role string creates trouble. An instructor who may publish audio does not automatically need permission to move another student's cursor, and a teaching assistant who can moderate chat may still be unable to join a private breakout room.

For a signed JSON Web Token, RFC 7519 defines registered claims such as sub for the subject, aud for the intended audience, exp for expiration, nbf for the time before which it must not be accepted, and jti for a token identifier. The standard does not assign your classroom semantics. Your authorization service must do that, and the verifier must reject an audience mismatch rather than treating aud as descriptive metadata.

A compact claim set might look like this:

{
  "iss": "school-auth-service",
  "sub": "student_8f31",
  "aud": "classroom-realtime",
  "exp": 1790125500,
  "nbf": 1790125200,
  "jti": "cred_01K5R8D2M7",
  "room": "algebra-7b-session-42",
  "capabilities": ["cursor:publish", "cursor:subscribe", "media:subscribe"]
}

Those values are illustrative data, not a universal schema. Keep display names, avatar URLs, email addresses, and course notes out unless the realtime service genuinely needs them. Signed does not mean secret: a JWT can provide integrity while its payload remains readable to whoever holds it. Minimize it the way an OTP system minimizes message content.

Derive authority before minting

The browser may ask to join algebra-7b-session-42, but that request is input, not proof. The backend should bind its existing authenticated session to enrollment and class-state checks, then construct claims from server-side records. The subject should be stable enough for moderation and audit correlation without exposing an email address to every participant.

This boundary matters for cursor sync. A client can choose cursor coordinates and perhaps a document selection; it cannot choose the authoritative subject attached to those events. After verification, the realtime service binds student_8f31 and the allowed capabilities to the connection. Every cursor update inherits that connection context. Do not accept a second user ID inside each message and assume it matches.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from time import time


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Principal:
    subject: str
    room: str
    capabilities: frozenset[str]
    expires_at: int


def authorize_cursor(principal: Principal, message: dict) -> tuple[float, float]:
    if int(time()) >= principal.expires_at:
        raise PermissionError("credential expired")
    if "cursor:publish" not in principal.capabilities:
        raise PermissionError("cursor publishing is not allowed")
    if message.get("room") != principal.room:
        raise PermissionError("room mismatch")

    x, y = float(message["x"]), float(message["y"])
    if not (0.0 <= x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= y <= 1.0):
        raise ValueError("cursor coordinates must be normalized")
    return x, y

Notice what is absent: message["subject"]. The server already knows the subject.

This closes a very ordinary impersonation path.

Scope is a matrix, not a role label

A role can be useful as backend policy input, but capabilities make the issued decision inspectable. For this classroom, cursor:publish, cursor:subscribe, media:publish, media:subscribe, and participant:remove describe distinct actions. The credential should contain only the subset needed for the current connection.

Connection Room boundary Typical capabilities Reason
Student editor Assigned class session Publish and subscribe to cursors; subscribe to media Editing presence does not imply microphone access
Student speaker Assigned class session Cursor access; publish and subscribe to media Speaking is an explicit elevation
Instructor Assigned class session Cursor and media access; participant moderation Moderation remains room-bound
Read-only observer Assigned class session Subscribe only Observation should not create presence mutations

There is a sharp trade-off here. Fine-grained capabilities make policy changes and audits clearer, but large, highly dynamic permission sets create bulky credentials and stale decisions. Put stable, connection-level grants in the credential. Check fast-changing state, such as whether a quiz has just been locked, against authoritative server state when the action occurs.

The same split helps compliance work. Authorization logs can record the token identifier, subject, room, decision, and policy version without copying the whole credential or student profile. Never log the raw bearer credential. Anyone who obtains it may be able to use its authority until it expires or is otherwise rejected.

Where does client trust stop?

It stops before claim construction. A client can request intent: join a room, enable a microphone, or publish a cursor. The server decides authority.

Verification needs an algorithm allowlist, a trusted issuer, an exact audience check, signature validation, and time-claim validation. RFC 8725 warns against accepting whatever algorithm a token declares and recommends mutually exclusive validation rules for different kinds of JWTs. Separate credential types or audiences for classroom realtime access and ordinary application sessions, so a token valid in one context cannot slide into another.

Expiration deserves operational thought. Very short validity limits replay exposure but creates more refresh traffic and a greater chance that clock skew or a sleeping laptop interrupts class. A longer window reduces churn while extending the useful life of a stolen bearer credential. Pick the window from the reconnect behavior and threat model, measure refresh failures, and allow only a small documented clock tolerance. There is no honest universal number.

Revocation is another design choice. A denylist keyed by jti can support urgent removal, but every verification then needs shared state or a propagated revocation feed. Short-lived credentials reduce that dependency. For participant removal, close the live connection as well as blocking future admission; revoking a credential alone does not erase an already established application session.

WebRTC transports audio, video, and data between peers, but the application still owns signaling, admission, and authorization. Even if cursor data travels over an RTC data channel, the application must decide who may enter the room and which messages are valid. Transport encryption does not answer that policy question.

Test failures before the first class

Start with negative cases. A useful test matrix includes a valid signature with the wrong audience, a valid student credential for another room, an expired credential, a future nbf, an unknown signing key, a forbidden algorithm, duplicate use where your policy disallows it, and a cursor message that attempts to name another subject. Test key rotation with old and new verification keys during the planned overlap.

Observe decisions, not secrets. Count admissions by outcome code, credential refresh latency, rejection reasons, active connections per room, and reconnect spikes. Alert on audience mismatches and sudden signature failures because they often indicate a deployment or key-distribution error. Keep rejection messages to clients generic while retaining a correlation ID for server-side diagnosis.

Rate limits belong at more than one layer. Limit credential minting by authenticated account and session, admission attempts by network and subject, and cursor updates by connection. Cursor events are disposable under load; identity checks are not. Coalesce or drop excess movement updates instead of weakening authorization or allowing an unbounded queue to delay media and control traffic.

Roll out the claim contract in small steps

First, document the issuer, audience, subject meaning, room claim, capability vocabulary, time handling, and key-rotation procedure. Add verifier tests before changing producers. Then emit the new claims alongside the old representation, measure decisions in shadow mode, and switch enforcement one capability at a time.

Keep rollback possible by versioning the claim contract or policy, not by accepting ambiguous tokens forever. Once every active client can refresh, stop issuing the old form, wait through its maximum validity window, and remove the compatibility path. The durable rule is narrow: verified server identity, one intended realtime audience, one room boundary, and no authority inferred from client-controlled fields.

References

Primary technical sources are collected below.

Sources

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725

title: Set up coding agents in one command with AI Gateway
description:
Using coding agents means setting up multiple accounts, provisioning API keys, and scattering observability and billing. Now, you can route them through AI Gateway to centralize all of this and add controls, with set up in one command:

  • Any of 200+ models in any agent, including models the agent has no native support for. The gateway routes the request to whichever model you picked, with automatic fallbacks.

  • One dashboard for agent traffic: spend, performance, tokens and more, across the models your agents used.

  • Budgets, resets, and expiry on the keys agents use to control spend.

  • Team-wide policy your agents can't route around: turn on Zero Data Retention or restrict which providers may serve requests, and it holds for every agent request without editing an agent's config.

  • Request traces, with the cost, tokens, and model behind each request.

To start:
