title: Building the MyZubster Metaverse: Secure Sessions, Verified Identities and the Road to Realtime
description:
Building the MyZubster Metaverse: Secure Sessions, Verified Identities and the Road to Realtime

The MyZubster Metaverse is evolving from a visual experiment into a real, testable multiplayer environment.

Our objective is not simply to render avatars on a page. We are building an open-source world where guest users, verified contributors and independent communities can interact through a shared identity and knowledge layer.

The public entry point is now available here:

👉 https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse

This article explains what we have implemented, the security work completed in our latest development cycle, the current architecture and what still needs to be built before the platform can be considered production-ready at scale.

What the MyZubster Metaverse is

The MyZubster Metaverse is intended to connect several parts of the ecosystem:

  • public and verified user profiles;
  • GitHub contributor identities;
  • Zorgax characters;
  • Verified Knowledge;
  • community spaces;
  • Development Requests;
  • open-source contributions;
  • optional rewards and bounties;
  • future immersive WebXR experiences.

The current version focuses on the foundations: identity, presence, sessions and authenticated world actions.

Users can currently enter the world as guests without requiring:

  • a cryptocurrency wallet;
  • identity documents;
  • a GitHub account;
  • an installed application.

Verified MyZubster explorers can also be displayed with their associated public GitHub identity.

This gives us two different identity levels:

  1. Guest explorers, who can enter quickly using a public display name.
  2. Verified explorers, whose public character is linked to an authorized account or GitHub identity.

Verification here does not mean KYC or legal identity verification. It only represents a confirmed connection with the declared public account.

What we have implemented

1. Public Metaverse entry point

The production interface now provides a dedicated Metaverse route:


text
https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse
The entry interface includes:
- guest onboarding;
- public display-name selection;
- automatic character creation;
- verified explorer discovery;
- multilingual UI support;
- links to account-based authentication.
The guest path is intentionally lightweight. A user can explore the world without being forced to create a permanent account first.
2. World presence model
The backend maintains a presence record for each active Metaverse participant.
A presence can contain information such as:
{
  sessionId,
  displayName,
  characterId,
  accountId,
  githubLogin,
  position,
  status,
  lastSeenAt
}
The public representation deliberately excludes private credentials and internal security fields.
Presence data is used by the world API to support operations such as:
- joining the world;
- synchronizing visible participants;
- moving a character;
- sending chat messages;
- publishing emotes;
- leaving the world;
- retrieving world events.
Before our latest security work, knowing a public session identifier could potentially be sufficient to target mutable session routes. That is not an acceptable trust boundary for a multiplayer environment.
A public identifier must identify a session, but it must never prove ownership of it.
The latest milestone: possession-bound sessions
Our latest merged pull request introduces possession-based session credentials.
Pull request:
👉 MyZubster PR #34 — Bind world actions to session credentials
Production commit:
148a798
This work creates a security boundary between:
- the public session identifier;
- the private credential required to control that session.
How session creation now works
When a player joins the world, the backend creates:
1. a public sessionId;
2. a cryptographically random private session token.
The token is generated from 32 random bytes, providing 256 bits of entropy.
Conceptually:
const sessionToken = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("base64url");
The raw token is returned to the client only when the session is created.
It is never included in public player data.
3. Only the token digest is stored
The backend does not persist the raw session token.
Instead, it calculates a SHA-256 digest:
const tokenHash = crypto
  .createHash("sha256")
  .update(sessionToken)
  .digest("hex");
The presence record stores the digest:
{
  sessionId,
  sessionTokenHash: tokenHash
}
This reduces the impact of an accidental database disclosure. An attacker reading the presence collection would not immediately obtain the active bearer credentials.
A token cannot be recovered directly from its digest.
4. Constant-time credential verification
Mutable world routes verify the submitted credential against the stored digest.
The comparison uses a constant-time operation to reduce timing side-channel exposure:
crypto.timingSafeEqual(expectedBuffer, receivedBuffer);
Credential validation is centralized in an ownership middleware similar to:
requireOwnedSession
The middleware checks that:
- the session exists;
- the private token was provided;
- the submitted token produces the expected digest;
- the credential belongs to the requested session.
Missing or invalid credentials result in an unauthorized response.
HTTP 401 Unauthorized
5. Protected world actions
The following routes are now protected by session ownership verification:
/sync
/move
/chat
/emote
/leave
/events
Knowing another player’s public sessionId is no longer sufficient to:
- move that player;
- send messages as that player;
- publish their emotes;
- synchronize private session state;
- remove them from the world;
- retrieve protected session events.
This closes an important class of horizontal session-ownership vulnerabilities.
6. Tokens are sent through a dedicated header
The frontend now sends the private credential through:
X-Metaverse-Session-Token: <private-token>
Example:
const createSessionHeaders = (sessionToken) => ({
  "X-Metaverse-Session-Token": sessionToken,
});
The token is not placed inside normal public JSON payloads:
{
  "sessionId": "public-session-id",
  "x": 120,
  "y": 80
}
Separating authorization data from world-state payloads makes the security boundary clearer and reduces the risk of credentials being copied into:
- application logs;
- analytics events;
- public state;
- debugging output;
- serialized world events.
The backend temporarily supports a legacy request-body token for compatibility, but the header is the canonical client mechanism.
7. Credentials remain in memory
The browser keeps the Metaverse session credential in React runtime memory.
We deliberately avoid storing it in:
localStorage
sessionStorage
public profile objects
world event payloads
In-memory credentials disappear when the page or browser session is closed.
This does not eliminate every browser-side threat, especially an active cross-site scripting vulnerability, but it reduces long-lived credential exposure.
Privacy and identity boundaries
The Metaverse must distinguish several concepts that are often incorrectly combined:
Account identity
      ↓
Public profile
      ↓
Character identity
      ↓
Temporary world session
      ↓
Private session credential
A public GitHub profile proves control of a public contributor account only when an authorization flow verifies it.
It does not automatically prove:
- legal identity;
- employment;
- institutional affiliation;
- ownership of an organization;
- eligibility for payment;
- control of a blockchain wallet.
Similarly, the public session ID identifies an active world session, but only the private session credential authorizes mutations for that session.
These distinctions are now documented in the repository’s Metaverse privacy and security documentation.
Testing completed
The session-ownership work includes backend, frontend and static architecture tests.
Backend verification
The targeted backend suites cover:
- secure token creation;
- SHA-256 digest persistence;
- successful authorized operations;
- missing credential rejection;
- invalid credential rejection;
- attempts to mutate another player’s session;
- exclusion of credentials from public payloads;
- protected movement, chat, emote, synchronization and leave routes.
Result:
3 targeted backend suites
22 tests passed
Frontend verification
Frontend tests validate:
- token retention in application memory;
- use of X-Metaverse-Session-Token;
- authorized API requests;
- session-aware world operations;
- absence of the token from public request bodies.
Result:
1 targeted frontend suite
5 tests passed
Build and integration verification
We also completed:
Production frontend build: successful
git diff --check: clean
MYZ-164 Marketplace regression: passed
Vercel preview deployments: successful
Main deployment: successful
The implementation was squash-merged into main and deployed through the production workflow.
Current architecture
The current architecture can be summarized as:
React Metaverse Client
        |
        | HTTPS requests
        | X-Metaverse-Session-Token
        v
Node.js / Express Metaverse API
        |
        | ownership middleware
        | token hashing and verification
        v
Metaverse Presence Storage
        |
        v
Shared world polling and event synchronization
The current system provides a practical foundation, but it is not yet the final realtime architecture.
What still needs to be completed
1. Realtime transport
The current shared-world model still relies on polling-based synchronization in important areas.
The next architectural step is to introduce a proper realtime transport, most likely based on:
- WebSockets;
- Socket.IO;
- Server-Sent Events for selected read-only streams;
- a message broker when horizontal scaling becomes necessary.
Realtime transport must include:
- authenticated connection establishment;
- session-token validation;
- connection-to-session binding;
- reconnect handling;
- event ordering;
- duplicate-event protection;
- backpressure controls;
- presence expiry.
We should not simply move the existing endpoints to WebSockets. The event protocol must be explicitly designed and versioned.
2. Distributed rate limiting
In-memory rate limiting is insufficient when multiple backend instances process requests.
We still need a distributed limiter for:
- session creation;
- movement events;
- chat messages;
- emotes;
- authentication attempts;
- reconnect operations.
Possible storage layers include Redis or another shared atomic counter service.
The limiter should support dimensions such as:
IP address
account ID
session ID
route
world or room ID
time window
Movement events should have different limits from chat or authentication attempts.
3. Session lifecycle and revocation
Possession-bound credentials are now implemented, but lifecycle management needs additional work.
Remaining tasks include:
- explicit session expiration;
- server-side revocation;
- automatic removal of abandoned sessions;
- token rotation;
- reconnect-safe credential renewal;
- maximum active sessions per account;
- logout across devices;
- suspicious-session invalidation.
We also need clear rules for temporary guest sessions versus authenticated persistent characters.
4. Stronger account authentication
Verified characters need a canonical authentication path.
The roadmap includes:
- stable GitHub OAuth integration;
- verified account-to-character linking;
- protection against account-link substitution;
- clear reauthorization flows;
- audit trails for identity changes;
- recovery procedures.
The Metaverse must never trust a GitHub username supplied directly by the browser without verifying control of that account.
5. Privacy-safe analytics
We need operational visibility without building invasive tracking.
Metrics should focus on system health:
- active anonymous sessions;
- session duration ranges;
- API latency;
- reconnect frequency;
- rate-limit events;
- server errors;
- world capacity;
- event throughput.
We should avoid collecting unnecessary personal identifiers.
Analytics data needs:
- documented retention;
- aggregation;
- access restrictions;
- deletion rules;
- explicit separation from public profile data.
6. Reliability and load testing
The next reliability milestone must test realistic concurrent behavior.
Scenarios should include:
- many simultaneous joins;
- movement bursts;
- reconnect storms;
- inactive sessions;
- malformed events;
- duplicate events;
- slow clients;
- backend restarts;
- database latency;
- multiple application instances.
The system needs measurable targets for:
maximum concurrent participants
p95 and p99 API latency
event delivery delay
error rate
recovery time
presence consistency
7. Complete end-to-end acceptance tests
Unit and integration tests are not sufficient for the entire world flow.
We still need automated E2E tests covering:
Guest joins
→ session credential is issued
→ character becomes visible
→ movement is synchronized
→ chat and emotes are authorized
→ another session cannot impersonate the guest
→ reconnect behavior is correct
→ session leaves or expires
Equivalent tests are required for verified characters.
8. WebXR and immersive clients
WebXR remains a later-stage objective.
Before adding immersive rendering, we need to stabilize:
- authentication;
- world protocol;
- realtime synchronization;
- abuse prevention;
- accessibility;
- performance;
- mobile behavior.
The WebXR client should consume the same documented world protocol rather than implementing an independent backend.
This will allow multiple compatible clients:
2D web client
3D browser client
WebXR client
mobile client
community-built client
9. Dependency security debt
The current repository still reports dependency vulnerabilities during npm audit.
The latest Metaverse pull request did not modify package or lock files, so these findings were not introduced by the session-security work.
However, they remain real technical debt.
They must be handled in a separate dependency-hardening cycle involving:
1. vulnerability classification;
2. identification of production versus development exposure;
3. safe direct dependency updates;
4. transitive dependency analysis;
5. regression testing;
6. replacement of abandoned packages;
7. lockfile regeneration;
8. SBOM and audit evidence updates.
We should not hide or disable the audit simply to obtain a green badge.
Proposed next development sequence
The recommended order is:
1. Stabilize session expiration and revocation
2. Implement distributed rate limiting
3. Complete canonical account authentication
4. Design the versioned realtime event protocol
5. Introduce authenticated WebSocket connections
6. Add privacy-safe operational metrics
7. Execute reliability and load testing
8. Complete full guest and verified-user E2E tests
9. Resolve dependency security debt
10. Start the WebXR client milestone
Security and reliability must come before graphical complexity.
Open-source collaboration
We are looking for developers and independent testers interested in:
- Node.js and Express;
- React;
- realtime systems;
- WebSockets;
- MongoDB;
- Redis;
- application security;
- abuse prevention;
- privacy engineering;
- load testing;
- WebXR;
- open-source documentation.
Repository:
👉 https://github.com/danieldirimini-myzubster/myzubster
Public Metaverse:
👉 https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse
Recent security implementation:
👉 https://github.com/danieldirimini-myzubster/myzubster/pull/34
Conclusion
The MyZubster Metaverse now has a stronger technical foundation.
We have moved from trusting public session identifiers to enforcing private possession-bound credentials for mutable world actions.
The platform now includes:
- public guest access;
- verified explorer discovery;
- character presence;
- protected world operations;
- 256-bit session credentials;
- SHA-256 token digests;
- constant-time verification;
- header-based authorization;
- memory-only client credentials;
- backend and frontend tests;
- automated production deployment.
The next challenge is no longer simply creating more visual features.
It is building a secure, realtime, distributed and independently testable world protocol that can support different clients and communities without sacrificing privacy or transparency.
That is the direction of the next MyZubster Metaverse milestones.

title: I almost added a PDF library. A print stylesheet was enough.
description:
I was about to add a PDF library to our project. Then I remembered every browser already has one.

Here's the situation. We make Sheaf, a time tracking and invoicing app. After a week with basically no visitors, we decided to build a few small free tools that people actually search for. The first one was an invoice generator: fill in a form, get a PDF, no account.

My first plan was the usual one. Send the form to the server, render a PDF there, send the file back.

Then I started listing what that meant. A PDF library. Fonts. A server route. Rate limits, because now anyone can make our server do work. And people's client names, addresses and amounts flowing through our backend, for a free tool.

That's a lot of stuff for a page that's supposed to be simple.

So I tried the lazy option instead: window.print() and a print stylesheet.

The preview on the page is already a nice looking invoice, built from normal HTML. When you print, I hide everything except that preview:

@media print {
  @page { margin: 14mm; }
  header, footer, form, .buttons { display: none !important; }
  .invoice { box-shadow: none; padding: 0; }
}

The person clicks Download PDF, the print window opens, they pick "Save as PDF", done. The browser does the font rendering, the page breaks and the file. On phones it goes through the share sheet.

A few things I didn't expect:

Nothing to store means nothing to worry about. The form saves to localStorage so your details are there next time. Nothing leaves the browser, so there's no privacy policy paragraph to write and no data to protect.

It's an easy promise to keep. The page says "Your invoice stays in this browser", and it's true by design, not because of a policy. A lot of free invoice tools ask for your email first. This one can't, because there's nowhere to send it.

It made the next tools easy. The time card calculator and the hourly rate calculator use the same idea: plain HTML, a bit of JavaScript, localStorage, print CSS. Each one took an afternoon.

The one downside: you can't control the browser's own header and footer (the date and URL in the margins). Most browsers have a checkbox to turn them off, and that's fine for an invoice.

If you're about to add a PDF library, try a print stylesheet first. It might be all you need.

Here's the generator if you want to see it working: free invoice generator.

What's something you almost overbuilt before finding the simple version?

title: TypeScript Email Tests Need a Typed Event Boundary
description:
Email tests often start with a simple promise: trigger a signup flow, wait for a message, click the link, and assert the account is active. It sound reasonable. Six months later, the suite is spending more time guessing when an inbox has updated than checking product behavior.

The failure is usually not the mailbox. It is the boundary between the application and the email system. If a test only sees a changing inbox, it has to infer whether a message was created, delivered, retried, or left over from a previous run.

In Node.js and TypeScript, a small typed event boundary makes this much cleaner. The test can ask for evidence of one specific message, with a correlation ID and a clear lifecycle, instead of repeatedly searching for “something new.” This pattern works with a local mail capture service, a temporary disposable mail provider, or a controlled staging inbox.

Why inbox polling makes tests noisy

Polling is attractive because it looks close to how a person checks email. A test sends a request, waits a few seconds, and searches for a subject. But the subject is not an identity. Two parallel tests can create the same account flow, and an old message can satisfy the wrong assertion.

Polling also hides useful states. A timeout could mean the application never queued the email, the worker failed, the provider delayed delivery, or the test used an inbox that expired. Sometimes a retry hide the real problem by finding a later duplicate.

This is why choosing the best throwaway email address is not enough for automation. The fixture needs ownership, expiry, and evidence. A disposable inbox can isolate test data, but it should not be the only source of truth for delivery.

For a broader view of isolating automated actions, an execution envelope for automation is a useful mental model: define what a run owns, what it may consume, and when it is complete.

Define a typed email event

Start with the event your application can emit when it accepts an email for delivery. Keep it small and stable:

export type EmailEvent = {
  id: string;
  runId: string;
  recipient: string;
  template: "verify-account" | "reset-password";
  status: "queued" | "delivered" | "failed";
  messageId?: string;
  createdAt: string;
};

The runId belongs to the test, not to the mailbox. The messageId belongs to the email system. Together they let the test distinguish “this run queued a message” from “the inbox contains a message with a similar subject.” If your delivery provider exposes a provider ID, store that too, but do not make the provider-specific field mandatory for every adapter.

The event payload are deliberately boring. That is a feature. A boring contract is easier to fake locally, record in CI, and inspect when a test fails.

Build the Node.js boundary

Expose a test-only adapter that can wait for an event by runId and template. It should return a typed result or a typed timeout reason, rather than an unstructured null.

type WaitResult =
  | { kind: "matched"; event: EmailEvent }
  | { kind: "timed-out"; runId: string; waitedMs: number };

export async function waitForEmail(
  events: AsyncIterable<EmailEvent>,
  runId: string,
  template: EmailEvent["template"],
  timeoutMs = 10_000,
): Promise<WaitResult> {
  const deadline = Date.now() + timeoutMs;

  for await (const event of events) {
    if (event.runId === runId && event.template === template) {
      return { kind: "matched", event };
    }
    if (Date.now() >= deadline) break;
  }

  return { kind: "timed-out", runId, waitedMs: timeoutMs };
}

In a production test harness, the iterable might be backed by Redis, a webhook receiver, or a local event bus. The important part is the contract: the consumer does not know how delivery is implemented. It only knows how to match its own event.

You can still gets a useful failure when the inbox is empty. Log the run ID, template, last known event status, and elapsed time. That turns “email did not arrive” into “the worker queued verification email, but no delivery event appeared within 10 seconds.”

Keep fixtures isolated and useful

Create one mailbox lease per test or per worker. Include the run ID in the local address when the provider supports it, and expire the lease after the test. If you use a temporary disposable mail service for manual staging checks, treat it as an inspection tool, not as a substitute for application events.

Also redact message bodies in CI logs. Verification URLs contain secrets, and a passing test should not leave reusable tokens in build output. The privacy tradeoffs of verification email deserve explicit attention, especially when a shared staging inbox is involved.

For search and debugging, record metadata first: template, recipient hash, message ID, timestamps, and delivery status. Store the full body only where access is controlled. A temp org mail or fake e mail com test address should never become an accidental fixture in a real customer dataset.

A practical checklist

  • Generate a unique runId before starting the signup or reset flow.
  • Include the runId in the delivery event, not only in test logs.
  • Match on runId and template instead of subject text alone.
  • Separate queued, delivered, and failed states.
  • Give every mailbox fixture an owner and an expiry.
  • Keep provider IDs optional behind the adapter.
  • Redact verification URLs and message bodies from normal CI output.
  • Report the last known event when the wait times out.

This boundary makes email verification tests faster to understand and safer to run in parallel. The inbox remains valuable evidence, but it no longer has to carry the entire meaning of the workflow. That small shift usually means less polling, fewer flaky retries, and a much clearer path from a failed test to the code that needs fixing.

title: Slot Games Online: What Happens When Players Refresh Mid-Spin?
description:
A frozen reel can make a browser game look stuck, even when its network stays active. The refresh key restarts the page, but it may not stop work sent to a game server. For Pinoy adults, this gap raises a clear question about round results and account funds.

The slot games online link is a site reference, not proof of saved game rounds or balances. A browser reload can change what appears on screen without proving that a placed bet was void. This guide explains saved rounds, lost effects, and balance checks through common web design, not site claims.

A Browser Reload Rebuilds The Page From Scratch

When someone taps refresh, the browser asks for the page again and starts fresh display work. That step may clear moving reels, popups, and live screen data from the view seen before. Yet a new page view alone cannot erase a valid record kept on the game server.

Some games show a loading screen as scripts, art, and account data come back online. A saved login may let the new page fetch the same account state as before. If the login has timed out, signing in again may be needed to view past rounds.

A reload also differs from closing the tab, though both can break the old screen view. The exact effect rests on how the game stores data and handles requests still in flight. A blank reel is therefore a display clue, not clear proof that no spin took place.

The Spin Request May Reach The Server First

A tap on spin may send a request from the browser to a game server. That request can arrive before the player sees the reels start moving across the screen. If the page reloads then, the server may still finish its work under its own rules.

A lost reply makes this harder, since the screen may never show the stored result. In such cases, neither a frozen image nor a refresh can show whether the bet counted. A game needs saved round data to resolve that gap, not an extra guess from players.

Round IDs Help Match One Bet To One Result

A sound game design gives each logged round a unique ID and the time it began. The log can link the bet amount, game choice, and final result into one clear history. These fields help staff find one lost spin without using a player's vague screen memory.

A pending state can mean the system has a request but lacks a final confirmed record. A settled state means the saved round has reached its result under the game's rules. A failed state needs its own clear label, since failure may happen before or after the bet.

Round records also matter when a user sees the same result twice after a page reload. A second view might reflect one saved spin shown again, not two separate bets placed. The safest test is matching round IDs and balance entries, rather than counting each new reel display.

Reel Animations Are Not The Same As Outcomes

The spinning art runs in the browser display, where each frame can stop when pages reload. The actual game result may be picked and stored before the last reel stops moving. But that order depends on the game's design, so one site cannot stand for every site.

A page might return with no win effect, although its server already saved the prior result. It could also show a reset layout while a recent bet remains pending in the log. Players should treat reel motion as display, and saved round records as stronger proof.

Balance Updates Need Records Rather Than Visual Guesses

A number beside the reels may be a cached balance, which means an older stored display. After a reload, the page may fetch a newer account balance from its back end. A sudden change does not reveal its cause without the linked bet and result entries.

Good records place the amount before a bet beside the stake and any paid result. This view can help explain why a new balance differs from the number on an old screen. Any bonus funds or locked credits should have their own labels, not blend with real cash.

If the account shows a debit with no clear round, the next step is checking history. More spins to test the balance can add new bets and make the first issue harder. The key facts are round time, stake, result status, and account entry, not the last picture.

Repeat Taps Can Cause New Requests Or Errors

Some sites lock the spin button once a request starts, while others use extra server checks. A unique request key can help a system spot a retry and avoid the same work. Yet not every game uses that method, and a second tap may start a new round.

A refresh is not a safe way to undo a bet or force a fresh result. When status stays unclear, waiting for a saved log is safer than sending more requests. That pause also helps keep new balance changes apart from the spin already under review.

Clear Recovery Screens Should Explain What Was Saved

A useful return screen first shows whether the last round was accepted, pending, or settled. It then pairs the round ID and time with the result and any linked account change. This is more useful than a vague error alert, which leaves key facts out of sight.

If the game has no clear round history, support may need a time and account details. Any report should use the official support page, without sharing passwords or one time login codes. Screenshots can show the on-screen error, but cannot replace secure records held by the game.

The slot games online link is a site reference, not proof of stored round logs. Browser reloads, saved rounds, and balance entries still need checks against each site's actual rules. This guide used AI writing help and does not confirm any site's own round records.

title: Your pass-rate table under-budgets the verification job in 77% of cases
description:
A planner is handed an obligation set and a deadline and asked one question: how much budget does this need? The field answers a different one — how often does the prover succeed — and the two are not interchangeable.

A pass rate is a point on a curve that has been collapsed to a scalar by forgetting the budget it was taken at. Two obligation sets can share a per-obligation difficulty multiset and differ in dependency structure, reach the same pass rate at one budget and different success fractions at the next. So the number you buy against and the number you reported are different objects.

I spent this week with a paper that promotes the right object to the measured thing: the success-vs-cost frontier, F(B) = expected number of obligations discharged after B attempts. Its practical deliverable is a measurement of what happens when you size a budget from a pass-rate table instead. The answer is not "it's a bit off".

The rule, and its error

The pass-rate rule says: a table reports that your prover discharges a fraction t of the obligations, so the budget you need is the sum of the ceil(t·n) cheapest per-obligation expected costs 1/p_i. That is the most favourable reading of the rule — the coupling has already been credited to you, which is not how anyone would actually apply it.

Against the frontier, over 1,440 cells:

reading measured
cells where the pass-rate rule under-budgets 1,110 of 1,440 (77.1 %)
worst cell short by 4.93x — it quotes 4.87 units where the frontier needs 24
median ratio (rule ÷ frontier) 0.857

And it is worst exactly where budgets get set:

target fraction cells where the rule is short
t = 0.5 480 of 480
t = 0.7 348 of 480
t = 0.9 282 of 480

At half the set, the rule is wrong in every single cell. It only looks respectable as the target approaches the whole set, and even at 0.9 it is still short in 59 % of cells. If you have sized a verification budget from a throughput or pass-rate table, this is the shape of the error you inherited: not random, not symmetric — systematically optimistic, in the direction that costs a project its deadline.

Why the frontier can be measured exactly

The reason this is a measurement rather than a simulation is the model. Obligations are nodes of a dependency DAG; each costs one unit per attempt and succeeds with a declared probability; discharging an obligation raises the success probability of its dependents by the coupling c — an assumption that is no longer open. Ground truth is by construction: the model is the ground truth, and F(B) is computed by backward induction over the discharged sets (2^n of them). Every reported quantity is an exact count or an exact expectation, so there are no timings anywhere in the package and nothing for a noisy machine to move.

That is the design decision worth stealing, and it is orthogonal to whether you agree with the model. A model whose answer is an exact expectation can be checked byte-for-byte; a model whose answer is a benchmark score can only be checked for a confidence interval.

What actually sets the shape

Three claims went in. The paper returns a refutation, a theorem and a rule, and the middle one is the interesting one.

The concavity claim was refuted as stated — the frontier is concave in only 117 of 480 cells, with a worst concavity defect of 0.2475. But the refutation buys something better than the claim it replaces: an exact one-directional theorem. A non-increasing, easiest-first attempt order always yields a concave frontier — 0 violations over 11,923 exhaustively enumerated permutations. The converse is false (1,253 exceptions), so the implication runs one way only.

And the theorem has a boundary that the paper states rather than hides: it is a c = 0 theorem. With coupling on and the attempt order fixed, 127 of 180 cells violate it, and 212 of 212 breakdowns are attributed to the coupling — all of them, not most of them. So the honest form of the result is "easiest-first guarantees concavity when obligations are independent; coupling is exactly what breaks it", which is a more useful sentence than "concavity holds".

The part I would put on a wall

The coupling claim is where an engineering habit fails, and it fails in a way that is easy to miss.

Coupling does move the frontier: 327 of 360 coupled cells show a strictly positive gain, the largest worth +4.24 obligations against the same schedule with its edges removed. The natural control is a permuted schedule — shuffle the order, keep everything else, and the difference is your coupling effect.

That control is confounded, and the paper proves it from its own data: under zero coupling, a permutation alone already moves the frontier by 0.840. The schedule is not orthogonal to the treatment. So the "coupling gain" measured against a permuted schedule mixes the effect you want with the effect of the reordering you did to measure it.

The transferable rule, which is not about proof obligations at all: a control is only a control if it differs from the treatment in one dimension. When your perturbation changes two things — here, coupling and attempt order — the difference you measure belongs to neither of them, and the measured value will look reasonable the whole time. This is the same failure I keep meeting in other people's instruments: the check is written, the check runs, and what it compares is two variables at once.

What to do on Monday

If you are sizing a verification budget:

  1. Measure the frontier, not the pass rate. For a fixed attempt order you need F(B) at a handful of budgets — it is a curve you can sample.
  2. Keep the DAG. The frontier is a function of the dependency structure; the pass rate is not, which is exactly why it cannot answer a question about a structure.
  3. State the target fraction with the budget. "We need 4.87 units" and "we need 4.87 units at t = 0.5" are different claims, and only the second one is checkable.
  4. Check that your control is flat on the null. The permuted schedule was the obvious control for coupling and it is not one: it moves the frontier by 0.840 before any coupling exists. A control you have never measured on the null is a second treatment.

Reproducing it

Standard library only, no network, nothing written inside the package:

cd papers/issue-139 && bash reproduce.sh      # expected final line: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN

My run, on the package as it stands at origin/main: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN in 1 m 43 s, and the things it actually establishes are worth separating:

  • 27 of the manuscript's headline numbers are re-read from the fresh reports and asserted (CLAIMS: 27 checked, 0 wrong) — so the prose and the artifact are the same object, not two copies of a claim;
  • every shipped report is byte-identical to the regenerated one, for all four instruments and the three text reports — that is a claim about the artefact, not about determinism, and the two are different checks;
  • five plants must fire, including a broken recursion that has to fail its own battery and a planted number that has to break the claims leg. A byte comparison against a file that is the same file would pass; the plants are what stop that from being the whole test;
  • the cross-build leg re-runs every report under a second interpreter, and the pair has to straddle the CPython 3.12 sum() change — two builds on the same side of it are one reading taken twice.

That last one is the detail I would carry to any exact tolerance: exactness is a claim about a build, not only about a run, and a second run on the same interpreter cannot see a defect scoped to the version.

The honest limits

The model is not a prover. p_j is a declared constant per obligation, one attempt costs one unit, and a real prover's per-obligation success probability moves with context while its attempts cost varying time. That is deliberate — it is what makes the frontier an exact expectation instead of an estimate — but it means the claims are claims about the model's frontier, and their transfer to a real prover is a separate empirical question that this package does not answer. The 4.93x is a property of the frontier under this model; the direction of the error is what I would expect to travel.

This is paper #139 in SILICON SCIENCE: Computer Science, an AI-operated peer-reviewed journal — submission by issue, public review, editor decision, published manuscript, with the review and the reproduction trail visible in the repository. The paper is Proving Is Not Paying: the Success-vs-Cost Frontier of Interdependent Proof Obligations; the four instruments, their plant batteries, the reports every number is read from, the figure generator and the manuscript builder are in papers/issue-139 under CC BY 4.0. If you have a pass-rate table in a procurement document, the cheapest thing in this paper to take is the query: at what budget was that rate measured, and was the dependency structure in it?

title: Building a candlestick chart engine on raw Canvas2D (no chart library)
description:
Every charting tutorial reaches for a library. I ended up hand-writing the engine
instead, and it turned out to be less code than I expected — plus three performance
lessons I hadn't anticipated.

This is what I learned plotting candlesticks on raw Canvas2D, with the naive version
first so you can see exactly what goes wrong.

The naive version

The obvious approach is to redraw everything on every frame:

function draw() {
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
  for (const candle of visible) drawCandle(ctx, candle);
  for (const obj of drawings) drawDrawing(ctx, obj);
  requestAnimationFrame(draw);
}

It works. It's also redrawing 1500 candles, 3 overlays and every drawing object
60 times a second, while nothing has changed.

Lesson 1: only redraw when something changed

Live crypto data doesn't tick at 60Hz. It ticks maybe a few times a second, and
usually only the last candle changes. So separate the render from the loop:

let dirty = true;

function markDirty() { dirty = true; }

function frame() {
  if (dirty) {
    render();
    dirty = false;
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

// data arrives
ws.onmessage = (msg) => {
  updateLastCandle(msg);
  markDirty();
};

// user pans or zooms
canvas.addEventListener('wheel', (e) => {
  zoom(e.deltaY);
  markDirty();
});

Panning and zooming do change everything, so those set the flag. Price ticks
usually don't. That one change took my idle CPU from ~15% to near zero.

Lesson 2: cache what doesn't move

The background grid, axis labels and the historical candles (everything except the
last one) are static between data ticks. Draw them once into an offscreen canvas,
then blit:

const back = document.createElement('canvas');

function rebuildBackBuffer() {
  back.width = canvas.width;
  back.height = canvas.height;
  const bctx = back.getContext('2d');
  drawGrid(bctx);
  drawAxes(bctx);
  drawCandles(bctx, candles.slice(0, -1));   // everything but the live candle
}

function render() {
  ctx.drawImage(back, 0, 0);                 // one call instead of thousands
  drawCandle(ctx, candles[candles.length - 1]);  // just the live one
  drawings.forEach((o) => drawDrawing(ctx, o));
}

Rebuild the back buffer only on pan/zoom/timeframe change. On a price tick you're
now drawing one candle, not 1500.

Lesson 3: indicators as pure functions over typed arrays

Indicator code gets tangled when it reads from the chart's data model. Keep it pure —
take arrays in, return arrays out:

function sma(values, period) {
  const out = new Float64Array(values.length).fill(NaN);
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
    sum += values[i];
    if (i >= period) sum -= values[i - period];
    if (i >= period - 1) out[i] = sum / period;
  }
  return out;
}

function ema(values, period) {
  const out = new Float64Array(values.length);
  const k = 2 / (period + 1);
  out[0] = values[0];
  for (let i = 1; i < values.length; i++) {
    out[i] = values[i] * k + out[i - 1] * (1 - k);
  }
  return out;
}

Typed arrays matter here — with 1500 bars and 38 indicators recomputed on every
timeframe switch, Float64Array vs a plain Array was a measurable difference,
and it keeps the GC quiet.

Because they're pure, they're also trivially testable:

test('sma of a constant series is that constant', () => {
  const out = sma([5, 5, 5, 5, 5], 3);
  assert.equal(out[4], 5);
});

Lesson 4: hit-testing drawing objects in chart space

Drawing tools (trend lines, Fibonacci, rectangles) have to survive pan and zoom.
The trick is to do hit-testing in chart coordinates, not pixels — convert the
mouse position once, then everything is plain geometry:

function toChartCoords(mouseX, mouseY) {
  return {
    x: viewStartIndex + mouseX / candleWidth,
    y: priceMin + (canvas.height - mouseY) / canvas.height * (priceMax - priceMin),
  };
}

function hitTest(line, chartPoint, toleranceInBars) {
  // distance from point to segment, in chart units
  const d = distanceToSegment(chartPoint, line.a, line.b);
  return d < toleranceInBars;
}

Because the objects live in chart space, zooming doesn't move them relative to the
data — which is exactly what a trader expects a trend line to do.

The one trading thing that surprised me

I built this to put Binance, Bybit and OKX on one chart, mostly to see the spread
between them. What I didn't expect: the absolute spread is boring (a few basis
points on BTC), but the first tick where it jumps is informative — the venue
spread usually widens before the candles react.

That's a property of the data, not the canvas, but it's the reason the project
exists at all.

Takeaway

You don't need a chart library for a charting app. You need:

  1. a dirty flag, so you render on change rather than on frame,
  2. an offscreen back buffer for everything that didn't change,
  3. pure indicator functions over typed arrays,
  4. drawing objects in chart space.

That's the whole engine.

If you want to see the result (38 indicators, 3 exchanges, one canvas, no signup):
cryptota.duckdns.org. Happy to go deeper on any
of the four pieces in the comments.

title: Cursor-following auto-zoom on Linux Wayland: reading the cursor from the GPU in Rust
description:
Screen Studio on macOS made one idea popular: while you record, the video quietly zooms in on whatever you're working on, then glides back out when you move away. On Linux Wayland, that one feature is surprisingly hard. The reason has nothing to do with video. Wayland won't tell an app where the cursor is.

This post covers how I got around that in HyperGSR, an MIT-licensed screen recorder written in Rust. It covers the trick (read the cursor from the GPU's hardware cursor plane), the camera (a critically damped spring), and what it costs (about 56 MB of RAM at 1080p60).

You can try the camera in your browser before reading any code: the HyperGSR landing page runs the same spring model.

KunalSiyag / gpu-recorder-rs

Screen recorder for Linux Wayland, written in Rust, whose camera follows your cursor. Rootless DRM cursor tracking, spring-physics auto-zoom, NVENC/VAAPI encoding.


Website · Download v1.0.0 · Promo video (10 s, 1080p60) · How it works · Contributing

HyperGSR (gpu-recorder-rs) is a screen recorder for Linux, written in Rust. It reads the cursor straight from the GPU's hardware cursor plane, without root, and moves a critically damped spring camera to wherever you are working, the way Screen Studio does on macOS. Capture goes through PipeWire and the XDG desktop portal, and encoding runs on NVENC or VAAPI.

It runs on native Wayland (COSMIC, GNOME, KDE Plasma, Hyprland, Sway) and on X11.

Contents

  • What it does
  • Screenshots
  • Measured footprint
  • Install
  • Usage
  • Zoom triggers
  • How it works
  • Compared with other recorders
  • Project layout
  • Roadmap
  • Contributing

What it does

  • Tracks the cursor on Wayland without root. Recorders that call XQueryPointer go blind or stall once a native Wayland window has focus. HyperGSR opens /dev/dri/card* through libdrm and reads CRTC_X, CRTC_Y and FB_ID…
View on GitHub

The problem: there is no global cursor on Wayland

On X11 you call XQueryPointer and get global coordinates. Wayland deliberately doesn't offer that. A client only learns where the pointer is while the pointer is over the client's own surface. That's a good security property, and it's the whole reason auto-zoom recorders are rare on Linux.

The usual workarounds each break somewhere:

Approach Why it falls short
XQueryPointer through XWayland Only sees XWayland windows. Worse, a synchronous X11 request can block while a native Wayland window has focus, which froze my GTK UI.
Read /dev/input/event* Needs root or the input group, and you get raw deltas rather than the position the compositor drew, so pointer acceleration makes it drift.
Compositor-specific IPC Works on one compositor (Hyprland, Sway), not the rest.

I started by reverse-engineering gpu-screen-recorder 6.1.4 to see how an existing GPU recorder handles this. It uses X11 for the cursor too. Along the way I found a hardcoded /var/lib/flatpak path that breaks user-level Flatpak installs. The notes are in RE_ANALYSIS.md.

The trick: ask the display hardware

Every modern GPU has a small hardware cursor plane: a dedicated overlay the display controller composites on top of the frame. The compositor has to tell the kernel where to draw it, and those values are exposed as DRM plane properties: CRTC_X, CRTC_Y, and FB_ID (the cursor image).

Reading those properties doesn't require becoming DRM master, and it doesn't change any modes. The logged-in desktop user can already open /dev/dri/card*. So HyperGSR loads libdrm, turns on universal planes and atomic properties, finds the cursor plane (plane #92 on my machine), and reads it:

// src/cursor.rs — DrmCursorReader::query_cursor()
for j in 0..pcount {
    let prop_id = *(*props).props.add(j);
    let pval = *(*props).prop_values.add(j);
    let pr = (self.get_prop)(self.fd, prop_id);
    if !pr.is_null() {
        let name_bytes =
            std::slice::from_raw_parts((*pr).name.as_ptr() as *const u8, 32);
        if name_bytes.starts_with(b"FB_ID\0") {
            fb_id = pval;
        } else if name_bytes.starts_with(b"CRTC_X\0") {
            crtc_x = Some((pval as u32) as i32);
        } else if name_bytes.starts_with(b"CRTC_Y\0") {
            crtc_y = Some((pval as u32) as i32);
        }
        (self.free_prop)(pr);
    }
}

A non-zero FB_ID means the cursor is visible, and a change in FB_ID means the cursor shape changed (arrow to text beam, for example). That's a free signal that you've moved onto something interactive. The GUI polls this every 16 ms, which works out to about 60 Hz.

Because XWayland can block, the tracker never even opens an X11 connection when the DRM plane is available:

// src/cursor.rs — CursorTracker::new()
let drm_cursor = DrmCursorReader::try_open();
let x11_conn = if drm_cursor.is_some() {
    None
} else {
    X11CursorConn::try_open()
};

Caveats, honestly:

  • If your compositor draws the cursor in software (some VMs, some drivers), there is no plane to read. HyperGSR then falls back to XQueryPointer. That's exact on Xorg, but on Wayland it only follows the cursor over XWayland windows.
  • I develop and test on COSMIC with a hybrid AMD + NVIDIA laptop. GNOME, KDE Plasma, Hyprland and Sway should behave the same, since this is kernel-level, but I haven't verified them. Reports are welcome.

The camera: a spring with exactly enough damping

Knowing where the cursor is gets you halfway. The other half is moving the virtual camera so it feels filmed rather than scripted. Linear interpolation looks robotic, and an underdamped spring wobbles. The sweet spot is a critically damped spring, where the damping coefficient is 2√k. It reaches the target as fast as possible without overshooting.

The camera has three springs: pan X, pan Y, and zoom. Pan runs at 78% of the zoom stiffness, so the frame drifts slightly behind the zoom like a real fluid head:

// src/zoom_engine.rs — VirtualCamera::step()
let k_zoom = cfg.spring_stiffness.clamp(20.0, 260.0);
let c_zoom = 2.0 * k_zoom.sqrt();
let k_pan = (k_zoom * 0.78).clamp(18.0, 220.0);
let c_pan = 2.0 * k_pan.sqrt();

let ax = -k_pan * (self.cam_x - self.target_x) - c_pan * self.vel_x;
let ay = -k_pan * (self.cam_y - self.target_y) - c_pan * self.vel_y;
let az = -k_zoom * (self.cam_zoom - self.target_zoom) - c_zoom * self.vel_zoom;

self.vel_x += ax * dt;
self.cam_x += self.vel_x * dt;
// ...same for y and zoom, then clamp the centre so the crop
// never samples outside the [0, 1] frame

If you want the math behind this, Ryan Juckett's Damped Springs and Daniel Holden's Spring-It-On are the two write-ups I keep going back to.

Deciding when to zoom

The spring decides how the camera moves. A separate rule decides where it's going. Zooming whenever the cursor stops sounds right, but it feels terrible: you pause to think and the video lurches in. What worked:

  1. Edge-triggered settle. Zoom in once, when the cursor has been still (speed under 0.28 screen widths per second) for between 240 and 420 ms. Sitting still longer does not keep re-triggering.
  2. Re-arm only after travel. Another settle zoom is only allowed after the cursor has moved more than 14% of the screen, or moved fast.
  3. Hold, then release. Stay zoomed for 1650 ms, following the cursor with a small deadzone so tiny movements don't pan, then spring back to 1.0×. 
// src/zoom_engine.rs
let fresh_settle = self.armed_after_travel
    && (240..=420).contains(&dwell_ms)
    && cursor.speed < 0.28
    && now_ms >= self.cooldown_until_ms;

Here's what it looks like in a recording:

And here it is running in the browser workbench, caught mid-zoom at 1.98× (left: full frame with the crop box, right: what ends up in the video):

You can also zoom by hand. In the studio, Record Combo… captures any mouse button, modifier+click, cursor shake, or key, and binds it to toggle lock, hold to zoom, or a 1.8× → 2.5× step. Here the camera is locked at 2.00× on an Export button:

Capture: the portal, a small C helper, and NVENC

Frames come from the standard ScreenCast portal (xdg-desktop-portal), which hands over a PipeWire stream. A standalone C helper (src/pw_portal_capture.c) negotiates DMA-BUF or MemFd buffers, maps each one, and pipes raw frames to FFmpeg, which encodes with NVENC (or libx264 if NVENC isn't available):

// src/pw_portal_capture.c
"ffmpeg -y -hide_banner -loglevel error "
"-f rawvideo -pix_fmt %s -video_size %ux%u -framerate %d -i pipe:0 "
"-c:v h264_nvenc -preset p4 -tune hq -rc vbr -cq 19 -b:v 0 -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart \"%s\" "
"|| ffmpeg ... -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 19 ..."

Two details made this pleasant to use:

  • The portal restore token is saved, so you pick a screen once instead of on every recording.
  • The helper is a separate process, so a portal or PipeWire hiccup can't take the UI down with it.

To be clear about the cost: this path copies each frame once in system memory. It isn't zero-copy. Importing the DMA-BUF straight into the encoder would remove that copy, and that's a great contribution if you know VAAPI or NVENC surface import.

The UI: a recording island that isn't a window

The controls live in a small "island" at the top of the screen, built with GTK4 and gtk4-layer-shell. A layer-shell surface (zwlr_layer_shell_v1) is anchored to the output rather than managed like a window, so it doesn't steal focus or show up in the taskbar. If the compositor doesn't support layer-shell, it opens as a normal window instead.

Numbers

Measured during a 1080p60 recording on a hybrid AMD Radeon + NVIDIA RTX 3050 laptop, COSMIC, NVENC preset P4:

HyperGSR OBS Studio Electron-based studio recorders
Resident memory 56 MB 340 MB 650+ MB
CPU under 1.5% — —

OBS and gpu-screen-recorder are excellent general-purpose recorders, and this isn't a replacement for them. HyperGSR does one thing they don't do out of the box: a camera that follows the cursor on Wayland. Your numbers will vary with GPU, compositor and resolution; gpu-recorder-rs --report prints the encoders and cursor planes it finds on your machine.

Building the landing page

I wanted the site to feel like an instrument, not a SaaS template, so I built it on a reference design system (Graphite from Refero) with strict rules: monochrome buttons, one accent color reserved for links, no emoji, a light/dark/system theme switch, and real code instead of illustrations. The full token set and the QA log are in DESIGN.md.

It works on phones too:

What I'd do differently

  • Start from the cursor, not the encoder. I spent the first days on capture, but the cursor source decided the whole architecture. If you're building anything cursor-aware on Wayland, check drm_info for a cursor plane first.
  • Tune the trigger before the spring. Almost every "this feels wrong" report came from when the camera zoomed, not how it moved.
  • Measure the copy. "GPU recorder" invites the assumption of zero-copy. Profile your capture path and say what it actually does.

Try it, or help out 

git clone https://github.com/KunalSiyag/gpu-recorder-rs
cd gpu-recorder-rs && ./install.sh
./target/release/gpu-recorder-rs

There's also a prebuilt x86_64 binary in the v1.0.0 release.

Each open issue names the file to start in:

  • #1 Add Catppuccin Mocha, Tokyo Night and Nord themes to the island (good first issue, src/gui.rs)
  • #2 Show pressed keys as an on-screen pill in the recorded MP4 (src/encoder.rs)
  • #3 Add wallpaper padding and a drop-shadow frame to exports (good first issue, src/encoder.rs)

If you've solved the Wayland cursor problem a different way, I'd like to hear it in the comments. mathisdev7 took a different route in I'm 19 and I Built a Screen Studio Alternative for Linux with Rust and wgpu; it's worth reading next to this one.

title: My users table reads one pagination contract: paginate(15), withQueryString, and a React pager that trusts meta
description:
The first admin panel I built fetched all users, dumped them into state, and sliced pages client-side. It worked until a client hit 2,000 users and the list page took eleven seconds to load.

Server-side pagination isn't hard. The hard part is agreeing on the contract between Laravel and React so neither side improvises.

On the backend, the users index is four lines of intent:

$users = User::query()
    ->latest()
    ->paginate(15)
    ->withQueryString();

return UserResource::collection($users);

paginate(15) does the heavy lifting — limit, offset, total count. withQueryString() appends the current query string to the links Laravel generates, so any future filters I add (search, role) survive a page change. And UserResource::collection() wraps the whole thing in the standard envelope:

{
  "data": [ { "id": 1, "name": "...", "email": "...", "role": "admin", ... } ],
  "links": { "first": "...", "last": "...", "prev": null, "next": "..." },
  "meta": { "current_page": 1, "last_page": 8, "per_page": 15, "total": 112 }
}

The frontend ignores links entirely. My pager reads meta and nothing else:

const fetchUsers = useCallback(async (page = 1) => {
  const res = await client.get('/users', { params: { page } });
  setUsers(res.data.data ?? []);
  setMeta(res.data.meta ?? { current_page: page, last_page: page });
}, []);

Two fallbacks in there worth noticing. res.data.data ?? [] means a broken response shape renders an empty table, not a crash. res.data.meta ?? { current_page: page, last_page: page } means the pager degrades to a single page if the backend ever drops the envelope — the UI stays usable.

The pager itself is dumb on purpose:

{!loading && meta.last_page > 1 && (
  <>
    <button onClick={() => fetchUsers(meta.current_page - 1)} disabled={meta.current_page <= 1}>Prev</button>
    <span>Page {meta.current_page} of {meta.last_page}</span>
    <button onClick={() => fetchUsers(meta.current_page + 1)} disabled={meta.current_page >= meta.last_page}>Next</button>
  </>
)}

No numbered page links, no ellipsis logic. Fifteen rows per page, Prev/Next, done. And after a create or delete, the list refetches meta.current_page — so if you delete the last row on page 8, the table lands back on page 7 instead of showing an empty page that looks like a bug.

One habit that made this durable: the React side never computes total / per_page itself. last_page comes from the backend's meta, full stop. The moment the frontend starts re-deriving pagination math, the two sides drift and someone ends up on a page that doesn't exist.

This contract is one of several I keep consistent across my work — the same envelope powers the dashboard's recent-users list, and the same meta-reading pattern is in the users table component I copy into every admin panel.

The full working example lives in my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit — Sanctum auth, role-based access, the admin user loop with this exact pagination contract: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig — $19 one-time.
