title: 8% of My Capterra Reviews Arrived as the Three Characters $62
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The half of my week that is not visas goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads B2B software reviews — Capterra, Software Advice, GetApp, TrustRadius — and returns all four with the same field names.

Last night I was grepping my own output for junk. Not looking for anything in particular, just running a regex for field values that look like machinery rather than text. One hit came back often enough to stop me:

{
  "reviewId": "Capterra___7209002",
  "title": "Slack: Essential for remote work productivity...and employee engagement",
  "overallRating": 5,
  "pros": "$62",
  "cons": "Honestly, not much. The only time I get frustrated with it is when I need to invite partners (from external companies) into our workspace for targeted deal collaboration…",
  "comments": "$61"
}

cons is a real review. pros is the string $62. Not an empty field, not a truncation, not a price — a three-character pointer where 1,309 characters of someone's opinion of Slack should be.

How often, and to whom

I keep every run's dataset, so this is measurable rather than anecdotal. Across 16 runs and 409 Capterra review rows, 35 rows — 8.6% — carried a pointer in at least one text field: 34 in pros, 12 in comments, never in cons. On Software Advice, 5 pointer fields across 150 rows. On TrustRadius, 0 across 1,330.

The TrustRadius zero is the clue. TrustRadius goes through a completely different code path in my Actor — one that reassembles each review out of a slice of markup. Capterra and Software Advice share a path that reads structured objects out of the page. So this was not a site change. It was my parser, and it had been wrong since at least late September.

What $62 actually is

Capterra runs on Next.js App Router, which means the page does not ship a single JSON blob. It ships a React Server Components stream, pushed into the document in pieces:

<script>self.__next_f.push([1,"1:\"$Sreact.fragment\"\n3:I[339756,[\"/assets-bx-capterra/…"])</script>

Concatenate those pushes and you get a flat wire format of numbered rows. Mostly they are component references, but some are text:

61:T425,Slack has been part of the corporate toolkits of the companies I've worked for since 2017…

Row 61, type T, length 0x425 = 1,061 bytes, then the text. And in the review object that owns that text, React leaves this:

{"reviewId":"Capterra___7209002","overallRating":"5.0",
 "consText":"Honestly, not much. The only time I get frustrated with it is when…",
 "generalComments":"$61","prosText":"$62"}

That is React's reference syntax. A $-prefixed string in an RSC payload is a pointer to another row, not a value. The serializer outlines a long string — hoists it out of the object graph into its own row — and substitutes the pointer. The threshold in React's flight serializer is 1,024 characters.

I had read none of this. My parser pulled balanced JSON objects out of the stream, found "prosText": "$62", and dutifully wrote $62 into the dataset as the review.

Why a line-based reader misses the rows

The obvious fix is to build a lookup table of rows and resolve pointers against it. My first attempt did it by splitting the stream on newlines and matching ^([0-9a-f]+):T([0-9a-f]+),. It found row 61 and reported rows 62 and 63 as missing — even though 62:T51d, is right there in the HTML.

Here is the reason, lifted from the raw stream:

…companies should seriously consider adopting it.62:T51d,Since 2020, I've worked remotely as…

A text row declares its length, so it does not need a terminator — and it does not get one. The next row id begins immediately after the last byte of the previous row's text. On a line-based split, the only text rows you find are the ones that happen to follow a newline-terminated row. Every text row that follows another text row disappears, which is exactly the case when a page has several long reviews in a row.

So the rows have to be walked in order, and the length has to be honoured in bytes, not characters — T counts UTF-8 bytes, and review text is full of smart quotes and emoji:

_RSC_ROW = re.compile(rb'([0-9a-f]{1,8}):')
_RSC_TEXT = re.compile(rb'T([0-9a-f]+),')

def rsc_text_rows(blob: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Map every length-prefixed text row in the stream to the text it carries."""
    raw = blob.encode('utf-8')
    rows, position, size = {}, 0, len(raw)
    while position < size:
        head = _RSC_ROW.match(raw, position)
        if not head:
            newline = raw.find(b'\n', position)
            if newline < 0:
                break
            position = newline + 1
            continue
        body = head.end()
        text = _RSC_TEXT.match(raw, body)
        if not text:
            newline = raw.find(b'\n', body)
            position = size if newline < 0 else newline + 1
            continue
        start = text.end()
        end = min(start + int(text.group(1), 16), size)
        rows.setdefault(head.group(1).decode(), raw[start:end].decode('utf-8', 'ignore'))
        position = end + 1 if raw[end:end + 1] == b'\n' else end
    return rows

Then resolving is a recursive walk over the parsed object, replacing any string that is exactly $<row id> with that row's text. One detail worth stealing: React escapes a string that genuinely starts with $ by doubling it, so a reviewer who wrote $62 a month is fair arrives as $$62 a month is fair. That means a single-$ value is always a pointer and never literal text — and that a parser which ignores all of this also silently doubles the dollar sign on any review starting with a price. I had zero of those in 2,947 rows, so that half is read from React's source rather than measured, but it costs one line to handle:

if value.startswith('$$'):
    return value[1:]

The bias is the real damage

8.6% of rows losing a field sounds survivable. It isn't, because the loss is not random.

Here are the longest text values on one Capterra page for Slack — the 25 reviews on page 1 — split by whether React kept them inline or outlined them:

Characters
Longest inline value 927
Shortest outlined value 1,061
Other outlined values 1,309 and 1,966

There is no overlap, and there can't be: the cut is React's 1,024-character rule. So the fields that went missing were precisely the three longest pieces of writing on the page. The 150-character "great tool, love it" reviews all came through perfectly.

If you are scraping reviews to feed a summarisation prompt, sentiment model or RAG index, that is the worst possible sample to lose. Short reviews are noise; the 2,000-character one from the IT executive explaining what Slack replaced and why is the entire reason to buy review data. My dataset was quietly dropping the signal and keeping the filler, and every run finished green with the expected row count.

That is the part I keep coming back to. The run succeeded. The row count was right. Nothing errored, nothing timed out, no site blocked anything. The only symptom was a two-byte string in one field of one row in twelve, and the only reason I found it is that I ran a regex looking for values that don't look like prose.

After

Same page, same 25 reviews, after the fix — and verified on the platform, not just on my laptop:

reviews: 25   pointer fields: 0
longest pros lengths: 1966, 1309, 926, 843, 805

Rows 1,966 and 1,309 are the two that used to be $63 and $62. The 926 was always fine. Both Actors that share this code path — Capterra & SaaS Reviews Scraper and its sibling — went out the same evening.

What to take from this if you scrape Next.js

  • Any $-prefixed string value in an RSC payload is a pointer. If your scraper reads App Router pages and never resolves them, you are losing your longest strings right now and your row counts look fine.
  • Length-prefixed rows are not newline-terminated. Walk the stream; don't split it.
  • Add a junk canary to your validator. Mine is one regex over every string field: ^\$[0-9a-f]{1,8}$. Values that look like machinery — pointers, $undefined, bare [object Object], NaN — are cheap to detect and are the ones that pass every other check.
  • Headless browsers don't have this problem. Read the rendered DOM and React has already resolved its own pointers for you. You pay a browser per page for it, which is why I parse the stream instead — but if you're scraping a handful of pages a day, that trade may not be yours.
  • Check field-length distributions, not just fill rates. A fill-rate check would have given this a clean bill of health: pros was populated in 100% of rows. It was populated with $62.

The reviews were there the whole time, 1,061 bytes further down the same response. I just never followed the pointer.

title: “This app might stop working soon”: Atlassian Connect apps
description:
On 9 October an admin wrote on Figma's forum that they had "received a notification indicating that your app may stop working after January 2027", and asked what it meant for their site. Connect end of support begins on 31 January 2027, 106 days from the day I'm writing this. On our own test site the admin screen gave two different dates for it.

Figma answered the next day. They assumed the admin meant Figma for Jira and said they plan to move it to Forge "by the end of the year". I liked that answer, because for most apps only the vendor can give it.

If you've seen "This app might stop working soon", or one of its cousins, on a Jira or Confluence app, Atlassian is telling you the app still has Connect parts. On our test site the Connected apps page tagged 4 of its 57 entries Legacy. Its banner said January 2027, and the tooltip on the Legacy tag said December 2026. Same page. Weird, I know.

Finding the affected apps takes a few clicks per site, and most of what's left after that is emails to vendors. If you want the background on why Atlassian is retiring Connect, Mihai covered it in Atlassian Connect end of support: 31 January 2027. This one is the admin's to-do list.

Our Connected apps page: 4 Legacy tags, two dates, no Connect column

We opened Connected apps on our wolfaenpak test site on 16 October 2026 and clicked through its three pages and the details screens. We read Atlassian's documentation the same day.

  1. No column, tag or filter says Connect or Forge. The list has the columns App, Edition, Installed by, Connections and Actions. The end-of-support signal is a yellow "Legacy" tag, on 4 of 57 entries. The word Connect only shows up inside a Legacy app's details, as a link to Atlassian's post.
  2. One page, two dates. The banner says "unsupported after January 2027". The tooltip on the Legacy tag says "This app may stop working after December 2026". The tooltip is a month earlier.
  3. The colour of the panel tells you the vendor's plan. Blue means the vendor has told Atlassian it will migrate before end of support. Yellow means the vendor said no, is undecided or said nothing, or that a newer version of the app is waiting for you.
  4. Atlassian's own Connect integrations aren't tagged. 12 of them are on our site, all with versions ending in -AC, and we found nothing that says whether end of support applies to them.
  5. Two shortcuts for spotting Connect didn't help. The details URL looked the same for the Legacy apps and our Forge app, and the old app-management API doesn't list Forge apps at all.

What “This app might stop working soon” means, and why a Forge app can still show it

The wording you see depends on when and where you saw it. "This app might stop working soon" is the title of a developer-community thread from 20 May 2026 that's had 2,382 views, about a banner that appeared inside apps. Atlassian staff said in that thread the message was meant only for non-Marketplace apps, rolled it back the same day, and later said it had been "scoped to canary tenants only". yasoon titled a support page after it, and that page still gives December 2026.

What admins see now is quieter. Atlassian documents the current copy on What admins see on the Connected Apps page, last updated 10 September 2026: "This app is running on a platform that will be unsupported after January 2027." Exalate quoted a third version in its support post, "This app may stop working after January 2027", and admins on Lucid's and Figma's forums repeat the same words. All three are the same warning about the same thing.

A Forge app can still get it, too. That one surprises people. Atlassian set the rule in its March 2025 timeline post. In its words, "an app that has a Forge manifest and a mix of Connect and Forge modules will be considered a Connect app until all Connect modules are removed." Exalate said exactly that about its own app in September: its package "still includes a Connect component alongside its Forge implementation", so the warning shows. A vendor telling you "we're on Forge already" and the warning are both true at the same time, until the last Connect piece is gone.

Connect end of support: December 2026 or 31 January 2027?

It's 31 January 2027. Atlassian moved it on 3 August 2026, in Getting Ready for Connect End of Support: "we're extending the end of support date from December 2026 to January 31, 2027." The developer changelog repeats it on 7 August. The pages updated after that use the new date too. They include the private-apps page and the migration-module page (both 10 August), what admins see (10 September) and the app migration page (23 September). The last one even says the date "was extended from December 2026".

December survives in older pages nobody went back to edit (the March 2025 timeline post says "Q4 CY2026", the August 2025 post on custom apps "the end of 2026"), on some vendor pages, and in our tooltip.

So plan for 31 January 2027. If someone in your company has December in a slide, they're probably reading the tooltip or a 2025 post, and it's an easy mistake when the product says it too.

How to identify if an app is Forge or Connect: four checks

Atlassian's own knowledge-base article for this question tells you to open each app's Marketplace listing and look for a descriptor link. It was last updated in September 2025, before the admin labels existed, and it's slow with more than a handful of apps. These are the checks I'd run instead, in this order.

Check 1: open Connected apps and look for the Legacy tag

Go to Atlassian Administration, select Apps, then Sites, pick your site, and select Connected apps in the left navigation (Atlassian's Manage an installed app page has the same path). From the organization's Atlassian apps page there's also a link, "Looking for your Marketplace and third-party apps?", which opens a site picker and lands you in the same place. You need to be an organization admin or a site admin.

Inside a product, the old Manage apps screen is gone. On our site both Jira and Confluence now say "App management has moved to Administration", with a "Take me there" button. The Jira sidebar item is still called "Manage apps", while the message says "Apps > Manage your apps". A bit confusing, but both take you to the same page.

Then page through the list. All of it. Our test site needed three pages for 57 entries, and 16 of those were Rovo MCP connectors that the system installed. The four Legacy tags were all third-party Marketplace apps:

App on our test site Vendor Tag Details panel
ScriptRunner for Jira The Adaptavist Group Legacy blue, links the vendor's Forge plan
Navigation Menus for Confluence (quick & easy orientation) Seibert Legacy blue
STAGIL Navigation Menus and Themes for Confluence STAGIL by catworkx Legacy not opened
User Management for Confluence (bulk & timed inactive users) TechTime Initiative Group Legacy not opened

Keep in mind the tag is a pointer. It tells you nothing about how far along the vendor is. An Atlassian staff member called the "at risk" signal "complicated and conservative" in a September thread and said to expect "false positives", many with simple fixes. So a Legacy tag means "look at this one": the app has Connect parts, and the vendor may already be most of the way off them.

Check 2: open View app details and read the panel colour

A Legacy app's details page has a panel at the top. Atlassian's banner table says the wording is the same whatever the vendor declared, and the colour carries the meaning: blue when the vendor declared willMigrateToForgeBeforeEOS: YES, yellow when it declared no or undecided, and yellow by default when it declared nothing. A vendor whose app has no Forge manifest yet can't declare anything, so it always gets the generic yellow message. Both Legacy apps we opened, ScriptRunner and Seibert's Navigation Menus, were blue. We didn't see a yellow one on our site.

If the panel is blue, click "Learn more", because it goes to the vendor's own migration page (for ScriptRunner that's Adaptavist's "moving to Atlassian Forge" page). If it's yellow and has a Learn more link, that's the vendor's plan, and the plan may well be "no". If it only points you to the Marketplace listing, the vendor hasn't declared anything, so contact them there.

There's also a yellow "Update your app now" variant. It appears when your version is older than one with a Forge manifest. Updating removes that message, and if the new version still has Connect parts you'll get the regular panel instead.

Check 3: look at the Authorization tab

This one's for when you want to see the difference with your own eyes. On our site, ScriptRunner's Authorization tab mixes plain-English permissions with old Connect-style ones in capitals: ACT_AS_USER, ADMIN, DELETE, PROJECT_ADMIN and READ. Our own Forge app, Sentinel Vault, lists only plain permissions such as "Read Confluence detailed content" and "App Storage scope".

I wouldn't use this as a test by itself. It's a hint. I find it most useful when you're talking to a vendor and want to ask which of those permissions will change after the move.

Check 4: find Atlassian's own Connect apps

The Legacy tag skips Atlassian's own apps. I didn't expect that. On our list, six entries have a details link containing /user-connected-apps/connect/jira/ and an app key: Atlassian Assist, Atlassian Home for Jira Cloud, Automation for Jira, Jira Service Management Widget, Opsgenie and Statuspage for Jira. Opsgenie's details page shows version 2.0.3-AC and a "Descriptor URL" link. Connect apps have a descriptor; Forge apps have a manifest.

Six more are easy to miss. Confluence Cloud for Microsoft Teams, Confluence Cloud for Slack, and Jira Cloud for Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Slack and Spreadsheets sit at the top of our list with no details link at all, so the URL trick can't see them, but the Marketplace lists all six as Connect. So for Atlassian's own integrations, I'd simply note down every row that says "by Atlassian".

I couldn't find an Atlassian statement on whether these are in scope for end of support, are exempt, or are being migrated. A developer asked "Why hasn't Atlassian migrated its own apps?" on 21 August, and nobody from Atlassian answered in the thread. I'm not going to guess. If your teams depend on one of them, Automation for Jira especially, ask your Atlassian account team or open a support ticket and get the answer in writing.

Two shortcuts that didn't help on our site

Atlassian's August 2025 post on custom apps said you could tell Connect from Forge by the details URL: Connect apps had /connect/<product>/<app-key>/ in it and Forge apps an opaque ID. On our site only Atlassian's own Connect apps had /connect/ in the URL. All four Legacy apps had the same opaque ID format as our Forge app, Sentinel Vault. (The two we opened had blue panels, which need a Forge manifest, so they're probably Connect apps partway to Forge. The test may still work for a pure Connect app. We didn't have one to try.)

The other shortcut is the old app-management REST API (/rest/plugins/1.0/), which older inventory scripts call. We called it on our site: Jira returned 206 entries, 10 of them flagged as Connect, all of them Atlassian integrations with an -AC version. Confluence returned 211 entries with 2 Connect ones. None of our own four Forge apps appeared, and neither did the other third-party apps, Legacy ones included. It looks like an inventory and it isn't one, so I'd stick to the Connected apps page and page through it by hand.

What admins see on the Connected apps page: end-of-support warnings and LEGACY apps since July 2026

Atlassian rolled the admin messages out in stages from mid-July 2026: apps with no declaration, a "no" or "undecided" in late July, and apps whose vendor declared "yes" in September. Some apps are blocked on a missing Forge feature that Atlassian accepted as a blocker. Those are left out of the messages for now, and get them a month after the blocker is resolved.

One Atlassian page still reads as if none of this has happened. The overview page for adopting Forge, last updated in March 2025, says the migration-intent feature is "only available to a canary cohort of developers" and that "the messaging will not be visible to all users yet". The page about what admins see is newer (10 September) and says the messages rolled out to all customers, which matches what we saw on our site.

For private apps, the ones your company built itself or had built and installed by link, Atlassian's guidance uses the same "LEGACY" status and the same Connected apps page. Atlassian's March 2025 timeline said installing new private Connect apps would stop from March 2026, so most private Connect apps you find will be older than that.

What to ask each vendor about its Connect to Forge migration

For Marketplace Connect apps, Atlassian's FAQ says "No action is required at this stage from you as an admin". It tells you to contact the vendor through the app's listing. I'd do that now rather than in January, because a vendor's support queue in the last weeks before a deadline is not a fun place to be. These are the questions that get you a usable answer:

  1. When will a version with no Connect modules be out? Ask for a month, and ask whether it's "Forge" or "Forge with remaining Connect modules", since Atlassian still counts the second as Connect.
  2. Will the move need my approval? A Forge update that changes permissions, adds outside connections or changes remote backends is usually a major version, and major versions wait for an admin to consent. Atlassian's Limitations and differences page for apps adopting Forge says the first Forge version may or may not need approval. If it does, find the "Update" tag on Connected apps, open View app details, review the new permissions and select Update. Mihai wrote up the 11 changes that force a Forge major version from the vendor's side, if you want to know what to expect.
  3. Will my data and configuration come across? Atlassian staff confirmed in September that data migration only works within the same Marketplace listing. If you're thinking of swapping to a different vendor's Forge app, there's no built-in way to bring your data along.
  4. Where will my data live afterwards, and does the app send anything outside Atlassian? Atlassian's data residency glossary says Connect app data "may be stored outside of the Atlassian cloud environment by a third-party app vendor". An app can also qualify for the Runs on Atlassian badge, which needs Atlassian-hosted compute and storage, matching data residency and admin control over data egress. Others keep their own servers. Either can be fine, as long as you know which one you're getting.
  5. Will the Runs on Atlassian badge change? Atlassian's Manage an installed app page warns that an update can gain or lose eligibility. Its absence doesn't prove an app is still on Connect, because the badge has extra requirements on top of Forge. We went through what the badge does and doesn't promise in our post about Sentinel Vault's AI review.

A good vendor answer looks like K15t's Forge transition page, which lists each app with a dated status ("Migration done (July 2026)", "Migration in progress. Target: end of October 2026"). A worrying one is no answer, or a date that still says "late 2026" without saying what happens in January.

Here's the email I'd send, adjusted for the app:

Hi, we run <app name> on <site>.atlassian.net. Our Connected apps page tags it
Legacy ahead of Connect end of support on 31 January 2027.
1. In which month will you release a version with no Connect modules left?
2. Will that update need admin approval, and which permissions change?
3. Will our data and configuration carry over automatically?
4. Where will our data be stored afterwards, and does the app send data outside Atlassian?
Thanks, <name>

If the vendor says no, or never answers

Give it two weeks, then ask once more through the support link on the Marketplace listing. If the answer is "no plan" or silence, treat the app like one of your own private apps (that section is below): find out who uses it, look for a native feature or another app that does the job, and plan the switch before January. Keep in mind Atlassian's data migration only works within the same Marketplace listing, so with a different vendor's app your data comes across only if that vendor offers an import, and otherwise you start fresh. A blue panel needs less of this. I'd still send the email, mostly to get the approval and data questions answered.

What stops working after 31 January 2027, and what keeps running

Nothing in Atlassian's pages says your Connect apps switch off on 31 January. The March 2025 post says customers "won't lose access to the app". The August 2026 post says Atlassian will "share more detail on timelines and next steps for Connect beyond end of support". There's no shutdown, block or uninstall date published anywhere I looked.

What does change, from the August 2026 post: "Atlassian will only address critical security patches. Support SLAs will be relaxed, and Connect will no longer evolve alongside the Atlassian platform." Connect capabilities can be removed "with significantly less notice". And the sentence I'd put in front of anyone who wants to wait it out: some platform changes "will cause apps to stop functioning without advance notice". The 2025 post put it more bluntly, that end of support means "use at your own risk".

Is that a reason to panic about each Legacy tag? I don't think so. Atlassian says "over 95% of paid app seats have been migrated to Forge", counted in paid seats rather than apps. It doesn't say whether apps that still have Connect parts count as migrated, and ScriptRunner, one of the biggest paid apps, still carries the Legacy tag on our site. So I'd expect the gaps to sit mostly with small apps, free apps and private ones, but check the big ones too.

There's also an audit angle. An Atlassian staff member wrote in June that for enterprise customers with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 obligations, an unsupported framework is "a material risk". Those customers were already asking how to find their Connect apps. If your auditors ask, the Connected apps page and the vendor answers are your evidence.

Private Connect apps you built yourselves: rebuild, replace or uninstall

I think private apps are where admins have most of the work. There's no vendor to email. Atlassian says it "won't directly update or rewrite installed apps" and won't support apps left on Connect after 31 January 2027. Its private-apps guidance boils down to a short audit for each LEGACY private app. Work out what business problem it solves and who uses it. Check whether a native Jira or Confluence feature, or a simpler workflow, could replace it. Then rebuild it on Forge, replace it, or uninstall it.

Atlassian's August 2025 post lists the signs of a private app. It was installed by link or in developer mode and isn't in Marketplace search. You hold its source code, and it has no licensing information. On the Connected apps page, a Marketplace app has a related-links sidebar and a private one doesn't.

If nobody knows who built it, Atlassian's advice is to bring in a Solution Partner. Any team with Forge experience and access to the code can do the rebuild. It's work we do too, and our Forge app development page is the place to start, but please check the uninstall option first. A private app nobody can name an owner for is often an app nobody uses.

An admin checklist for the 106 days before 31 January 2027

This is the order I'd work in, starting this week:

  1. Open Connected apps for each site you own and write down the apps with a Legacy tag or an Update tag, plus every row that says "by Atlassian".
  2. Open View app details for each Legacy app and note whether the panel is blue or yellow, and the "Learn more" link if there is one.
  3. Apply pending updates on apps that show the "Update your app now" message, after reading the new permissions.
  4. Email the vendor of each Legacy app with the questions above, yellow ones first. Keep their answers with your audit evidence.
  5. Ask your Atlassian account team about the "by Atlassian" rows from step 1 that your teams rely on.
  6. Decide on each private app: rebuild, replace or uninstall, with an owner and a date before January.
  7. Check again in December. The tags and panels change as vendors declare and ship, and Atlassian said it will eventually show migration notices inside the apps themselves, with advance notice and a testing period first. I couldn't confirm whether those in-app notices are live yet.

Planning a migration around the same January date? Mihai's post on why Cloud Fortified keeps probing an old Connect URL shows what a vendor's half-finished move can look like from the inside.

Where we stand, and where I could be wrong

We're a vendor too, so you should know where we sit: our four apps (CogniRunner, Sentinel Vault, LeanZero Management and Cost Slasher) have no Connect modules, and the Marketplace marks their current versions as not Connect.

This is one test site on one morning. Keep that in mind. Our list is full of development installs and test apps, so the 4-of-57 figure says nothing about a normal company's site, where I'd expect more Marketplace apps and more tags. I didn't open the details panels for STAGIL or TechTime. I didn't see an end-user banner inside an app either. And the wording has varied a lot this year, so yours might read differently. If you see a version I haven't quoted here, send a screenshot to office@leanzero.net and I'll add it.

My recommendation: do steps 1 to 4 of the checklist before the end of October, so the vendors have had three months to answer before January. Then spend whatever time is left on your private apps, because nobody else is going to fix those for you.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: iPhone Duo Apps: Arabic RTL, Banking & Super-App Readiness Checklist (Xcode 27.1, Vertical Tab Bars, Screenshots)
description:
The short answer

iPhone Duo apps have six days to get ready. Apple opened iPhone Duo pre-orders on Friday 16 October 2026 (5 a.m. PT, which was 4 p.m. in Dubai and 3 p.m. in Riyadh), and the first foldable iPhone reaches customers from Friday 23 October 2026. The UAE is in Apple's first wave, and on 17 October apple.com/sa also showed "Available starting 23/10". Every existing app will run, but only apps rebuilt with the iOS 27.1 SDK in Xcode 27.1 (released 15 October) use the full display. On the outer display, and in landscape on the inner one, toolbars and tab bars move to a vertical column on the side. For Arabic-first products, the detail that matters most is in Apple's Human Interface Guidelines: that vertical column stays on the same physical side in right-to-left languages. This article turns Apple's primary documentation into a checklist for MENA banking, government-ID, super-app and e-commerce teams. Wherever Apple does not document Arabic behaviour, we flag it as something to test, not a promise.

Key facts, with dates and primary sources

  • 9 September 2026, unveiling: Apple introduced iPhone Duo as "the first foldable iPhone". It has a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer display (7.58 and 5.36 inches measured as rectangles), and both displays share the same aspect ratio. It runs on A20 Pro, has Touch ID in the side button for unlocking open or closed, uses an eSIM-only design worldwide, ships with iOS 27.1, and starts at US$1,999 (256GB to 2TB). (Apple Newsroom: Apple unveils iPhone Duo)
  • 18 September 2026, tools: Xcode 27.1 beta arrived with an iPhone Duo simulator, along with Figma and Sketch design kits in Apple Design Resources. (Apple Developer News: Build for iPhone Duo with new resources)
  • 5 October 2026, submissions open: Apple said apps optimised for iPhone Duo can be submitted now. Apps that submit iPhone Duo screenshots get an "optimized for iPhone Duo" badge on the App Store, and from April 2027 submissions will need iPhone Duo screenshots. (Apple Developer News: Prepare and submit your apps for iPhone Duo)
  • 15 October 2026, Xcode 27.1 (27A9275) released: It includes Swift 6.4 and the iOS 27.1 SDK and needs macOS Tahoe 26.6 or later. Known issues: the iPhone Duo simulator runtime doesn't support StandBy or running and debugging most app extensions, and the first simulator launch can take several minutes. (Apple Developer Releases; Xcode 27.1 Release Notes)
  • 16 October 2026, pre-orders: More than 70 countries and regions, including the UAE, could pre-order from 5 a.m. PT. Availability starts 23 October, and 28 more countries and regions follow from 30 October. (Apple Newsroom, 15–16 Oct)
  • Gulf store pages (checked 17 October 2026): apple.com/ae listed iPhone Duo "From AED 8,499" and apple.com/sa listed "From SAR 9,499". Both showed "Pre-order iPhone Duo. Available starting 23/10." Prices can change, so check the store before you quote them. (Apple UAE; Apple Saudi Arabia)
  • Screenshot sizes: the outer display takes 1398 × 2034 (or 2034 × 1398) and the inner display takes 2007 × 2853 (or 2853 × 2007). (App Store Connect: Screenshot specifications)

Do existing iPhone apps work on iPhone Duo without an update?

Yes, they run, but how well depends on the SDK you build with. Apple's "Prepare" page describes three tiers:

  1. iOS 26 SDK or earlier: the app runs but does not adapt. On the open inner display it sits in the centre with empty space around the window. On the closed outer display, content appears to the left of the status bar and camera.
  2. iOS 27 SDK: the app fills most of the inner display but still avoids the status bar on the right edge.
  3. iOS 27.1 SDK or later: the app is optimised. It extends to the full display, and toolbars and tab bars appear vertically below the status bar. Apple warns that before you ship a 27.1 build, you must make sure your content adapts to the bars becoming vertical.

For a Gulf bank or a Saudi super-app, tier 1 looks old the moment a customer unfolds the phone, and tier 3 is where the RTL work starts. Apple's own advice is to rebuild, and the screenshot rule makes that unavoidable by April 2027. (Apple Developer: Three steps to make your app shine on iPhone Duo)

What Apple tells every team to fix first

Apple's checklist is short and very concrete. Its Xcode coding assistant has a resizability skill: ask it to "get my app ready for iPhone Duo". Teams using another agent can export the skill with xcrun agent skills export. Apple says the skill "finds most issues, but not all of them", so review its findings against this list:

  • Stop sizing from the main screen. Replace UIScreen.main.bounds with view.bounds or window.bounds, or use GeometryReader / onGeometryChange in SwiftUI. Create windows with UIWindow(windowScene:).
  • Re-read size when it changes. A fold can resize your app in the middle of a session. Put size-dependent layout in layoutSubviews or viewDidLayoutSubviews, and use viewWillTransition(to:with:) for work that has to run when the size changes.
  • Don't use orientation for layout. Remove layout logic based on UIDevice.current.orientation, statusBarOrientation or interfaceOrientation, and compare width with height instead.
  • Don't treat "regular width" as "iPad". With iPhone Duo, an iPhone app can have any combination of size classes. Code that shows an iPad-only layout whenever horizontalSizeClass == .regular will now run on an iPhone.
  • Remove device-size checks such as bounds.height == 844.
  • Check full-bleed media. Hero images set to aspect-fill "can lose important content on wider displays". Choose between fill and fit, or set a focal point.

Test in the resizable simulator in Device Hub, in iPhone Mirroring on macOS 27 (resize the window to extremes), and in the iPhone Duo simulator in Xcode 27.1. Apple calls the Duo simulator "the best way to test the full native experience".

How do vertical tab bars behave in Arabic RTL on iPhone Duo?

This is the section MENA teams can't skip. Apple's HIG page "Designing for iPhone Duo" (new on 9 September 2026) and the developer article "Preparing your app for iPhone Duo" say the following:

  • On iPhone Duo, toolbars, tab bars and navigation controls move to the side, except on the inner display in portrait, which keeps standard horizontal bars.
  • The side column holds the Dynamic Island, the status bar, the toolbar (including navigation buttons) and the tab bar, from top to bottom.
  • Controls on the vertical axis "stay aligned with the hardware", so they "stay on the same side in right-to-left languages". Apple's tech talk "Raise the bar with iPhone Duo" says the same thing: the bar stays fixed and the content adapts around it.
  • In Split View multitasking, each app puts its controls along its outer edge, so "the left app has controls on the left".
  • In a split view, bars stay horizontal for the sidebar or content column and go vertical for the detail column. On the inner display, sheets get a horizontal toolbar for centred or leading placements and a vertical one for trailing placements.
  • A toolbar item with a title but no icon, or with a custom view, is not shown vertically. The system uses icons in the vertical column.

What this means for Arabic products (our analysis, not Apple's wording): in an LTR app, the side column sits on the trailing edge. In Arabic, the column doesn't flip, so it ends up on the side where Arabic reading starts. Right-aligned Arabic titles, list rows, back affordances and price labels will meet the control column on the same edge. If you used leading/trailing constraints and safe-area insets, the system should handle the spacing. If your Arabic build uses hard-coded left/right offsets, mirrored custom bars or semanticContentAttribute hacks, expect overlaps. Treat these as tests to run, not outcomes we've seen on a device:

  • Run every primary flow in ar-SA / ar-AE and in English on the closed outer display, in landscape on the inner display, and in Split View on both the left and right side.
  • Check that the Arabic Back control at the top of the vertical column uses the system glyph and direction. Don't ship a custom mirrored chevron.
  • Give every toolbar action an SF Symbol plus an Arabic title. Text-only items, such as Arabic "Done" or "Cancel" labels with no icon, stay in a horizontal bar, and the overflow menu shows the icon and title together.
  • Set visibilityPriority so that "Transfer", "Pay" or "Add to cart" stay visible when the column compresses, and choose the compression behaviour: a minimised tab bar for task flows, an overflow toolbar for navigation-heavy screens.
  • In SwiftUI, GeometryProxy.reservedRegions(kind:options:layoutDirectionBehavior:) takes a layout-direction parameter. Test it in Arabic for any custom view that avoids the fold or camera, rather than assuming mirrored frames.
  • Keep amounts, IBANs, card numbers and OTP codes in LTR isolation inside RTL text, and recheck them at every width. Truncation moves when the side column takes space.

Our earlier guides on multilingual product design and the Figma code layers RTL checklist cover the general RTL basics. iPhone Duo adds a fixed, non-mirroring hardware edge to the list.

What should banking and government-ID apps test on a foldable?

Gulf and Egyptian fintech flows include steps that break easily: OTP entry, app switches to Nafath or UAE Pass, card and ID scanning, and biometric prompts. iPhone Duo touches each of them in ways Apple documents:

  1. Biometrics are Touch ID. Apple's press release puts Touch ID in the side button, working whether the device is open or closed. If your Arabic or English copy, onboarding illustrations or settings toggles say "Face ID" without checking LABiometryType, they will be wrong on iPhone Duo. Make the strings come from the biometry type you detect.
  2. Mid-session resizing. Apple says a fold can resize your app mid-session. Open the device on the OTP screen, on the transfer-confirmation screen and while a 3-D Secure web view is loading. Check that entered digits, the timer and the focused field survive, and that the keyboard doesn't hide the Confirm button at either width.
  3. App switch in Split View. iPhone Duo allows two apps side by side for the first time on iPhone. A customer can open the bank app next to Nafath, UAE Pass or an authenticator. Test that universal links and callbacks return to the correct window and that your session timeout doesn't fire while the other app is in front. Our Nafath and UAE Pass onboarding guide lists the return-path failures to look for.
  4. Camera direction can flip. Apple notes that when someone opens, closes or rotates the phone, "the camera you're using may point in the opposite direction". Card, Emirates ID, Iqama and passport scanning should choose the camera by the direction it faces and keep the capture frame clear of the fold.
  5. eSIM-only. iPhone Duo is eSIM-only worldwide. Remove "insert your SIM" steps and support articles that mention SIM trays from Arabic and English onboarding, and check any device-binding logic that assumed a physical SIM.
  6. Tap to Pay and payments UI still use the same system sheets. Re-test them at both widths. Our SAMA Tap to Pay on iPhone article covers the mada trust cues that need to stay visible.

Super-app and e-commerce layouts on the 7.6-inch inner display

Catalogue-heavy apps in the region, including grocery, fashion, electronics retail and ride-hailing super-apps, get the most from the larger screen and have the most to break:

  • Even-column grids. The HIG recommends an even number of columns "so content divides cleanly" at the fold. A 3-column product grid will put the fold through the middle card.
  • Arrangement views. The new ArrangementView (SwiftUI) and UIArrangementViewController (UIKit) offer split and overlay styles. In an overlay arrangement on a partially open device, Apple puts the primary view in the trailing or bottom part relative to the fold. Check which pane Arabic users see first. A map with a ride-request card or a product image with a buy box is a natural fit.
  • Banners with baked-in Arabic text. Promo artwork set to aspect-fill will crop on wider displays, and Arabic headline text inside images is the first thing to disappear. Use live text over images, or set focal points per locale.
  • Two windows. Apple says users can open two windows of the same app, like Safari, for comparison shopping. If your app supports multiple scenes, a "compare two products" or "two accounts" view is a real feature, not a gimmick.
  • Siri AI is English-first. Apple says Siri AI is rolling out in beta in English with iOS 27, and Arabic isn't in its current Apple Intelligence language list. Don't build Arabic marketing around Siri onscreen awareness on iPhone Duo yet. See our Siri AI and iOS 27 article.

Are iPhone Duo screenshots required on the App Store?

They aren't required yet, but they are already worth adding:

  • Now: submitting iPhone Duo screenshots adds a badge to your product page. App Store Connect has a new preview tool that shows your screenshots, product page headers and metadata on iPhone Duo. You can also send a featuring nomination saying the app is optimised for iPhone Duo, "including support for all device poses".
  • April 2027: Apple's news post says submitted apps "will need to include screenshots for iPhone Duo". The screenshot-specifications page frames it as apps using the iOS 27.1 SDK or later. Plan for both readings.
  • Arabic storefronts: prepare ar-SA / ar-AE screenshot sets at 1398 × 2034 (outer) and 2007 × 2853 (inner), and show the Arabic UI with the vertical column on its real side. Apple's design templates include the new product page headers and search result assets.

A one-week plan before 23 October

  1. Day 1: install Xcode 27.1 (macOS Tahoe 26.6+), rebuild on the iOS 27.1 SDK, and run "get my app ready for iPhone Duo".
  2. Day 2: fix UIScreen.main, orientation and idiom checks. Move layout into viewDidLayoutSubviews and size-class logic.
  3. Day 3: audit the bars. Use system containers (NavigationStack, TabView, UINavigationController), add icons and titles, and set visibility priorities.
  4. Day 4: run the Arabic RTL matrix in the Duo simulator across all six poses Apple illustrates (closed, tent, open wide, partially folded, open tall, laptop), in Split View left and right, with Dynamic Type at the largest size.
  5. Day 5: run the fintech regressions (OTP, 3-D Secure, Nafath/UAE Pass return, ID scanning, Touch ID copy), then record EN + AR screenshots and preview them in App Store Connect.

If your design system already separates leading/trailing tokens, as we recommended in fintech design systems and product engineering and the Material 3 and Liquid Glass dual-compile guide, most of this week is testing rather than rewriting.

Frequently asked questions

When can customers in the UAE and Saudi Arabia get iPhone Duo?

Apple opened pre-orders on 16 October 2026 at 5 a.m. PT (4 p.m. UAE, 3 p.m. KSA), with availability from 23 October 2026. The UAE is named in Apple's first-wave list, and apple.com/sa showed "Available starting 23/10" on 17 October. Store prices started from AED 8,499 and SAR 9,499 on that date.

Do existing apps work on iPhone Duo without an update?

They run, but apps built with the iOS 26 SDK or earlier appear centred with empty space on the inner display. Apps built with the iOS 27 SDK fill most of it. Only apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK in Xcode 27.1 use the full display with vertical toolbars and tab bars.

Which Xcode version do I need to build iPhone Duo apps?

You need Xcode 27.1 (build 27A9275, released 15 October 2026). It includes the iOS 27.1 SDK, Swift 6.4 and the iPhone Duo simulator, and requires macOS Tahoe 26.6 or later. The Duo simulator runtime doesn't support StandBy or debugging most app extensions.

How do vertical tab bars behave in Arabic on iPhone Duo?

Apple says controls on the vertical axis stay aligned with the hardware and stay on the same side in right-to-left languages. The bar doesn't mirror and the content adapts around it. Arabic layouts that use leading/trailing constraints and safe areas should adapt, but hard-coded left/right offsets and custom mirrored bars need testing.

Are iPhone Duo screenshots required on the App Store?

Not yet. Submitting them now adds an "optimized for iPhone Duo" badge. Apple says that starting April 2027, submissions will need iPhone Duo screenshots: 1398 × 2034 for the outer display and 2007 × 2853 for the inner display, in portrait or landscape.

title: Enséñale a tu agente a usar AWS
description:
Cada día que pasa estamos sorprendidos por lo capaces que los agentes de código se han convertido. Muchos incluso predicen que ya no necesitamos ingenieros o ingenieras en el futuro y que se viene un apocalipsis donde las computadoras se van a rebelar contra nosotros y contra aquellos que no le decían por favor y gracias a sus agentes después de terminar una tarea.

Nada más alejado de la realidad. Cuando le preguntas algo a tu agente seguramente has notado que se inventa cosas que ni siquiera existen o que te da una solución que quizás no es la adecuada. Y es que el agente no tiene la culpa en sí de que no pueda darte la última versión de la API de una librería porque ellos tienen un corte en la información. Es decir, quedan congelados en el tiempo.

Por supuesto, existen herramientas que le ayudan al agente a encontrar información actualizada y con eso puede ponerle un parche a lo que le falta de información y completar la tarea. Hemos visto cómo pasamos de MCPs a skills y luego a un mix entre ellas.

Y es por eso que hoy quiero platicarte acerca de una herramienta que le va a ayudar a tu agente a hacer las cosas de la forma correcta cuando trabajas con AWS.

AWS no tiene que ser complicado

Sí... yo sé que alguien te dijo que usar AWS es difícil o que necesitas configurar demasiadas cosas. Pero algo que quizás nadie te ha dicho todavía es que mejoramos la plataforma para que puedas construir de manera más sencilla con AWS sin que tengas que gastar tantas horas configurando tu cuenta antes de empezar siquiera a construir.

La nueva experiencia de AWS te permite comenzar de manera más sencilla y sin tanto rollo. Aquí te dejo un blog post adicional por si quieres leer más al respecto.

Uno de los principales cambios para personas como tú y como yo que les gusta empezar rápido y sin tanto trámite es la forma en que puedes conectar tus agentes de IA para que trabajen por ti y te ayuden a construir en AWS.

¿Qué hace esta herramienta?

Como te dije antes, los agentes únicamente aprenden hasta cierta fecha y lo que hace esta herramienta es que te permite utilizar herramientas que quizás ya son familiares para ti como MCP y los Agent Skills para brindarle conocimiento a tu agente de cómo debe trabajarse en AWS de la forma CORRECTA, utilizando las mejores prácticas y aprovechando las bondades de la nueva experiencia.

Si quieres que tu agente tenga estas habilidades solo tenemos que realizar unas configuraciones. Pero lo bueno es que podemos copiar un prompt y pegarlo en nuestro agente para que haga el trabajo por nosotros. Sencillo, ¿no?

Vamos a instalarlo

Iniciemos sesión en nuestra cuenta. Si no tienes una cuenta todavía, te dejo un recurso para que crees tu cuenta. ¡Ahora puedes iniciar sesión hasta con GitHub!

Copiamos el prompt que aparece en nuestra pantalla:

El prompt le dice a nuestros agentes que deben configurar el Agent Toolkit. Y además, les da instrucciones para que usen la nueva experiencia de AWS.

Pegamos el prompt en nuestro editor y esperamos a que el agente termine. Solo necesitaremos ir dando permisos, ya que lo que hará es instalar la AWS CLI en caso de que no la tengamos, o la actualizará y muchas otras cosas.

Después de pegar el prompt empieza con esto. Verificando las herramientas que necesita:

Ya aquí mi agente verificó todo lo que necesita para empezar con la configuración:

En mi caso me pidió que le diera un nombre de perfil. Así que le puedo decir que use el default o darle un nombre. Yo elijo el default.

Esto sirve por si quieres trabajar en diferentes proyectos. Le dices al agente que proyecto tiene que usar y utilizará ese perfil.

Una vez definido el perfil me pide que inicie sesión. Solo necesitas aws login y se abrirá una ventana en tu navegador para terminar de hacer login y seleccionar el proyecto al que quieras acceder.

En mi caso yo estoy colaborando en un proyecto con un compañero por eso se ven dos tarjetas para elegir. Una que en particular dice: Owned by Ramsés.

Si quieres saber más acerca de los proyectos, checa este link, ya que es una ¡nueva feature!

Seleccionamos la opción que necesitemos y vamos a ver la siguiente pantalla:

Después de que haya seleccionado el proyecto se crean credenciales temporales para que pueda acceder a mi cuenta desde la terminal (este acceso lo usará el agente. Ojo, el agente nunca tiene acceso a mi token o contraseña).

Ya que tenemos el acceso listo, el agente configura las Agent Skills que contienen buenas prácticas para trabajar con AWS.

Esto le dará a nuestro agente instrucciones adicionales para que sepa qué hacer en ciertos momentos y que no invente cosas.

Después instalará las nuevas reglas e instrucciones para aprovechar al máximo la nueva experiencia de AWS.

Esto agregará las instrucciones a las guías de tu agente. En mi caso, estoy usando Kiro, así que configurará esas instrucciones en los Steering Files.

Al finalizar, el agente tiene todas las herramientas necesarias para trabajar con nuestra cuenta. Incluso a mí me aparece que puedo pedirle una nueva webapp.

Algo que también es útil es que le podemos preguntar acerca de la nueva experiencia de AWS.

Otra cosa que está genial en la nueva experiencia son los límites de gastos, que también nos los menciona.

Empecemos a crear

Ya que tenemos esto podemos crear lo que nosotros nos imaginemos y desplegarlo de inmediato en nuestra cuenta. Ya no tenemos que desperdiciar tanto tiempo configurando. Ahora podemos aprovechar ese tiempo construyendo, ya que AWS se encarga de darnos una cuenta con configuraciones sensatas por default para que no nos preocupemos.

Recuerda: cada vez que vayas a trabajar con AWS, únicamente escribe aws login para crear las credenciales temporales y que tu agente pueda desplegar tus recursos. ¡Ojo! No te olvides revisar cada acción que el agente tome por ti para siempre estar seguro de lo que estás haciendo 🙂.

¿Qué es lo primero que vas a crear con esta nueva experiencia? Deja tu comentario.

title: 三丰云免费服务器实测：博客+备份脚本跑半年，这些坑要提前排
description:
之前一直写“零事故”，今天换个角度——把我会踩的坑先摘出来。折腾云服务器半年以上，最大的收获不是学会了多少命令，而是知道哪里会疼。三丰云这个免费云服务器，我用它跑 Typecho + Nginx + 自动备份脚本，资源常年很轻松，但有几个设置不做好，后期真的很麻烦。

开机自启：别指望它能自己醒

我第一次部署完，重启机器发现博客挂了。Nginx 没设开机自启，Typecho 依赖的 PHP-FPM 也没跟着起。Linux 服务管理很直接， systemctl 或 chkconfig 都要手动配。

现在的做法是写个启动脚本，加入 rc.local 或者用 systemd 服务文件。每次开机，服务自动拉起，不用 SSH 进去手动敲命令。这一步做了，后续省掉很多“为什么挂了”的困惑。

备份清理：磁盘会涨，记得定期删

我观测到的情况是，磁盘每周涨几百 MB。原因很简单：Nginx 日志、Typecho 上传的图片、数据库备份文件。我的自动备份脚本每天跑一次，如果不加清理逻辑，一个月后磁盘就满了。

现在设定了保留策略：最近 7 天的备份保留，更早的每周清理一次。用 find 命令加上 -mtime 参数，配合 crontab 定时执行。磁盘空间从不满仓变成始终有余量，心态也稳。

提醒设置：续期靠自觉，但别忘了

这和上一篇文章里说的 7 天续期一样。我设了手机日历提醒，每周一早上弹一下。不只是续期，还有实例重启、证书更新这类琐事。没有提醒，大概率会忘；忘了，实例可能就被回收了。

数据方面，负载常年 0.2~0.5，内存占用不到一半。1 核 1G 的机器跑一个 Typecho 博客，确实绰绰有余。5M 带宽日常访问没问题，没遇到过限速或降权的情况。日志和流量统计对得上，没有暗扣。

为什么还愿意用这种“手动维护”的模式

  • 自启配置一次，省去后续手动启动的麻烦
  • 备份清理脚本自动化，磁盘空间可控
  • 日历提醒续期，避免实例被回收
  • 资源充足，博客运行流畅无卡顿
  • 没有复杂账单，只有明确的 7 天周期
  • 故障自愈能力强，脚本挂了能手动拉起
  • 学习 Linux 运维的绝佳沙盒环境
  • 稳定性经受过半年考验，非短期尝鲜
  • 适合个人技术栈沉淀，非商业生产依赖
  • 客服响应及时，工单处理有保障

适合谁这样折腾

如果你是学生、自学开发者，或者想搭个 Typecho 博客、跑个小工具、练手 Linux 命令——这台机器够用。不适合高并发、重要数据长期存放。它是轻量实验场，不是生产级高可用方案。

想试的自己搜三丰云官网。新手建议先了解 Linux 基础命令，再动手配置自启和备份脚本。如果只想搭个静态页面或简单应用，也可以试试 免费虚拟主机，门槛更低。

title: eve adds new Slack event hooks and session controls
description:
eve agents on Slack can now keep replying in a thread without repeated mentions, cancel an in-progress response or reset a conversation entirely, and react to any event your Slack app subscribes to.

Continue conversations without repeated mentions

Mentions no longer have to carry the conversation. Once a thread has an active session, your agent can reply on its own.

The new onMessage hook receives incoming Slack messages, and two helpers decide which ones to handle: ctx.isBotMentioned() detects an explicit mention, and ctx.isSubscribed() checks whether the message belongs to a thread with an active eve session:

When routing depends on who has joined the thread, the new ctx.thread.listParticipants() helper returns unique human Slack user ids in first-appearance order. Public channel messages require the message.channels trigger event type and the channels:history bot scope; private channels also need message.groups and groups:history.

Cancel a turn or reset the conversation

Message hooks also receive two thread-bound session helpers.

ctx.cancel() stops the current turn while keeping the session: call it before returning { auth } to queue the new message as replacement input, so a mid-turn correction drops the stale work and the agent responds to the latest message.

When the conversation should start over instead, ctx.reset() terminally retires the session that owns the thread. The next delivered message begins a new session with fresh history, state, and sandbox. Inside your onMessage dispatch logic, a reset command takes three lines:

Handle any Events API callback

Your agent can now react to any event your Slack app subscribes to.

The new onEvent hook receives raw events such as reaction_added, team_join, and channel_created. Inside the hook, call ctx.receive() to start an agent turn, or call it several times to fan one event out to multiple targets. The team_join event, for example, can kick off onboarding in each of your welcome channels.

Read the Slack channel documentation to get started, or add the channel to your eve agent with eve channels add slack.
