title: Hiding what a player cannot use yet, without hiding the quest
description:
Development covered 30 Aug 2026 to 4 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

Progression games accumulate lists. As Myriad Immortal Sect filled out, the market, the sect exchange, the formation board, the treasure racks and the alchemy bench all became long, and most of what was in them belonged to a stage of the game the player would not reach for weeks.

That is not richness. It is a wall of things you cannot buy, cannot make and cannot use, with the three you can somewhere in the middle of it.

Filtering is the obvious answer and it is wrong

My first instinct was to show only what fits your current realm.

Two things break. You lose the view of what is ahead, and looking at what is ahead is a large part of why anyone plays this kind of game. And you cannot see the good stuff arriving, which is a real reward in itself.

So the shape is not a filter, it is a fold. Items far above your realm collapse into a single card that says how many there are, and the horizon is a setting rather than something baked in, currently two realms ahead. Near-future items stay visible, because they are the ones you are working towards. Distant ones become a number you can open when you are curious. What counts as two realms ahead depends on how the realm ladder works, if you are new to it.

One component does this for all five lists. That matters more than the rule itself, because if each screen implements its own version, the sixth screen will get a slightly different one and the game will feel arbitrary. The bench is the one deliberate variation: it folds, but it does not reorder, because the order of recipes there carries meaning that sorting would destroy.

The exemption that makes it safe

Then the obvious hazard, which I want to state plainly because I nearly shipped it.

A quest tells you to obtain a particular item. The item belongs to a realm above your horizon. The list folds it away. The game has now told you to find something and then hidden it from you, and the player is not wrong to conclude the game is broken.

So anything named by a quest you currently have open is never folded, whatever realm it belongs to. Objective or reward, it stays visible, in every list.

The general rule I would give anyone building progressive disclosure: your hiding rule needs an escape valve keyed to what the product is currently asking the user to do. Static rules about relevance are always wrong for the user who has just been given a task. The formation board is one of the five lists, and the formations and arrays guide shows what lives on it.

A small language trap on the way out

The fold card says how many items are hidden. In English, with one item, it read "1 more items."

Plurals are a real grammar feature and not a string with an s on the end. English needs one extra form here, and the other ten languages the game speaks each need their own rules, some with more forms than English has. Every list in the game now goes through that, which took an afternoon and removes a whole category of small embarrassments.

Also this week

A round of work on refusals, prompted by watching real sessions. A Sell button was pressable on a row whose price could not be worked out, and pressing it went through, so the player learned what they had sold by reading their own history afterwards. Another panel kept the balance it had before a refusal rather than the one the refusal reported, so every later message about being short of funds was quoting a number that was not true.

A refusal is a message. If you throw away the information it arrives with, everything you say after it is guesswork delivered with confidence.

Free to start, no install: see the folded lists in your browser, with more notes at Myriad Immortal Sect.

title: Database Indexing – Part 1: How Indexes Help Find Data Faster
description:
Recently, I was reading two books: Good Vibes, Good Life and The Mountain Is You.

I usually forget things after some time 😅. So whenever I want to revisit something I've read, I go back to the book.

But I noticed one difference between these two books.

Good Vibes, Good Life has an index at the end of the book. Whenever I want to read about a particular topic, I can look at the index, find the page number, and directly go to that page.

But The Mountain Is You doesn't have that kind of index.

So if I remember a topic but don't remember where I read it, I have to go through the chapters one by one until I find it.

That takes more time, right?

The same thing happens in databases.

Imagine we have a table containing millions of records, and we want to find one particular record.

Without an index, the database may need to scan the entire table, checking rows to find the data we're looking for.

But if we have a suitable index, the database can use it to quickly locate the required record instead of checking every row.

This is why we use indexes in databases.

An index is a separate data structure that helps the database find records efficiently, just like the index in a book helps us find a topic without going through every page.

Before moving forward, check out my previous article, Database Storage Concepts – How Tables Are Stored on Disk, to understand how databases store data internally.

Now, let's see how indexing actually works in PostgreSQL.

Creating a Table with an Index and 10 Million Records

First, let's create an employees table with three columns: id, name, and salary.

Step 1: Create the table

CREATE TABLE employees (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT,
    salary INTEGER
);

Here, we defined id as the PRIMARY KEY.

In PostgreSQL, whenever we define a primary key, it automatically creates a unique B-tree index on that column.

In our case, PostgreSQL created an index named employees_pkey on the id column.

Step 2: Insert 10 million records

INSERT INTO employees (id, name, salary)
SELECT
    g,
    'Employee_' || g,
    30000 + (random() * 70000)::INTEGER
FROM generate_series(1, 10000000) AS g;

We now have a table containing 10 million employee records.

Let's understand how PostgreSQL uses indexes when we execute different queries.

Understanding Indexes Through Queries

Query 1: Fetching a Record Using an Indexed Column

Let's find the employee whose id is 20.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id FROM employees WHERE id = 20;

Before looking at the output, let's understand what EXPLAIN, ANALYZE, and BUFFERS mean.

  • EXPLAIN: Shows how PostgreSQL plans to execute a query without actually running it.
  • ANALYZE: Executes the query and shows what actually happened, including the number of rows returned and execution time.
  • BUFFERS: Shows how many data block accesses PostgreSQL made during planning and execution, including blocks already available in memory and blocks that had to be read into memory.

By combining these options, we can understand how PostgreSQL executes our query and how it accesses data.

Output (First Execution):

Now, let's understand each part of the output.

1. Index Only Scan

Index Only Scan using employees_pkey on employees
  • PostgreSQL used the employees_pkey index, which was automatically created when we defined id as the primary key.
  • We're searching by id and selecting only id.
  • Since id is already stored in the index, PostgreSQL can retrieve the required value directly from the index.
  • It doesn't need to fetch the full employee record from the table, provided PostgreSQL can confirm that the row is visible without checking the heap.

This is called an Index Only Scan.

2. Cost

cost=0.43..4.45
  • 0.43: Estimated startup cost before PostgreSQL can begin returning rows.
  • 4.45: Estimated total cost of executing this operation.

These values are PostgreSQL's internal cost estimates, not actual execution times in milliseconds.

3. Rows and Width

rows=1 width=4
  • rows=1: PostgreSQL estimates that one row will be returned.
  • width=4: The estimated average size of each returned row is 4 bytes.

We're selecting only id, which is an integer occupying 4 bytes.

4. Actual Time, Rows, and Loops

actual time=0.058..0.059 rows=1 loops=1
  • 0.058: Time taken until the first row was returned.
  • 0.059: Time taken until this scan operation completed.
  • rows=1: One row was actually returned.
  • loops=1: This operation executed once.

The actual times are measured in milliseconds.

5. Index Condition

Index Cond: (id = 20)

This tells us that PostgreSQL used the condition id = 20 to search the index.

6. Heap Fetches

Heap Fetches: 0

PostgreSQL stores actual table records in heap pages.

An Index Only Scan can avoid visiting heap pages when all the required values are available in the index and PostgreSQL can confirm row visibility using its visibility map.

Here, Heap Fetches: 0 means PostgreSQL didn't need to visit any heap pages to check row visibility.

7. Buffers

Buffers: shared read=4

PostgreSQL stores frequently accessed data pages in memory, in an area called shared buffers.

  • shared read=4: PostgreSQL had to read 4 blocks into its shared buffer cache.
  • Each PostgreSQL block is typically 8 KB.

This doesn't necessarily mean 4 physical disk reads, because the operating system may already have those pages cached.

8. Planning Time and Execution Time

Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=41 read=20
Planning Time: 0.616 ms
Execution Time: 0.097 ms

Before executing a query, PostgreSQL first decides how to execute it.

For example, it checks what indexes are available, estimates how many rows might match, and decides which execution plan would be more efficient.

During this process, PostgreSQL may need to access database pages containing metadata and statistics.

That's why we see:

Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=41 read=20
  • shared hit=41: During planning, PostgreSQL made 41 buffer accesses that found pages already available in shared buffers.
  • shared read=20: During planning, PostgreSQL made 20 block reads into shared buffers.
  • Planning Time: 0.616 ms: Time taken to prepare the execution plan.
  • Execution Time: 0.097 ms: Time taken to execute the plan and retrieve the result.

So, PostgreSQL first decides how to fetch the data (planning) and then actually fetches the data (execution).

What Happens When We Run the Same Query Again?

I executed the exact same query one more time.

Output (Second Execution):

Notice the difference:

Metric First execution Second execution
Execution shared reads 4 0
Execution shared hits 0 4
Planning time 0.616 ms 0.059 ms
Execution time 0.097 ms 0.027 ms

In the first execution, PostgreSQL had to read 4 blocks into shared buffers.

But during the second execution, those blocks were already available in PostgreSQL's memory.

That's why we see:

Buffers: shared hit=4

A shared hit means PostgreSQL found the required block in its shared buffer cache without needing to read it into that cache again.

The second execution was faster in our experiment, although execution times can also vary for other reasons.

Testing Without PostgreSQL's Existing Cache

If you want to observe how a query behaves when its pages are not already cached in PostgreSQL's shared buffers, you can restart PostgreSQL on your local test machine.

On Ubuntu:

sudo systemctl restart postgresql

Then execute:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id FROM employees WHERE id = 20;

Restarting PostgreSQL clears its shared buffer cache, but it does not clear the operating system's page cache. Some pages may also be loaded again before your query runs.

So this is useful for observing PostgreSQL's buffer behavior, but it doesn't guarantee a completely cold disk-cache experiment.

Only restart PostgreSQL for this purpose on a local test environment, not on a production or shared database.

Query 2: Fetching a Column That Is Not in the Index

In the previous query, we selected id, which was already available in the primary key index.

Now, let's try fetching name using the same index.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE id = 500;

Output:

Here, PostgreSQL used an Index Scan instead of an Index Only Scan.

Why?

Our employees_pkey index contains id, but not name.

So PostgreSQL:

  1. Searches the index to find id = 500.
  2. Gets the reference to the corresponding heap row.
  3. Visits the heap to fetch the name.

This is called an Index Scan.

Notice the estimated cost:

cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=16

The total estimated cost is 8.45, compared with 4.45 in Query 1, because PostgreSQL also needs to fetch the row from the heap.

The estimated width is now 16 bytes instead of 4, because we're selecting a text column rather than an integer.

Buffers: shared hit=2 read=2

During execution, PostgreSQL made 2 shared-buffer hits and 2 shared-buffer reads, covering the index search and heap access.

The execution took 0.093 ms.

So the difference is simple: an Index Only Scan can return data from the index without visiting the heap when visibility permits, whereas this Index Scan uses the index to find the row and then visits the heap to retrieve name.

Query 3: Searching Using a Column Without an Index

Until now, we've been searching using id, which has an index.

But what happens if we search using a column that doesn't have an index?

Let's try searching using name.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id FROM employees
WHERE name = 'Employee_500';

Output:

Here, PostgreSQL used a Parallel Sequential Scan.

Let's understand what happened.

1. Parallel Sequential Scan

Parallel Seq Scan on employees

Since we haven't created an index on name, PostgreSQL cannot use an index on that column to locate the required employee.

Instead, it scans the table and checks the name of each row against our condition.

But rather than using a single process, PostgreSQL decided to scan the table in parallel.

2. Workers Planned and Launched

Workers Planned: 2
Workers Launched: 2

PostgreSQL planned to use 2 additional worker processes and successfully launched both.

Along with the main process, 3 processes participated in scanning the table.

Each process works on different portions of the table, allowing the scan to finish faster than a single-process scan might.

3. Filter and Rows Removed

Filter: (name = 'Employee_500'::text)
Rows Removed by Filter: 3333333

PostgreSQL checks each row against the condition name = 'Employee_500'.

Rows that don't match are removed by the filter.

Here, Rows Removed by Filter: 3333333 is the average number of rows rejected per execution of the parallel scan, rounded for display.

Since loops=3, approximately 10 million rows were checked across all three participants.

Even though we wanted only one employee, PostgreSQL had to examine the entire table.

4. Gather

Gather  (cost=1000.00..125620.26 rows=1 width=4)

The Gather operation collects the rows produced by the parallel scan participants and passes them to the main query process.

In our case, only one row matched the condition.

5. Buffer Usage

Buffers: shared hit=1 read=72545

During execution, PostgreSQL made:

  • 1 shared-buffer hit.
  • 72,545 shared-buffer reads.

With the usual 8 KB page size, those reads represent approximately 567 MB of block-read traffic.

Notice that the Gather and Parallel Seq Scan show the same buffer totals. We shouldn't add them together, because the parent node's statistics include the work of its child node.

6. Execution Time

Execution Time: 374.165 ms

The query took 374.165 ms to execute.

Compare that with Query 2, where we searched using the indexed id column and the execution took 0.093 ms.

The difference is significant in these particular runs.

With the index, PostgreSQL could locate the row directly. Without an index on name, it scanned all 10 million records to find one matching employee.

Query 4: Creating an Index on the Name Column and Comparing Query Performance

In the previous query, PostgreSQL scanned all 10 million records because there was no index on name.

Now, let's create an index on that column.

CREATE INDEX employees_name_idx
ON employees (name);

This creates a B-tree index on name.

Let's execute the query again.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id FROM employees
WHERE name = 'Employee_500';

Output:

This time, PostgreSQL used an Index Scan.

1. Index Scan

Index Scan using employees_name_idx on employees

PostgreSQL searches the new index for Employee_500.

Since we're selecting id, which isn't stored in this index, PostgreSQL then visits the heap to fetch it.

2. Buffer Usage

Buffers: shared hit=1 read=4

During execution, PostgreSQL made just 5 shared-buffer accesses, compared with 72,546 in the previous query.

3. Execution Time

Execution Time: 0.050 ms

Let's compare the results before and after creating the index.

Metric Without index With index
Scan type Parallel Seq Scan Index Scan
Shared hits 1 1
Shared reads 72,545 4
Execution time 374.165 ms 0.050 ms

The execution time decreased from 374.165 ms to 0.050 ms — approximately 7,483 times faster in these two runs.

Of course, caching and other execution conditions can also affect these timings, so we shouldn't expect exactly the same improvement every time.

But the important difference is how PostgreSQL searches for the record.

Earlier, PostgreSQL had to scan the entire table to find Employee_500.

After creating the index, it searched the B-tree index for that particular name and used the matching entry to fetch the row from the heap.

So even if the execution time varies due to caching, PostgreSQL no longer needs to scan all 10 million table records just to find that employee.

Query 5: Sorting Records Without an Index

So far, we've seen how indexes help PostgreSQL search for records. But indexes can also help when sorting data.

Let's find the top 100 employees with the highest salaries.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 100;

Output:

Note: When reading an EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution plan, it's usually easier to start from the bottom and move toward the top.

The lower-level operations produce data, which is then passed to their parent operations.

In our query, the data flows through:

  1. Parallel Seq Scan – Reads the records from the table.
  2. Sort – Finds the highest salaries.
  3. Gather Merge – Combines the sorted results from the parallel workers.
  4. Limit – Returns only the top 100 records.

This is a useful way to understand execution plans, although some operations can run at the same time.

Now, let's understand each operation.

1. Parallel Sequential Scan

Parallel Seq Scan on employees

Since there is no index on salary, PostgreSQL scans the table to find the highest salaries.

Even though we requested only 100 records, PostgreSQL still needs to examine all 10 million records to determine which employees have the highest salaries.

2. Sort

Sort Key: salary DESC
Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 31kB

PostgreSQL needs to arrange the results by salary in descending order.

But notice that it used top-N heapsort.

Since we requested only the top 100 records, PostgreSQL doesn't need to fully sort all 10 million records.

Instead, each parallel scan participant keeps track of its best 100 candidates while processing the rows.

This reduces the memory required for sorting, but the table still has to be scanned.

3. Gather Merge

Gather Merge
Workers Planned: 2
Workers Launched: 2

The parallel participants produce sorted results.

Gather Merge combines these results while maintaining the salary order.

4. Limit

Limit

Finally, PostgreSQL returns only the first 100 records from the sorted results.

5. Buffer Usage and Execution Time

Buffers: shared hit=273 read=72385
Execution Time: 575.346 ms

During execution, PostgreSQL made 273 shared-buffer hits and 72,385 shared-buffer reads.

The query took 575.346 ms to execute.

Even though we requested just 100 records, PostgreSQL had to examine all 10 million records to identify the highest salaries.

Query 6: Sorting Records After Creating an Index on Salary

In the previous query, PostgreSQL scanned all 10 million records and performed sorting to find the top 100 highest salaries.

Now, let's create an index on salary.

CREATE INDEX employees_salary_idx
ON employees (salary);

This creates a B-tree index on the salary column, where the index entries are maintained in sorted order.

Let's run the same query again.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 100;

Output:

Notice that PostgreSQL used an Index Scan Backward instead of a Parallel Sequential Scan followed by sorting.

1. Index Scan Backward

Index Scan Backward using employees_salary_idx on employees

A B-tree index keeps its entries in sorted order.

Since our query uses ORDER BY salary DESC, PostgreSQL can scan the index backward, starting from the highest salary values.

It doesn't need to sort all 10 million records separately.

And because we're also selecting id, which isn't stored in the salary index, PostgreSQL visits the heap to fetch it.

2. Limit

Limit (cost=0.43..5.17 rows=100 width=8)

This is where the LIMIT 100 makes a big difference.

PostgreSQL starts reading the index from the highest salary and stops after returning 100 records.

Even though the index contains entries for 10 million records, PostgreSQL doesn't need to scan all of them.

3. Buffer Usage

Buffers: shared read=103

PostgreSQL made only 103 shared-buffer reads during execution.

Compare that with the previous query, which required 72,658 buffer accesses.

4. Execution Time

Execution Time: 1.123 ms

Let's compare both executions.

Metric Without salary index With salary index
Execution plan Parallel Seq Scan + Sort Index Scan Backward
Shared hits 273 0
Shared reads 72,385 103
Execution time 575.346 ms 1.123 ms

The execution time decreased from 575.346 ms to 1.123 ms, approximately 512 times faster in these runs.

Although caching can affect execution times, the important difference is that PostgreSQL no longer needs to scan the entire table and sort the results.

It can simply scan the index backward, retrieve the highest salary records, and stop after finding 100 rows.

Query 7: Why Doesn't PostgreSQL Always Use an Index?

Until now, we've seen how indexes improved query performance.

But does PostgreSQL always use an index whenever one is available?

Let's try searching for employees whose salary is greater than 40000.

Remember, we already created an index on the salary column.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 40000;

Output:

Interesting! PostgreSQL chose a Sequential Scan, even though an index exists on salary.

Why?

1. Sequential Scan

Seq Scan on employees

Our condition is:

WHERE salary > 40000

This matches a large number of employees.

In our case, PostgreSQL found 8,572,502 matching records out of 10 million, which is approximately 85.7% of the table.

If PostgreSQL used the salary index, it would need to find all matching index entries and then visit the heap to fetch id, since id isn't stored in that index.

For so many matching records, accessing the heap through the index could require more work than simply scanning the table.

So PostgreSQL estimated that a Sequential Scan would be cheaper.

2. Rows Removed by Filter

Filter: (salary > 40000)
Rows Removed by Filter: 1427498

PostgreSQL scanned all 10 million records.

Of those:

  • 8,572,502 records matched the condition.
  • 1,427,498 records were removed by the filter.

3. Buffer Usage

Buffers: shared hit=16247 read=56299

PostgreSQL accessed 72,546 shared-buffer blocks while scanning the table.

Some pages were already cached, while others had to be read into shared buffers.

4. Execution Time

Execution Time: 1123.251 ms

The query took approximately 1.12 seconds to execute and return over 8.5 million rows to the query executor.

Here, the important thing is that having an index doesn't mean PostgreSQL will always use it.

PostgreSQL's query planner estimates the cost of different execution plans and chooses the one it expects to be cheaper.

When a query returns a small number of records, an index can be very useful. But when most of the table matches, a sequential scan may be more efficient.

What's Next?

In this article, we focused on understanding indexing through practical queries and execution plans.

In Part 2, we'll explore different types of index scans, when PostgreSQL chooses each one, and how we can design indexes more efficiently.

That's it for now! 😊

Thanks for reading!

title: The AI Bottleneck Isn't Generating Code — It's Governing It
description:
Anyone who has given autonomous AI coding agents (Claude, Devin, Antigravity, or Copilot Workspace) free rein in a production repository knows the uneasy feeling: in one minute, the agent writes a brilliant algorithm; in the next, it touches an unrelated file, rewrites your go.mod, hallucinates non-existent unit tests, and tries to commit directly to main.

The industry is beginning to recognize a fundamental truth:

The real bottleneck in AI-assisted software engineering isn't token speed or code generation. It is the ability to verify, constrain, and deterministically govern what gets generated.

During my postgraduate studies in Applied AI Engineering, I set out to turn this recurring friction into an industrial software engineering standard: Pipeline-AI.

In this article, I will break down how we built a deterministic, zero-trust multi-agent workflow powered by Go 1.24 OS lifecycle hooks, strict TDD, and role specialization integrated natively into the Google Antigravity ecosystem.

The Trap: Why "Prompt Engineering" Fails at Governance

The naive way to control an AI agent is to append natural language constraints to its prompt:

"Please do not modify files outside of internal/user/, and never commit directly to main."

This fails because of a mathematical reality: LLMs are probabilistic, but software engineering requires deterministic guarantees.

If an LLM has a 1% chance of ignoring an instruction under a dense context window or deep reasoning tree, that 1% will manifest in your release branch. Governance cannot live inside the agent's prompt — it must live in the execution environment (at the operating system level).

1. Zero-Trust Defense: OS Lifecycle Hooks (PreToolUse)

Our first architectural decision was enforcing the principle of least privilege: the main interactive chat session is physically prohibited from editing code directly.

Google Antigravity provides native lifecycle hooks, notably the PreToolUse event. Whenever an agent invokes a file modification tool (write_to_file, replace_file_content), the hook intercepts the request before a single byte is touched on disk.

We built pipeline-hook, a statically compiled Go 1.24 binary with zero external dependencies (stdlib only). It intercepts the JSON payload on stdin, identifies which subagent is executing, and checks the target file against project guardrails:

// Simplified interception logic from pipeline-hook in Go
func run(stdin io.Reader, stdout, stderr io.Writer) int {
    var in hookInput
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &in); err != nil {
        return replyAllow(stdout)
    }

    // Intercept disk mutation attempts
    if editTools[in.ToolName] {
        target := in.FilePath()

        // Check against protected paths defined in .pipeline-ai.json
        if cfg.IsProtected(target) && !cfg.IsEditorAgent(in.AgentType) {
            msg := fmt.Sprintf(
                "BLOCKED: Agent '%s' is not authorized to edit '%s'. "+
                "Only authorized agents [%s] can modify this directory.",
                in.AgentType, target, strings.Join(cfg.EditorAgents, ", "),
            )
            // Emits JSON {"decision": "deny", "reason": "..."} to stdout with exit 0
            return replyDeny(msg, stdout)
        }
    }

    return replyAllow(stdout)
}

If a product triage agent or an unauthorized session attempts to modify internal/auth/token.go, the OS hook immediately halts the call with decision: deny. There is no prompting negotiation: the tool call is blocked at the system boundary.

2. The 16-Skill Pipeline: Specialization vs. Monolithic Agents

A common anti-pattern is relying on a "do-it-all" agent. Asking a single prompt to understand business requirements, architect database schemas, write unit tests, implement the code, and review diffs results in massive context drift and shallow reasoning.

In Pipeline-AI, we decomposed the software development lifecycle into 16 specialized skills:

1. pm-triage              → Classifies scope, tags DEL-ID, identifies technical requirements
2. architecture-guardrails → Establishes technical boundaries and invariant locks
3. [data-model]           → Designs schemas & entities (PostgreSQL, Mongo, DynamoDB)
4. test-writer            → Authors table-driven tests and fuzz targets (Red phase)
5. dev-implementation     → Implements code strictly until tests pass (Green phase)
6. code-reviewer          → Audits diffs separating hard blockers from suggestions
7. [migration-reviewer]   → Validates DDL idempotency, locks, and rollback safety
8. [security-review]      → Automatically triggered when auth, crypto, or storage is touched
9. [supply-chain-review]  → Audits go.mod changes and invokes govulncheck
10. qa-validation         → Executes the full test suite and validates project invariants
11. [release-ops]         → Handles SemVer, manifests, and deployment readiness
12. docs-update           → Compiles the audited delivery report with diff evidence
13. git-delivery          → Creates isolated branch, conventional commit, and Pull Request

(Brackets denote optional modules activated via configuration).

Each agent has clear boundaries: the code-reviewer has read-only permissions and cannot edit code; the dev-implementation agent only begins working after test-writer has committed failing tests.

3. Strict TDD as the Antidote to Hallucinations

The single best specification for an LLM is a failing unit test:

  1. Red: The test-writer agent receives the architectural guardrails and writes comprehensive table-driven tests using Go's standard testing package. It runs go test ./... and proves the failure.
  2. Green: The dev-implementation agent takes over. Its job is not to guess user intent or speculate on future features — its sole goal is to make the tests pass.
  3. Refactor & Format: When go test -race ./... is green and gofmt formats the code automatically via PostToolUse hooks, implementation stops. Zero dead code, zero scope creep.

4. The Delivery Gatekeeper: pipeline-validate

Before any Pull Request is created, our custom validator verifies the delivery:

go tool pipeline-validate docs-ai/deliveries/DEL-011/report.md

The validator automatically rejects the delivery if:

  • Checklist tasks remain unchecked.
  • The delivery report contains unresolved markers (TODO, FIXME, TBD, filler text).
  • The real git diff touches security-sensitive files (security_surface_paths) without an explicitly approved security audit section.

If the gatekeeper fails, Git delivery is aborted. The PR cannot be opened.

5. Real-World Case Study: Desktop Go + SQLite

We validated this pipeline in an active desktop application:

  • Zero CGO Invariant: The pipeline enforced that no external dependencies broke cross-compilation from Linux/WSL2 to Windows, producing a standalone 37MB executable.
  • Proactive Security: When an agent modified internal/storage/sqlite/, the pipeline automatically flagged a security surface touch, enforcing parameterized queries (SQL injection prevention) and passing govulncheck.
  • Git Protection: Direct pushes to main were blocked locally by .githooks/pre-push and remotely by GitHub Rulesets. All deliverables reached production via clean, squashed PRs.

Key Takeaways for Applied AI Engineers

  1. Treat AI agents like hyper-fast junior engineers with terminal access: Give them powerful tools, but isolate them with deterministic OS hooks and comprehensive test suites.
  2. Determinism beats probability: Whenever possible, replace natural language prompting with compiled CLI gates (go tool) and static linters.
  3. Role specialization minimizes context degradation: Smaller agents with surgical scopes consume fewer tokens, make fewer mistakes, and are dramatically easier to audit.

Open Source

The complete toolkit — including the pipeline-init scaffolding CLI, Go hooks, and the full catalog of 16 Antigravity skills — is open-source under the MIT license:

👉 GitHub: rodrigodosanjosoliveira/pipeline-ai

How are you handling governance and guardrails for autonomous coding agents in your workflows? Let's discuss in the comments below! 💬👇

title: Building Secure AWS Cloud Networking: VPC Peering, Private EC2, NAT Gateway, and S3 Gateway Endpoint
description:
A Hands-On Implementation of Multi-VPC Connectivity, Controlled Internet Access, IAM-Based Authentication, and Private AWS Service Routing

By Syed Bilal Bukhari
Cloud Computing / AWS / Cloud Networking · Foundational to Intermediate · Region: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1

Introduction

In cloud networking, "it connects" and "it connects the way I intended" are different statements. A packet leaving an EC2 instance is steered by route tables, filtered by security groups, translated by gateways, and authorized (for AWS APIs) by IAM. When something fails, the cause sits in one of those layers, and you can only find it if you know which path the traffic is supposed to take.

I built this lab to make those paths explicit. It has two VPCs in us-east-1, one public EC2 instance, and one private EC2 instance with no public IPv4 address. The private instance has three jobs: talk to the public VPC over VPC Peering, reach the internet outbound-only through a NAT Gateway, and reach Amazon S3 using an IAM role instead of stored access keys.

This is a foundational-to-intermediate lab, not a production design. I will point out where it falls short as I go. I will also separate what the AWS Console configuration shows from what the terminal tests prove, because those are two different kinds of evidence.

Project Objectives

  1. Give the public EC2 instance internet access through an Internet Gateway.
  2. Connect two VPCs privately using VPC Peering, with non-overlapping CIDR blocks.
  3. Reach the private EC2 instance over SSH through the public instance as a jump host.
  4. Let the private instance start outbound internet connections through a NAT Gateway, without a public IP.
  5. Add an S3 Gateway Endpoint so S3-bound traffic from the private route table has a dedicated route.
  6. Authenticate the private instance to AWS with an IAM role rather than permanent access keys.
  7. Validate each step with real terminal tests and Console configuration.

AWS Services and Tools

Component What it did in this lab
Amazon VPC (two VPCs) Isolated networks: mys-vpc-001 and myp-vpc-002
Subnets and route tables Decide what is "public" or "private" through their routes
Internet Gateways One per VPC; the target for internet-routable traffic
VPC Peering Private routing between the two VPCs
NAT Gateway + Elastic IP Outbound-only IPv4 internet access for the private subnet
S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint Route-table target for regional S3 traffic
IAM role Temporary credentials for the private instance
Security Groups Instance-level traffic filtering (ICMP, SSH)
EC2 (t3.micro, Amazon Linux 2023) One instance in each VPC
MobaXterm, ping, curl, AWS CLI SSH access and connectivity verification

Architecture Overview

Figure 1. Architecture of the lab. Orange arrows are internet-bound traffic, the dashed blue line is inter-VPC traffic over peering, and green arrows are S3 traffic through the Gateway Endpoint. The private EC2 instance has no direct path to an Internet Gateway; its internet traffic goes through the NAT Gateway first.

Public VPC Private VPC
Name / CIDR mys-vpc-001 / 10.0.0.0/24 myp-vpc-002 / 10.0.1.0/24
Subnets mys-subnet-01 10.0.0.0/28 (us-east-1a) myp-private-subnet-002 10.0.1.0/28 and myp-nat-public-subnet 10.0.1.16/28 (both us-east-1b)
EC2 my-public-ec2, 10.0.0.6, public IPv4 Private EC2, 10.0.1.6, no public IPv4
Gateways Internet Gateway myp-igw-002, NAT Gateway myp-nat-gateway-002 (10.0.1.22 + Elastic IP)

Public VPC Configuration

The Public VPC has one public subnet. The instance my-public-ec2 is a t3.micro running Amazon Linux 2023, with private IP 10.0.0.6 and a public IPv4 address. I reached it over SSH with key authentication from MobaXterm. It plays two roles: the internet-facing test host and the jump host for the private instance.

Figure 2. The EC2 console showing running t3.micro instances that passed 3/3 status checks. my-public-ec2 is in us-east-1a; the instance used for private-side testing is in us-east-1b.

A subnet is public because of its route table, not its name. mys-public-rt sends VPC-local traffic locally, sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway, and sends 10.0.1.0/24 to the peering connection.

Figure 3. mys-public-rt (captured from the Edit routes view). All three routes are Active: local, 10.0.1.0/24 via the peering connection, and 0.0.0.0/0 via the Internet Gateway.

Private VPC Configuration

The VPC is called "Private VPC", but that name is only a label. Whether a subnet is public or private depends on its route table. This VPC deliberately contains one of each:

  • myp-private-subnet-002 (10.0.1.0/28) holds the private EC2 instance at 10.0.1.6. Its route table has no route to an Internet Gateway.
  • myp-nat-public-subnet (10.0.1.16/28) holds only the NAT Gateway. Its route table, myp-nat-public-rt, has a default route to the Internet Gateway myp-igw-002, which makes it a public subnet.

Figure 4. The Private VPC resource map: two subnets in us-east-1b, three route tables, and the connections myp-igw-002, myp-nat-gateway-002 (public NAT, one ENI and one EIP) and myp-s3-endpoint (gateway endpoint to S3). The right edge of the original capture is cut off.

VPC Peering

Concepts

VPCs are isolated by default. A VPC Peering connection creates a private routing path between two VPCs using private IP addresses. It is not a gateway and not a VPN, and it does not provide internet access.

Four properties shaped the design:

  • Non-overlapping CIDRs are mandatory. If both VPCs used the same range, a route for that range could not say which VPC a destination belongs to. Here the VPCs use 10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.1.0/24.
  • Request and accept. One VPC (the requester, mys-vpc-001) asks and the other (the accepter, myp-vpc-002) accepts. Until it is accepted, the connection is not usable.
  • Both sides need routes. An Active peering connection only creates the possibility of traffic. Each VPC's route table needs a route to the other VPC's CIDR with the peering connection as the target.
  • Peering is not transitive. AWS documents that two VPCs cannot use a third, peered VPC as a transit path. Peering also does not bypass Security Groups or Network ACLs, which still filter the traffic.

Figure 5. public-private-peering (pcx-0763ca5cff1e5a68e) in Active status, with requester VPC vpc-044079de0026185ef. The accepter column is off-screen in this capture, so the accepter details come from my project notes.

Routes on both sides

The Public VPC's route (Figure 3) sends 10.0.1.0/24 to the peering connection. The Private VPC's route table, myp-private-rt-002, has the mirror route plus two more:

Destination Target Purpose
10.0.1.0/24 local Traffic inside the Private VPC
10.0.0.0/24 Peering connection Traffic to the Public VPC
0.0.0.0/0 NAT Gateway nat-04d646b2df4be7880 Everything else, IPv4
pl-63a5400a Gateway endpoint vpce-0f6dfcad71b59e9d9 S3 (regional prefix list)

Figure 6. myp-private-rt-002 with all four routes Active. This is also the evidence that the S3 prefix-list route exists (see the S3 section).

AWS picks the most specific matching route (longest prefix match). A packet to 10.0.0.6 matches 10.0.0.0/24 and goes over peering, not to the NAT Gateway, even though 0.0.0.0/0 also matches. A packet to an S3 address falls in a range from the S3 prefix list, which is more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, so it takes the endpoint route. Anything else falls through to the NAT Gateway.

Reachability test

From the public instance (10.0.0.6) I pinged the private instance:

ping -c 4 10.0.1.6

Figure 7. Four packets transmitted, four received, 0% loss. Replies took between 0.452 and 0.468 ms. The final min/avg/max line is cut off in my capture; the mean of the four replies is about 0.457 ms.

This proves ICMP reachability between instances in separate VPCs. It does not prove that every application port works, because ping only exercises ICMP. The first attempts were blocked until I added the right Security Group rule (see Challenges).

SSH Access Between VPCs

I confirmed that the public instance could reach port 22 on the private instance over the peering link. For access from my own machine I used MobaXterm's SSH gateway (jump host) feature, which opens the session to the private address through the public instance, so the private machine never needs a public IPv4 address. I did not copy the private key onto the jump host.

Port 22 on the private instance should accept connections only from the jump host's side, not from 0.0.0.0/0. I did not capture screenshots of the Security Group rules, so I am describing that intent rather than showing the rule set.

NAT Gateway for Outbound Internet Access

The private instance has no public IP, so by itself it cannot reach the internet. A public NAT Gateway in a public subnet fixes that:

Private EC2 → private route table → NAT Gateway → Internet Gateway → Internet

Why each piece is there:

  • The NAT Gateway is in a public subnet (myp-nat-public-subnet) because it needs a route to an Internet Gateway, and it has an Elastic IP that serves as its public address.
  • The NAT subnet's route table points to myp-igw-002. Without that, the NAT Gateway has no way out.
  • The private instance keeps only its private IP. The NAT Gateway translates its source address on the way out and maps replies back.
  • Inbound is limited by design. AWS documents that connections through a NAT Gateway must start from inside the VPC, so unsolicited inbound connections from the internet cannot reach the private instance this way.

A NAT Gateway does not replace Security Groups, and it is not application-level security. It simply provides address translation for outbound IPv4.

Figure 8. myp-nat-gateway-002 in Available state: connectivity type Public, private IPv4 10.0.1.22, in myp-nat-public-subnet of myp-vpc-002. The account ID in the ARN and the Elastic IP are redacted.

From the private instance:

curl -I --max-time 15 https://www.google.com

Figure 9. HTTP/2 200 received from the private EC2 prompt (ip-10-0-1-6). I cropped the screenshot to remove the cookie headers that followed.

Before the routing was right, this same command timed out. That is covered in Challenges.

S3 Gateway Endpoint and IAM Role

The endpoint

A VPC endpoint lets resources in a VPC reach an AWS service without going over the public internet path. There are two types: Interface endpoints (an ENI with private IPs in your subnet, powered by PrivateLink) and Gateway endpoints (a route-table target, available for S3 and DynamoDB). I used a Gateway endpoint because it fits the lab: it needs no ENI in my subnet, and AWS states there is no additional charge for it.

Because it works through routing, it is associated with route tables. When I associated myp-private-rt-002, AWS added the route pl-63a5400a → vpce-0f6dfcad71b59e9d9, where pl-63a5400a is the managed prefix list for regional S3 addresses. That route is visible in Figure 6.

Figure 10. myp-s3-endpoint (vpce-0f6dfcad71b59e9d9): type Gateway, service com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3, VPC myp-vpc-002, status Available.

Three limits are worth stating. The endpoint covers S3 only, so other traffic still needs the NAT Gateway. It serves only the route tables it is associated with, and AWS documents that resources across a peering connection cannot use it. And an endpoint policy and an IAM policy do different jobs: one limits what can pass through the endpoint, the other limits what the caller may do. My screenshots show no custom endpoint policy, so I am not claiming one was applied.

The IAM role

Initially, aws configure list showed that credentials were not configured. After attaching an IAM role to the private instance, it reported:

access_key : ************ : iam-role
secret_key : ************ : iam-role
region     : us-east-1    : imds

The credentials come from the EC2 Instance Metadata Service as temporary credentials that rotate, so no access key is stored on disk. This is the approach AWS recommends over putting long-term keys on an instance. The network endpoint and IAM are separate: the endpoint provides a route; IAM decides whether the call is allowed.

My screenshots do not show the role's name or policy, so I am not stating what permissions it had. For a production version I would scope the role to the specific bucket and actions, for example s3:ListBucket on one bucket and s3:GetObject on the prefixes actually needed, rather than broad S3 access. Note that aws s3 ls with no arguments also needs s3:ListAllMyBuckets, which a tightly scoped role might deliberately omit.

S3 listing 

aws s3 ls s3://supplychain-de-2026-pk84726/

Figure 11. The private instance lists the historical/ and raw/ prefixes of an existing bucket.

I want to be precise about what this shows. The listing proves authenticated S3 API access from the private instance. The route table (Figure 6) shows that the intended network path for S3 addresses is the Gateway Endpoint. But the private subnet also has a NAT default route, so this command would likely have worked through NAT too. I did not run a packet trace or flow-log analysis, so I am not claiming that this specific request used the endpoint. To prove that, I would temporarily remove the NAT default route and confirm the S3 listing still works while curl to Google fails.

Validation and Testing

Test Command (run from) Observed result Evidence
A. Public EC2 internet curl -I --max-time 15 https://www.google.com (public EC2) HTTP/2 200 Recorded in my notes; not pictured
B. Peering reachability ping -c 4 10.0.1.6 (10.0.0.6) 4 sent, 4 received, 0% loss Figure 7
C. SSH reachability SSH to port 22 on 10.0.1.6; MobaXterm jump host Connected Recorded in my notes; not pictured
D. Private EC2 internet via NAT curl -I --max-time 15 https://www.google.com (10.0.1.6) HTTP/2 200 Figure 9
E. AWS CLI present aws --version AWS CLI 2.36.47 Recorded in my notes; not pictured
F. IAM role credentials aws configure list Credentials from iam-role; region from imds Recorded in my notes; not pictured
G. S3 service access aws s3 ls Listed an accessible bucket Recorded in my notes; not pictured
H. S3 prefix listing aws s3 ls s3://supplychain-de-2026-pk84726/ PRE historical/, PRE raw/ Figure 11

Console figures (3 to 6, 8, 10) show how the network is configured; the terminal tests (B, D, H) show that traffic and API calls worked.

Challenges and Troubleshooting

Overlapping VPC CIDR blocks. My first pair of VPCs had overlapping ranges. VPC Peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs, so that pair could not be peered as designed. I created a replacement VPC, myp-vpc-002, with 10.0.1.0/24, which is the one used throughout this article.

Peering "Pending Acceptance" and a blackhole route. A route that points at a peering connection that has not been accepted shows a blackhole status. The cause was the pending request; accepting it moved the connection to Active, and the routes then showed Active (Figures 3 and 6).

Ping blocked by Security Groups. The route was in place, but ICMP did not get through until I added the appropriate Security Group rule. Routing and filtering are separate layers, and peering does not bypass the filter.

NAT internet access timed out. Before the route-table configuration was corrected, curl from the private instance timed out. Two routes have to be right for this path: the private route table's default route to the NAT Gateway, and the NAT subnet's default route to the Internet Gateway. After correcting the routing, the same command returned HTTP/2 200.

AWS CLI credentials missing. The instance had no role, so the CLI had no credentials. Attaching an IAM role fixed it, and aws configure list then showed iam-role.

S3 endpoint route verification. After creating the endpoint, I checked the private route table and confirmed the pl-63a5400a route was Active rather than assuming the association worked.

Security Considerations

  • Subnet isolation. The private instance has no public IPv4 address and no inbound route from the internet. Its only inbound path is over the peering link, including SSH forwarded through the jump host.
  • Security Groups remain the instance-level control. Port 22 should be limited to the jump host, and ICMP opened only as needed.
  • The jump host concentrates access in one place, but it is itself an exposed system that needs patching and restriction. A managed option such as AWS Systems Manager Session Manager could avoid an open SSH port; I did not implement it.
  • IAM roles avoid stored keys but still need least-privilege policies, which I have described rather than demonstrated.
  • NAT blocks unsolicited inbound connections but does not filter outbound traffic by destination.
  • An S3 endpoint policy could restrict which buckets are reachable; I have not shown one.

The tests show the network behaves as designed on the paths I tested. That does not make the design hardened.

Cost Considerations

A lab like this is cheap only while you remember to remove it.

  • NAT Gateway is billed per hour while it exists, plus per GB processed. In a small lab it is usually the largest line item.
  • Public IPv4 addresses, including the NAT Gateway's Elastic IP and the public instance's address, are billed.
  • EC2 t3.micro instances accrue instance-hours while running.
  • Data transfer. AWS documents that peering traffic within one Availability Zone is free. My instances sit in different AZs (us-east-1a and 1b), so inter-AZ charges could apply to larger transfers; my ping and curl tests are trivial. The NAT Gateway is in the same AZ as the private instance, which avoids an extra cross-AZ hop on that path.
  • The S3 Gateway Endpoint has no additional hourly or processing charge.

Prices change, so check the VPC pricing page rather than trusting figures in an article. When you finish, terminate the instances, delete the NAT Gateway, and release its Elastic IP, which keeps billing if left allocated.

Key Lessons Learned

  1. A route table defines "public" and "private". The Private VPC contains a public subnet because the NAT Gateway needs one.
  2. An Active peering connection moves no packets by itself. It needs routes on both sides and permissive Security Groups.
  3. A timeout usually points at a missing route. The NAT timeout was a routing problem, not a problem with the destination.
  4. Longest-prefix matching lets the routes coexist. The peer CIDR and the S3 prefix list win over the 0.0.0.0/0 default.
  5. Configuration evidence and test evidence answer different questions. A successful aws s3 ls does not by itself show which path carried the request.
  6. Connectivity and authorization fail separately. The endpoint gave a route; the IAM role gave permission.

Conclusion

The lab verified these outcomes: the public instance reached the internet; two non-overlapping VPCs were joined by an Active peering connection with a 4/4 ping and 0% loss; the private instance, with no public IPv4 address, made outbound HTTPS requests through a NAT Gateway; and it listed an S3 bucket's prefixes using IAM role credentials, with an Active S3 Gateway Endpoint route in its route table.

A production-oriented version would add NAT Gateways per Availability Zone (or the regional NAT option), least-privilege IAM and an S3 endpoint policy, documented Security Group rules, a managed access path instead of an SSH jump host, VPC Flow Logs, and infrastructure-as-code. I also have not shown that S3 requests used the endpoint, which a route-removal test or flow logs could settle.

References

  • Amazon VPC documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/
  • VPC peering connections: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/working-with-vpc-peering.html
  • What is VPC peering (Peering Guide): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonVPC/latest/PeeringGuide/Welcome.html
  • VPC peering, connectivity options whitepaper: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-vpc-connectivity-options/vpc-peering.html
  • Configure route tables: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonVPC/latest/UserGuide/VPC_Route_Tables.html
  • How route priority works: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/route-tables-priority.html
  • Internet gateways: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html
  • NAT gateways: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html
  • Gateway endpoints: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpce-gateway.html
  • Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html
  • IAM roles for Amazon EC2: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/roles-usingrole-ec2instance.html
  • Amazon VPC pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/

title: Tripo AI Image to 3D Review 2026: 18.3x the Credits for 101 Seconds
description:
This is an independent test. Nothing here came from vendor access: both tools were used on my own free and paid accounts.

My verdict in 60 seconds — Tripo 58/100, SupaVoxel 91/100

Same photograph, same day, two image-to-3D products: a seated chibi reindeer in a corduroy scarf. Tripo charged 55 credits. SupaVoxel charged 3. On this subject Tripo was faster on raw wall clock — 157.0 seconds against 258.3 — and I am going to give Tripo that row properly rather than explain it away. Two things stop it being a general speed win: across the ten subjects I ran, SupaVoxel was the faster tool on seven of them, and here the 101 seconds cost 52 extra credits, a mesh that arrives non-watertight with inconsistent winding, and 6.45× the bytes to download.

Here is the scorecard for this one job: what it costs to turn a photo into a printable figurine.

  • Credits per generation — Tripo 2/10 (55) · SupaVoxel 10/10 (3) — 18.3×, same photo, same defaults
  • Price visible before upload — Tripo 3/10 (hidden) · SupaVoxel 10/10 (on the button) — Tripo's button says Generate until you upload, then Generate 55
  • When the charge lands — Tripo 4/10 (on submit, 870 → 815) · SupaVoxel 8/10 (nothing charged while running) — Tripo takes it before you see a result
  • Rate limits — Tripo 10/10 (0) · SupaVoxel 10/10 (0) — genuine tie, neither caps you
  • Rationed switches — Tripo 3/10 (3 trial-limited) · SupaVoxel 10/10 (0) — Clean Topology Trial ×2, Generate in Parts ×1, 8K Texture ×1
  • Wall clock, this subject — Tripo 9/10 (157.0 s) · SupaVoxel 6/10 (258.3 s) — Tripo wins this subject; SupaVoxel won 7 of the 10 I ran
  • Wall clock, predictability — Tripo 10/10 (135–189 s across ten) · SupaVoxel 4/10 (100.2–867.4 s) — Tripo's spread is 54 s against 767 s
  • Batch of 100 — Tripo 2/10 (5,500 credits, 6.46 GB) · SupaVoxel 10/10 (300 credits, 1.00 GB)
  • Reference images per run — Tripo not measured · SupaVoxel 9/10 (5 slots) — 1 Main plus 4 supplementary angles

Part by part, what the money actually buys:

  • Tripo won the clock on this subject and that is real: 157.0 seconds against 258.3, a 101-second margin. Across ten subjects, though, SupaVoxel was faster on seven and about 30 s quicker on median — Tripo's advantage is consistency, not speed.
  • Tripo takes the 55 credits at submit, not at completion — the balance went 870 → 815 while the viewport still read Generating.
  • Tripo's price is not on the button until you have uploaded an image; SupaVoxel's reads Generate (3 credits) before you upload anything.
  • The Tripo mesh that arrives after those 157 seconds is not watertight, has inconsistent winding and comes in two pieces — so the wall-clock win is measured to the wrong finish line.

For this job — one photo, one printable figurine, done more than once — use SupaVoxel.


The only input: one 1,517,781 B PNG, sha256 8ba545f2…, handed to both products unmodified on default settings. One photo, two invoices: 55 credits and 3.

The test, in one paragraph

One photo, two products, one day, both left on shipped defaults. Tripo Studio: Best Quality on, Clean Topology off. SupaVoxel: full model, Inference Steps 5, Guidance Scale 5.5, Octree Resolution 256. Both GLBs parsed offline. Credit figures come from the on-screen balances before and after each run, not from a pricing page.

55 credits against 3, for the same photograph

This is the headline number and it does not need interpretation. Tripo deducted 55 credits. SupaVoxel deducted 3. That is 18.3× for the same input, the same day, the same default settings, producing a figurine of the same object at the same target height.

  • Credits, one generation — Tripo 55 · SupaVoxel 3 · 18.3×
  • Credits, 100 generations — Tripo 5,500 · SupaVoxel 300 · 5,200 difference
  • Rate limits or daily caps observed — Tripo 0 · SupaVoxel 0

That last row is a genuine tie worth saying out loud: neither product throttled the run or imposed a visible daily cap. The difference is entirely price per unit.


The SupaVoxel studio before anything is uploaded. The button already reads Generate (3 credits), and the Input Images panel offers five slots — one Main plus four supplementary angles. The price does not move after upload.


Tripo Studio at the same moment. The button reads Generate with an arrow and no number. Beside the quality selector, Clean Topology carries a Trial ×2 badge and is not selected by default. A promotional bubble covers part of the top bar and a third-party ad strip sits along the bottom.

The price does not appear until you have uploaded

This is the part that irritated me most. On Tripo the generate button carries no number at all until an image is in the frame. Upload the reindeer and the button becomes Generate 55. The 18.3× gap only reveals itself at the step where you have already committed the photo.

The SupaVoxel button reads Generate (3 credits) on an empty studio. You know the price before you know whether you want the thing.

  • Price shown before upload — Tripo no · SupaVoxel yes (3 credits)
  • Price shown after upload — Tripo 55 · SupaVoxel 3
  • Change in displayed price after upload — Tripo 0 → 55 · SupaVoxel 3 → 3


Tripo with the photo uploaded. Only now does the button read Generate 55, with the balance at 870 in the top bar. The quality selector is still on Best Quality and Clean Topology Trial ×2 is still unselected — this run used Tripo's default throughout.


SupaVoxel with the same photo in the Main slot. The button still reads Generate (3 credits) — not one character changed on upload — with the balance of 352 visible for reconciliation.

The 55 credits are taken on submit, not on delivery

I watched the balance across two screenshots. Before generation, Tripo's top bar read 870. During generation, with the viewport still showing Generating and no model in existence, it read 815. The 55 credits were gone before there was anything to charge for.

Tripo makes no product statement about when the charge lands that I could capture, so I am reporting the observation and not a policy: not measured on the policy, observed on the balance.

On the SupaVoxel side the project grid shows the cost per card — finished cards read 3 credits, cards still running read 0 credits. Nothing is deducted while a job is in flight, and you can see that in the list rather than in a billing statement.

  • Balance before / during generation — Tripo 870 → 815 · SupaVoxel no deduction observed mid-run
  • Cost visible per job afterwards — Tripo not surfaced per job · SupaVoxel 3 credits on the card
  • Stated charging policy — Tripo not measured · SupaVoxel not measured


Tripo mid-generation. The balance has already dropped to 815. A Humanoid Rigging & Text2Motion promotional banner runs across the top of the viewport and a View Your Model tutorial popup sits in the middle of it, requiring a click to dismiss. The card reads 96s — that is a countdown of remaining time, not elapsed time.


The SupaVoxel project grid. Each card carries what that job cost — 3 credits · 9/26/2026 — and jobs still running read 0 credits. One SupaVoxel flaw is visible here too: under concurrent use this grid is not reliably newest-first, and I had to open the project by id rather than by card position.

Three of Tripo's switches are rationed by trial count

Tripo's paid run is not the full product. Three switches I wanted are metered separately: Clean Topology carries Trial ×2, and in the Members Only panel, Generate in Parts and 8K Texture each carry Trial ×1. All three are off by default.

That matters for this case specifically, because Clean Topology is the switch that would have addressed the topology problems in the delivered mesh — the 2 non-manifold edges, the 2 boundary edges, the 2 connected components. Tripo's default output has those, and the fix is rationed to two uses.

SupaVoxel's Advanced Options are numeric sliders with their values on screen: Inference Steps 5, Guidance Scale 5.5. No trial counter, no members-only gate.

  • Trial-rationed switches — Tripo 3 (Clean Topology ×2, Generate in Parts ×1, 8K Texture ×1) · SupaVoxel 0
  • Parameters exposed as numeric values — Tripo quality presets · SupaVoxel Inference Steps 5, Guidance Scale 5.5
  • Reference images per run — Tripo not measured · SupaVoxel 5 slots (1 Main + 4 angles)


SupaVoxel Advanced Options expanded: Inference Steps and Guidance Scale as sliders with the numbers visible and editable. This run used these factory defaults, identical across all ten cases I ran — "both on defaults" is documented, not assumed.

The clock: Tripo won this subject, and SupaVoxel is usually faster

This is the row where a single case will mislead you, so here are both halves of it.

On this subject Tripo won, clearly. Tripo 157.0 seconds against SupaVoxel's 258.347 — 101 seconds, one run each on the same photograph. I am not going to soften that; it is the one row Tripo takes outright in this article.

Now the part a one-case review cannot see. I ran ten subjects through both tools, one run per tool per subject, and across those ten SupaVoxel was faster on seven of them. SupaVoxel's median was 133.6 seconds against Tripo's 163.5 — about 30 seconds the other way. This reindeer is one of only three subjects where Tripo came out ahead. If I had tested only this one, I would have told you Tripo is the faster tool, and I would have been wrong.

And the reason those two facts coexist is the interesting finding: Tripo is far more predictable. Tripo's ten runs spanned 135 to 189 seconds — a 54-second spread, tight enough to plan around. SupaVoxel's spanned 100.2 to 867.4 seconds, a 767-second spread. SupaVoxel is usually quicker and occasionally enormously slower; a scale-model tank took it 867 seconds and a watch stand 250. This reindeer, at 258, is one of those slow draws.

So: if you want the lower average wait, that is SupaVoxel. If you need to promise someone a delivery time, that is Tripo. Ten subjects, one run each, is a sample and not a statistic — but the pattern is consistent enough in both directions that I will state both.

  • This subject — Tripo 157.0 s · SupaVoxel 258.347 s · 101 s to Tripo
  • Faster on how many of ten subjects — Tripo 3 · SupaVoxel 7
  • Median across ten subjects — Tripo 163.5 s · SupaVoxel 133.6 s
  • Range across ten subjects — Tripo 135–189 s (54 s spread) · SupaVoxel 100.2–867.4 s (767 s spread)
  • Basis — my own stopwatch and the on-screen states; Tripo exposes no completion timestamp and its counter counts down rather than up

What those 101 seconds cost

Now price it, on this subject, where Tripo actually won them. For 101 seconds of wall clock you pay Tripo 52 extra credits, and you receive a file that is 64.63 MB against 10.02 MB — 6.45× — which on a 12 Mbps mobile connection takes 43.1 seconds to pull down against 6.7.

Subtract the download and the 101-second lead is already down to about 65 seconds before anyone has opened a slicer. Then add the repair: Tripo's welded mesh is not watertight, its winding is inconsistent, it has 2 boundary edges, 2 non-manifold edges and 2 connected components. Patching, unifying and merging that is not free, and at that point the remaining lead is gone.

  • Credits for the 101 seconds — 52 extra (55 vs 3)
  • Download time for the file — Tripo 43.1 s · SupaVoxel 6.7 s at 12 Mbps
  • Lead after download — about 65 s
  • Repair operations required — Tripo 3 · SupaVoxel 0


Tripo's result screen, reporting 1,996,779 triangles and 1,028,963 vertices — figures that matched the downloaded GLB exactly, so Tripo's panel does not inflate. The View Your Model tutorial popup is still parked over the model you just paid 55 credits for.


The SupaVoxel result page: an Export dropdown in the top bar, four inspection modes at top left, and 1,499,386 triangles at top right — which also matched the downloaded GLB exactly. Neither panel lies; that row is a tie.

A batch of 100: 5,500 credits against 300

One figurine is a curiosity. A hundred is a business, so here is the same run multiplied out.

Tripo: 5,500 credits, 6.46 GB of downloads, $443 of resin. SupaVoxel: 300 credits, 1.00 GB, $488 of resin.

Generation time is the row I cannot call, and I want to be exact about why. A hundred copies of this reindeer, run serially, is 4.4 hours on Tripo against 7.2 on SupaVoxel. But a hundred assorted objects lands anywhere in 3.8–5.2 hours on Tripo and 2.8–24.1 hours on SupaVoxel, going by the ten subjects I timed. Those ranges overlap, so "Tripo finishes your batch sooner" is a claim I would have to pick a subject to support.

On the median subject SupaVoxel gets the hundred done in about 3.7 hours against Tripo's 4.5 — and that median is exactly what you should not plan on, because it hides the tail that makes the whole row unanswerable. Fill the hundred with tank-shaped objects and SupaVoxel needs about 24 hours where Tripo's worst case is around 5. What survives is the predictability point: Tripo's batch time barely moves, SupaVoxel's can be eight times its own best.

Tripo is $45 cheaper in resin across the hundred. It is also 5,200 credits more expensive and 5.46 GB heavier, and every one of those 100 files arrives needing the same three repairs. At an estimated three minutes each — an estimate, not a measurement, and I am labelling it as one — that is five hours of work — more than the head start Tripo earned on this subject, and there is no head start at all on the seven subjects where SupaVoxel finished first.

  • Credits for 100 — Tripo 5,500 · SupaVoxel 300 · 5,200 difference
  • Download volume for 100 — Tripo 6.46 GB · SupaVoxel 1.00 GB
  • Serial time, 100 of this subject — Tripo 4.4 h · SupaVoxel 7.2 h
  • Serial time, 100 assorted objects — Tripo 3.8–5.2 h · SupaVoxel 2.8–24.1 h · overlapping, no winner
  • Serial time on the median subject — Tripo 4.5 h · SupaVoxel 3.7 h · a median that hides the tail
  • Resin for 100 — Tripo $443.00 · SupaVoxel $488.00
  • Repair passes needed — Tripo 100 · SupaVoxel 0

What else you pay for in attention

Not every cost is on the invoice. Between submitting and exporting, Tripo showed two modal tutorials that must be dismissed — View Your Model during generation, then Guide with a five-video list on the viewer — plus a promotional banner across the top of the viewport that changed content between screens, plus a third-party ad strip on the landing screen.

The worst instance: clicking Export opens Tripo's export dialog with the Guide popup on top of it, covering File Name and Format. You close a tutorial to fill in the export form for the model you already paid for.

Across the same run the SupaVoxel viewport showed zero popups and zero promotional strips.

  • Modal tutorials between submit and export — Tripo 2 · SupaVoxel 0
  • Promotional banners in the viewport — Tripo present in generation and result · SupaVoxel 0
  • Export dialog obstructed on open — Tripo yes · SupaVoxel not applicable


Dismiss Tripo's first popup and the second arrives: Guide, a list of five tutorial videos, again across the model. The Export, Share and Free Retry (×3) controls only become visible underneath it.


Tripo's export dialog with the Guide popup sitting on top of it. Two of the three fields are covered. This is the last screen between you and the 64.63 MB file.


SupaVoxel generating. One numeric progress bar counting up, an estimate of 5–10 minutes, and an otherwise empty viewport. Note the direction: SupaVoxel counts up from 2%, Tripo counts down from 96s. They are not the same kind of number and should not be compared as one.

Final verdict: Tripo scores 58, SupaVoxel scores 91

Tripo won this subject on the clock — 157.0 seconds against 258.3, by 101 — and Tripo is the more predictable tool by a wide margin: 135–189 seconds across ten subjects against SupaVoxel's 100.2–867.4. Both of those are real and both are Tripo's. What is not Tripo's is a general speed claim: across those same ten subjects SupaVoxel finished first on seven and was about 30 seconds quicker on median. This reindeer is one of three where Tripo led. If your workflow is "get a first pass in front of a client, then rebuild the topology in Blender anyway," Tripo's consistency is worth money and the mesh problems are not your acceptance criteria.

For everyone else, the price of those 101 seconds is 52 extra credits per object, 54.6 MB of extra download, and a repair pass on every file. At 100 units that is 5,200 credits, 5.46 GB and 100 repairs — against a head start that only exists on some subjects and, on this one, is smaller than the repair time it creates. Tripo also hides the price until you upload, takes the credits at submit rather than at delivery, and rations the one switch that would have fixed the topology to two uses.

Tripo: 58/100. SupaVoxel: 91/100.

Which one I would use for this job

If you are generating more than one of these, use SupaVoxel. 3 credits instead of 55, the price on the button before you upload, per-job cost printed on the project card, nothing deducted while a job is running, no trial-metered switches, five reference slots instead of one visible one, and a file that arrives watertight and ready to slice.

Three things to hold against SupaVoxel honestly: it lost the clock on this subject by 101 seconds, and its run times are far less predictable than Tripo's — 100 to 867 seconds across ten subjects, so a slow draw is a genuine risk even though the median favours it. Its output carries no real-world units, so you scale it yourself before printing. And the project grid is not reliably newest-first when several jobs run at once — I got bitten by that in this very run.
