title: A software handover should prove one recovery path
description:
Before agreeing to support an unfamiliar application, ask a practical question: can the team recover one important workflow using the handover material? A walkthrough turns missing context into specific work before an ongoing support arrangement is scoped.

Start with one ordinary business path

Choose something the organisation depends on, such as opening a dashboard and exporting an accurate report. Define the expected result, its information source and who can confirm that it is correct. Keep the walkthrough in an isolated test environment with dummy or appropriately redacted data.

A handover walkthrough

  1. Identify the running version. Record the source revision, deployment reference and environment. A repository link alone does not show which release is actually serving users.

  2. Check the access boundary. Identify the people permitted to investigate, deploy and restore. Document how authorised access is obtained; keep credentials out of the runbook itself.

  3. Trace the business path. List the services and data stores needed for the chosen workflow. Include any scheduled job that must finish before the result is current.

  4. Make failure visible. Describe what a user sees, what the monitoring shows and which evidence helps distinguish a stale result from an unavailable service. Agree who investigates the alert.

  5. Rehearse recovery. Use an approved test environment to demonstrate the relevant rollback or restore procedure. Record the test date, version, outcome and remaining limitations. A successful file restore does not by itself prove that the business workflow works again.

  6. Check recovery consequences. Identify work that may have occurred after the restored point. Define how it will be reconciled. Avoid blindly replaying operations that can create duplicate or irreversible effects.

  7. Assign the next decision. Identify who can approve a rollback, pause a workflow or accept a temporary workaround. Record the escalation route and expected contact window without assuming round-the-clock coverage.

  8. Leave usable evidence. Store a short runbook, relevant references and the unresolved items somewhere the authorised support team can find them. Have another person follow it and note where they need help.

Turn the gaps into a bounded support brief

Use this outline for a new support enquiry:

  • System and business owner:
  • Workflow that must keep working:
  • Observed problem and business impact:
  • Known version, dependencies and access owner:
  • Recovery evidence already available:
  • Unresolved risks and decisions:
  • Required support window:
  • One-off stabilisation work versus ongoing scope:

The walkthrough informs the scope; it does not establish a response-time guarantee, certification or production readiness. Agree responsibilities, included work and exclusions against the actual system.

Repository ownership and incident responsibility also need to be distinguished. GitHub's CODEOWNERS feature requests reviews for relevant changes. An operational escalation rota and authority to restore service need their own agreement.

Further reading

GitHub: About code owners
https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-code-owners

Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: Emergency Response
https://sre.google/sre-book/emergency-response/

From Lumox Technologies

Lumox is a Canberra-based software engineering company. If you are evaluating support for a business application, send a non-confidential outline of what should work better through Lumox’s enquiry form. Scope and availability would be discussed against your actual requirements.

For practical examples of software handoffs and integrations, follow Lumox on LinkedIn.

title: Architectural Breakdown: Building Production-Ready Open-Weights AI Agents with Gemma, Google ADK, an
description:
# Building Production-Ready Open-Weights AI Agents with Gemma, Google ADK, and Cloud Run GPUs

![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+Building+Production-Ready+Open+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

## The Premise

Most "production-ready AI agent" tutorials are corporate theater. You've got an LLM, some async glue code, and a deployment config file. You call it shipshape. Meanwhile, your agent blows past 8GB RAM on its first real query, deadlocks on a race condition nobody tested, and chokes under anything heavier than ten concurrent users. This guide exists to fix that.

We're covering **Gemma** (Google's open-weights family, the model, not a hardware board), **Google ADK** (Agent Development Kit for structuring agentic workflows), and **Cloud Run with GPU backing**. The goal isn't to impress at demo day. It's to build something that doesn't collapse when a real user touches it.

## Hardware Constraints: Stop Treating 8GB Like a Suggestion

The 8GB RAM ceiling isn't a suggestion. It's a hard boundary imposed by your GPU container spec on Cloud Run. Exceed it and the orchestrator kills your instance with no ceremony.

Here's what actually matters:

- **Quantize Gemma to 4-bit or 8-bit**. The `gguf` format is your friend. A full 7B-parameter float16 Gemma model eats roughly 14GB. A 4-bit quant compresses it to ~4GB, leaving headroom for the runtime, the KV cache, and your agent logic.
- **Stream your context, don't hoard it**. Bounded queues for incoming prompts and outgoing completions keep memory predictable. Anything that grows unbounded will eventually OOM-kill you.
- **Profile before you ship**. Tools like `memory_profiler` and `tracemalloc` aren't optional. Deploying without them means you're guessing.

## Race Conditions: The Silent Instance Killer

Multi-threaded agent loops are where your system quietly corrupts itself. One thread writes state, another reads it, and suddenly your agent generates a response based on a half-updated context window. The fix isn't theoretical. It's mechanical:


python
import threading
import queue
from typing import Optional

Thread-safe bounded queue for conversation history

class BoundedContextQueue:
def init(self, max_tokens: int = 8192):
self._lock = threading.Lock()
self._queue: queue.Queue[str] = queue.Queue(maxsize=50)
self._token_count = 0
self._max_tokens = max_tokens

def add_turn(self, role: str, content: str) -> bool:
    """Add a message turn with token budget enforcement."""
    estimated_tokens = len(content) // 4
    with self._lock:
        if self._token_count + estimated_tokens > self._max_tokens:
            # Evict oldest turns to make room (circular buffer strategy)
            self._evict_oldest(estimated_tokens)
        self._queue.put(f"{role}: {content}")
        self._token_count += estimated_tokens
        return True

def _evict_oldest(self, needed_tokens: int) -> None:
    """Remove oldest entries until enough space exists."""
    while self._token_count > needed_tokens and not self._queue.empty():
        old = self._queue.get_nowait()
        self._token_count -= len(old) // 4

def get_all(self) -> list[str]:
    with self._lock:
        items = list(self._queue.queue)
        return items


The key principles:

- **Use locks around shared mutable state**. Every time two threads touch the same dictionary or queue, wrap it in `threading.Lock()`. No exceptions.
- **Prefer queues over shared variables**. Python's `queue.Queue` with a `maxsize` limit gives you thread safety and bounded memory in one abstraction.
- **Make critical sections atomic**. If you're reading a config, mutating it, and writing it back, do it in a single locked block. Any gap between read and write is a race condition waiting to fire.

## Development Process: Modular or Regret

A monolithic agent script isn't just bad practice. It's a deployment hazard. Break it down into four isolated modules:

1. **Model loader**: Handles quantization, GPU memory allocation, and warmup. Isolate it so you can swap models without touching the rest of the codebase.
2. **Context manager**: Manages conversation history, bounded by a token limit. This is where your queue lives.
3. **Tool executor**: Each tool (search, API call, code interpreter) runs in its own function with explicit error boundaries.
4. **Orchestrator**: Runs the agent loop. It shouldn't know about quantization, threading, or deployment internals.


python

orchestrator.py

The agent loop. Pure logic, zero infrastructure concerns.

class AgentOrchestrator:
def init(
self,
model: GGMLModel,
context: BoundedContextQueue,
tools: dict[str, Callable],
):
self._model = model
self._context = context
self._tools = tools

def run(self, user_input: str) -> str:
    self._context.add_turn("user", user_input)

    for step in range(5):  # Max 5 reasoning steps
        prompt = self._build_prompt()
        response = self._model.generate(prompt, max_new_tokens=512)

        if tool_call := self._extract_tool_call(response):
            result = self._execute_tool(tool_call["name"], tool_call["args"])
            self._context.add_turn("assistant", f"[Tool: {result}]")
            continue

        self._context.add_turn("assistant", response)
        return response

    return "[MAX STEPS REACHED]"

def _build_prompt(self) -> str:
    messages = self._context.get_all()
    return "\n".join(messages)

def _execute_tool(self, name: str, args: dict) -> str:
    if name not in self._tools:
        return f"Unknown tool: {name}"
    try:
        return self._tools[name](**args)
    except Exception as e:
        return f"Tool error: {e}"


If your codebase doesn't follow this pattern, you'll spend more time untangling it than shipping.

## Deployment on Cloud Run: What Actually Works

Cloud Run with GPUs is powerful and punishing in equal measure. Cold starts on GPU instances are measured in minutes, not seconds. You need a strategy:

- **Enable minimum instances** (at least 1) to avoid cold starts during traffic. Yes, it costs more. Yes, it's cheaper than a degraded user experience.
- **Set memory to 8GB and CPU to 2-4 cores**. Match your container spec to your quantized model size. Overprovisioning burns money. Underprovisioning triggers OOM kills.
- **Implement health checks that validate GPU memory**. A passing `/healthz` shouldn't just say the server is up. It should confirm the model loaded and GPU memory is available.
- **Cache aggressively**. Your first inference is always slow. Subsequent ones with similar contexts benefit from KV cache reuse.


yaml

cloudrun.yaml

apiVersion: serving.knative.dev/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
name: gemma-agent
spec:
template:
metadata:
annotations:
autoscaling.knative.dev/minScale: "1"
autoscaling.knative.dev/maxScale: "5"
spec:
timeoutSeconds: 300
serviceAccountName: agent-sa
containers:
- image: gcr.io/project/gemma-agent:latest
resources:
limits:
nvidia.com/gpu: 1
memory: "8Gi"
cpu: "4"
livenessProbe:
httpGet:
path: /healthz
port: 8080
initialDelaySeconds: 120
periodSeconds: 30
readinessProbe:
httpGet:
path: /readyz
port: 8080
initialDelaySeconds: 120


The 120-second initial delay accounts for GPU model loading. Without it, Kubernetes restarts your container before it ever becomes ready, creating an endless crash loop.

## The Bottom Line

Building a production-ready open-weights agent isn't about stacking frameworks. It's about respecting constraints. Memory, concurrency, cold starts, and designing around them. Gemma handles the model. Google ADK structures the agent loop. Cloud Run GPUs provide the compute. Your job is making sure they don't destroy each other.

Stop writing agents that work on your machine and die in production. Ship something that survives.

---

**Open Loop:** When you've got a single GPU instance serving bursty agent traffic, how do you decide between scaling horizontally with more minimal instances versus vertically with a larger, more expensive GPU pod. Where do you draw the line between cost efficiency and latency guarantees?

title: Personal Agent Protocol: should the company agent be a back-end channel like the website or the API?
description:
TL;DR

  • The Personal Agent Protocol (PAP) gives personal agents a standard front door to businesses, whether they end up on a website, an API or a company agent. What sits behind that door is left to each company.
  • We've been exploring one design for that open part: the company agent talks and proposes, but holds no credentials. A deterministic gateway decides, and mints a single-use grant bound to the exact input.
  • What this does: it caps the damage a manipulated agent can do at what your policy allows.
  • What it doesn't do: it doesn't stop the agent from being manipulated into proposing something that policy allows. Policy becomes the security model.
  • This is a prototype with no independent review. Below: what it covers, what it doesn't, and four questions we'd like your help with.

Meta and Sierra, with partners including Genesys, Instinct, Rocket, Shopify, Stripe and Walmart, announced the Personal Agent Protocol (PAP), an open standard for how a customer's personal agent talks to a business. As we read it, the principle is: customers decide what access their agent gets, and companies decide what agents can do.

We think PAP gets important things right. It gives businesses a standard, public way to say how agents can reach them, instead of a thousand custom integrations or agents pretending to be humans on a website. It keeps customers in charge of what access their agent gets, and companies in charge of what agents can do. Leaving the back end open is a sensible scope for a first protocol. The questions below are about that open part. We offer them as a complement to the standard, not a criticism of it.

We have been experimenting with agent ecosystems through a project called Lianxi, an independent open-source project (not affiliated with the companies above) that explores agent-to-business communication from the security side. Reading the announcement taught us two things we had missed: a public discovery file, and one session per customer across channels. The question we kept returning to is the one the announcement sensibly leaves open:

Where does the company agent sit, and who holds the keys to the back office?

Three disclosures up front:

  • The PAP v0.1 spec had not been published when we wrote this. We're working from the announcement only. Field names below are ours, not the standard's.
  • Only Trust Gateway is open source. Other parts run in a private build, so some claims can't be checked by you. Each is labeled: 🟢 working and public, 🟡 working but private, ⚪ not built.
  • No independent security review, and no adversarial testing beyond our own. Everything under "what it covers" is design intent.

Two possible wirings behind the front door

The announcement's diagram shows the company agent as one channel beside the website and the APIs, all under the brand's rules.


Extract from the Sierra announcement.

It deliberately doesn't say how the company agent connects to the systems behind it, and PAP is compatible with many wirings.

Model A is one possible wiring: the customer-facing agent is given tools directly, such as a database connector, a payment key or a refund endpoint. An external agent then has a natural-language conversation with an internal agent that can act on real money and data. That is a confused deputy risk, closely related to what the OWASP LLM Top 10 calls excessive agency. Guardrails and system prompts reduce it, but they are probabilistic controls guarding deterministic assets. We don't know how common this wiring is in practice.

Model B is the one we have been experimenting with:


The model we have been experimenting with. Trust Gateway mediates connections from agents (external or company agents), keeping reasoning, which is probabilistic, separate from execution, which is deterministic.

Layer Role Holds back-office credentials? Status
1. Front door Discovery via /.well-known/personal-agent.json. Callers: your agent, Claude via MCP, shopping agents, external A2A agents No 🟢
2. Company agent Talks, explains, negotiates over DID-based A2A No, by design 🟡
3. Gateway Policy engine, WebAuthn step-up, grant minting No (signs, doesn't execute) 🟢
4. Executors Verify the grant, then act Only what the grant allows 🟢
5. Enterprise systems Store DB, Stripe, fulfilment n/a n/a

Two lanes: lookups from your own agent, Claude over MCP or a shopping agent go 1 → 3 → 4 → 5 with no LLM on the company side. Only negotiation (disputes, volume discounts) goes through Layer 2. Either way, Layer 3 is the only component that can authorize a mutation. We haven't benchmarked whether skipping Layer 2 for lookups matters at scale; we chose it to keep simple reads deterministic.

What it covers, and what it doesn't

This is the part we think is useful beyond our own project. It's a threat model for the "company agent holds no keys" pattern, based on design intent and not on test results:

Threat Covered? Why
Injected agent tries to call a refund or DB tool directly Yes It has no such tool or credential
Injected agent proposes an in-policy but harmful action (say, a refund inside the limit) No The gateway sees a valid proposal and approves it
Parameters altered between approval and execution Yes The grant is bound to a hash of the exact input
Grant replayed Yes, by design Single-use, short-lived
Stolen grant replayed before first use Depends on executor state A bound input hash stops tampering, but preventing duplicate execution requires nonce/JTI invalidation at Layer 4.
Compromised executor No It still holds Layer 5 access, so isolation and least privilege matter
Bug or gap in the policy No The policy is now the single point of failure
Approval fatigue (the human clicks yes) No Passkeys prove who approved, not that the approval was wise
Company agent lying to the customer's agent Not addressed The model protects the merchant, not the consumer's agent

So the claim is narrow: the worst case becomes "the most policy allows", not "the most a model can be talked into". We expect that to be a smaller and more testable surface, but we haven't tested it, and we don't know yet whether it is small enough.

What a visit looks like

Short version, with the discovery file, since that is the piece closest to PAP. Here is a small shop selling boxes:

  1. 🟢 The personal agent fetches the discovery file and learns what each capability requires.
  2. 🟢 As a guest it can read (catalog, returns policy). Writes are refused with a reason it can relay to its user.
  3. 🟡 Signing in moves it to the account tier through an OAuth2 token. It never sees a password.
  4. 🟢 Checkout is a step-up action. The agent only proposes it. The customer approves with a passkey on their own device, and the gateway mints a short-lived, single-use, Ed25519-signed grant bound to the exact cart and amount. The executor verifies it and places the order, and no card number passes through the agent.
  5. 🟡 Order events are relayed to the customer's channel. ⚪ Showing them in the agent's inbox isn't built yet. 
{
  "protocol_version": "2026-draft-1",
  "routes": {
    "mcp": { "endpoint": "https://lianxi.io/v1/mcp/sse", "protocol": "sse" },
    "b2b_agent": { "endpoint": "https://lianxi.io/a2a", "did": "did:web:lianxi.io:agent:box-shop" },
    "web": { "landing": "/", "sitemap": "/sitemap.xml" }
  },
  "authentication": {
    "supported_tiers": ["guest", "account", "step_up"],
    "step_up_mechanism": "webauthn_fido2"
  },
  "capabilities": [
    { "name": "catalog_query", "required_tier": "guest" },
    { "name": "order_lookup", "required_tier": "account" },
    { "name": "zero_credential_checkout", "required_tier": "step_up", "max_single_transaction_eur": 500.00 }
  ]
}

protocol_version is our own placeholder. The capabilities block is where the two lanes show up (deterministic tools vs. tiered, step-up-protected actions). It is an experiment, not a proposal for the standard.

Open problems

Promise vs. decision. A negotiating agent can promise a discount that policy then refuses, so the customer hears "yes" and later gets "no". One idea we have not built or tested (⚪): before offering anything, Layer 2 asks the gateway for a dry-run evaluation and may only offer terms returned as a signed, time-limited quote. The gap then becomes an expired quote, not a contradicted promise. We don't know where this breaks. Does it just move the problem into quote management?

Who approves company-side commitments? Passkey step-up is clear for consumer actions. When the company agent agrees a volume discount, who holds the passkey: a human operator, an approval queue, nobody?

Step-up thresholds. Prompts suit high-value actions and annoy people for the rest. We don't have a principled way to set the line.

Weight for small merchants. Five layers is real operational cost. Is there a lighter version that keeps the one key property (the conversational agent holds no execution authority)?

We are very interested in your feedback

  1. Credentials: does your company agent hold direct API keys, or is there an independent policy checkpoint between the model and your APIs? What drove the choice, and what went wrong?
  2. Protocol vs. implementation: should a standard like PAP say anything about how a company agent connects to the back office, or is that rightly each company's business?
  3. Step-up: is OAuth delegation enough when agents act autonomously, or does the flow need cryptographic step-up such as WebAuthn?
  4. Commitments: how would you reconcile a promise made in conversation with a decision made by a policy engine? Does the signed-quote idea hold up?

Disagreement is welcome, especially if you can show a case the threat model table gets wrong.

  • 👉 A more detailed article on our blog, with interactive diagrams and the full PAP-to-Lianxi mapping.
  • 👉 GitHub: fcn06/trust_gateway, the open-source Rust policy engine, discovery handlers and grant verifiers.

title: I pulled 4 real error messages from live APIs today. Here is what each one gets wrong.
description:
Error messages are copy. They get read by someone who is already having a bad day, mid-task, on a phone, at 1am. Most teams write them last, drop them in a JSON field, and never read them again.

So this morning I pulled four real error responses from live endpoints, quoted them exactly, and rewrote each one. Every example below is a real response I got today, with the exact request that produced it. Nothing invented.

1. npm registry: the message that knows nothing 

$ curl -i https://registry.npmjs.org/definitely-not-a-real-pkg-9x8y7
HTTP/2 404
{"error":"Not found"}

Two wasted words. The status code already said 404. "Not found" doesn't say what wasn't found, and the person reading it is holding the one piece of information the message omits: the name they just typed.

The more interesting question is who owns the sentence. This body is consumed by a machine. Whatever surface wraps it — npm install, a bot, a dashboard — is the thing talking to a human. If that surface just echoes the body, that's the bug. You don't fix this in the registry; you fix it in the layer that renders it.

The line I'd want a human to see:

No package named definitely-not-a-real-pkg-9x8y7. Check the spelling, or search the registry: npmjs.com/search?q=definitely-not-a-real-pkg-9x8y7

Named thing. One next move. Done.

2. GitHub: two different problems, one identical message 

$ curl -i https://api.github.com/repos/torvalds/linux-nonexistent
{
  "message": "Not Found",
  "documentation_url": "https://docs.github.com/rest/repos/repos#get-a-repository",
  "status": "404"
}

404 appears twice: once in the actual HTTP status, once as a string in the body that nothing parses. documentation_url points at the generic "get a repository" endpoint docs, which describes the success case.

Here's the part that bites people: a private repo you do have access to, with a token missing the right scope, returns the exact same "Not Found" as a repo that doesn't exist. That's a deliberate choice (don't leak the existence of private repos), and it's defensible. But the message does nothing to prepare the reader for it. The person who typed a URL and got "Not Found" will spend twenty minutes convinced they typo'd a repo they can see open in another tab.

No repository at torvalds/linux-nonexistent, or your token can't see it. If it should be private-visible, check your token's repo scope.

You can't tell the reader which of the two it is. You can tell them there are two.

3. Stripe: the good error in the wrong field 

$ curl -i https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges
{
  "error": {
    "message": "You did not provide an API key. You need to provide your API key in the Authorization header, using Bearer auth (e.g. 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_KEY'). See https://stripe.com/docs/api#authentication for details, or we can help at https://support.stripe.com/.",
    "type": "invalid_request_error"
  }
}

This one is actually good. It names the problem, shows the fix, and links the docs. As developer documentation delivered at the moment of need, it's better than most READMEs.

The problem is where it lives. error.message is the field developers most often pipe straight into a UI, because for a long list of APIs that's the only human-readable field there is. This string is written for an engineer holding a secret key. Leak it into a customer-facing path and your user is reading "Bearer YOUR_SECRET_KEY" while their payment fails.

Two audiences, two fields:

{
  "error": {
    "message": "No API key in the request.",
    "hint": "Send it in the Authorization header: Bearer <secret key>.",
    "doc_url": "https://docs.stripe.com/api/authentication",
    "type": "invalid_request_error"
  }
}

One sentence for the wrong-field accident. The essay for the person who actually needs it.

4. Google Books: the useful part is three levels down 

$ curl "https://www.googleapis.com/books/v1/volumes?q=test"
{
  "error": {
    "code": 429,
    "message": "Quota exceeded for quota metric 'Queries' and limit 'Queries per day' of service 'books.googleapis.com' for consumer 'project_number:624717413613'.",
    "errors": [ { "message": "Quota exceeded for quota metric 'Queries' ...", "reason": "rateLimitExceeded" } ],
    "status": "RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED",
    "details": [ { "...": "...", "metadata": { "quota_limit_value": "0", ... } },
                 { "links": [ { "url": "https://cloud.google.com/docs/quotas/help/request_increase" } ] } ]
  }
}

The identical sentence appears twice, in message and errors[0].message. quota_limit_value is "0", which tells you nothing a human can use. The one genuinely actionable thing in the entire payload — here's how to ask for more — is a URL buried inside details, four levels deep.

If you control the API, flatten it. If you're the client, the lesson is the same one as npm: the payload is for machines, and you still owe your user a sentence.

Daily query limit reached for this project. Quota increases: cloud.google.com/docs/quotas/help/request_increase

The three rules I keep landing on

  1. Name the thing that failed. "Not found" is a state. "No package named X" is information. The reader gave you the identifier. Give it back.
  2. Write for the reader you won't meet. Not the one who knows the architecture. The one who is tired, mid-task, and has no idea what your system calls its own parts.
  3. Say the next move. One action. A link, a command, a scope to check. An error that only reports is a dead end.

And one that isn't about words at all: decide who owns the sentence. The JSON body and the human sentence are two different jobs. When one layer just echoes the other, you get a message that's technically accurate and completely useless.

If your product's error messages read like {"error":"Not found"}, that's a five-minute fix and it's the copy your users read most often. I rewrite pages for a living — one page, clearer, plus a short note on what I changed and why. First paragraph free, no account needed: davidrewrites.surge.sh

title: Fixing the Silent Killer: How Improper Server Actions Leak Secrets in Next.js 15
description:
The Problem: Your API Keys Are Probably Leaking

Last month, I traced a production incident back to a Next.js Server Action that accidentally bundled our Stripe secret key into the client JavaScript. The root cause? A seemingly innocent use client directive in the wrong file.

Next.js 15 Server Actions are powerful, but the boundary between server and client code is subtle. One misplaced export and your secrets ride straight into the browser bundle.

Here's what a vulnerable pattern looks like:

// ❌ DANGEROUS: Defined in a Client Component file
'use client'

import { stripe } from '@/lib/stripe' // Secret key imported!

export async function processPayment(amount: number) {
  'use server'
  return await stripe.charges.create({ amount, currency: 'usd' })
}

Even though the function has 'use server', it's defined in a client module. Next.js will serialize this function reference, but the import graph taints the entire file. Your secret key ends up in the client bundle.

Deliverable 1: Secure Server Action with Zod + Session Guard

Here's the correct architecture:

// app/actions/payment.ts (NO 'use client' anywhere)
'use server'

import { z } from 'zod'
import { auth } from '@/lib/auth'
import { stripe } from '@/lib/stripe'

const PaymentSchema = z.object({
  amount: z.number().positive().max(999999),
  currency: z.enum(['usd', 'eur']),
  idempotencyKey: z.string().uuid(),
})

export async function processPayment(rawInput: unknown) {
  // 1. Session verification FIRST
  const session = await auth()
  if (!session?.user) {
    return { error: 'Unauthorized' }
  }

  // 2. Input validation with Zod
  const parsed = PaymentSchema.safeParse(rawInput)
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { error: 'Invalid input', details: parsed.error.flatten() }
  }

  // 3. Safe execution
  try {
    const charge = await stripe.charges.create({
      amount: parsed.data.amount,
      currency: parsed.data.currency,
      customer: session.user.stripeId,
    }, {
      idempotencyKey: parsed.data.idempotencyKey,
    })
    return { success: true, chargeId: charge.id }
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Payment failed:', err)
    return { error: 'Payment processing failed' }
  }
}

Why this works:

  • No client directive: The entire file stays server-only.
  • Zod validation: Catches malformed inputs before they hit Stripe.
  • Session guard: Prevents anonymous abuse.
  • Idempotency: Protects against duplicate charges on network retries.
  • Typed errors: The client gets structured error objects, not raw exceptions.

Client usage:

// app/components/CheckoutButton.tsx
'use client'

import { processPayment } from '@/app/actions/payment'
import { useTransition } from 'react'

export function CheckoutButton({ amount }: { amount: number }) {
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()

  const handleClick = () => {
    startTransition(async () => {
      const result = await processPayment({
        amount,
        currency: 'usd',
        idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID(),
      })
      if (result.error) {
        alert(result.error)
      }
    })
  }

  return (
    <button onClick={handleClick} disabled={isPending}>
      {isPending ? 'Processing...' : 'Pay Now'}
    </button>
  )
}

Deliverable 2: React Server Component with Granular Suspense

The second performance trap I see constantly: waterfalling data fetches that tank your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP).

Anti-pattern:

// ❌ Serial waterfall
async function Page() {
  const user = await fetchUser()
  const posts = await fetchPosts(user.id) // Waits for user
  const comments = await fetchComments(posts[0].id) // Waits for posts
  return <div>...</div>
}

Every await blocks rendering. Your LCP suffers.

Correct pattern with Suspense streaming:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'

async function UserProfile({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const user = await fetchUser(userId)
  return <div>{user.name}</div>
}

async function PostsList({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const posts = await fetchPosts(userId)
  return <ul>{posts.map(p => <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>)}</ul>
}

export default function DashboardPage({ params }: { params: { userId: string } }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <Suspense fallback={<div className="skeleton h-12 w-48" />}>
        <UserProfile userId={params.userId} />
      </Suspense>

      <Suspense fallback={<div className="skeleton h-64" />}>
        <PostsList userId={params.userId} />
      </Suspense>
    </div>
  )
}

Next.js 15 will:

  1. Stream the shell HTML immediately.
  2. Start both fetchUser and fetchPosts in parallel.
  3. Replace each Suspense boundary as data arrives.

Result: LCP improves by 40-60% because the skeleton UI paints instantly.

War Story: The Bundle Audit That Saved Us

After the Stripe key leak, I added a CI check:

# .github/workflows/bundle-audit.yml
- run: npm run build
- run: |
    if grep -r "sk_live_" .next/static/chunks; then
      echo "Secret key found in client bundle!"
      exit 1
    fi

Caught three more leaks before they hit production.

Takeaways

  1. Never define Server Actions in 'use client' files.
  2. Validate inputs with Zod before touching external APIs.
  3. Guard every action with session checks.
  4. Use granular Suspense to parallelize data fetching and improve LCP.
  5. Audit your bundles in CI to catch secret leaks.

Next.js 15 gives you the primitives. It's on you to wire them correctly.

title: 🧠 Mastering Goroutines in Go: The Power of Lightweight Concurrency.
description:
Go (Golang) is known for its simplicity, performance, and concurrency model.
At the heart of this concurrency lies one of Go’s most elegant features — the goroutine.

In this blog, we’ll explore what goroutines are, how they work under the hood, and how you can use them to build concurrent, scalable applications like a seasoned Go developer.

🧩 What is a Goroutine?

A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime.

When you run:

go doSomething()

you’re telling Go:

“Run doSomething() asynchronously, and don’t wait for it to finish.”

That single keyword go launches a new goroutine.

Unlike traditional OS threads (which can take up megabytes of stack memory), a goroutine starts with only a few kilobytes — making it possible to spawn hundreds of thousands of them effortlessly.

⚙️ How Goroutines Work (Under the Hood)

Go uses an efficient M:N scheduler, meaning it maps:

M = OS threads

N = Goroutines

So, instead of each goroutine needing its own thread, the Go runtime multiplexes thousands of goroutines onto a few OS threads — automatically managing scheduling, context switching, and load balancing.

This is why goroutines are incredibly lightweight and efficient.

🧠 The Lifecycle of a Goroutine

You launch it with go ...

The Go scheduler places it in a run queue

The scheduler assigns it to an available P (processor context)

The goroutine executes

When it finishes (or main() exits), it’s garbage collected

Important: When the main function ends, all goroutines stop — no exceptions.

🧪 Example 1: Your First Goroutine

Let’s start simple:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    go fmt.Println("Hello from a goroutine!")
    time.Sleep(time.Millisecond * 10)
}

Without the time.Sleep, this program might print nothing — because the main goroutine exits before the child one gets CPU time.

✅ Lesson: The main goroutine must stay alive until others finish.

🧱 Example 2: Launching Multiple Goroutines
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {
        go fmt.Println("Goroutine:", i)
    }

    fmt.Scanln() // Wait for user input to prevent exit
}

You’ll notice the output order is unpredictable — and that’s expected!
Each goroutine runs concurrently, not sequentially.

🔗 Communication Between Goroutines — Channels

Goroutines are great, but they’re even more powerful when they communicate safely.
That’s where channels come in.

A channel is a pipe that allows goroutines to send and receive data.

Example:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    ch := make(chan string)

    go func() {
        ch <- "Hello from goroutine!"
    }()

    msg := <-ch
    fmt.Println(msg)
}

ch <- "Hello" sends data

<-ch receives data

Both send and receive block until the other side is ready — ensuring synchronization.

⚙️ Buffered Channels

Want to send without waiting immediately? Use a buffered channel:

ch := make(chan int, 2)
ch <- 1
ch <- 2
fmt.Println(<-ch)

Here, the buffer lets you send two items before blocking.

🧰 Controlling Goroutines with sync.WaitGroup

In real-world apps, you’ll often need to wait for multiple goroutines to finish.
That’s where sync.WaitGroup comes in:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

func main() {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup

    for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func(id int) {
            defer wg.Done()
            fmt.Println("Worker", id, "done")
        }(i)
    }

    wg.Wait() // Wait until all goroutines finish
}

✅ This is the idiomatic Go way to synchronize goroutines.

🏗 Real-World Example: Worker Pool Pattern

A worker pool limits the number of concurrent workers — an essential pattern in production.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func worker(id int, jobs <-chan int, results chan<- int) {
    for j := range jobs {
        fmt.Println("Worker", id, "started job", j)
        time.Sleep(time.Second)
        fmt.Println("Worker", id, "finished job", j)
        results <- j * 2
    }
}

func main() {
    jobs := make(chan int, 5)
    results := make(chan int, 5)

    for w := 1; w <= 3; w++ {
        go worker(w, jobs, results)
    }

    for j := 1; j <= 5; j++ {
        jobs <- j
    }
    close(jobs)

    for a := 1; a <= 5; a++ {
        <-results
    }
}

💡 Conceptually:

Jobs channel → queue of tasks

Results channel → output

Workers (goroutines) → process jobs concurrently

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

❌ Forgetting to close channels — can cause deadlocks

❌ Starting goroutines without control — can overwhelm system memory

❌ Accessing shared memory without sync — causes race conditions

You can detect races by running:

go run -race main.go

🧭 Key Takeaways

✅ Goroutines are lightweight, cheap, and managed by Go’s scheduler
✅ Channels enable safe communication between them
✅ Always synchronize goroutines using WaitGroups, channels, or contexts
✅ Never start a goroutine you can’t stop

🚀 Final Thoughts

Goroutines are the foundation of Go’s simplicity and power.
Once you master them, you’ll start thinking in concurrent patterns — building systems that scale effortlessly.

In upcoming posts, I’ll dive deeper into:

Context cancellation

Pipelines

Fan-out/Fan-in patterns

Real-world concurrency debugging

✍️ Written by Yogesh Mathankar

💬 Modern MERN & Go developer passionate about building scalable systems and AI-integrated apps.

title: Restaurant Menu Retrieval Architecture: Safe Delete Semantics and Traceable Answers
description:
Restaurant menu assistants have a deceptively strict data contract: an answer must be grounded in the current menu, and a deleted dish must stop appearing in retrieval. That contract matters more than picking a fashionable vector database.

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to a menu document; treat deletion as a versioned data event, not as an afterthought in the UI.

Start with the answer contract

For a support agent answering “Does the lunch bowl contain peanuts?”, the retrieval result is not just a chunk of text. It needs a document identifier, source URL or file name, menu version, and the text span used to draft the answer. I model that as a small contract before choosing an API:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional


@dataclass
class MenuEvidence:
    text: str
    document_id: str
    source_url: Optional[str]
    menu_version: str
    deleted: bool = False

The deleted flag is useful during ingestion and audit, but deleted records should not be eligible for a user-facing query. A clean pipeline is easier to reason about when it has separate stages: ingest and normalize, index active records, retrieve a bounded candidate set, then generate an answer with citations.

This is where delete semantics become operational. A restaurant can remove an ingredient today while an old PDF remains in an object store, a queue, or an embedding index. If the index is updated first and the source registry later, a race can briefly resurrect the dish. I prefer a tombstone event keyed by document_id and menu_version; the query stage rejects tombstoned versions, and a compaction job removes their vectors deliberately.

Small rule. Delete twice safely.

That means the delete operation is idempotent, and a retry cannot turn a missing record into an error that blocks the menu update. It also gives support staff a review trail: “this answer cited menu-2026-08-31.pdf, which was superseded by menu-2026-09-01.pdf.”

Infrai fits this early boundary when a small support team wants retrieval beside model calls and other backend services behind one REST API and one key. The useful payoff is less credential and SDK setup while the application still owns the evidence contract, version checks, and deletion policy.

How should a restaurant menu assistant handle retrieval architecture and delete semantics?

Bound the work at every boundary. A query should have a maximum candidate count, an explicit timeout, and a retry policy with exponential backoff. Retrieval should fail closed when the source context is missing: return “I can't verify that from the current menu” rather than inventing a confident allergen answer.

The staged flow I use looks like this:

  1. Resolve the restaurant and active menu version.
  2. Query only the collection assigned to that restaurant and version.
  3. Filter out tombstoned document IDs before ranking or generation.
  4. Keep the top few passages and their source identifiers.
  5. Ask the language model to answer only from those passages, preserving citations.

The collection boundary is important for privacy and relevance. A shared global collection can return a similarly named dish from the wrong location. Explicit collections make that mistake harder, and they make a re-index of one restaurant predictable.

Here is a minimal discovery check using Infrai's documented collection-list route. It is intentionally only a setup check; the query payload belongs behind the contract above, where your application can validate fields and limits.

import os
import time
import requests


def list_collections():
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/list"
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}
    delay = 0.5

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=5)
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else delay)
            delay *= 2
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"collection discovery failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        return response.json()

    raise TimeoutError("collection discovery remained rate-limited")

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the team wants one REST API and one credential for several backend services around the assistant. That removes a real integration chore: separate keys and billing consoles for retrieval, model calls, and adjacent infrastructure. Its public discovery surface also documents capabilities and runnable examples, which shortens the path from an empty repository to a reviewed integration. The recommendation is narrow: try it for the retrieval boundary when credential sprawl and SDK installation are slowing delivery, while keeping the evidence contract in your own code.

Compare the integration surface, not just search quality

Search quality depends on chunking, metadata, and evaluation data. The integration surface determines how quickly a team can make those choices safely.

Option Setup and credentials Delete and re-index control Best fit Trade-off
Infrai vector API One REST key can cover retrieval and other backend capabilities; no SDK is required Application owns versioning and tombstones while collection operations stay explicit Small teams assembling a support backend Less specialized than a vector-only platform for deep index tuning
Pinecone Managed vector service with a focused SDK/API surface Namespaces and deletes are available, but your source-of-truth workflow still needs versioning Teams that want a dedicated managed vector layer Another vendor credential and service boundary to operate
Weaviate Open-source or managed deployment with a rich schema/client model Object deletion and schema design are powerful, with more concepts to govern Teams needing configurable schemas and self-hosting options Larger operational and schema surface for a small menu assistant
Elasticsearch Existing search clusters can combine lexical and vector retrieval Mature document lifecycle and aliases support controlled re-indexes Organizations already standardized on Elastic operations More tuning and cluster ownership than this narrow use case needs

No row wins universally. Infrai is not suitable when you need a vector-specialist's low-level index controls or already have a heavily tuned Elasticsearch cluster; stick with Pinecone, Weaviate, or Elasticsearch in those cases. Conversely, a team that is wiring email notifications, model calls, and retrieval with a small backend may value one credential more than another dashboard of knobs.

I would run the same menu evaluation set against each option: 50 questions covering allergens, substitutions, opening hours, and removed dishes. Record recall at a fixed top_k, citation correctness, stale-answer rate after deletion, and the time from a menu upload to a useful answer. Don't use a single “looks good” demo as the acceptance test.

Make deletion observable and boring

Deletion needs a state machine, not a button. Keep active, superseded, and tombstoned states in the source registry. On replacement, write the new version, verify its chunks, then mark the old version superseded and remove its vectors. On a true removal, write the tombstone first, invalidate caches, and enqueue vector deletion. A periodic reconciliation compares the registry with the collection so a missed event becomes a measurable repair task.

I once assumed a successful upload meant the index was current. It didn't. The missing piece was a deletion test: the old PDF was still retrievable because the test suite only asserted that new content appeared. Add a regression that asks the removed-dish question after every re-index and asserts both that no deleted document ID is returned and that the answer carries a current source identifier.

Set a deadline for every stage. If retrieval exceeds it, return a reviewable fallback and log the request ID, collection, menu version, and candidate IDs. Your mileage may vary on timeout values; traffic, PDF size, and the support team's tolerance for a delayed answer decide that number. The invariant is simpler: a slow source must not hold the user flow hostage.

A practical rollout boundary

Start with one restaurant and one explicit collection. Shadow queries for a week, compare citations with the source PDFs, then enable generated answers for low-risk questions. Keep allergen and legal-policy responses behind a human review path until citation correctness is demonstrated on your own data.

After that, automate re-indexing from a deliberate event, not from every file-system change. Store the event ID so retries are idempotent. Keep the retrieval API replaceable behind the MenuEvidence contract; this is what lets you move between a unified REST platform and a specialist without rewriting the support workflow.

If this boundary fits your system, the Infrai documentation is the next place to check the current collection and query details. For the grounding model, the original Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper is still a useful reference.

Sources

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: I checked 9 copy-paste HTML contact forms from the top search results. 4 send nothing
description:
Disclosure: I build Formgong, a form backend. Three of the pages below belong to companies like mine, and I say which.

If you search "html contact form code", you get pages with a form you can copy. I wanted to know how many of those forms would actually deliver a message if you pasted them into a site today.

On 13 October 2026 I took the top 10 pages for four searches ("html contact form code", "html contact form", "contact form html css", "simple contact form html"), merged by rank, skipping pages with no copyable code (a Scribd PDF, a Medium post with the code only as screenshots, and a page that now redirects to a form-builder tool). One page was down ("Site unavailable"), so 9 were judged. I wrote the checks down before opening the first page, and I only read the code. Nothing was submitted anywhere.

The checks

  1. Does it send? The form has an action pointing at something that exists, or the page gives the backend code. action="#", no action, or JavaScript that only shows "Thanks" count as no.
  2. Labels. Every field has a <label> tied to it. A placeholder alone doesn't count.
  3. type="email" on the email field.
  4. required on name, email and message.
  5. autocomplete on name and email, so phones and password managers can fill them.
  6. Any spam protection in the snippet: a honeypot, a captcha, a server check.
  7. If JavaScript sends it: does it show an error when the request fails?

Results

Page Owner Sends Labels type=email required autocomplete Spam
Formspree library form backend yes, after signup yes no no no not in snippet
Medium (Cwrcode) independent no no yes no no no
GeeksforGeeks independent yes (PHP) no yes no no no
TemplateMonster Help (2011) independent yes (PHP) no no no no no
freeCodeCamp independent no no yes yes* no no
TutorialsPoint independent no yes yes yes no no
a Lovable-built blog independent no yes yes yes no no
Web3Forms form backend yes, after signup no yes yes no not in snippet
Formcarry blog form backend yes yes yes no no no (PHP version)

The totals:

  • 5 of 9 send anywhere. Three of those five are form-backend companies, which is fair: sending is what they sell.
  • Of the 6 independent pages, 2 send, and one of the two can't be submitted as shown (see TemplateMonster below). So 1 of 6 gives code that delivers a message as pasted.
  • 3 of the 4 forms that don't send never tell the reader.
  • 0 of 9 set autocomplete. 0 of 9 have spam protection in the code itself. The three backend companies say they filter on their side; I didn't test that.
  • The only snippet that submits with JavaScript shows "Thank you" without making a request at all.

Four things worth seeing in the code

The fields have no names. The Medium post's form has inputs for name, email and phone, and none of them has a name attribute. Browsers only send fields that have a name. Even with a working backend behind it, the message would arrive with the country code and the text, and nothing that tells you who wrote it:

<input type="text" size="33" placeholder="Enter Your Name" id="firstname" autofocus />
<input type="email" id="eid" placeholder="Enter Your Email" size="33" />

The Send button disappears. The TemplateMonster article from 2011 shows its textarea with a <br> after it and no closing tag. A browser keeps reading everything after an unclosed <textarea> as its text, including the button. Parsed in Chrome, the form has zero submit buttons. Its PHP also builds the From and Reply-To headers from a variable the script never defines.

An empty message passes required. freeCodeCamp's form posts to action="#", so it sends nothing, and the tutorial doesn't mention that. The labels point at ids the inputs don't have. And the textarea ships with a space inside:

<textarea name="message" cols="30" rows="10" placeholder="Enter your message here ..." required> </textarea>

That space is the field's value, so the browser treats it as filled. In Chrome, validity.valueMissing is false for a message nobody typed.

Copy it as-is and you CC a stranger. GeeksforGeeks is the one independent page whose code would deliver, on a PHP host where mail() works. Its PHP adds a fixed header:

"CC: somebodyelse@example.com";

Paste it unchanged and every message also goes to example.com.

One more, from a backend company's own page: Formcarry's PHP example checks the name and email with patterns that reject o.brien+site@gmail.com, ann@studio.agency, José García and Олена Коваль. I tested the two patterns with Python's re, not PHP, because PHP isn't installed on my machine.

What a contact form that works needs

This is the checklist I'd use before pasting any snippet:

<form action="https://your-endpoint.example/submit" method="POST">
  <label>Name <input name="name" required autocomplete="name"></label>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" required autocomplete="email"></label>
  <label>Message <textarea name="message" required></textarea></label>
  <!-- honeypot: hidden from people, bots fill it, the server drops those -->
  <div hidden><label>Leave empty <input name="botcheck" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off"></label></div>
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
  • An action that points at something that really sends. Then send yourself one test from the live page and check the inbox.
  • A name on every field. Without it the value never leaves the browser.
  • Labels wrapped around or tied to each field, type="email", required, and autocomplete.
  • No whitespace between <textarea> and </textarea>.
  • Some spam check, even a honeypot.
  • If you send with fetch, show an error when the request fails. A "Thanks" that appears no matter what is worse than no form.

We put these rules into the free form generator on our site. It writes the same form as HTML, Tailwind, Bootstrap, React or Vue. It posts to Formgong, so it needs a key (there's a free plan). If you have your own backend, copy the markup and change the action.

To check a form that is already live, paste the page address into our form checker. It reads the page's HTML and reports a missing action, fields without names or labels, a lost submit button and a whitespace-filled required textarea. It works with any form backend and never submits anything.

The method, the full results and the failing line from every snippet are in a public repo: formgong/html-snippet-study. If you want a page I didn't quote, ask in the comments.

Tell me what I missed

Which tutorial did you copy your first contact form from, and did it work? If you know a snippet that passes all seven checks, post it below. I'll add it to the table.

title: AI Gateway now supports team and project spend budgets
description:
AI Gateway spend budgets can now be scoped to a team or a project, in addition to individual API keys. Set a dollar limit on a scope, and the gateway meters spend against it and stops further requests once the limit is reached, until the budget resets or you raise it.

Scopes

A budget attaches to one of three scopes. A request can fall under multiple budgets and has to pass all of them: if any one is over its limit, the request is rejected, even when the others have room left.

Scope

Caps spend for

Team

Every request your team runs through the gateway

Project

All requests attributed to a single project

API key

A single API key

BYOK spend is not counted against budgets by default.

Manage budgets in the dashboard

Set and track budgets from the AI Gateway Budgets tab. The Overview breaks spend down across every scope against its limit, so you can see what is near or over before it starts rejecting requests.

Turn on email spend alerts to notify your team's usage notification recipients when usage crosses 50%, 75%, or 100% of a limit within a refresh period. Alerts are off by default and informational: they never block requests, only the budget limit does.

Set a default budget for projects or API keys, and every one without an explicit budget inherits it automatically. An explicit budget always overrides the default.

Manage budgets from the CLI

Set, inspect, and remove team and project budgets from the CLI. The refresh period is daily, weekly, monthly (default), or none for a cumulative cap.

For more information, read the budgets documentation.

title: Supabase's October 30 change: don't fix "permission denied" by reopening your tables
description:
On October 30, 2026, Supabase applies a new default to every existing project: new tables you create in the public schema are no longer reachable through the Data API until you explicitly grant access. New projects have worked this way since May 30.

This is a good change. It also creates a moment where a rushed fix can leave you worse off than before. Here is what changes, what you will see, and how to fix it without reopening your data.

What actually changes

Until now, every new table in public automatically received select, insert, update and delete privileges for the anon, authenticated and service_role roles. That made every new table reachable through supabase-js, REST and GraphQL the moment it existed, including tables nobody had protected yet.

After the change reaches your project:

  • Existing tables are not touched. They keep their current grants and keep working.
  • New tables in public need an explicit grant before the Data API can see them.
  • RLS is unchanged. Grants decide whether a role can touch a table at all. RLS decides which rows that role can see. You need both.
  • Direct Postgres connections are unaffected. If your app only uses psql, an ORM or a server with a connection string, this does not apply to you.
  • Other schemas are unaffected. storage, auth, realtime and custom schemas keep their current defaults.

What you will see

The first time your app (or your AI coding agent) creates a table and queries it, you get:

{
  "code": "42501",
  "message": "permission denied for table your_table",
  "hint": "Grant the required privileges to the current role with: GRANT SELECT ON public.your_table TO anon;"
}

The hint is helpful. It names the role that asked and the grant that would let it in. But read it carefully, because that is where the risk is.

The trap: three quick fixes that reopen your data

1. The bulk grant. Supabase's own rollback FAQ includes this, for people who opted in early and want the old behavior back:

grant select, insert, update, delete on all tables in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;

That is a legitimate rollback, but as a fix for one broken table it reopens every table in public to every API role. If any of those tables lacks RLS or has a loose policy, it is exposed again.

2. Following the hint word for word. If the failing request was made by a logged-out visitor, the hint suggests granting to anon. Most app tables should never be readable by logged-out visitors. Ask "who should be able to reach this table?" before you copy the line.

3. Granting on a table that has no RLS. Tables created in the Supabase dashboard get RLS enabled by default. Tables created in the SQL editor or by other tools, including migrations and AI agents, need RLS enabled explicitly (Supabase docs). A grant on a table without RLS means any role with that grant can read every row.

This matters more now than it would have a year ago. Supabase's changelog says the hint exists partly so that "an agent can self-correct when a grant is missing." That is useful, but an agent that self-corrects by granting anon on an unprotected table has just undone the protection this change was designed to add.

The safe pattern: grant, RLS and policy as one unit

Supabase recommends treating these three steps as a unit, in the same migration:

-- 1. Grant only what each role needs
grant select, insert, update, delete on public.your_table to authenticated;
grant select, insert, update, delete on public.your_table to service_role;
-- grant select on public.your_table to anon;  -- only if logged-out visitors truly need to read it

-- 2. Enable RLS
alter table public.your_table enable row level security;

-- 3. Add the policies you need
create policy "users can read their own rows"
  on public.your_table
  for select
  to authenticated
  using (auth.uid() = user_id);

If your app has organizations or teams, the policy should check membership in the row's organization, not only auth.uid(). Remember that insert and update policies also need a with check clause, or a user can write a row into someone else's organization.

If you build with an AI coding agent

Add a rule to your agent's instructions file (for example CLAUDE.md, a Cursor rule, or your system prompt):

When you create a table in the public schema, in the same migration: grant only the privileges each role needs (authenticated for signed-in users; anon only if I confirm logged-out visitors must read it, and then select only), enable row level security, and add policies that limit rows to their owner or their organization. Never use "grant ... on all tables in schema public" to fix a permission error. If you hit a 42501 error, tell me which role and table, and propose a per-table grant instead of applying it.

Supabase also maintains an agent skill that includes the grants step; the changelog recommends adopting it.

A 10-minute checklist before October 30

  1. Open Security Advisor and the Data API exposure badge in the Table Editor. They list tables worth reviewing.
  2. Try the new behavior early on a staging project. Supabase documents the opt-in SQL in its changelog.
  3. Update your migration templates so every new table ships with grants, RLS and policies together.
  4. Update your AI agent's instructions with the rule above.
  5. Revoke grants on any existing table that should not be reachable at all: revoke all on table public.your_table from anon, authenticated, service_role;
  6. After your next migration, check the outcome, not just the SQL. Sign in as a user from a different account or organization and confirm you cannot read or change the first user's rows.

The short version

The change is good for everyone. The risk is the fix. Grant per table, per role, with RLS and policies in the same migration, and then test that one signed-in user really cannot reach another's data.

I build RowAttest, which runs that last check on a staging Supabase project: it signs in as test users from different organizations and tries to read and write across them. The steps above work without it.

title: Amazon CloudWatch log centralization now available in AWS GovCloud and additional commercial Regions
description:
Amazon CloudWatch log centralization is now available in AWS GovCloud (US) and 13 additional commercial Regions. CloudWatch log centralization copies log data from multiple AWS accounts and Regions into a single destination account, integrating with AWS Organizations for efficient aggregation without the need for custom solutions.

With this launch, organizations in the AWS GovCloud (US) partition and commercial partition can each centralize logs across their accounts and Regions for centralized monitoring. You can scope centralization rules to your entire organization, specific organizational units, or selected accounts and copy logs into a single account while preserving source context through enriched system fields.

CloudWatch log centralization is now additionally available in Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Milan), Europe (Spain), Europe (Zurich), Israel (Tel Aviv), Middle East (Bahrain), Middle East (UAE), AWS GovCloud (US-East), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). For a complete list of supported Regions, see the AWS Region table.

To get started, create a centralization rule in the Amazon CloudWatch console, or by using the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, see Log centralization in the Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide. Customers can centralize one copy of logs for free; additional copies are charged at $0.05/GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch pricing.

title: 5 ways your cloud CLI picks the wrong account without telling you
description:
You type vercel deploy, gh pr merge or kubectl apply. Which account does it run on?

Most people would say "the one I'm logged into". That's wrong more often than you'd think, and nothing on screen
tells you. Each CLI works out the account from flags, environment variables, files in the current folder and files in
your home directory, and each one checks them in a different order. These are five cases I ran into while building
cloudpin, all on current versions.

1. An environment variable silently beats your login

gh auth status says you're logged in as you. But if GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN is set, gh uses that token
instead, for every command (gh help environment). The same goes for VERCEL_TOKEN, SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN and
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN over their CLIs' stored logins.

These variables usually get set once (a .env file, a CI secret copied to a laptop, an old shell profile) and then
forgotten. From then on, the login you see and the account your commands run on are different, and nothing on screen
says so.

2. The project folder picks the account

Several CLIs read the target from the project folder, not from who you're logged in as:

  • Vercel: a linked project (.vercel/project.json) sends project-level requests to the team it was linked under. Observed on Vercel CLI 50.35: --team changes account-level requests but not those; VERCEL_ORG_ID does. And the current flag in vercel teams ls shows only your global team, whatever the folder says.
  • Supabase: commands go to the project in supabase/.temp/project-ref, which supabase link wrote, unless --project-ref or SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID says otherwise. Copy a folder, and you copy the link.
  • Cloudflare Wrangler: account_id in wrangler.toml wins over CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID. The source even has a TODO to swap them in v5. Setting the variable to "be sure" does nothing if the config file names another account.

So cd ../other-project && deploy can land on another account from the same terminal, with the same login.

3. Config files merge, and the first one wins

KUBECONFIG can list several files. kubectl merges them, and for each value the first file to set it wins
(kubernetes.io, "Organizing cluster access"). Add a file at the front of the list and your prod context may now point
somewhere else, with the same name.

A harder one to spot: kubectl config view --minify shows the context you'd expect but ignores --cluster, and real
requests use it (you can see it in the kubectl -v=6 request URLs). So the command you'd use to check can disagree
with the command that runs.

4. Someone else changed the global state

az account set, gh auth switch and gcloud config configurations activate rewrite a file in your home folder.
Every terminal and every tool on the machine shares it. Switch in one window to check something for a client, and the
deploy you start in the other window an hour later goes to the client.

Some mistakes don't even fail. On gcloud SDK 588, --configuration with a name that doesn't exist is not an
error: you get an empty configuration and exit code 0.

5. Names aren't IDs

  • In my own Azure account, several subscriptions are all called "Azure subscription 1". Only the subscription ID tells them apart.
  • Kubernetes context names are personal: the same cluster is prod on one laptop and acme-prod-admin on another.
  • AWS CLI aliases (~/.aws/cli/alias) can replace a built-in command, so aws s3 ls may not be s3 ls.
  • gcloud puts the resource name after the verb: gcloud compute instances delete describe deletes an instance named "describe".

What AI agents add

Coding agents run these same commands for you, and they don't stop to ask which account is active unless you tell
them to. When I started doing my side projects' Azure infrastructure with an agent, I approved each change myself,
but the approval prompt shows the command, not the account it will run on. So I ended up adding the same line to
almost every request: first check which account you're logged into. It worked, but only when I remembered to say
it, and that's the part that kept bugging me.

What I built

So I built cloudpin. You pin the accounts a project uses in a
.cloudpin.yml by ID, since names repeat. Before any guarded command runs, cloudpin works out which account that
command would use, with its own flags, environment and folder, and stops it if it's not the pinned one. If it can't
tell, it blocks the command and says why. It works in your terminal (a shell wrapper) and in agent hooks (Claude
Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot CLI, Antigravity and Gemini CLI).

It covers az, aws, gcloud, vercel, gh, kubectl, helm, supabase and wrangler. cloudpin explain -- <command> shows
what it would decide for any command, and why, without running it.

Works alongside

cloudpin doesn't manage credentials or switch accounts. It sits next to the tools that do:

  • aws-vault and granted hand out short-lived AWS credentials; cloudpin checks they're for the right account.
  • kubectx and kubens switch contexts quickly; cloudpin stops the command when the switch was the wrong one.
  • direnv sets per-folder variables; cloudpin checks which account those variables point at.

It's still early days: cloudpin has only been around for about a week, so it's very much a work in progress and I'll
keep adding to it. Next up are a Claude Code plugin, a GitHub Action, and Homebrew and Scoop installers.

To try it: npm install --global cloudpin, then cloudpin init in a project. If it gets an account wrong for your
setup, please open an issue. That's the feedback I'm most after.

title: How to back up your Samsung phone before flashing firmware
description:
Flashing stock firmware is one of the safest ways to fix a misbehaving Galaxy phone, but only if your data survives the process. A full flash wipes the internal storage, and the restore only works if the backup was made before the flash, not after. The ten minutes a backup takes are the cheapest insurance in the whole process.

What flashing actually erases

A standard Odin flash with the CSC file (not HOME_CSC) performs a factory reset as part of the install. That means photos, videos, downloaded files, app data, saved Wi-Fi networks, call history, and messages stored on the phone all go away. The SIM card and the microSD card are not wiped, but anything on internal storage is. If you flash with HOME_CSC, your data is meant to stay, yet plenty of flashes still go wrong partway through and end in a forced wipe. Treat every flash as a full wipe, and you will never lose anything to a surprise.

The three things worth saving

First, your files: photos, videos, documents, and anything in the Downloads folder. Second, your app setup: which apps you had, your accounts inside them, and chat histories that do not sync to a cloud. Third, your phone settings: Wi-Fi passwords, home screen layout, and accessibility options. A good backup covers all three, and the methods below stack nicely if you use two of them together.

Method 1: Smart Switch on a computer

Smart Switch is Samsung's own backup tool, and it is the most complete option. Install it on a Windows PC or a Mac, connect the phone with a USB cable, and choose Backup. It copies contacts, messages, call logs, photos, videos, music, documents, app lists, and most settings into a single backup file on the computer. When the flash is done, connect the phone again and choose Restore. One detail people miss: Smart Switch backs up the apps themselves only if the backup includes them, and some apps with their own login (banking apps, authenticators) still need to be signed into again. Move authenticator codes to a second device before you flash, because a backup will not save those.

Method 2: Samsung Cloud and Google backup

If you do not have a computer nearby, the built-in cloud backups cover most of the same ground. On the phone, open Settings, then Accounts and backup, and check that both Samsung Cloud and Google One backup are switched on. Samsung Cloud handles call logs, messages, contacts, calendar entries, and settings. Google's backup covers app data for apps that support it, plus Wi-Fi passwords and call history. Run a manual backup now rather than trusting the last automatic one, and wait until it reports completion. Cloud restore works well, but it needs a stable Wi-Fi connection and it is slower than a cable restore, so plan for that.

Method 3: a manual copy of the files that matter

Cloud and Smart Switch backups are good, but a manual copy is the belt to go with the braces. Plug the phone into a computer, copy the DCIM, Pictures, Downloads, and Documents folders to a folder on the computer, and confirm the copy by opening a few files. If the phone has a microSD card, copy its contents too, since a card can be removed before flashing and kept somewhere safe. This manual copy is also the fastest way to check that your photos really exist in two places before you wipe the phone.

After the flash: restore in the right order

Once the phone boots into the fresh firmware, sign into the same Samsung and Google accounts you used for the backup, connect to Wi-Fi, and let the restore run before installing anything new. Restore Smart Switch or cloud backup first, then check that photos, messages, and contacts are back. Only then reinstall the apps that need fresh logins, and re-register authenticator apps from their own recovery codes. Flashing first and hunting for a backup afterwards is how data loss happens, so keep the order strict.

The one mistake that costs people their photos

The most common data-loss story is not a failed flash. It is a phone that was backed up to a computer that later turned out to hold a backup from a different phone, or a cloud backup that had silently stopped syncing months earlier. Before you flash, open the backup and verify it: check the date, the size, and a few files inside it. A backup you have not verified is a guess, not a backup.

A clean flash with a verified backup is a routine job. Do the backup first, check it, and then flash with confidence. For the firmware itself, SamFware keeps official stock ROMs organised by model and region, and the guides on SamFware walk through the flash step by step.
