title: Postgres "deadlock detected": Fix the Lock Order First, Then Add a Retry
description:
Postgres raises ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01) when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The durable fix is to make every code path lock rows in the same order; a retry on 40P01 is the safety net, not the cure. If you only add the retry, you hide the bug and pay for it in latency.

What does the error actually say?

This is the shape of the message you get in the application and the server log:

ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 8121 waits for ShareLock on transaction 90417; blocked by process 8130.
Process 8130 waits for ShareLock on transaction 90416; blocked by process 8121.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,12) in relation "accounts"

Read it as a cycle. Process 8121 is waiting for a transaction that process 8130 owns, and 8130 is waiting for one that 8121 owns. Postgres notices the cycle after deadlock_timeout (1 second by default), picks one transaction as the victim, and aborts it. The other one proceeds as if nothing happened.

Two things trip people up. The victim is not necessarily the "wrong" transaction, so you cannot fix this by blaming one code path. And the CONTEXT line names only the row the victim was waiting on when it was killed, not the whole story. The server log, not the client error, has the full query text for both sides.

Takeaway: a deadlock is a cycle between two or more transactions, and the error message is only the last edge of that cycle.

Why does it only happen under load?

A deadlock needs two transactions to interleave at exactly the wrong moment, so it passes every test you run alone. The classic version is a transfer between two accounts:

-- Transaction A (transfer 1 -> 2)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

-- Transaction B (transfer 2 -> 1), running at the same moment
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 5 WHERE id = 2;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 5 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

A locks row 1, B locks row 2, then each reaches for the row the other holds. Neither can finish. Nothing about this is a Postgres quirk; any database with row locks behaves this way.

The less obvious sources, in the order I tend to find them:

  • Batch updates with no stable order. UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...) locks rows in whatever order the plan visits them. Two workers updating overlapping sets can lock in opposite orders. Postgres does not guarantee the order from the IN list.
  • Foreign keys. Inserting a child row takes a FOR KEY SHARE lock on the parent row. Concurrent inserts of children plus an update of the same parent can form a cycle you never wrote explicitly.
  • Upserts and unique indexes. Two transactions inserting overlapping sets of keys with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT in different orders can deadlock on the index entries.
  • Mixed application paths. One endpoint locks orders then inventory; a background job locks inventory then orders.

Takeaway: most production deadlocks come from two code paths touching the same rows in different orders, not from a single bad query.

How do you find the two queries involved?

Turn on lock-wait logging so the server log tells you who waited on whom. These are standard settings; set them in postgresql.conf or through your managed provider's parameter UI:

ALTER SYSTEM SET log_lock_waits = on;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

With log_lock_waits on, any wait longer than deadlock_timeout is logged, and a deadlock entry includes the statements for each process involved. Pair that with log_line_prefix containing the process id (%p) so you can match Process 8121 to its query. If you ship logs to a hosted service, search for deadlock detected and read the two statements side by side. The ordering mismatch is usually visible in thirty seconds.

Takeaway: turn on log_lock_waits before you need it, because a deadlock you cannot attribute to two specific statements is a deadlock you cannot fix.

How do you fix it: consistent lock ordering

Lock the rows you are about to modify up front, in a deterministic order, then do the writes. For the transfer example:

BEGIN;

SELECT id
FROM accounts
WHERE id = ANY(ARRAY[1, 2])
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE;

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;

COMMIT;

Both directions of transfer now lock id 1 before id 2. The second transaction waits for the first instead of forming a cycle, and waiting is fine; only circular waiting is fatal.

In application code, sort the keys before you touch them. A Python sketch with psycopg 3:

import psycopg

def transfer(conn: psycopg.Connection, src: int, dst: int, amount: int) -> None:
    with conn.transaction():
        # Lock both rows in a fixed order, regardless of transfer direction.
        conn.execute(
            "SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id = ANY(%s) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE",
            ([src, dst],),
        )
        conn.execute(
            "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - %s WHERE id = %s",
            (amount, src),
        )
        conn.execute(
            "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + %s WHERE id = %s",
            (amount, dst),
        )

For batch jobs, the same idea applies: select the target ids with ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE, or use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED if workers should divide work rather than queue behind each other. Also keep transactions short. A transaction that holds locks while it calls an external API widens the window for every cycle.

Takeaway: if every transaction acquires locks in one global order (for example ascending primary key), a lock cycle cannot form.

What should the retry look like?

Ordering fixes the cycles you know about. Foreign-key and index locks can still produce rare ones, so wrap write transactions in a retry that catches only the deadlock error:

import random
import time
import psycopg
from psycopg import errors

def run_with_deadlock_retry(conn, fn, attempts=4):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn(conn)
        except errors.DeadlockDetected:  # SQLSTATE 40P01
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, 0.05 * 2 ** attempt))

Retry the whole transaction, not the single statement that failed, because Postgres has already rolled it back. Make sure the function is safe to run twice, which means no external side effects inside it. Jitter matters: without it, the two transactions can collide again in lockstep.

Approach Removes the cycle? Cost Use when
Consistent lock order (ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE) Yes One extra statement per transaction Always, as the primary fix
Retry on 40P01 No, it recovers Latency on the rare collision As a safety net behind ordering
Shorter transactions Narrows the window Refactoring Locks held across slow calls
SKIP LOCKED Avoids waiting Rows may be skipped this pass Worker pools draining a queue
Raise deadlock_timeout No Slower detection Rarely; it just delays the failure

Takeaway: ordering prevents deadlocks, retries absorb the leftovers, and raising timeouts does neither.

FAQ

Is a Postgres deadlock a bug in my database?

No. Postgres is behaving correctly by detecting the cycle and aborting one transaction; the bug is in the application's lock ordering.

Should I just retry on deadlock detected?

Retry as a safety net, but fix the ordering first. A retry on its own turns a correctness bug into intermittent latency spikes.

What is SQLSTATE 40P01?

It is the code Postgres returns for deadlock_detected. Catch that code specifically instead of retrying on every error.

Bottom line

If you see deadlock detected, enable log_lock_waits, find the two statements, and make both paths lock rows in the same order, usually ascending primary key via SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE. Then wrap write transactions in a small jittered retry on 40P01 for the cycles you cannot predict. Do not treat a longer deadlock_timeout as a fix. As of late 2026 this behavior is stable across supported Postgres versions, though the exact log wording can differ slightly.

title: Why my business simulator replays every run bit for bit
description:
I started Ventute in December 2022 as a rough idea. For the first couple of years it was mostly sketches and throwaway code. Most of what exists today was built in the last year, and I built it alone.

Ventute is a business simulation platform. You run a company, make decisions, and the engine plays out what happens next. Simple enough, until you realise a simulation you cannot replay is a simulation you cannot debug or trust.

Events instead of state

Every action in Ventute is stored as an event. The state of a company is never saved directly. It is rebuilt by folding the event log from the beginning. Same events in, same state out.

The hard part is making that true every single time. Wall clock time, randomness, iteration order and floating point all love to break replay quietly. So the kernel treats each of them as something that has to be controlled, not trusted. The goal was replay that matches bit for bit, not just close enough.

Monte Carlo without the GIL

Forecasting means running a lot of possible futures. In pure Python the GIL turns that into a queue. I moved the hot loop into Rust and call it through PyO3, so the simulations run on real threads in parallel while the API stays in async Python with FastAPI. PostgreSQL (serverless on Neon) and Redis handle storage and caching.

Parallel code and determinism usually do not get along, so every run has to produce the same answer no matter which thread finishes first.

Pulled out as open source

Three patterns from Ventute turned out to be useful on their own, so I published them on GitHub under m4xkushnir. An event driven replay kernel, a deterministic AI guardrail, and a small PyO3 bridge between Rust and Python. They are deliberately small so they are easy to read.

I am curious how others handle determinism in their own systems, especially around floats and parallel work. If you have fought the same battle, I would love to hear how it went.

title: Vercel Sandbox now runs on Vercel Managed Images
description:
Today we are introducing Vercel Managed Images (VMI), a set of versioned, open-source base images you can use as-is or extend. The source for every image lives in the public vercel/sandbox repository.

Managed images replace Sandbox runtimes, which are now deprecated. Starting with version 3 of the Sandbox SDK, new sandboxes default to vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. It ships with Node.js, Python, common coding agents and standard utilities, so most users never build a custom image or install packages at boot.

The universal image switches our default operating system from Amazon Linux to Ubuntu, a lighter and more widely used system across the industry.

Secure by default

Every managed image gets a nightly release. Rolling tags such as latest and the major-version tags pick up operating system and dependency updates automatically, including security patches and new releases of Node.js, Python, and the preinstalled coding agents.

Within each release, dependencies are pinned to specific versions wherever possible, so a given image version stays consistent.

If you need a fully immutable, reproducible environment, pin to an image digest (SHA). Digest-pinned images opt out of automatic updates.

Choose a managed image from the catalog

Each managed image targets a different starting point:

  • vercel/sandbox/universal:latest is the new default, a rolling release on Ubuntu 26.04 with Node.js 24, Python 3.14 with uv, the opencode, claude-code, codex, and pi coding agents, and utilities including git, vim, nano, tmux, ripgrep, jq, and fzf.

  • vercel/sandbox/node:22, node:24, and node:26 provide Node.js versions on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/python:3.14 provides Python on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/ubuntu:latest provides base Ubuntu 26.04 with no extra tooling.

  • vercel/sandbox/arch:latest provides Arch Linux, regularly updated, with no Node.js or Python preinstalled. Its large package repository makes it useful for agents that install tools on the fly.

Reference an image and migrate from runtimes

Sandboxes can use an image from any repository in your project, a repository which has been shared with your team or any public repository.

Images are addressed by their full path, team-slug/project/repo:tag, for example vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. The SDK types the image property so built-in images autocomplete while any string is still accepted. The previous runtime property is deprecated, not removed, so existing code keeps working.

Amazon Linux runtimes are not part of the managed image catalog, so teams that need AL2023 can stay on runtime. Managed images run as the default ubuntu or arch user with passwordless sudo, rather than the vercel-sandbox user.

Open an issue or a pull request to improve them, and read the Vercel Sandbox images documentation to get started.

title: Let Your Users Talk a Workflow Into Existence (ByteChef Embedded, Part 9)
description:
Your users rarely know their automation up front. They discover it while they describe it: "when a deal closes... actually only enterprise deals... and loop in the account manager... and skip weekends."

A template can't handle that. A drag-and-drop canvas scares half of them off. So in part nine of the ByteChef Embedded series, we give them a chat: they describe what they want, and ByteChef's workflow agent builds it in their account while they watch.

On your side, it's one React component, one callback and a button.

TL;DR

  • EmbeddedWorkflowChat takes the connected user's JWT, starter suggestions, an optional system prompt, and an onWorkflowReady callback.
  • On mount it creates an empty draft workflow. The agent edits that draft directly, turn by turn.
  • Every turn streams over AG-UI from POST /automation/workflows/{uuid}/copilot/chat.
  • When the agent needs something, it renders a card in the thread: a question, an option picker, a connection picker, or a Connect button.
  • After the first turn, onWorkflowReady(uuid) fires and you can send the user to the editor.

Where chat fits

In the embedded sample app, open Automations. The split button lists every way to start a workflow:

Option The user... Best when
New from Template (part 8) Picks a workflow you built You know the common automations
New from Embedded Workflow Builder Drags nodes on ByteChef's canvas The user likes visual builders
New from Prompt Writes one description, gets one result The request is short and clear
New from Chat (this part) Talks it through with an agent The request is fuzzy, or the user doesn't know the apps' vocabulary
New from Custom Workflow Builder (part 7) Fills in a UI you designed You want full control

Chat is the most forgiving option. Your users don't need to know Slack's action is called Send Channel Message or that a schedule trigger has a dayOfWeek property. The agent knows. When it isn't sure what they mean, it asks.

The page

Click New from Chat and you land on /automations/chat:

Three parts:

  1. A collapsed System prompt (optional) field where you, the integrator, add house rules.
  2. The chat, centered while empty.
  3. Suggestion chips. Clicking one sends it as the first message, so a blank chat isn't intimidating.

Once the conversation starts, the composer docks to the bottom. After the first turn, an Open workflow button appears top right.

Mounting the component

Here's app/automations/chat/page.tsx, trimmed:

export default function GenerateFromChatPage() {
    const [jwtToken, setJwtToken] = useState<string | null>(null);
    const [systemPrompt, setSystemPrompt] = useState('');
    const [workflowUuid, setWorkflowUuid] = useState<string | null>(null);

    const router = useRouter();

    useEffect(() => {
        getToken().then(setJwtToken);
    }, []);

    return (
        <div className="flex h-screen w-full flex-col p-4">
            <div className="mb-3 flex items-center justify-between gap-4">
                <details className="flex-1 text-sm">
                    <summary>System prompt (optional)</summary>

                    <Textarea
                        onChange={(event) => setSystemPrompt(event.target.value)}
                        placeholder="e.g. Always prefer Slack over email; keep workflows under five steps."
                        value={systemPrompt}
                    />
                </details>

                {workflowUuid && (
                    <Button onClick={() => router.push(`/automations/${workflowUuid}`)}>Open workflow</Button>
                )}
            </div>

            <div className="min-h-0 flex-1">
                {jwtToken && (
                    <EmbeddedWorkflowChat
                        baseUrl={BYTECHEF_APP_BASE_URL}
                        environment={BYTECHEF_ENVIRONMENT}
                        jwtToken={jwtToken}
                        onWorkflowReady={setWorkflowUuid}
                        suggestions={[
                            {
                                title: 'Search for an action',
                                label: 'that can send an email',
                                action: 'Search for an action that can send an email',
                            },
                            // ...
                        ]}
                        systemPrompt={systemPrompt}
                    />
                )}
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}

getToken() asks the sample's back-end to sign a connected-user JWT, the same as in part one. The chat waits for the token, because everything it does is on behalf of that user.

Props

Prop Type What it does
jwtToken string (required) The connected user's JWT, sent as Authorization: Bearer ...
baseUrl string Your ByteChef instance. Defaults to https://app.bytechef.io
environment `'DEVELOPMENT' \ 'STAGING' \
{% raw %}suggestions {title, label, action}[] Starter chips. action is the message that gets sent
systemPrompt string Your house rules, applied to every turn
onWorkflowReady (workflowUuid: string) => void Called once, after the first turn
className string Extra classes for the container

The component fills its parent's height, so give the parent one (the sample uses min-h-0 flex-1 inside an h-screen column).

It's source, not a package

Unlike useConnectDialog or EmbeddedWorkflowBuilder, the chat isn't an npm export. It lives in the sample app under front-end/src/components/embedded-workflow-chat/, and you copy the folder:

embedded-workflow-chat/
├── index.ts
├── EmbeddedWorkflowChat.tsx           # the public component
├── EmbeddedCopilotRuntimeProvider.tsx # AG-UI agent and event handling
├── workflow-chat-thread.tsx           # messages, composer, chips
├── dataComponents.tsx                 # interactive cards
├── store.ts                           # zustand transcript store
├── api.ts, constants.ts               # skeleton workflow, endpoints
├── chat-config-context.tsx            # JWT, base URL, environment for cards
├── EmbeddedChatBoundary.tsx           # error boundary
└── assistant-ui/                      # markdown, tool card, reasoning renderers

That's on purpose. A chat is the most visible thing in your product, so it should look like your product, not ours. It's built on assistant-ui primitives with Tailwind, so restyling is ordinary React work.

Dependencies: @ag-ui/client, @assistant-ui/react, @assistant-ui/react-markdown, zustand, lucide-react, tailwind-merge, and @bytechef/embedded for the ConnectDialog.

On mount: a skeleton workflow

The agent doesn't generate a workflow and hand it back at the end. It edits a real one, in place, during the conversation. So before the user types anything, the component creates it:

export const SKELETON_WORKFLOW_DEFINITION = JSON.stringify({
    description: '',
    inputs: [],
    label: 'New Workflow',
    tasks: [],
    triggers: [],
});

const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/api/embedded/v1/automation/workflows`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${jwtToken}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-Environment': environment,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({definition: SKELETON_WORKFLOW_DEFINITION}),
});

const workflowUuid = (await response.text()).replace(/"/g, '').trim();

The draft lands in the connected user's personal project for that environment. While the request runs, the component shows Starting.... If it fails (expired JWT, wrong baseUrl), the error shows in red instead of the chat.

That UUID anchors the whole conversation. A ref latch makes sure only one skeleton is created, even under React StrictMode.

One thing to plan for: every visit creates a draft, even if the user leaves without typing. More on that in Hardening.

On each turn: AG-UI streaming

When the user sends a message, the component posts the conversation with an AG-UI HttpAgent:

const agent = new HttpAgent({
    agentId: 'workflow_editor',
    url: `${baseUrl}/api/embedded/v1/automation/workflows/${workflowUuid}/copilot/chat`,
    headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${jwtToken}`,
        'X-Environment': environment,
    },
    threadId: conversationId,
});

agent.setState(
    trimmedSystemPrompt
        ? {additionalSystemPrompt: trimmedSystemPrompt, mode: 'BUILD', workflowUuid}
        : {mode: 'BUILD', workflowUuid}
);

await agent.runAgent({runId: randomUUID()}, subscriber);

Of that state, the server uses only the system prompt. It rebuilds everything else itself (see What the agent can and can't do).

The response is a text/event-stream. The subscriber turns events into UI:

AG-UI event What the user sees
TEXT_MESSAGE_START, _CONTENT, _END An assistant message, streamed token by token
TOOL_CALL_START, _ARGS, _END A tool card (e.g. searchTasks, updateWorkflow) with its arguments filling in live
TOOL_CALL_RESULT The card gets its result and a success or error icon. Interactive results add a card below
RUN_ERROR A red callout, e.g. The copilot run failed. Reference: 3f2b...
RUN_FINISHED The turn is over. The first time, onWorkflowReady fires

The server closes the open text message whenever the agent calls a tool, so a turn reads in the order it happened: "Let me find the right trigger", the tool cards, then the next message.

Errors users can act on

When a run fails for a reason the user can do something about, ByteChef sends a fixed sentence plus the run ID:

Cause What the user reads
No AI provider for the environment No AI provider is set up for this environment, so the chat can't answer.
Rate limiting The AI provider is rate limiting requests right now. Try again in a minute.
Overloaded The AI provider is overloaded right now. Try again in a minute.
Bad API key The AI provider rejected its API key. Ask an administrator to check it.
Context too long This conversation is too long for the AI model. Start a new chat.

Anything else reads The copilot run failed. Reference: .... The text is fixed, never the exception message, because exceptions can name tables, internal hosts or keys. The full cause goes to the server log under the same run ID. When a user reports a failure, ask for the reference and grep for it.

The controls users expect

  • Stop aborts the run.
  • Edit on a user message rewinds and reruns from there.
  • Refresh regenerates the last assistant message.
  • Copy and Export as Markdown under assistant messages.

Edit and Refresh rewind the agent too, not just the screen. The agent's memory lives on the server, keyed to the user, the workflow and the conversation. Before each run, ByteChef trims that memory back to the last user message both sides agree on. The server only ever removes messages this way. It never takes the client's word for what was said.

Interactive cards: when the agent needs the user

A text-only agent would ask "which channel? please type its exact name" and hope. Instead, some tools return a small JSON envelope with a kind, and the chat renders a card for it:

{
    "kind": "create-connection",
    "componentName": "slack",
    "componentLabel": "Slack"
}

Here the agent looked up the trigger, then stopped to ask which time zone "9am" means:

The sample maps four kinds in dataComponents.tsx:

kind Card On click
ask-user-question Multiple-choice questions, one at a time (Question 1 of 3, Previous) Answers go back as "User picked: ..."
select-property-option Searchable list of valid values, like Slack channels or Google Sheets The label and real value go back, and the agent writes the value into the workflow
select-connection Searchable list of the user's connections for an app Name and ID go back. With one connection, it's picked automatically
create-connection A Connect Slack button Opens the ConnectDialog. When done, the card shows Connected Slack

Three of them do nothing on the server except hand the question to the browser. The property picker does a bit more: it fetches the property's real options first, using a connection the user may use.

When the agent shows a card, its turn ends. It doesn't guess and carry on. It waits. The user's pick goes back as an ordinary message, which starts the next turn with exactly what the agent asked for. Answered cards collapse to a short summary with a green check (Picked: #standup), so the thread stays readable.

Connect, right in the conversation

This is where the whole series comes together. The user asks for a Slack reminder but hasn't connected Slack. The agent calls createConnection, and the chat shows Connect Slack. Clicking it:

  1. Calls GET /api/embedded/v1/integrations with the user's JWT and finds the integration whose componentName is slack.
  2. Opens the ConnectDialog from part one via useConnectDialog.
  3. Watches the dialog's portal and marks the card connected when it closes.

The user goes through the same OAuth or API-key flow as on your Integrations page, without leaving the chat. Then the agent picks the new connection with select-connection.

createConnection is signaling only. The agent never sees or stores credentials, and the tool call creates nothing on the server. If the app isn't one of your integrations, the card says No integration is available for Slack.

Your house rules: the system prompt

The user decides what the workflow does. You decide how it's built.

Good system prompts encode decisions your users shouldn't have to make:

  • Always notify the team in Slack, never by email.
  • Keep workflows under five steps.
  • Use the Europe/Berlin time zone for every schedule unless the user names another.
  • Never delete CRM records; update a status field instead.

How ByteChef treats it:

  • Read every turn. Change it mid-conversation and the next turn picks it up.
  • Trimmed and capped at 4,000 characters on the server.
  • Can't override the core rules. It's appended under a heading that marks it as additional instructions from the integrating application, applied only where it doesn't conflict with the build rules, the workflow-definition contract or safety constraints. Your rules steer the agent. They can't turn it into something else.

In the sample it's a text box so you can experiment. In production it belongs in your code: build it from your product's conventions and what you know about the user (plan, time zone, approved apps).

What the agent can and can't do

The chat is a public surface. It runs with the connected user's JWT, and the browser controls the request body. So the copilot endpoint trusts none of the AG-UI state it receives. On every turn, ByteChef:

  • Checks the workflow belongs to the user. The {workflowUuid} must be in the user's own project for that environment.
  • Rebuilds the agent state from scratch. It keeps only the additional system prompt, then sets the rest itself: BUILD mode, non-autonomous, the verified workflow ID, the user's project, the environment from X-Environment (PRODUCTION if missing), and a conversation key built from tenant, user and workflow. Editing the request can't switch modes, change workspaces or read someone else's conversation.
  • Keeps the agent inside the user's project. Every workflow tool checks ownership, and project-level changes are off limits. Talk the model into opening another workflow and the tool refuses: "This chat can only work with the projects and workflows of its own project."
  • Allows only the user's own connections. The agent sees only connections the user owns or was given, and every connection ID it binds or queries is checked against that list: "This chat can only use connections its user is entitled to use." No borrowing another customer's Slack.
  • Limits the agent to your catalog. It can use only enabled integrations for that environment, plus connection-free components (schedules, conditions, loops, data mappers). Anything else doesn't show up in search, can't be looked up, and is rejected anywhere in a saved workflow, including inside conditions, loops and AI agent nodes.

That last one is easy to miss. If you offer HubSpot and Slack but not Salesforce, a user asking for "Salesforce to Airtable" gets a conversation about what's possible, not a workflow that could never run:

Handing off the result

The chat produces a real ByteChef workflow, so it's not a dead end. After the first turn, the component calls onWorkflowReady with the UUID from mount:

<EmbeddedWorkflowChat
    // ...
    onWorkflowReady={setWorkflowUuid}
/>

{workflowUuid && (
    <Button onClick={() => router.push(`/automations/${workflowUuid}`)}>Open workflow</Button>
)}

When the build is done, the agent says what it made:

Two things about the callback:

  • It fires once, after the first turn, not when the workflow is "done". That turn may have built three steps or only asked a question. The UUID never changes and the agent keeps updating the same workflow, so opening it later always shows the latest. Read it as "there's a workflow worth linking to now".
  • It's a callback, so you decide what it means. A button, a live preview next to the chat, a Save button, an analytics event.

/automations/{uuid} renders the same EmbeddedWorkflowBuilder from part eight. Chat to draft, canvas to polish.

From draft to running

A chat-built workflow is a draft. Nothing runs until it's published and enabled, which is the right default for something an AI just wrote. The calls from part seven take it live:

// Freeze the current definition as the first version
await fetchWithAuth(`/api/embedded/v1/automation/workflows/${workflowUuid}/publish`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
    body: JSON.stringify({description: 'Created from chat'}),
});

// Turn it on (DELETE to turn it off)
await fetchWithAuth(`/api/embedded/v1/automation/workflows/${workflowUuid}/enable`, {method: 'POST'});

In the sample the user does this by hand: Publish in the editor, then the toggle on the Automations list. A more guided product could add an Activate button under the chat.

Prerequisites

Your ByteChef instance needs:

  1. The copilot enabled: bytechef.ai.copilot.enabled=true. Without it, /copilot/chat doesn't exist.
  2. An AI provider configured. The run's environment decides which settings apply.
  3. Integrations enabled for the environment. With none, the agent can still build schedules and logic, but nothing that talks to an app.

Embedded workflows and the copilot endpoint are Enterprise Edition features.

Hardening the demo for production

The sample is intentionally small. Before you ship:

  • Clean up abandoned drafts. Create the skeleton on the first message, or DELETE /automation/workflows/{uuid} untouched drafts when the user leaves.
  • Write suggestions for building. The sample's chips come from ByteChef's editor copilot, where a workflow already exists. On an empty one, try "Post a Slack message every Monday at 9:00" or "When a HubSpot deal closes, create a Jira ticket".
  • Own the system prompt. Generate it in code. Don't hand end users a text box.
  • Pass environment explicitly. It defaults to PRODUCTION, and a JWT signed for another environment is rejected when the skeleton is created.
  • Decide what "ready" means. For a stricter signal (a trigger exists, no open issues), fetch the workflow when the callback fires and check.
  • Support multi-select questions. The sample renders every question as single-select and ignores the multiSelect flag for now.
  • Fix the error boundary. EmbeddedChatBoundary hides a harmless assistant-ui unmount error, but renders nothing for any other crash. Replace that null with a fallback and report the error.
  • Add a New chat button. Remount the component (change its key) to get a fresh skeleton, a new conversation and an empty agent memory.
  • Surface the error reference. Make the run ID easy to copy and teach support to search logs for it.

Who owns what

  • You own where the chat appears, how it looks (it's your source code), the suggestions, the system prompt, which integrations exist, and what happens when a workflow is ready.
  • ByteChef owns the agent and its tools, the AG-UI stream, component search and property lookups, validation, per-user storage, the security boundary around every turn, the ConnectDialog and credentials, and the engine that runs the result.

Your code is one component, one callback and a button. Behind it is an agent that knows every action in your catalog and can turn "remind my team about standup every weekday" into a scheduled Slack workflow on the user's own account.

The series so far

  1. Connect your users' apps (the JWT and ConnectDialog everything rests on)
  2. Act on connected apps directly with the ComponentKit
  3. Chat with an AI assistant that uses the ComponentKit's tools
  4. Trigger workflows from your product's events
  5. Call a workflow like a synchronous API
  6. Agent over MCP: the same tools, discovered through an open protocol
  7. Author workflows in a builder you designed
  8. Start from a template you curated
  9. Talk a workflow into existence (this part)

Parts three and nine both put an AI chat in your product, but they do opposite jobs. The ComponentKit chat acts on the user's apps right now: it sends the email, creates the ticket. New from Chat builds something that acts later, on its own, every time the trigger fires. One is an assistant. The other is an automation author.

Try it: enable the copilot and an AI provider in ByteChef, run the embedded sample app, and open Automations → New from Chat. Ask for a weekday Slack reminder and watch it build.

Originally published on the ByteChef blog. ByteChef is an open-source workflow automation and AI agent platform: github.com/bytechefhq/bytechef.

title: Website Error Logs: A Practical Way to Investigate Without Exposing Secrets
description:
An error page tells you that something failed. Logs can help explain why, but only when they are collected with enough context and handled responsibly.

Record a reproducible symptom

Note the affected URL, approximate time, action taken, and response status. Include the timezone. A request identifier is useful when the application provides one.

Avoid immediately changing several settings. Preserve the relevant evidence so later observations can be compared with the original failure.

Match the right logs

A reverse proxy, web server, application runtime, and database may each record a different part of the same request. Start at the public symptom and follow the request through the relevant layers.

An HTTP 500 status alone does not identify a database failure. Read the associated error and investigate the dependency it actually names.

Protect sensitive information

Do not publish raw logs in a forum without review. Remove access tokens, cookies, passwords, personal information, and confidential query data. Keep the surrounding error context needed for diagnosis.

In production, avoid displaying detailed stack traces to visitors. Use controlled logging and restricted access instead.

Make one justified change

Form a hypothesis, apply a targeted correction, and repeat the failing action. Confirm both the visible behavior and the relevant log output.

Document what changed and how it can be reversed. If the cause remains unclear, share a sanitized excerpt and the reproduction steps with the responsible support team.

Retain logs deliberately

Set retention and rotation appropriate to the service. Logs that fill the disk can become an availability problem themselves.

Published for Alif Host. Good troubleshooting improves observability without making private data public.

Example: a form fails only after submission

A visitor can load a contact page but receives an error after submitting it. The initial page request and the form submission are separate operations. Checking only the page response will miss the failing action.

Record the time, route, request method, and visible error. Use a safe test message without confidential customer data. Then inspect the application error associated with that submission and any downstream email or queue service it uses.

A recent change is a useful lead, not proof of the cause. Compare the failure with deployment records and verify the actual dependency named by the evidence. Avoid disabling security controls merely because they are a convenient explanation.

Make the evidence easy to correlate

Use consistent timestamps and record the timezone. If the system generates request identifiers, keep the identifier with the support report. That helps connect a proxy entry with the corresponding application event.

Different layers can use different status codes or wording. An upstream timeout at the proxy can correspond to a slow database call deeper in the application. Follow the chain rather than assuming the first message tells the entire story.

Do not enable unrestricted debug output on a public production page. If additional logging is necessary, limit its scope, protect access, and turn it off when the investigation ends.

Share a sanitized support packet

Include a short description of expected behavior, actual behavior, reproduction steps, time, recent relevant changes, and a carefully reviewed log excerpt. Remove secrets and unrelated personal information.

Keep enough context to make the message meaningful. Replacing every field with asterisks can hide the component or error type support needs. Preserve safe structural details while redacting sensitive values.

Store detailed evidence in an appropriate controlled location. A public comment thread is not a substitute for the provider's secure support channel.

Common questions

Should every warning be treated as the outage cause?

No. Some warnings are incidental. Correlate the event with the failing request and test a specific hypothesis.

Can a restart fix the problem?

It may temporarily change the symptom, but it can also remove useful evidence. Preserve relevant logs and investigate why the failure occurred.

What should happen after recovery?

Record the established cause, correction, verification, and any monitoring or documentation improvements. If the cause remains uncertain, state that clearly rather than inventing certainty.

Related Alif Host resources

For the platform specific steps, see How to Fix the 500 Internal Server Error in WordPress.

To review the relevant service scope and plan details, visit Alif Host WordPress hosting. Confirm the features you need before choosing a plan.

title: Make a Flaky Test Fail on Demand Before You Hand It to Your Coding Agent
description:
• Book: Ship It — the pragmatic startup tech stack
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Say the checkout test fails one CI run in fifty. You paste the link into your coding agent and type "fix the flaky checkout test." It runs the test and gets green. It wraps an assertion in a retry, runs the test again, gets green again, and reports the task done.

Two green runs are exactly what the broken version produces most of the time. The agent proved nothing, and you wouldn't have either with the same two runs.

The Claude Code best-practices page names the problem: "Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, 'looks done' is the only signal available." A flaky test is the worst case for "looks done".

So before an agent touches it, you make the test fail on demand and write down the command and seed that did it. Then you hand over a check that has to pass hundreds of times in a row, whether the suite runs on Go, pytest, Vitest or Jest.

Which kind of flake you have

A reproducible failure is a command plus a seed that fails within minutes, not a CI link that fails sometimes. To get one, you need to know which kind of flake you have.

The first kind fails in any order: a data race, a timeout that's too tight, a clock, shared state inside one test. You find it with volume, running the same test hundreds of times. The second kind depends on what ran before it: a global left dirty, a database row from another test, a cache. You find it by running many different orders, each from a seed you can replay.


One failure in hundreds of runs: you have to go looking for it.

Go: -count repeats the order, -shuffle picks it

go test can do both. -count n will "Run each test, benchmark, and fuzz seed n times". -shuffle on randomises the order of tests, and "the seed will be reported for reproducibility". -race turns on the race detector. Start with volume on the one test:

go test ./internal/cart -run '^TestCheckoutTotals$' \
  -count=500 -race -failfast -timeout=30m

-failfast stops at the first failure, so the output stays short. The -timeout matters too. The default is 10 minutes, and the race detector docs say that for a typical program "memory usage may increase by 5-10x and execution time by 2-20x". If 500 race-checked runs go past 10 minutes, the test binary panics, and that reads like a failure that has nothing to do with your bug.

If the test alone never fails, it probably depends on another test, and now you need orders. Here Go's source has a detail that changes the command. In testing.go, M.Run shuffles the top-level tests once, prints the seed with fmt.Println("-test.shuffle", n), and only then enters the -count loop. So -count=500 -shuffle=on is one random order, run 500 times. It is not 500 orders.

For many orders, run many test binaries, each with a seed you pick:

log=$(mktemp)
for i in $(seq 1 50); do
  seed=$RANDOM
  if ! go test ./internal/cart -count=10 \
      -shuffle="$seed" -race >"$log" 2>&1; then
    echo "FAILED: -shuffle=$seed"
    tail -n 40 "$log"
    break
  fi
done

When it fails, go test ./internal/cart -count=10 -shuffle=<seed> -race replays the same order. Go also caches passing results when you name packages, so an agent that runs go test ./internal/cart twice with no change in between can get a cached pass on the second run instead of a real one. The docs call -count=1 "the idiomatic way to disable test caching explicitly". Put a -count on every command you hand over.

pytest: pytest-repeat for volume, pytest-randomly for order

Python needs two plugins. pytest-repeat adds --count, and its README notes you can pair it with -x "to force the test runner to stop at the first failure." pytest-randomly shuffles the test order, prints the seed at the start (its example is Using --randomly-seed=1553614239), and resets Python's global random seed "before each test setup, run, and teardown". So one seed replays both the order and any data drawn from random.

python -m pip install pytest-repeat pytest-randomly
pytest "tests/test_cart.py::test_checkout_totals" \
  --count=500 -x -q

Same catch as Go: one pytest run is one seed, so those 500 copies all run in one shuffled order. For many orders, put this in the loop from the Go section and pass the seed yourself:

pytest tests/ -x -q --randomly-seed="$seed"

--randomly-seed=last reruns the previous seed, as long as pytest's cache provider plugin is enabled.

Then turn the plugin off and give each test the same 50 runs in file order: pytest tests/ -x -q -p no:randomly --count=50. Don't add -p no:randomly to the loop itself, because with the plugin off pytest no longer knows --randomly-seed and every pass exits with a usage error. If it fails shuffled but never in file order, the test depends on another test's leftovers. If it fails either way, look at time, threads, the network or the database.

Vitest and Jest: pick the seed yourself

Vitest 5 can do both from the command line. --repeats <number> will "Repeat every test a specific number of times regardless of the result", and --sequence.shuffle with --sequence.seed gives you a seeded order. The sequence config docs say the seed defaults to Date.now(), and they don't say Vitest prints it. So pass your own, and you always know which one failed:

npx vitest run src/cart --repeats=50 --bail=1
npx vitest run --sequence.shuffle \
  --sequence.seed="$seed" --bail=1

Jest 30 has --randomize, which shuffles tests within a file and displays the seed, and only works with the default jest-circus runner. --seed=<num> sets the seed, which Jest also uses to shuffle the order test suites run in, and it must sit between -2147483648 and 2147483647. In bash, $RANDOM stays between 0 and 32767, so it fits. For Jest, the loop does the repeating:

npx jest src/cart --randomize --seed="$seed" --bail

The check script and the brief

Put the loop in one script that exits 0 only when every run passes. You run it, the agent runs it, and nobody has to judge whether "it looked fine".

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/flaky-check.sh
# Exit 0 only if RUNS seeded runs all pass.
set -u
RUNS=${RUNS:-50}

run_once() {
  go test ./internal/cart -count=10 -shuffle="$1" -race
}

log=$(mktemp)
for i in $(seq 1 "$RUNS"); do
  seed=$RANDOM
  if ! run_once "$seed" >"$log" 2>&1; then
    echo "run $i/$RUNS FAILED, seed $seed"
    tail -n 40 "$log"
    exit 1
  fi
done
echo "$RUNS/$RUNS runs passed"

Fifty runs of -count=10 is 500 executions of every test in the package, across 50 orders. For pytest, the body of run_once becomes pytest tests/ -x -q --count=10 --randomly-seed="$1". For Vitest or Jest, use the commands above with "$1" as the seed.

How many runs is enough depends on the failure rate, so measure that first with the loop, counting single executions of the test. If it failed 1 execution in 50 and the "fix" changed nothing, the chance that all 500 executions in the script (50 runs × -count=10) still pass is 0.98^500, about 1 in 24,000. At 1 in 1,000, a test that is still broken passes those same 500 executions 61% of the time (0.999^500). Rare flakes need bigger numbers. An order-dependent flake has no steady per-execution rate, because it fails only in some orders, so for those raise RUNS to try more orders.

Now the brief. 8812 below stands for the seed your loop printed:

Fix the flaky test TestCheckoutTotals in ./internal/cart.

Reproduce first. This fails within a few minutes:
  go test ./internal/cart -count=10 -shuffle=8812 -race
Run it before you change anything and confirm it fails.

Failure:
  <paste the failing assertion and any race report>

Rules:
- Find the cause. No retries, sleeps, t.Skip or
  longer timeouts.
- Don't change the test's assertions or
  scripts/flaky-check.sh.

Done when both pass:
  go test ./internal/cart -count=10 -shuffle=8812 -race
  scripts/flaky-check.sh

Reproducing first is the Claude Code docs' own advice for bugs: "write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it." If you want the gate enforced inside Claude Code itself, the same docs describe a Stop hook that "runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes".

Running the loop next to the agent in Hermes

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Everything above works in any terminal. Hermes puts the agent, your repro loop and the verdict in one window.

Press ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) and paste the brief as the task. The agent, Claude Code or Codex for example, starts in a real terminal with your own sign-in, on its own hermes/<name> branch and in its own worktree, with the brief as its first prompt.


The ⌘N New task sheet: the task, chips for Claude Code, the orders-api project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, model and effort, and the "Hermes will run" preview of the claude command.

Then split the pane, right or down, and open a plain shell beside the agent. git worktree list shows the task's folder. cd there and run the seeded repro yourself, once before the agent's first edit and once after its last. One caution: your loop and the agent's own test runs compete for CPU, and that changes timing. A race can show up more often or less often while both are busy, so run the final check when the agent is idle.


Two sessions in split panes: Codex on orders-types and Claude Code on orders-api, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with the sessions sidebar (status, context use, cost, branch) on the left.

Your script stays the definition of done, so run it in that pane before you land. Then open the Review Desk (⌘G, or Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows and Linux) and read the change turn by turn. You're checking that the rules held: no new sleep, no retry, no loosened assertion. For the check script, plain git answers in one line:

git diff main...hermes/<name> -- scripts/

Empty output means the agent left your check alone.

If this was useful

A flaky test is a CI problem before it's an agent problem: once a pipeline goes red at random, people learn to hit rerun, and the real failures hide in the noise. Ship It covers everything between localhost and production for a small team, from hosting, payments and auth to CI/CD and monitoring, which is where a check like this one ends up living.

Hermes IDE is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and isn't affiliated with Anthropic, OpenAI or Nous Research. If it saves you a rerun, a star on GitHub helps other developers find it.

title: How to search the Internet Archive from Python and get direct download links
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit.

The Internet Archive holds millions of free books, films, recordings and software, and it has public APIs. But turning "every Mark Twain audiobook, with MP3 links" into a clean table still means juggling two APIs, Solr query syntax, a 10,000-result paging limit and metadata that's sometimes a string and sometimes a list.

I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I wrapped all of that in an actor called Internet Archive Scraper. This post shows how to call it from Python and Node, what the data looks like, and one small project: a public-domain reading list with direct EPUB links.

How it works, briefly

The actor calls archive.org's own search API (advancedsearch.php) and, if you ask for files, the metadata API (/metadata/{identifier}). No browser, no login. Plain-word searches are limited to title, subjects and creator by default, because archive.org's full-text search is very noisy: when I sorted "moby dick" by downloads over full text, the top hit was a 1948 film noir. With the default, the top hits are actual Moby-Dick editions.

Python example 

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/internet-archive-scraper").call(run_input={
    "queries": ["apollo 11"],
    "mediaTypes": ["movies"],
    "sortBy": "downloads",
    "maxResults": 20,
})

for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item["title"], item["year"], item["downloads"], item["url"])

Node example 

npm install apify-client

import { ApifyClient } from "apify-client";

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: "<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>" });

const run = await client.actor("rel8ble/internet-archive-scraper").call({
  queries: ['creator:"Mark Twain"'],
  mediaTypes: ["audio"],
  sortBy: "downloads",
  maxResults: 50,
  includeFiles: true,
  fileFormats: ["mp3"],
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const it of items) console.log(it.title, it.filesCount, "MP3 files");

What comes back

One item per archive.org item. This is a real row from a test run ("moby dick", sorted by downloads, file formats limited to PDF/EPUB), trimmed:

{
  "query": "moby dick",
  "identifier": "mobydickorwhale01melvuoft",
  "title": "Moby-Dick; or, The whale",
  "mediaType": "texts",
  "creator": "Melville, Herman, 1819-1891",
  "year": 1922,
  "publisher": "London Constable",
  "collections": ["robarts", "toronto", "university_of_toronto"],
  "downloads": 135030,
  "downloadsLastWeek": 678,
  "pageCount": 398,
  "url": "https://archive.org/details/mobydickorwhale01melvuoft",
  "filesCount": 2,
  "files": [
    {
      "name": "mobydickorwhale01melvuoft.epub",
      "format": "EPUB",
      "sizeBytes": 1433807,
      "url": "https://archive.org/download/mobydickorwhale01melvuoft/mobydickorwhale01melvuoft.epub"
    }
  ]
}

You also get subjects, language, license URL, rights, favorites, ratings, runtime for video and audio, ISBNs and a thumbnail URL. One detail I cared about: archive.org lists users' personal favourite lists as fav-<username> collections, and the actor strips those out.

Use case: a public-domain text corpus with direct links

The goal: the 50 most downloaded English books in archive.org's Project Gutenberg collection, with a direct link to each plain-text file, saved as CSV. That's a small, clean corpus for NLP experiments or a reading list.

import csv
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/internet-archive-scraper").call(run_input={
    "collection": "gutenberg",
    "mediaTypes": ["texts"],
    "language": "eng",
    "sortBy": "downloads",
    "maxResults": 50,
    "includeFiles": True,
    "fileFormats": ["txt"],
})

with open("gutenberg-top50.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["title", "creator", "downloads", "txt_url", "bytes"])
    for it in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
        txt = (it.get("files") or [{}])[0]
        w.writerow([it["title"], it.get("creator"), it["downloads"], txt.get("url", ""), txt.get("sizeBytes", "")])

In my test run, the top result was Amusements in Mathematics by Henry Ernest Dudeney (2,767,810 downloads), with its text at https://archive.org/download/amusementsinmath16713gut/16713-8.txt.

queries is empty here on purpose: when you only set filters, the actor lists the whole collection. Swap gutenberg for prelinger (old films) or oldtimeradio and change the format filter to h.264 or mp3. One thing I learned: Gutenberg items on archive.org carry text and HTML files, not EPUBs, and most have no year, so don't add a year filter to this one.

What it costs

Pricing is $1.00 per 1,000 results, and one result is one archive.org item, with or without its file list.

  • The corpus above: 50 items = $0.05
  • A 1,000-item catalog of a collection = $1.00
  • Apify's free plan gives $5 of monthly credit, which covers about 5,000 items

Limits

These come straight from my testing:

  • 10,000 results per query. archive.org's search API won't page further. Split by year or media type.
  • File lists add one request per item. Audiobooks can have hundreds of files, so a 300-item run with files took about 5 minutes locally at concurrency 5. The default is now 10.
  • Metadata is whatever the uploader entered. In a 300-item test, 78% had a date, 44% a license URL and 26% a publisher.
  • It doesn't download files, it gives you the URLs. Check each item's license before reusing anything.
  • One oddity I hit while building it: archive.org's newer "scrape" API cached responses and returned the same results for different queries. The actor uses the older, stable search API instead.

If something breaks or a field is wrong, the Issues tab on the actor page reaches me directly.

Internet Archive Scraper on Apify

This article was drafted with AI and published by me.

title: Building a Personal Portfolio Website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
description:
Building a Personal Portfolio Website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

A personal portfolio website is a useful way for developers to present their skills, projects, and learning journey in one place. It allows recruiters and other developers to understand what you can build and which technologies you have used. As part of my Full Stack Web App Development Internship at Valentius Kryptix, I worked on creating a responsive portfolio website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Creating the Website Structure with HTML

HTML provides the foundation of the website. I organized the content into important sections, including Home, About, Skills, Projects, and Contact. I also used semantic HTML elements to make the structure more meaningful and easier to maintain.

The Projects section highlights two of my development projects:AgriVista – Smart Crop Recommendation System and a School Management System. These projects demonstrate my experience with different technologies and help visitors understand my practical development work.

Designing a Responsive Interface with CSS

CSS was used to create the website's visual appearance, including its layout, colors, spacing, typography, and project cards. I focused on keeping the interface clean and professional so that visitors could find information easily.

Responsive design was another important part of the development process. By using flexible layouts and media queries, I worked to make the website usable across desktop, tablet, and mobile screen sizes. A responsive portfolio is important because visitors may access it from different devices.

Adding Interactivity with JavaScript

JavaScript adds interactive behavior to the website. I implemented a mobile navigation menu that can be opened and closed, making navigation easier on smaller screens.

This feature also helped me understand how JavaScript can work with HTML elements and CSS classes to update the user interface in response to user actions.

Key Lessons from the Project

Building this portfolio helped me practice several important frontend development concepts:

  • Structuring web pages with semantic HTML.
  • Creating layouts and responsive designs with CSS.
  • Adding interactive features using JavaScript.
  • Organizing project information clearly.
  • Using Git and GitHub to maintain and share project code.

The project also showed me that a portfolio is not just about appearance. Clear project descriptions, working links, readable content, and a consistent design are equally important.

Conclusion

Creating a personal portfolio website was a valuable step in my web development journey. It gave me an opportunity to combine HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into a practical project while presenting my work professionally. I plan to continue improving the website by adding more projects, screenshots, and detailed project documentation.
