title: Is this test flaky, or is it a real bug?
description:
A flaky test failed and then passed on a retry without anyone fixing anything, and a real bug fails for a reason no retry changes. Nexus Studio, by Verdict System LLC, tells them apart by recording every retry: FLAKY for a failure that a retry passed, BREACHED for a real finding, and BREACHED_FLAKY for a failure that is itself inconsistent. A retry never turns a defect into a green run.

By the Nexus Studio team, Verdict System LLC. October 7, 2026.

What is a flaky test?

A flaky test is one whose attempts disagree: it fails once and passes on another try, with the code and the test unchanged. In Nexus Studio the word has one meaning. FLAKY is a test that failed, then passed on a retry, with nothing healed. Something is unstable, in the application or in the test, and nothing was fixed.

A hard failure that happens on every attempt is not flaky, even when the self-healing step tried and failed to repair a selector. An earlier version of the engine filed that case as FLAKY. Teams read FLAKY as "the test is bad" and move on, so a broken application shipped as noise. The engine no longer does that.

Do retries hide real bugs?

They can, and the reason is the number of states. With pass and fail only, a retry that passes turns a red run green, and an intermittent defect in the application becomes invisible. That is one of the most expensive kinds of bug to find. When red can also mean a blinked network or a dead browser, the team learns to rerun reds instead of reading them, and the suite loses trust.

Nexus Studio keeps the retry visible. A test that failed and then passed is not SECURE. It exits 0 in CI, so it does not break the build, but it shows in the report and in History as FLAKY, a pass with a reservation. See how the 14 verdicts are decided for the full order of checks.

What is the difference between FLAKY, BREACHED and BREACHED_FLAKY?

  • FLAKY: failed, then a retry passed it, and nothing was repaired. Read the failed attempt's raw-data.json, then the History trend. It exits 0.

  • BREACHED: the test failed on a single attempt, and no environment or harness pattern explains the error. An assertion failed. This is the bug report, and it exits 1.

  • BREACHED_FLAKY: the test failed on its last attempt after an earlier retry, and no environment or harness pattern explains it. The failure itself is inconsistent. Compare the attempts before you file a bug. It exits 1.

Two neighbors keep the picture honest. AUTO_RECOVER is a pass where self-healing replaced a selector, so the author's locator is dead and the test is not clean. A first attempt that failed only on time and then passed on retry is SECURE, because that shows latency, not instability.

Before a failure can be BREACHED or BREACHED_FLAKY, the classifier rules out the other explanations in a fixed order: a harness error, a crash, a block, an unreachable host and a timeout. Only a failure that none of those explains is a finding. That is why a timeout or a CAPTCHA does not arrive as a bug report.

How are retries counted?

The engine reads the attempt number of the run. A passing test with a retry number above zero is FLAKY, unless a selector was healed, in which case it is AUTO_RECOVER. A failing or timed-out test with a retry number above zero, and no environment explanation, is BREACHED_FLAKY. A clean pass needs retry zero and no healed selector.

FLAKY means the attempts disagreed, and nothing else. A failure on a single attempt, with zero retries, is never labeled flaky. Each History row also records retry_attempt and attempts, so the count stays with the run.

What evidence does each verdict leave?

  • FLAKY: screenshot.png, metadata.json and raw-data.json. The folder keeps the failed attempt's raw-data.json, so a retry that hid the failure still leaves its log. This follows the setting Keep evidence of a FLAKY / AUTO_RECOVER pass, which is on by default.

  • BREACHED_FLAKY: report.md, metadata.json, raw-data.json and screenshot.png, and its failure video is kept by default.

  • BREACHED: the same files, with the video kept by default.

The verdict is in the evidence folder's name, for example a name that ends in [BREACHED]. The Evidence page follows one failed test through every file.

How does History spot a test that flips?

History keeps one row per run for each test and browser or device, with the verdict, the retry attempt and the error signature. From those rows it shows trends by session, day or week: Regressed, Recovered, Still broken and Slower. A test that goes green, red and green again shows up there instead of disappearing into reruns.

The risk ranking, in the Evidence Locker and in Patrol, orders tests by how often they flip, break or cost time. It also shows a predicted risk from a logistic regression over your history, with an EWMA fallback when data is thin. Nothing is called flaky below five runs, because one or two runs cannot show a pattern.

Limits

  • Retries are what separate FLAKY from SECURE and BREACHED_FLAKY from BREACHED. With retries off, an intermittent failure is a BREACHED.

  • FLAKY says the attempts disagreed. It does not say why. Finding the cause in the application or in the test is still work for a person.

  • The classification reads error text, so a custom assertion message that contains words such as 403 or Forbidden can read as an environment problem. Open metadata.json when a verdict surprises you.

  • Below five runs, History and the risk ranking call nothing flaky.

Where to go next

The Evidence page shows every file a failed test leaves, and How Nexus Studio decides 14 test verdicts explains the order of the checks. The 30-day trial runs the same engine on your own tests.

title: CSP Nonces and Hashes: Building a Strict Frontend Policy
description:
• Why strict CSP matters
  • How to choose between CSP nonces and CSP hashes
  • How to implement nonce-based CSP in the browser
  • How to use hash-based CSP to tame static assets and builds
  • How to monitor, report, and migrate to a strict policy
  • Practical application: checklist and code recipes

A strict Content Security Policy built around cryptographic nonces or hashes can make script injection impractical at the browser edge — but the wrong policy or a half-baked rollout will either break functionality or push teams to weaken protections. The goal isn't a policy that "blocks everything"; it's a policy that blocks the bad stuff while remaining predictable and automatable.

The site is full of small failures: analytics stops firing after a CSP rollout, A/B tests vanish, vendors complain their widgets were blocked, and someone reinstates unsafe-inline because "we had to ship." Those symptoms come from policies that aren't strict, are overly permissive, or were rolled out without an inventory and testing window — and that is why most CSP rollouts stagnate or regress into a false sense of security. CSP can protect you from script injection, but it only works when designed to match how your app actually loads and runs code.

Why strict CSP matters

A strict Content Security Policy (one that uses nonces or hashes instead of long allowlists) changes the attack model: the browser becomes the final gatekeeper that refuses to execute scripts unless they present a valid cryptographic token. That reduces the practical impact of reflected and stored XSS and raises the bar for exploitation.

Important: CSP is defense in depth. It reduces risk and attack surface but does not replace input validation, output encoding, or secure server-side logic. Use CSP to mitigate exploits, not as a substitute for fixing vulnerabilities.

Why a strict approach beats host-based allowlists

  • Allowlist policies grow brittle and large (they often require enumerating dozens of domains to integrate common vendors).
  • Strict CSPs based on nonce- or sha256-… don't rely on hostnames, so attackers can't bypass them by injecting a script tag pointing at an allowed host.
  • Use tools like CSP Evaluator and Lighthouse to verify policies and avoid subtle bypasses.

Quick comparison

Characteristic Allowlist (host-based) Strict (nonces/hashes)
Resistance to injected inline script Low High
Operational complexity High (maintain hosts) Medium (inject nonces or compute hashes)
Works well with dynamic scripts Can be OK Nonce-based: best. Hash-based: not ideal for large dynamic blobs.
Third-party support Needs explicit hosts strict-dynamic + nonce makes third-party easier to support.

How to choose between CSP nonces and CSP hashes

Start here: choose the mechanism that maps cleanly to how your UI is built.

  • Nonce-based CSP (nonce-based CSP)

    • Best when pages are rendered server-side or you can inject a per-response token into templates.
    • Nonces are generated per HTTP response and added both to the Content-Security-Policy header and to the nonce attribute on <script> and <style> tags. This makes dynamic inline bootstraps and SSR flows straightforward.
    • Use strict-dynamic to allow scripts that your trusted (nonced) bootstrap loads; that’s very helpful for third-party loaders and many libraries. Be mindful of older browser fallbacks when you rely on strict-dynamic.

  • Hash-based CSP (CSP hashes)

    • Best for static inline scripts or build-time-known fragments. Generate a sha256- (or sha384-/sha512-) for the exact contents and place it in the script-src list. Changes to the script change the hash — include this in your build pipeline.
    • Hashes are ideal when you host static HTML and still need one small inline bootstrap or when you want to avoid templating to inject nonces.

Trade-offs at a glance

  • Generate nonces per response to avoid replay or guessing; use a secure RNG (see Node example later).
  • Recalculating hashes is operational work, but it’s stable for static files and enabling SRI workflows.
  • strict-dynamic paired with nonces/hashes reduces allowlist sprawl but changes how legacy fallbacks behave; test older browsers if you must support them.

How to implement nonce-based CSP in the browser

The core pattern:

  1. Generate a cryptographically secure, unpredictable nonce for each HTTP response. Use a secure RNG and base64 or base64url encode the result.
  2. Add the nonce to the Content-Security-Policy header as 'nonce-<value>'. Use the same nonce value in the nonce attribute of inline <script>/<style> elements that you trust.
  3. Prefer strict-dynamic in modern browsers to reduce host-based allowlists; provide a safe fallback if you must support older clients.

A minimal Node/Express pattern

// server.js (Express)
const express = require('express');
const crypto = require('crypto');

const app = express();

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  // 16 bytes -> 24 base64 chars; you can choose a larger size
  const nonce = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('base64');
  // Store for templates
  res.locals.nonce = nonce;

  // Example strict header (adjust directives to your needs)
  res.setHeader(
    'Content-Security-Policy',
    `default-src 'none'; script-src 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'`
  );

  next();
});

// In your templating engine (EJS example)
// <script nonce="<%= nonce %>">window.__BOOTSTRAP__ = {...}</script>
// <script nonce="<%= nonce %>" src="/static/main.js" defer></script>

app.listen(3000);

Notes and gotchas

  • Generate a unique nonce per response; don't reuse across users or over time. Use crypto.randomBytes (Node) or a secure RNG on your platform.
  • Do not implement a dumb middleware that re-writes every script tag to add a nonce after the fact; templating is safer. If an attacker can inject HTML into the template stage, they will get the nonce alongside their payload. OWASP warns against naive noncing middleware.
  • Avoid inline event handlers (e.g., onclick="...") — they are incompatible with strict policies unless you use unsafe-hashes, which weakens protection. Prefer addEventListener.
  • Keep the CSP header on the server (not in meta tags) for reporting and Report-Only flexibility. Meta tags can't receive report-only reports and have limitations.

Trusted Types and DOM sinks

  • Use the require-trusted-types-for 'script' and trusted-types directives to enforce that only sanitized, policy-created values reach DOM XSS sinks like innerHTML. This makes DOM-based XSS much easier to audit and reduce. Treat Trusted Types as the next step after you have nonces/hashes in place.

How to use hash-based CSP to tame static assets and builds

When you have static inline blocks (for example, a small inline bootstrap that sets up window.__BOOTSTRAP__), compute the base64 SHA hash and add it to script-src. This is perfect for CDNs, static hosting, or very small inlines that rarely change.

Generating a hash (examples)

  • OpenSSL (shell): 
# produce a base64-encoded SHA-256 digest of the exact script contents
echo -n 'console.log("bootstrap");' | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 -A
# result:  <base64-hash>
# CSP entry: script-src 'sha256-<base64-hash>'
  • Node example (build step): 
// compute-hash.js
const fs = require('fs');
const crypto = require('crypto');
const script = fs.readFileSync('./static/inline-bootstrap.js', 'utf8');
const hash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(script, 'utf8').digest('base64');
console.log(`sha256-${hash}`);

Add to your CSP header or inject into HTML meta in build-time pipelines. For long-term maintainability:

  • Integrate the hash generation into your build (Webpack, Rollup, or a small Node script).
  • For external scripts prefer Subresource Integrity (SRI) plus crossorigin="anonymous"; SRI protects supply-chain tampering, while CSP prevents execution of injected inline payloads.
  • Remember: any change (even whitespace) alters the hash. Use CI to regenerate hashes automatically and fail builds when mismatches occur.

Browser compatibility nuance

  • CSP Level 3 expanded some hash semantics and added features like strict-dynamic; older browsers may behave differently with certain hash-and-external-script combos. Test the set of browsers you must support and consider a fallback (e.g., https: in the policy) for legacy clients.

How to monitor, report, and migrate to a strict policy

A staged rollout avoids breaking production users and gives you data to make the policy precise.

Reporting primitives

  • Use Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only to collect violation reports without blocking. Browsers send reports that you can consume and analyze.
  • Prefer the modern Reporting API: declare endpoints with the Reporting-Endpoints header and reference them with report-to inside your CSP. report-uri remains present in the wild but is deprecated in favor of report-to/Reporting API.

Example headers (server-side):

Reporting-Endpoints: csp-endpoint="https://reports.example.com/csp"
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: default-src 'self'; script-src 'nonce-<token>'; report-to csp-endpoint

Collect and triage

  • Accept application/reports+json on your report endpoint and store minimal metadata (URL, violated directive, blocked URI, user-agent, timestamp). Avoid logging user-supplied content verbatim to your logs.
  • Run two parallel stages: a broad report-only rollout to collect noise, then a tightened policy in enforcement mode for a subset of routes before full enforcement. Web.dev's guidance maps this process.

Use automated tools in your pipeline

  • Run policies through CSP Evaluator to spot common bypass patterns before deploying.
  • Use Lighthouse in CI to catch missing or weak CSPs on entry pages.

A conservative migration timeline (example)

  1. Inventory: scan your site for inline scripts, event handlers, and third-party scripts (1–2 weeks).
  2. Create a draft strict policy (nonce or hash) and deploy in Report-Only site-wide (2–4 weeks of collection; longer for low-traffic services).
  3. Triage: sort reports by frequency and impact; fix code to stop relying on blocked patterns (replace inline handlers, add nonces to legitimate bootstraps, add hashes for static inlines).
  4. Stage enforcement on a subset of traffic or routes. Monitor.
  5. Enforce globally once violations are rare or have known mitigations. Automate hash regeneration in CI for hashed policies.

Practical application: checklist and code recipes

Practical checklist (high-signal tasks)

  • Inventory: export a list of pages with inline code, external scripts, and event handlers.
  • Decide policy style: nonce-based for SSR/dynamic apps; hash-based for static sites.
  • Implement nonce generator with a secure RNG and pass it to templates. crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('base64') is a sensible default in Node.
  • Add Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only and Reporting-Endpoints to collect violations.
  • Triage and fix top violations; remove inline handlers and move to addEventListener.
  • Convert Report-Only to Content-Security-Policy and enforce.
  • Add require-trusted-types-for 'script' and allow-listed trusted-types policies when ready to lock down DOM sinks.
  • Add SRI for critical external scripts to protect supply chain risk.
  • Automate policy checks in CI with CSP Evaluator and browser-based smoke tests (headless runs capturing console errors).

Report endpoint example (Express):

// small receiver for Reporting API / CSP reports
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

// browsers POST JSON with Content-Type: application/reports+json
app.post('/csp-report', express.json({ type: 'application/reports+json' }), (req, res) => {
  // Persist to a datastore or analytics. Avoid echoing the full report into public logs.
  console.log('CSP report received:', JSON.stringify(req.body, null, 2));
  res.status(204).end();
});

Automated hash generation (build step snippet):

// build/hash-inline.js
const fs = require('fs');
const crypto = require('crypto');

function hashFile(path) {
  const content = fs.readFileSync(path, 'utf8');
  const hash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(content, 'utf8').digest('base64');
  return `sha256-${hash}`;
}

// example usage
console.log(hashFile('./static/inline-bootstrap.js'));

Policy example (final enforcement header):

Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'none';
  script-src 'nonce-<server-generated>' 'strict-dynamic';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
  require-trusted-types-for 'script';
  trusted-types myPolicy;

Key operational rules

  • Verify your policy with CSP Evaluator before enforcement.
  • Keep the report endpoint accessible only from browsers (rate-limit and validate).
  • Don't fall back to unsafe-inline as a permanent fix. That defeats the purpose of strict CSP.

Strong finishing thought

A strict, well-instrumented CSP built from nonces and hashes turns the browser into an active defender without needlessly breaking functionality — but it requires planning: inventory, secure nonce generation, build-time automation for hashes, and a patient report-only rollout. Treat CSP as an operational feature that your CI and monitoring pipelines own; do the work once, automate it, and the policy becomes a stable, high-leverage protection for years to come.

Sources:

Content Security Policy (CSP) - MDN - Core CSP concepts, examples for nonce and hash-based strict policies and general guidance.

Mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) with a strict Content Security Policy (web.dev) - Practical rollout steps, strict-dynamic guidance, and browser-fallback recommendations.

Content Security Policy - OWASP Cheat Sheet - Operational cautions, nonce warnings, and rollout advice.

Content-Security-Policy: script-src directive - MDN - nonce, strict-dynamic, unsafe-hashes, and event-handler behavior.

Reporting API - MDN - Reporting-Endpoints, report-to, report format (application/reports+json) and collection guidance.

Content-Security-Policy: report-uri directive - MDN (Deprecated) - Notes deprecation and suggests migrating toward report-to / Reporting API.

Node.js Crypto: crypto.randomBytes() - Use secure RNG for nonces (crypto.randomBytes).

Trusted Types API - MDN - Using trusted-types and require-trusted-types-for to lock down DOM sinks.

Subresource Integrity (SRI) - MDN - Generating integrity hashes and using SRI for external resources; examples for openssl command usage.

google/csp-evaluator (GitHub) - Tooling to validate CSP strength and detect common bypasses.

Ensure CSP is effective against XSS attacks (Lighthouse docs) - Integration points for audits and CI checks.

title: How to Preview a Weave Router Benchmark Run Before Launch
description:
A benchmark launch can fan out across tasks, attempts, and model routes. Before spending model or sandbox time, inspect the exact plan.

Weave Router's public weave-bench CLI has a --dry-run option for that step. It resolves the benchmark manifest, builds one Harbor command per comparison arm, prints the commands and version pins, then exits before launching any Harbor jobs. In this walkthrough, the plan selects one Terminal-Bench task and two arms. It produces no benchmark result.

Install the benchmark CLI

The harness requires Python 3.12 or newer and uv. This guide is pinned to Router commit cbe7584, so the source and manifest match the behavior described here:

git clone https://github.com/weave-os/router.git
cd router
git checkout cbe758442460ca68db8f4fe9837db087c50cf1e5
cd bench
uv sync --locked --extra harbor

Cloning the repository and syncing dependencies use the network. After that setup is complete, the planning command below builds and prints a local plan; it does not call the Router or model APIs or start Harbor jobs.

Print a one-task plan

This command compares the Router's router arm with a direct GPT-5.6 Luna control, using the benchmark's pinned smoke task:

uv run --locked --extra harbor weave-bench run terminal-bench-4 \
  --arms router,luna \
  --smoke \
  --dry-run

Representative output:

# terminal-bench-4 run_id=<generated-run-id>
# tasks=1 (manifest has 66); harbor=0.22.0 (published: 0.22.0) codex=0.150.0
...
--include-task-name terminal-bench/cad-model

The CLI generates the run ID. The important details are the selected task and the pinned versions, followed by the Harbor command for each arm.

What the plan means

  • One task, not 66: --smoke selects terminal-bench/cad-model from the 66-task manifest.
  • Two arms, two Harbor jobs: router sends requests through Weave Router's /beta policy; luna calls GPT-5.6 Luna directly. This is not a same-model comparison because the Router policy chooses a model per request.
  • Two attempts per arm: the pinned configuration sets two attempts and up to 12 concurrent tasks per job. For this one-task example, a real run is configured for up to four task attempts in total. An attempt can make multiple model requests, so that number is not an API-call count or a cost estimate.
  • No credentials in the plan: dry-run output shows the names of environment variables a real job would use, not their secret values. Keep credentials in the environment; do not paste them into a report.

--smoke only limits task selection. Remove --dry-run and the CLI launches the Harbor jobs, which can make model calls and incur compute and provider costs. Review the generated commands, budget, credentials, and sandbox configuration before launching. Treat a plan as a plan, never as benchmark evidence.

Sources

  • cmd_run returns before job launch when --dry-run is set
  • Benchmark package and Python version requirement
  • Terminal-Bench task, attempt, concurrency, and version pins
  • Router and direct Luna arm definitions
  • Weave Router benchmark methodology

This walkthrough explains the public CLI at the cited commit. No benchmark was launched and no new performance or cost result is claimed.

title: How do you test code that drives an AI coding agent?
description:
I'm building a desktop app that starts the real agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI) and talks to them over their protocols. That makes tests awkward. A test that starts a real agent spends someone's usage, needs a login and gets a different answer every run.

What I do for end-to-end tests: launch the built Electron app with Playwright, with fake claude, codex and gemini commands first on PATH. The app also gets a temporary user-data folder seeded with demo data, an in-memory keychain and a fixed clock. Each run starts from the same place and ends the same way.

That covers what I need most: the chat, an access request being answered, undoing a turn, the board. A test never starts a real agent or spends anyone's usage. Each fake has a .cmd twin for Windows, because a bare script on PATH doesn't run there.

The gap is that a fake only knows what I taught it. If a real CLI changes the events it sends, the fake keeps passing and the app breaks for users.

If you wrap or drive an agent CLI from your own code, how do you test it? Fakes on PATH, recorded sessions, a cheap real model on a schedule, something else? And how do you find out when the real CLI changes under you?

This came out of building Styx, an open-source app that runs these agents side by side.

title: What is scale-to-zero and how does it change cloud cost?
description:
What is scale-to-zero?

Scale-to-zero flips the traditional cloud billing model: you pay only for the time your code is actually processing requests, not for the time a virtual machine simply exists. When traffic stops, the platform pauses the instance and your compute meter drops to zero. The next incoming request triggers a wake-up, the instance serves the request, and then it returns to a paused state after the idle timeout expires. This means idle hours generate no cost, while active hours are metered precisely to the work done.

Our internal billing data shows the impact of always-on compute. In a recent 16-day window, a customer’s total platform consumption was 1,305 credits, of which 1,096 credits,about 84 %, came from a single line: vCPU-hours on a virtual machine that never slept. The VM averaged under one vCPU of real work but ran for every hour in the period, so the per-hour meter charged for idle time as if it were doing useful work.

The math of always-on

Always-on billing has a fixed exchange with wall-clock time. A machine that never turns off accrues 730 metered hours in a 31-day month, one for each hour whether it served a million requests or zero. At our published rates, $0.036 per vCPU-hour and $0.004 per GB-hour of memory, the always-on baseline looks like this:

Machine Idle cost per month
1 vCPU, 1 GB about $29
2 vCPU, 2 GB about $58
4 vCPU, 8 GB about $141

That is the cost of existence before the machine does any work. In the example above, the customer’s database stored only a few megabytes and object storage held less than a gigabyte, so the non-compute portion of the bill was roughly 210 credits. The compute line was five times larger, and most of those hours contained no traffic at all. This is not a Scalix-specific trap; it is the outcome of two decades of cloud habits where the default is to pick a size, boot it, and leave it running.

Scale-to-zero: bill while serving, not while existing

With scale-to-zero the meter only runs while the instance is actively serving. When the request stream stops, the platform parks the instance and the compute cost drops to exactly zero. When the next request arrives, the instance wakes, serves the request, and then parks again after the idle timeout. Between requests you pay nothing.

On Scalix this model appears in three places:

  • Functions - billed per invocation and scale to zero between calls. Nothing runs, nothing bills, until a request arrives.
  • Run services - autoscale based on traffic; setting the minimum instance count to zero lets a service park when idle and wake on request.
  • ScalixNova shared Postgres - suspends to zero when unused, so you only pay for storage and the brief compute bursts needed to serve queries.

Wake latency

The trade-off is latency on the first request after an idle period. Our production benchmarks measured a parked service waking to serve TCP in roughly 200 ms median, and a full first request through the TLS edge taking about 600 ms median. For APIs, dashboards, and internal tools this delay is imperceptible. For sub-ten-millisecond p99 paths you would keep the workload warm with an always-on instance or a higher minimum count.

When to keep an always-on VM

Keep an always-on machine when:

  • Traffic is steady around the clock.
  • You rely on persistent connections such as WebSockets or long-running database sessions.
  • The workload is stateful and latency-sensitive to the point that even a few hundred milliseconds of wake-up time hurts your SLO.

A simple audit is to compare your billed compute hours to your request volume. Hours without requests are the portion you are renting for nothing; those are the hours scale-to-zero would eliminate.

Which Scalix products support scale-to-zero?

  • Functions - per-invocation billing, automatic scale-to-zero.
  • Run services - autoscale with min-instance-count set to zero.
  • ScalixNova Postgres - suspends to zero when unused, waking on the first query.

If you want to see scale-to-zero in action, try deploying a function from our docs or start a Run service with a zero minimum. The free tier provides a starting line for experimentation, and you can move to a paid plan as your usage grows.

Read the functions quickstart to deploy your first scale-to-zero endpoint today.

title: What is a neocloud? A practical definition for modern AI workloads
description:
What is a neocloud?

A neocloud is a cloud platform engineered from the ground up to serve AI and data-centric workloads while keeping data within the customer’s jurisdiction. It bundles native AI services, serverless compute, and sovereign data hosting into a single, cohesive experience. This eliminates the need to stitch together separate AI, database, and storage providers, and it removes the hidden cost of always-on virtual machines that dominate traditional cloud bills. In practice, a neocloud lets you deploy an inference service, a stateless API, and a database that all stay in the same region, all while paying only for the compute that actually processes requests.

The core ingredients of a neocloud

  1. AI-native services - The platform exposes high-performance inference endpoints, model training pipelines, and data-science tooling that are tightly integrated with the underlying compute fabric. These services are built to scale automatically and to run without the overhead of provisioning and managing separate GPU clusters.

  2. Serverless compute - Functions, event-driven microservices, and container-based workloads are executed in a scale-to-zero model. The billing model is per-invocation or per-second of active execution, so idle time costs nothing. This directly addresses the cost leak that occurs when a traditional VM runs 24/7 but receives traffic only a fraction of the time.

  3. Sovereign data hosting - All data, whether it is a relational database, object store, or cache, is stored within the legal jurisdiction of the customer. The platform provides audit logs, encryption at rest, and access controls as platform primitives. Data never leaves the country unless the customer explicitly opts in.

  4. Unified management - A single dashboard, API, and CLI let you provision, monitor, and scale all components. There is no need to juggle multiple cloud accounts or to write custom scripts to move data between services.

How it compares to the old model

In a traditional cloud, you might spin up a VM for your inference service, a separate managed database, and a storage bucket for training data. Each of those resources lives in its own namespace, has its own billing, and requires separate access controls. The bill is a patchwork of compute, storage, and network charges, and the customer often ends up paying for idle compute that never processes a request. In a neocloud, the same workloads are co-located, share a single billing stream, and the platform automatically scales resources to zero when idle. This eliminates the hidden cost of a VM that runs 24/7 but serves traffic only 10% of the time.

Real-world metrics

  • In 2025, 73 % of our customers used the neocloud for at least one AI inference workload (Scalix internal survey).
  • The average first-request latency for serverless functions in the neocloud is 120 ms, compared to 650 ms for a traditional VM that must wake from sleep (Scalix performance benchmark).
  • The platform’s autoscaling engine can spin up a new inference instance in under 200 ms, ensuring that traffic spikes are handled without manual intervention (Scalix real-time monitoring data).

A deeper dive into the components

AI-native inference

The inference service is built on a custom runtime that can run models in TensorFlow, PyTorch, or ONNX format. It exposes a REST API that automatically scales based on request volume. Because the runtime runs on the same hardware that hosts the database, the network latency between model and data is minimal. This is a key advantage over traditional clouds where inference services often sit in a separate region from the data store.

Serverless compute

Functions in the neocloud are billed per second of active execution, with a minimum of one second. The platform keeps a pool of pre-warmed containers that can be reused for subsequent invocations, reducing cold-start latency. When traffic drops to zero, the containers are automatically de-allocated, and the cost for that period is zero. This is the same scale-to-zero model that powers our managed database, which suspends to zero when idle.

Sovereign data hosting

All data is stored in an object store that is physically located in the customer’s chosen country. The platform enforces encryption at rest using keys that the customer controls. Audit logs capture every read, write, or delete operation, and the logs themselves are stored in a separate, tamper-evident bucket. This architecture gives regulated buyers the substrate their regime asks for, without bolting on a separate compliance service.

Unified management

The dashboard lets you view all resources in one pane, see real-time usage, and set up alerts. The CLI and API expose the same set of commands, so you can automate provisioning with scripts or Terraform. The platform also supports role-based access control, so you can grant developers read-only access to the inference API while restricting database credentials.

How to get started

If you’re curious about how a neocloud can simplify your AI workflows, start by exploring our documentation. The docs walk you through creating a new project, deploying a model, and connecting it to a sovereign database. Once you’re comfortable, you can sign up for the free tier to experiment with a small inference service and see the cost savings for yourself.

Explore the documentation → /docs/neocloud-intro

Final thoughts

A neocloud is more than a marketing buzzword. It is a concrete architecture that brings together the most common pain points of AI-centric development: high-performance inference, cost-efficient compute, and data sovereignty. By building these capabilities into a single platform, we remove the friction of juggling multiple services and let you focus on building the next generation of intelligent applications. We look forward to seeing what you build.

title: Model Stock Counts So Variances Explain Themselves: CountSession, BlindCountLine, Recount and StockAdjustment
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In many inventory systems, a stock count is modelled as one operation: "set quantity on hand to X." It is simple, and it destroys information. The difference between what the system expected and what was counted disappears into an overwrite, along with the reason it happened.

For food and agro manufacturers that is a real problem. A variance usually means something upstream was not recorded: a goods receipt, a production issue, a dispatch. If your data model cannot hold the variance, its recount and its cause, your users will keep "fixing" the same gap every month.

This piece is for developers modelling inventory in manufacturing ERPs. The factory-floor checklist behind it is on the FactoraERP blog (canonical link above).

The domain objects you need

  • StockBalance: quantity by item_id, lot_id, location_id and status (released | hold | quarantine | rework | returns | scrap). Lot and status are part of the key, not optional attributes.
  • CountSession: id, type (full | cycle), cutoff_at, scope (locations or items), state.
  • BlindCountLine (table count_line): session_id, item, lot, location, status observed on the floor, counted_qty, uom, counted_by, counted_at.
  • Recount: a second BlindCountLine for the same key, by a different user.
  • Variance: expected_qty (snapshot at cut-off), final_counted_qty, difference, value, reason_code.
  • StockAdjustment: an immutable movement posted from an approved variance, with approved_by and approved_at.

Invariants worth enforcing

  1. Snapshot at cut-off. When a CountSession moves to counting, store expected_qty per key from the ledger as of cutoff_at. Movements posted after cut-off must not change the expected figure.
  2. Blind counting. The count API and UI never return expected_qty while the session is in counting. Expose it only in reconciling.
  3. Separation of duties. recount.counted_by != original.counted_by, and adjustment.approved_by must not be any user who counted that key.
  4. Thresholds trigger recounts. If abs(difference) > threshold(item) (quantity or value), the variance cannot be approved until a recount exists.
  5. No adjustment without a reason. reason_code is required (timing, production_issue, intake, dispatch, expiry_damage, uom_error, unexplained). Flag unexplained for escalation.
  6. Adjustments are movements, not overwrites. Post a ledger entry dated at the count's cut-off. Never UPDATE stock_balance SET qty = counted.
  7. Status mismatch is a finding. If the observed floor status differs from the system status (a "released" pallet in the quarantine bay), record it even when quantities match.

A minimal state machine 

CountSession: draft -> counting -> reconciling -> approved -> posted
                         |             |
                         +--(recount)--+
  • draft -> counting: freeze scope, snapshot expected quantities.
  • counting -> reconciling: all lines counted; variances calculated.
  • reconciling -> approved: every variance above threshold has a recount and a reason; approver passes the role and limit checks.
  • approved -> posted: write StockAdjustment movements in one transaction.

Schema sketch 

create table count_line (
  id bigserial primary key,
  session_id bigint not null references count_session(id),
  item_id bigint not null, lot_id bigint, location_id bigint not null,
  observed_status text not null,
  counted_qty numeric(14,3) not null, uom text not null,
  counted_by bigint not null, counted_at timestamptz not null,
  is_recount boolean not null default false
);

create table variance (
  session_id bigint not null, item_id bigint not null,
  lot_id bigint, location_id bigint not null,
  expected_qty numeric(14,3) not null,
  final_qty numeric(14,3) not null,
  value numeric(14,2) not null,
  reason_code text,
  approved_by bigint, approved_at timestamptz
);

Reporting that pays off

Once variances persist with reason codes, the useful report is trivial: variance value by item and reason across sessions. An item that shows production_issue week after week points to a recording gap on the line, not to a counting problem.

Records

In Kenya, section 23 of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015 sets a general five-year retention period for documents required under a tax law (with exceptions). If count sheets and approved adjustments are part of your users' record set, design for retention and audit trails rather than deletes.

The full operations checklist, with FAQ, is here: Stock Count Reconciliation Checklist.

title: Page Cache and Object Cache in WordPress: Different Jobs, Different Tests
description:
A page cache and an object cache can both reduce work, but they store different things. Treating them as interchangeable makes troubleshooting harder.

What page caching does

Page caching stores a generated response so the server can reuse it for eligible requests. It can reduce repeated application execution for public pages.

Eligibility matters. Logged in pages, shopping carts, checkout screens, and personalized responses need careful exclusions. Accidentally caching private output is a correctness and privacy problem, even when a benchmark looks faster.

What object caching does

Object caching stores reusable application data. A persistent object cache can retain selected data between requests when the application and infrastructure support it.

It does not automatically replace page caching or repair inefficient queries. Cache invalidation, memory limits, and connection overhead can affect the result.

Test them separately

Begin with a repeatable baseline. Record the requested page, user state, response time, cache status, and server resource use. Compare cold requests with repeated requests rather than mixing both into one unexplained average.

Enable one change at a time. Verify that updates become visible and that session specific information stays private. For stores, verify product prices, cart contents, and stock behavior.

Diagnose before adding another layer

A slow external API, an oversized image, and an expensive database query require different fixes. More caching is not a universal answer.

Document how to clear each cache and who owns it. A CDN cache, server page cache, plugin cache, and browser cache can all influence the final result.

Published for Alif Host. Confirm supported cache integrations with your hosting provider before enabling them.

A practical comparison for a small online store

Imagine a store with a public catalogue, customer accounts, and checkout. The public product description may be a good candidate for page caching, while a cart response contains information specific to the current shopper. Serving the same cart response to several shoppers would be incorrect regardless of its speed.

Object caching has a different opportunity. The application may repeatedly request shared configuration or product data. Reusing suitable cached objects can reduce repeated work, but the application still needs correct invalidation when a price or stock value changes.

For this example, define separate tests for an anonymous catalogue visit, a logged in account page, an empty cart, and a cart containing products. Record which cache should apply to each case. The expected behavior is a testable specification, not just a performance target.

Build a measurement sheet

Record the page address, request type, authentication state, cache state, response time, response status, and relevant resource measurements. Repeat under comparable conditions. A request served after another test warmed the cache should not be compared with a cold request without explaining the difference.

Also record correctness checks. Change a product description and confirm that the intended version appears. Sign in as two test users and ensure that account information does not leak between sessions. Empty and refill a cart to verify the right state at each step.

Do not use real customer accounts for experiments when safe test accounts will do. Keep load tests within the hosting provider's rules and the application's operational capacity.

Have a rollback plan

Before changing cache settings, export or document the previous configuration. Know how to disable the integration and clear the relevant cache. If a separate object cache service is introduced, confirm what happens when the connection fails.

Monitor memory use, errors, and latency after rollout. A cache with poor hit rates or frequent evictions may add complexity without providing useful benefit. Investigate the access pattern before increasing capacity automatically.

Common questions

Does Redis replace every other cache?

No. Redis can support several application patterns, but the integration determines its role. A persistent object cache and a CDN response cache solve different problems.

Should every page be cached?

No. Personalization, authentication, and transaction state affect eligibility. Use the application's supported cache rules and test the resulting behavior.

What matters more than the headline score?

A correct response delivered consistently to the intended user. Measure both performance and correctness, then retain a documented configuration that the team can maintain.

Related Alif Host resources

For the platform specific steps, see How to Configure LiteSpeed Cache and Redis Object Caching for WordPress.

To review the relevant service scope and plan details, visit Alif Host WordPress hosting. Confirm the features you need before choosing a plan.

title: Your Dashboard Says "Live" — Prove It With Freshness Watermarks
description:
I once shipped a monitoring page that said LIVE in confident green letters. It stayed green for eleven days while the ingest job behind it had been dead for nine of them. The label was a CSS class. It had never once looked at the data.

That was the week I stopped treating freshness as a display feature and started treating it as a data property — something each row carries, something every query can be tested against, something that fails loudly. This post is the pattern I use now: freshness watermarks.

The label is a claim; the row is the evidence

A dashboard badge claims "the view you're seeing is current." The only evidence for that claim lives in the data itself: when was this record last observed? If rows don't carry that answer, every freshness claim downstream is theater — CSS, not evidence.

So step one is embarrassingly simple: every record gets an as_of timestamp, and it means last time the source confirmed this, not last time my pipeline touched the file. A re-ingest of a two-week-old snapshot must not launder the timestamp. If your ETL rewrites as_of = now() on replay, it is manufacturing freshness out of thin air, and it will lie at exactly the worst moment.

Watermarks: freshness as a queryable object

Once rows carry as_of, freshness becomes computable per feed:

watermark(feed) = max(as_of) over rows in feed
lag(feed)      = now() - watermark(feed)

Two feeds can both be "today's data" and mean opposite things: a channel that updates hourly and a watermark from 09:00 is fine at 10:00; a quarterly registry with the same watermark is screaming. Which gives the honest alarm rule — lag is only meaningful against expected cadence:

alarm(feed) = lag(feed) > k × expected_interval(feed)

with k around 3 for feeds you rely on. The cadence table is the artifact everyone skips and nobody regrets skipping loudly: write down, per source, how often updates should arrive. You can estimate it from history (median inter-arrival over 30 days) on day one; the discipline is reviewing the estimates when the alarms lie.

The four failure modes watermarks catch

  1. Silent death. Job dies; badge stays green. With watermarks, lag crosses the threshold and the page turns amber-red in the header, not in a log line nobody reads. The UI shows data age per feed — a number like "3m" or "9d", never the word "live."
  2. Partial death. One shard, one region, one channel of twelve stops. Aggregate row counts wobble inside normal noise; per-feed watermarks expose it the same day. (My volume-band alarm catches "how much," the watermark catches "who." They are not redundant — I run both.)
  3. Replay laundering. Backfills that rewrite timestamps and make nine-day-old facts look fresh. The defense is two timestamps: observed_at (source's last confirmation) and ingested_at (when my pipe saw bytes). Any query that claims freshness reads observed_at; audits diff the two columns and flag rows where ingestion is younger than observation by a suspicious margin.
  4. Consumer-side staleness. The reader-side mirror of my own sin: downstream caches, CDN pages, exported files. If you publish data products, the artifact should ship its watermark in the artifact — a header line, a manifest field. My OSINT dumps do this (each bundle opens with its collection window and per-channel as_of table) for the boring reason: a data product without a freshness manifest is a rumor with good formatting.

Ship the age, not the adjective

The cheapest version of this, deployable in an afternoon to anything you run:

  • one as_of per row (source-confirmed, never replay-laundered),
  • one watermark + expected-cadence alarm per feed,
  • one visible data-age number on every view and every exported artifact,
  • and the word "live" banned from interfaces until it can be computed.

Green text is an aesthetic. A watermark is a property. Only one of them fails safe — and it's the one your readers can audit.

Part of a series on building trustworthy data pipelines from public sources. Previous: From 1,271 Raw Messages to Three CSV Files — the dedup layer that sits downstream of everything described here.

Every figure in my shop bundles carries a freshness stamp like this one: free Telegram OSINT sample (pay what you want). The ingest-death story behind the watermark rule: “No New Posts Today” Is the Most Dangerous Line.

title: Edge Config is now Global Config
description:
Edge Config is now Global Config. This rename better reflects that it is a globally replicated data store with ~1ms reads in every region, built for the configuration that applications read at runtime, such as feature flags, redirects, and experimentation settings.

Global Config stores can now hold up to 1 MB on every plan, and Pro and Enterprise teams can create unlimited stores with more writes per day. The rename also ships with a new server-side SDK, @vercel/global-config, and a new environment variable.

What changed

  • Name: Global Config is the new name for Edge Config. The store itself is unchanged.

  • Package: @vercel/global-config replaces @vercel/edge-config as a drop-in replacement.

  • Environment variable: Connecting a Global Config store to a project creates a GLOBAL_CONFIG environment variable instead of EDGE_CONFIG.

  • Limits: Raised on every plan. Pricing is unchanged.

What you need to do

  • Existing projects: no action required. Deployments, connected stores, and the EDGE_CONFIG environment variable continue to work.

  • Upgrading proactively is safe. The new SDK reads GLOBAL_CONFIG by default and falls back to EDGE_CONFIG, so it works with stores connected before and after the rename. You can switch packages today without touching your stores.

  • Creating stores and pushing new config values work without upgrading. Neither depends on which SDK version your project uses.

  • Upgrade before connecting new stores to a project. Connecting a store now creates a GLOBAL_CONFIG environment variable, and the legacy SDK only reads EDGE_CONFIG by default. A project still on @vercel/edge-config cannot read a newly connected store.

To upgrade, install the new package and update imports:

New limits

Limit

Hobby

Pro

Enterprise

Stores

1 (unchanged)

Unlimited (was 3)

Unlimited (was 10)

Writes

250/month (unchanged)

100/hour (was 480/day)

100/hour (was 480/day)

Store size

1 MB (was 8 KB)

1 MB (was 64 KB)

1 MB (was 512 KB)

Pricing is unchanged at $3 per 1,000,000 reads and $1 per 100 writes.

See the Global Config migration guide for custom setups and the full list of changes.

title: Model saved places as decisions, not just pins
description:
A collection of saved places is often treated as a map problem. The harder product problem may be choosing between those places when a real situation arrives.

“Where can we get coffee near the station before the train?” includes location, purpose, and a time constraint. A saved pin without any context answers only one part of that question.

Keep place data and personal context separate

For a first design, I would use two conceptual records. The place record holds its name, location, and source. The save record holds who saved it, their note, and their intended use.

That separation matters because several people can save the same café for different reasons. One wants a working spot; another wants somewhere to meet a friend. Neither note needs to become a universal claim about the venue.

Let uncertain details remain uncertain

Personal notes such as “looked quiet in the video” should remain visibly personal. They should not turn into a verified amenity like “quiet workspace.” Likewise, an old save is not proof of current opening hours.

Show the source and provide a way to recheck details when someone is making a plan. A tool can preserve an idea without pretending every detail is current.

Design the result card around the decision

A compact card could display the place name, the user's reason for saving it, and its source. Filters might reflect practical questions: city, intended activity, or a person associated with the plan. Start with filters users actually ask for rather than an elaborate taxonomy.

Evaluate with a scenario

Give someone a collection of ten saved places and a specific plan: a short visit, a coffee meeting, or a weekend walk. Watch what information they need to choose confidently.

The design goal is to move from “I remember saving somewhere” to an informed next step. That connection between a save and its purpose is a recurring Némos theme.

title: Enterprise Managed Users is now generally available
description:
Enterprise Managed Users (EMU) gives organizations full control over the Vercel accounts tied to their verified domains. It makes the organization's identity provider the single source of truth for authentication and account lifecycle, so accounts on company domains are governed centrally rather than owned by individuals.

Now generally available

  • IdP-enforced sign-in: Managed users sign in through SAML SSO only. All other login methods, including email OTP, GitHub, Google, and GitLab, no longer work for managed accounts.

  • SCIM provisioning & lifecycle: Directory Sync creates, updates, and deprovisions managed users automatically, keeping accounts in sync with your IdP.

  • Owned by your organization: Profile settings are managed through your IdP rather than by the individual.

  • Self-serve enablement: Turn EMU on for a verified domain in Team Settings under Security & Privacy, and extend it across multiple eligible teams in a single step.

Requires an Enterprise plan, enforced SAML SSO, active Directory Sync, and at least one verified domain.

In Beta, available on request

  • Hobby team transition: Members with an existing personal account on a newly managed domain are guided to add a personal email (keeping their hobby projects) or delete the account, then continue to their work through SSO.

  • Automatic conversion: Personal accounts with no content or activity are archived automatically, and their owners land in a new managed account at their next SSO sign-in.

To request access, contact your account team.

title: How to Call Gemini 4 Argon with the OpenAI SDK: Streaming, reasoning_effort and the Real Cost of Each Request
description:
You send Gemini 4 Argon a one-line question, get a one-word answer, and the usage block says you paid for about 70 output tokens. That is not a bug. Argon thinks before every answer, and thinking is billed as output.

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is Google's flagship reasoning model, available on the paid tier of the Gemini API since 13 October 2026, with a 1M-token context window shared by input and output and up to 65,536 output tokens per response. This tutorial calls it through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with the official openai Python package, streams long answers, sets the thinking level with reasoning_effort, and reads back exactly what each request cost.

Disclosure up front: the endpoint in the examples is apimodels.app, the API gateway I work on. The same code runs against Google's own OpenAI-compatible endpoint if you swap the base URL; I note the differences where they matter. This post was drafted with AI assistance from our docs and test notes, and every command was checked against those sources.

What you need

  • Python 3.9 or newer and the OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • curl for the first check
  • An API key, stored as an environment variable (placeholder below, never a real key in code): 
export APIMODELS_API_KEY="sk_your_key_here"
  • Base URL: https://api.apimodels.app/v1 (with Google directly, it is https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/ and a Gemini API key)

Why Argon costs more than the text you see

Argon always reasons before it answers, and Google bills those thinking tokens at the output rate. Google's pricing page says it plainly: "Output price (including thinking tokens)". Google's thinking guide lists three levels for Argon (low, medium, high), sets medium as the default, and thinking cannot be turned off.

Our own measurements show the effect. On 14 October 2026, asking Argon to reply with just "OK" used 66 thinking tokens. On 15 October, the same prompt used 105 thinking tokens at low and 302 at high. On one hard reasoning prompt, high ran for 8 to 10 minutes. So two habits matter from the first line of code: set the thinking level on purpose, and read the thinking count from every response.

Step 1: make the first call with curl

This request asks a short question at the lowest thinking level, which keeps the first test fast.

curl https://api.apimodels.app/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIMODELS_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gemini-4-argon",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence: what does a database index trade off?"}],
    "reasoning_effort": "low",
    "max_tokens": 4000
  }'

You get a standard chat-completion object. Look at usage: completion_tokens already includes thinking, and completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens tells you how much of it was thinking.

Step 2: call it from Python and read the usage

The OpenAI SDK needs only a different base_url. Using with_raw_response keeps the response headers, which carry the request ID and, for non-streaming calls on apimodels.app, the amount charged.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["APIMODELS_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.apimodels.app/v1",
    timeout=900,  # high-effort runs can take minutes
)

raw = client.chat.completions.with_raw_response.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the N+1 query problem in two sentences."}],
    reasoning_effort="low",
    max_tokens=4000,
)
resp = raw.parse()
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

u = resp.usage
thinking = getattr(u.completion_tokens_details, "reasoning_tokens", 0) or 0
print("input:", u.prompt_tokens, "| output incl. thinking:", u.completion_tokens, "| thinking:", thinking)
print("request id:", raw.headers.get("x-apimodels-request-id"))
print("charged (USD):", raw.headers.get("x-apimodels-cost"))

The last two lines are apimodels.app-specific headers; with Google directly they are absent and you calculate cost from usage yourself.

Step 3: stream long answers and keep the usage

Streaming is the safe default for Argon, because a long, high-effort answer can take minutes. Ask for usage in the final chunk with stream_options.

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a step-by-step plan to migrate a Flask app from SQLAlchemy 1.4 to 2.0."}],
    reasoning_effort="medium",
    stream=True,
    stream_options={"include_usage": True},
)

usage = None
for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.choices and chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="", flush=True)
    if chunk.usage:
        usage = chunk.usage

print("\n\nusage:", usage)

In one test on 15 October 2026, a stream of 16,599 output tokens took 144 seconds, with the first token after 8.7 seconds, about 120 tokens per second after that. On api.apimodels.app a streamed Argon response can run for up to 30 minutes; a non-streaming request is cut off at 13 minutes (limits as of 17 October 2026). Use the api.apimodels.app host for long jobs.

Step 4: pick the thinking level with reasoning_effort

reasoning_effort maps to Argon's three thinking levels. apimodels.app sends none and minimal as low (Argon cannot turn thinking off), medium as medium, and high, xhigh and max as high; any other value is dropped and the model's default (medium) applies. Google's own OpenAI-compatible endpoint maps minimal to low for Argon as well.

A practical split:

  • low: extraction, short answers, formatting, anything a user waits on
  • medium: everyday coding and analysis
  • high: hard multi-step problems, run in the background and streamed

Do not use max_tokens as your cost control. Google's docs warn that when the limit is hit during reasoning, the answer can come back truncated or empty while the thinking tokens are still billed. Lower the thinking level instead, and keep max_tokens generous. The ceiling for a normal request is 65,536; anything above that returns a 400 error.

Step 5: pass tools without the $schema key

Tool calling works through the same endpoint: in our tests on 15 October 2026, single tools, three parallel tools, streaming and multi-turn tool conversations all passed. One schema detail trips people up. Some JSON Schema generators add a top-level "$schema" key, and Gemini rejects it:

Invalid JSON payload received. Unknown name "$schema" at 'tools[0].function_declarations[0].parameters'

Strip it before you send the tool definition:

def clean_parameters(schema: dict) -> dict:
    schema = dict(schema)
    schema.pop("$schema", None)
    return schema

Verify it works: look up what the request cost

Every successful LLM response from apimodels.app carries an x-apimodels-request-id header, streaming included. Pass that ID to the records endpoint to get the settled amount.

curl https://api.apimodels.app/v1/records/<request-id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIMODELS_API_KEY"

When data.settled is true, data.credits is the final USD amount taken from your balance, and data.usage holds the token counts. A failed request always shows 0, and the lookup itself is free.

Where apimodels.app fits, and when to skip it

apimodels.app is a multi-model API gateway: one API key and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, plus native Gemini and Anthropic formats, for more than 140 image, video, audio and language models. For Argon that means more than one upstream channel with automatic failover, no charge for failed requests, and the per-request lookup above. As of 17 October 2026 Argon costs $1.10 per million input tokens and $5.50 per million output there, 55% of Google's $2 / $10 list. Google's list rises to $4 / $20 on 1 December 2026, and apimodels.app moves to $2.20 / $11.00 at 00:00 UTC that day, still 55%, with no code change. Argon supports Google's implicit caching only: explicit cache objects are not supported, and whether a repeated prefix hits is decided on Google's side and is not guaranteed. Cached tokens bill at $0.055 per million ($0.11 from 1 December), but budget as if nothing is cached. Details are on the Gemini 4 Argon model page.

Skip it if you need more than 65,536 output tokens in one answer: that is Google's long-decode mode, which needs Google's background execution API, and apimodels.app does not expose it. Skip it too if you need a contract, compliance terms or provisioned throughput directly with Google.

Common errors

  • Invalid JSON payload received. Unknown name "$schema": your tool parameters contain a $schema key. Remove it (Step 5).
  • Empty content with finish_reason: "length": thinking used up max_tokens. Raise max_tokens or lower reasoning_effort.
  • 400 when max_tokens is above 65,536: that is Google's synchronous output cap for Argon.
  • 401: the key is missing or wrong. The OpenAI-format endpoint expects Authorization: Bearer <key>.
  • Client timeout on a long answer: switch to stream=True, or raise the SDK timeout for non-streaming calls.

FAQ

Does reasoning_effort work with Gemini 4 Argon? Yes. It maps to Argon's thinking levels low, medium and high, and it changes the bill: the same prompt used 105 thinking tokens at low and 302 at high in our test. Argon cannot turn thinking off, so none behaves like low. Set it per request rather than globally, and use high only for work that runs in the background.

How do I know what a single Argon request cost? Read usage.completion_tokens (thinking included) and usage.prompt_tokens from the response. On apimodels.app, non-streaming responses also carry the charged amount in x-apimodels-cost, and GET /v1/records/{id} returns the settled amount for any request, streaming or not.

Limits of this walkthrough

  • Timings are single runs from our tests on 14 and 15 October 2026; your prompts and context sizes will differ.
  • Google's long-decode mode, search grounding and code execution are not covered.
  • Prices change on 1 December 2026. Recheck them before you plan spend.

What do you set reasoning_effort to for coding agents: one global level, or per task?

This post was written with AI assistance from apimodels.app's docs and our test notes, and reviewed before publishing. I work on apimodels.app.

title: Inside the Vercel intern experience
description:
The best way to learn is by shipping product to users in production, and that's why we don’t treat our interns as temporary guests. Every intern at Vercel is expected to operate like a core part of our engineering team from day one.

This past winter, we welcomed a small cohort of those interns to our headquarters in San Francisco. Over an intense four months, they contributed to some of our most important products: the CDN, v0, financial infrastructure, AI Gateway, and more. They shipped features used by millions, helped close the gap for enterprise deals, and in more than a few cases, left a mark that will outlast their time here.

Meet the Winter '26 intern cohort

Yash Kothari, CDN Team

University of Waterloo

What Yash shipped:

Yash's internship spanned the full CDN stack, from infrastructure to CLI to UI in the dashboard.

His first major project was Project-level routing, which is part of the new CDN tab in the Vercel dashboard. This feature lets customers update routing rules, including redirects, rewrites, and header transforms, from the dashboard, API, CLI, or SDK, without needing to redeploy their project or touch a single line of code. Yash built the underlying API endpoints (including a staging/publish workflow), the vercel routes CLI commands, and contributed AI-powered route generation. Right after launch, hundreds of teams immediately adopted it and created thousands of rules.

"One of my favorite things about my internship was that at Vercel you get a lot of autonomy and ownership," Yash said. "I hopped on calls with enterprise customers, saw my work featured on Vercel's changelog, and demoed my work in a live YouTube community session."

In the second half of his internship, Yash worked on Vercel's Firewall and Security products. He shipped the vercel firewall CLI command, enabling users and AI agents to configure custom rules, IP blocks, and firewall controls directly from the terminal. He also built an AI-powered Firewall Rule Builder that lets users describe a desired rule in natural language and generates a WAF custom rule automatically.

Kavin Valli, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kavin shipped:

Kavin worked across the full v0 platform over four months, taking on projects that ranged from user-facing features to cost efficiency for the system’s backend infrastructure.

He started by building Folders and v0 Projects end-to-end: core CRUD operations, a library page redesign, favoriting, visibility controls (private/team/public), and folder sharing. He also closed a critical gap in v0's version history by shipping the manual commit button, which ensured that manual edits in the VM editor properly created commits and blocks, which closed the loop between manual edits and v0's iteration model.

His highest-leverage work came later in the term, when he focused on VM and sandbox infrastructure. By splitting VMs into tiered pools and routing smaller projects to a cost-efficient default pool, Kavin significantly reduced memory usage and infrastructure cost for roughly 80% of sandboxes.

"I worked on v0 and got thrown into the deep end pretty quickly, especially around the v1 launch," remembered Kavin. "It was a bit chaotic at times, but that's something I actually enjoyed."

His final and most involved project was taking ownership of the v0 Slack agent. He shipped Slack preview deployments for safe testing, rebuilt the router agent with improved thread history and SAML re-auth resume, redesigned project context tracking, and built out the full PR flow including v0 labels, Slack thread links, and merged/closed state tracking. The result was an agent that went from rough around the edges to something teams can genuinely rely on.

Mingchung Xia, Financial Infrastructure Team

University of Waterloo

What Mingchung shipped:

Mingchung pushed over 250 PRs in four months and became one of the top contributors on Vercel's central control systems monorepo.

His most externally visible project was the v1/billing/charges API endpoint and the vercel usage CLI command, which let users view their usage and costs in the standardized FOCUS v1.3 FinOps format. Originally scoped as a full-internship project, Mingchung completed it early and expanded its scope into a joint launch with Vantage. The work was subsequently adopted by Meta, Notion, Porsche, and other prominent companies to analyze their Vercel spend in a modern, compliant format.

His most technically complex project was designing and building Vercel's core entitlements system, which is the infrastructure that enables granting, revoking, and provisioning entitlements across project-based monetization, add-ons, enterprise, and marketplace work streams. The system architecture incorporated strong and eventual consistency guarantees, async and synchronous derivations, transactional outboxing, write-ahead logs, plan change manifests, stale-validation sentinels, and materializations. It was rolled out to production and backfilled across all active subscriptions.

"Most companies don't give interns or even existing engineers the opportunity to touch payment systems or billing infrastructure, let alone own it end to end," explained Mingchung. "Correctness is imperative when you're working with money, and I got to experience that firsthand at Vercel."

He finished his internship by shipping Vercel Buy, a new billing service supporting frictionless purchasing for agent credits, gateway credits, v0 credits, and pro subscriptions, complete with a CLI surface.

Mingchung will be joining Vercel full-time on the Financial Infrastructure team after completing his degree.

Kevin Thomas, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kevin shipped:

Kevin's work spanned ML infrastructure, enterprise features, reliability engineering, and incident response, often simultaneously.

His most ambitious self-directed project was v0's auto model routing system: a full pipeline that automatically routes user prompts to the right model tier based on complexity. Kevin proposed the system, built the labeling pipeline, experimented with multiple classifier architectures (embedding-based MLP classifiers, TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned TinyBERT), and integrated everything into TypeScript-only functions for production deployment. By launch, the system had processed over 1.4 million v0 messages and became the default for all non-enterprise users, reducing decision fatigue and latency for a very large share of v0's user base.

"From working on on-call incidents and vulnerabilities in month one to working directly with enterprise customers in April, I've gotten to work on an unusually wide range of meaningful problems," Kevin said at the end of his internship.

In the latter half of his internship, Kevin focused on enterprise work, most notably the v0 × Snowflake integration. He built enterprise admin controls for model access, RBAC for team skill management, resolved issues in SAML and isolated tenant environments, and shipped the integration itself. This work directly unblocked enterprise customers, supported renewals, and addressed live customer issues.

Kevin also served as a primary investigator for several incidents around signup, billing, auth, and account access, staying at the center of v0's reliability work throughout his term.

Sylvie Zhang, AI Gateway Team

University of Pennsylvania

What Sylvie shipped:

Sylvie worked across the AI Gateway service, contributing to everything from database and backend logic to observability, the frontend, and documentation.

Her first project was Price Strikethrough, surfacing provider MSRP as a strikethrough price alongside Gateway pricing, making provider discounts visible to end users. It touched the full stack and gave her a complete view of the AI Gateway product from the start.

"All that sounded daunting to a student like me with little experience," Sylvie said, "but it was the best learning experience I could have asked for."

Her most impactful and technically demanding project was the AI SDK v5 → v6 endpoint migration for AI Gateway's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. As the AI provider landscape had grown significantly more complex since v5 was designed, maintaining the legacy version had become a bottleneck, especially for handling token usage granularity differences across providers. Sylvie led the migration with a disciplined approach: deep cross-provider knowledge to catch incorrect AI-generated assumptions, systematic multi-turn and cross-provider testing scripts, concurrency testing to surface race conditions, proactive customer communication, and a deliberate fallback strategy that left legacy code in place until the migration proved stable.

The result was a cleaner, more maintainable Gateway service better equipped to handle the continued evolution of AI providers and models.

Advice for future interns

We asked these interns to share their top advice for future cohorts.

Take ownership from day one

Vercel gives interns real autonomy, but that means it's on you to use it well. Don't wait to be assigned work. Take initiative, identify what needs to be done, and start shipping.

Ask questions

Every intern said the same thing: no one at Vercel makes you feel like a burden for asking. The team genuinely wants you to succeed, so use that to your advantage and ask.

Work in public

Share your PRs in team channels. Post updates. Present at Demo Days. The feedback loop is fast, and the visibility helps you iterate and build trust faster.

Talk to people outside your team

Some of the best conversations happen across team lines with engineers, designers, finance, and people in roles you've never considered. Go to the office. Grab lunch with someone new.

Give yourself time to ramp up

The codebase, the culture, and the pace can be a lot at once. Don't rush. The first few weeks are for absorbing, not sprinting. Take time to ramp well, and you will be able to run fast.

Apply to become a Vercel intern
