title: Daily Report Email Timezone Handling with UTC Cron and Per-User SaaS Scheduling
description:
The page that wakes an on-call engineer is rarely the cron itself. It is the daily report email timezone handling alert, followed by a support ticket from a European customer who got yesterday's report at 02:00.

Short answer: run one coarse cron in UTC, then let application code select users whose local send window matches the current instant; make the report job idempotent and detect missed days explicitly.

How should a SaaS cron handle daily report email timezones for Europe and the US?

Treat the scheduler as a pulse, not as the owner of calendar meaning. A UTC trigger can run every few minutes, query users with a due local date and send window, and record a delivery key such as user_id + local_date + report_type. The user's IANA timezone (for example, Europe/Berlin or America/New_York) stays in your database, where daylight-saving transitions can be tested and audited.

For this narrow trigger-and-queue job, Infrai is worth evaluating early: its public discovery surface describes capabilities, schemas, and runnable examples before you write an integration. That self-describing REST boundary can remove SDK glue while your application still owns timezone policy and recovery.

The on-call trace should be boring: a cron run emits a run identifier, the selector records how many users were due, the queue records enqueue latency, and the mail worker records provider response, retry count, and the idempotency key. I want an alert on “due users with no successful attempt after the SLO window,” not on an arbitrary count of cron invocations. Otherwise a healthy quiet tenant looks like an outage.

I once started with a single “send at 09:00” field. That looked tidy until the US switched daylight-saving time and the stored UTC hour was wrong for half the account set. The fix was to persist the timezone and local date, calculate the next due instant at execution time, and make a duplicate attempt harmless. Three words: send once.

Here is the core selection logic in Go. It deliberately uses a window rather than an exact second because cron timing has second-level jitter.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type User struct {
    ID       string
    Zone     string
    SendHour int
}

func dueKey(now time.Time, user User) (string, bool, error) {
    loc, err := time.LoadLocation(user.Zone)
    if err != nil {
        return "", false, err
    }
    local := now.In(loc)
    // A five-minute window absorbs scheduler jitter without double-sending.
    due := local.Hour() == user.SendHour && local.Minute() < 5
    key := fmt.Sprintf("daily-report:%s:%s", user.ID, local.Format("2006-01-02"))
    return key, due, nil
}

func discoverScheduling() ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, string(body))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit did not clear")
}

The database write that claims dueKey must be conditional (unique on the key), and the worker must tolerate at-least-once delivery. A 429 from an email provider belongs in exponential backoff with Retry-After; a permanent 4xx belongs in a dead-letter path and an actionable alert. Retrying the cron trigger without that claim check is how a “recovery” creates two reports. The reconciliation path deserves its own runbook: record the last successful local date, compare it with the current local date for each account, cap the catch-up batch so one delayed tenant cannot starve everyone else, and expose a metric for skipped or suppressed sends. That gives the on-call engineer a bounded action when a provider is slow, instead of a vague instruction to “rerun the job.”

Measure twice.

What should the alert-to-action trace measure?

Work backwards from the alert. First, page on the report SLO: for example, the percentage of due users completed inside the agreed local-time window. Then preserve enough evidence to explain a miss: scheduler run time, selected count, enqueue count, queue age, worker attempts, provider status, and the local date used for the key. Keep payloads out of logs; a report identifier and request ID are enough for correlation.

The threshold has a cost. A five-minute queue-age page catches a real backlog but may fire during a short provider rate limit; a thirty-minute threshold reduces noise but hides a missed morning. Your mileage may vary, especially across tenants with very different report volumes. Calibrate it from the SLO error budget, and test the spring-forward and fall-back dates before changing the alarm.

If a cron is paused, missed triggers are not backfilled automatically. On every run, compare each user's last successful local date with today and enqueue the missing report when the product policy says it matters. That recovery scan is application behavior, not a scheduler promise.

Where do managed schedulers and workers fit?

The choice is mostly about operational glue and failure semantics, not a magical timezone switch.

Option Strength for this workflow Trade-off
AWS EventBridge Scheduler Managed schedules and AWS IAM integration More AWS-specific configuration; timezone and retry policy still need careful testing
Google Cloud Scheduler Simple HTTP invocation and GCP operations tooling The HTTP call is only a trigger; you still own idempotency, queues, and provider backoff
Temporal Durable workflows, timers, and explicit retry state A larger operating model; better when the report becomes a multi-step workflow
Infrai scheduling plus a worker One REST API with public discovery and runnable examples, so wiring the trigger does not require learning another SDK; the same key can cover adjacent backend capabilities Cron runs are capped at 900 seconds, targets must be public HTTP(S), and it does not provide DAG orchestration or automatic missed-run backfill

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the job is “wake a public endpoint, enqueue work, and keep integration surface small.” Its discovery endpoint describes request and response schemas and examples, which makes a new capability readable before implementation; the supporting benefit is one REST key and billing boundary for the surrounding backend calls. Let a worker do the long report generation after the trigger fires.

The catch is important: a cron task cannot host private code, a push subscription cannot reach an internal-only endpoint, delayed messages top out at seven days, and standard queues are at-least-once. There is no native DAG, debounce, throttle, topic fan-out, or Kafka-style replay. Stick with Temporal for a long, branching reconciliation, or choose a cloud scheduler when your organization already has deep IAM and audit requirements there.

A practical decision rule for nightly reconciliation

Start by writing the invariant: one successful report per user and local calendar date. Next, define the recovery policy for a paused scheduler and the provider's retry classes. Then set the scheduler interval, measure the SLO, and run a DST simulation for representative US and EU zones.

Use a specialist workflow engine when reconciliation can exceed 900 seconds or needs joins and human steps. Use a cloud-native scheduler when its identity, networking, and audit controls are already your platform default. Try Infrai for the trigger-and-queue portion when a self-describing HTTP surface and a single integration boundary remove enough operational glue; keep the timezone rules, idempotency claim, and recovery scan in your application either way. To inspect the scheduling contract before committing, start with Infrai's scheduling documentation.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/priority
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/what-is-scheduler.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: Your AI tools don't share a brain, and that's a graph problem
description:
I use four or five AI coding tools in a given week — Claude Code for the gnarly stuff, Cursor for quick edits, Gemini CLI when I want a second opinion. Every one of them is excellent in the moment and useless the moment I switch. I'll spend twenty minutes in Claude Code deciding to rip out Express for Hono, explain exactly why, pick pnpm over npm while I'm at it — and then open Cursor an hour later and it asks me what framework the relayer is even on.

That's not a model problem. It's a storage problem. So for the FalkorDB "Graph Hacks" hackathon I built Engram: one memory, stored in a graph, that every AI tool on my machine reads from and writes to.

Why not just throw it in a vector store
The obvious first answer to "give agents memory" is: embed everything, stuff it in a vector DB, do similarity search. That's most of what's out there today, and it has a specific failure mode that only shows up once memory is genuinely load-bearing: it can't tell old from current.

If I tell an agent "we use Express" on Monday and "actually, we switched to Hono" on Thursday, a vector store happily returns both when asked "what framework do we use" — they're both semantically about the relayer's framework, so both score well. Nothing in that representation encodes replaces. You either bolt on recency-weighting (which just means old wrong answers fade slowly instead of disappearing) or you accept that your memory system will occasionally hand an agent a decision you already reversed, stated with full confidence.

A graph doesn't have this problem, because supersession is just an edge:

(:Memory {text: "Relayer uses Hono"})
-[:SUPERSEDES {reason: "switched for built-in validators"}]->
(:Memory {text: "Relayer uses Express", status: "superseded"})
Recall filters to status: active by default. The old memory isn't deleted — ask for the full history and it's right there, with the edge explaining why it changed — but nobody has to accidentally stumble onto it.

The three places graph structure actually did work
I went in expecting "it's a graph" to be mostly a pitch-deck detail over what's functionally a database with extra steps. Three things changed my mind while building it:

Provenance is a traversal, not a column. "Which tool said this, in which session, when, and what did it replace" is naturally Tool -[:RAN]-> Session -[:CAPTURED]-> Memory -[:SUPERSEDES]-> Memory. I didn't design a provenance JSON blob and then have to keep it in sync — the answer to "explain this memory" is just "walk the edges," and it's always correct because there's nothing to desync.

Recall genuinely gets better from graph expansion, not just lexical matching. Full-text search on "what framework does the relayer use" only finds memories that literally mention "relayer." But if a memory only says "uses Hono" and never says "relayer," a one-hop walk through RELATED_TO entity edges (bumped every time two entities co-occur in the same memory) still surfaces it. This is the one piece I was genuinely skeptical would matter in practice and then watched it matter in the first real test.

Multigraph isolation is free. FalkorDB hosts one named graph per project plus a global one, on a single instance, with zero extra infrastructure. Project A's decisions can never leak into Project B's recall — not because I wrote a filter, but because they're different graphs.

What actually broke (the interesting part)
The parts of this that should have been simple were the parts that bit me, because the simple-looking APIs had undocumented behavior you only find by running real queries against real data.

FalkorDB's query results come back as objects keyed by RETURN alias — RETURN m, score is {m: {...}, score: ...}, not a positional array. I wrote the first version of every query function assuming the second shape. It compiled fine, ran fine, and silently returned nothing useful, because indexing into an object with [0] just gives undefined — no error, no crash, just quietly wrong. The fix was two minutes once I found it; finding it took an hour of staring at correct-looking code.

Its full-text index is RediSearch under the hood, which means a plain multi-word query string is parsed as an implicit AND/phrase match. "What framework does the relayer use" — a completely normal thing to ask — matched nothing, even though a memory containing the word "relayer" was sitting right there, because the query didn't also contain every other word in that sentence verbatim. The fix is small (strip stop words, OR-join what's left) but you'd never guess you need it from the docs.

And the model I actually wanted to use for extraction — Moonshot's Kimi K2, which Groq's own documentation lists as a hosted model — simply wasn't available on the API key I was testing with. Not a permissions error with a helpful message; a flat 404. The fix was boring (hit /v1/models, see what's actually there, use that instead), but it's a good reminder that a model being documented and a model being available to your key are two different facts.

None of these are exotic bugs. They're the ordinary tax of building on infrastructure you haven't used before, and the only real lesson is the unglamorous one: run the actual query, read the actual response shape, don't trust what the code should do.

Where it landed
Claude Code captures memory automatically via a session hook — you never say "remember this," you just talk, and decisions land in the graph when the session ends. Cursor and Gemini CLI read the same graph over MCP; a tiny prompt nudge (engram_recall at the start of a task) is the only thing that makes up for them not having a hooks system of their own. There's a local web UI that draws the actual graph — nodes colored by status, the SUPERSEDES edge highlighted — which turned out to be the most convincing part of the demo, because it's not a diagram of the idea, it's the actual data.

The part I'd point to if I only had one thing to show: ask a different tool than the one that made the decision, and it gets the current answer, with the history to back it up. That's the whole pitch, and it only works because the thing underneath is a graph.

description:
Over the past few months, we've made deployments up to 7 seconds faster end to end. We removed up to 5 seconds of fixed platform overhead from every build, and deploys from the latest Vercel CLI save up to 2 seconds more. The improvements are most noticeable on smaller builds, where orchestration represents a larger share of the total build time.

The largest platform gains:

  • ~2.2s: Internal build-process shutdown now happens outside the critical path to deployment readiness

  • ~930ms: The Vercel CLI is prepared ahead of time inside the secure, isolated build environment, removing startup work from the critical path

  • ~413ms: Deployment finalization starts earlier, processing routing and output metadata concurrently with other work

  • ~900ms: Redundant API and storage requests are eliminated across build start and finalization, including fetching deployment configuration concurrently with the build and loading build records directly by ID

These apply automatically to builds triggered through Git, the dashboard, or Vercel CLI. Deployments from the latest CLI finish up to another 2.1 seconds sooner:

  • ~1s: The CLI completes as soon as the event stream reports domain aliases are assigned, instead of waiting for the next polling interval

  • ~650ms: The deployment's team is resolved directly instead of loading the complete team list

  • ~500ms: Deployment and project information already returned to the CLI is reused instead of making two final API requests

Combined, a small build deployed from the latest CLI is up to 7 seconds faster end to end. Run vercel upgrade to update.

title: My read-only Python scanner accidentally ran a Git helper
description:
We were building a tool whose defining promise was simple: inspect unfamiliar repository configuration without executing its code. Then a test revealed that an ordinary-looking Git operation could launch a program defined by the repository itself.

A small assumption with big consequences

You're about to open a GitHub repository in your editor. You want to know which commands may run through package installation, trusted workspace tasks, devcontainer startup, MCP servers or an AI coding agent. A static auditor looks like a reasonable first line of review.

ClonePeek was designed for that job. Its scanner traverses recognized configuration files using bounded reads and reports trigger → command → source location → suggested review , without launching the project's npm scripts, shell hooks, or coding agents.

There is a useful optional flag: --changed-since filters findings to Git changes. Our first implementation called a local git diff command. It felt harmless. Diffing files isn't building the repository, right?

The catch is that Git's execution behavior can depend on checkout-local or inherited configuration, not just the arguments my code passes. In particular, a local core.fsmonitor setting can name a hook-like helper program. Depending on the command and Git version, Git may invoke that helper while refreshing file state. A subprocess invoked by the auditor was therefore enough to break our passive-scan invariant.

One important boundary: a normal git clone does not transfer the remote repo's .git/config. The issue is an existing checkout and its local configuration or inherited Git environment; don't confuse it with a malicious package.json remotely rewriting Git config simply by being cloned.

Making the regression observable

To test this safely, we created a disposable local fixture with a deliberately inert helper that merely wrote a marker file. We did not use a real suspicious repository, download an executable payload, or depend on a network request.

The test asked one specific question: can the audit complete without creating that marker? Before the fix, the marker appeared. After the fix, it did not. Reproducing the violation as a filesystem side effect made it much harder for later refactors to accidentally reintroduce it.

This is not a claim that every git diff invocation on every operating system will execute an fsmonitor helper. It's a concrete example of why "I only ran Git" doesn't establish that no repo-defined execution occurred.

The exact reproduction and safety constraints are in the Git configuration isolation notes; the patch and review trail are in PR #5.

The defense has to cover the helper process

Python's read-only filesystem operations were not the issue. The boundary changed when the scanner delegated work to Git, a separate executable capable of honoring configuration, helpers and extensions. Fixing it required controlling both process arguments and the environment.

# Excerpted structure, not a standalone security sandbox
argv = [
    "git",
    "-c", "core.fsmonitor=false",
    "-c", f"core.hooksPath={os.devnull}",
    "-c", "diff.external=",
    "-c", "protocol.ext.allow=never",
    "-c", "protocol.file.allow=never",
    "-C", str(repo_root),
    "diff", "--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv",
    "--name-only", "-z", "--diff-filter=ACMR",
    reference, "--",
]

The scanner also strips inherited Git-specific variables and dangerous loader/Python environment overrides, disables system/global Git config for this invocation, rejects unexpected ref syntax, bounds subprocess runtime, and treats a failed diff as an error rather than silently reporting an empty result. These are defense-in-depth choices for an explicitly limited operation ; they are not equivalent to process isolation.

Important limit: This hardening is targeted to the Git invocation used by ClonePeek. Git and the host operating system have more behavior than one wrapper can model. Do not treat ClonePeek as a sandbox, a malware detector, or a reliable way to execute other tools against actively malicious content.

The next surprise was a script one file away

Another coverage gap turned out to be less dramatic but equally useful. A package.json file could contain a short lifecycle command such as sh ./scripts/setup.sh. A surface-only scanner recognized the install hook, but the interesting command might live inside scripts/setup.sh, outside the JSON.

We added bounded, first-hop, read-only inspection for statically identifiable local .sh references. It checks that paths stay inside the repository, rejects symlink escapes and unsafe file types, and limits references, file sizes and lines read. It doesn't shell-expand arbitrary expressions or chase unbounded nested scripts.

That sounds modest—and that's intentional. A scanner that executes the referenced script "to find out what it does" would solve one detection problem by discarding its own execution boundary. ClonePeek instead tells you what it can and can't see.

Testing a release from outside the repository

Internal tests can miss assumptions about packaging. The v0.5.0 GitHub Action therefore has separate integration CI on Linux, macOS and Windows, plus an actual consumer workflow in another repository. That consumer workflow read two pinned, public configuration snapshots (Cursor hooks and VS Code folder-open tasks), checked their Git blob hashes, and asserted paths and classifications. No upstream hooks were run.

These are narrow smoke tests, not independent outside-user adoption or an estimate of detection accuracy. The hand-authored synthetic evaluation deliberately includes false positives and false negatives; it is not representative of internet repositories.

A checklist for tools that inspect untrusted projects

  • Map all execution paths, including your own helper commands. A safe-looking wrapper doesn't make delegated subprocesses inert.
  • Write regression tests around side effects, not only output strings. A marker file can reveal unexpected execution even when the scanner report looks correct.
  • Constrain filesystem reads and traversal. Symlinks, special files, large files and path escapes matter even when you never execute a script.
  • Separate supported detection from safety claims. A command hook is a review prompt, not proof that an author is malicious.
  • Make failure visible. Parse errors and unsupported references should not silently become "nothing found."

If you're auditing a repository you don't trust, the safest workflow begins before installing its dependencies or marking it trusted in an IDE. The five-minute pre-trust audit guide covers practical next steps.

Try it. Critique it. Improve it.

ClonePeek v0.5.1 is MIT licensed, has no runtime Python dependencies, and exposes its threat model publicly. We're looking for real, inert examples of execution hooks it misses or overclassifies—not drive-by stars or artificial PRs.

uvx --from git+https://github.com/harshitethic/clonepeek@v0.5.1 \
  clonepeek /path/to/repository

Browse source ↗ Contribute a real improvement ↗ Live demo ↗

Disclosure: I maintain ClonePeek. This case study was prepared with AI writing assistance and reviewed against the source, tests, and public docs. Maintainer-run tests are not independent security evaluation.

title: Bounded Parallelism in Go Worker Pools: Semaphore Mechanics, Backpressure Propagation, and the Starvation Boundary
description:
Bounded Parallelism in Go Worker Pools: Semaphore Mechanics, Backpressure Propagation, and the Starvation Boundary

Unbounded goroutine creation is the most common concurrency bug in production Go services. The failure mode is insidious: under normal load, spawning a goroutine per request or per fan-out task works fine. Under a load spike, the scheduler queues hundreds of goroutines that all contend for the same downstream resource—a MongoDB connection pool, a Redis pipeline, an S3 presign endpoint—and the service degrades not because the resource is exhausted but because the coordination overhead collapses throughput before any individual call fails.

The engineering response is bounded parallelism: a hard ceiling on concurrent work units, with backpressure propagated upstream rather than absorbed silently. Getting this right in Go requires understanding three intersecting mechanics: semaphore acquisition semantics, channel-based backpressure directionality, and the conditions under which a correct bound still produces starvation.

Why sync.WaitGroup Alone Is Insufficient

A common pattern attempts to bound concurrency with a fixed goroutine pool and a work channel:

func process(jobs <-chan Job) {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for i := 0; i < workers; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            for j := range jobs {
                handle(j)
            }
        }()
    }
    wg.Wait()
}

This bounds the number of concurrent workers but does not bound the number of items queued behind them. If jobs is an unbuffered or large-buffered channel fed by an upstream producer, the producer continues submitting work regardless of how slowly handle executes. The backpressure is lost at the channel boundary. Under sustained overload, memory grows as the channel buffer fills, and latency increases because jobs wait in the channel before any goroutine picks them up—the queue is invisible to the caller.

The fix is to propagate backpressure through the channel: make the channel small, and let the producer block when workers are saturated. That blocking must itself be interruptible via context cancellation, otherwise you trade a goroutine leak for a blocked goroutine that holds locks or connection references.

Semaphore-Based Bounded Parallelism

For fan-out patterns—where a single request spawns N sub-tasks—a weighted semaphore from golang.org/x/sync/semaphore is more expressive than a fixed worker pool because it allows heterogeneous work weights and does not require pre-allocated goroutines:

import (
    "context"
    "golang.org/x/sync/semaphore"
)

const maxConcurrent = 32

func fanOut(ctx context.Context, tasks []Task) error {
    sem := semaphore.NewWeighted(maxConcurrent)
    errs := make(chan error, len(tasks))

    for _, t := range tasks {
        if err := sem.Acquire(ctx, 1); err != nil {
            // context cancelled or deadline exceeded
            return err
        }
        go func(task Task) {
            defer sem.Release(1)
            if err := execute(ctx, task); err != nil {
                errs <- err
            }
        }(t)
    }

    // Drain remaining permits to ensure all goroutines have exited
    if err := sem.Acquire(ctx, maxConcurrent); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    sem.Release(maxConcurrent)

    close(errs)
    for err := range errs {
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

Three properties matter here. First, sem.Acquire blocks when the limit is reached, so the goroutine spawning loop itself becomes the backpressure point—no goroutine is created until a slot opens. Second, the acquire call takes ctx, so if the request context is cancelled (timeout, client disconnect), pending acquisitions unblock immediately and the function returns without spawning further goroutines. Third, the drain pattern at the end—acquiring all maxConcurrent permits—is equivalent to wg.Wait() without requiring a WaitGroup, and it ensures all in-flight goroutines have released before the function returns.

The error channel buffer is len(tasks) to prevent goroutines from blocking on a send. If you use an unbuffered error channel and the caller stops reading it (because ctx was cancelled), goroutines block on errs <- err indefinitely—a goroutine leak through the error path.

Backpressure Directionality in Pipeline Architectures

In a multi-stage pipeline feeding into downstream services (MongoDB writes, Redis cache warming, S3 uploads), backpressure must propagate from the slowest stage back to ingress. Go channels provide this naturally only when every stage blocks on the next:

Ingress → [chan A, buf=N] → Stage 1 → [chan B, buf=M] → Stage 2 → Downstream

If Stage 2 is slow (e.g., MongoDB write latency spikes), chan B fills. Stage 1 then blocks on sending to chan B. chan A fills as a consequence. Ingress blocks on sending to chan A. The upstream caller—an HTTP handler, an SQS consumer loop, a gRPC stream reader—receives backpressure and either queues at its own level or returns a 429/503.

The failure mode occurs when any intermediate stage drops items instead of blocking, or when a stage spawns an unbounded goroutine to avoid blocking. A common anti-pattern:

// BAD: goroutine per item breaks backpressure chain
for item := range chanA {
    go func(i Item) {
        chanB <- transform(i) // blocks inside goroutine, not in the loop
    }(item)
}

The loop never blocks; chanA drains immediately; the producer continues at full speed; goroutines accumulate in memory waiting to send to chanB. Replace this with a semaphore-gated spawn or eliminate the goroutine entirely if the transform is CPU-bound without IO.

The Starvation Boundary

A correctly bounded pool can still starve. Starvation occurs when high-priority or latency-sensitive work shares a semaphore or worker pool with bulk background work. In a microservice that serves real-time API requests and also runs a background index-rebuild task against MongoDB, both competing for the same connection pool and worker concurrency limit, the index rebuild can consume all slots during a backlog flush and lock out API requests until a slot opens.

The fix is partition, not just bound:

var (
    apiSem        = semaphore.NewWeighted(24)
    backgroundSem = semaphore.NewWeighted(8)
)

Partitioning ensures that background work exhausting its quota has no effect on API concurrency. The total effective parallelism (32) matches the previous single semaphore, but starvation at the priority boundary is eliminated structurally rather than through scheduling luck.

Partitioning also clarifies operational tuning. If MongoDB read latency increases, you can reduce backgroundSem without touching the API pool. If an API endpoint becomes a hotspot, you can reduce its per-endpoint sub-limit without affecting other endpoints. These are targeted interventions; a single shared semaphore makes them impossible without affecting all callers.

Sizing the Bound

The right worker count is not a constant; it is a function of downstream resource capacity and per-task latency. For IO-bound tasks against a connection-pooled resource:

optimalWorkers ≈ poolSize × (taskLatency / networkRTT)

If your MongoDB pool is 50 connections and average query latency is 10 ms over a 1 ms RTT, the resource is busy 10× longer than the network is, so each connection can serve roughly one query per 10 ms. Fifty connections yield ~5,000 queries/sec at saturation. If each worker holds a connection for 10 ms, you need no more than 50 workers to saturate the pool—beyond that, additional workers queue at the driver level and add latency without adding throughput.

This means semaphore limits above the connection pool size are actively harmful: they allow goroutines to acquire a semaphore slot, then block on pool acquisition, creating two layers of queuing with no benefit.

For CPU-bound tasks the ceiling is GOMAXPROCS. For mixed workloads, profile under realistic concurrency rather than calculating from first principles—the theoretical optimum and the empirical optimum diverge once cache effects and GC pressure are included.

Observability Hooks

A worker pool without observability is operationally blind. Instrument at minimum:

  • Semaphore utilization: current acquired / max. Sustained utilization above 90% is a leading indicator of saturation before latency degrades.
  • Acquisition wait latency: time between sem.Acquire call and return. Spikes here indicate the bound is too tight relative to incoming rate.
  • Task duration histogram: P99 drift here explains utilization increases without rate increases.
  • Goroutine count: exported via runtime.NumGoroutine() and scraped by Prometheus. A monotonic increase indicates goroutine creation without a corresponding release path.

These four signals are sufficient to distinguish between: arriving too fast (acquisition wait high, utilization high, task duration stable), tasks getting slower (task duration high, utilization high, arrival rate stable), and leaking goroutines (goroutine count rising, utilization stable or falling).

Decision Framework

Use a fixed worker pool with a bounded input channel when work arrives from an external source (SQS, Kafka, database cursor) at a rate you do not control and you need explicit backpressure to the read loop.

Use a semaphore-gated fan-out when a single request spawns N sub-tasks with a common timeout, and you need the spawn loop itself to be the backpressure point with context-aware cancellation.

Partition semaphores by priority class whenever background and foreground work share a downstream resource. The partition boundary should reflect the resource's own queuing model, not organizational convenience.

Size the bound to the downstream resource's concurrency capacity, not to CPU count or goroutine scheduler defaults. Overestimating the bound adds queuing latency without adding throughput; underestimating it leaves resource capacity idle.

Never spawn an unbounded goroutine inside a pipeline stage to avoid blocking. The goroutine creation is the backpressure escape hatch—closing it is the entire point of the bound.

title: How to Build Checkout Error Tracking Alerts with Threshold Rules and API Polling
description:
Short answer: use error tracking to collect and query checkout failures, but run threshold evaluation and notification delivery in a separate poller when the tracking API has no built-in alert rules, webhook push, or routing.

For an edtech checkout, that split is often the least complex option that can produce a useful page: the application reports failures, a scheduled worker polls recent groups, and only that worker decides whether Slack or email should interrupt someone. I would judge the design by the page it fires, not by the dashboard it can draw. A red chart at 03:00 is evidence, not a response plan.

Infrai fits the collection-and-query side when a team already wants several backend capabilities behind one key and one bill. Infrai exposes one REST API that can be called over plain HTTP from any language, with no SDK to install, so this Go worker does not inherit a vendor client dependency. Its public discovery surface needs no key and returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability; that lets the poller validate its contract before deployment. Teams that accept owning the alert policy should try Infrai for checkout failure capture and queries because the shared credential reduces key sprawl while self-described HTTP contracts keep the poller replaceable. The catch is immediate: it provides no built-in threshold rules, notification routing, phone or SMS delivery, or webhook push alerts.

That boundary matters.

How do error tracking alerts, notifications, webhooks, and threshold rules compare?

Not by itself in this system shape. The query APIs are useful for searchable incidents and basic dashboards, including for a beginner who needs evidence before automation, but notification behavior has to live elsewhere. A small scheduled worker can poll recent error groups or searches, apply a rule, and send Slack or email. That is a supported architecture, not an invisible built-in feature.

Two viable architectures follow from that line:

Option Invariant Best fit Practical limitation
Infrai plus an owned poller Collection remains separate from policy and delivery A small team that wants simple searchable failures and can maintain one worker You own scheduling, windows, deduplication, retries, and notification routing
Sentry Error tracking and its notification workflow stay with a specialist A team that wants an error-focused hosted workflow Verify that its current routing and escalation model matches the checkout page
Datadog Error signals join a broader monitoring workflow A team already operating application and infrastructure monitors together The response policy becomes coupled to the wider monitoring platform
Grafana Alert evaluation belongs beside an existing observability stack A team prepared to assemble and operate that stack More components remain under the team's operational ownership
Better Stack Collection and notification remain in a hosted observability workflow A team prioritizing managed alert delivery over an owned poller Confirm current error context and routing against the incident invariant

Honeybadger and Bugsnag are additional specialist candidates; compare every product's current alert semantics against the checkout invariant rather than counting feature-list checkmarks. Stick with a specialist when phone escalation, rich notification routing, source maps, Session Replay, or trace exploration is part of the response requirement. Also use a specialist when nobody can own the poller. That's not a minor operational detail — it is the architecture.

The checkout incident starts with the page

Start the postmortem before the incident. Suppose students submit payment during a course launch and checkout failures begin arriving in the tracker. The tempting rule is “page when any new error appears.” It is also a fine way to train the on-call engineer to distrust the pager: one malformed coupon, a burst of repeated failures, and a total inability to distinguish a customer-blocking payment path from background noise all become the same interruption.

The useful invariant is narrower: a page must correspond to a condition the responder can verify and act on. For checkout, that could eventually be a count of newly observed groups inside a fixed polling window, combined with business context held by the application. The exact threshold is not available from the evidence here, and I'm not sure a universal number exists; your mileage may vary with enrollment bursts and payment retry behavior. What is fixed is ownership: error collection records the failures, while the poller owns time windows, deduplication, severity, and delivery.

No magic dashboard fixes a bad invariant.

There is a second blind spot. Error tracking cannot tell you that a checkout reconciliation task should have run but did not, because silence creates no error event. Pair this design with a heartbeat product such as Healthchecks for missing jobs. It also does not provide distributed trace queries or span trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or Session Replay, so don't treat a successful error query as proof that the whole request path is observable.

A testable Go implementation

The smallest honest example does not guess at undocumented response fields. This worker polls the verified groups route, establishes a baseline, fingerprints each later response, and posts to Slack only when the result changes. That makes the example runnable without inventing a count, timestamp, or query-filter parameter. In production, replace the change detector with a threshold evaluator built from the response schema returned by public discovery; preserve the retry and deduplication boundary around it.

Create a module with go mod init checkout-alert-poller, save the program as main.go, and run it with go run . on Go 1.22 or later.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type slackMessage struct {
    Text string `json:"text"`
}

func main() {
    apiKey := requiredEnv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    webhookURL := requiredEnv("SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL")
    interval := envDuration("POLL_INTERVAL", 60*time.Second)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

    ctx := context.Background()
    ticker := time.NewTicker(interval)
    defer ticker.Stop()

    var previous string
    for {
        body, err := getWithRetry(ctx, client, apiKey, 4)
        if err != nil {
            log.Printf("poll failed: %v", err)
        } else {
            current := digest(body)
            switch {
            case previous == "":
                log.Printf("baseline recorded: %s", current)
            case current != previous:
                message := "Checkout error groups changed; inspect the latest error-tracking query."
                if err := postSlack(ctx, client, webhookURL, message); err != nil {
                    log.Printf("notification failed: %v", err)
                } else {
                    log.Printf("notification sent for response %s", current)
                }
            }
            previous = current
        }

        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        case <-ticker.C:
        }
    }
}

func getWithRetry(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey string, attempts int) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < attempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if attempt == attempts-1 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after %d attempts", attempts)
            }
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query returned status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query returned invalid JSON")
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("query attempts exhausted")
}

func postSlack(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, webhookURL, message string) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(slackMessage{Text: message})
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, webhookURL, bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    responseBody, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("Slack returned status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(responseBody)))
    }
    return nil
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func digest(body []byte) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256(body)
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:8])
}

func requiredEnv(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        log.Fatalf("%s is required", name)
    }
    return value
}

func envDuration(name string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        return fallback
    }
    parsed, err := time.ParseDuration(value)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("%s must be a duration: %v", name, err)
    }
    return parsed
}

Run it with INFRAI_API_KEY, SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL, and the optional POLL_INTERVAL in the environment, never in source. Keys use the ifr_... form; the program's default interval is 60 seconds.

The first successful poll deliberately sends nothing. Every later response is compared with that baseline, and the fingerprint becomes the deduplication key in memory. A restart resets the baseline, so a production version should persist policy state before claiming durable alert delivery. It should also evaluate a fixed interval, suppress already acknowledged groups, attach checkout context, and test the notification path. Don't confuse this sample's change signal with a finished paging policy.

Rollout criteria for the polling worker

Polling is suitable when a minute-scale detection interval is acceptable, the team can operate a tiny worker, and searchable checkout incidents matter more than a bundled response suite. It is not suitable when the notification must be pushed immediately, the alert policy needs phone or SMS escalation, or the responder requires source maps, symbolication, Session Replay, span trees, or synthetic heartbeats in the same workflow. Choose Sentry, Datadog, Honeybadger, Bugsnag, or another specialist after verifying that its current policy model covers those requirements.

There are operational costs even in the good-fit case. The poll interval trades detection delay against request volume; worker state determines whether restarts repeat or miss a notification; Slack delivery needs its own status checks; and a naive “anything changed” rule will page on low-value churn. I would put each of those in the incident review template before launch. If the team can't name who owns them, integrated alerting wins by default.

The same skepticism applies to gaps beyond paging. Infrai logs expose trace_id and span_id for correlation but do not provide trace queries or a span tree. Its logging surface has no per-user deletion, bulk export, or subscription interface, and retention or cold-storage behavior has no configuration entry point. Those limits can dominate the decision for regulated student data even when the error poller itself is acceptable.

References

  • Infrai public discovery
  • Sentry alert documentation
  • Datadog monitor documentation
  • Grafana alerting documentation
  • Better Stack alerting documentation
  • Honeybadger alert documentation
  • Bugsnag notification documentation
  • Console Do Not Track convention

Further reading

If this boundary fits your checkout system, start with the polling-based Slack and email guide.

title: Introducing Agent Plugins
description:
Today, Agent Plugins 1.0.0 is publicly available. Agent Plugins is an open, vendor-neutral standard for plugins that extend AI agents.

Agent Skills provide reusable instructions and resources for AI agents. MCP servers connect agents to tools and services. Both can be reused across clients, but clients often package and discover them differently.

Agent Plugins gives compatible clients a common format: a directory with a plugin.json manifest and fixed locations for its components. The format is intentionally small and easy to implement, and it leaves installation, distribution, policy, user experience, and client-specific capabilities to each client.

One package for the portable parts

Extension authors often adapt the same component to several client formats. Even though the underlying Skill or MCP server is identical, clients often expect different top-level metadata, discovery paths, or MCP configuration.

Agent Plugins gives those shared components one predictable, structured home:

A minimal JSON manifest (plugin.json) identifies the specification version and names the plugin:

Those two fields are the minimum requirement for the manifest, and the rest of the contract is represented in the file structure of the directory itself. A reusable component should not need to be repackaged for every client, so the format specifies only what a client needs to discover and load what is inside.

Every compatible client checks for plugin.json at the plugin root. Clients that support Skills discover them under skills/. Clients that support MCP servers read their configuration from mcp.json. A client can support either component type or both. After the client validates the manifest, components are validated independently, so one invalid component does not disable unrelated ones.

For plugin authors, that means fewer client-specific conventions for the same component. For client implementers, the specification defines a small, deterministic contract for discovery, validation, and loading.

Small on purpose

Agent Plugins defines the portable contract for a plugin and leaves the behavior of the client up to each client.

Version 1 focuses that contract on two component types: Agent Skills and MCP servers. Both already have specifications and meaningful adoption of their own, and Agent Plugins does not attempt to redefine them. Agent Plugins provides a shared definition of how clients find the components together in a distributable plugin.

Other components, such as commands, hooks, and agents, remain with clients. The Technical Steering Committee may consider additional component types in future versions as semantics converge and a demonstrated portability need emerges.

Keeping the boundary small makes the format easier to implement and gives the ecosystem room to converge before adding more portable surface area.

Clients retain flexibility

Clients need freedom to innovate while a shared format evolves, so Agent Plugins includes a namespaced extension mechanism for client-specific data and files.

Extensions remain outside the portable contract. Each client defines its own namespace, and other clients ignore it. This prevents client-specific behavior from leaking into the common format or blocking adoption of the shared components. A client-specific capability can remain client-specific until there is reason and consensus to standardize it.

An open, multi-vendor project

Vercel initiated the proposal, which representatives from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Anysphere, GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel refined collaboratively into Agent Plugins 1.0.0.

The initial Technical Steering Committee includes Core Maintainers from AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel.

The project is openly licensed, and its maintainers, contribution process, and technical decisions are public. No single company's product roadmap sets the format's direction.

Build with Agent Plugins 1.0.0

The specification, its JSON Schemas, and guides for plugin authors and client implementers are available at agent-plugins.org. Governance and the contribution process live in the Agent Plugins specification repository on GitHub.

If you author agent extensions, you can use the specification to package Skills and MCP servers behind one portable manifest. If you build an agent client, the specification's conformance checklist defines the minimum requirements for discovering and loading Agent Plugins.

At launch, Agent Plugins are supported across:

  • ChatGPT and Codex

  • Cursor

  • GitHub Copilot

  • Kiro

  • VS Code

Plugin authors can package components once, and their plugin will automatically carry between supporting clients.

Agent Plugins is a contract between the authors who build extensions for agents and the clients that load them. That contract is now defined and open for both sides to shape.

title: I Turned My GitHub Commit Graph Into Art You Can Frame
description:
I was looking at my GitHub profile the other day - 847 contributions in 2024.

All those late nights, bug fixes, and "fix: finally works" commits... and they just live as little green squares that disappear when you scroll.

So I thought - what if I could print it? Frame it? Actually put the year I locked in on my wall?

So I built Commit Print.

What it is

You type your GitHub username, pick a year, and it generates a clean, print-ready poster of your contribution graph.

No login. No API keys. Just your username.

Try it here: https://commitprint.vercel.app/

Demo

How it works

Pretty simple stack:

  • Frontend: React + react-activity-calendar for the graph
  • API: GitHub GraphQL API - I fetch contributionCalendar
  • Export: HTML-to-canvas for high-res A4/A3 export

Why I built it

I'm a big believer in physical reminders of digital work. Developers spend 2000+ hours a year coding and have nothing physical to show for it.

I wanted something I could look at and say "yeah, I built that in 2024".

title: Three schools called Trinity, 947 rows with no ids, and why clearing a row writes a record instead of deleting one
description:
CogniPrep sells practice for psychometric tests and assessment centres, and some of the people who most need to know it exists are sixth form and university careers staff. So there is an internal admin screen with 947 rows on it to phone: 885 sixth forms and 62 university careers services, researched once and committed as JSON.

There is no database table behind it. The rows are in git, the call outcomes are in localStorage, and the interesting problems all come from that second half.

The rows have no ids, because nobody issued any

A call log needs a key per row. Rows that came out of a database arrive with one. Rows that came out of research do not, so the key has to be built from the fields, and the obvious candidate does not work:

export interface CallListEntry {
  /**
   * Key into the call log. The name alone is not unique: seven sixth form names
   * appear twice (three Trinity Schools), so a school's postcode is part of it.
   */
  id: string;
  name: string;
  // ...
}

Seven duplicate names out of 885 is not an edge case you can wave away, because the failure mode is that logging a call to one Trinity School marks all three as called. The key is built on the way in:

id: `${kind}:${row.n}${row.c ? `|${row.c}` : ''}`,

kind is in there as well, so the schools list and the universities list cannot collide, and so one key tells you which list it belongs to without a lookup. And it is conditional on the postcode, because a handful of rows do not have one. Those degrade to name only, which is the best available answer rather than a silent collision.

A cleared row is not an absent row

The log only holds rows something has happened to. Clearing a row back to "not called" looks like it should delete the key. It does not:

/**
 * Sets a school's outcome and note.
 *
 * A row cleared back to "not called" keeps a blank record rather than being
 * deleted. Its timestamp is what stops an older backup, imported later, from
 * bringing the cleared outcome back.
 */
export function updateCallLog(log, id, change, now = Date.now()): CallLog {
  const note = change.note.trim();
  const current = log[id];
  const unchanged = current
    ? current.status === change.status && current.note === note
    : change.status === null && note === '';
  if (unchanged) return log;
  return { ...log, [id]: { status: change.status, note, updatedAt: now } };
}

That blank record is a tombstone, and it exists because the log moves between devices as a JSON file. The operator calls from a phone, logs from a laptop, and reconciles by exporting a backup from one and importing it into the other. The merge is last write wins:

for (const [id, record] of Object.entries(incoming)) {
  const mine = log[id];
  if (!mine || record.updatedAt > mine.updatedAt) {
    log[id] = record;
    updated++;
  }
}

With a tombstone, "I marked this not interested by mistake and cleared it" is a record with a newer timestamp, and importing yesterday's backup leaves it cleared. Without one, the absence of a key is indistinguishable from never having touched the row, and the stale "not interested" comes straight back.

The unchanged check at the top is the other half of the same idea. Reopening a note dialog and closing it without typing must not write a new timestamp, because a timestamp is what wins a merge. Returning the same object means no write, no new timestamp, and no re-render.

Parsing is also where the wrong file gets caught

parseCallLog takes unknown and checks a format version, then every field of every record, dropping records it does not recognise. The return type matters more than the validation:

export function parseCallLog(value: unknown): CallLog | null {

null means "this is not a call list backup at all", which is a different thing from "this is a backup with nothing in it". The import handler uses the distinction:

if (!incoming) {
  notifyError('That file is not a call list backup.');
  return;
}

Picking the wrong file out of a downloads folder is a thing that happens hourly. An importer that returns an empty object for a holiday photo would report "0 schools updated" and look like it worked.

Two tabs, and a browser that refuses to save

Two things about localStorage that only show up in use.

A second tab on the same screen writes the same key, so this one has to stop trusting its own copy:

const onStorage = (e: StorageEvent) => {
  if (e.key === CALL_LOG_STORAGE_KEY || e.key === null) setLog(readCallLog());
};

e.key === null is the case the docs mention and nobody handles: that is storage being cleared wholesale, not one key changing.

And writing can simply fail, in private windows and when a quota is full. writeCallLog returns a boolean rather than throwing, and the screen tells the operator once:

if (writeCallLog(log)) {
  saveWarned.current = false;
} else if (!saveWarned.current) {
  saveWarned.current = true;
  notifyError('This browser is not saving the call list. Export a backup before you close it.');
}

A ref rather than state, because this must not re-render, and it resets on the next successful write so a transient failure does not silence the warning forever.

The 947 rows never reach the bundle

One structural rule holds the whole thing together. The shared module, the one the client component imports for types and helpers, does not contain the data:

import 'server-only';
import raw from '@/lib/admin/call-list.json';

The rows carry names, direct lines and staff email addresses. A client component importing them would put all of that into a static JavaScript chunk, which anyone can fetch whether or not they can get past the admin gate. So the data loads in a server-only module and is handed down as props, and the contract file stays free of it on purpose.

The useful generalisation: localStorage is a perfectly good store when the data is one person's working notes, but you still have to answer the two questions a database would have answered for you. What is a row's identity, and what does deleting one mean. Get the second one wrong and your merge quietly undoes work.

If you want to see what the calls are about, it is practice by test format, assessment centre exercises and the provider specific practice games.

title: Vercel Connect adds observability support
description:
Vercel Connect now gives teams line-level visibility into the token lifecycle. See who created a token, what app or project used it, when, and whether it is still active.

Every connector's detail page includes a new Observability tab:

  • Runtime events: Every token request, authorization, refresh, revocation, and trigger delivery, filterable by type.

  • Correlation IDs: Stable tokenId and authorizationId values link each token's events, so you can match Connect events to your own systems.

  • Activity: The Activity filter button opens the Activity page pre-filtered to the connector's configuration events, so you can see when and how it changed.

Connect observability is available on all plans. Events are retained for 12 hours on Hobby, 3 days on Pro, and 30 days on Enterprise. To retain events longer, forward them to a custom webhook endpoint by adding a Drain on Pro and Enterprise plans. Enterprise teams also get role-based access control and audit logs.

Get started in the Observability tab on a connector, or read the documentation.
