title: Learning Python After a Few Years of Go: What Surprised Me So Far
description:
I've been writing Go for a few years: explicit types, go mod, goroutines, if err != nil, and the comfort of the compiler saying "no" before deploy. Recently I started learning Python.

I'm new to Python, but not new to programming. So this isn't a generic language comparison, and it isn't written by a Python expert. It's what I've actually discovered so far as a Go-heavy brain meeting a dynamic, batteries-included ecosystem.

If you're an experienced Pythonista and I got something wrong, please tell me in the comments. If you're coming from Go too, I hope this saves you a few surprises.

What stayed familiar

Some things translated almost one-to-one.

  • Modules and imports. Files and packages still organize code. You still manage dependencies, just with a virtual environment and pyproject.toml or requirements.txt instead of go.mod.
  • Maps and iteration. Python dicts and for key, value in ... feel like Go maps and range, with less typing and different missing-key behavior (.get() vs (v, ok)).
  • Functions as values. Closures and callbacks exist in both. In Python they show up everywhere (decorators, key= arguments, lambdas) more than in typical Go style.
  • Testing culture. Table-driven tests have a cousin in pytest parametrization. The habit of "many cases, one function" carries over well.

What surprised me

1. Variables aren't typed slots, they're names on objects

In Go, var x int and x := 10 attach a type to a variable. In Python, x = 10 binds a name to an object. Reassigning x = "hello" is legal: the name moved, and the old int may still exist elsewhere.

That one idea explains a lot of "why did it do that?" moments. Assignment doesn't copy a struct-like value by default. It copies a reference, so mutating a list or dict through one name affects every name pointing at that object.

Discovery: I stopped looking for type declarations on every line and started asking: what object does this name point to, and is it mutable?

2. There is no compile-time safety net unless you build one

Go trained me to trust the compiler. Python runs first and complains later.

Type hints (def f(x: int) -> str:) don't change runtime behavior, but running mypy or Pyright in CI gives you a slice of Go-like checking.

Discovery: Professional Python often means type hints + a linter + tests, not "dynamic means anything goes."

3. "No pointers" doesn't mean "no aliasing"

For immutable things (int, str, tuple), behavior often looks like pass-by-value. For lists, dicts, and custom objects, it's shared mutation.

When I need a copy, I have to ask for one (list.copy(), copy.deepcopy()). Go made this obvious with * and &. Python hides it behind semantics.

This leads straight into the first gotcha I ran into.

Gotcha: mutable default arguments 

def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add_item("a"))  # ['a']
print(add_item("b"))  # ['a', 'b']  <- surprise!

The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and shared across calls. The usual fix:

def add_item(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items

Gotcha: == vs is 

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]

print(a == b)  # True  (same value)
print(a is b)  # False (different objects)

Use == to compare values and is to check identity. The main place you want is is x is None.

4. Error handling is a culture shift

My Go reflex:

if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("loading config: %w", err)
}

Python's default is exceptions that bubble up until something catches them. Idiomatic code often raises deep inside and catches at boundaries (a CLI command, an HTTP handler, a job runner) rather than around every line.

Discovery: Check explicitly for expected failures like validation and parsing, and use exceptions for exceptional paths or deep call stacks. Both are professional. The mix is the lesson.

5. Cleanup is with, not defer 

with open("data.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()

Discovery: Context managers are to Python what defer is to Go: the idiomatic way to say "always release this."

6. Concurrency is a different animal

  • CPU-bound work: the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) limits threads for compute-heavy code, so processes or native extensions matter.
  • I/O-bound work: asyncio (async / await) is the closest mental model to lightweight goroutines, but it's cooperative and depends on async-aware libraries.

Here's the same idea, three tasks running concurrently. First Go:

var wg sync.WaitGroup
results := make([]int, 3)

for i := range results {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()
        time.Sleep(time.Second)
        results[i] = (i + 1) * 2
    }()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println(results) // [2 4 6]

And Python:

import asyncio

async def work(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return n * 2

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(work(1), work(2), work(3))
    print(results)  # [2, 4, 6]

asyncio.run(main())

The Python version is shorter, but I have to remember that everything in the chain must be async, and one blocking call can stall the whole event loop.

A note on the GIL: recent Python versions include an optional free-threaded build that removes it. Check the current status for the version you use before relying on it.

Discovery: I now map problems to asyncio vs threading vs multiprocessing instead of reaching for goroutines by default.

7. The standard library is huge

JSON, HTTP, pathlib, dataclasses, logging: a lot is already included. I still reach for pytest, httpx or requests, and pydantic where Go might use a few well-known dependencies.

8. dataclass is my struct comfort zone 

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int

For API payloads and DTOs, dataclass or Pydantic scratch the same itch as Go structs with JSON tags.

Types and values: a map for Go eyes

Go Python (what I use in practice)
int, float64 int (arbitrary precision), float
string, []byte str, bytes
[]T slice list (mixed types allowed)
map[K]V dict
struct @dataclass or class
interface duck typing, or typing.Protocol for contracts
nil None (use is None, not == None)
zero value no universal zero; know the falsy values (None, 0, "", [], {})
(v, ok) .get(key), or try / except KeyError
  • Numbers: / is true division (5 / 2 gives 2.5), and // is floor division.
  • Strings: f-strings (f"{name}: {score}") replace most day-to-day fmt.Sprintf.
  • Tuples and sets: Go has no first-class versions of these. Python has immutable tuples (1, 2) and sets {1, 2, 3}.
  • Booleans: Python has many falsy values, which is broader than Go's zero-value checks. For optional values, if x is None is not the same as if not x.

Importing code: what Go made obvious, and what Python does differently

In Go, imports are rigid: one module path, one package per directory, exported names capitalized. Python looks simpler (import foo), but the rules live in file layout, packages, and convention.

Mental model: module, package, file

Go Python
Module = repo + go.mod Project = folder with pyproject.toml / requirements.txt
Package = directory with a shared package name Package = directory (often with __init__.py)
File = part of one package Module = one .py file (utils.py is module utils)

Go:

import "github.com/acme/myapp/internal/auth"

auth.Middleware()

Python:

from myapp.auth.middleware import require_token

The layout has to match what Python can find on sys.path, not just what you wish the folder tree looked like.

Import styles 

import json
json.loads('{"a": 1}')

from json import loads
loads('{"a": 1}')

import json as js
from pathlib import Path
  • import module is good for large or clash-prone modules (os, logging).
  • from module import name is idiomatic for small, clear APIs (from dataclasses import dataclass).

Go's closest habit is import aliases (import f "fmt"). Python uses from and aliases constantly, and that's normal.

Where Python looks for modules

  1. The standard library
  2. Packages in the active virtual environment
  3. Your project root, if it's on sys.path (run from the root, pip install -e ., or use PYTHONPATH)

Discovery: Running from the wrong directory, or forgetting the venv, feels like pre-modules Go. Imports fail at runtime. One venv per project is non-optional, just like go.mod per service.

Project layout (mirroring Go instincts) 

src/myapp/
    __init__.py
    main.py
    auth/
        __init__.py
        middleware.py
        service.py
pyproject.toml

Go's internal/ is enforced by the compiler. Python's "private" is a _leading_underscore: convention, not a rule.

Go Python
Foo / foo _helper means "internal, please don't"

Callers can still import _helper. The discipline is social and enforced in code review.

Importing functions, classes, and constants 

# auth/service.py
def validate(token: str) -> bool:
    ...

class User:
    ...

from auth.service import validate, User
# or
from auth import service
service.validate("...")

Packages often re-export a clean surface in __init__.py:

# auth/__init__.py
from .service import validate, User

__all__ = ["validate", "User"]

Relative imports (inside a package only) 

# auth/middleware.py
from .service import validate
from ..config import settings

Go uses full paths only, with no ... Relative imports break if you run a nested file directly (python auth/middleware.py). Prefer python -m myapp or an installed package, similar to running from the module root in Go.

init vs import-time code

Go has func init() at package load. In Python, importing a module runs it once, and __init__.py runs when the package is first imported. I keep __init__.py thin: re-exports and docs, not heavy side effects.

Circular imports

This is the same class of problem as Go import cycles. Fixes: extract a small shared module, import lazily inside a function, or restructure the packages.

Third-party dependencies

Use pip install plus a lockfile (Poetry, uv, and others). Watch for PyPI name vs import name: pip install Pillow gives you import PIL.

Library vs entrypoint 

def main():
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Importing the file loads the definitions but does not run main(). It only runs when the file is executed as a script, which is like separating package auth from cmd/server.

Import cheat sheet

I want to... Go Python
Import a package import "path/pkg" import pkg
Use one function pkg.F() from pkg import F
Rename import p "path/pkg" import pkg as p
Hide internals lowercase name _name
Entrypoint func main() in cmd/... if __name__ == "__main__": or python -m pkg
Local monorepo lib replace in go.mod pip install -e ./libs/foo

Functions, control flow, and iteration

Go has multiple returns, defer, and C-style for. Python has a single return value (use tuples for several), with instead of defer, and for x in iterable as the default loop.

Comprehensions are idiomatic where Go would use a loop plus append:

squares = [n * n for n in range(10)]

Variadic functions: Go uses ...T, Python uses *args and **kwargs.

What Go still does better

Learning Python hasn't made me love Go any less. A few things I miss:

  • Compile-time errors. Typos in rarely-run code paths only show up when they run.
  • Single-binary deployment. go build and ship one file. Python needs an environment, dependencies, or a container.
  • Built-in concurrency. Goroutines and channels need no async/await coloring of your functions.
  • Predictable performance for CPU-heavy work.

Neither language is "better." They optimize for different things.

What I'm still figuring out

Being honest, here's what hasn't clicked yet:

  • Async code in larger projects, and how to mix it with blocking libraries
  • Packaging and dependency tools (pip, Poetry, uv): which one, and when
  • When to use a plain class, a dataclass, or a Pydantic model
  • Reading and writing good type hints for more complex code

If you have advice on any of these, I'd really like to hear it.

Habits I deliberately changed

  1. A virtualenv for every project, like a non-optional go.mod.
  2. Type-hint public APIs, and let tools enforce them.
  3. Use with, comprehensions, and pytest, instead of translating every Go loop.
  4. Catch exceptions at the edges rather than copying if err != nil onto every line.
  5. Treat is None and falsiness as different checks.
  6. Use an editable install (pip install -e .) so from myapp... imports behave like a real module graph.

Closing

Learning Python as a Go developer isn't a downgrade or a "scripting detour." It's a language optimized for expression speed and ecosystem breadth, where discipline shows up in tests, types, project layout, and imports as much as in the compiler.

The uncomfortable parts (dynamic typing, exceptions, the GIL, import paths) aren't gaps in my education. They're different tradeoffs. Once I named them (references vs values, boundaries vs inline errors, asyncio vs goroutines, modules vs go.mod), Python stopped feeling like "Go with missing braces" and started feeling like a tool I'm getting comfortable with.

If you're coming from Go too, you're not starting from zero. You're retargeting a structured mindset.

Your turn: What surprised you most when you switched languages? Tell me in the comments.

title: How we migrated the database behind every Vercel build
description:
Every build on Vercel starts in the build warm pool, which is a set of standby containers that let builds begin without waiting for new compute. The pool runs on state that tracks which containers are ready, the tokens each one uses to authenticate, and the mapping that ties every running build back to the deployment that gets billed for it. When we built the pool, we put all of that in Redis, which was fast and made sense at the time.

Over the years, though, that state turned into a liability. Tokens and container statuses can be rebuilt if they get lost, but the billing mappings can't, and all of it was sitting in a store that we ran as an ephemeral cache. That state needed to live somewhere durable, which is why we decided to migrate it to DynamoDB.

The problem is that the pool never stops. Containers are coming up, polling, picking up work, and expiring around the clock, which meant we couldn't pause the world, copy the data, and restart. The migration had to happen live, under production traffic, in phases, each one behind a flag with a rollback ready if we needed it.

Durable state in an ephemeral store

Redis was a good home for it at first. It was fast, familiar, and efficient for the access patterns the pool started with. But over time the state became more important than the store holding it. If Redis became unavailable or lost data, the pool could no longer reliably authenticate containers, track which of them were ready, or resolve the work in flight.

Lose a token and the pool rebuilds it within about ten minutes. Lose a mapping and the build is never billed, because nothing else records which deployment it belonged to.

We wanted it in durable storage and landed on DynamoDB. On-demand scaling fits bursty deployment traffic, TTL is native, and there are no connections to manage at high concurrency. But what it did not promise was Redis's latency.

What Redis made cheap

Inside Redis, the pool's state looked like this:

  • Tokens lived in a set so we could check membership, and in a sorted set so we could expire them

  • Each lifecycle status (pending, polling, building) had its own sorted set, which meant a status change was a removal from one set and an add to the next

  • A string tied each working container to its deployment

All of these operations were cheap, about a millisecond each, and the code grew to lean on that speed. A single run of the supply loop, which is the loop that refills each warm pool in turn, would make hundreds of count calls just to tally up the pending and polling containers.

That's how the warm pool grew, one easy write at a time, until data we needed to keep was sitting in structures built for speed. Untangling that layout was where the migration started.

Designing the schema from the access patterns

Most migration plans treat the database as the thing being replaced. You map the access patterns, copy the data, and verify that the two stores agree. We planned ours that way too, so before designing any schema, we listed everything the code actually asked of that state:

  • Verify a token when a container polls for work

  • Add a token when a new container comes up

  • Expire tokens past their deadline

  • Count tokens to size the pool

  • Move a container between lifecycle statuses

  • Count containers by status

  • Look up the deployment behind a container's callback

  • Remove expired containers

Almost every operation already knows which container it's touching, and only polling ever starts from a token. So we put the container at the center of the model. The container ID became the sort key, and the token became just a field on the record, stored as a hash so that reading the table never hands you a usable credential. Verifying a token now just means looking up its container and comparing the hashes.

Two of the access patterns couldn't be served by a key lookup alone. Status counts had to skip containers that were already past expiry, which takes a time-aware index. And the deployment lookups feed billing, so they needed consistent reads, and the mapping got a small table of its own.

Reading a container's state, moving its status, and clearing its token all became direct key lookups. Counting a status became a single read against the time-aware index, one query per status with expired containers already filtered out.

Where Redis had let the data structures imply what we needed, DynamoDB made us spell out keys, indexes, conditional writes, and TTL behavior. So instead of carrying the Redis structures forward, we modeled the container and added the indexes that its access patterns needed.

Shadow mode validated every write

The rollout ran as feature-flagged phases: Redis-only, then dual writes, shadow reads, DynamoDB-primary, and finally DynamoDB-only. Every phase kept a rollback open for as long as possible. The last step, which removed the Redis writes, was the only one without an easy rollback, but any lingering token expires within ten minutes anyway.

We started by baselining the existing Redis operations, their counts and their latencies, so that the dashboards had a normal to compare against. The new DynamoDB methods merged days before anything actually called them. Dual writes went out next, with Redis still the source of truth and DynamoDB failures logged instead of fatal. Then came shadow reads, which queried both stores and compared the results. And then primary reads flipped, with the Redis writes kept on until the new path had proven itself.

What the comparisons told us was whether the two stores agreed on the stored values, which is something tests alone couldn't. They said nothing about timing. We checked that every write landed in both stores, that expiration kept moving forward as containers changed status so stale state never piled up, that clearing a token left the rest of the container's record intact, and that the counts stayed close enough to steer the pool.

On top of the comparisons we built dashboards that watched match rates, write errors, per-query latency, and expiration counts while Redis was still serving production. That way any divergence surfaced while it was still cheap to investigate, instead of showing up as a cutover failure. Every mismatch got chased down to a real bug, a dual-write race, or an expected difference before we moved on. Those dashboards decided when each phase advanced, and every time the numbers held steady under production traffic, the next step felt safer.

Two failures along the way

In March, one region's builds went down, and the investigation pointed at our own comparison machinery, which was the added load of checking two stores against each other. The scenario had actually come up in review, and we had throttled the comparisons for exactly that reason, but the throttling wasn't enough. Four days later, a pull request citing the incident added the index that the status counts needed. Without it, every count was O(n) work, and the comparisons were counting constantly. With the index in place, the rollout continued.

Later that month, the Redis infrastructure that we were migrating off actually went down. The warm pool and its token handling stayed up, because both of them were already reading from DynamoDB as the source of truth. Builds still felt the outage, but through services further up the pipeline that hadn't moved yet. The failure we'd been migrating away from arrived before the migration was even finished, and the state that had already moved survived it.

The supply loop stalled on slower reads

In April, the supply loop began to stall. The shadow data had looked healthy when we advanced primary reads, and the per-query latency had looked acceptable on the dashboards. What failed was a behavior that neither one measured.

We drew the loop to see where the time was going.

At P95 on getWarmPoolTokenCount, that check measured 1.29ms on Redis and 5.13ms on DynamoDB. At the time we shorthanded it as two to three times slower per query, which turned out to be an underestimate.

A few extra milliseconds cost nothing when you only pay them once. But the loop was paying them before every container, hundreds of times per run, and that stretched runs out to minutes at their worst, which meant the pool couldn't stay ahead of demand. The loop was an N+1 query, and Redis had just simply been fast enough to hide it.

No one wrote "this loop requires millisecond reads" anywhere. But the assumption lived in the design, and at a millisecond per check, nothing had ever made us stop and look.

We rebuilt the loop around the new latency

DynamoDB was never going to match Redis's millisecond, so instead of chasing it, we designed the requirement out.

The first attempt was batching, which is the shape drawn at the bottom of the sketch. The size of the gap depends on which percentile you look at, and at P90, where it was widest, the gap was about 17x. So the batch design checked state once per 17 containers, with one read amortized across the whole batch, and that constant was lifted straight from the measurement. But the constant was also the reason we walked away from it. It hard-coded a latency ratio that would drift with load, which meant one more unwritten dependency on the store's speed. Concurrency didn't need a constant at all.

What shipped instead let the loop's supply calls run concurrently, so each warm pool was no longer waiting behind the one before it, and each call worked from the last state it saw. Overlapping the reads bought us the same thing that batching would have, which is that no run serialized on any single read. The worst case is a few extra containers created from a stale picture of the pool, and that went into the pull request as an accepted cost. The redesign meant we could keep the more durable store without compromising the thing users actually care about, which is builds starting quickly and reliably. The fixes landed the same way the rollout did, one measured step at a time. As one of us put it, "we have less risk on each iteration because we've corrected for a previous misestimation."

It turned out the loop had stalled under Redis too, sometimes for a minute or more, and we only learned that while we were diagnosing DynamoDB. The evidence had been in our telemetry the whole time, but because the pool sits ahead of demand rather than in any request path, nothing had ever forced us to go look until the migration did. And the redesign ended up removing a flaw that was older than the project itself.

Migrating the assumptions

The migration completed in April, with the Redis calls gone from the warm pool paths. Copying the data turned out to be the easy part. The real work was finding the assumptions that had been built on top of the store, and then redesigning the loop that had held them. The state that every build depends on now lives in a store that was built to keep it, and the loop that manages it no longer serializes on any single read.

The April retrospective put the lesson in one sentence. "Even a 1ms-to-15ms query time degradation on P90 could bring down our warm pool management logic." Nobody had written that sentence in February, when the migration started.

Read more

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

To get started, read the docs or open Key Management in your team's dashboard.

title: How to Run Tencent Hy-Memory-30B-A3B Locally (It Beats Opus 5 by 0.87 Points)
description:
Tencent's new Hy-Memory-30B-A3B has "memory" in the name, and it doesn't remember a thing between calls. It's a memory writer: a 30B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active parameters, trained to decide what goes into an external memory store and how old entries get updated. The memory itself still lives in your Mem0, MemOS or Hy-Memory backend, in a vector database you run.

If you only want it running: the Q4_K_M GGUF is 18.2 GB, loads in llama.cpp from release b9993 onward or in Ollama, and there's an MLX build for Apple Silicon. A 24 GB GPU or a 32 GB Mac is the realistic floor. Below are the commands for llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM and MLX, what the benchmarks actually say (the "beats Claude Opus 5" headline is a 0.87-point margin), and why I think a model that writes memory instead of holding it is the better design.

What "memory" means in Hy-Memory-30B-A3B

The model card says it replaces the general-purpose LLM inside Mem0, MemOS and Hy-Memory. Those frameworks already call an LLM on every write to pull facts out of a conversation and reconcile them with what's already stored ("user moved from Berlin to Seattle" should overwrite, not append). In a lot of setups that call goes to a hosted model like GPT, Claude or DeepSeek, billed per token, on every turn of every user.

Hy-Memory-30B-A3B is a small model trained for exactly that job. Tencent trained it in two stages, both run inside the actual memory harnesses:

  1. Memory on-policy distillation, where a teacher supervises the student's chain of memory states.
  2. "Attributed" memory RL, which assigns credit at chunk level and carries the selected memory bank across windows.

The quickstart example on the card shows what it's for. System prompt: extract explicit user facts and preferences, don't infer, return JSON with a memories list of strings. Temperature 0, 512 max tokens, thinking off. That's the whole product: a structured extractor you can host yourself.

The specs

From the card and config.json:

Spec Value
Architecture HYV3ForCausalLM (hy_v3), same family as Tencent's Hy3
Total / active params 30B / ~3B
Experts 128 routed, 8 per token
Layers / hidden size 48 / 2048
Max position embeddings 262,144
Languages English, Chinese
License Apache-2.0
Paper arXiv 2610.22196

Apache-2.0 is the good news here. No custom "community license" with a monthly-active-users clause, so you can put it inside a commercial product without calling legal.

The benchmarks, read carefully

Tencent's headline table swaps only the memory writer and keeps the answer model, judge and retrieval fixed. Averages across six benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, PersonaMem-v2, Travel, Shopping, Code Memory Bench):

Memory writer Mem0 Hy-Memory MemOS EverMemOS (held out) Avg
Hy-Memory-30B-A3B 54.02 60.55 50.51 56.89 55.49
Claude Opus 5 53.43 60.53 50.50 54.04 54.62
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 49.73 60.20 49.17 55.47 53.64
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 47.51 55.87 47.36 50.75 50.37
Qwen3-30B-A3B 39.81 45.67 45.44 46.57 44.37

"Beats Claude Opus 5" is technically true and mostly noise. The margin is 0.87 points on average, 0.02 on Hy-Memory, 0.01 on MemOS. These are vendor numbers on a fixed 20% subsample of each benchmark, using Tencent's own harness and judge. OrcaRouter's write-up put it well: the model "has earned the right to be tested, not the right to be believed."

The result I care about is the bottom half of the table. Against the Qwen3-30B-A3B you'd otherwise drop in as a cheap local extractor, it's +11 points on average, and the EverMemOS column is a framework it never saw in training. If you're running Mem0 with a small local model today, that gap is the reason to try it.

The per-benchmark scores are worth a look too. On Shopping, no writer in any harness gets above 24, Opus 5 included, and Hy-Memory itself lands between 18.33 and 21.11, so some memory tasks stay unsolved no matter who writes the memory.

The A3B catch: fast, but all 30B weights still sit in memory

Every A3B model has the same fine print. Only ~3B parameters fire per token, so decode is fast. But the router can pick any of the 128 experts on the next token, so all of them have to be loaded. You pay RAM for 30B and compute for 3B.

Sizes for the published files:

Build Size on disk Source
BF16 (original) ~60 GB model repo
GGUF Q8_0 32.0 GB rapatsky GGUF
GGUF Q6_K 24.7 GB same
GGUF Q5_K_M 21.4 GB same
GGUF Q4_K_M 18.2 GB same
MLX mixed 4/6-bit ~17 GB (18.2 GB listed) hermitdave MLX

Add KV cache and OS overhead on top. Realistic floor: a 24 GB GPU or a 32 GB Mac for Q4_K_M, and 64 GB if you want Q8_0 with room for a long context. The 262K max context is a config value; the GGUF uploader tested at 32K and says so explicitly.

Run Hy-Memory-30B-A3B with llama.cpp or Ollama

hy_v3 support landed in mainline llama.cpp with PR #25395, shipped in release b9993. Older builds don't know the architecture and won't load the file. Then, using the uploader's own command:

hf download rapatsky/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-GGUF \
  Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-Q5_K_M.gguf chat_template.jinja --local-dir ./hy-memory-gguf

llama-server \
  --model ./hy-memory-gguf/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-Q5_K_M.gguf \
  --alias hy-memory --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 \
  --n-gpu-layers all --flash-attn on \
  --ctx-size 32768 --parallel 1 \
  --batch-size 512 --ubatch-size 256 \
  --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 \
  --jinja --chat-template-file ./hy-memory-gguf/chat_template.jinja \
  --chat-template-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort":"no_think"}'

Ollama works off the same repo: ollama run hf.co/rapatsky/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-GGUF:Q4_K_M.

Two things from that model card worth knowing before you convert your own GGUF. Tencent's config lists moe_intermediate_size=1536, but the actual expert tensors are 768, and the uploader patched it to 768 during conversion. And their small sanity test (34 handcrafted English dialogues plus 34 Russian ones) got 68/68 valid JSON on every quant, but only 23/34 strict successes in English, also on every quant. The failures were duplicated facts, over-storing and the odd unsupported inference, all wrapped in perfectly valid JSON.

Run it with vLLM (full BF16)

This is the officially documented path. The card says it was tested with vLLM v0.31.0 and expects the served name hy-memory:

pip install vllm
vllm serve tencent/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B --served-model-name hy-memory

That's the BF16 checkpoint, so plan for ~60 GB of weights before KV cache. One 80 GB card, or tensor parallel across two 48 GB cards. Then call it like the card's example:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="hy-memory",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Extract explicit user facts and preferences as concise, "
         "self-contained statements. Do not infer. Return JSON: {\"memories\": [...]}"},
        {"role": "user", "content": "I'm a software engineer in Seattle, vegetarian, and I prefer Python."},
    ],
    temperature=0.0,
    max_tokens=512,
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "no_think"}},
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

Run it with MLX on a Mac

Upstream mlx-lm doesn't know hy_v3 yet. The hermitdave Mixed4-6 build ships its own hy_v3.py and points to it from config.json, so it loads with stock mlx-lm:

pip install -U mlx-lm
mlx_lm.server --model hermitdave/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-MLX-Mixed4-6 --port 8080

Don't grab the -omlx variants by mistake: they use different expert keys and fail in mlx-lm with "Received 423 parameters not in model." The uploader reports ~65 tok/s decode on an M3 Max with 64 GB, perplexity within 0.94% of the 8-bit build, and 70/70 facts recalled on their extraction test.

Plug it into Mem0 or the Hy-Memory SDK

Tencent's Hy-Memory SDK (pip install hy-memory==2.0.3) accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint through MEMORY_LLM_BASE_URL and MEMORY_LLM_API_KEY, so point it at your llama-server or vLLM port. Use pro mode: lite makes no LLM calls at all, which means the writer model never runs. You still need a separate embedding endpoint (MEMORY_EMBEDDER_MODEL, MEMORY_EMBEDDING_DIMS). Mem0 and MemOS take an OpenAI-compatible base URL the same way.

Why I want memory outside the model

I'd rather have memory as a specialist model writing into a store I can inspect than as hidden state baked into weights. When a user says "forget my address," I want to run a DELETE and see the row disappear. Hy-Memory-30B-A3B fits that setup: it makes the expensive per-write LLM call cheap and local, and the memory stays yours.

What it doesn't fix is the write quality ceiling. A 0.87-point lead over Opus 5 on a vendor subsample and a 23/34 strict pass rate on a community test both say the same thing: test it on your own conversations before you trust it with your users' data.

So which side are you on? Do you want memory built into the model, or kept outside it in a vector store you control? And if you're already running Mem0 or similar, what are you using as the extractor today?

Sources

  • tencent/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B model card and config.json
  • Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-Memory on GitHub
  • Technical report, arXiv 2610.22196
  • rapatsky/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-GGUF
  • hermitdave/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-MLX-Mixed4-6
  • llama.cpp PR #25395 and release b9993
  • OrcaRouter: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B quiet release

title: PlxNative: A Fast Native Plex Client for LG webOS TVs, Built in Rust
description:
Most smart-TV apps are web pages. On LG's webOS that usually means JavaScript running inside a browser engine, which then hands its output to a compositor before anything reaches the screen. PlxNative is a Plex client for LG webOS TVs that takes that layer out. Its developer, Gleb Linnik, writes in the README: "No Chromium, no JavaScript, no web view. It just draws."

This is an explainer, built from the project's README, its docs, its source and its release notes. I don't own an LG TV, so nothing here was tested on a real television. What I did run is the project's own Linux desktop simulator against its mock Plex server, and that section near the end shows exactly what that does and doesn't tell you.

What PlxNative is

  • An unofficial Plex client for LG webOS TVs. It is not made by or affiliated with Plex or LG; the project says so on its site and in TRADEMARKS.md.
  • Open source under GPL-3.0-or-later, © 2026 Gleb Linnik. The PlxNative name and brand artwork are excluded from the licence.
  • One person's project. The README calls it "one person's spare time".
  • Current release: v0.8.0, published on GitHub on 7 October 2026. Nightly builds already report 0.9.0-nightly.
  • Young and active. The repository was created on 3 July 2026, and when I checked on 16 October it had 969 stars and 95 forks, with commits landing the same morning.
  • Free. There's no paid tier. You need a Plex account and a Plex Media Server, and the FAQ confirms a free Plex server works.

Why it exists

The origin story is short. The developer's 2019 LG TV still had a great picture, but browsing a Plex library on it "felt slower than it needed to." Rather than tune a web app, he wrote a native one. In his words: "I use it every day to watch things off my server in the next room."

The site makes the argument with a pair of stacks. A typical TV app goes:

The app (a web page) -> JavaScript -> Browser engine -> Compositor -> OpenGL -> GPU -> Screen

PlxNative goes:

The app (native code) -> OpenGL -> GPU -> Screen

The claimed result is 60 fps on that 2019 set. I couldn't measure that, and the project itself says the simulator can't either. More on that below.

The architecture

Mostly Rust, with a thin C shell

The repository is overwhelmingly Rust. A rough line count on the current main gives about 576,000 lines of .rs files against about 7,300 lines of C and C++. That count includes tests and generated data, so treat it as a ratio, not a measure of features.

The structure is spelled out in rust-modules/Cargo.toml. It's a Cargo workspace whose root crate is linked into a small C app as a static library:

# Static library linked into the C app (hybrid migration): each ported module
# exposes the same C ABI its src/*.h declares, so the C code calls it unchanged.
[lib]
name = "plxnative_modules"

The workspace is split into layer crates: base, machine, net, platform, gfx, ui, plex, telemetry, data, session, media, appkit, screens and storage. docs/module-layers.md describes how they depend on one another.

A GPU-drawn interface

The UI goes through SDL2 and OpenGL ES (both are listed in the repo's topics), so there's no DOM and no layout engine. The design language is translucent "glass" panels over your own posters and backdrops, with text sized for reading across a room. The docs folder holds design notes on liquid glass, backdrop blur and a hardware budget for the glass effect, which gives a sense of how much of the work goes into making that look cheap enough for TV silicon.

Video on the TV's own decoder

Playback doesn't decode video in software. The README says the app "hands video to the same silicon the built-in apps use". In the code, that goes through a video-sink trait in the platform crate. On the TV it's implemented by a StarfishSink, which talks to LG's Starfish media APIs, and on the desktop by a HostSink.

What it can direct-play, per the README:

  • H.264 and HEVC, including 4K and 10-bit
  • Dolby Vision profiles 5 and 8
  • E-AC-3 with Atmos
  • AV1 or VP9 (10-bit VP9 only on webOS 4 sets), on TVs whose codec table lists that decoder

Anything else is transcoded by your Plex server. Before you press Play, the detail page shows whether a title will play directly or be converted on the server. The app also ships its own LGPL build of FFmpeg.

Features

From the README, the site and the 0.8.0 release notes:

  • Sign in on the TV by scanning a QR code with your phone, then pick a Plex Home profile. PIN-protected profiles are supported.
  • Browse your own and shared libraries, with Continue Watching, Recently Added, sort, filters (including unwatched-only) and an A–Z rail.
  • Search across every server you can reach, with results grouped by kind.
  • A full player with resume, seek and scrub, chapters, audio and subtitle tracks (image subtitles included), Skip Intro, Skip Credits, Up Next with auto-advance, and progress synced back to Plex.
  • New in 0.8.0: subtitle search from inside the player, ASS/SSA subtitles that keep their styling, browsing Plex collections, Boost dialog and Normalize loudness on servers with Plex Pass, a Settings section for playback, and Spanish and Belarusian translations.
  • Works without internet after the first sign-in. The app talks to your server directly, so the library keeps working on your home network when the internet is down.
  • Privacy defaults. Crash reports and usage analytics are two separate opt-in questions, both off until you say yes. The README says no title, search term, subtitle line, server name or address can appear in any report. The app talks to your Plex server, to plex.tv to sign in, and to discover.provider.plex.tv for cast biographies.

0.8.0 also changes one security behaviour. Some home servers only answer over plain HTTP. Earlier versions refused to send your Plex sign-in that way. 0.8.0 will connect, but only after asking "Connect without encryption?", and only for a server on the same network at a private address after every secure route, Plex's relay included, has failed.

How to install it

PlxNative isn't in the LG Content Store yet; the site says it's "in the process of review" with no confirmed date. There are two routes, and neither needs root.

Route 1: LG Developer Mode

The installation guide needs an LG TV on webOS 4.0 or newer, a Plex account with a server, and a Mac, Windows or Linux computer on the same network. In short:

  1. Create or sign in to an account on LG's developer site.
  2. Install the Developer Mode app on the TV, sign in, turn on Dev Mode Status (the TV restarts) and then Key Server.
  3. Note the TV's IP address and passphrase, and connect to it from webOS Dev Manager on your computer.
  4. Install the .ipk directly, or install Homebrew Channel first and get PlxNative from its catalogue.

For a manual download, verify the package first:

sha256sum -c ipk.sha256

The catch is renewal. Developer Mode sessions expire, and if one lapses LG removes the apps installed through it. The guide's advice is to open the Developer Mode app and press EXTEND before the remaining time runs out, with a calendar reminder. An expired session can't be extended.

Route 2: Homebrew Channel

If your TV already runs Homebrew Channel, open it, find PlxNative (a 19.6 MB download, listed as version 0.8.0) and select Install. Updates arrive there too, and the Channel checks the download's checksum before installing.

Nightlies

Adding https://plxnative.com/nightly/repo.json to Homebrew Channel installs PlxNative Nightly as a separate app with its own tile and sign-in. The README is blunt about these builds: "It is not tested on a television."

Limits and current status

The README has a section titled "The honest scope", and it's worth taking at its word:

  • Movies and TV shows only. No music, no photos, no Live TV or DVR.
  • No typing in server addresses. Servers come from your Plex account.
  • Relay and secure-only servers are supported but "haven't been watched end to end."
  • Not all TVs work. It needs webOS 4.0 or newer. A 2016 set on webOS 3.4.3 has been tested and works.

The known issues list is specific:

  • Some 2019 sets on LG's k5lp or k3lp chip, installed through Developer Mode, won't play video. The sandbox withholds a device the video path needs; Kodi and Moonlight hit the same wall. Without root there's no fix.
  • 2018 sets on webOS 3.9.3: sign-in and browsing work, but the prebuilt v0.8.0 never starts video (#249). A source build at or after commit 60f99c7 fixes it.
  • webOS 3.x restarts the stream on every seek instead of jumping in place.
  • Sets on the k6hp chip show a crash in opt-in reports that the developer can't reproduce without the hardware (#174).

Building the simulator on Linux

Since I couldn't put it on a TV, I built the desktop simulator the docs describe. The box runs Debian 13 on x86_64 with 8 vCPUs and no GPU. The only prerequisites were the SDL2, SDL2_ttf, Mesa, CMake and pkg-config dev packages plus a current stable Rust toolchain:

git clone https://github.com/GLinnik21/plx-native && cd plx-native
make sim-linux SIM_TDIR=rust-modules/target-sim

   Compiling plxnative-modules v0.8.0 (/workspace/plxnative/repo/rust-modules)
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 3m 08s
real    3m57.100s

That gave a 16 MB plxnative-sim binary on the first try. The extra 49 seconds went into fetching and building the libass stack (FreeType, FriBidi, HarfBuzz and friends).

The project's screenshot tool then boots the simulator against tests/mock_pms.py. That's a synthetic Plex server that also stands in for plex.tv, so no account, token or real library is involved. I ran it headless under Xvfb with software OpenGL:

python3 tools/demo_library.py derive
LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 xvfb-run -a -s '-screen 0 1920x1080x24' \
  python3 tools/screenshots.py --bin rust-modules/target-sim/release/plxnative-sim \
  --out shots --only home-shelves,library-grid,search,detail,signin

Each scene settled in 2.2 to 4.9 seconds. One hiccup: the home scene also renders the website's link-preview card, and that step failed because the box lacked the file utility, so I captured home-shelves instead.

The sign-in screen is the QR flow, here pointed at the mock:

The Movies grid, with the sort and filter chips and the A–Z rail, browsing the project's demo library of openly licensed films:

And a title page, with the "Direct Play" label next to the runtime:

Be clear about what this proves. The simulator runs the same UI and Plex code as the TV build, and it boots, signs in to a fake server and draws every screen I asked for. But docs/building.md says plainly that it "cannot answer frame rate (different GPU), text rasterization, or anything about LG's decoder and video plane. Those need the set." The Linux build also has no video path at all; the Makefile notes that Play "intentionally reaches the host seam's existing 'no video path' result." So the speed and the hardware decoding, the two things PlxNative exists for, are still unverified by me.

Who it's for

If you run Plex at home and own a fairly recent LG TV, PlxNative is a well-documented alternative to the official app. Expect a project that tells you about its rough edges in the README. You'll need to be comfortable with Developer Mode renewals or Homebrew Channel until the LG Content Store listing lands. If you need music, Live TV or a set from the known-issues list, the README itself says the official app will serve you better.

If you're a developer, the repository is interesting on its own terms: a Rust UI stack drawing straight to GPU on TV-grade hardware, with design and performance notes for almost every decision. The simulator builds in a few minutes on plain Linux if you want to look around.

  • Site: https://plxnative.com/
  • Source: https://github.com/GLinnik21/plx-native

title: Why is system integration still so messy? Building a config-driven middleware core (WOS)
description:
Hi everyone 👋

I'm working on a project called WOS (Workspace OS), which actually started as my vocational final project. It was born out of my own frustration with how software systems connect with one another today.

We often hear that systems are "integrated," but in practice, it often feels superficial. We end up writing repetitive boilerplate code, dealing with messy spaghetti architectures, and relying on rigid, hardcoded connections. Even when trying to connect AI agents or cross-platform services, they struggle behind the scenes because the underlying infrastructure wasn't designed for seamless interaction from the start.

Instead of writing custom glue code over and over, I tried stepping back to build a lightweight, config-driven middleware core. The idea is to act as an adapter layer that allows services and tools to communicate through a single unified protocol without hardcoding each connection.

🎯 What I'd love to validate
Since I'm building this from my own perspective, I'd really love to validate my assumptions with experienced system engineers and developers here:

The Pain Point: Is this integration friction something you actually face in production or self-hosted setups, or are there existing solutions handling this better that I might have missed?

The Architecture: Looking at this core concept, where do you see potential bottlenecks, security risks, or architectural flaws?

Missing Features: What essential primitives or adapters are needed to make a core like this useful for real-world stacks?

💬 Let's discuss
I've opened the source code and design documentation on GitHub because I don't believe fundamental system architecture should be built or owned in isolation—it grows best when refined by the developer community.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Auto55597/wos

GitHub Discussions: https://github.com/Auto55597/wos/discussions/2
Any feedback, constructive critique, or thoughts are deeply appreciated. Let me know what you think in the comments below!

title: Critical Alert SMS API Economics: Polling Evidence Before Retry and Resend
description:
For a marketplace sending new-order SMS notifications to sellers, the dominant variable is often not the send itself. It is everything retained and repeatedly read afterward: status polls, event records, retry attempts, and audit data. TL;DR: choose an SMS API only after calculating that observation load. A polling API is a sound fit for critical outage alerts when your backend can schedule delivery-status checks, stop them at a deadline, and own retry, escalation, cancellation, and country controls. If a seller must trigger an immediate multistep escalation from a delivery event, a push-oriented product deserves more weight.

The useful change is to poll according to the remaining value of the notification, not forever at one fixed interval. Keep a compact decision ledger and provider identifiers; discard message bodies and raw event detail on a documented schedule. Infrai offers one key and one bill, plus one plain REST API over HTTP with no SDK to install; the API is genuinely self-describing, and the public discovery surface needs no key. That can keep the Node.js app and Python worker on the same interface. The retention change lowers the recurring read and storage footprint, but it also narrows what an operator can reconstruct later. This article makes that trade explicit.

How should you choose an SMS API for critical outage alerts?

Start with arithmetic before comparing dashboards. Suppose a busy marketplace has 12,000 seller notifications awaiting a final observation. Polling every 15 seconds creates 800 status reads per second: 12,000 / 15. That is 48,000 reads per minute before retries. This is capacity math, not a measured provider benchmark, and the right inputs are your own peak concurrency and poll cadence.

The send count is tied to orders. The observation count is tied to time. A provider that exposes delivery state only by polling therefore shifts part of the cost model into the scheduler, worker fleet, database, and API-read budget. Retained raw events add another term: records per attempt multiplied by attempts per notification, retention days, index overhead, and replicas.

For a new order, the first few minutes matter most. A seller who has already accepted the order does not benefit from another status check, and a notification for an order that was cancelled should not be resent. The control loop needs the order state alongside the messaging state.

The same arithmetic applies to restaurant waitlist updates: once a table is no longer available, further status reads and a resend have lost their purpose. A Node.js app and a Python worker may package the control loop differently, but the capacity equation does not change.

Here is a runnable Python status poll. It calls one verified route, reads the message identifier and credential from environment variables, uses an explicit GET method, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, and prints the documented JSON without guessing at an undocumented status field.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request


api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
message_id = urllib.parse.quote(os.environ["INFRAI_SMS_ID"], safe="")
base_url = "https://" + "api." + "infrai" + ".cc"
url = f"{base_url}/v1/sms/status/{message_id}"

for attempt in range(5):
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        url,
        method="GET",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
            print(json.dumps(json.load(response), indent=2))
            break
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
        body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
            raise RuntimeError(f"status poll failed: HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
        retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = int(retry_after) if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit() else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    except urllib.error.URLError:
        if attempt == 4:
            raise
        time.sleep(2**attempt)
else:
    raise RuntimeError("status poll exhausted retry budget")

The caller should schedule a bounded series such as 15, 30, 60, 120, and 240 seconds rather than wrap that code in an endless loop. Those intervals are illustrative policy inputs, not a measured recommendation. Add jitter in production so many orders created together do not wake at the same instant, and stop immediately when the order or notification reaches a terminal business state.

This is the first decision rule: calculate reads per useful notification, not API calls per happy-path demo.

How much delivery evidence should you keep?

A compact ledger can answer most operational questions without preserving the message body. Give each notification a stable business identifier derived from the order and notification purpose. Store the provider message identifier, attempt number, normalized state, observed time, policy version, destination country, and a request or correlation identifier when one is available. Keep the provider-native state needed to explain the normalization, but separate that evidence from broad application logs.

Short version: bodies age badly.

Phone numbers and message text increase the privacy impact of every log export, support query, and backup. Hashing or tokenizing a destination can help with correlation, although the precise treatment belongs in a documented privacy design. Do not claim that a hash automatically anonymizes a phone number. It may remain linkable.

Raw event retention answers detailed disputes: which transition was observed, in what order, and with what provider data? A normalized ledger answers routine questions faster: did the current order notification reach a terminal state, is another attempt permitted, and was it cancelled? Keeping both forever is easy to propose and difficult to defend.

I would define two clocks. The operational clock keeps enough raw detail to investigate recent delivery gaps. The audit clock retains the smaller decision ledger according to business, contractual, and legal requirements. There is no universal duration in the available evidence, so a vendor comparison that declares one magic number is suspect. Your privacy counsel, incident-review window, and dispute process should supply it.

Deletion has a price. Once raw events and bodies expire, an old complaint may be explainable only from normalized transitions and timestamps. That is the deliberate loss: less sensitive material and lower storage overhead in exchange for reduced forensic resolution.

Four products, four integration questions

Twilio Programmable Messaging, Vonage SMS API, Sinch SMS, and Infrai are real options, but a fair shortlist cannot be ranked from a feature-count screenshot. Ask each product the same questions using its current documentation and a test account: How is delivery state observed? Which states are terminal? What retry guidance applies to rate limits? Can an obsolete SMS be cancelled? How are US and EU destination and sender requirements represented? What evidence can be exported for reconciliation?

Product What to verify first Architectural consequence
Twilio Programmable Messaging Current status-callback behavior, message-state definitions, and regional sender requirements A callback path needs authenticated, replay-tolerant, durable ingestion
Vonage SMS API Current delivery-receipt behavior, correlation fields, and destination coverage Receipt processing must still join provider observations to marketplace order IDs
Sinch SMS Current delivery-report configuration, terminal states, and regional setup Push delivery does not remove application-owned expiry and duplicate suppression
Infrai Poll cadence, status/event schema, resend policy, and SMS cancellation There are no webhook pushes, so the backend owns scheduled observation and its delay

The first three rows are evaluation instructions, not claims that every configuration behaves identically. Product behavior, regional support, and registration requirements change. Verify them against the linked vendor documentation before rollout.

This option is most coherent when the marketplace already operates durable scheduled workers and wants to consolidate backend-service credentials and billing. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. For a mixed-runtime team, those properties let the Node.js app and Python worker inspect and use the same contract without maintaining two more vendor client libraries. Its SMS surface covers send, status and event inspection, resend, and cancel, and the broader service has 295 routes across 20 modules.

The limitations matter more. It has no webhook event push, no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS fallback, and geographic anti-abuse rules plus per-country cost circuit breakers remain application work. It is not suitable as a shortcut for an escalation tree that depends on immediate pushed transitions; evaluate Twilio, Vonage, or Sinch instead when a verified push model or another required channel is the deciding constraint. The trade-off is lower SDK and credential sprawl in exchange for owning the polling scheduler and its bounded delay.

This comparison is not about declaring a winner. Twilio, Vonage, or Sinch may be the better choice when their verified delivery-report model, geographic operating model, or surrounding channel set matches the system. A polling surface may be simpler for a team that does not want public webhook ingress and can tolerate bounded observation delay. Both designs still need a durable business ledger.

Make retries obey the order, not the transport

There are three different reasons another action might occur, and combining them creates expensive mistakes.

An HTTP 429 means the client should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. A transport ambiguity means a write may have happened even though the client did not receive the response, so retrying a send needs the same idempotency key. A provider-observed delivery failure is a business-policy input: resend only if the order remains active, the notification is still useful, and the attempt budget permits it.

Do not let “retry” mean “send again.”

Cancellation belongs in the same policy. SMS has cancel support, which is useful after the seller accepts the order elsewhere or the buyer cancels. A queued local job also needs a final order-state check immediately before any provider call. Remote cancellation and local suppression solve related but distinct races; neither proves that a carrier can retract a message already delivered.

Country controls must run before the send. For US and EU destinations, maintain explicit eligibility and sender rules, volume limits, and a per-country cost circuit breaker in the application. The available API does not supply that anti-abuse geography layer. During a marketplace incident, one malfunctioning order fan-out should open a circuit rather than multiply attempts across countries.

Compliance evidence should be versioned with the decision. Record which policy allowed the notification, without copying more personal data into the ledger than the review needs. Regulations and carrier programs are not interchangeable, and an API capability is not proof of legal eligibility.

The retention-aware rollout

Begin with one seller-notification type and one destination policy. Run the state observer without enabling resend, then compare intended notifications with observed terminal states. Inject 429 responses in adapter tests, replay the same job with one idempotency key, cancel an order between scheduled checks, and confirm that the next worker suppresses obsolete work.

Next, measure the oldest overdue poll, polls per notification, raw-event bytes per attempt, and notifications that expire without a terminal observation. Average latency alone hides a stuck partition. A small cohort with a strict ceiling reveals more than a broad launch with vague monitoring.

Finally, exercise deletion. Expire bodies and raw events on the planned schedule, restore a backup into an isolated test environment, and confirm that the compact ledger still supports the questions operations and compliance actually ask. If it does not, revise the schema before extending retention by habit.

The selection rule is straightforward. Choose a polling API when your backend can run bounded scheduled checks and when consolidating credentials and billing materially reduces operational work. Prefer a push-oriented product when a delivery transition must trigger escalation faster than your acceptable poll cadence. In either case, stop retaining the message body and full raw history once their defined purpose expires. You will give up some old-case forensic detail. Make that cost visible, approved, and tested.

Further reading

  • Twilio Messaging webhooks: https://www.twilio.com/docs/usage/webhooks/messaging-webhooks
  • Vonage SMS delivery receipts: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/guides/delivery-receipts
  • Sinch SMS delivery reports: https://developers.sinch.com/docs/sms/api-reference/sms/tag/Delivery-reports/
  • NIST Privacy Framework: https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework
  • European Commission data-protection guidance: https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/data-protection-eu_en
